After Trump launched a fierce crackdown on immigrants in the Los Angeles region in spring 2025 and residents took to the streets en masse, Essayli aggressively targeted Angelenos accused of interfering with immigration officers. “If you impede our agents or strike them, you will end up in handcuffs,” he posted on his X account in June, accompanied by the mugshot of one person he had charged.

The cases, often stemming from minor, chaotic clashes between militarized officers and angry or frightened residents, were atypical for the DoJ, and reports in the LA Times and Bloomberg suggested Essayli in some cases overruled prosecutors who advised against charges due to insufficient evidence.

In one instance, the sources told both publications, Essayli was overheard shouting at a subordinate to ignore the DoJ “justice manual”, which says prosecutors generally should only bring charges they can win.

Since spring 2025, Essayli’s office has prosecuted 113 people for alleged crimes against immigration officers, mostly charges of impeding, conspiring against or assaulting agents, according to data the DoJ shared with the Guardian. As of mid-September, 33 of them had charges dismissed, and nine people were acquitted by juries. Only four people were found guilty at trial, only two of which were felonies. Thirteen pleaded guilty to felonies, and the remainder were resolved as misdemeanor pleas, with a handful of trials still pending.

These are “unprecedented” results for federal prosecutors, who normally have a conviction rate well above 90%, said Laurie Levenson, a Loyola law professor and former DoJ attorney.

Some protester cases quickly collapsed because prosecutors had relied on uncorroborated officer statements or because video footage contradicted the chargers. For others, the cases dragged on.

One Angeleno profoundly affected by Essayli’s mission was Jonathon Redondo-Rosales, a 37-year-old jailed for six months on charges that he assaulted a federal officer – with a cloth hat.

Video from an August 2025 anti-ICE protest at a federal building showed Redondo-Rosales dancing in front of a government vehicle that slowly made contact with him, then briefly rolling on the hood of the car, at which point an officer lunged at him. Redondo-Rosales appeared to stumble backwards and swat back at the officer with his sun hat in his hand. Multiple officers took Redondo-Rosales to the ground, pepper-sprayed him and left his face bloodied. An officer said Redondo-Rosales had hit him with a fist, according to court filings from the defense. But the DoJ’s case faltered when footage contradicted the officer’s claim that he was punched, and records revealed the officer in a separate case had failed to disclose his own criminal conviction for harassment.

Just before the start of the trial in February, prosecutors moved to dismiss the case “without prejudice”, which would have left the door open to refile charges. The federal judge overseeing the case said that move by the government was in “bad faith” and dismissed the charges “with prejudice” – case closed.

Recounting his six months in jail denied bail in a recent interview, Redondo-Rosales said: “Not knowing when you’re going to get out, that stressed me the most. People inside said: ‘Plead guilty and you’ll go home,’ but I wasn’t going to do that, because I wasn’t guilty. I didn’t assault him.” He said he was grateful the dismissal allowed him to keep protesting: “They’re just trying to shut us up … but I wanted to be able to continue documenting all of this. People need to see what’s going on.”

Essayli’s office charged Sandra Samame, 25, with “stalking” and “conspiracy” to dox an ICE agent, after she and others followed an officer driving away from the federal building in August 2025. The group thought the agent was going to a raid, she recalled in an interview, but ended up inadvertently following him to his home. Unlike Redondo-Rosales, Samame went to trial – and won. Two co-defendants were convicted, but she was found not guilty of both charges after her attorney argued she had simply exercised her free speech. She was freed after spending about three months in jail, during which time she lost her job as a vet tech and failed her classes.

“The administration is trying to make ICE agents out as heroes, so they need villains, which is why they try to villainize us activists and undocumented people,” Samame told the Guardian. Her message to Essayli, she said, is: “The truth prevails always and people are not scared to stand up for their community, no matter to what extent the government is willing to go, to put us away, to criminalize us.”

Essayli’s office declined repeated interview requests and did not respond to inquiries about the cases.

Essayli has brought other splashy “tough on crime” cases that turned out to be shockingly thin – and in one case appeared to be based on false identification.

In two unconventional operations, federal officers swarmed MacArthur Park in May and Skid Row in October, for “takedowns” targeting “drug markets” and “high-crime areas of Los Angeles”. Typically, street-level drug crimes would be handled by local law enforcement, but Essayli, targeting an area known for its unhoused population, said the government was “reclaiming MacArthur Park from criminals and drug addicts”.

He charged 25 defendants with drug crimes and, in a press release, suggested the DoJ was going after big-time dealers and gang leaders. But for some defendants, their charges told a different story.

Anthony Solis, a defense lawyer, represented one man in the MacArthur Park case accused of selling 0.4 grams of meth for $20 to an informant. In his 25-year career, Solis said, he had never seen a quantity that small in federal court – even 10 times that amount would not normally warrant federal charges: “It’s not a big conspiracy. It’s not large quantities. It’s teeny-tiny amounts of drugs.” His client could face years in prison.

Wallach, the defense lawyer, represents another defendant who sold 0.15 grams of fentanyl to an informant. His client has no criminal convictions and a medical assistant degree, but had been struggling with addiction, the lawyer said in a court filing. If the defendant’s case were brought in state court, he would likely be placed in a diversion program, where he could get treatment and have the charges dismissed; now that he has a felony conviction, that will severely diminish his job prospects.

“It’s not the ‘worst of the worst’, it’s the ‘neediest of the needy’. What public benefit does this provide?” Wallach said.

In the Skid Row cases earlier this month, Essayli announced 23 arrests, saying he was working to “dismantle the networks flooding Skid Row with deadly drugs”. But when defense lawyer Robert Bernstein arrived at court to represent one of the arrested men, he noticed the DoJ’s complaint included a photo that was clearly not his client appearing before him – the man in the photo was also Black, but had different features. Bernstein said he pleaded for his client to be released, but prosecutors demanded he remain jailed.

Bernstein soon learned his client was actually at a probation office at the time prosecutors said he was on camera selling fentanyl. Prosecutors dismissed the case – after the man had spent two nights in jail.

Bernstein said it appeared the mistake originated with investigating officers, but argued the charges should never have been brought: “They are pursuing these improperly investigated cases with no review by the federal prosecutors – in this case, seeking a criminal complaint and arrest warrant for the wrong person, then arguing he be detained without bail. It’s ridiculous.”

Some of Essayli’s failed prosecutions have flown under the radar, but others have been high profile. In June, Essayli’s office suffered a bruising mistrial in an arson case against a man accused of igniting the 2025 Palisades fire after defense attorneys poked holes in prosecutors’ theories. In September, his prosecutors were dealt a not guilty verdict in a murder-for-hire trial against Lil Durk, after the Chicago rapper’s lawyers attacked the credibility of witnesses.

And last month, a judge dismissed Essayli’s lawsuit seeking to force California to ban trans girls from women’s sports. That case targeted Abigail Jones, whom Essayli had attacked at the school board years prior. Jones, identified as “Student 2” and “male” in Essayli’s complaint, said she felt some relief at the dismissal: “This was not a case the DoJ could win.” But she still worries Essayli will find other ways to target her and other trans girls.

Meanwhile, Essayli’s office has undergone dramatic change. Already by July 2025, reports indicated the office had lost roughly one-third of his legal staff, some senior prosecutors resigning after Essayli reportedly intervened to negotiate a cushier deal for a former sheriff who had already been convicted of excessive force. Essayli also faced heat for dismissing corporate fraud charges against a restaurateur who was a Trump donor.

“Many people left because they felt the Department of Justice had really lost the mission of justice,” said Julius Nam, a former California central district prosecutor, who was working in a different DoJ division when Essayli started. “The internal policies were not being followed – they were being bent to serve the political statements that the higher-ups were trying to make.”

Essayli’s campaign against “voter fraud” is his latest departure from DoJ traditions. But his ability to continue leading the charge is now being called into question.

For months, defense attorneys have sought to have Essayli disqualified from his position because of his lack of Senate confirmation, as required by law for US attorneys.

Since Essayli’s “interim” appointment officially ended last July, the Trump administration has maneuvered to keep him in charge, giving him an “acting” title and keeping him on as “first assistant” after a judge ruled he was unlawfully serving as “US attorney”. But Essayli’s position keeps facing challenges in court and similar schemes by Trump’s DoJ have failed. Alina Habba, Trump’s former personal lawyer, was disqualified from the top prosecutor job in New Jersey in December. A federal appellate court ruled against a Nevada DoJ leader in a similar case in August.

On Tuesday, the same judge who ruled against Essayli last year again decided he was “unlawfully serving as a ‘de facto’ United States attorney”. The judge disqualified Essayli from overseeing two cases where lawyers had challenged his position. The order does not go into immediate effect, and the DoJ intends to appeal.

Essayli’s office said in a statement that the matter would ultimately be decided by the US supreme court.

When reporters followed Essayli out of a recent court hearing in the disqualification case, he smirked and delivered a statement he seemed to have rehearsed: “The president runs the executive branch, and nothing here is going to change that.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/no-hel.title: ‘You have to believe’: Qwan’tez Stiggers, the New York Jets player who went from delivery driver to the NFL
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/no-hel.author: Gavin Willacy
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/no-hel.text:
When Stiggers’ father died, he dropped out of college to help his mother and 12 siblings. He thought his football dream had ended but made it in the end

Qwan’tez Stiggers had only been in college for a few days when his world fell apart. Seven months after the car crash that put him in a coma, Stiggers’ father died. Stiggers quit college and returned home to support his mother, Kwanna, and 12 siblings. It was a huge blow to the 18-year-old. His partner, Cheyenne, was also processing a tragedy after her teenage sister had been killed by a stray bullet. Over the last six years, Cheyenne and Qwan’tez have helped each other off the bottom of an emotional well.

Working as a delivery driver and washing trucks while his old teammates progressed in their football careers could have driven him off the rails. “I wouldn’t necessarily say I was envious but I wanted better for myself,” says Stiggers. “I had a child, was living with my wife – my girlfriend at the time – and got those late-night delivery jobs to pay the bills.

“But you can’t base your life off of someone else’s path. You’ve got to create your own success and opportunities. You have to believe in yourself. That’s what I’ve been doing since I was a kid, wake up each day and keep putting that foot forward. You got to get around people that believe in you, too.”

Stiggers’ certainly had that. His mother wrote to every football team she could find asking for a trial, desperate to see her son back doing what he loved. She found Fan Controlled Football on Facebook – a professional seven-on-seven indoor football league where fans vote on play calls – and they signed him up. It wasn’t the NFL but it was a start: his first paying gig in his sport.

Was her determination annoying at the time? “I really didn’t know how to feel,” admits Stiggers. “I was telling her: ‘You know, football might just be the least of my worries. I just want to focus on getting a job and having you take care of my siblings. But then, look what she did. It all worked out in the end.”

Stiggers only needed to attend one try-out. “I went there, killed it and ended up making the team. I’ll always believe in myself, mentally, physically and spiritually.” Stiggers was then spotted by a Toronto Argonauts scout, who sent him up to Ontario for a trial. Sixteen games later he was voted the outstanding rookie in the Canadian Football League – the first defensive back to be crowned in 25 years – and every NFL team knew who he was.

He was drafted by the New York Jets in the fifth round in 2024, making him the first player this millennium taken straight from the CFL without doing time in college football. When the Jets’ first-round pick, Olu Fashanu, was starring for Penn State at Beaver Stadium in front of 100,000 fans, Stiggers had been playing seven-a-side in a former fertiliser processing plant.

If Stiggers had impostor syndrome, he did not show it. His route to the top was unusual but the 24-year-old has benefited from his varied experiences. “It’s really your mindset,” he says. “I still joke with my old Argonauts coach about him telling me: ‘Just to let you know, you might be the first person we cut.’ I’m just like: ‘Hmm, no, I don’t think so.’ And I went out there and pretty sure I led the defence and interceptions.”

“No dream is too big, no dream is too small. As long as you work hard, you could do whatever you want. I always knew I had the skill set to be a professional. Competition is competition: you just gotta go out there and be a dog about it. You can’t let anyone take your food. You gotta protect me, eat your own food.”

Stiggers played in 29 games in his first two NFL seasons, sparkling on special team plays, especially on kickoffs. “Right now it’s about knowing my role and not letting nobody minimise it, whether that’s running down on special teams or going to the game at cornerback. It’s all about just wearing my opportunity.”

He is the fifth of 13 siblings and feels a responsibility for his family. “Everybody older than me has jobs, one younger brother is going to trade school, and I think my youngest brother is in ninth grade. They all play football. I had one sister who passed away and my other sister is manager of a PetSmart warehouse in Georgia. She probably makes more money than me.”

That seems unlikely. Two years after being paid $400 a week by FCF, Stiggers was getting more than $1m a year from the Jets. Stiggers has been wise to invest that. “The money is really for everybody. I just bought 13 acres in Georgia and am going to build a house. I’m putting money up for my kids for college and helping my little brothers: buying them clothes, shoes and food, because, unfortunately, when I went to college I wasn’t able to have all the luxuries by getting money from my parents. But, money is money. It will come and go. I’m all about the memories.”

He recognises that the tragedy of losing his father, sister and sister-in-law shaped his approach to life. “I’m grateful for just waking up every day. A lot of people take that for granted. Any opportunity is great, no matter how big or small. It’s all about just waiting. And, you know, my time probably came.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Mark Carney is celebrated abroad – while consolidating power at home | Shiri Pasternak
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Shiri Pasternak
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The Canadian prime minister’s reckoning with Trumpism in Davos clashes with his attacks on environmental, Indigenous and labour rights

The Canadian prime minister is a hero around the world for his Davos speech that reckoned with a reconfiguration of power in the shadow of Donald Trump.

But at home, Mark Carney is mirroring the US president by radically centralizing power within his office and cabinet and taking a hatchet to dozens of laws protecting environmental, Indigenous and labour rights, all in order to enact his economic agenda.

His global sale of Canadian land and resources comes just weeks after another major Canadian export – wildfire smoke – decimated First Nations communities in northern Ontario, leading to mass evacuations and warning the world of the impact of a fossil fuel economy.

The Building Canada Strong Act, Bill C-39, is a 250-page piece of omnibus legislation introduced on 21 September by the transport minister and House leader, Steven MacKinnon.

The new bill expands his previous legislation that created an expansive fast-tracking designation for “projects of national interest” to “regions of national interest”, which could exempt vast areas of Canada from labour and Indigenous rights, and environmental protections.

Geographic regions can be given this sweeping new designation by federal ministers, diminishing the sovereignty of parliament and bypassing local elected officials and affected citizens in these special economic zones.

Arms-length environmental review boards are also being done away with. Decision-making for new pipelines, nuclear facilities, highways and other major infrastructure has been shifted to the very bodies charged with promoting these sectors. The Canada Energy Regulator now directly assesses energy projects, while the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission directly approves nuclear/uranium projects.

Cabinet approval has also been removed entirely for most pipelines under the amended framework, now strictly reserved for pipeline projects requiring more than 300km of new right of way. Even if a significant pipeline is proposed, if it hews close to existing corridors, it is now exempt from federal cabinet oversight.

This is what Carney believes it takes to make good on his oft-repeated promise that Canada “has what the world wants”.

As Narwhal magazine reported, these changes follow lobbying by the oil and gas industry in the form of a literal wishlist of demands to speed up project reviews for fossil fuel projects. A public pressure campaign by the CEOs or executive chairs of 14 companies was released last March, calling on the prime minister to undo the former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s modest climate policies.

It is not only environmental protections that are impeding the economy Carney hopes will stabilize Canada’s GDP. The new bill also explicitly adds the power to end a legal strike in the Canada Labour Code.

For Indigenous peoples, the rollback is just as massive. They have fought for decades to constitutionally enshrine their rights to consultation on development affecting their lands.

But with fast-tracked projects and a new guarantee to industry of a one-year timeline for decisions, communities must determine all cumulative impacts in the early stages of assessment, virtually wiping out their opportunity to influence the project direction, given the time-consuming nature and costly nature of impact assessment.

What is the former central banker’s vision for Canada? To what image of nationalism is Carney hewing?

Carney’s approach has been called a “carve-out” system of legal exceptionalism. These aren’t the sensational executive orders of Trump’s bombastic political style, but more sophisticated and sly swipes at our existing framework of law.

It is no coincidence that this omnibus legislation came down following the major Canada Investment Summit that Carney held in Toronto in September. It replaced what many feared was the worst rollback in rights Canadians had ever seen – Bill C-5 - with something even worse.

The leaked pitch book for the Investment Summit showed 167 projects being sold to the highest bidder among the 200+ private equity and sovereign wealth funds reps who attended. The projects include AI datacentres, publicly owned airports, defence manufacturing, and dozens of energy and mining projects.

Carney has claimed the summit raised over $500bn in new foreign investment commitments to Canada. But how will he accommodate the needs of capital to make these projects viable? The Building Canada Strong Act is the most crucial way, through regulatory concessions. But it’s part of a buffet of public wealth on the table.

Only one day after the summit, Carney introduced the Productivity Mega Deduction, allowing businesses to deduct the cost of a much broader range of assets right away, including pipelines, mining property, aircrafts and bridges. The effective tax rate went from 13% to 6.4% – the lowest of any major economy, including the US.

Carney also promised to distribute C$280bn in federal subsidies to industry by way of tax write-offs and shifting risk from capital to taxpayers via cheap credit and loans from the Canada Growth Fund, the Canada Infrastructure Bank, and Export Development Canada.

To survive Trump’s trade war, the doors of Canada have been flung open to a giant sale of resources to industrial projects that would not be viable without the public backstop of financing and corporate license to plunder.

Though Carney is popular, Canadians are waking up to this elitist agenda. Rather than rescuing Canada, it is endangering the survival of our country and people.

Shiri Pasternak is an associate professor in criminology at Toronto Metropolitan University and a member of the Infrastructure Beyond Extractivism research team, a collaboration between critical scholars and Indigenous land defenders across North America

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Max Dowman’s Fleetwood fracas leaves him, Arsenal and Arteta red-faced
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Ed Aarons
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Teenager was maybe harshly sent off in the Carabao Cup tie but his reaction was a mistake he will learn from, while his manager might also have regrets

Mikel Arteta’s reaction said it all. As Max Dowman trudged towards the touchline after becoming the youngest player sent off in a League Cup match at 16 years and 300 days, the Arsenal manager could not help himself.

Arms folded across his chest like an angry father who has caught his teenage son sneaking in after midnight, Arteta leaned over and aimed a few choice words in Dowman’s direction before the forward headed sheepishly down the tunnel. What he said remains unknown, although that hasn’t stopped the amateur lip-readers speculating on social media. “Get in the changing room. Now,” appears the most likely guess.

There is no doubt Arteta had made up his mind about the incident that ended with Dowman seeing red for reacting to an overly aggressive sliding tackle from Fleetwood’s Harrison Neal. Although Arsenal intend to appeal and Arteta told Sky after the shock penalty shootout defeat by the League Two side 84 places below them in the pyramid that he wanted to watch it again before “assessing the situation”, the Spaniard made no excuses for Dowman in his post-match press conference.

“It was something that we discussed before the game,” he said when asked about their touchline exchange. “We knew when we prepared the context of the match, we were very clear on the things to expect, the things that emotionally we have to dominate.”

Whether Dowman’s reaction warranted a straight red card remains open to debate given there was minimal force when he lifted his right knee towards Neal. The referee, Michael Salisbury, could easily have decided to give both players a yellow and defused the situation, especially given Cole Palmer was booked for barging into Tottenham’s Matheus Fernandes off the ball on Saturday in what seemed a far more aggressive act. But, as Wayne Rooney and David Beckham infamously found to their cost while playing for England at the World Cup, acts of petulance are not usually tolerated by officials. Dowman was deemed to have overstepped the line.

It is a pressure Arteta has warned the record-breaking teenager would have to deal with as Dowman’s reputation has grown. Only last month Dowman was sent off playing for England’s under-19s against the USA after a poorly timed tackle that most present at the behind-closed-doors match deemed a harsh decision. He is said to have been on the receiving end of a host of strong challenges in that match. Last year, Arteta urged Dowman to follow the example of Bukayo Saka after revealing Dowman was fouled nine times in a the first half of an England under-19s game against Spain.

“It’s going to happen, he’s going to have to learn when to release the ball and when to attract his starting position,” Arteta said. “Very similar to Bukayo in the beginning as well. Those players are going to attract players, contact, attention and they have to be very smart about when you want that contact and when you don’t want it, and what you have to do to avoid it.”

Asked how Dowman tends to react, he said: “He just gets up … very rare! Sometimes I get surprised emotionally how cool he can be. I think it’s about repetition. He’s so used to it that now he knows to let the referee deal with it and my teammates probably to defend me, and I will carry on playing.”

When the dust settles after a seismic defeat that ranks alongside Arsenal’s League Cup upsets against Swindon, Birmingham and Bradford, Arteta may come to regret such a public admonishment of a 16-year-old. His actions were criticised by Paul Merson, who questioned whether Areta would “do it differently” given another chance. But part of Arteta’s frustration will be that Dowman took the bait. He also knows opponents will now target Dowman even more to see whether they can provoke a reaction.

If Arsenal’s appeal fails, Dowman’s immediate punishment will be a three-match domestic suspension, causing him to miss Sunday’s trip to Liverpool and games against Hull and Newcastle. The timing is far from helpful: Saka’s thigh injury, expected to keep him out for several weeks, had opened up the possibility of more game time in the Premier League, and Noni Madueke did not travel to Fleetwood owing to an ankle issue.

Dowman burst on to the scene last year by becoming the first 15-year-old to play in the Champions League, then broke the Premier League’s youngest goalscorer record against Everton in March, and this is the first major setback in his fledgling career.

He has been training with the first team since he was 14 and Arsenal have been extremely careful not to overexpose one of the most talked-about players to emerge from their Hale End academy. Arteta resisted the temptation to give him many more minutes in the Premier League after Dowman scored twice against Ipswich in the previous round of the Carabao Cup last month. The challenge will be how Dowman responds to the extra scrutiny – on and off the pitch – that is bound to come his way.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Fernandes tells Carrick he is committed to turning season around in clear-the-air talks
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Jamie Jackson
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Michael Carrick and Bruno Fernandes held clear-the-air talks on Tuesday after the Manchester United captain criticised the manager’s tactics last week, with him now expected to start at Chelsea on Saturday.

Carrick and Fernandes met before training on Tuesday morning at United’s Carrington training base. The 32-year-old, it is understood, offered the manager assurances that he is fully committed and intent on trying to turn the team’s season around. There was also a squad meeting with Carrick at which the rest of the players made the same vow.

Dismal results have left Carrick’s job in the balance. Later on Tuesday it emerged that the 45-year-old will remain in charge for the trip to Chelsea after Jason Wilcox, the director of football, decided he should be given more time.

But to remain as the head coach for the long-term, Carrick has to start winning games. So having dropped Fernandes, who is considered United’s best player, for Sunday’s 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth due to the criticism, him now being available for Chelsea is a considerable boost.

After last Wednesday’s 4-1 loss at Como, Fernandes questioned the team’s strategy. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man,” he said. As Carrick decides tactics this was seen as a direct attack on the manager.

On Wednesday morning Kobbie Mainoo was back in training after missing the last four games due to injury.

Carrick’s side have won twice in 12 games and were eliminated from the Carabao Cup by Brighton. United are 16th in the Premier League, a point above the relegation zone.

United host Roma in the Champions League three days after playing Chelsea, then Aston Villa in the league the following Sunday before a two-week international window, which would offer a longer period for the board to assess the situation.

Carrick’s reprieve may be a move to allow time for Wilcox to secure a replacement should the decision be taken to sack him. The director of football’s prime candidate is Eddie Howe, the former Newcastle manager, while Christopher Vivell, the head of recruitment, favours the former Germany head coach Julian Nagelsmann.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘Les the bare-handed beekeeper asked if he should put them on his face. I said: Sure!’ Holly Lynton’s best photograph
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Interview by Chris Broughton
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
‘Les didn’t wear gloves as he needed to be able to feel the bees so he didn’t crush them. He looks like something out of The Odyssey’

The jumping-off point for my Bare Handed series was a bird becoming trapped in the netting around the raspberry bushes in my backyard. It made me think of the problem humans have interacting with the natural world. How do we navigate obtaining food and the other things we need while still being good stewards of the land? I’d seen work by photographers demonstrating how Big Agriculture was destroying the environment. I wanted to find people who took a respectful approach, tried to work in tandem with it, but who might be in a fearful or dangerous situation.

I approached Les, the man in this picture, after speaking to the director of an exhibition space in Albuquerque, New Mexico, who had hired him to remove a feral beehive from his tree. I’d already tried to photograph another beekeeper who wore a full protective suit, but he might as well have been an astronaut. With Les, I was able to stay nearby and work with him over three days. The first couple involved straightforward documentary pictures of him tending his hives. Then, on the third day, his apprentice Amber showed up to help.

Les had the queen bee in a cage in his shirt pocket and asked Amber to take it out. Wherever the queen is, the rest of the colony will swarm. There’s a picture I made where Les and Amber are joined together by bees, and that was my “ah ha!” moment. Amber took out the queen and placed her in Les’s hand, which is where the bees went next. He looked at me with his hands full of bees and said: “Should I put them on my face?” I said: “Sure!”

Les slowly moved his hands up to his face. Bees don’t like hair, which is why they’re not in his beard or the top of his head. He closed his eyes for a few minutes, and I photographed. Afterwards, he said: “You know, I couldn’t hear anything but the buzzing.” I don’t think he’d ever done that before. People sometimes have their own ideas, which I just go with. One of the reasons I like spending some time with them is that when they’re engaged in work, it’s almost like watching a dance and waiting for the right gesture.

Les didn’t wear gloves when handling the bees. He said he needed to be able to feel them so he didn’t crush them, and that it was too hot to wear a suit. I wore a shirt that buttoned up tight at the wrists and tried wearing a beekeeper’s veil, too, but I abandoned that after finding it hard to focus through the mesh. I did get a bee buzzing in my ear and had to walk away until she let up.

I was using a medium-format analogue camera, and the bees were also landing on my hands while I was looking through the lens. I could feel them but not see them. That was disconcerting, but Les advised me just to move slowly, as he did. That worked: I didn’t get stung.

For a while, the photograph of Amber and Les joined together by bees was the one I preferred. I was worried people would find the bees on his face over the top. The themes of the project were quickly reinforced when I photographed wolves in a sanctuary with their trainers, and then went out with a family of catfish noodlers in rural Oklahoma. “Noodling” involved them catching these fish with their bare hands – even though they can weigh 45kg and really fight back. I realised none of these people had any fear. They were all experts at whatever it was they were doing, and for them this was a spiritual, meditative practice. That became the focus for the series.

Before I started taking photography classes, I planned to be a psychologist and a writer. But what I love about photography is that you can create ambiguous narratives, a multilayered story in a single frame. A lot of my work references cultural memory. Rather than straight documentary, I’m aiming for something more mythic, and gestures that happen spontaneously can sometimes seem to reference a certain myth or biblical allusion. This photograph leans more towards Greek mythology, even if it doesn’t directly reference an exact story. Les isn’t Odysseus but, like him, he elects to hear rather than protect himself, which makes him feel like he’s a part of The Odyssey, somehow.

High point: High points occur when my photographs are both made and shown. When photographing, a high point is when everything aligns – the light, content, composition – and I create an unanticipated image that transcends the moment. One that elicits allusion, mystery and wonder. In terms of exhibitions or publications, it’s often what is recent. In the past few years, institutions as varied as the Nelson-Atkins Museum in Kansas City and Bristol Cathedral in England have exhibited my work. I’m thankful that institutions have enabled people from many different backgrounds and perspectives to see my photographs. Talking with viewers and hearing their reactions has been a real gift. My book Bare Handed, published by L’Artiere, was another high point.

Top tip: Right now, the quest for authenticity instead of artifice feels crucial, and what I’d urge photographers to undertake. I’d also say there is no such thing as too much curiosity (even though some people might make you think so). Don’t be afraid to change your mind about what you are working on, the meaning behind it or how to go about it. Reframing is what I like to call it. Follow your intuition. And find the joy in the practice of making work and being creative. Difficult moments will occur, and ones that feel like failures, but it’s the journey, not the end goal.

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: When the weather is frightful, you don’t need to be: everything you need to stay cozy during cold months
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Filter contributors
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
Here are some of our writers’ best ways to stay toasty and occupied, even during cold weather, from teas to pajamas

When the weather starts to take a turn for the brisk, the impulse to stay inside and hibernate is nothing new – but there are ways to optimize your time spent inside for maximum coziness and pleasure.

From a limited-edition candle to a plush, furry comforter that does double duty, here are some of the ways our writers stay toasty even when the weather outside turns frightful.

This tea is a delectable blend of two green tea varieties, nutty genmaicha a blend of toasted rice and sencha green tea and matcha, powdered green tea with a bright umami note. Together they make for a smooth, perfectly balanced cup I crave every afternoon, especially the dreary ones. (And because green tea has less caffeine than black tea or coffee do, I get a small pick-me-up that’s long gone by bedtime.) The cozy icing on the cake is that the teabags and their hemp wrappers are compostable. I don’t know about you, but that certainly gives me a feeling of warmth and comfort. June DeMelo

I am deeply committed to a cozy lifestyle, and have piles of favorite soft blankets, warm socks and comfy pajamas around my home. But I also love having cozy rituals to round out my evenings, and one of them is having a nice cup of herbal tea. Tension Tamer, along with homemade chamomile and lavender blends, is a comforting classic and eases me into the end of the day gently. (It’s also perfect to pair with a book!) I love Tension Tamer because it is gently spiced and full of flavor without being overpowering, and it’s flavorful enough to stand in on those nights I kind of want a cocktail but don’t really want to drink. Julia Skinner

I have always preferred tea over coffee. While I appreciated the rich flavor of dark roast coffee, I sometimes found it too bitter. To get a decent cup from French roast beans requires grinding and pressing or an attentive slow pour. That is more effort than I want to expend first thing in the morning. That led me to explore roasted teas, starting with dandelion root, which comes surprisingly close to coffee. Still, something was missing. I wanted the deep round notes of coffee without losing the subtle flavor of tea. When I discovered roasted yerba mate, I knew I was close. My current favorite is Celestial Seasonings Morning Thunder, a blend of mate and black tea. It’s dark and smooth, with a satisfying roasted depth that doesn’t overpower the sweet, grassy notes I love in green mate. Morning Thunder has enough caffeine for a gentle lift without the intensity of coffee, and its warm, earthy aroma makes brewing a cup feel like a small daily ritual. Whether I’m starting a chilly morning or taking a midday break, it’s a cozy way to recharge. Alan Truly

I have burned this newly released candle from Trudon weekly since getting my hands on it earlier this fall. It has an amazing throw (how far the candle’s scent travels) that somehow trickles into every room of my apartment without feeling overpowering, and I love how its woodsy scent leans more floral and delicate, without being too musky or earthy. When lit, the cedar notes are most noticeable, which makes it ideal for the holiday season. Oset Babür-Winter

The scent of something baking always makes a home feel a bit more welcoming. This candle collaboration between Levain Bakery and Snif is a fun alternative to having to whip up chocolate chip cookies for that same effect, with luxurious notes of vanilla, chocolate and even a bit of toasted walnut that really does smell like a morning at Levain Bakery. Lighting the candle and sipping a hot beverage while reading or having relaxing music playing certainly makes my evenings feel very snuggly and cozy – and bonus, I didn’t have to dirty a single dish to get that just-baked cookie aroma. Bernadette Machard de Gramont

I got this comforter set for my son’s room, now that he is at university and the room will be used as a guest room for much of the year. The base of the set is a prewashed comforter that snaps on to a furry, sherpa-style blanket, so you have options: get cozy in the fabulous fluff or just use the comforter for the bed and the blanket for movie nights. Tobey Grumet Segal

In the three weeks since buying this nursing pillow, it has not left my lap. I use the crescent-shaped blob to support my son’s head and neck during feeds (and his hours-long contact naps that ensue), but you don’t have to be a breastfeeding parent to benefit: it serves as the ideal lap desk, allowing me to prop up my laptop or notebook while offering the ample elbow support that your typical lap desk doesn’t. Free of any rigid and harsh “corporate-friendly” materials such as wood, metal or plastic, you’ll find yourself hitting a flow state with unprecedented comfort. Luckily, this thing isn’t all business. It’s got a ledge designed to prop up your phone, should an endless scroll down TikTok lane sound like an appealing way to hibernate. Marissa Miller

A few days each month, I help my wife, Tracey, at a small art gallery in Nova Scotia. Art2Sea’s brick building has an enormous display window and a drafty glass door, so chilly mornings used to mean bundling up and relying on hand warmers. Now I drape my Vankada heating pad over the office chair while opening up. By the time we’re finished, the seat is warm, and I drape the pad over my lap and sit comfortably without cranking up the space heater. The soft fabric immediately feels cozy, and the adjustable heat lets me dial in just the right warmth. The heating pad has six heat levels up to 140F and a safety timer that switches off in an hour or two. I start at the warmest setting but progressively lower the temperature as needed. It heats up again quickly whenever I want. There’s an energy-saving benefit as well. Running two 120W heating pads for six hours uses less electricity than running a typical 1,500W space heater for one hour. I love being comfortable without drying out the air or making the room stuffy for visitors. AT

There’s nothing inviting about climbing into a cold bed on a frosty winter night. Even in autumn, that initial chill can be startling, and cold feet make it harder for me to settle down and fall asleep. A hot water bottle works but the bulging rectangular shape is surprisingly unfriendly. Fortunately, I found Urbzue’s long, narrow hot water bottle, which has a much more practical and comfortable design. Its slender shape and 29in length make it easy to tuck alongside a cold leg or cuddle against my torso without awkward corners digging into me. The soft, fuzzy cover adds another layer of comfort. I appreciate how something so inexpensive and simple can make bedtime feel luxurious. There is no cord to plug in, no controls to fiddle with, and no need to warm the whole room. I just fill it carefully with hot water, cap it and slip the warm tube under the covers to enjoy a cozy retreat from the cold until I wake in the morning. AT

I am generally warmer than I want to be in the colder months, thanks to the powerful steam heat that comes shrieking out of the radiators of my New York City apartment, but sometimes I want the best of both worlds: to be cozy on the sofa with the window ajar, blowing in a crisp, autumnal breeze. This sort of situation is only tolerable until, say, November. And when I really want to feel cozy, I turn to the Bearaby Lounger – a heated, weighted thing that’s really more comfortable to use than a full-on weighted blanket. Unlike traditional heated blankets, the Lounger requires no electricity. You just stuff it in the canvas bag it comes with, microwave it for a minute and drape it over whatever part of your body needs it. It’s filled with something called Terraclay – which the brand says has heat-retaining qualities – and the weight itself is gentle at just 6lbs, so it’s perfect for beginners. Megan Reynolds

I think getting older makes you care more about looking and feeling like an adult. Take sleepwear: I didn’t start setting aside clothes just for bed until well after college. Gym clothes had always seemed fine to sleep in, but purpose-made sleepwear feels even better. I don’t mean goofy holiday pajamas. I mean pants and a shirt so comfy you look forward to bedtime. This matching set is made from modal, a fabric derived from beech trees. It drapes beautifully and feels so smooth it makes cotton seem rough by comparison. It’s also breathable and wicks away sweat at night. Thoughtful details abound, including flat seams to reduce chafing, hand pockets, and a drawstring that won’t disappear into the waistband – and in the end, this is what makes them feel like the equivalent of Sunday morning pancakes. Sal Vaglica

Earbuds designed for sleep have become a category of their own, and I have tested plenty. Still, I keep coming back to the Soundcore A20s – even after the company released a newer version. They’re small, with grippy silicone that keeps them in place through a night of tossing and turning, and they’re comfortable enough that you barely notice them. Side sleepers may want to try a pillow with an ear-shaped cutout to keep pressure off the earbuds. The A20s also have an intuitive app with customizable white noise. I start the night with a boring ESPN baseball podcast, then let the earbuds switch to my soothing mix of a washing machine, traffic and rain on a tent. SV

This eye mask ticks all the boxes I have for finding the perfect eye mask. Not only does the soft satin exterior feel comfortable next to my skin, but it offers a secure strap to keep it in place all night and comes weighted with subtly scented lavender microbeads to help me fall asleep. JS

It may be a cliche choice, but when it’s chilly, I turn to my Uggs to keep my toes warm. These sheepskin-lined slippers do the trick and slip on and off easily – no hands required. I especially love them for walking the dog, or for heading to yoga since sneakers can be a pain to deal with. The rounded toe gives your feet room to spread out, and the suede exterior is fairly easy to keep clean with light brushing every so often. The soles are good for indoor and light outdoor use, so I wouldn’t wear them for heavy walking days, but I do like them for running quick errands in the car. If the classic chestnut colorway isn’t your jam, you can pick from a handful of other color options, including black. BMDG

Fluffy slippers lined with lofted fleece or shearling seem cozy – until you flatten the insoles into oblivion or stink up the insides. Enter Glerups. Made from breathable 100% wool that is felted into these nearly indestructible flexible leather soles, the unisex slippers come in 16 colors and two additional heights. (And if you plan to wear them for coffee runs or trips to the mailbox, you can opt for a rubber sole instead of leather.) After six years, mine recently developed a small hole where my big toe rubs against the felt. I was about to replace them with a new pair when I discovered that the company will send a felt patch free of charge. Here’s hoping an easy repair keeps them in my closet and out of the landfill for many more years to come. JD

After many visits struggling with the cold stone floors at my in-laws’ 16th-century countryside home in south-west France (a niche problem, I know), I discovered the Bombas Gripper Slipper. Built like a soft bootie, these are made of a thick blend of merino wool and nylon, and have grips on the bottom so you can easily walk on hardwood and tile flooring without sliding. The footbed is padded, so you get a little more support than you would from wearing just socks. They are very effective at keeping my feet warm, and they have their own storage bag that you can pack them in, making them perfect for travel. BMDG

I’m no Kelly Wearstler, but I know a thing or two about lighting choices that make a space feel inviting. First stop: I have foregone use of my godawful overhead pot lights in favor of these charming and rechargeable Shark Tank-famous wall sconces. I especially appreciate that they’re renter-friendly and suitable for the commitment-averse, as they stick on in seconds, leaving no damage behind. They impart a range of comforting (and flattering!) light settings, whether you need real visibility to read or an ambient glow to set a vibe (it is cuffing season, after all). MM

There’s always a puzzle in progress at my house, pieces strewn all over the coffee table. It’s the ultimate cozy activity during evenings at home, often with a comfort movie playing in the background. This high-quality wooden jigsaw puzzle is one of my favorites – the nostalgic artwork and “whimsy” ski shapes of each piece make it a joy to put together, and a few posters evoke fond memories of visits to those destinations. Paige Triola

Nothing makes me happier than snuggling up with a good novel, and I have been a steadfast Kindle user since 2008, when I used to read while I nursed my son (and could use one hand to turn the pages). As a Brooklyn apartment dweller, ebooks are the perfect alternative to the real thing because I only have so many bookshelves I can fill. The newest iteration of the Kindle Paperwhite is bigger and brighter than the previous version, and still comes with an IPXG waterproof rating – so I can even take it for a long soak in a hot tub. Plus, its screen is now totally flush, which makes it a little more comfy to hold. TGS

Sweatshirts are an incredibly personal item of clothing because what makes a good one is different for everybody. As a particularly picky individual, I have a lot of inside-the-house sweatshirts that are just about perfect, except for one little thing – but this guy, bought at the Wellfleet Oyster festival a decade ago, is ideal. The sweatshirt itself is from Comfort Colors, printed with the Wellfleet Oyster festival’s logo, and was perfectly smooth, soft and broken-in from the jump – and has only gotten better with age. It’s the right weight for layering under whatever strange assemblage of outwear required for late fall’s hot, then cold, weather. Nothing in life is perfect, but this comes close enough for me! MR

Ladies and gentlemen, I give you the most comfortable blazer I’ve ever worn. Like a cozy blanket I can wrap around my shoulders, the blazer is crafted from soft shetland tweed with a snug, vintage fit. Form and function in the best ways possible: it keeps me warm on chilly days, it’s perfect for work or play, and it’s my favorite travel companion for the plane and beyond. TGS

When it comes to cozy knits, &Daughter is the brand I save up for. Each piece is a bit of an investment, but I wear mine often enough that the cost-per-wear comes out to be a much better decision than spending, say, $250 on a sweater with acrylic or polyblend. This gorgeous V-neck has a plush, five-gauge knit (100% wool, obviously) that somehow feels incredibly lightweight and warm; I’ve yet to find another sweater that does both so well. I also love layering different colors of tees underneath, from a pop of red to classic white. OBW

This lightweight jacket has gotten me through 11 winters and counting in rainy Portland, Oregon. When it’s wet and cold outside, I layer it over a sweater and under a rain shell. And on dry days when the temps are in the 40s and 50s, it’s warm enough to wear on its own. The ripstop outer is windproof and water-repellent, while 800-fill-power goose down gives it a high warmth-to-weight ratio. Use the adjustable cords at the hood and hem to seal in warmth and the internal zippered chest pocket as a stuff sack for travel. One of my favorite features? The velvety “zipper garage” at the top, which keeps the jacket from rubbing against your chin when it’s zipped all the way up. JDM

The warmth and roomy fit of this fleece make it a great choice for chilly weather – but it’s the soft natural hues, charming floral pattern, and corduroy collar and pockets that make it my go-to for pumpkin picking or lounging by the campfire. For me, it perfectly captures the feeling of being at home in nature. (There is also a half-snap, unisex sherpa jacket available, so everyone can be cozy outside.) PT

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump’s midterms mindset: ‘If his side wins, elections were honest’
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Guardian staff
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
Late-night hosts discussed Trump discrediting midterms results, and Don Jr’s friendship with a Russian oligarch

Late-night hosts looked into Republicans’ efforts to discredit election results ahead of the US midterms and Donald Trump Jr’s questionable friendship with a Putin-aligned oligarch.

On Tuesday’s Jimmy Kimmel Live!, the host opened with the latest wrinkle in a scandal involving the president’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, and Umar Kremlev, a Russian oligarch who paid for some of the cost of renting a private island and staging a fireworks display for Don Jr’s Bahamas wedding in May.

The latest report is that in August, “DJTJ and his bro-ligarch went on a hunting trip together to Mongolia”, Kimmel explained. During the trip, Trump’s son reportedly shot and killed an Altai argali, the largest sheep in the world that is also an endangered species, “so of course Junior jetted in to kill it, as is the Trump way”.

“But the bigger issue is, this buddy of his is a close friend of Putin,” Kimmel continued. “The son of an American president is pal-ing around Mongolia with a known Russian security asset. It raises very serious concerns about counter-intelligence.

“And if you think about it, pretty much everything the Trumps do is counter to intelligence.”

Kimmel offered a theory on the questionable relationship: “I believe this whole thing – the wedding, the hunting, all of it – is a big conspiracy cooked up to make it look like Don Jr has a friend.”

Kimmel then turned to next week’s midterms, “which will decide whether the Republicans maintain control of Congress or whether it was stolen by a caravan of woke, dog-eating transgender immigrants”.

“You must get out and vote,” he urged. “Every vote counts, assuming the Trump administration allows the states to count the votes,” especially given that Trump’s justice department will deploy thousands of employees to “observe” poll workers as they count the votes.

“I will say, there is something funny about Republicans accusing Democrats of cheating while their leader is offering everyone $5,000 to vote Republican,” Kimmel noted. “Everyone’s worried Trump is going to do something crazy if there’s a big, beautiful, blue wave next week, but does this to you sound like a man who might refuse to accept the outcome of an election?”

Asked if he would respect the results of the election, Trump answered: “I will – if they’re honest elections.”

Kimmel offered a translation: “If his side wins, the elections were honest. If they lose, they were not. It’s really very simple. I don’t know what you people don’t understand about it.”

And on Late Night, Seth Meyers opened with disbelief that the midterm elections are only a week away. “Hard to believe, isn’t it?” he said. “Only two more weeks until there’s two more years until there’s 90 days until the next insurrection.”

During a rally in Iowa last week, the Republican congressional candidate Joe Mitchell gave Trump the “man of the century award”, which Meyers pointed out is “not a real award”.

Mitchell claimed that he came up with the honor, delivered via framed certificate, himself. “Sorry, that’s the award?” Meyers laughed. “For being the best man of the whole century? That looks like he graduated from an eight-week computer class at night school.”

In other campaign news, while speaking to reporters on Saturday after voting early in Florida, Trump said that his uncle invented radar. “And you know what that means: time to ace another cognitive exam!” Meyers quipped.

And during a rally on Friday, Trump again said that he wanted to change the name of New Mexico to “New America”.

“Dude, you can’t call it ‘New America’ when it’s in America,” Meyers corrected. “Do you think that Rome has a neighborhood called ‘Little Italy’? If anything, they might have a New America.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Racism needs to be understood as a global phenomenon – our humanity depends on it
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Anna Spain Bradley
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
In order to eliminate global racism, we must dismantle the ideological architecture that allows it to thrive worldwide

Around the world, racism is fueling a new wave of global unrest. In recent weeks, demonstrations in France turned violent amid mounting frustrations over socioeconomic and racial inequities, led by a younger generation that has had enough. Earlier this month, the Green party of England and Wales’s decision to define Zionism as a form of racism sparked controversy and renewed public debate about what racism is and who gets to decide it. In September, electoral gains by Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party raised alarms in a nation with a dangerous history of racist, antisemitic fascism. And for the past year, the Trump administration has pushed ahead white supremacist agendas throughout the United States, highlighted by violent Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids targeting people by race, regardless of citizenship status.

To understand each of these examples of racism in isolation would be a mistake. They are connected. Racism is not merely a series of random occurrences affecting certain people in certain places. It is more than institutional discrimination in schools or workplaces or even systemic inequalities in healthcare and policing. Racism is an interconnected, global phenomenon, spreading throughout our human ecosystem and embedded in world order. This global racism, which I name and define in my new book Global Racism: A Challenge for the World, is dangerous – it underpins wars and threatens our very humanity.

Global racism is an old story and an evergreen one. It is often powered by leaders who seek to divide humans through dehumanizing “us v them” narratives. In 1095, for example, Pope Urban II called upon Frankish nobles and common folk alike to take up arms against the Seljuk Turks, urging them in one account of his speech “to destroy that vile race from the lands of our friends”. Nearly nine centuries later and a continent away, the Hutu Ten Commandments, published in 1990 in a Rwandan newspaper, invoked ideologies of racial superiority that created the conditions in which the Rwandan genocide unfolded four years later. The worst things we humans have ever done to one another – slavery, genocide, segregation, apartheid – have been justified and sustained by ideologies underlying global racism. When this racist fervor subsides, we realize that such acts have not only killed countless people but diminished our humanity.

Today, evidence of racism’s global disruption is clear. According to the United Nations, racial discrimination is among the most common forms of discrimination worldwide, often intersecting with gender discrimination against women and girls. A Pew survey found that across 36 countries a median of 68% of adults consider racial or ethnic discrimination as a significant worldwide problem. The international community recognized the need to confront such challenges back in 1965 when nations created the first treaty banning racial discrimination, defined as certain acts of discrimination on the basis of race, color, descent, national or ethnic origin (but not nationality). A laudable first step, the treaty failed to define and ban racism, alongside racial discrimination.

Understanding global racism reveals why this gap matters. Racism can’t be eliminated by banning acts of racial discrimination, nation by nation, alone. Racism’s deeper roots are embedded not only in how humans and the institutions we create behave, but in what we believe. White supremacist movements, for example, teach followers to believe that being white makes someone inherently superior to everyone else. This ranking of humans by group based on a construct that has no basis in biology isn’t accidental. It is by design and always has been. Today, because of social media and new technology, global racism moves throughout our human ecosystem with rapid speed, making it possible anywhere and everywhere people are.

Consider the racist, anti-immigrant riots that erupted last June across Northern Ireland after a knife attack in Belfast, where people violently targeted minority communities, setting fire to homes and vehicles. It exposed how far-right ideologies amplified online could help drive people to commit racist crimes. Like a spark that turns into a raging wildfire, racism doesn’t go viral without hot, dry, windy conditions in the air that allow it.

Launching an effective campaign to combat global racism starts with dismantling the ideological architecture that allows racism to thrive. Many governments, however, have been reluctant to do this, privileging free speech and ideas even when the unfettered exercise of those freedoms enables the spread of racial hatred. But protecting the right to express an idea, however objectionable, should not mean allowing racist beliefs to become systems of power. An idea, after all, is not the same as an ideology. The difference, according to Merriam-Webster, is between an idea as a “formulated thought or opinion” and an ideology as a “systematic body of concepts”. The goal isn’t to police an individual’s ideas; it is to stop national leaders who command military power and vast resources from spreading ideologies of racial superiority that threaten peace and security.

WEB Du Bois warned of precisely this danger in 1935 in an unpublished essay, A Pragmatic Program for a Dark Minority. He described a world in crisis, where leaders of nations amassed power built on platforms of racist ideologies that promised a bleak future for everyone. “All this,” he wrote, “must inevitably move toward an increase of race hate and war.” History proved him right. The Holocaust, the Rape of Nanjing, and US internment of Japanese Americans, among other horrors, were all built on ideologies of racial superiority. Du Bois understood something we still miss today: racism is not a national peculiarity but a global force, one that degrades those who wield it as surely as those who suffer under it – and that, left unchecked, threatens to plunge the world into chaos and war.

Racism is, indeed, a global force, but so is our ability to overcome it. Recognizing global racism is the first step. For nations, this requires banning racism, alongside racial discrimination, under international law. For the rest of us, this means giving up the allure of ideologies of racial superiority. Like all global challenges, real solutions will require collective action. We can start by demanding dignity from our leaders and from ourselves. Why should we try? Because the future of our human species depends upon us acting as one.

Anna Spain Bradley is the author of Global Racism: A Challenge for the World and a professor of law at the UCLA School of Law

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Chiefs reportedly signing Tucker in wake of sexual misconduct allegations as Butker struggles
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The Kansas City Chiefs are reportedly signing the former Baltimore Ravens kicker Justin Tucker to their practice squad after Harrison Butker’s poor start to the season.

Tucker was widely considered one of the best kickers in NFL history until the Ravens released him in May 2025. The Ravens said his departure was a “football decision” after a slump in form, but the move came months after he was accused of inappropriate sexual behavior by massage therapists. Tucker denied the allegations and never faced criminal charges but he served a 10-game NFL ban for violating the league’s personal conduct policy.

More than a dozen massage therapists from spas and wellness centers in the Baltimore area accused Tucker of inappropriate sexual behavior. One therapist who spoke to the Baltimore Banner, which broke the story, described Tucker’s alleged behavior as “really degrading”. Another said: “I can’t watch sports anymore. I see his face everywhere.”

The 37-year-old has not played in the NFL since he was released by Baltimore. During his time with the Ravens, he made seven Pro Bowls and won the Super Bowl in his rookie season. His final season in Baltimore, in which he made just 73.3% of his field goals, was statistically the worst of his career. Tucker’s career average for field goals is 89.1%.

Butker, who has won three Super Bowls with the Chiefs, has missed five of his 16 field goal attempts this season. The 31-year-old Butker has also been involved in off-field controversy. During a commencement address at Benedictine College in 2024, he criticized Pride month, working women, Joe Biden’s leadership during the Covid-19 pandemic and abortion.

“I think it is you, the women, who have had the most diabolic lies told to you,” Butker said during the speech. “Some of you may go on to lead successful careers in the world, but I would venture to guess that the majority of you are most excited about your marriage and the children you will bring into this world. I can tell you that my beautiful wife Isabelle would be the first to say her life truly started when she started living her vocation as a wife and as a mother.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US lawmakers demand action on overcharging at 7-Eleven, Dollar General and other chains
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Barry Yeoman
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Democrats urge FTC to tackle ‘systemic failure’ of biggest convenience and dollar stores over pricing practices after Guardian investigations

Thirty-four members of Congress are calling on the Federal Trade Commission to investigate reports of widespread overcharging by some of America’s most-recognized brand-name retailers.

The 28 October letter to the FTC comes in direct response to Guardian investigations of four of the nation’s largest dollar-store and convenience-store chains. Both investigations revealed pervasive mismatches between shelf labels and register prices.

The first, published in December, found that Dollar General had failed more than 4,300 government price-accuracy inspections in 23 states over a three-year period on items such as peanut butter, spaghetti sauce and Flintstone vitamins. Its smaller rival, Family Dollar, failed 2,100 price inspections in 20 states over the same period.

The second, published last month, found a similar pattern at convenience store chains 7-Eleven and Circle K. Consumer complaints, along with state and local inspections, revealed overcharges for snacks, beverages, toiletries, tobacco and medications. In addition, some stores charged more at the pump for gasoline than the prices displayed on their big road-facing signs.

“These reports show that these incidents are not isolated to a geographic area or to a handful of stores,” the Congress members’ letter said. “Instead, the scale of documented violations seems to be the result of systemic failure within corporate operations, leading to customers overpaying for their groceries, potentially without knowing.”

All four companies have told the Guardian in written statements that they try to keep register prices consistent with shelf prices.

The letter, written by US House Democrats from 17 states and the District of Columbia, was addressed to the FTC chair, Andrew N Ferguson, a Trump appointee.

It was sent two days after the FTC, along with 20 states, filed a federal lawsuit accusing Dollar General of a “pattern of inaccurate pricing” that “affects millions of purchases”. The lawsuit claims the company knew about the problem for years without correcting it.

Dollar General, in a statement, vowed to “defend this litigation vigorously”, saying it aims for 100% price accuracy and that it cooperated with the FTC’s investigation.

“While this step is positive,” the lawmakers wrote of the FTC’s lawsuit, “the widespread nature of the issue revealed by public reports and state inquiries warrants a full-scope probe.”

The congressional letter comes on the eve of a midterm election in which affordability has emerged as the major concern. In a recent Harris Poll conducted for the Guardian, voters listed gas prices, grocery prices and living expenses as their top three election issues.

In another poll, released by AP-Norc Center for Public Affairs Research, nearly 80% of voters disapproved of Donald Trump’s handling of the cost of living.

“Gas prices are at $4.50 a gallon in my district,” US representative Nikki Budzinski of Illinois, the letter’s lead author, told the Guardian. “Any uptick in a gas price, or any uptick in the price of a banana or the price of ground beef, means families, in reality, making very difficult decisions as to whether they’re even able to afford that item any more … They’re making decisions as to whether to fill their gas tank up completely or fill their grocery basket up.”

Back in December, Budzinski and 29 colleagues wrote to the CEOs of Dollar General and Family Dollar seeking internal documents about their pricing disparities. Neither company complied, she said, “so we’re taking the next step of going to the FTC and asking them to do enforcement”. The federal agency is charged with policing unfair, deceptive and anti-competitive business practices.

Budzinski and her co-authors noted that many of their constituents live too far to walk or drive to independent grocery stores or chain supermarkets. A Dollar General or 7-Eleven might be the closest place for them to buy food.

“Because these stores are often the sole option for essentials in underserved neighborhoods and rural communities, these companies occupy a unique position of trust and responsibility,” the letter said. “It is deeply troubling to see that these limited options have been exploited to the detriment of working families.”

For one of the lawmakers who signed the letter, the issue is personal. US representative Shontel Brown lives near a Dollar General in Warrensville Heights, Ohio. She visited earlier this year to buy some soda pop. When she reached the register, she said, the total cost didn’t match the advertised price.

“I asked the cashier, ‘Wait a minute, how am I paying X amount when these items are on sale and I’ve applied these coupons?’” Brown recalled. “And she said, ‘Well, the system does that. It does it a lot with the pop.’”

The congresswoman left without making the purchase. “I have the luxury of not counting every single dollar in my budget,” she said. Many of her constituents don’t have that leeway. “I can’t imagine folks who are coming in there, who have to itemize every dollar, dealing with something like this. So when the letter was brought to my attention, I was a ‘hell yes’.”

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Tommy Robinson found guilty of harassing journalists
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Ben Quinn
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Judge says he will consider all options when sentencing far-right activist who trial heard deployed ‘bullyboy, intimidatory tactics’

Tommy Robinson faces up to 10 years in prison after being found guilty of harassing two journalists to the point it caused them fear of violence.

Journalists from the Daily Mail and their family members fled their homes after “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics” were deployed by the far-right activist, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, his trial was told.

Robinson had shared pictures of the family of one of the journalists online and said he had “tagged and bagged” all three reporters who worked on an article about his alleged role influencing unrest that broke out after the 2024 Southport murders. The charges related to two of the journalists, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber.

Dirnhuber and his partner had to leave their home, while Young and his family were provided with a close protection officer after an alleged campaign of intimidation that also included a call to the editor of the Daily Mail, saying he would make the journalists and their families “famous”.

Robinson was found guilty on both counts against him on Wednesday at Southwark crown court. The jury had deliberated for two days and had to be directed by the judge that they could return a majority verdict rather than a unanimous one.

A number of journalists had to be given an escort by security after they were threatened inside the court by one of Robinson’s supporters, after the man was ejected from the press gallery and later from the courtroom.

Robinson, a former member of the British National party and co-founder of the English Defence League, had said ahead of the trial that his legal bills were being paid for by the billionaire tech mogul and owner of X, Elon Musk.

He was accused of harassment causing fear of violence through posts shared with his hundreds of thousands of followers on X and by direct messages. He called Young on 5 August 2024 and told him that he would visit his house, saying: “I’m coming to get you.”

Robinson, who attended court each day with a large number of supporters, was said to have become enraged after the Mail tracked him down to a hotel in Cyprus, where he was commenting on events in the UK following the Southport murders, and published a story about him with the headline “Stoking race riots from his sunbed”.

Dirnhuber said in a witness statement he did not know how Robinson had obtained his address, or who he had shared it with, adding: “I was concerned about the risk of being intercepted on my way to work, either by Robinson for a livestreamed interview or by an unpredictable supporter of his hoping to cause me or my partner physical harm.”

Young said he felt his family was under threat and he was fearful of what might happen next. “It was clear to me that Tommy Robinson was following through on his threats. My main concern was that while he may not physically harm me, he had 800,000 followers on X at the time who might have been tempted to seek revenge on me, or my home, or my family for what I had written.”

A third Daily Mail journalist, George Odling, said in a witness statement that he, his wife and young child had to leave their home through a neighbour’s house because they feared being followed by Robinson’s supporters.

The trial heard that Robinson’s “angry” and “retaliatory” posts began on 5 August 2024, as he questioned the Daily Mail’s decision to photograph and write the story about him in Cyprus.

In a post on X, which has been viewed 244,000 times and made reference to the newspaper’s front page headline “Stoking riots from his sunbed”, he wrote: “Quick question, these lies have a direct result on threats to my family.

“Is it ok if I track down the journalists addresses + families details + dox them. Would that be journalism. This has been coordinated from the top down because my latest documentary humiliates their lies.

“They have purposely doxxed where my children are is it fair for me to do the same to them.”

Robinson said in evidence he had been in “a panic” after the Mail had in effect identified the hotel in Cyprus where he had gone with family and friends and published a photo of his ex-wife, which he said put her at risk. He said he had only wanted to “question” the journalists and said they “knew” he was “not coming to beat them up.”

After he was found guilty, the Crown Prosecution Service said Robinson had “weaponised social media”. Frank Ferguson, the head of the CPS’s special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “Nobody should be made to fear violence because of the work they do. Journalists play an important role in a democratic society and should be able to carry out their professional duties without being subjected to harassment.

“We will always seek to work with the police to prosecute those who break the law and I hope these convictions provide reassurance that such behaviour will be treated seriously by the criminal justice system.”

Robinson is due back in court on 16 December for a sentencing hearing. Mr Justice Cavanagh said after the verdict he would be considering all options, including a custodial sentence, whether in full or suspended. Harassment causing fear of violence can carry a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Dolores Huerta, California labor leader and civil rights champion, dies aged 96
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Richard Luscombe
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Huerta co-founded United Farm Workers union with Cesar Chavez, improving pay and conditions for farm workers

Dolores Huerta, an iconic 1960s labor union leader and civil rights activist, died on Wednesday in California at the age of 96, her family said.

Huerta was co-founder with Cesar Chavez, another veteran unionist and political activist, of the United Farm Workers union (UFW), which was credited with improving pay and conditions for agricultural workers through a series strikes, boycotts and protests in the 1960s and 1970s.

Huerta was born in New Mexico in 1930, and followed her father, a miner and farm worker, into union activism. As a political operative, she worked on the presidential campaigns of several Democratic party candidates, including helping Robert F Kennedy to secure the party’s 1968 nomination before he was assassinated, and aiding the elections of Barack Obama and Joe Biden.

“We are deeply saddened to announce that our beloved mother, Dolores Huerta, has passed away today at the age of 96,” her family said in a statement on social media.

“As you can imagine, this is an incredibly difficult time for us, and we ask for privacy as we grieve this incredible loss to our family. We know that many of you around the world share in our mourning, and we will be following up on plans to recognize and celebrate her incredible life and legacy.”

Huerta is credited with coining the phrase “Si, se puede!” (yes, we can), which became the slogan of the UFW, and which Obama adapted as a rallying cry for his successful 2008 campaign for the White House.

As well as serving as Chavez’s right hand at the UFW, the union said on its website, “she could also be the greatest thorn in his side.”

It said: “The two were infamous for their blow out arguments, an element that was a natural part of their working relationship. Dolores viewed this as a healthy and necessary part of the growth process of any worthwhile collaboration.”

It emerged only in interviews Huerta gave to the New York Times, published in March, one month before her 96th birthday, that their relationship was much darker than it was publicly portrayed. As allegations emerged that Chavez, who died in 1993, groomed and sexually abused a number of teenage girls, Huerta revealed that he had raped her during the winter of 1966 in a vehicle in a secluded California grape field.
