Though McMahon is reportedly planning to furnish her new office at the department, her overall goal is to diminish staffing and remove responsibilities that her department oversees, in effect shutting it down.

Shortly after returning to office in 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order directing McMahon, a former executive at World Wrestling Entertainment turned cabinet member, to close the Department of Education.

The Department of Education was established by Congress and can only be dissolved at the direction of Congress, but the Republican-controlled chambers have not moved to do so. But the administration has taken steps to reduce the department’s power. So far, the administration has nearly halved the department’s staffing through workforce reductions and moved department-specific responsibilities to other agencies through “interagency agreements”.

Among those, special education services have been moved to the Department of Health and Human Services and civil rights enforcement efforts have been moved to the justice department.

Trump and McMahon have insisted that effectively shuttering the Department of Education will give states more authority over education, despite states already controlling most of their education policies, and eliminate unnecessary bureaucratic processes.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.title: ‘We sold out tickets within 13 minutes’: new novel from romantasy author Sarah J Maas sparks fan mania
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.author: Emma Loffhagen
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.text:
Move over Oasis – 6,000 people tried to buy 220 tickets to a masquerade ball to celebrate the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony, while specialist bookshops catering for the genre report huge sales

When The Spicy Librarian, a romance bookshop in Leamington Spa, announced a masquerade ball to celebrate the new Sarah J Maas novel, 6,000 people tried to buy 220 tickets. “We sold out within 13 minutes,” says the shop’s co-founder Ali Maynard James. “As soon as tickets went on sale, our website crashed”.

The shop was one of many across the UK marking the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony, the first instalment of Maas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses series in more than five years. On Monday night, bookshops threw parties and opened past midnight – and The Spicy Librarian hired a stately home to mark the occasion.

The book, the sixth in the series known to fans as Acotar, went on sale at 12.01am on Tuesday. Few releases carry as much commercial weight – the first book, a dark retelling of Beauty and the Beast, was published in 2015, with later books following the adventures of Feyre across the faerie lands of Prythian. By 2021 the series had sold 13m copies, and across her three interlinked fantasy series, Maas has now sold more than 75 m books in 40 languages.

The Spicy Librarian, which bills itself as Europe’s largest independent romance bookshop, held its ball at Ragley Hall in Warwickshire, where riders dressed as “fae warriors” carried torches on horseback. Tickets were £149 – the shop ran the event again the following night, which also sold out, and ordered about 750 copies to cover both balls and its pre-orders.

“We gave everyone the books at midnight, and people started reading them immediately,” says Maynard James. “Some people stayed up and devoured the whole thing in a few hours.”

Maas is the biggest name in romantasy, a genre combining fantasy and romance which has grown from an online niche into one of publishing’s most lucrative categories. Last year, Onyx Storm by Rebecca Yarros – another romantasy star – had the biggest first week for a hardback novel in the UK since Harper Lee’s Go Set a Watchman in 2015. In 2024, booming sales of romance and fantasy helped push UK fiction revenue above £1bn for the first time. The genre’s readers are largely young women, and much of its growth has played out on TikTok.

“It’s been such a long wait for this book, people are just itching to get their hands on it,” says Starlin Marot, owner of Bad Girl Books in Oxford, the UK’s first romantasy-only bookshop. “For so many of us, the series has been like a gateway drug into the genre, or into reading itself.”

In Oxford, Marot had only planned to open Bad Girl Books for half an hour after midnight, for a couple of readers who had asked on Instagram. Instead, a queue formed outside. “It was just crazy, like a flurry of people came in,” she says. “I was honestly not expecting that many people just for half an hour. But it shows how popular these books are!”

Her midnight release doubled as a pyjama party. “It was cute and cosy vibes,” Marot says. “We had Acotar-themed cakes and drinks.”

In London, romance bookshop Main Character Books decided against a midnight opening, serving breakfast to readers collecting pre-orders instead and holding an evening party for 45 people. “We decorated the entire store,” says owner Cassie Simmons. “In early October we had more pre-orders than we expected … we doubled our order at the publisher.” After Tuesday’s sales, the shop ordered again. “We’re going through stock even faster than we expected.”

The latest book is the first part of a four-part story. A Court of Forgotten Melody, out on 12 January, contains the next two parts, and the last is still being written.

“I think it’s definitely the five-year wait and the hype that’s been going up online,” says Simmons.

Maynard James, who says Acotar got her reading for pleasure again after becoming a mother, believes its heroines are a big part of the draw for its largely female fanbase. “They aren’t women that are damsels in distress that need rescuing or saving,” she says. “They almost prioritise themselves before they prioritise love. We want the women to be the centre of their own story.”

For the specialist shops, the boom is showing up in the till. “Sales are so much higher than I even anticipated for the year already,” says Marot. “It’s so exciting.”

While a Hulu adaptation of Acotar was announced in 2021, Maas has now bought back rights. “I want to see everything adapted the way I envision it, and the way I know fans want it”, she said in March.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: EU backs away from offer to Canada to start ‘associate member’ talks
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Lisa O’Carroll in Brussels and Leyland Cecco in Toronto
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Watered-down version of statement to be issued at end of Montreal summit instead offers ‘ever closer association’

The EU has backed away from its offer to Canada to start talks on becoming an “associate member” after disagreements between members states just as an EU-Canada summit was set to begin in Montreal.

A draft of a joint statement to be issued after the end of the summit, which runs Thursday and Friday, showed a watered-down version offering “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself”.

The issue was triggered after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, surprised nearly everyone by announcing in last month’s state of the union address that the EU would consider “associate membership” for Canada.

The declaration had been hailed as a landmark in EU history, offering a non-EU country such close ties to the bloc, which has not allowed any state membership since Croatia joined in 2013.

It was also seen as a sign that the call by Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, at the Davos summit in January for “middle powers” to work together was paying off.

But instead of announcing a work programme on developing “associate membership”, the draft communique, seen by the Guardian, states the two sides would “work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself, to reflect, through this even closer association, our common endeavour and cooperation towards our shared goals of prosperity, economic security and strategic autonomy”.

Associate membership had been mooted, and rejected, previously for countries such as Ukraine.

Von der Leyen’s declaration caught EU capitals by surprise and led to pushback politically and legally. Given “associate status” has no definition, diplomats wondered about such issues as whether Canada could join the European Council, legislative bodies or decision-making processes without a vote.

At a meeting on Monday, ambassadors in the EU raised concerns about the dramatic offer, but vowed to make efforts to seek a diplomatic path to rescinding the offer of “associate” membership without embarrassing Von der Leyen. It is understood that Italy suggested “associate membership as proposed by the commission”, with the definition to be thrashed out later by member states.

Germany walked back further, suggesting the wording “an ever closer association of Canada” to the EU.

“Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [Von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem. Many member states, including Germany, were not happy. This is all about fixing the plane while it is flying,” said one diplomat.

Germany had argued that “associate membership” should be reserved as an interim step for prospective candidate countries, such as Ukraine or Montenegro, noting that the status has no formal grounding in current EU treaties.

Donald Trump, the US president, previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable”, and said if he ​interpreted the move as a “hostile act” the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things”.

A bitter trade war with the US, a longtime ally, has seen Carney seek out new trading partnerships around the world. Ahead of the summit in Montreal, one of Canada’s largest banks released a report suggesting there was “meaningful” upside for Canada if it were to deepen economic ties with Europe. Tens of billions of dollars in additional trade would be possible if barriers were removed in areas of overlapping interest such as defence, energy, critical minerals and digital markets, TD Economics said.

Carney has spoken specifically about the need to lessen reliance on Elon Musk‘s Starlink satellite network, following a decision to throttle its usage over Ukraine.

Earlier this week, Carney posted on social media that Canada would join the popular music competition Eurovision. But despite fears raised by political rivals, Carney has said Canada has no interest in formally joining the EU. Changing Canadian laws to bring it in line with European nations would probably prove unpopular, despite public support for stronger ties.

Carney told reporters on Tuesday that the summit this week was the launch of further formal negotiations that will take place another year.

“The good news is it doesn’t matter about ⁠specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will ​make to the lives ​of Canadians.”

A previous draft statement ​had included at least two references to Canada as an “associate member”, ​including an acknowledgment that ‌defining the ​term would take ​another year.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: New book makes fiery claims about Jared Kushner’s finances in Trump’s first term
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Martin Pengelly
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Kushner threatens to sue, denying allegations that two slush funds were set up to influence his Middle East role

A new book containing incendiary claims about Jared Kushner’s financial dealings during Donald Trump’s first term has ignited a political and media firestorm.

The book by author Matthew Cole is called Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East and was released in the US this week. An excerpt was published by Vanity Fair last Thursday, and immediately drew a furious response from Kushner, who called its claims “completely insane”. The book contains numerous allegations about Kushner, whose father-in-law is Trump and who has served as one of his top diplomatic envoys in the Middle East – the most explosive of which are claims linking him to huge bank accounts allegedly funded by Gulf states.

Kusher denounced the book on his site last week, and writing on X: “We denied every one of these claims on the record, yet the author failed to provide a single shred of evidence to substantiate any of them.” He has demanded that Vanity Fair retract the excerpt and has threatened legal action against the book’s publisher, Simon & Schuster.

He added: “During the period in question, I was one of the most scrutinized people in the world, subjected to intense media coverage, multiple congressional investigations, and a special counsel investigation. I voluntarily cooperated with these investigations, providing over 30 hours of testimony. None of these allegations ever surfaced, because none of these events ever happened.”

The Guardian contacted Kushner’s legal counsel from Clare Locke as well as Chad Mizelle for comment and received no response.

Cole’s sources are predominantly anonymous and he does not print images of emails or other documentation to support his reporting. Extensive footnotes indicate sources of information, including confidential interviews.

In the book, the top intelligence official in the United Arab Emirates, Ali Al Shamsi, is reported to have called Kushner “the most expensive employee we’ve ever had”. The book details alleged payments into two “slush fund” bank accounts allegedly set up for Kushner by Emirati prince Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ) and Saudi Arabian prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) during Trump’s first term. The Guardian contacted the Saudi Arabian and Emirati embassies for comment and did not receive a response.

In the book, Cole claims the accounts were partially managed by Kushner on an iPhone hacked by Russian and Dutch intelligence.

But despite the Emirati spymaster’s opinion of Kushner, Cole alleges that the New Jersey real estate scion was not entirely trusted. Cole describes a dangerous world in which blackmail is as common a tool of statecraft as torture and murder, as in the cases of the Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, killed on the orders of MBS in Turkey in 2018, and the Emirati journalist and poet Habib Al Sayegh, whose killing by agents of MBZ in 2019 is described by Cole.

Kushner continues to steer US foreign policy despite having no official role, with questions about his business interests accompanying him as he travels the world with New York real estate magnate Steve Witkoff, this week seeking peace in Ukraine, if on terms favorable to Russia.

In response, an attorney “who has represented President Trump in multiple defamation lawsuits”, Alejandro Brito, told Cole that, “during his time working for President Trump, Kushner ‘always represented and sought the interests of the United States and the President of the United States and did not make any agreements or arrangements with leaders or officials in foreign countries that were not agreed by the President of the United States and in the best interests of the United States.’” He further said that “[a]ny allegation that Kushner knew of, had access to, had authorization for or engaged in or directed any conduct related to any government-funded or government-linked bank account is totally false and defamatory”.

Brito told Cole that “‘there are no accounts and never were.’” Cole writes that the Dutch government refused to comment in response to his questions about the alleged hacking of Kushner’s phone.

According to Cole, MBZ and MBS wanted Kushner to help achieve their “vision of a new Middle East, one in which Israel would become an integral part of the region, recognized diplomatically by Gulf Arabs today and eventually by the rest of the Arab world; the Palestinians would end their conflict with Israel and accept a peace built on prosperity; Islamic extremism would be defeated; and Iran’s expansionism and militancy would retreat, either by persuasion or force.”

Nearly 10 years later, the US and Israel are planning new strikes in their eight-month war with Iran; Saudi Arabia is at war with Houthi rebels in Yemen, and Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza since the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023.

Kushner entered Trump’s first administration with his wife, Ivanka Trump, as close presidential advisers. MBZ and MBS, Cole claims, saw a chance to secure the best access money could buy. Cole alleges that in early 2017 the two princes “proposed to give Kushner a fund, a bank account, which the two leaders, working with Jared, would use to identify and pay for projects and foreign policy goals to advance for President Trump’s benefit”.

According to Cole, an idea to fund Trump’s proposed wall on the US border with Mexico apparently did not work out but the author claims that “MBZ and MBS initially, and then MBZ alone, put at least $2bn into at least two banks for Kushner.” Classifying the accounts as “Alpha” and “Beta”, Cole claims the Alpha account was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank, the largest in UAE, and contained “roughly $750m” to be “used as a foreign policy fund” overseen by Kushner and MBZ and meant to help end the Israel-Palestine conflict.

Cole quotes a source who says he knew of the UAE’s alleged deal with Kushner as saying: “‘Jared was looking for shortcuts in his diplomacy.’” Cole writes: “This person held discussions with both senior UAE and Israeli officials about the secret financial arrangement between Kushner, the UAE, and, at least initially, Saudi Arabia. ‘Jared promised MBZ that he’d push their agenda with Trump if they participated in a fund. He wanted normalization with Israel so that business could take off,’” the source alleged.

The same source claimed that “a slush fund – a shared pool of money for off-the-books diplomatic objectives – was a common form of Gulf Arab government corruption … ‘The Emiratis and the Saudis do this once a year. A billion or two is nothing for them, and if it gets them what they want, it’s money well spent.’”

Citing “a person briefed on the Beta account”, Cole claims it contained “roughly $1bn” and at the suggestion of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, was moved by MBZ to the Israeli Central Bank via Azerbaijan, a favored conduit for laundering money.

“It is … unclear how Kushner used the money the UAE deposited into the Beta account for him,” Cole alleges, “but according to the person with knowledge of the money, its allocation was for Kushner’s personal benefit.”

Kushner’s attorney, Brito, told Cole his client “had no financial relationships with any foreign countries or leaders”, adding that his “complete financial disclosures are publicly available in his OGE [office of government ethics] form 278e filings during this period.”

Cole alleges that the “Alpha” account established for Kushner in Trump’s first term was drained by failed schemes and Kushner’s access was cut off. “It is unclear if the Israeli government allowed Kushner access to the Beta bank account” after the end of Trump’s first term, Cole writes.

Cole also examines the widely reported story about how Kushner ultimately secured Qatari investment in 666 Fifth Avenue, a marquee Manhattan property, thereby profiting from interests on both sides of a bitterly divided Middle East, given Saudi Arabia and UAE’s rivalry with Qatar. (Kushner has denied engaging in any conflicts of interest.)

In Trump’s second term, Kushner’s diplomatic work has been dogged by questions about another massive financial asset: a $2bn investment by the Saudi sovereign wealth fund in Kushner’s Affinity Partners private equity firm, made after Trump left power in 2021. Cole quotes an unnamed Arab official and Affinity investor who claimed: “We don’t pay Jared because he’s a savvy investor. We pay him to keep him happy. That keeps his father-in-law happy.”

Cole writes: “Deep relationships with MBZ, MBS, Emir Al Thani [of Qatar], and Bibi Netanyahu were useful as [Kushner] shuttled between capitals, trying to find a way to end the daily slaughter in Gaza. But as it had been when he was a government employee, there was little record of what his investors were negotiating with him.”

In his epilogue, Cole writes that Kushner “declined multiple requests for an on-the-record interview for the book”, adding that he “first contacted him with a list of questions in May 2026 and followed up via email twice more, asking additional questions.”

Through his lawyers, Kushner denounced all of Cole’s reporting. Also on X, Chad Mizelle, a Trump administration lawyer who identified himself as “Jared’s attorney”, said: “The central allegation in this book is categorically false. These are not questions of interpretation or competing recollections: there are no bank accounts. They don’t exist. These are egregious and defamatory claims without a shred of evidence to substantiate them.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: California weather is ‘well into extreme territory’ with historic high tides
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Gabrielle Canon in San Francisco
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Seawater surges into low-lying communities from San Diego to San Francisco Bay Area, submerging streets, homes and businesses

Historic high tides have caused chaos up and down the California coast this week, as parts of the state were inundated by record-breaking water levels. Seawater surged into low-lying communities from San Diego to the San Francisco Bay Area, submerging streets, flooding homes and businesses, and jamming important transportation corridors and train routes.

Kayakers and paddle boarders could be seen gliding through typically busy thoroughfares in Marin county, north of San Francisco, on Monday and Tuesday. Several drivers had to be rescued from floating cars in the area, while cyclists who had attempted to cross the temporary lagoon that had formed quickly found themselves waist-deep. Further south, in cities such as Newport Beach, water pounded the emergency infrastructure set up to keep out the swelling sea, which seeped through berms, seawalls and sandbag blockades along the shoreline.

Up and down the state, all-time records were smashed. Near Los Angeles and San Diego, tides rose above 8ft. San Francisco registered its highest reading for the month of October on Wednesday, breaking a record set the day before.

The National Weather Service has issued a swathe of flood advisories and warnings that will last for days. In San Diego and Orange counties, forecasters said significant coastal flooding was expected during high tides through Thursday. “Numerous roads may be closed. Low lying property including homes, businesses, and some critical infrastructure will be inundated,” they said in a Wednesday outlook. In Los Angeles, moderate flood risks extended into the weekend, though tides would begin to drop after Thursday. Shoreline erosion is expected across the California coast.

The repeated onslaught from the rising sea has made for a tumultuous autumn, especially in southern California, which has been hammered several times over the last two months. Los Angeles has already logged 12 coastal flood days in 2026, according to records from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) – outpacing any year in the last 50 – with months left to go.

But the dangers won’t recede when the tides do, and the newly set records won’t be held for long. The worst flooding may be to come as severe impacts from an exceptionally strong and still-strengthening El Niño unfold in the months ahead, experts warned, with the potential to raise tides several feet above the levels recorded this week.

“What we are seeing now could be the beginning of what could be significantly more disruptive conditions later this year,” climate scientist Daniel Swain said during an online briefing Tuesday.

The sharply rising waters are the result of thermal expansion from a record-breaking oceanic heatwave layered on top of higher sea levels fueled by the human-caused climate crisis, Swain explained. A coastally trapped Kelvin wave – a massive underwater band of warm water that has crept across the Pacific and up the North American shoreline – has also added to the fray, and the California coast could see plenty more of them through the winter and into early next year. “I would expect these water levels to be exceeded multiple times this winter,” Swain said.

San Diego, La Jolla, Los Angeles and Santa Monica all have above an 80% chance of high tide flooding in December according to a Noaa outlook. Most of the stations near coastal communities to the north, going all the way to the Canadian border, were in the 60-80% category.

The floods seen this week were not so-called king tides, which are the highest predicted tides for the year. Those will show up right in time for busy holiday weekends, around Thanksgiving and Christmas this year, and around 20-23 January next year.

King tides can add an additional foot or two to water levels, which are already elevated by roughly a foot due to human-caused warming, the effects from El Niño and Kelvin waves. If each of these layers align as they are expected to, they will create up to 5ft of sea level rise above average, in many places at once.

“We are well into extreme territory – and really in record-breaking territory,” Swain said. That will set the stage for disastrous flooding, should a storm arrive when waters are high.” Swain said that’s when things “get really hairy”.

The historic El Niño brewing in the Pacific has the power to unleash extreme weather around the world, and in California that could mean supercharged storms. Southern California especially tends to get doused during the El Niños, and this year the climate phenomenon, characterized by warmer-than-average equatorial sea surface temperatures, could pack an extraordinary punch.

Should a strong storm occur during the windows when the tides are highest, flooding could be disastrous. “There’s at least a 30-40% chance we stack all of these this winter, and potentially more than once,” Swain said.

https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/o.title: Embattled Bari Weiss says she is not ‘focused’ on declining 60 Minutes ratings
https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/o.author: Jeremy Barr in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/o.text:
CBS News editor-in-chief sidesteps viewership concerns and says flagship show doing ‘tremendously well’

CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss has spoken publicly for the first time about the ratings challenges the network has experienced under her year-long tenure, sidestepping concerns about diminished viewership at the Sunday show 60 Minutes by saying it was not her top priority.

“I could never build anything if I were focused on the precise number of people that happen to tune in to the second feature on 60 Minutes on a given Sunday,” she said at an industry conference on Wednesday organized by the tech publication the Information. The news organization did not offer press credentials.

Weiss completely overhauled 60 Minutes in late May, ousting the show’s executive producer and parting ways with three top correspondents, including Scott Pelley. But the show has struggled to even match last season’s viewership, which averaged 9.1 million viewers per episode.

The show’s most recent episode drew just 5.64 million viewers, “one of the smallest audiences for the program in years”, Variety reported. The show was the lowest-rated sixth episode of the weekly show this century, a feat also achieved by the fourth episode of the show.

The show’s ratings are heavily dependent on whether it is preceded by a highly watched NFL football game. Ratings for the show have been low despite a strong run of guest bookings and news-making segments. Viewership hasn’t been all bad, either – the 4 October edition of the show drew an average of more than 10 million total viewers.

Weiss was also asked about parent company Skydance’s recent merger with Warner Bros Discovery, the parent company of CNN. While Weiss was initially rumored to potentially lead the cable news network, chief executive David Ellison instead opted to keep CNN chief executive Mark Thompson in place – for the time being, at least.

Asked whether she might be interested in running CNN, Weiss replied: “I want to focus on doing CBS News, trust me. This is a big enough challenge.”

Weiss said she is not focused on criticism of her tenure at CBS News, which has come from inside and outside the building. Her strategy has been to “put the blinders on, tune out the noise and focus”, adding: “I’m not doing anything I’m doing for popularity’s sake.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Non-profit group leaks data of more than 40,000 homeland security workers
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Reuters
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Information released by Distributed Denial of Secrets is the third such government data disclosure in the last month

The leak website Distributed Denial of Secrets said on Wednesday it has released data on more than 40,000 Department ⁠of Homeland Security (DHS) employees, including details about officials working in sensitive fields such as surveillance and human intelligence.

The disclosure – which the ⁠non-profit data transparency group says draws ⁠on information obtained ​by an entity calling itself “Department of Peace” – is the third government data leak to have made headlines in the past month.

In September, the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed ⁠the theft of a massive trove of data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, including sensitive job details and medical information from thousands of bureau employees. Last week, the defense department was hit with ⁠a class action lawsuit following a breach that exposed data on millions of current and former military personnel.

The DHS data includes ​names, phone numbers and email addresses of employees from Immigration ‌and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border ‌Protection, Homeland Security Investigations, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and other DHS component agencies.

Also included in the data were job ‌titles and email groups, which, among other details, showed which agents were assigned to special operations, surveillance jobs, computer forensics and undercover work.

In a statement, Emma Best, a Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder, said the hacktivist known as “maia arson crimew” developed a search tool for the data that would allow the public to browse it. Best said the tool would “replace anonymity with accountability” and empower journalists, guide public records requests and boost congressional oversight.

The Department of Peace did not immediately respond ‌to a request for comment, but in a statement included with the data, it said that DHS employees “have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped the data “can ​be used to limit further harm by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction”.

The Department of Peace in March claimed responsibility for hacking DHS and posting documents related to contracts with outside vendors.

Best’s statement said Department of Peace harvested the data from the Okta sign-on service used by DHS. Reuters could not immediately corroborate the claim. Okta said in response to a Reuters query: “Okta is ⁠secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised.”

Reuters could not immediately ​verify the authenticity of the entire data ​trove but it was able to match ​personal information of about six DHS employees named in the leak to credit bureau records and breach data ​carried by the dark ‌web intelligence platform District 4 ​Labs. In other cases, ​Reuters called three DHS employees directly and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details. One said it was the first they had heard of a breach.

In several cases, the data tracked information available on DHS employees’ LinkedIn profiles. But in others, the data revealed nonpublic data about internal DHS organization charts or previously undisclosed programs or operations.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Tributes pour in for labor leader Dolores Huerta: ‘Fought for farm workers to the very end’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maanvi Singh
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Lawmakers, activists and union leaders across the US remember the co-founder of United Farm Workers union

Following the news that Dolores Huerta – the civil rights icon who popularized the rallying cry “Sí, se puede! – had died at the age of 96 on Wednesday, activists, lawmakers and civil rights leaders paid tribute to Hureta’s long and lasting legacy.

In California – where Huerta helped found the United Farm Workers (UFW) union – her death was deeply felt. It was in California’s central valley that she laid the foundations for the United Farm Workers, and helped organize the 1965 Delano grape strike – a national boycott of table grapes that resulted in better wages and working conditions for grape pickers. Several schools in California bear her name, and murals across the state depict her likeness. And in 2018, California declared 10 April – her birthday – Dolores Huerta Day.

“From the fields of California to the halls of Congress and the White House, Dolores dedicated her life to ensuring that every voice – especially those too often silenced – was heard,” said Hector Sanchez Barba, the president of the voter mobilization organization Mi Familia Vota. “Her historic rallying cry, ‘Sí, se puede,’ is not just a slogan; it is a living call to action that continues to unite and inspire millions across the world.”

“Our greatest monument to her memory is for the union she helped found to continue to grow. Dolores fought for farm workers to the very end of her life,” said UFW president Teresa Romero. “The greatest possible tribute to her life is for her work of organizing to continue.”

Huerta’s legacy is national and international; her portrait hangs at some US embassies and schools in several US states are named after her. She helped negotiate national immigration policy, and remained, until her death, intimately involved in promoting civil and labor rights in Washington DC and across the US.

Tributes also came from some of California’s biggest political names, including Nancy Pelosi, the former House speaker, Gavin Newsom, the governor, and former vice-president Kamala Harris.

“Dolores was a dear friend, and we all responded to her rallying cry, ‘Sí se puede,’ which inspired generations of Americans to believe in the power of collective action,” said Pelosi. “May it be a comfort to her family and loved ones that so many mourn their loss and are praying for them at this sad time.”

“I was blessed to know Dolores for many years and proud to organize alongside my dear friend to champion working families and immigrant rights,” said Harris. “I will always be grateful for her support and friendship. We will honor her legacy by continuing the fight for the dignity of every person.”

“Dolores Huerta represented the best of us,” said Newsom. “California – and the United States – would not be what we are today without her resolute spirit, her passion for justice and fairness, and her commitment to those overlooked and forgotten.”

“The best tribute we can pay is to carry on the work, which means standing with workers, defending civil rights and organizing for a more just California,” echoed Alex Padilla, US senator representing California.

“¡Adiós, Dolores! You were everywhere. You did everything,” said Xavier Becerra, the former California attorney general and former US health secretary who is running for governor. “If you want to know where a leader will take you, know where they come from. Dolores never let us forget where she came from. Si, se pudo [Yes, we did].”

Lawmakers across the US, including Alexandria Ocasio Cortez, the New York congressperson, also hailed her trailblazing legacy. “For decades after the Delano Grape Strike, she continued to organize for the rights of working people, women and immigrants. She continued to fight for the idea that when ordinary people come together, they can change the course of history,” said Ocasio Cortez. “While we mourn her devastating loss, we will continue her fight to build a country where every worker, regardless of race, gender, or economic status, is treated with dignity.”

Lawmakers thanked Huerta for her efforts to promote female candidates to public office.

Eloise Gómez Reyes, the state senator who brought legislation in 2018 to mark 10 April as Dolores Huerta Day in California, said that she was mourning “the loss of someone who profoundly shaped my own life”.

“Dolores Huerta taught generations of us that we did not have to accept the world as it was. That ordinary people, working together, could challenge powerful institutions, overcome injustice, and build something better. She didn’t simply open doors for women like me. She taught us that we had the power to open them for others,” Reyes said.

Hilda Solis, a former Democratic congresswoman who became the first Latina to serve in a cabinet position as Barack Obama’s labor secretary, thanked Huerta for her mentorship. “Growing up in the San Gabriel Valley, I rarely saw Latinas in positions of leadership. Dolores was one of the few women who showed me what was possible,” she said. “From the state legislature to Congress and my time serving in President Barack Obama’s cabinet, Dolores remained a constant in my life. We joined demonstrations and rallies, stood with workers fighting for their rights and demanded action when people in power looked away … Dolores understood the importance of showing up, bearing witness and refusing to let the suffering of women go ignored.”

Huerta for years was considered the second-in-command to UFW co-founder César Chávez – and spoke about how she had to fight the sexism within the movement, and was often forced to cede credit to Chávez. Earlier this year, in the aftermath of a New York Times investigation uncovering Chávez’ pattern of sexual abuse of women and girls, Huerta revealed that Chávez had raped her, too.

“I believed that exposing the truth would hurt the farmworker movement I have spent my entire life fighting for,” she said, explaining why she had stayed silent about her abuse for so long.

But after sharing her story, she learned that her fear would not bear out. Across the US, officials looked to renaming streets that once bore Chávez’s name with Huerta’s. Murals centering Chávez were replaced with Huerta’s image, or images depicting the larger farmworker movement.

“Her guidance transcended generations, nationalities, and borders. She touched so many people as she fought for justice, peace and equality. She never backed down,” said actor Rosario Dawson, who portrayed Huerta in a 2014 biopic of César Chávez. Dawson, who cofounded the organization Voto Latino, had worked with Huerta to rally voter turnout, and at times had openly disagreed with her politics, said that the civil rights leader had been a “mentor and a beacon of light”.

“¡Sí, se puede, Dolores! May we carry your light and joy as we forge the path for new generations,” she added.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: I’ve mailed off my vote in the US midterms. It will be a nail-biting watch, but easier from outside Trump’s America | Eleanor Limprecht
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Eleanor Limprecht
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
I’m hopeful these elections will be a win for democracy rather than dictatorship, for peace rather than war, and humanity rather than hubris

Recently I made my own envelope out of a sheet of paper and sticky tape, signed it and affixed a sticker. Then I took it to my nearest Australia Post shop in Sydney and mailed it.

In other words, I voted from abroad in the US midterm elections. Because my last place of residence in the US was the state of Virginia, I can register to vote and request a ballot online, but the ballot still needs to be printed, signed, sealed in an envelope made of folded paper, signed again, placed inside another (store-bought) envelope and mailed in. There was no sausage sizzle or cake stall to reward me for my civic duty, and no spectre of a fine if I didn’t complete it.

I give a wide berth to anything resembling a craft project (haunted by the ghosts of Easter hat parades past) but I would cross-stitch a ballot if it lessened the power that President Trump wields over my country of birth. Hell, I would papier-mache an airplane and decoupage a pilot’s licence to deliver my vote in person.

Unfortunately, not everyone is as fervent: voter turnout in the midterm elections in the US is typically less than half the eligible voting population. The midterms are viewed as less important; in-person voting is arduous and inconvenient (with long queues, on a weekday rather than a Saturday) and some voters view state-based elections as secondary to the presidential election.

The current administration is trying to reduce voter turnout even more because things are not looking good for Republican candidates. They have gerrymandered, sued the state of California for refusing to disenfranchise 20,000 voters, tried to restrict mail-in voting (this was blocked by the supreme court) and already made a challenge to Alaska’s Senate election results if the incumbent Republican senator Dan Sullivan does not win.

Can you smell it from here? That’s not raw sewage overflow from the recent heavy rains, that’s Trump’s fear.

Democrats only need three seats to gain majority in the House of Representatives and four to gain majority in the Senate. If the Democrats control Congress it will be far more difficult for Trump to get his laws through. They could create committees to investigate the president and even begin an impeachment trial.

Trump’s egregiously named Operation Epic Fury has caused the price of fuel to skyrocket and most Americans (two-thirds) now view the ongoing war against Iran as a mistake. As the price of fuel goes up, Trump’s approval rating sinks. (His dismantling of democracy and campaign of disinformation didn’t seem to disturb voters in the same way that this hit to the hip pocket does.)

I am cautiously hopeful. I’ve spent the past two years wishing I was Canadian and rushing to turn off the radio or television at the sound of Trump’s hyperbole. Perfecting my simultaneous sigh and shrug when people hear my accent and ask me to explain how and why the bully-in-chief was re-elected.

But I keep recalling the awful events of 6 January 2021, when in the wake of a Trump rally, an angry rightwing mob attacked the US Capitol building after his defeat in the 2020 elections. Five people died and 174 police officers were injured while the rest of the world watched in horror. As a child in Arlington, Virginia, I visited those rotundas and chambers on field trips. As an adult here in Australia, I worried over friends and family who live and work in Washington DC. If the Republican candidates are defeated in these elections, will the administration accept the results?

There are three million Americans who live abroad and more than 110,000 here in Australia (around 60% of us have Australian citizenship). It will be nail-biting to watch the 3 November midterm elections, but easier from afar than from within Trump’s America: a country where immigrants are endangered, abortion rights have been eroded, artificial intelligence has grown without regulation and foreign aid, environmental protections and domestic social services have been gutted. Even Trump’s tariffs are backfiring for the United States, uniting the countries they are aimed against, such as Canada. Elbows up!

These midterms, I am hopeful it will be a win for democracy rather than dictatorship, for peace rather than war, and humanity rather than hubris.

Just please, whatever happens, don’t ask me to explain the electoral college come 2028.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Liverpool beat Chelsea on penalties yet again to secure Carabao Cup progress
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Andy Hunter at Anfield
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Chelsea must have known their fate as soon as the last 16 tie at Anfield went to penalties. Four times they had faced Liverpool in a penalty shoot-out previously and four times they had lost. Make that five, after Wesley Fofana’s woeful attempt sailed high into the Kop and sent Andoni Iraola’s side into the Carabao Cup quarter finals.

The defender was not the only culprit as Chelsea’s catalogue of penalty misery against Liverpool gained a new chapter to add to the 2007 Champions League semi final, the 2019 Uefa Super Cup final and the FA and League Cup finals of 2022. Emmanuel Emegha could have won it for Xabi Alonso’s visitors but his effort was saved superbly by Giorgi Mamardashvili.

Kostas Tsimikas could also have reprised his match-winning role from Wembley in 2022 but fired over when Liverpool were a kick away from the last eight. Ryan Gravenberch and Valentin Barco also failed to convert in the shoot-out after Morgan Rogers and Cody Gakpo had both scored penalties in normal time.

Former Liverpool midfielders Alonso and Jordan Henderson received lukewarm receptions on their return to Anfield, certainly in comparison to previous visits with Bayer Leverkusen, Real Madrid and Brentford. That was the best they could have hoped for given the club they were returning with. The Chelsea manager was warmly embraced before kick-off by his childhood friend Iraola, however, while Henderson had to make do with some pantomime booing whenever he took possession.

Both Basque coaches sprang selection surprises for the last 16 tie, more in terms of positioning than personnel. Lewis Koumas – one of seven changes that Iraola made from Sunday’s win over Brighton – started on the right of Liverpool’s attack withGakpo leading the line. In the absence of the injured João Pedro and the suspended Cole Palmer Alonso deployed the veterans as he sought a reaction to Chelsea’s home defeat by Tottenham. Danny Welbeck being closely supported by a roving Henderson in the number ten role would not have been on anyone’s Chelsea bingo card before this season. There was still no room in the starting line-up for Estêvão, a talent who appears not to fit the Alonso approach.

The Premier League rivals served up a fast-paced, committed cup tie that was just lacking goalmouth incident before they exchanged penalties in the space of four minutes. Koumas picked up an early booking for a challenge on Maxence Lacroix, who caught the Liverpool forward as he attempted to clear his lines and not vice-versa. Rio Ngumoha stirred the home crowd with a few mesmerising runs down the left but the final ball from his teammates was lacking.

Neither goalkeeper had been seriously troubled before Chelsea were awarded the first of two quick-fire spot-kicks. Moisés Caicedo was released inside the Liverpool area by a cleverly disguised pass from Malo Gusto and clipped from behind by Ryan Gravenberch as the pair headed away from goal. The boos for Henderson intensified as he carried the ball to the spot with a wry smile on his face and handed it to Rogers, who sent Mamardashvili the wrong way with an emphatic penalty kick.

Liverpool soon had a spot-kick of their own when Caicedo and Fofana challenged Virgil van Dijk at a Kostas Tsimikas corner and the ball struck the Chelsea defender’s raised hand. Gakpo went low to Mike Penders’s right with his penalty while the Chelsea keeper dived to his left.

The referee, Darren England, called both penalties instantly and correctly, showing officials do not always have to rely on video assistance. The game benefited as a spectacle from the absence of the video assistant referee, although Iraola might well have disagreed had Rogers scored after appearing to control Pedro Neto’s chip with his arm. Mamardashvili’s save spared us that controversy.

Chelsea needed to take control of the contest before Iraola introduced the insurance policy of Liverpool’s big names from the bench. Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola would arrive in the 59th minute with the game still evenly poised and the visitors struggling to break down a resolute home defence. Gusto fuelled the atmosphere by twice collapsing in apparent agony following a touch from Penders, keen to atone for his costly error against Spurs, took centre stage for Chelsea when saving a flying header from Ronald Araujo at close range.

The Liverpool central defender had been supplied by a fine cross from Joe Gomez and, with two defenders pushed forwards, Rogers almost punished them on the counter attack. Gomez, however, worked tirelessly to chase back and block the forward’s eventual shot. Penders also saved impressively from Barcola when the France international cut inside from the right and his low shot was deflected towards the bottom corner.

Rogers was involved in several promising openings for Chelsea as Alonso’s team – improved more than Liverpool by their substitutes – finished strongly. Marco Palestra had the best of them when released by the England forward’s perfectly weighted pass but Mamardashvili produced an excellent save low to his right. Wirtz also had a late chance to seal victory but his attempt from Gakpo’s knock-down struck Levi Colwill and was eventually cleared. And so to penalties, and a familiar feeling for the men from Stamford Bridge.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Investors turn on Google owner Alphabet after profit miss, ad slowdown and high spending
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Net profit slid 25% from a year earlier to $26.2bn, well short of expectations, though revenue rose to $127.6bn

Shares in Google parent Alphabet fell more than 10% in after-hours trading Wednesday, erasing tens of billions of dollars in stock market value from the $4tn tech giant. The company had reported lower-than-expected profit and a slowdown in its advertising business while it maintained big spending on AI.

Net profit slid 25% from a year earlier to $26.2bn in the July-to-September period, or $2.12 a share, well short of expectations by analysts surveyed by FactSet.

Alphabet booked an $8.7bn loss on its equity investments, which it attributed to its stake in SpaceX, the Elon Musk-led company where shares have struggled since going public in June.

Revenue, however, rose 25% to an enormous $127.6bn. The figure was slightly below the roughly $128bn analysts had forecast.

Advertising revenue grew 11% to $82bn, short of expectations. Revenue from Google’s search business, still the company’s largest source of income, rose 12% to $63.4bn, slowing from 17% growth in the previous quarter.

YouTube, now the most-watched content provider on American TV screens, saw advertising revenue grow 9% to $11.2bn, down from 13% growth in the previous quarter. YouTube Music and Premium passed 150 million subscribers worldwide, including trials.

Google Cloud, which rents computing power and AI tools to businesses, saw revenue jump 103% to $30.7bn, ahead of analyst expectations.

The company said sales of its in-house AI chips, known as TPUs, contributed significantly to that growth. Operating income for the unit tripled to $11.1bn.

Google is also selling its TPU chips to outside companies, in a growing challenge to market leader Nvidia. OpenAI reportedly plans to buy some of the chips.

Alphabet’s “Other Bets” division, which includes robotaxi company Waymo, posted revenue of $372m and an operating loss of $2bn.

Waymo now provides more than 500,000 paid rides per week across 15 US metropolitan areas and aims to reach 1m weekly rides by the end of the year.

Alphabet spent $51.4bn on capital expenditures during the quarter, mostly on datacenters and AI chips, more than double the $24bn a year earlier.

Its latest forecast for capex spending is between $195bn to $205bn in spending for 2026.

The company said it would continue to increase capex spending significantly in 2027.

“I would broadly think of all of this as a long-range planning process, not a short-term allocation exercise,” Sundar Pichai, the Google CEO, told analysts of the company’s investment splurge.

The company’s spending, which included a fine paid to the European Union, outstripped the cash generated by Alphabet’s businesses for a second straight quarter, leaving a $9.1bn gap.

During the quarter Alphabet raised $28.7bn by selling bonds and $12.4bn by issuing new shares to help pay for its AI ambitions.

Google has stepped up the pace of its AI releases since a delay to a flagship model in July raised questions about whether it was falling behind rivals OpenAI and Anthropic.

It launched Gemini 4 at the end of September and later released a version focused on cybersecurity.

The Gemini app has reached 1bn users. Google’s AI models now process nearly 32bn tokens, or units of text, per minute, more than four times the level of a year ago, the company said.

Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, is also one of Google’s largest cloud customers. It has committed to using up to one million Google AI chips.

In September, a US judge declined to order Google to sell off parts of its advertising technology business, imposing restrictions on how it operates instead.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Judge rebuffs Trump DoJ’s bid to order California to set aside 20,000 ballots
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sam Levine
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Justice department had demanded state segregate ballots from people it claimed were non-citizens

A federal judge declined to order California election officials to segregate ballots from people the Trump administration claimed were non-citizens, rebuffing a legally thin request from the justice department that appeared designed to cast doubt over the results of the midterms.

The ruling from US district judge David Carter, nominated to the federal bench by Bill Clinton, comes about two weeks after the justice department delivered a USB drive to election officials in Los Angeles and Sacramento that it said contained the names of 20,000 non-citizens on the state’s voter rolls. There are more than 23 million registered voters in California and non-citizen voting is extremely rare.

“This case is about the right of every American citizen to vote in a free and fair election,” Carter wrote in his Wednesday evening ruling. “Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch.”

“In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign,” Carter continued. “But California and its people are sovereign, too.”

The justice department gave officials just 48 hours to review the list and said it would sue the state if officials did not sequester ballots from those whose citizenship it could not confirm. The department refused to provide more details about its methodology and Los Angeles officials found preliminary indicators the list was inaccurate. The justice department then sued California on 15 October to try and force the state to sequester the ballots and verify citizenship.

The justice department separately has threatened to prosecute election officials in the state if they tabulate ballots from non-citizens. Such a move would be without a legal basis, Sam Trepel, a former prosecutor at the justice department, wrote in a blogpost this month. After filing the lawsuit, the Trump administration began providing lists to other counties of suspected non-citizen voters. When election officials began reviewing them, they found the department had flagged voters who were not on the rolls and had provided insufficient information to verify their citizenship status, according to CalMatters.

Carter’s ruling came after the justice department tried to bypass him entirely. After Carter set a 27 October hearing on the justice department’s emergency motion, the department took the unusual step of appealing to the US court of appeals for the ninth circuit, saying Carter was not considering the case fast enough. A panel of ninth circuit judges ruled 2-1 against the justice department earlier this week.

Legal experts have been skeptical about the justice department’s efforts in California since the outset. In July, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced it had identified up to 190,000 non-citizens on California voter rolls. The DHS did not provide more details to the state until after ballots had already gone out in the state.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘They mobilized a whole government response to that joke’: Obama laughs off Trump attacks in rally for Ossoff
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: George Chidi in Atlanta
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Former US president comes to Georgia to support Jon Ossoff for US Senate and Keisha Lance Bottoms for governor

Barack Obama, speaking at a Wednesday campaign rally in suburban Atlanta, offered a closing argument for Democrats in the final week of the midterm election campaign.

“These are not serious people,” he said of Donald Trump and the Republican party. “And we’re all paying the price for their lack of seriousness.”

Obama came to Georgia to support the campaigns of US senator Jon Ossoff, former Atlanta mayor and gubernatorial hopeful Keisha Lance Bottoms, and an array of down-ballot Democrats as part of his cross-country campaign tour before next week’s election. From 3,500 to 4,000 people filled the Discovery Center of Clayton county for the late election season stop, just south of Atlanta.

Obama has been casting caltrops behind him with each campaign stop, offering pointed criticism of Republican candidates and Donald Trump that has been unusual for the former president. He continued to do so on Wednesday, again invoking the image of Trump’s gilded renovations of the White House and noting Trump’s strident reaction to his crack last week likening it to Saddam Hussein decorating a Cheesecake Factory.

“The Saddam Hussein thing didn’t bother him. But he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory,” Obama said. “I mean, it’s all crazy, but this is the crazy part: they mobilized a whole government response to that joke.

“The White House even called the secretary of the treasury,” the former president continued. “The guy who is trying to figure out how to lower inflation … they told him he should hold a press conference in front of the Cheesecake Factory.”

He also rebuffed Republicans’ accusations of snobbery for referencing the popular chain restaurant.

“I am the father of two daughters,” Obama said. “Do you think I could have survived their childhood without going to the Cheesecake Factory?”

But he turned that discussion to the problems of affordability for American voters, in contrast with the corruption of the presidency.

“We have never seen a president so intent on selling favors,” Obama said. “The guy has made billions of dollars while in office. Understand that this has not been done in modern times.”

The construction of a new ballroom on the site of the former East Wing of the White House featured in the comments of many speakers at Wednesday’s rally, including Ossoff.

“Each day, Donald Trump digs the moral pit deeper,” Ossoff said, accusing the president of leading “the most corrupt administration of all time, and everybody knows it”.

“If you’re involved in any of this, next year you’ll be raising your hand to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth,” Ossoff said, in reference to Democrats pledging to impeach Trump if they take control of Congress next year.

Bottoms, meanwhile, contrasted her candidacy with that of her Republican opponent Rick Jackson, tying the billionaire healthcare executive to Trump and describing them as “two out-of-touch billionaires who want to keep getting rich on the backs of taxpayers”.

Invoking the legacies of US Representative John Lewis and Coretta Scott King, Bottoms characterized her candidacy as transcending politics. “They may have the money, but they will never overtake our movement,” she said.

Despite a broad wave of Democratic support buoying candidates across the country – and the eight- to 10-point polling lead Ossoff has on his Republican opponent, US Representative Mike Collins – Bottoms is statistically tied in polls with Jackson. If elected, Bottoms would break the state’s Republican trifecta – where the GOP has controlled both chambers of the legislature and the governor’s office – which began in 2004.

Rev Raphael Warnock, Georgia’s other senator, warned of “spiritual wickedness in high places” while describing the effects of deep cuts to Medicaid and Snap nutrition support for children.

“This is about the character of the country,” Warnock said. “This is about who we are and whether we are here for one another … I am concerned about the spiritual health of our country. There is brokenness, because only a broken nation could manage to elect Donald Trump twice.”

Trump, who was campaigning in Ohio at the same time as the Georgia rally, has also been on a national rally blitz, holding near-daily events in the final days of the midterm campaign. Trump has made two appearances in as many weeks in Georgia, both in what would otherwise seem to be congressional districts that are safe territory for Republicans.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: US ambassador suggests Trump could blame Canada if midterms don’t go his way
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Pete Hoekstra, controversial US ambassador to Canada, has also accused Canadian officials of interfering in US elections

The US ambassador has suggested Canada could be blamed if Republicans perform poorly in next week’s midterm elections, the latest intervention from a controversial figure who has been accused of inflaming a bitter dispute that has angered and baffled residents of both countries.

On Wednesday, CTV news reported that Pete Hoekstra told business leaders at a closed door meeting that if a number of swing races – including Maine and Michigan – go to the Democrats, it could make things harder for Canada because Donald Trump might try to blame the loss on it.

“That’s an interesting way of framing it,” the prime minister, Mark Carney, told reporters when asked about the allegations.

For months, Canada and the US have been locked in a bitter tariff war, with Ottawa retaliating against illegal US tariffs and targeting goods in states that rely heavily on trade with Canada.

Carney said that Canada “will pursue” such a deal if it presents itself, but that Ottawa’s trade negotiators are “not in that position right now”.

Hoekstra is a deeply polarizing figure in Canada, particular for his response to Trump’s rhetoric about making Canada the 51st US state. Speaking to a Michigan radio station last year, he described the threats as a “sign of affection” and questioned why Canadians were offended by what he characterized as a “generous offer”. He had previously described Canada’s 2025 federal election as “anti-American”.

This year a House of Commons petition signed by more than 225,000 Canadians called for his expulsion, suggesting his statements violated diplomatic protocols, including the prohibition on diplomats interfering in the internal affairs of a host country.

More recently, Hoekstra has accused Canadian officials of interfering in US elections, pointing to Canadian politicians who have criticized the tariffs in US media, and the province of Ontario’s anti-tariff advertisement that ran on US television.

“We see all of that. We are monitoring it. We are evaluating it. And if some of it becomes election interference, America will respond to it,” Hoekstra, who comes from Michigan, recently told a Canadian podcast, adding that Canadians should “keep your nose out of American politics”.

Canada’s industry minister, Mélanie Joly, who was a target of Hoekstra’s comments, told reporters in Ottawa that her country “would never do that” and said Canada would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada”.

Carney, while in Turkey, told reporters there was “no merit” to the claims of interference and that he was “disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions”.

Roland Paris, the director of the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs at the University of Ottawa and a foreign affairs adviser to the former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, said the remarks were an “extraordinary thing” for a US ambassador to say about his host country and looked like an effort to “manufacture a pretext for the Trump administration’s own political difficulties”.

“The job of an ambassador is to represent the interests of his country, but it’s also to maintain channels of communication and build relationships and manage disagreements,” he said.

“His comments have repeatedly aggravated tensions instead of helping to manage them. I don’t think that he’s serving American interests very well. I’m not even sure that he’s serving the interests of his president.”

Paris points to polling in the US that shows voters have increasingly linked tariffs, the war and cost of living. There is also widespread confusion over why the White House has chosen to treat Canada as a trade adversary.

“It’s certainly not working in Canada. It’s on the contrary. It seems that every time Mr Hoekstra opens his mouth, the Canadians are more determined than before to stand up to the bullying of the Trump administration,” he said. “That’s not serving American interests.”

The US embassy denied Hoekstra said Canada would face blame for a poor Republican showing, suggesting the remarks were “grossly taken out of context” from a broader discussion.

“The ambassador has consistently said that the Canadian media is attempting to overstate the relevance of Canadian issues in American elections. As we have previously stated, Americans will decide American elections based on issues that are important to them,” the embassy said in a statement.

At a Canadian American Business event last year, Hoekstra delivered what witnesses say was an expletive-laden tirade at Ontario’s trade representative after the province ran a series of anti-tariff ads in the US that featured Ronald Reagan. Ontario’s premier called the outburst “absolutely unacceptable” and “unbecoming of an ambassador”.

Last week, Barack Obama noted the unusual choice to attack a longtime ally while speaking at a Democratic campaign rally in Detroit, mocking Trump’s fixation on Canada and jokingly referring to his northern neighbor as a “well-known evil empire”.

“That historical adversary of ours: Canada,” the former US president said. “It’s your neighbor! It’s a few minutes drive over the bridge. These are the people who gave us Martin Short … and maple syrup. They are the nicest people. And somehow we’ve gotten them so mad.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Utah files criminal charges against prediction market Kalshi and company co-founders
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Firm calls charges, which include violating state gambling ban and profiting from illegal activity, ‘crazy overreach’

Utah on Wednesday filed criminal charges against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, months after a federal judge rejected Kalshi’s effort to prevent Utah from enforcing its strict anti-gambling laws against the activity.

The felony charges could represent a new tactic in how states try to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity, a clash that appears headed to a showdown at the US supreme court.

The charges include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity.

The state’s charging documents name Kalshi and its co-founders, chief executive officer Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara.

In a statement, Utah attorney general Derek Brown said Kalshi has continued to operate in Utah, despite a federal court ruling that Utah’s gambling laws apply to the company.

“Gambling is illegal in Utah, whether you place the bet, run the game, or promote it. Calling it a ‘prediction market’ doesn’t change what it is, and being federally registered doesn’t put a company above the law,” Brown said in a statement.

The attorney general’s office did not immediately say what sort of criminal penalties it would seek in the case, although the felony charges carry the possibility of jail time.

In a statement, Kalshi called the charges a “crazy overreach” and said that “Utah is clearly playing politics”.

“We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona,” it said.

Utah has been on the front lines of a battle between states and the federal government over who regulates the markets. Litigation has spread across roughly 20 states, creating a fragmented legal landscape that analysts say will likely be settled by the supreme court.

Kalshi has maintained that prediction markets fall exclusively under federal jurisdiction and are not governed by state gambling laws.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign reportedly recruited second Dan Sullivan in Alaska Senate race
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Chris Stein
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Republicans have condemned the presence of two Dan Sullivans on the ballot, calling it a ploy to split votes

Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign was behind an effort to recruit a challenger with almost the same name as the Republican US senator Dan Sullivan, both of whom will appear on the ballot in next week’s midterm elections, the New York Times reported on Wednesday.

Republicans have condemned the presence in the race of two candidates named Dan Sullivan – one the two-term US senator, the second a retiree living in south-eastern Alaska with scant political experience – calling the newcomer a ploy by Democrats to cost the incumbent re-election by splitting his supporters.

Peltola’s campaign has denied involvement with the other Dan Sullivan, but the Times reports that her officials together with the party’s campaign arm, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), worked to find other people named Dan Sullivan in Alaska, and encourage them to run. Their reporting is based on interviews with Peltola’s former campaign manager and other sources, together with documents and text messages related to the recruitment effort.

“Alaskan voters need to know,” Elisa Rios, whom Peltola fired in August, told the Times, which added that she later tried to retract her interview with the outlet.

Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sullivan’s campaign, said: “Alaskans deserve the truth.”

“Not one player in this operation has acted in good faith with Alaska voters. Mary Peltola and her campaign have spent months gaslighting Alaskans, denying a scheme they were running all along. We always knew this was a concerted effort to deceive Alaskans, and Mary Peltola was hoping it would stay covered up until after the election,” he added.

Donald Trump shared a link to the Times’s article on Truth Social, calling it proof of “election fraud”.

“I don’t think Mary Peltola, after perpetrating such a terrible scheme, should be allowed to run,” he added. Last week, he acknowledged ordering the justice department to file a lawsuit attempting to block the certification of the election results, if Sullivan loses.

A spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign said: “The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign. Like Mary, our campaign is focused on lowering costs and fixing the rigged system in DC.”

Sullivan’s bid for a third term in the US Senate against Peltola, a former US congresswoman, is one of the most important contests of next week’s midterm elections. Alaska is one of a handful of states with Senate races this year that Democrats are targeting in order to win back a majority in the chamber, where they hold 47 seats to the GOP’s 53, and recent polls have shown Peltola in the lead.

Election authorities in the state attempted to disqualify the other Dan Sullivan before the August primary, but the state supreme court ruled that he can appear on the ballot. Together with Sullivan and Peltola, the challenger was one of the top four vote-getters in the non-partisan primary.

On the general election ballot, the senator will be listed as “Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent” and the challenger “Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.”

At a rally in Alaska this month, Trump urged the senator’s supporters to vote for the “real” Dan Sullivan, and warned that errant votes for the challenger could cost the senator re-election.

“The DSCC is not involved with Dan J Sullivan,” a spokesperson for the Democratic Senate campaign arm said. They added that “Republicans have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns”, including in Alaska’s and Ohio’s Senate races this year, and in previous elections in North Carolina and Montana.

The Times reports that Democrats began considering ways to get a spoiler candidate on to the midterm ballot in the summer of 2025. The DSCC introduced the Peltola campaign to a political operative and Ohio native named Jerid Kurtz, who specialized in such activities, which are typically legal. The aide unsuccessfully approached another potential candidate, who did not share a name with the senator, and ultimately recruited the other Dan Sullivan, the Times reports.

Peltola campaign officials also discussed with the DSCC creating a rightwing party to field a candidate in a race, but that did not pan out, according to the Times. After a second Democrat advanced through the August primary, the operative met with him and convinced him to drop out. He was replaced on the ballot by another Republican, Gerald Heikes, who told the Times he was recruited to run “by a guy from the midwest”, though the person did not resemble the Democratic operative from Ohio.

Heikes is a perennial candidate, who has previously run unsuccessfully for governor, US senator and House representative.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Canada women snap eight-game skid against USA to avenge Olympic hockey heartbreak
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Guardian sport and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Canada ended an eight-game losing streak against the United States with a 5-3 victory on Wednesday night in Windsor, Ontario, as newcomers Caitlin Kraemer and Rosalie Tremblay scored their first senior international goals in a rematch of February’s Olympic gold-medal game.

The win marked Canada’s first victory over their archrivals since 2025 and came eight months after the Americans snatched Olympic gold in Milan, where captain Hilary Knight scored the equalizer with 2:04 remaining in regulation before Megan Keller struck in overtime to deny Canada a fifth Olympic title.

Sarah Fillier scored the winner with 8:15 remaining in the third period after the Americans had erased a two-goal deficit at the WFCU Centre. Laura Stacey added an empty-net goal with six seconds left to seal the victory in the first of two exhibition games ahead of next month’s women’s world championship in Denmark.

Daryl Watts opened the scoring on a first-period power play before Kraemer, 20, doubled the lead off a pass from Nicole Gosling. Knight pulled a goal back for the Americans at 5:37 of the second period, but Tremblay, an 18-year-old freshman at the University of Wisconsin, restored Canada’s two-goal advantage just over four minutes later with a rebound goal.

The Americans mounted their comeback in the third period, with Abbey Murphy cutting the deficit to 3-2 at 3:48 before Caroline Harvey tied the game at 7:53. Fillier put Canada back in front with a shot high past US goaltender Aerin Frankel, and Ann-Renée Desbiens made several late saves to preserve the lead.

The Americans entered the two-game series with all 23 members of their Olympic gold-medal team among a 31-player training camp roster. The teams meet again on Friday in Plymouth, Michigan.

The women’s world championship will take place in Herning and Esbjerg, Denmark, from 6 to 16 November.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Milwaukee Brewers close out Tampa Bay Rays to end 57-year wait for first World Series title
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The Milwaukee Brewers captured their first World Series championship on Wednesday night, defeating the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 to complete a four-games-to-one victory and end more than half a century of waiting for baseball’s biggest prize.

Cooper Pratt drove in two runs and Jacob Misiorowski pitched five and two-thirds scoreless innings as Milwaukee put the finishing touches on a charmed season that began with championship ambitions and ended with the first title in the franchise’s 57-year history.

Trevor Megill secured the final out when Richie Palacios grounded to second baseman Brice Turang, who threw to Jake Bauers to seal Milwaukee’s long-sought maiden title.

Fri 23 Oct Game 1: Milwaukee 3, Tampa Bay 2Sat 24 Oct Game 2: Milwaukee 5, Tampa Bay 4Mon 26 Oct Game 3: Milwaukee 10, Tampa Bay 1Tue 27 Oct Game 4: Tampa Bay 4, Milwaukee 3 (12 innings)Wed 28 Oct Game 5: Milwaukee 4, Tampa Bay 1

In the US, all World Series games will air on Fox and Fox Deportes, with streaming available through Fox One. In the UK, the series will be carried by TNT Sports. In Australia, fans can watch on ESPN, with streaming available through Disney+ and Kayo Sports.

“I know the city’s waited a long, long time for this and we’re so happy to bring it home to them,” Christian Yelich said. “Can’t wait to get back there and celebrate.”

The Brewers, who arrived in Milwaukee in 1970 after one season as the Seattle Pilots, had reached the World Series only once before. Their seven-game defeat to the St Louis Cardinals in 1982 remained the closest they had come until this year, when a team blending young talent with October experience finally went one step further.

Milwaukee had been three outs from completing a sweep on Tuesday night in Game 4 before surrendering a 12th-inning lead. Given another opportunity on Wednesday, the Brewers built a four-run advantage behind Misiorowski, who allowed two hits and one walk while striking out two before departing following an injury delay in the sixth.

Tampa Bay’s best early opportunity came in the fourth, when Liam Hicks was hit by a pitch and Chandler Simpson singled, with Sal Frelick’s fielding error leaving runners at second and third with two outs.

Misiorowski induced a groundout from Ben Williamson, whose pinch-hit single had won Game 4, to leave both runners stranded. He then retired the Rays in order in the fifth.
