“I don’t even have words,” Misiorowski said. “I know they’re going crazy in Milwaukee.” Asked about the fans’ support, he added: “Damn it, I’m getting emotional.”

Pratt, the rookie who had collected four hits in Tuesday’s defeat, again supplied an important part of Milwaukee’s offense. Brice Turang doubled in the second inning and, after Frelick was hit by a pitch, scored on Pratt’s single to center. Pratt was caught trying to reach second, but the Brewers had the lead.

Tampa Bay starter Drew Rasmussen, pitching on three days’ rest, kept the deficit at one through four innings before manager Kevin Cash turned to his bullpen.

Milwaukee immediately added another run. Pratt singled off Kevin Kelly, Garrett Mitchell followed with another single and David Hamilton’s ground-ball single to right brought Pratt home for a 2-0 advantage.

The Brewers widened the gap in the sixth. Christian Yelich was hit by a Garrett Cleavinger pitch and scored on William Contreras’s double to left. Turang singled, then stole second after Tyler Wells entered. Following a Frelick strikeout, Pratt lifted a sacrifice fly into foul territory in right, scoring Contreras to make it 4-0.

The Rays threatened with two outs in the ninth. After Liam Hicks doubled and Jonny DeLuca struck out, Chandler Simpson lined an RBI double to right off Megill, cutting Milwaukee’s lead to 4-1 and bringing the potential tying run into the on-deck circle. But Megill induced a groundout from Richie Palacios to seal the title and set off celebrations among Brewers fans everywhere.

The championship capped a season in which Milwaukee posted a major league-best 103-59 record before winning the National League pennant for the first time.

For Pat Murphy, it was the crowning achievement of his third season managing the Brewers. The 67-year-old, previously Craig Counsell’s bench coach, had already won consecutive National League manager of the year awards before guiding Milwaukee to the promised land.

The Brewers established their advantage with three consecutive victories: a narrow win in the opener, a comeback from four runs down in Game 2 and a 10-1 rout in Game 3. Tuesday’s setback delayed their celebration but ultimately did not change the outcome.

Tampa Bay, who won an American League-best 98 games, were left with a third World Series defeat following losses in 2008 and 2020.

The Brewers’ triumph marked the city of Milwaukee’s first World Series championship since 1957, when Lew Burdette’s three complete-game victories powered the Braves past the New York Yankees in a seven-game classic, delivering the city’s first professional sports title. The Braves relocated to Atlanta nine years later.

This year’s Fall Classic guaranteed a first-time champion, only the second such World Series in 107 years and the first World Series since Philadelphia faced Kansas City in 1980. Milwaukee claimed that distinction, leaving the Rays, Colorado Rockies, San Diego Padres and Seattle Mariners as the four active major league franchises still seeking their first title.

Amid the celebrations, Yelich remembered the beloved Brewers broadcaster Bob Uecker, who died last year aged 90. “He’s smiling, man. He’s smiling. I really wish he could have been here to see this,” he said. “This one’s still for Bob and this is still for you.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘Feels like we’ve gone backwards’: Indonesia’s choking haze provides spark for wider protests
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Kate Lamb
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
After two years, President Prabowo Subianto is struggling with economic malaise, policy blunders and a devastating fire season in the world’s third-largest democracy

As almost 2m hectares has gone up in smoke in Indonesia’s worst fire season in a decade, enveloping the region in a thick dystopian haze, 33-year-old university researcher Nurul Amalia has grown increasingly exasperated.

“The government claims to be continuously increasing the number of personnel to extinguish it. But we have yet to see any significant progress,” she says.

“People in Kalimantan continue to report toxic air conditions, and now we hear news of firefighters losing their lives,” she adds, of four volunteers killed fighting fires this month.

On Wednesday, Amalia joined hundreds in Jakarta protesting against the government, the second demonstration in a week. Chief among their demands was that President Prabowo Subianto declare the fires a national disaster.

The demand is just one on a list of grievances amid brewing anger in the world’s third-largest democracy, where analysts say a confluence of policy blunders, economic stress and a government seen as increasingly out of touch is sending Indonesia into a period of volatility unseen for decades.

Civil society groups have criticised the Prabowo presidency for wasteful government programs, increasing militarisation and centralisation of power, deepening patronage, attacks on the press, and what they say is a weakened judiciary.

The government communications agency said in a statement on Wednesday that it welcomed the aspirations of student protesters as part of an effort to nurture democracy, and that concerns raised about the environment, economy and legal reform were being addressed.

Some 70,000 firefighting personnel, it added, had been sent to fire-hit regions, and it was investigating corporations and individuals allegedly involved in starting the fires.

Prabowo marked two years in power this month, but some who voted for him say the country is, at best, stagnating.

“Not only has there been no progress,” says Ika Anastasia, a PR professional and Jakartan mother of three, “it actually feels like we’ve gone backwards.

“In my 32 years, I think this government is probably the worst,” says Aryana, a private-sector employee. “The problems keep coming one after another, and before one is solved, another appears.”

Prabowo, a former military general and the ex-son-in-law of former dictator Suharto, ran in 2024 on a platform of continuity, cuddly vibes and a multibillion-dollar free meals program intended to target malnutrition.

In June this year the head of the national nutrition agency responsible for rolling out the program was arrested on allegations of corruption. Since it began, thousands of schoolchildren have been inadvertently poisoned after eating tainted meals. Among their complaints have been maggots and glass in their rice.

“This current government is strong at agenda setting in public policy, but it is very weak at delivery,” says Yanuar Nugroho, a former presidential staffer for Prabowo’s predecessor and a visiting fellow at Singapore’s ISEAS Yusof Ishak Institute.

“Never have I seen the situation like this,” he adds. “I think this is the worst and the most messy.”

In a statement on Wednesday, the government said it would strengthen supervision and involve local government in implementing the free meals program, with many children, pregnant women and lactating mothers benefiting from it.

But a poll this month by Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting showed that about 62% of Indonesians now oppose it.

The same poll gave Prabowo an approval rating of 44.5%, the lowest of any Indonesian president since polling started 20 years ago.

“It’s just a horrific result. It shows that Prabowo has lost the country,” says Kevin O’Rourke, a longtime Indonesia analyst.

“I think that it’s the programs that he’s put out are failing, and those are things that people see in their communities,” he says, referring to the free meals and a costly village cooperatives program.

This year the Indonesian rupiah sank to record lows against the US dollar, while the country is up to its third finance minister in two years. In recent weeks footage has shown people forming snaking lines for fuel in Bali, Sulawesi and Kalimantan.

And, in what could be a major setback for south-east Asia’s biggest economy, this month global index provider MSCI threatened to downgrade Indonesia to “standalone market” status over unclear share ownership and suspected coordinated trading.

The government pointed out the economy had grown 5.29% in the second quarter of this year and poverty had fallen by 8%, while it had accelerated market reforms to address the issues raised by the MSCI.

Some analysts say the MSCI, which is not a regulator, may have gone too far.

“Our country continues to face all sorts of disturbances, including the MSCI. They are trying to intimidate us,” he told his cabinet. “I simply want to tell MSCI: the Indonesian nation fears no one and will never back down.”

Amid the turbulence, analysts say Prabowo has developed a reputation for being stubborn, and reluctant to accept advice. The government disputed this claim, saying Prabowo holds continuous dialogue with various stakeholders.

“I can sense on the one hand, he is detached from the reality,” observes Yanuar Nugroho. “On the other hand, he has very, very strong ideas of him as like a saviour.”

“There is a lot of uncertainty at the moment and we’ve seen there is a lot of potential for demonstration,” says Kennedy Muslim, an analyst from Indonesian pollster Indikator. “What it needs is a trigger, but that couldn’t be predicted.”

Indonesia is now in a situation unprecedented since its reform era began after Suharto stepped down in 1998, says O’Rourke, noting that in previous administrations there were flaws but more democratic openness, independent institutions and checks and balances.

“In the past, actors always had to respect democracy and the rules of the elections and the rights of opponents in parliament. None of that exists now,” he says.

“Prabowo has a free hand. And so it’s very ugly and very unpredictable, volatile.”

https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.title: Fake film deals and emails from top agents: who is behind the explosion in literary scams?
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.author: Snigdha Poonam
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.text:
Writers are being bombarded daily with invitations from fake book groups and offers to publicise their work. For the scamming industry, aspiring authors can be a soft touch This piece first appeared in the Dial

‘Hello Professor Snigdha Poonam,” the email began. I read that again. Nobody has ever called me “professor” for the obvious reason that I am not a professor. Bracing myself, I read on. The email was from Timothy Firth, organiser of a Seattle-based life-drawing community with 1,943 members that regularly has “thoughtful discussions inspired by creative works”. A recent inspiration was my first book, Dreamers: How Young Indians Are Changing Their World. The group wanted to discuss it, the email said, at one of its upcoming meetups. Attendees would be encouraged to post reviews on Goodreads and Amazon after.

I looked up CAM Life Drawing and found an events page and an Instagram account. The latter had some photos of Timothy Firth – white, male – as well as testimonials from members who said he worked “day and night to create more community space”. Something told me this wasn’t the man who had reached out to me.

Why would a hyperlocal life-drawing community in Seattle be interested in a nonfiction book about the shifting aspirations of young people in India’s small towns? The book was published seven years ago. What did they want from me?

I accepted the invitation. The next email had a slick poster promoting the Zoom event, with the book cover as the backdrop and blurbs from the Economist and other publications. My attention was drawn to something more intriguing: a request for a “contribution fee”, with no amount specified. It would cover promotion, coordination and administration. But, oddly, this email didn’t come from Timothy. Signing off this time was Stephen – “Organiser, Community Improv LA”, which was another group in another city. According to the improv community’s Facebook group, Stephen is indeed the name of the organiser. However, Stephen had written to me using Timothy’s email address. To add to the chaos, Stephen/Timothy had also left what I suspect was an AI prompt in the email, which included the line: “MAKE IT MORE PROFESSIONAL.”

This was undoubtedly a scam. Genuine book clubs don’t ask for money from authors. But who was behind it?

Had these individuals actually read my work, they would have wanted to stay away from me. I have spent the last 10 years reporting on transnational fraud. My first book, Dreamers, closed with a chapter on fake call centres in India; my second, Scamlands, travelled to other low-income countries in Asia to portray an invisible empire that thrives on inequality, technological change and the erosion of trust.

Along the way, I met and interviewed the scammers whose labour keeps this empire running. For some, fraud was a route to upward mobility; for others, an act of revenge against the privileged. Though I have formally emerged from this underworld, I can never delete a scam email without wanting to know more.

I agreed to pay the book club – but after rather than before the event. After clarifying that “Stephen” was a typing error, “Timothy” sent me a Google Meet link for the book discussion. I joined the meeting to find about 20 people already in there: Alexander, Andrew, Mira, Rajnish, another Alexander, and several others. Timothy was also there and so was Stephen. None of them had their cameras on. Going by the profile pictures they used, most of them appeared to be white.

While the questions may have been AI-generated, the voices seemed human. They did not always align with their pictures. Timothy seemed to be a woman, not a man, judging by the voice. Who were these people? They left only one clue. All these ostensibly white people, men and women, spoke with a west African accent.

I am not the only author to have found myself stuck in a Zoom book club with fake readers. Countless writers with published books have been receiving invitations from reading communities that start to unravel after a basic Google search.

As often happens with scams, most invitations sound too good to be true – thousands of members, incredible Goodreads clout and, at times, something even more alluring for an author: a deep understanding of their book.

One author who engaged with a book-club impersonator was told a $100 (£75) contribution for the online event would cover snacks for the participants; she withdrew without asking how they would partake of the snacks while on Zoom. Novelist Marsh Rose, playing along, exchanged 29 emails with the Chicago LGBTQ Book Club. “The individuals whose voices I heard on the Zoom didn’t seem to be speaking from Chicago. They all sounded like my friend in Nigeria,” she wrote in a blog post for WritersWeekly.com, an online resource for authors that offers writing opportunities and industry news.

Writers are also being bombarded with offers to publish our next book, market our book, handle social media for us, represent us as agents and get us book-to-movie deals with Netflix and Paramount. Every major publisher, agent, editor, author union and literary award executive is at risk of being impersonated.

The money requested often seems small. “Amounts reported to me range from $55 to $350. In one case, the scammer offered three ‘spotlight packages’ – basic, essential and premium – for between $100 and $200,” Victoria Strauss, co-founder of Writer Beware, an anti-scam watchdog, wrote in a blog post. Often, the paper trail leads to Nigerian third parties holding bank accounts in the US. Author Jon Cocks paid $478.65 to one “Mary Brown,” who claimed a wide network of book clubs across the US, the UK and Australia, only to later notice the name Dayo Oguntuase listed as the recipient on the PayPal statement.

The Writers’ Guild of Great Britain (WGGB) reports “an explosion” in the number of members seeking advice about unusually enticing offers in recent months. “Even the most vigilant of writers are understandably falling prey to these scams,” WGGB’s general secretary, Ellie Piers, said in a statement commenting on new guidance, co-issued with the Society of Authors in May, to help authors protect themselves against scammers. “Our advisory team receives at least a dozen reports of scams each week,” Anna Ganley, chief executive of the Society of Authors, said in her own statement, tracing the spike to the emergence of generative AI. The US Authors Guild says it hears from authors who have been scammed, or nearly scammed, every day. Angela Hoy, the founder of WritersWeekly.com, told me she is in touch with “authors all day long, every day, thinking they got an offer from one of the top five publishers in New York or thinking they’ve been contacted by a famous literary agent”.

A prominent trendsetter was the PageTurner scam, named after a fictitious US-registered publishing company that operated between 2017 and 2024. Call centre staff in Cebu, the Philippines, claimed PageTurner was an intermediary between authors and literary agents, film studios and streaming services and persuaded authors to pay so-called taxes, transaction fees and other costs before their books could be published or adapted.

The scale of the operation became clear after US authorities launched an investigation into the business. According to the Department of Justice, more than 800 authors were defrauded of upwards of $48m (£36m). Writer Beware received hundreds of complaints about PageTurner. One author reportedly lost more than $600,000 (£450,000). The prosecutors found that at least $42m in proceeds were laundered through accounts in the Philippines. One defendant pleaded guilty in May of this year, while three others are awaiting trial.

Judging by the surge in both the number and range of baits used on authors over the past couple of years, the scams seem to be launched from multiple territories. Anyone who has researched publishing would know most authors don’t have bundles of cash lying around. So why are the scammers coming after us?

Hoy, who has dealt with thousands of writers at WritersWeekly.com, puts it down to ego. Brian Whiddon, the site’s managing editor, elaborated: “Not every author is a narcissist, but they all want to be recognised. That’s exactly what these scammers are targeting. They have identified a very, very lucrative niche.”

Writers are waiting “for somebody to read their writing”, Hoy added. She argued that is why many writers believe the praise scammers heap on them. AI makes many of the compliments sound nuanced and personalised. Elderly authors are particularly vulnerable. As Hoy explained, a significant number of people who have a book in them leave off the writing until they have retired. Something else also kicks into the picture at this life stage: a sizable retirement fund. Scammers know American people have worked their whole lives and have retirement accounts, Hoy said.

Some authors are so hell-bent on signing up for the deals the scammers promise that they disregard Hoy’s counsel. Others come to Hoy when it’s too late. She has said one of the writers in her community paid more than $100,000 for a fake book-to-movie deal.

“I’ve actually used some of the verbiage from these emails talking about how fantastic my book is in my advertising,” author Donna Strong commented in the Goodreads discussion forum Readers Group Scams.

Even as a new category of literary scams emerges every few days, authors have very little information about the people behind them.

In August, Danny de Hek, a New Zealand-based scam buster, forwarded me an Excel spreadsheet he received from a scammer in Karachi, Pakistan, with permission from the sender. Titled “LinkedIn Outreach 2026”, it has monthly data on targeted authors from March until August. One sheet has 403 names, each neatly labelled: new author, cookbook author, religious author, investigative author, poetry author, New York Times bestselling author and so on. Most are based in the US; the rest are in Canada, Australia or Europe.

It’s an incredibly detailed document, with columns for the name of the person who found the profile, the person who first reached out, the service the author needs (website development, illustrator, social media visibility), the department handling the author, meeting links shared with the author. In a few cases, the document also lists the outcome of the outreach.

“Meeting booked Wed 12 Aug, 10pm PKT, number confirmed, deep trust-built relationship, ready to invest, needs custom package built around limited budget and multi-project scope.”

Some of the details only make sense if you know the context. 10pm PKT would mean 10am on the US west coast and 1pm in the east. Danny told me that most of the people working on this scam are Pakistani, yet the names of the callers are all American-sounding – Ashley, Jocelyn, Megan – probably to fool the authors into thinking they are Americans working for US-based companies and groups.

Scam recipients often find the emails they receive haphazard and random. But the modern scam industry is a highly organised system modelled on the global corporate setup, with clearly laid out deliverables, salaries, incentives and reporting structures. Even though the schemes are mind-boggling in range, the young people joining these “companies” are given the same targets: Americans on top, followed by gullible foreigners in other western countries. I spent several years reporting from India on its massive scam call-centre network, which employs hundreds of thousands of educated young people trying to beat the dim economic prospects offered by the domestic labour market. Similar Excel spreadsheets are used to organise schemes where Indian scammers in Delhi or Kolkata impersonate Microsoft tech support, the Internal Revenue Service or even the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

De Hek, who exposes transnational scams on his blog and YouTube channel with relentless zeal, told me Pakistan’s fake companies offering literary services operate in a similar fashion to India’s scam call centres. The majority of them maintain physical offices in Karachi and Lahore and employ people aged 20 to 24. Upon joining, the young employees typically get assigned to a unit, each designed around a specific literary swindle. While entry-level employees may only be tasked with outreach, the more experienced ones are entrusted with building long-term relationships aimed at selling multiple “packages” to clients over months and sometimes years.

The most profitable service targets authors lurking outside the notoriously gatekept realm of traditional publishing. Rather than through a cold call or email, the scammers lure them through websites offering self-publishing or vanity publishing.

Scam companies in Pakistan trap writers by impersonating known publishing houses and paying thousands of dollars to influence search results on Google. As a result, someone with a finished manuscript who searches online may find sites such as penguinwriters.com or amazonglobalpublishers.com before any legitimate self-publishing platform. Unlike traditional publishing websites, these feature open calls for new writers. WritersWeekly.com estimates there are at least 3,000 such sites. The biggest tell: a chat box pops up in the bottom right of all fake publishing websites as soon as the page opens, followed by a message from someone with an American-sounding name (such as Mark Anderson or Jessica Parker) and a white person’s face: “How can I help you today?” “Talk to a live agent, not a bot!” claims a ticker. And that much is absolutely true: the person messaging you is a scammer whose shift is dictated by the waking hours in your time zone.

None of the five major trade publishers has sued alleged impersonators. The only recorded instance involves Amazon, which took nearly 20 individuals and associated companies to court in California for falsely claiming affiliation with Amazon Publishing and Kindle Direct Publishing to deceive authors. Amazon won $36.4m (£27m) in February 2025.

M L Stark, a Danish self-published author of several psychological thrillers, is one of the rare victims who has met – and confronted – her scammer in person. Last year, she flew to Thailand to meet with Ethan Williams, a man she believed had become her longtime editor at an LA-based self-publishing house affiliated with Amazon – and a close friend. By this time, she had been talking to him over Zoom and email for more than a year and paid his company about $100,000 for different author services, from editing and cover design to coverage in the New York Times and the Los Angeles Times.

While most of the services she paid for never materialised, the company did follow through on some. They signed her up on IngramSpark, a self-publishing platform, which enabled her to release two books, and Amazon, which made the books available on the platform. Most notably, in 2024, one of her titles was displayed on a digital billboard in Times Square.

“I had paid $10,000 for that,” she told me. Only later, she told me, did she come to see these deliveries as strategic concessions, held back for moments when a long-term client reached the end of her tether. “Each time, it happened when I told them, after months of them stalling, that I wanted my money back.”

The scammers’ last pitch was a Netflix adaptation that they claimed the film-makers wanted to shoot in Thailand – an important setting in her upcoming book, a thriller based on her own life. Stark and Williams were meeting in Thailand to scout locations.

He had told her he was a British citizen, half English and half Arab; as a light-skinned Pakistani, his story was plausible. “He is an artist, he knew how to play the role,” she said. Still, she asked him to show an ID. He produced one that looked clearly faked. “I demanded he show me his passport,” she said. That exposed his real name and citizenship. He came clean. “He said, ‘Yeah, this has been a scam from the beginning. Even Peter is using a fake name; even Ronald is using a fake name. Everybody in the company that you have talked to is a scammer. It’s a huge scam operation, and we are not based in Los Angeles. We are based in Karachi.’” She is still processing her shock.

I clicked on a random website from a list of known scam sites; it happened to be impersonating Red Rock, a real literary agency based in London whose authors have been published by major publishers such as Hurst, which published my first book in the UK. Bold promises greeted me on the homepage.

A chat window opened, and someone with the username “Rae Donnaelly” asked how she could help. I told her I had an idea for a book. She asked for my contact, then called me on WhatsApp from a US number. She spoke like a South Asian imitating an American accent, something I could easily recognise because I’m South Asian myself, and we’ve all tried it at one point or another.

I told her the truth: I was writing an article about author-baiting scams, and I was hoping she could tell me about her experience working for a fake publishing house.

She told me she wasn’t “authorised” to talk about the company she works for, and she refused to tell me her real name. But she had no qualms spilling the beans on her ex-employer.

Rae has a law degree but found it difficult to find a job in law after university. Her first job after graduating was at a fake publishing company in Karachi. “I started working for a company which was a scam – a guaranteed scam – and I didn’t know it when I started off with them. I was an intern trying to learn how the system really works; what the pros and cons are.”

It took Rae only a few days to figure out the company’s business model: proxy sales. They would tell the author they would get them a guaranteed sale order for 1,000 copies, or something like that, making “fake commitments”. The scam rarely stopped there. After a client signed up for developmental editing, they would be offered a discount on book-cover design, and once they paid for that, the scammer would dangle social media management. “It could start off from as little as $400- $500, and it could go up to the skies, like $10,000, $15,000.”

As with all scams, those executing the con learned how easily people can be manipulated if you know what they desired. “You could see how the human brain works. It’s actually scary when you think about it,” Rae admitted.

She believes Americans make easy scam targets. “People in the US are very nice, they’re very good-hearted people. They trust you. Whatever you’re saying, they trust you. That’s the problem.”

At times, the clients only noticed they had been scammed after they had paid all the way up to a Times Square display and Broadway adaptation. “When the authors did not see results, they would either reverse the charge on their card or accuse us of being scamsters,” Rae recalled.

According to Talal Choudhary, an Islamabad-based tech journalist, there are about 1,000 Pakistani companies running scam sites. “One company runs as many as 25 websites. I personally know a company that had about 200 employees, just offering services to writers.” These companies are “very, very profitable”, he said. “From one client, you can make $60,000.”

In Pakistan, Choudhary told me, the workforce of the author-baiting scams is largely made up of high-school and university graduates. They earn an average salary of about 50,000 Pakistani rupees (£136) a month. For high performers, there is commission. For every sale worth $1,000, they might get a 10-20% commission, he said, upselling until the author backs out.

According to Rae, any guilt the scammers felt was cancelled out by the increasingly skewed conversion rate between the American dollar and Pakistani rupee. “Generally, the mentality was: when you’re making income in dollars, you have a stable life, you have sustainability. So that’s what they did. They just ripped people off.”

I have heard multiple versions of this statement since I first reported on the rise of organised transnational fraud. Earlier this year, Hoy received a message on Facebook from a Nigerian man who offered to market her latest novel. Convinced he was part of the suspected author-scam network, she made him an offer of her own: write an article for Writersweekly.com about how the company he worked for scams Americans while being based overseas.

But he wrote it using AI, which is against the site’s submission rules. He also ignored the brief. Instead, he chose to highlight, as Hoy recalls, “how it’s so hard for people in Africa and therefore it’s OK to scam Americans because all of us are rich over here”.

Salil Mahmood, who asked that I change his name, is another self-described ex-scammer from Karachi. He reached out to me after hearing from Danny de Hek about the article I was writing. Compared with some of the more outrageous deals his seniors offered their clients, his job, as an entry-level recruit, was low-key. He cold-emailed published authors with a proposal to create their official pages on Wikipedia and have those approved. However, many of the pages he created – largely based on information provided by the authors – failed verification because the citations he supplied were fabricated. “The pages would remain active for a while and then disappear.” The authors never got their money back.

While he only worked there for a few months, he said the setup was highly aspirational for those who wanted to make serious money. “The bosses would show us pictures of their lifestyles: mansions, fast cars, parties and lots of alcohol. If you met your targets, they would have a rented car drive you around.” But in keeping with the nature of such enterprises, failure was not an option. “If an employee did not meet the target, they and their families were threatened with violence,” he said.

Rae left the company she had been working for after a disagreement with her manager less than a year into the job. But rather than go back on the job market, she and a few friends started a new company that, as she described, provides American authors with tailored services.

She insisted her company did not defraud its clients. I could have asked her why, if it was a genuine publishing house in Pakistan, it gave clients the impression that it was based in the US; why the website featured books it had not published; or why the individuals who popped up in the chat boxes used fake, American-sounding names, including her. But I left it at that. I could sense she wanted me to believe she had nothing to do with the scammers. She even pointed out that her religion does not allow her to earn money from fraud.

“You can look out for us at the next Frankfurt book fair,” she said. I told her I would.

I still get emails from Timothy Firth – the impersonator – reminding me to send my voluntary contribution in gratitude for the book club discussion. The person writing to me as Timothy probably knows it is not coming. I have a feeling the scammers know I am on to them because of how the meeting ended. After running through all the questions they had prepared, the moderator asked if I had any final comments.

I asked if any of them had thoughts to share about the last chapter in my book. Reported from fake call centres in Delhi, I explained, it is the story of ambitious young people being drawn into an underworld of scams and fraud.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: How did a fishmonger who starred in an adult movie make Rocky? The film about Sylvester Stallone’s amazing triumph
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Gwilym Mumford
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
Belittled for his speech and looks, and so short of cash he had to sell his dog, Stallone managed to write and star in one of the greatest boxing movies ever. How does Anthony Ippolito feel about playing his hero?

Fifty years ago this December, cinema’s greatest underdog story hit the screen, a tale about a Philadelphia ham-and-egger who takes the world heavyweight boxing champ all the way to the final bell, losing the fight on a judge’s decision but winning the hearts of a nation. That film, of course, was Rocky. Its creation, famously, was no less remarkable an underdog story – one about an out-of-work character actor with the curious name of Sylvester Stallone who wrote his own boxing movie then managed to convince a studio not only to finance it, but also to cast him in the title role. He then went one further than the character he was playing by earning the top prize: a best picture Oscar.

If you thought, half a century on, Rocky’s punching power – its unerring ability to make heroes out of zeroes – has faded, think again. This, after all, is a movie franchise whose stirring qualities are enough to make thousands of people hurtle up all 72 of the Philadelphia Museum of Art’s steps every year in homage to its plucky pugilist.

And now Rocky has birthed a third great underdog story. This one is about a 27-year-old New Yorker who, through grit, persistence and a never-ending stream of unsolicited audition tapes, bags the role of a lifetime and propels himself into the Oscar running, alongside the likes of Tom Cruise, Matt Damon and John Malkovich. His name is Anthony Ippolito and he’s playing Sly Stallone himself in Peter Farrelly’s rousing, making-of movie I Play Rocky.

The role, which follows Stallone from his early struggles in New York to movie greatness in LA, is one Ippolito has been circling – like Ali or Tyson rounding their prey – for years, before the project even had a script. Such was his desperation to play Stallone, he started sending in self-taped performances of what he thought those making the film might be after, an experience that felt like “sending your work into the abyss – even more so when no one’s asking for your audition in the first place”.

It’s a process, Ippolito remembers with a wry smile, that could feel “a little discouraging”, particularly when film websites were tipping big names for the role – Superman David Corenswet, Jacob Elordi, even Timothée Chalamet. Ippolito recalls: “People around me said, ‘Don’t get your hopes up, they’re probably looking at bigger names. That’s Hollywood.’”

He would not be deterred, though, and his self-confidence was justified: according to Farrelly, Ippolito was the first person he and the film’s producers looked at for the part. And once they saw him there was no point in auditioning anyone else.

Speaking to Ippolito by video call from a hotel room in Rome, it’s not easy to discern immediately what made those producers so convinced of his Sly-ness. Granted, he doesn’t look dissimilar to Rocky-era Stallone – the square jaw and mop of dark hair are present and correct – but his features are softer, more boyband, and his voice is noticeably higher than Stallone’s bassy drawl. You’d be more likely to compare him to a young Al Pacino – fitting, as Ippolito played Pacino in another making-of project, The Offer, a TV series about the protracted creation of The Godfather.

Yet the moment the opening credits of I Play Rocky roll, a remarkable transformation occurs. Ippolito’s voice drops an octave, and he affects that stuffy sinus-heavy delivery of Stallone’s. His eyes droop, his chin juts, his shoulders seem to grow rounder and he starts to move in that loping shuffle. He looks broader and more imposing, too – the result, Ippolito says, of a bulking-up regime that involved “a lot of eating, a lot of protein … it required an entire lifestyle shift”.

It’s a performance that could so easily lapse into lazy caricature – or even worse, punching down, given that Stallone’s drooping features and slurred speech are the result of forceps injury at birth. But Ippolito is so note perfect that even Stallone has been in touch to offer his approval. “He had a positive reaction and I’m very grateful – because this is, in a lot of ways, a love letter to what he persevered through.”

The film, Ippolito says, covers a “very dark, lonely time” in Stallone’s life, when he worked in a fishmonger’s and appeared in an adult movie to scrape together rent. What serious roles he did get tended to be bit parts as tough guys, cops or thugs. He was routinely belittled for his speech and looks – particularly by his domineering father, played by Matt Dillon in the film. But Stallone had a remarkable raw talent hidden under the surface. “There’s this incongruence,” Ippolito says. “People would mistake him for being, um, maybe not smart – just a strong, burly guy with this slur. And then he’s actually a brilliant writer. Burt Young [his Rocky co-star] called him ‘an orphan in life’ with ‘a big fire burning and no place to put it’. You can feel this great depth and intensity.”

I Play Rocky doesn’t seem terribly preoccupied with these roiling internal dynamics – though that isn’t to its detriment. It’s not hard to see why crowds have chimed with the film, which turns Stallone’s story into part inspirational sports movie, part comedy caper. Farrelly has great fun in depicting the scrappy, seat-of-its-pants production of the original film, which couldn’t go a day over for risk of its studio shutting the whole thing down: scenes are rattled off in single, frenzied takes; Stallone limps through filming with a strained leg tendon, then a broken hand from punching a frozen side of beef in the film’s famous meat-locker scene; at one point, cast and crew have to squeeze into a walk-in freezer with their equipment to hide from a union rep threatening to take their filming permit away.

The most entertaining section, though, comes before Rocky has even been greenlit, when the film’s producers are trying desperately to convince Stallone to give up the title role in return for a life-changing sum of money. No matter how many zeroes are added, Sly stands firm: no starring role, no deal. This despite him having few career prospects and a heavily pregnant wife. It’s a remarkable act of brinkmanship – at one point, Stallone is forced to sell his own dog to make ends meet – but it proves successful.

Stallone turned down $300,000, the equivalent of almost $2m today. Would Ippolito have gone to such extremes? “I don’t know, it’s a lot of money,” he laughs “I don’t want to make myself sound spineless! But it’s certainly tempting. I guess that’s what makes it so incredible, maddening almost. I think there’s a certain naive quality. Like he was able to just, at a young age, almost not know the rules so he could break them.”

In another life, rather than playing an actor playing a boxer, Ippolito might have been a baseball player. At three years old, he was a pitching prodigy able to throw a ball at “40 miles per hour or something”, a talent that led him to appear on an episode of Ripley’s Believe it or Not!. For much of his childhood, playing baseball professionally was “the main goal”, and he carried on at a high level at college. “I learned a lot about acting inadvertently,” he says, “because there’s a ton of failure in that sport.”

By his late teens, he had started to take acting seriously. He began picking up walk-on parts in films: David Chase’s coming of age movie Not Fade Away, where he got to watch James Gandolfini from afar; Julianne Moore comedy-drama The English Teacher; and Adam Sandler vehicle Pixels, where he first understood the appeal of doing this thing full-time. “I was like, ‘Wow, these guys look like they’re really having fun at work.’ That stuck out.”

After college, his career moved up a gear: there was a main role in edgy Netflix high-school drama Grand Army, then his appearance as Pacino in The Offer. How does it feel to play not one but two of the most famous actors alive? “It’ll throw you, for sure. But it’s also an incredible opportunity to explore stuff. There’s almost a voyeuristic quality to it – like an infinity staircase.”

Now, with the success of I Play Rocky, Ippolito is finding himself among the big names, rather than impersonating them. He recently met Andrew Garfield and “is still recovering”. More encounters will surely come in awards season: his Stallone performance is being talked up for a best actor nomination, which would put him up against “people I’ve looked up to for the last 20 years”. Don’t count Anthony Ippolito out yet.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: The rise and fall of mid-century modern: how millennials fell out of love with their favourite look
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Sarah Phillips
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Once coveted for its clean lines and timeless design, the functional furniture is no longer seen as cool. Anyone for cottagecore and chrome?

“I definitely don’t think it is cringe,” says Laura Budds, a vintage furniture dealer based in Norfolk. “But I do think we have reached the peak, and we’re on the descent.” Budds is talking about mid-century modern furniture, which has recently come under fire from younger generations for being – like so many things, including trainer socks and high-waisted jeans – a deeply millennial aesthetic. As the Wall Street Journal declared: “Midcentury modern design has met the fate of pumpkin spice lattes, cocktails in mason jars, no-show socks, leggings and other aspects of millennial culture: it has become cringey.”

Budds, 44, is resigned to the fact that she is a “mid-century millennial”. She’s even made a career out of it: she sells furniture and vintage clothes at Williams & Parfitt, a modern antiques centre in Wymondham, Norfolk. But she says she has had to diversify in recent years to cater to changing tastes among younger customers, who are moving away from the “wall-to-wall mid-century” look beloved by the generation above them. She says of gen Z: “I don’t think they are so bound by the eras or designers – they just buy what they like. They aren’t afraid of older antiques and will have a bit of whimsy or taxidermy.”

The term “mid-century modern” was originally coined to refer to architecture and design that became popular from the 1940s to the 1970s, largely in the US, Brazil and Europe. Famed for its clean lines and simplicity, the style had visual forebears in the Bauhaus movement and classic Scandinavian design, along with the philosophy of beautiful yet functional furniture for the masses that spread to the US, UK and beyond in the postwar era. British-made items include Ercol and Robin Day chairs and G Plan teak sideboards, all of which are still coveted. (Anglepoise’s timeless industrial lighting, too, was associated with the aesthetic.)

The book Mid-Century Modern: Furniture of the 1950s, written by Cara Greenberg and published in 1984, is often seen as being responsible for popularising the phrase. Today, she says, the term has “become meaningless, applied to everything from museum-quality material to made-in-China repros on eBay”.

Greenberg lives in Brooklyn, New York. Her first mid-century purchase was an Eames plywood lounge chair bought at a street market in NYC in the 1970s, which she still owns. These days, she is more interested in a comfy sofa: “not a mid-century modern speciality”, she says, given the aesthetic’s tendency for furniture to be fairly upright and firm, often designed with polite conversation in mind rather than slouching and scrolling.

But, Greenberg says, she will still defend the best of it “as the most innovative and stylish furniture America ever came up with”: Charles and Ray Eames, the husband and wife duo who revolutionised design with multipurpose chairs; George Nelson’s industrial looks for the furniture company Herman Miller; Eero Saarinen’s Tulip chair for Knoll. Since then, she says, “there have been many cycles of revival, including the reissue and mass marketing of ‘best of’ classics by the original companies in the 1990s”.

Affordability has always been a cornerstone of mid-century design. “The philosophy of modernism and mid-century design, when it first started, was accessibility,” says Keith Stephenson, who lives in Camberwell, south-east London with his partner, Mark Hampshire. Together they run the design and homewares company Mini Moderns and co-authored the 2019 book Mid-Century Modern Living: The Mini Moderns Guide to Pattern and Style. “It was never supposed to be an elitist thing,” he says. “It was about bringing good design at a good price to as many people as possible. Reaching more people with good design is never a bad thing.”

It is also ideal for smaller spaces, which is one of the reasons Hampshire thinks it has “endured many a cycle of trends” to become “the endlessly go-to period of design”. The postwar period was “the first time that designers considered function and aesthetics together – so furniture was designed to solve a specific problem as well as to fulfil a function. The results of this level of considered design have, in many cases, proved hard to beat, thus becoming the template for subsequent designs.”

He gives an example: “If you look at a classic mid-century style sofa, it is on legs, so you can see the floor underneath it – and that makes a place feel much bigger, because you can read the room around the piece of furniture. There’s room to breathe. All of those things are classic interior design tricks to make a place look and feel more spacious.”

Mid-century modern’s design quality and price point made it irresistible to millennials who were starting to live independently in the 2010s. It fitted with the vintage aesthetic of the time and there were still bargains to be found. Even as late as 2019, says Budd, “you could find sideboards at auction for £50. Now you’re lucky to get one for less than £300-£400.” A lot of British mid-century modern has been shipped abroad in recent years, to Europe and as far as Japan, where consumers have cottoned on to British brands such as Ercol, G Plan and McIntosh. This has pushed prices up and “made it a bit too elitist. Only certain people can afford the really good quality stuff now,” says Budd.

The interior designer Natasha Landers has lived in her home in Walthamstow, east London, for 26 years. Her mid-century bookcase cost £30 when she bought it, and her £50 coffee table would now sell for £200. “It’s not as accessible as it was when I first started collecting,” she says. Still, she’s reluctant to write off the whole aesthetic just because it has been widely used. “Good design doesn’t have to become bad design because it is popular,” says Landers. “There is something slightly snobbish about deciding something is no longer cool simply because more people can enjoy it. What I do have a problem with is when everyone’s houses look the same.”

The proliferation of millennial style on the go-to interior design sources Pinterest and Instagram has inevitably meant that the high street and large webstores have capitalised on the trend. New furniture clearly inspired by classic mid-century modern pieces can now be found everywhere from Marks & Spencer and Dunelm to H&M and Temu.

“That craze for buying a full set of mid-century tables, sofas and lighting is definitely gone,” says Carina Harford, an interior designer from west London. “It had a paint-by-numbers experience to it that might have felt safe to its devotees but began to feel too commonplace.” The climate impact of “fast furniture” is also a consideration. “The imitation mid-century furniture that was coming out a lot in the last five or so years really irked me,” says Harford. “Stop buying new things if you don’t need them.”

It is this desire to avoid having identikit homes that is fuelling the mid-century modern cringe. “I really don’t want to have the same things as everyone else,” says Sheree Millington, a copywriter based in Margate, who is renovating her Victorian terrace. Lucy Hayes, a writer and director in east London, agrees. “I like a mix of styles and ages, and things that don’t feel rooted to a particular decade or era. I want my home to feel like it exists now rather than as a time capsule.”

Millington thinks a more quintessentially English style is coming back in, “whether that is cottagecore, or more like an English townhouse, with lots of mismatched things, more pattern, more print”. She is noticing chrome – a staple of 1990s homeware that has since fallen out of favour – becoming more popular again, too.

Harford’s home is kitted out with secondhand treasures spanning many different eras and styles: “It’s all just sort of mushed together, and I think it works.” Most of it was bought from auctions and cost about £100 or less. Highlights include a Victorian fold-out card table (bought for £110), lighting from a shuttered billiards hall (£40), a 1940s Anglo-Indian table (£30) and a set of 1980s stools (£90 for four). Although bidding can seem more complicated than buying new online for next day delivery, you quickly get the hang of it, she says, and the result is, “something much more special and unique”.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: I set up a free school for Afghan girls – and the Taliban blindfolded me and broke my nose and jaw
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Sonia Lambert
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
When Basir Arian was summoned to the Taliban headquarters, he knew he had to go. To defy them meant death. The torture left him devastated and sure he had to leave the country

‘I knew that sooner or later, they would come for me,” says Basir Arian. After the Taliban regained control of Afghanistan in August 2021, he had set up an online English study programme for girls when they were banned from attending school. In May 2022, he was eating lunch in the western city of Herat, when he got a call from an unfamiliar local number. A Talib official told Arian to come to the intelligence directorate within 20 minutes and to bring his phone.

“I’ll never forget that moment,” he says. “If you disobey this order, they will kill you. You have to try not to make them angry.” He told a friend where he was going, and they hurriedly discussed what to do if he didn’t return.

Taliban fighters searched him at the gate. Inside, there was a huge courtyard with military vehicles. Armed Taliban with long beards and dusty slippers were everywhere; even the men sitting behind desks had guns. Arian tried to stay calm. He finds it very hard to talk about this part, but wants people to know what happened.

He was told to sit in a hallway, where he was left waiting for a few hours. Then a tall, bald young Talib called him into an office. Here, a senior official played a WhatsApp voice message in which Arian encouraged some of the students not to lose hope, to motivate them. He accused Arian of working with infidels, being a puppet of the west and “an apostate”. He insulted his appearance. Then he spoke to the tall Talib, saying: “Let’s teach him.”

The tall young man blindfolded Arian and led him through a long hallway, down about two floors and into a basement room. He tied Arian’s hands. Arian could hear that two or three others were there. They spoke in Pashto: “His excellency says we must teach him a lesson.” They called him “an infidel”, and “a dog”. Something hard struck his nose and jaw – he realised it was the butt of a rifle – and he was kicked until he lost consciousness.

He came to, lying in a lot of blood. One of his fingers was broken, his upper body was beaten and his nose and jaw were badly injured. He asked to have his blindfold removed and his hands untied, which a different man did. He was in a small and very dirty cell.

Arian was born in 1997, in rural Afghanistan, near the border with Iran, into a community already broken by the Soviet invasion in 1979 and the civil war that erupted after it left in 1989. His father – a tailor – had a talent for maths, but only had a few years of primary education and wanted something better for his son. “My dreams began because of my father’s belief in me,” says Arian.

He remembers the excitement of walking with his cousins to the village’s first school, on the day it opened in 2003. There were no buildings, just tents, which – like the books, pencils, even the biscuits they were given at break – were all provided by the United Nations Children’s Fund.

There were landmines buried for miles across this dry, sandy region. The wind carried dust – some days, they could barely see a metre in front of their faces. Every few weeks a schoolmate gathering firewood or a mother fetching water would step on a mine and lose a leg or an arm, or sometimes, says Arian: “There was nothing left to save.”

There was not enough rainfall to grow much, although people kept trying. When he was about 10, for the first time, Arian saw a rose that someone had brought from the city. Drinking water came from a spring, and Arian walked for miles with his father and their donkey to fetch it. Once, they saw the distant shape of an aeroplane in the sky, and Arian’s father pointed upwards and said to his young son: “One day, you’ll travel in one of those.”

His family were poor but, unusually, their home had books, which Arian’s father ordered from Iran or brought from the city. Arian read Robinson Crusoe and The Little Prince, and his father introduced him to classical Persian poetry. He passed every exam with top marks, but people laughed at his father’s belief in education, and thought it unrealistic. By the time he was 15, Arian was the only student left in his class.

In 2012, he left his village to continue his schooling in Herat. His new classroom had walls, desks and chairs, and better trained teachers, but he worried about being teased for his country accent. Two years later, he was the first person from his area to be admitted to the engineering faculty at Herat University. “My parents were overjoyed,” he says. The family moved so that his siblings and cousins could keep studying as well.

When he started university, Arian was skinny and fragile, and he began going to the gym. “The gym was my therapy,” he says. He read hungrily, to try to understand the situation in his country. He noticed newer versions of “political Islam”, which were “hostile towards women”. He went to poetry readings, took part in debates and spoke on local television about social issues, corruption and human rights. He became well known locally, and started to get threats from various religious groups. “I was not alone,” he says, but “part of a network of brave men and women.”

In 2017, he graduated and was keen to help rebuild the country. The following year, he was in a taxi in Kabul, looking for work, when a suicide bomber exploded his device 100 metres away. The blast wave caused a cloud of dust, smoke and body parts to hit the car windows and the smell was terrible. Arian’s ears were ringing as the taxi driver reversed away from the explosion. He was deeply shocked and it dawned on him how very hard it was to respond with logic to that sort of violence. “All of a sudden, you can be wiped out,” he says.

In 2019, Arian was elected as a youth representative to the Loya Jirga, a traditional assembly of political, community and religious leaders called upon at critical points in Afghanistan’s history to debate issues of national importance. Here, he saw the division and mistrust between urban professionals with smartphones and men from remote rural areas with very traditional dress and beliefs. By the time he took part in a second Loya Jirga in 2020, the country was on the verge of collapse. The US had withdrawn most of its troops: Arian says he could guess “the end of this story”.

More people were coming to the city, displaced by fighting and the climate crisis, and Arian decided to study for a master’s in urban planning over the border in Iran. He was home on a visit in August 2021, when Afghanistan finally fell to the Taliban. Arian felt that the world had abandoned them. It was like watching a building collapse, he says, or “like an emotional breakdown”. His mother cried a lot, because she had lived through the first Taliban era (which had ended in 2001, after the US invasion). Arian and his friends stayed awake all night, in shock, exchanging messages and going through their social media accounts, hiding content that put them at risk.

Women stopped being seen in public. The city was flooded with Taliban fighters, roaring around on motorbikes or crammed into military vehicles they had captured, celebrating with flags and songs. It was surreal and frightening: many had never been to a city before, and wanted to try ice-cream and pizza, but Arian knew they could kill without hesitation. His friends exchanged hushed news of raids, revenge killings and disappearances.

Arian’s sister was in secondary school. A few weeks later, the driver of the vehicle that normally collected her from the end of the road said that girls were no longer allowed. Arian saw her standing in her uniform with her schoolbag, crying. She wanted to become a doctor.

Something inside him “exploded” and he decided to act. He made contact on LinkedIn with an American teacher and film-maker, and they came up with a plan for a free online English school. Arian registered hundreds of Afghan girls as students, and the American teacher recruited 23 volunteer English-language teachers from around the world. Some classes were held in the middle of the night, because of the different time zones.

In May 2022, Arian had to return to Afghanistan to renew his visa. It was during this visit that he received the call from the Talib official to come to the intelligence directorate. After he awoke in the cell, he was given bread and water, and was told he could pray. He objected, saying that in Islam it is forbidden to pray with blood on your clothes. He couldn’t sleep, thinking about his mother, suffering from his injuries, and worrying that his face would be disfigured. Before dawn, he was taken to a washroom and again told to pray, which he did. When he touched his face, it was in spasm.

In the morning, he was once again blindfolded, and taken back up to the same office as before, where he was forced to sign a statement saying that he was sorry, and warned not to talk about it, or he would be killed. He got his phone, was released, and took a tuk-tuk to the hospital.

An X-ray showed that his nose was broken in four places and his jaw was broken. The doctor had to wait a few weeks for Arian’s face to heal a little before he could operate on his jaw. After that, he had surgery on his nose, before returning to Iran as soon as he could.

He didn’t want “to let the girls down”, so he tried to keep the online classes going with the help of a volunteer, but stopped any new recruitment. His face healed, but he was “mentally devastated”, and struggled to recover. “It was just not fair. I couldn’t forgive them,” he says. After about a month, he was able to return to the gym, which helped him unwind. He finished his dissertation and graduated.

He wasn’t allowed to work in Iran and was on the verge of homelessness when he applied for a Chevening scholarship – a prestigious, fully funded chance to study for a one-year master’s degree in the UK. It was a long, complex and competitive process, followed by a two-hour visa interview. Against the odds, he won a place to study international development at the Institute of Development Studies based at the University of Sussex. He flew from Tehran in September 2024. As the plane descended towards Gatwick, he thought of his father’s prediction, years before. He was worried he might be stopped, but the woman at passport control smiled and said: “Welcome to the UK!”

His new life was not easy. Some international students on his course were hostile and made racist comments about Afghans. “I did not expect the sense of isolation I sometimes felt,” he says. Arian gave an interview on BBC Persian criticising the Taliban’s policies. When the course ended, most other students flew home, happy and proud, with gifts for their families. Arian had nowhere to go. Returning, especially after the BBC interview, could mean death. Applying for asylum was not something he chose freely, he says, but was “a decision that reality forced upon me”.

He arrived at the Home Office in Croydon with only a few pounds left. They asked lots of questions and told him to call a helpline and ask for urgent accommodation. He phoned again and again, but, he says: “They just said someone will call you, send this or that document.” He was homeless for six days, spending the nights in a park, and the days in Starbucks, where he charged his phone.

Then he was told to go to Croydon police station, where a taxi picked him up. Two women, one from China, the other from Hong Kong, were already in it. The driver told them they were heading for Liverpool. The only thing Arian knew about Liverpool was the football team.

He was taken to an asylum hotel, arriving late at night. The staff were kind, but it felt “like being in detention”. Everyone was traumatised and depressed. There was not enough food, and what was available was terrible quality – Arian lost weight, couldn’t sleep and felt very low. There were other Afghans “all fleeing from torture by the Taliban”, some because of their beliefs or ethnicity, some because they had served in the previous regime. There were also Iranians and refugees from other conflicts. Sometimes, they were warned to stay inside, because of the risk of protests. They got £1.30 a day and were not allowed to work.

Arian didn’t have a solicitor and knew little about the asylum process, but handled it himself, researching online. It was stressful, but swift compared with others in the hotel. He had an interview in October 2025, and a couple of days later got an email granting him refugee status. He left the hotel after two months.

After four months volunteering at a construction company to get UK experience, Arian got his first paid job as a civil engineer this summer. He is also translating into Farsi The Places in Between, a book about Afghanistan by Rory Stewart. He is grateful to be safe, and for the support he has had, and is excited about working and contributing to this country. He says the media are often “wrong and unjust” on these issues. “Migrants are the most defenceless group, and some politicians pin every problem on them. It’s not fair to reduce millions of people to a single threatening cliche.”

Arian rejects the idea that suffering “makes you stronger”, and says that some experiences just take things away from you. He has a sense of how fragile life can be, and doesn’t take stability for granted: “You start preparing yourself, almost automatically, for the worst.” He says his own life hasn’t given him confidence in a happy ending.

His father’s belief that a better future was possible, which he says he absorbed as a child, helped him to keep going. Reading and studying were always important to him, and he writes a lot of lists to instil a sense of order. Going to the gym has been crucial, especially when other parts of his life felt stuck or out of control. And “human connection really matters”, he says, including the random pleasant interactions which, in a new country, can make such a difference. All these things help him find the strength to move forward.

The impact of the torture stayed with him long after his physical injuries had healed. He says it was a feeling of violation, of having his dignity and control taken away: “Coming to terms with the fact that someone chose to do that was very difficult.” For him, recovery is about “finding a way to live with what happened, without allowing it to take over”.

He can’t forget the realities for so many people still in Afghanistan, especially women, without education, healthcare or other basic freedoms. In March, the UK government introduced a temporary ban on study visas for all Afghans, so, for now, the route he took is barred. It is a heavy burden – trying to use his voice and do the best he can with the opportunities he has, but also to be realistic about what he can’t change.

His message for other refugees is to “hold on to your human dignity”. He says it’s possible to “come out of even the deepest darkness, as I did”.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.title: Israel election results live: count of absentee ballots under way as coalition talks among Eisenkot bloc set to begin
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.author: Jonathan Yerushalmy
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text:
With the final count unlikely to shift results significantly, experts say Gadi Eisenkot’s hopes of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu rest on his willingness to work with Palestinian parties

Analysis: Israel’s choice: Netanyahu remaining in power or a Palestinian-backed coalition

With 91% of votes now counted, the current results show prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc projected to receive 53 seats, with the grouping of his opponent Gadi Eisenkot on 48 and the Palestinian parties on track to receive a record 19 seats.

The final tally of absentee ballots is not expected to significantly shift the results, and with no grouping managing to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, Israel could be in for weeks of uncertainty, as both sides try to gather enough support to form a government.

Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in Eisenkot’s bloc, has told Israeli media that he will meet leaders on Thursday for coalition talks. According to the Times of Israel, he will hold talks with Eisenkot, the leading opposition candidate and chair of the Yashar party, and Yair Lapid, the number-two in the opposition B’Yachad party.

This would mark the official start of coalition talks, and Golan has been the only opposition leader so far backing working with the parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, voiced hope that the country could avoid a second election. “We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” said Herzog, who is tasked with determining which candidate to tap to form a government, urging parties to keep “an open mind”.

Israel’s future hangs in the balance after it became clear that Benjamin Netanyahu has lost his governing majority. His political fate now depends on whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common front with Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday’s historic elections. Indeed, Gadi Eisenkot and his allies face a clear choice: either make a pact with Arab Israeli parties heading for a record result of 19 seats, or hand Netanyahu a political lifeline in the form of new elections or a unity government.

Yousef Jabareen, head of the Arab-majority Joint List, said the Israeli public had voted for new leadership and “anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu’s blood-soaked government will have to talk to us”. He told AFP that while he was willing to cooperate with an opposition-led government to unseat Netanyahu, he was not open to joining such a coalition outright. The ad hoc support of Palestinian lawmakers could enable Eisenkot to maintain a minority government, although few observers believe such an arrangement would survive for long.

Israel’s Central Elections Committee said it had received a Likud party complaint alleging that Arab parties had compromised election integrity and would examine the claims as part of its routine post-election review. Netanyahu’s party responded to partial election results showing Arab-led parties could play a king-making role in forming a new government by accusing them – without evidence – of “stealing” the election and demanding that the police and Shin Bet security service investigate the allegations.

UN rights chief Volker Turk has said that he hopes the next Israeli government will “change course massively” and respect international law. “The message is: don’t continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that’s what we have frankly seen in the current environment,” Turk told reporters in New York. He added: “Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them, and I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively.”

Hours before the final results from Israel’s elections were in, several things were clear. Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition had lost its mandate, and the opposition had a firm majority.

But most of Israel’s Jewish opposition ruled out governing with Palestinian-led parties, in the course of a racist election campaign in which Netanyahu painted Palestinian citizens as an enemy inside the state.

The self-imposed ban on a broader opposition alliance, if it holds, offers Netanyahu the prospect of turning his defeat into another term in office – or at least a prolonged mandate as caretaker prime minister and perhaps another round of elections.

This confected barrier to unseating Netanyahu became the focus of Israeli media and analysts. “No Clear Government” announced the newspaper Israel Hayom. “Road to Unity Government Has Been Paved”, read an article on Channel 12.

Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats, attacked that framing. “Netanyahu lost. I know how to count,” he said in a statement calling for a government with Palestinians, who make up about 20% of Israel’s population.

“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he said. “We have a majority. We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a change government in partnership with Arab citizens of Israel.”

While Palestinian-led parties do not describe themselves as Zionist, neither do some of the ultra-Orthodox groups who are a key part of Netanyahu’s current coalition.

A survey taken as polls closed on election day showed that a clear majority of opposition voters supported forming a government with the Palestinian-led Ra’am in order to unseat Netanyahu, political psychology researcher Eran Halperin said.

But opposition leaders were silent on Wednesday, as they apparently tried to balance their desire to unseat Netanyahu with promises against working with Palestinians.

Former general Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the biggest opposition party, has not directly ruled out governing with Palestinians but laid out conditions that made it politically impossible for them to join a coalition.

Palestinians have been clearer about their priorities. “We are ready and prepared to pave the way for the ousting of the Netanyahu government,” Yousef Jabareen, leader of the larger Joint List, said on Wednesday. “The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership.”

Israel’s elections committee has said it began counting absentee ballots at 1am local time. That count is expected to last until Thursday evening, with an estimated 500,000 ballots from military personnel and diplomats to be tallied up.

Under Israeli electoral law, each voter is assigned a specific polling station and can only vote at that station. However in exceptional circumstances, some voters are allowed to cast their ballot at special polling stations they are not registered at. Among those afforded this exception are soldiers stationed at IDF bases, diplomats working abroad, prisoners and prison guards and people in hospital.

These absentee ballots are transported directly to the Knesset where they undergo a series of checks before they are counted, which is why they arrive in the final count much later.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Outcry after Call of Duty maker uses real footage of deadly Seoul crowd crush in new video game
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Raphael Rashid in Seoul
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Bereaved families have urged the publisher of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 to remove a clip from the game that shows a figure performing CPR and bodies lying in the street

Bereaved families in South Korea have demanded that the makers of Call of Duty remove harrowing footage of the deadly 2022 Seoul crowd crush from the latest instalment of the video game.

The clips, which are seconds-long, appear in the opening moments of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and are used to represent a scenario of civilian casualties during a fictional North Korean invasion.

One shows a scene of chaos with a figure performing CPR on a victim lying in the street. Another shows rows of bodies laid out in the road, and a victim being carried away on a stretcher.

A total of 158 people were killed in a narrow alley in Seoul’s Itaewon nightlife district during the Halloween weekend in 2022. Two more have since been recognised as victims, having died from trauma caused by the disaster.

“We are appalled that the chaotic and desperate scenes, in which countless citizens performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the cold street, were used exactly as they were to create a scene in a game,” the bereaved families’ council and a coalition of civic groups said in a joint statement on Wednesday, demanding that the footage be removed.

They said people who had taken part in the rescue or witnessed the crush were still living with trauma, while hateful comments about the victims were spreading online in connection with the game’s premise.

Activision, the game’s publisher, told the Yonhap news agency that “some actual news footage included in the game’s opening cinematic was utilised as an element to convey the fictional story within the work.”

They added, “We had absolutely no intention of mentioning or treating lightly any actual tragic events, including the Itaewon tragedy.”

The demand comes as the country marks the fourth anniversary of the crush on Thursday.

Players in South Korea identified the clip after the game’s release, and Korean broadcasters have compared it side by side with footage filmed on the night of the crowd crush.

The Korean Game Users Association called for an apology and for the footage to be replaced.

Modern Warfare 4 follows a South Korean marine private fighting a North Korean invasion through recognisable Korean streets.

The title had already become a political talking point before its release, with conservative politicians urging president Lee Jae Myung – who is pursuing a more conciliatory approach towards North Korea – to play the game to understand what they described as the threat from Pyongyang.

It topped South Korea’s sales chart on Steam, the leading PC gaming platform, within days of its release.

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: Nocturne review – Stephen Graham is TV’s most evil serial killer … and it’s impossible to stop watching him
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Lucy Mangan
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
The star plays a sadistic murderer still pulling the strings from behind bars. With his high-pitched giggles and fatal whispers, it is a perfectly terrifying show for Halloween

It has taken a while, but I think the torch may finally have passed from Anthony Hopkins as the screen’s most profoundly unsettling and instantly-absorbed-by-the-cultural-imagination serial killer. From Hannibal’s hitherto unfailing hands it has been thrown to Stephen Graham, who plays multiple murderer Jurek Walter in the new 10-part psychological thriller Nocturne.

Walter, who draws out the deaths of his victims in order to torture their families as much as the individuals themselves, is incarcerated for life in the bowels of Riverside psychiatric hospital in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. He passes the time by doing push-ups, stashing contraband behind his toilet bowl for as-yet-unspecified purposes, and driving fellow inmates to suicide by whispering to them through the pipes. Graham – muscle-bound, preternaturally still and occasionally emitting a high-pitched giggle – is mesmerising and utterly terrifying.

He soon has his hooks into his new nurse, Karl (Rory Culkin), who is too young, inexperienced and tender-hearted to heed the staff’s warnings about the manipulative monster in the basement. Walter has a way, as one former nurse notes, of making you feel sorry for him – “a man who buried people alive”. Soon Walter has Karl offering up personal information and carrying illicit messages to his supposed lawyer.

In addition to the murders he was convicted for, Walter is also suspected of abducting and killing two children, Michael and Felicia Frost, though their bodies were never found. When Michael (Landon Valentin) stumbles out of the woods after three years, the man who was in charge of the Frost case, Jonah Lynn, comes out of voluntary retirement to work out if and how he was wrong, and where Felicia might be. Lynn (Liev Schreiber) is still grieving for the wife and son he lost in an accident and the partner who killed himself. The question of whether these many sorrows threaten to make him reckless in pursuit of the truth or merely relentless is one of the many uncertainties that will come to infuse the story.

His late partner’s child, Saga (Zazie Beetz), is an FBI agent who has become a surrogate daughter to Lynn. Which is why he is not best pleased when, as the police begin to suspect that Walter has smuggled out a note telling an accomplice to release Michael, she insists that the best way for them to find out more is for her to go undercover as a patient at the facility.

In she goes, parlaying her experience with a long-institutionalised mother into something useful – palming pills, fighting off assaults from other staff members and behaving badly enough to get herself sent down to the basement and become Walter’s neighbour.
