Can you pretend to be criminally insane without jeopardising your own sanity? Can you instigate a relationship with someone who lives to unearth weaknesses in others and exploit them without getting suckered in? Can you exist within a dehumanising system and keep your sense of self, let alone a professional self, intact? More uncertainties and ambiguities gather.

Nocturne is adapted, by Rowan Joffé, from two volumes of the Joona Linna series by Lars Kepler (the nom de plume of husband-and-wife team Alexander Ahndoril and Alexandra Coelho Ahndoril). As with most Scandi noir, their books are slow burns, and so too is Nocturne, though the series’ focus is narrower – there is less space given to the impact of Walter’s crimes on the community and more to his present influence on those around him.

This means that certain roles are underdeveloped, despite some beautiful work from the cast (particularly veteran character actors Bill Camp as the harrowed police chief and Chrissy Metz as the children’s mother). They do, however, give glimpses of how the series might have been strengthened by a little more emphasis on the trail of suffering caused rather than just its execution; if perhaps a few twists and revelations had been cleared for emotional delineation and investment instead. There is a slight but growing sense as the series wears on that it is just a bit less impressive than it was shaping up to be, a little more hollow than it thinks.

Then Graham appears again and the adrenaline that floods your system in the presence of his radiant evil pushes all rational thoughts from your mind, and you are captivated once more. It is the perfect watch for Halloween, especially for those of us who are always more horrified by the menace that stalks the earth in all-too-human form than by anything they say the supernatural can throw at us.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Serbia’s students achieved the impossible. Europe must not fail them now | Srđjan Cvijić
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Srđjan Cvijić
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Some EU leaders courted the authoritarian Vučić regime – they must offer this reborn democracy a future within the union

As polling stations closed across Serbia on Sunday evening, riot police were deploying around the presidency in Belgrade. Many of us feared the worst: massive electoral fraud, a refusal to recognise defeat or outright violence. After nearly 15 years of Aleksandar Vučić’s increasingly authoritarian rule, a peaceful transfer of power seemed implausible.

I had good reason to feel afraid. I am co-founder of an annual conference on the security and foreign policy challenges shaping the western Balkans, and sit on the international advisory committee of a civil society thinktank, the Belgrade Centre for Security Policy. Such work would be uncontroversial in most countries seeking European Union membership. Under Vučić’s regime, it was anything but.

Over the past two years, our organisation has faced cyber-attacks by actors suspected of links to Russian intelligence, spyware attempts and relentless vilification by pro-regime media. After one attack, investigators documented 28,000 email exchanges that had been hacked. At the same time, Serbian regime propagandists portrayed us as foreign conspirators, while the threat of Russian-style foreign agents legislation cast a long shadow over all of Serbian civil society. Had Vučić won another mandate, exile might have become a reality for many of us.

Others endured far worse. Journalists and activists had their homes set on fire. Students who were detained reported being beaten, females stripped naked and humiliated in police stations while activists were imprisoned for exercising their democratic rights. Among them were the Novi Sad 12 – students and activists prosecuted on politically motivated charges during the protests that followed the November 2024 railway station canopy collapsethat killed 16 people. Six were driven into exile; the other six endured imprisonment and house arrest.

Vučić conceded defeat. The student-backed list’s margin of victory was so overwhelming that overturning the result might have proved more dangerous than accepting it.

What convinced a man who had spent nearly 15 years concentrating power in his hands to relinquish it? Fear of popular resistance? International pressure, and if it was this, from where?

Uncertainty over the loyalty of Vučić’s security apparatus may have been a decisive factor. Days before the election, hundreds of serving and former police and intelligence officials, including former security leaders, signed an appeal urging their colleagues to uphold the constitution rather than obey unlawful political orders. It was a reminder that Vučić could not necessarily count on the entire security establishment to keep him in power.

An incumbent accepting electoral defeat is ordinary in an established democracy. In Serbia, it felt almost miraculous.

The students had achieved what many thought impossible. They had forced a system built around the impossibility of losing to accept that it had lost.

Their victory belonged equally to hundreds of thousands who marched, organised and endured intimidation. What began as grief over 16 lives lost in Novi Sad became a movement challenging the foundations of state capture.

For nearly two years, the students dismantled the regime’s most powerful weapon: the belief that resistance was futile, everyone had a price and political change was impossible.

But the significance of their victory is measured not only in votes. It is measured in lives.

I think of Mila, Anja, Doroteja, Branislav, Jovan and Dejan, the six Novi Sad activists forced into exile formore than a year and a half. They may finally be able to come home. Six of their comrades in Serbia are now free from detention and house arrest. But I have friends who have confronted authoritarianism in their countries with equal courage and have no prospect of achieving the same breakthrough. I am thinking of Marika from Georgia, Gökçe from Turkey and Andrei from Belarus. For them, exile remains a condition of life. Their fate reminds us that Serbia’s peaceful breakthrough was not inevitable.

Geography, too, played its part. Serbia lies at the heart of Europe, beyond Russia’s immediate reach and too close to the EU for its democratic struggle to remain Europe’s distant concern.

Serbia’s students deserve the credit, but what happens next also depends on Europe. For years, some European leaders tolerated, and sometimes effectively supported, Vučić’s authoritarian rule, preferring a predictable strongman to democratic uncertainty. Serbia’s breakthrough happened largely despite Brussels, not because of it.

Here lies the irony: while European leaders courted Vučić, much of Serbia’s genuinely pro-European constituency opposed him. Our research found that two-thirds of Serbians who supported EU membership also opposed his government. Brussels was looking for stability in the wrong place.

Serbia’s ability to consolidate its democracy relies on a future in Europe. And Europe now has an opportunity to regain the trust of those who fought for the very democratic values it professes to uphold.

Defeating an autocrat is an event, but dismantling authoritarian institutions is a process. Serbia must restore the rule of law, free its media and ensure that its police and security services serve citizens rather than a political party.

The students have won the right to change their government but the harder task lies ahead. And that means building a country where doing so will never again require such extraordinary courage.

Srđjan Cvijić is a writer, president of the international advisory committee of the Belgrade Centre for Security Policy and co-founder of the Belgrade Security Conference

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: From sex ‘obsession’ to losing friends, key takeaways from Russell Brand’s testimony at trial
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Matthew Weaver
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Comedian told jurors he now believed it was wrong to have used his fame for sex and said his life had been consumed by the allegations

Russell Brand was in the witness box for more than four hours on Wednesday at his trial at Southwark crown court. He denies three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one charge of attempted indecent assault.

Six alleged victims say the comedian switched suddenly after appearing charming and forced them into sexual activity in a toilet, a hotel room, workplace corridors and his bedroom, acting as if nothing had happened after the attacks.

Brand said in evidence that he had an “obsession” with sex when he was younger, but denied setting himself a “goal” to sleep with 5,000 women.

He said: “I do recognise I have been a very determined and focused man and with regard to the latter, with women, of course, which is the subject of my trial, I’ve been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond-reckless philandering and idiocy.”

Brand’s former friend, Mark Pinheiro, previously told the trial that Brand had boasted on a car journey to the Labour party conference in Bournemouth about his techniques for “pulling” women and allegedly revealed an ambition to sleep with 5,000 women.

Riel Karmy-Jones KC, prosecuting, asked Brand: “Is it a goal you may have had?” Brand said: “I don’t agree, I don’t recall the conversation you are referring to.”

Brand also suggested a reported conversation in 1999 about never leaving an interaction with a woman without a “conquest” was a riff on a Woody Allen joke.

Brand told jurors he now believed it was “wrong” of him to use his fame for sex. He said: “As I became more successful and famous I was very comfortable allowing that to facilitate sexual access which I agree with you was wrong.”

One of Brand’s alleged victims says she was raped after she met him at one of his Hammersmith Apollo standup performances in 2009.

The court heard he stored her name next to the letter T, which he said stood for “tart”. Asked what he meant by the word “tart”, he replied: “That was what I used to denote casual hook-ups.” He told jurors the woman had not said “no” or told him to stop as they were having sex.

Another allegation is that Brand sexually assaulted a Channel 4 worker in 2009 during a recording session, after she had been forced by members of his entourage to give him a massage. Brand agreed that, while he says he cannot remember that day, it would have been “petulant and childish” to refuse to continue the recording without first receiving a massage.

Asked if he had found thrusting his head into her lap funny, Brand replied: “I don’t remember. I don’t think it’s funny now.”

In his evidence Brand recalled only consensual encounters and told the court that “consent is more important than sex itself”.

The prosecution claimed he had constructed his evidence in response to the allegations. Karmy-Jones accused Brand of staying silent on the accusations in his police interviews so that he “forged” his account around the evidence.

“Were you waiting to see all that evidence before you gave your account?” she asked. Brand replied: “I was doing my best to participate.”

Brand blamed the media for his public fall from grace after reporting of sexual misconduct allegations in a 2023 Channel 4 Dispatches documentary and news stories. Asked about the impact of the Dispatches programme, Brand said: “It was devastating.”

Brand told the court that after the programme and the articles he was unable to stay with his son at Great Ormond Street hospital in London when he was having surgery. “Due to material that had been published in the public eye they had to bar my attendance and presence,” Brand said.

Brand told the court he had been unable to persuade any friend or acquaintance to give evidence on his behalf. The defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, asked him: “Will they touch you with a bargepole?” Brand replied “No.

Brand described the last few years as “deeply traumatic” and told the court that focusing on the allegations and trying to remember incidents from his past had damaged his personal life.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: ‘I’m no special guy. We can all do this’: Loek Hartog on rescuing Ollie Millroy from a burning car
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Donald McRae
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Last month in Shanghai, the Dutch driver saved Ollie Millroy’s life after a crash. The incident created a unique friendship and a shared determination to improve safety

Winter is coming and, at eight in the morning, Amsterdam is dark as Loek Hartog and I walk towards the park. The GT motor racing driver is only 24 but, after all he did last month, when he showed extraordinary courage in saving the life of his fellow racer Ollie Millroy, we talk easily about life and death.

Hartog sips a takeaway coffee and, as we stroll, he asks if the world seems to be in a worse state than usual. Paris is burning, Kyiv is reeling, Vladimir Putin is being hailed as “a humanitarian” by Donald Trump’s envoy and the robots are coming for us. These are grim times, but I remind Hartog that he gave us hope as, after ripping off the doors of Millroy’s burning car as if he had stepped out of a superhero movie, his humanity was remarkably moving. Hartog dragged Millroy to safety before trying to comfort the 36-year-old Briton after an accident that left him with six broken ribs, a damaged lung, a splintered collarbone, a broken hand, a fractured C6 neck vertebrae and a stunned sense that he had almost died at the China GT.

We sit near a small lake and Hartog explains he will soon fly to Shanghai again for the next round of racing in the GT World Challenge Europe Endurance Cup. This weekend he is back on the same track where he and Millroy shared something profound, and driving the same kind of car that almost killed his new friend.

A low sun rises over Vondelpark, the birds are singing and cyclists whir past in an unbroken hum as the young Dutch driver resists being called heroic. “Maybe the biggest thing to process was that a lot of people actually had the balls to tell me: ‘Oh, I would have never done the same,’” he says. “That made me more emotional than the actual circumstances and this is why I’m sitting here. We need to do better as a society. We need to stand up for each other. You already touched on this, with what we see in the news. We’re all humans and we need each other. Why be against each other?”

Has the accident changed Hartog? “Of course. I look at things with a completely different angle now. But it’s like an additional angle. It’s not that I’ve changed my character. I’m still the same guy with just one experience more.”

He adds: “The biggest thing I’m conscious of now is not every time somebody calls this a heroic act, which is a very nice appraisal. It’s when people say: ‘I wouldn’t have acted the same.’ I’d love to trust people. I know you can’t expect these things but the world would be a better place if we can. I came away from it unscathed and, as humans, it’s not that hard. Really, I’m no special guy. We can all do this.”

It’s worth recounting what “this” amounted to for Hartog. He was driving at “around 270km/h” down a straight when he saw fire engulf Millroy’s Ferrari after he had been hit by a car involved in a different collision. “I saw a lot of flames,” Hartog remembers. “I’m quite tall, 6ft 6in, but I think the flames were twice my height. So I knew there was a high chance of him not getting out himself. It was quite serious.”

Did he feel afraid? “It’s kind of similar to stepping on a surfboard for the first time. You don’t know what you’re doing. It was more that kind of feeling – not really scared. For me there was no other scenario than I would get him out.”

Hartog didn’t consider the danger that Millroy’s car might explode. “No, you don’t think of that. It was like the movies because it felt like slow motion. When I watched it back for the first time I was like: ‘That was it?’ It felt so much longer.”

He tried to open the driver’s door before running round to the other side of the car. Hartog yanked the doors off but says, with a smile: “It looks a lot more spectacular [than it was].”

When a marshal finally arrived, Hartog took the fire extinguisher from the man, who was not wearing flame-proof clothing. He doused the worst of the fire before, after two attempts, pulling Millroy out of the burning wreck. It took just over a minute and Hartog says: “Ollie was confused and not aware he was in a car in flames. It was like he was knocked out in a boxing match and not able to breathe. He kept repeating: ‘Where am I? What happened? I think I broke my back.’ The help was not the best because not many people were speaking English. So they kept moving him and I kept telling everyone [to stop]. That was maybe the worst thing for me because I felt the most helpless.”

Hartog and Millroy sat near a barrier as they waited for the medics. “That’s where we became a bit more emotional because I was telling him: ‘You’re going to be OK. There’s help on the way.’ I was making eye contact, but he was in shock.”

After Millroy was taken away, Hartog drove his car slowly back to the pits. “I was like: ‘I need to stop [racing].’ You think like that in those moments which is human and natural. But then you think of all that [racing] means to you. So [his doubts] very quickly turned into: ‘When can I go out back again?’ It’s like a drug, racing.”

Hartog visited Millroy in hospital that night. “He was very drugged, but I showed him on my phone what happened and he kept saying: ‘Oh my God, nobody told me it was this bad. Oh my God, is that me?’ He realised it would have been very different if I wasn’t there.”

It felt as if fate had intervened because, as Hartog says: “I was doing very bad in the race and, usually, I’m not running so far at the back. But that actually put me in the position to respond the way I did. So it’s such a strange turn of events that led to this. It’s unbelievable.”

Before the race on 5 September he had “a very bad feeling. I reflected more on myself, like something would be wrong for me. In the end, it turned out differently.”

Millroy has a wife, Fern, and three children. That night, everything they could have lost hit Hartog. “That was really emotional for me,” he says. “I couldn’t sleep because I was overloaded and then Wiep, my partner, sent me a picture of Fern, the kids and Ollie at Disneyland. She was like: ‘You did it for them.’ That really struck me.”

The deep gratitude felt by Ollie and Fern meant they flew to Amsterdam to surprise him this month. “My birthday is 5 October,” Hartog says, “and I thought I was going for lunch with Wiep. She said: ‘Oh, we need to get a big frame for my masters’ degree before lunch.’ I was like: ‘Why can’t we get it after lunch?’ She was saying: ‘We need to get it now.’ I was like: ‘OK, OK.’ Then we walked into this restaurant [near the framers] and I asked for a table for two. We were taken to one where Ollie and Fern were sitting.”

Hartog’s shock gave way to delight and then appreciation. “It was really special and they gave me a very special gift. They gave me a watch, because I gave them more time.”

That simple gesture is laced with deeper resonance and Hartog asks if I would like to see it. He spreads the Rolex across his open hand, and we think how time would have stopped for the Millroy family had he not saved Ollie’s life.

Did he and Millroy know each other before the accident? “No. We’d heard of each other but we’re from different generations. Ollie has been a benchmark and a competitor to some of my mentors.”

Despite their difference in age, Hartog and Millroy are determined to work together. “Absolutely. That’s the most important thing – that something positive comes out of this. If the headline had been ‘British racing driver had a fatal accident’ rather than ‘was saved’, it would have been a completely bad story for our sport. We don’t want that to happen, ever.”

It took 47 seconds for a marshal to appear and more than four minutes for medical assistance to arrive at the Shanghai track. We discuss the anger of Betty Chen, Millroy’s teammate at Ferrari, who wrote: “The measures taken by the organisers following today’s incident, particularly the lack of an immediate and adequate emergency response, are something we cannot accept. The safety of drivers and team members must always come before anything else. What happened today and the way the situation was handled is truly unacceptable.”

Hartog understands Chen’s anger. “Absolutely. First of all, an incident like this should never happen. And, secondly, there should be no driver that needs to stop to help in a case like this.”

He continues: “Lots of people told me the marshals are not allowed to cross the guardrails on their own, which makes total sense on paper. But once something like this happens in front of you, I cannot believe you’re telling people to go against their feeling. If your gut tells you to do something, it should be your cue to act. We should mandate rules that are more human.”

There is something deeply human in Hartog as, walking back to his apartment, he talks about his hope that he and Millroy may race each other again next year. But we sense the difficulties Millroy faces when we have a WhatsApp video call with him. The injured racer talks openly about how he is struggling since he took himself off his strong painkillers. He compares it to the withdrawal symptoms a heroin addict might suffer, while the pain has become excruciating.

We postpone our joint interview until the next morning. Hartog and I are convinced that Millroy won’t be well enough to talk and we agree to leave him in peace during his long and painful recovery. But 24 hours later Millroy messages me to say he is ready to chat on a Zoom call from Dubai.

“I was hoping to be in better shape six weeks on, but I’m really struggling,” Millroy says. “I’m in a lot of pain. It’s really hard and I’m getting frustrated. The meds gave me a false sense of security because the team are testing at Sebring [in Florida] in four weeks and I’d thought I might be all right for that. But since I’ve come off the painkillers, I can’t even imagine getting anywhere near a racing car. I can’t even get in a road car at the moment, it’s that sore. I’ve got an appointment this afternoon to work out a plan but it’s made me realise I’m a lot further away than I thought.”

Hartog leans towards his friend on screen and says: “It’s pretty insane what your body has been trying to heal the last six weeks.”

Millroy nods. “I guess this is one thing I can’t rush, I can’t force, I can’t influence, other than doing what I’m doing, which is eating the right things and trying to rest. But I’m in so much pain I can’t even sleep. It’s just in my head that I want to move on. It’s in our nature, right? I guess it’s why we do what we do. We’re not the most patient.

“It’s a really weird feeling because I’m also enjoying time at home with my wife and kids. So am I desperate to switch back to all the travel? I don’t think so. The bit I love about motorsport is driving a racing car and that’s not been impacted at all by what’s happened. I’m excited to get back behind the wheel and compete. But I don’t feel like my life’s been put on hold because I’m not at a circuit next weekend.”

The two friends talk engagingly about the addiction of racing and it’s striking that Millroy’s son, Mylo, has already fallen for karting. “It was pretty crazy,” Millroy says. “We were still in hospital when he had his first race. My wife flew out a couple of hours after the accident. She was watching it live on TV at home [in Dubai] and got the first flight to China. She told the kids I had food poisoning and she needed to come to China to help me get home. But news of the accident spread around the school and, even though they’re just eight years old, kids were seeing it on YouTube and parents were talking about it.

“On the Wednesday after the accident Mylo called us in tears because he’d seen it. He’d watched enough racing to know that that doesn’t happen very often. He said: ‘I want to be with you.’ We said: ‘The best thing you can do is have a great weekend and just enjoy everything on the track.’ And he did. Even at his age you can see the addiction and passion for racing.”

Mylo finished third and was awarded the top novice prize at the UAE International. “He’s off to a great start,” his dad says. “But the most important thing is that he’s enjoying it.”

Hartog had told me the previous day about his own start in motorsport that had been fuelled by his father’s love of GT racing. “The best thing is the time you get to spend with your parents or with your dad,” he says before talking directly to Millroy. “Ollie, you and Mylo will spend a lot of time together in the winter. That’s great.”

The drivers are determined to bring about change in racing. “We want to try to save more lives by pushing for better safety,” Millroy says of their joint objective. “Safety has improved so much in the last few decades. But we’ve got to a stage everybody has sat back and said: ‘Motorsport can’t get any safer than it is now.’ But my accident proved it can, especially in some parts of the world. It’s been a wake-up call for a lot of organisers, a lot of circuits. We’d like to get the whole motorsport community together to make sure steps are taken to make the sport safer – because it’s very clear there are still areas in need of improvement.”

This weekend Millroy will turn on his TV and watch Hartog race in Shanghai while remembering his traumatic accident. He says: “I’m not particularly angry about anything that happened. All the positivity since then massively overwhelms any anger.”

He amuses us as he recalls the look on Hartog’s face when he and Fern were surprise guests at his birthday: “It was pure shock as he had absolutely no idea. It was brilliant.”

I know how often Millroy has thanked Hartog but is there anything else he would like to say to the man who saved him? “Thank you again Loek and don’t change. I know you won’t. This is in your nature and you’re an inspiration to all of us in sport and life in general. Fern and I now think about life differently because you really put everything into perspective. So thank you for myself and also on behalf of so many millions of people that have seen this story. You’ve been really inspirational.”

Hartog’s face fills the screen and he says: “Thank you, Ollie. I’m really looking forward to the friendship that comes out of this, talking about Mylo’s career and the fun stuff which keeps us busy every day. In the three times we’ve met each other in person it has been very special and always too short. I look forward to it being normal and to seeing Ollie being fully himself again and smiling a big and really complete smile. That would be special.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Spain begins mourning period after deadly train crash
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Staff and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Emergency services combed through the wreckage overnight as Civil Guard sets up clinics for relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims

Spain has begun three days of mourning after a high-speed rail collision – its second this year – killed 68 people and injured scores, with relatives desperately seeking news about their loved ones.

The trains, one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling on Wednesday morning in the same direction on the line that stretches from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to the southern region of Andalusia. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near the town of Urda.

Officials said on Wednesday another 107 people had needed medical treatment in hospital, including 15 who were in a serious condition.

The disaster has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain’s rail network after the transport minister reported an “error” and “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the crash.

Emergency services combed through the wreckage overnight to find further victims, hoisting pieces of mangled metal with cranes, according to Agence France-Presse.

Emiliano García-Page, the leader of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, told reporters on Wednesday that more victims were likely as “it has not yet been possible to reach the bottom of the carriages”.

The Civil Guard has set up four offices in the cities of Madrid, Toledo, Córdoba and Seville to enable relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims. Blood donation points have also been set up in Castilla-La Mancha and Madrid.

A school in the nearby village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid, is being used to allow relatives to enquire about their loved ones. Teams of Red Cross workers offered support to groups of people who arrived, some of them in tears.

Red Cross psychologist Carmen Garcia said “long and hard hours” were in store because “every person will manage it in their own way”. “We have people who are in shock, who haven’t taken on board what has happened, angry people, sad, worried people. The grieving will be complicated,” Garcia said.

In January, 46 people were killed and dozens more injured after two trains – again, one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.

The prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said it was “unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in the same year, as we have”.

The causes of the accident were under investigation, he added. If it emerged that it was due to failures in the security system or negligence, these shortcomings would be addressed with the “utmost severity”, he said.

The first victims to be named included a 31-year-old Guardia civil agent, José Manuel Chacón.

The national law enforcement agency expressed its “deepest condolences” to his family, friends and colleagues. Spanish media said the missing included a former minister for the People’s party and several foreigners who were likely on holiday in the country.

The opposition People’s party leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, called for an immediate investigation into what had happened, as well as a “complete and independent review” of Spain’s entire rail network. “Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure,” he told reporters.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: A three-year-old soccer prodigy went viral. The adults have already let him down
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Jeff Rueter
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
From Ms Rachel to Roc Nation, the internet embraced a Florida toddler. Police records reviewed by the Guardian complicate the story – and raise troubling questions

There is real tragedy in this week’s story of the three-year-old Florida boy whose parents claimed he was so good at soccer that police were called to do what opposing defenders couldn’t. But it doesn’t lie where the outrage cycle wants you to think. It’s broader, implicates more people, and to me, is far more depressing.

You may have seen the video by now. Here was a toddler with fabulous soccer talent, running end-to-end and scoring goal after goal against opponents who have seemingly just found their feet. The cameraman, later identified as the child’s father, loudly and proudly cheers his son on. Way to go, kid.

Then, an abrupt cut to the parents speaking with two police officers from the Orlando suburb of Winter Park. “They called the police on a three-year-old, because he’s too good,” one of the parents says. An officer responds: “They’re wanting you guys to head out, OK?” The parents ask: “You’re confused too, right?”

In the final shot, his mother says: “This is the biggest part of it. We’re trying to put a show on in front of these people. It’s all on [TikTok] Live. There’s thousands of people watching this. He’s famous. There’s thousands of people watching this.”

The story quickly became national news. It was easy to see why. It appeared to take in so many flawed aspects of America: the commoditization of youth sports, overbearing parents, police called for seemingly minor infractions, a social media pile-on and race relations (the child and his parents are Black, the majority of the other children and their parents in the clip were white). Celebrities quickly weighed in to give the story even more life, among them US international Alex Freeman and children’s edutainer Ms Rachel. Civil rights attorney Ben Crump threw his hat in the ring.

But the story is more complicated than the viral video suggested. Police dispatch records, 911 calls and body-camera footage obtained and reviewed by the Guardian offer a fuller picture of what happened on Saturday morning. The organizer, who is also Black, acknowledged that the boy was unusually talented but told officers he had been pushing other children and that his parents had become argumentative. The organizer said he had been rotating players to ensure everyone got a turn, and that the parents had argued with other families. That approach was consistent with i9 Sports’ stated philosophy, which emphasizes fun, inclusion and equal playing time regardless of ability. In a 911 call obtained by the Guardian, the organizer complained of an allegedly disruptive parent who was following him around, calling him names and livestreaming their confrontation. He also referred to the family’s large Instagram following in remarks captured on body-camera footage. The parents offered a sharply different account, insisting that their son was being unfairly singled out because of his ability. Officers, who had not witnessed the dispute, treated it as a civil matter and discussed arranging a refund. No arrests were made.

When the scenes in Winter Park first landed on my feeds on Saturday night, my initial reaction was largely in line with the popular discourse. But even as I learned more, a shot near the end has continued to haunt me. The camera’s edge catches a glimpse of the youngster, visibly confused, already overwhelmed. He couldn’t have known that he’d become a main character of this week’s internet. An audience of mere thousands was about to seem tiny.

Neil Postman got famous arguing that modern media amounts to “amusing ourselves to death”. A few generations on, that phrase is showing its age. Not for its core messaging, but for the implication that amusement is the point. Platforms ensnare users with endless scrolling, fueled by algorithms to extract every penny from one’s pocket and every second from one’s existence. Even if this was the worst day of this kid’s life (or, at least, his worst day so far), that wasn’t the point. The idea that this is an incident with plenty of nuance to consider is immaterial. It was engagement fodder, fresh and meaty ragebait for the ravenous masses to consume and proliferate.

At this point, it’s worth acknowledging that even if the initial video had accurately conveyed the reason for the police’s summoning – which, understandably, the parents couldn’t immediately discern – we may have ended up in the same place. There are countless stories of parents crossing lines at youth sports events, including some that were more worthy of law enforcement. That aspect of this all has largely fallen on deaf ears.

The livestream raises another question, too: what about the other children playing that morning, whose images may have been broadcast to thousands of strangers without their parents ever consenting to such exposure? That point would seem salient enough, and is worth a closer look.

So quickly has this story gone viral that most of us have overlooked one crucial detail: the player involved at the heart of all this is three years old. A toddler. By any criteria, the boy is far too young to be platformed like this, whether by his parents or by the various companies that have leapt on to the story: Jay-Z’s sports and entertainment agency Roc Nation has offered to fly the boy to Spain for “an impactful athletic experience”.

Our culture has ignored any teachable moments from the hype trains that pushed LeBron James, Tiger Woods and Freddy Adu front and center well before they turned 18. Countless parents aspire to turn their children into the next viral sensation, as if that’s a healthy and wise idea. Three-year-olds often can’t keep within the lines of their coloring books, much less understand the ramifications of a grift.

As of Wednesday, the young athlete has nearly 900,000 followers on Instagram and 1.2 million on TikTok. One especially ghoulish post from Monday shows his likeness thrown into a dozen different AI-generated “ads” to position the toddler as a spokesperson for cereal, sugary drinks and athletic gear.

He’s clearly not making these posts himself. It’s hard to imagine he’s asking to become another in an endless and tired trend of athletes turned influencers. Yet his profile has two links: an email address for inquiries – introducing this winter’s hot toy, My Little Inbox – and a GoFundMe to “support [his] soccer journey”, with a claim that this is all about “protecting [his] passion for soccer”. As of Wednesday night, the fundraiser had raised more than $49,000, comfortably surpassing its $30,000 goal.

Hopefully he can soon enjoy the anonymity that nearly every other three-year-old enjoys. To grow up as a child rather than as a commodity. To continue playing sports because he loves them, not because there’s a buck to be made.

But maybe that window has already slammed shut. There were too many clicks to be generated, too much engagement to be had. In this case, across the board, the grownups and their machines have let him down. The question now is whether they’ll allow him to be a child again.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: Wicker review – Olivia Colman finds the perfect lover in intriguing folk-horror romance
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Peter Bradshaw
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
Colman stars as a depressed and bullied fisherwoman in medieval England. Fortunately, Peter Dinklage’s basketmaker delivers the answer to her dreams – an Alexander Skarsgård made of wicker

The spirit of mystery author Shirley Jackson is interestingly revived in this peculiar folk-horror romance, adapted from a 2006 story called The Wicker Husband by British writer Ursula Wills. It’s almost funny but not exactly, and almost disturbing but not exactly, occupying a strange and intriguing Venn-diagram overlap between macabre horror and sentimentality. Yet devotees of bucolic British screen-scariness will note that it is, after all, about a wicker man.

The scene is a fabular medieval-effect village that could be in central Europe or England, where there are bizarre patriarchal rituals, like the placing of metal collars on new brides. A depressed middle-aged fisherwoman (fiercely and naturalistically played by Olivia Colman) lives alone in a remote cottage and regularly brings her unappetising tench and gudgeon to market, where she is mocked and bullied by the nasty, closed-minded locals, including Richard E Grant as a lazy and incompetent doctor. Chief among her tormentors is the spiteful tailor’s wife, an elegant, sharp-faced woman played by Elizabeth Debicki.

But the fisherwoman, showing a good deal more imagination than everyone else, boldly approaches the Basketmaker (a droll performance from Peter Dinklage) and commissions him to make a wicker husband for her; this wicker hunk, magicked up in a secret workshop, is played by Alexander Skarsgård. His soulful eyes look out attractively from that weird wicker face.

This new husband turns out to be an amazing catch: attentive, sensitive, non-toxically masculine, a wicker man of few words, great at fixing things in the cottage as he creaks self-effacingly around the place. (This is just as well as it’s still Colman who is earning a living for them both.) And above all, he is a wonderful lover; we don’t see his wicker genitals but there is evidently no problem with abrasion discomfort. (A movie more conventionally aware of comedy might have felt the need to explain this away a little more.)

Instantly, the fisherwoman’s domestic bliss triggers poisonous envy among the sex-starved villagers, especially that noisome tailor’s wife. And it leads to an almost disquieting (and certainly amusing) climax of dismay.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: You be the judge: Should my girlfriend stop sending me 10-minute voice notes?
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Interviews by Georgina Lawton
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Elena records messages for Ayo because they’re often apart, but he would prefer a simple text or chat on the phone. Is he right to call her out?

double quotation markI haven’t got time to listen to 10-minute messages. I’d much prefer a simple text or phone call

I’m a simple man and I value direct communication. But I’m not a big texter and I find voice notes hard work. My family and friends know that if you want to reach me, you can pick up the phone and call as I nearly always answer.

My girlfriend Elena is the opposite. She’s super chatty and she loves texting and leaving a lot of voice notes. Sometimes she sends voice notes to ask a quick question that could be a text, like “What’s for dinner later? Shall I pick something up?” Or to check in when we’ve spent time apart. It’s cute, but also a bit annoying as I would nearly always rather have a call.

Sometimes Elena infers a lot of meaning from texts in a way that isn’t healthy. I’ve had to talk her down off a ledge after she’s read something into messages from friends that she thinks are mean or horrible. She will see a full stop or a lack of emojis and say: “They hate me. What have I done wrong?”

If I’m blunt with her in a text, she will think I’m mad at her. I’m just a bit less smiley on text and don’t want to send voice notes. I also don’t have time for analysing messages or to listen to a 10-minute voice note.

Elena’s longest voice note to me was 12 minutes. I just find they require so much more brain power than a phone call, where you can receive and process information in real time. By the time I’ve finished listening to one, I sometimes can’t remember what was said at the start, especially because Elena’s are quite rambling. If I’m on a work trip, I can’t store any more info in my brain and I sometimes forget to reply. Elena will bring it up later and ask me what happened. But by that time, I simply can’t recall.

One time she got really annoyed when I sent a heart in response to her voice note. But I was on the move and sent a message back asking for a call two days later. We’ve been together a year and I think we are on different pages with phone communication, but in real life we get on well. I just hate voice notes.

double quotation markHe’s often away, so I think voice notes are a nice way to give a window into the life you’re leading

Ayo calls himself a simple man, but sometimes I think that’s code for a “bad communicator”. The funny thing is that he’s great in person. He’s funny and a good listener, and even though he’s more introverted than me, our communication is great. The problem is his manner on the phone.

I love a voice note and a nice message. I will ask Ayo how his day is via voice note or text, and I make the effort to sound bright and enthusiastic. He will respond with a text, like “Fine thanks, you?” Or he’ll just ignore my voice note entirely.

We don’t live together and he travels for work often, so I think voice notes are a nice way to give a window into the life you’re leading. I’d send one while I’m walking somewhere, or cooking dinner or getting ready, and I like hearing someone’s tone of voice. A phone call requires both people to be free at exactly the same time, whereas a voice note can be listened to at your leisure.

Ayo makes it sound as if I’m sitting around analysing every full stop he sends me. I’m not, but he can be incredibly blunt over text and then act surprised when I wonder whether he’s annoyed. Apparently, after just a year, I’m supposed to be fine with his texting style. But I’m not – so if he could change, it would improve our relationship.

I’m not asking him to send long voice notes like me, but it would help if he didn’t reply to an eight-minute chat with one line. He’ll reply to the first thing I’ve said and completely miss something important two minutes later, or call me instead when I’m busy and then complain that I don’t pick up.

I’m not asking Ayo to start producing 40-minute podcasts every morning. Most of my voice notes are a few minutes long. The 12-minute one was never replicated because he ignored it. But if your girlfriend wants to tell you about her day, putting your headphones in for five minutes really shouldn’t be that much of an ordeal. Names have been changed

Voice note etiquette is a sacred practice in 2026 and it’s perfectly acceptable to leave fun, low-stakes voice notes for friends. But Elena needs to respect that that’s not Ayo’s preferred mode of communication and save the mini podcasts for her pals. Nicola, 35

A 12-minute voice note is an act of emotional terrorism! And two days of not replying is bad form too, Ayo. But overall, Elena is undoubtedly the biggest offender. If she will not cease and desist, my advice to Ayo is to play her voice-notes at double speed. Kitty, 34

I can understand why Elena feels limited by opportunities for phone calls and wants to share. I think Ayo could make a little more effort to listen, reply and show more interest, while Elena could send fewer lengthy tomes. Bryony, 31

Why should Elena conform to Ayo’s preferred communication style? She is putting care and thought into telling him how she is and what’s happening in her world while they’re apart – that’s what matters, not the medium. Trying to change people rarely ends well. Ayo should embrace their differences. Daniel, 48

I hate trying to access voice notes myself (even though I do actually like sending them!), so in my view Elena is guilty. If she refuses to stop leaving them, I suggest Ayo speeds them up – it makes the voice sound like a speedy android, but you can just about make out the words and the gist. Margie, 50

We asked whether Tony should stop letting the cat drink on the kitchen counter.

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.title: Pop prodigy Underscores: ‘I don’t think Gen Z is a loveless generation’
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.author: Shaad D'Souza
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.text:
With a sound inspired by the San Francisco tech boom, the hyperpop musician is entering the big leagues, and a slot on Charli xcx’s tour. First she needs to get over her own shyness – not to mention a fear of love songs

The life of a rising pop star: One day, you’re performing your own song with Charli xcx, her dancers emulating your choreography, an arena’s worth of fans screaming along. The next, you’re on a surgery table, with a healthcare professional yanking four superfluous teeth out of your mouth. Even pop stars need emergency dental work sometimes.

It’s all par for the course for April Grey, the San Francisco-born, Chicago-based musician who records as Underscores. Her 2026 has been, plainly, wild: her third album, U, released in March, was met with acclaim and attracted a small army of new fans. Many of the shows on her tour in support of U, earlier this year, were upgraded due to demand, and one expects the bump she’ll get from her current run supporting Charli xcx’s Music, Fashion, Film tour will push her into even bigger rooms. It’s a blow-up befitting the level of ambition Grey put into U, which is a taut, compulsively listenable pop record that sounds like a mid-2000s Now That’s What I Call Music! compilation as recreated by Aphex Twin. “As I was making it, it felt like a very big swing for the fences,” she says. “I wanted it to be big.”

Grey is video-calling from her tour bus a week after her wisdom tooth surgery. (“The swelling wasn’t too bad,” she says. “I don’t even think I got too chipmunky.”) She knew that this year would be crazy – any album release year is, given how much touring and promotion is required to sell a record – but getting the call to join the Charli tour kicked things up a notch. “On my headline tour, many of the shows were upgraded to larger venues, but some weren’t, so there was this whiplash of playing to 4,000 people and then 400 the next night. The main struggle has been trying to figure out how to adapt the show,” she says. “After getting the Charli call, it’s like: ‘How does this look in an arena?’ It definitely is chasing a moving target.”

Grey was born in the year 2000 and grew up amid the San Francisco tech boom. Her father is a musician who was “discovered by Elton John in a bar” but by the time Grey was born, he was “deep in startup world”. Her mother was a teacher, but now has a “crazy job selling jewellery to like, princes and stuff”. Grey “had a very vibrant childhood, and [San Francisco is] a really insane place to grow up … I think there’s an era before the tech boom that people romanticise a lot, but I can look at it now post-Covid and be like, wow, the tech boom, when it was first happening, was the glory days,” she says.

Grey started making music at a young age, but really began taking things seriously when she was about 12, she says. It was hearing the American dubstep producer Skrillex that really changed things. “After discovering Skrillex, I was like: ‘All right, I’m gonna start taking this shit seriously,’” she recalls. From there, she was very “one-track minded” in that she didn’t really do anything else: “I didn’t have other friends, so I was obsessed. Now, I think I have a better work-life balance, but I’m a pretty shy person. But if I’m being honest, I was always very confident about music. There wasn’t really a plan B.”

Away from Silicon Valley, a rowdier group of revolutionaries were congregating in the city, which was quickly becoming a hub for future bass producers such as Shawn Wasabi and the Nest HQ label in the mid-2010s. Grey was a teenager and fledgling producer around that time, and relished the opportunity to see stars of the scene so close to home. “I was like: ‘These people are legends’, and it was such a trip to be able to go to those [events]. I was trying to immerse myself in it, and then everyone left because they got priced out,” she says.

During high school, Grey realised that maybe she should have been spending more time cultivating a social life, as she saw people “going to parties and doing all these crazy things”. “I was like, ‘Damn! I haven’t done any of that shit,’” she recalls. But within a few years, it was clear she was on the right path. After spending a few years releasing brazenly avant garde music online, Grey released her debut album, Fishmonger, in 2021. It was an underground sensation and turned her into a critical darling.

Fishmonger and its follow-up, 2023’s Wallsocket, felt hugely accomplished, but they didn’t have the intense laser focus of U. Wallsocket was a sprawling, rock-adjacent concept album about three young women coming of age, and Grey says its reception made her feel “misunderstood”. “I was almost embarrassed that I had accidentally made a rock opera or something – I’m not a theatre kid, I’m a jazz band kid,” she says with a laugh. “Afterwards, I thought if I was going to try my hand at a pop record, now would be the time to do it.”

On U, Grey tried to write nine love songs, because she hadn’t written many previously. Before, she hadn’t thought that she was even able to. “I just don’t think I’ve really resonated with many love songs in ways that other people have, and growing up, I had issues with showing affection or intimacy. It was something I had to work at,” she says. Even so, she doesn’t buy the idea that gen z is a loveless generation. “I feel like there’s a lot of love to be had. Maybe we’re having less sex because it’s scary or something. That might be true.”

U, with its Britney-meets-Oneohtrix Point Never production, vaulted Grey out of the underground into a more mainstream arena. But it wasn’t until about a month ago – when she met her childhood hero Skrillex at a dinner – that she realised she was in a new echelon. “I was sitting next to him, and he was just really nice, trying to include me as much as possible, asking questions,” she recalls. “I think people like that are just so willing to talk to people, and I’m not as much like that. It’s hard for me to initiate, and I’m kind of realising like, damn, I’m 26. I can’t be shy any more. We gotta cut that out.”

Spending time on tour with Charli, too, has shown her a different side of celebrity and pop stardom. “She is one of the nicest people I’ve ever met. She pops in and checks on us, and she’s very supportive,” she says. “At a level like hers, you worry that anybody under that scrutiny will turn into some kind of diva, and she’s not like that at all. It reminds me to check myself when I get diva-y. Like: Charli doesn’t do that, so I shouldn’t.”

Whatever move Grey makes next, it seems likely that she’ll keep graduating to bigger and bigger stages. “If I think about it too long, it starts to make less and less sense,” she says. “But I gotta be ready for anything.”

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.title: Are You With Me Now? by Hanif Kureishi review – back to basics
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.author: Melissa Denes
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.text:
After his catastrophic accident, the rebel writer’s musings on everything from sex chatbots to film stars have become gloriously unleashed

Some months after returning home, after a grim year in hospitals in Rome and London, Hanif Kureishi begins to rebel. Not against his family, or the physical reality of being tetraplegic (and how could he?), but the liberal homogeneity of Shepherd’s Bush. He gets a diamond stud in his left ear at Westfield shopping centre, a piercing that enraged his father when he was 17. He sends off for a Maga cap and wears both to the farmers’ market, hoping for vitriol but getting nothing. “These quiescent scumbags only cared about themselves and their shopping,” he grumbles. “Being a fascist is far less thrilling than I imagined.”

Kureishi’s “re-punking” after decades in the metropolitan elite remains an ongoing project, just one response to his paralysis after a fall on Boxing Day 2022. His memoir Shattered was written in the long shock of that severance from a former life, which left him with no movement in his hands or legs, “a Beckettian chattering mouth”.

But Kureishi’s mind remains intact, even unleashed: free from the pull of a phone (he can’t scroll), he is funny, nostalgic, profound, petty and never sentimental, not even about the family he relies on. His latest collection of essays, co-written with his son Carlo, takes its title from a song he used to listen to while driving in Italy, his partner Isabella at the wheel while he smoked a fat joint. (It’s also a question his iPad asks him in Shattered – “Are you still there?” – when paralysis leaves him unable to hit refresh.) Now, Carlo is always with him as he dictates, each chapter the product of a conversation between 10am and 1pm. The book has a more outward-looking feel – less stunned, less homesick, sometimes transcribed as a dialogue.

These back-and-forths have a distinctive energy. An argument over what to write becomes a disquisition on art versus politics, Kureishi wanting to reflect on beauty, Carlo insisting that the only subject is Gaza. An experiment with a sex chatbot hits a wall of shared embarrassment. Carlo convinces his father of AI’s usefulness – but their collaboration is the perfect illustration of its limits: here are two humans with a long history of navigating each other’s weaknesses with love.

There are great, gossipy digressions on taking acid with Billy Idol, a schoolmate, and Kureishi’s friendship with David Bowie. Bowie would call at 2am with an urgent question about serial killers, when Kureishi was “a new father of twins, dressed in only my underpants”. Dennis Hopper, Kureishi’s co-juror at the 1992 Venice film festival, was a disappointing square. Isabelle Huppert was a “sweet and intelligent” ally as jury president at Cannes 2009, “a frantic, crazy party that you could never leave”. He misses it all, but these memories push the horrors of the spinal injuries ward – the patient crawling across the floor at 2am, the bodies removed at dawn – that bit further away.

Meanwhile, Kureishi has a house full of strangers, a drama he plays as comedy and farce. There are the carers fighting in the kitchen, and the nice woman who tells him “I really don’t like penises” as she washes his. Someone always has a finger up his arse. He and Carlo are working on a movie about his accident: who will play them, they wonder? But life is mostly a thousand small humiliations: in the park, an acquaintance pats him on the head.

Kureishi revels in a new kind of writing – the essays were originally drafted as Substack posts – discursive, energised by a readership that writes back. His best novels have a clear-eyed quality that can border on cruelty – the famous “fucks for which a person would have their partner and children drown” in the autobiographical novel Intimacy. Here, that deep attention to his own ego expands to the world around him and becomes fiercely illuminating. What a thrill it is to be here, he writes from the edge of the abyss, as well as frustrating and often boring.

The book ends with his marriage to Isabella, Elton John pulling up in a cherry-red Bentley. Kureishi is rawdogging life, he tells his son Sachin, in the gen Z sense of doing it without distraction: “I am compelled to be present”. Sex is difficult, but desire – for everything – remains. This exhilarating book looks death and decay in the face and asks: is that all you’ve got?

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: The NFL has a host of Hall of Fame caliber receivers. But which one is the best?
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Graham Searles
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Quarterbacks in 2026 have a series of dazzling weapons at their disposal. We rank the best of the receivers in the NFL at the moment

NB: We have restricted the list below to players in their prime years, so excellent, older receivers such as Mike Evans and Davante Adams have been left out.

The quality of receivers across the NFL at present is sky high. And Smith-Njigba is a cut above the rest. There are faster and more physical wideouts, but none have the precise, impossible to cover route running of JSN. Most receivers have a tell that hints at their next move. Not Smith-Njigba though: defensive backs have to guess and second guess his movements, which leads to consistent, easy separation and massive yardage totals.

The 24-year-old’s talent is so great that he quickly ended DK Metcalf’s time in Seattle and took over the offense, leading them to the Super Bowl last season. Smith-Njigba is the key to Seattle’s offense, not Sam Darnold at quarterback. Any league average passer could be elevated to playoff success throwing to Smith-Njigba.

After seven games this season he is closing in on 1,000 receiving yards. He almost broke 1,800 yards in 2025 but, at this pace, he could be the first NFL receiver to crack 2,000 yards in a season.

Not a lot was thought of Nacua heading into the 2023 draft. He was seen as a decent option as a slot receiver or a gadget guy. NFL analyst Lance Zierlein’s assessment wasn’t exactly glowing: “Nacua is an athletic wideout lacking the twitch or speed to attack man coverage at a successful rate. However, the ball skills and competitive nature he brings to the field give him a fighting chance to make a roster.”

Teams were put off by his lack of speed – his 40-yard dash was the 37th-best among wide receivers drafted in 2023 – and he fell to the Rams in the fifth round. But the NFL isn’t all about straight-line speed. He did well in the combine’s gauntlet drill – which involves running across the field while catching balls fired from either side – and Nacua reached the highest top speed of any receiver who did not miss a catch.

What’s even more special is how quickly he adapted to the NFL. His first game: 10 receptions for 119 yards. Lucky start? Nope. Game two: 147 yards. He had an off day on his third outing with “only” 72 yards. Game four he roared back with 163 yards and a touchdown. The only knock on the 25-year-old is his availability – he has only played all 17 games once in his career – and he has been mired in off-field issues. But when he’s on the field he has been ultra consistent, and could go for 1,500 yards this year, despite missing a couple of games.

The Bengals top receiver in yards this season is Tee Higgins by a wide margin, but Chase is still the leader – alongside Joe Burrow – of Cincinnati’s offense. That includes in the locker room too. On Sunday, Chase gave a stirring half-time speech after the Bengals went into the break 13-0 down.

“I came in here screaming, saying, ‘Somebody’s got to make a play for us, somebody got to make a play,’” Chase said after the game. “And I told our offense we can’t look at our defense the whole time. We’ve got to step this shit up and make something work.”

And they did. The Bengals scored five unanswered touchdowns to obliterate the Ravens for a vital victory in the ultra competitive AFC North. Chase’s elite speed, agility and phenomenal hands are a nightmare for defenders. He often starts seasons slowly, so expect great things to come from a player capable of unparalleled production. Chase’s has three career games of 200 or more receiving yards, the best in the NFL among active players.

The Vikings star is in a tricky spot. His talent is undeniable, as is his track record. At the start of the season his 8,480 yards receiving since 2020 were the most for any player in the first six years of their career. That total includes last year though, when Jefferson recorded his lowest total for receiving yards, touchdowns and first downs. Then again, he did have JJ McCarthy, Carson Wentz and Max Brosmer throwing him the ball.

And in another season in which Minnesota’s defense is doing the heavy lifting, Jefferson is still on good form despite an uninspiring cast of quarterbacks. He already has more touchdowns (3) than he did in the whole of last season, and there are signs that Kyler Murray could be able to give him the service he deserves.

Against the Saints, Murray went all-in with a fastball to Jefferson in the back of the endzone amid blanket coverage. It all looked so simple as Jefferson popped and came down with the ball, while falling backwards, for the touchdown. Hopefully Murray can give Jefferson a few more moments like that as the 6-0 Vikings builds towards the playoffs.

Zay Flowers, Amon-Ra St Brown, Chris Olave, CeeDee Lamb, Christian Watson, (honorary tight end inclusion) Trey McBride and Higgins all have a case here but Drake London gets the nod owing to untapped potential and immense physicality. He always appears to be open, thanks to a 6ft 4in frame, brilliant hands and great route running. He lacks speed but the 25-year-old is as close as it gets to a Mike Evans clone. He would be accruing similarly impressive stats if the Atlanta Falcons had more competent quarterback play. A rogues gallery of Desmond Ridder, Kirk Cousins, Marcus Mariota, Taylor Heinicke and Cooper Rush have stymied London’s numbers since he joined the NFL in 2022, but in 19 games with Michael Penix at quarterback he has 1,822 yards and 10 touchdowns. Penix is good but by no means great, and London still has much more to offer.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Everybody hates Pat: is a cabal of college kids really trying to bring down ESPN’s star meathead?
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Aaron Timms
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Pat McAfee’s reaction to a few mild jokes shows how the ubiquitous ESPN personality is happy to whip up a crowd into a hostile frenzy but is terrified of any criticism

It was all shaping up to be a golden year for Pat McAfee. The man who landed a five-year, $85m deal in 2023 to take The Pat McAfee Show to ESPN had cemented himself as the star attraction of the sports broadcaster’s bold new era of stunts, stupidity and memebrain swill. His persistently honking presence on the set of ESPN’s College GameDay had helped push ratings to new heights. ESPN executives were so impressed with McAfee they were reportedly in negotiations to award him a new contract worth between $60m and $65m a year; one even went so far as to describe him as a “generational” media talent.

Then, over the weekend, disaster struck. A handful of college kids attacked him online ahead of his appearance with College GameDay at the University of Utah. Well, “attacked” is maybe overstating things: they made a few mild jokes at his expense. But it was all too much for ESPN’s brightest blimp. Suddenly, McAfee’s world came crashing down. His initial reaction, to be fair, was mild: “The university’s Instagram account posted something talking a little trash about me last night, which I certainly love,” he said ahead of the Utes’ clash with the Houston Cougars last week.

But by Monday the narrative had changed. On his eponymous show, McAfee said he had “never felt more uncomfortable” than he did on the Utah campus, alluding to the assassination of Charlie Kirk as a reason for his unease: “I thought to myself: Has anything really scary happened at, like, a college gathering in the state of Utah recently? Do you think we should be amplifying reasons for why people hate my guts as a university? I don’t know.”

Well, Pat, neither do I. To read this comically melodramatic retelling of his time at Utah you might assume last week’s College GameDay was uncommonly vicious and antagonistic. Instead, it was the usual chop-up of hype, half-assed technical analysis and shouting, in which McAfee supplied his standard mix of meandering rants and basic crowd work and the gathered masses, in turn, responded with cheers and (good-natured) boos as expected. The video that McAfee implied had him fearing for his life, posted to the university’s Instagram and TikTok accounts, involved a handful of students poking very light fun at the ESPN host for ripping off his shirt on set (which he does often) and spouting “corny” lines in place of real analysis (ditto); one of McAfee’s would-be assassins even emphasized that “we love you bro” as he implored McAfee to “keep the shirt on”.

The wokes and the leftists are always the most precious snowflakes on earth until some kid does a mild impersonation of Pat McAfee ripping his top open; when that happens it’s a federal emergency and the national guard needs to be called in to set things right. Any more of this mild banter from the brutes and ingrates of the American undergraduate population and McAfee will be calling his buddy Donald Trump to request Secret Service protection.

Even more bizarre than McAfee’s amazingly thin-skinned overreaction to this absolute non-event is how seriously his claims of imminent danger to his life (stemming, once again, from a video in which a few students say they don’t want to see McAfee’s naked torso) have been taken by those around him. The school published a groveling apology for its actions and deleted the offending video from its social media channels, while ESPN issued a statement of support for McAfee and “the very real and valid concerns he has around safety and security”.

During his ascent at ESPN, McAfee has perfected all the attributes of a WWE-style heel – the gift for offense, the shirtlessness, the penchant for writhing on the ground like an upturned beetle – with the exception of one: he absolutely cannot stand it when he’s the butt of the joke. The man is a machine at whipping a crowd into a hostile frenzy then runs in fright the moment the first boos hit his ears. McAfee is perhaps the leading light of the rightwing sports bros who’ve come to prominence in the age of Trump: these men love sports, love their country, love their president, and are unsure what to make of women. Trump himself made his debut appearance on The Pat McAfee Show late last year, and over this summer McAfee was on hand to lend some primetime meat to the inaugural Patriot Games, the president’s Hitlerian exercise in uplift for the white youth of America.

It’s perhaps no surprise, then, that McAfee has absorbed completely the personality traits of the president: to the casual misogyny, the constant moaning about “woke”, the boorishness and the egomania can now be added McAfee’s Trumpian inability to take a joke or any kind of criticism, however mild or well-intentioned; in the deranged McAfee worldview it now seems even college kids, a big part of College GameDay’s own audience, are part of the shadowy network of villainy working to bring ESPN’s star beetroot down. Whether it’s punching across at critical media outlets or punching down at fans who don’t like the kind of shirt-ripping frattiness he’s introduced to College GameDay, McAfee never seems more engaged in his work than when snarling about the “rats”, “marks”, “losers” and “puppets” snapping at his feet.

It cannot be emphasized too much how stupid and overblown this whole concocted controversy is. What is really going on here? Is this all reflective of a desire for attention on McAfee’s part, another demonstration of his continuous need to make everything – in sport, on TV, in culture at large – About Him? Or is ESPN so heavily degraded and virality-brained now, so in thrall to the Magaverse and its perverse understanding of the world, that the empty suits who run the place genuinely feel the operation will collapse without a happy McAfee – placated and kept safe from the everyday terrorists roving the college campuses of America – at its core?

Perhaps it’s a bit of both. As Soft Pat’s star at ESPN has risen and he’s been handed more prestigious on-air assignments, the statements emanating from the C-suite hailing his “generational” and otherworldly talent have become more and more ludicrous; amid reports of his monster new contract, McAfee is now involved in Monday Night Football and there’s talk of potentially using his Super Bowl alt-cast for even higher honors on screen.

“Pat can do whatever he wants,” ESPN executive vice-president Mike Foss recently mused, and there’s a real sense that the whole network is under the spell of McAfee’s bare breast, that – if only as a cultural project – the erstwhile “Worldwide Leader in Sports” now belongs to McAfee. The wholesale enrollment of a once-proud network into the cult of McAfee does not reflect the man’s talent: he’s good for ratings, sure, but any old rightwing purplehead could curl up into a topless ball, screeching, and do what he does. Instead, it’s a sign of the profound confusion that has gripped traditional media in the post-cordcutting era of vertical video and endless slop. Nothing else works, seems to be the thinking; maybe this idiot will.

In another context, or another era, the TV triumph of the outcast, the oddball, the unlikely star might have heralded a deepening of the culture, a growing sophistication in our collective understanding of what it takes to be appealing as a popular media talent. But so much of what McAfee represents is the kind of meatheaded insensitivity that sports broadcasting – with its polish and professionalism – was historically designed to supersede, especially at a place like ESPN. Figures like McAfee drag us all back into the frathouse, the kegger, the swamp, and now they won’t even let us joke about it.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Democratic lawmakers decry Osha’s push to roll back worker respiratory protections
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Michael Sainato
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Elizabeth Warren and others joined by unions and industry experts in warning against the weakening of regulations

The senator Elizabeth Warren, the congresswoman Ilhan Omar and several other Democratic lawmakers are calling on the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Osha) to abandon a rollback of respirator mask regulations, a change the lawmakers say would weaken worker protections against hazardous substances.

Under the proposed rules, employers would face fewer requirements to provide workers with respirators masks when working with substances including “lead, asbestos, formaldehyde and inorganic arsenic, among other chemicals”, the lawmakers wrote in a letter to the Osha assistant secretary, David Keeling, a former UPS and Amazon executive.

The agency is also trying to end a requirement for employers to provide medical evaluations to employees who wear specific types of respirators in their work, the letter noted.

Lawmakers said the rules show how the Department of Labor, the parent department of Osha, “is endangering workers and prioritizing the interests of unscrupulous employers over Americans who work hard to provide for their families”, according to the letter.

On average, more than 5,000 Americans die annually from occupation-related respiratory illnesses. In recent years, the rates of silicosis and coal-related worker’s pneumoconiosis have been on the rise due to artificial stone used for countertops and increased silica exposure in coal seams.

The lawmakers noted that the agency issued the proposed rules in July 2025 without providing required evidence or requesting information needed to implement them. They also criticized the agency for holding a procedural hearing in August, during Congress’s recess when no lawmakers were on Capitol Hill to discuss the rules.

“Most Osha standards take years to move through the same steps these respirator rules have [moved through] in a matter of months,” the lawmakers wrote.

The letter was also signed by the senators Chris Van Hollen and Cory Booker; the congresswomen Pramila Jayapal, Rashida Tlaib and Jasmine Crockett; and more than 20 other congressional Democrats.

Unions and medical and industry experts, including the Advisory Committee on Construction Safety and Health, the American Industrial Hygiene Association, National Nurses United and North America’s Building Trades Unions, have warned Osha against pulling back standards.

The Associated General Contractors of America, a construction industry trade association, said in a comment against the rules that “quality safety regulations save contractors money in the long run and any deregulatory benefits associated with the proposed rule will be outweighed by potential liability down the line”.

Lawmakers said the rollback is part of a broader deregulatory effort at Osha under the Trump administration, which had proposed more than 60 deregulatory rule changes in the Department of Labor last year.

“The Trump administrations claims that it is a ‘champion of the American worker’, but the [labor department] has demonstrated its disregard for workers’ lives by trying to roll back the regulations that keep workers safe – even when industry leaders, safety experts and workers raise the alarm,” the letter said.

Republicans have proposed to cut Osha’s budget by over 8% for fiscal year 2027. In 2025, Osha inspections dropped by 20% and the agency lost 223 full-time employees to buyouts and early retirements amid efforts to significantly cull the federal workforce during Trump’s second term.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: New elementary school in Texas named after beloved longtime school custodian
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Marilyn Hampton, who regularly bought supplies for and gave rides to children, was honored at public meeting

US schools are often named after presidents, historical figures and civil rights leaders. And soon joining those ranks is a retired longtime Texas school custodian known for going above and beyond her duties by buying classroom supplies for children in need and helping students with their assignments.

That heartwarming story centers on Marilyn Hampton, whose former employer of 39 years – the Aubrey independent school district (AISD) – recently moved to rename its new elementary school No 5 in her honor.

The AISD’s tribute, announced at a 21 October governing board meeting recorded on video, brought Hampton to joyful tears and quickly went viral among circles dedicated to promoting uplifting news stories.

“I still can’t believe it,” Hampton later told the Dallas-Forth Worth news outlet WFAA. “I haven’t stopped crying.”

Before retiring in 2022, Hampton spent 39 years as an AISD custodian. But, as officials would later say, she took on much more than custodial work in her role, assisting students with their classwork; buying and delivering them school supplies if they needed them; and staffing the ticket booth at football games.

Thousands of AISD students, teachers and staff members came to draw inspiration from Hampton’s commitment, according to the district’s superintendent, Shannon Saylor.

So the AISD ultimately decided to invite her to its October meeting under the guise of speaking about a particular school-related issue – then Saylor asked her to unroll a red carpet and read what was emblazoned on it in navy blue letters.

“She may not have the official title of an educator – but she was in every meaningful sense a teacher and educator at heart,” Saylor remarked in reference to the namesake of the new school under construction and scheduled to open in August.

An emotional Hampton replied, “Y’all are too good.” Covering her mouth, she continued: “I wasn’t expecting this. Thank y’all. I love all of y’all – always miss y’all.”

She then composed herself and gazed at a monitor with an AI rendering of the school and a sign on it bearing her name. “They better keep it clean,” Hampton joked, eliciting loud laughter among those at the meeting.

When she reflected on the distinction with WFAA, she wore a new Marilyn Hampton elementary school T-shirt and recounted how she was the only one of eight siblings to graduate high school. She told the station she used to consider herself a failure for not going to college – but in time became “very happy with the way things turned out”.

She added: “I just thought, You know, Marilyn? God put you where you are supposed to be.’”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: FTC orders Delta, Uber and others to hand over data on algorithmic pricing
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Heather Timmons in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Regulator demands companies explain how and why they charge different prices for the same product or service

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is demanding some of the US’s biggest airlines, ride-share companies and retailers divulge how they are using algorithms and loyalty programs to target customers and drivers with different prices and wages.
