Nine companies – Delta, United, JetBlue, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Target and Walmart – were named in the inquiry, which comes after investigations and lawsuits alleging consumers are charged different prices based on their buying histories and drivers paid different fares based on their personal histories.

The FTC will “scrutinize the opaque methodology that some companies in these industries may be using to determine how much consumers pay or how much gig workers are paid for the same product or service”, chair Andrew Ferguson said in a statement.

US family budgets already burdened by inflation are being gouged by opaque and sometimes deceptive store pricing practices, including surveillance pricing and overcharges by Dollar General and convenience stores.

The FTC is tasked with policing “unfair or deceptive acts or practices” in industries except banking and airlines, which means it can not impose any fines or regulations on the airlines named. While the Trump administration has rolled back corporate regulations, the FTC’s consumer protection division has joined with states in some instances to pursue legal action and penalties against some companies.

Companies must “turn over information that will allow the agency to assess whether the pricing for a ticket, ride share, food delivery or other product or service varies from one person to the next based on factors such as participation in loyalty programs or analysis of personal data by super-intelligence algorithms”, the FTC said.

Several states have begun introducing legislation to ban surveillance pricing and electronic shelf labels that could be used to set different prices based on shoppers habits and online information.

The probe follows a July 2024 inquiry by the Biden administration into surveillance pricing, which demanded information from McKinsey, JPMorgan Chase and others that offered surveillance pricing products to consumer-facing companies.

“Details like a person’s precise location or browser history can be frequently used to target individual consumers with different prices for the same goods and services,” the FTC found in January of 2025.

Whether the inquiry will result in substantial changes in consumer laws or company practices is unclear.

“What we have seen so far is that they have not been using these studies that produce meaningful reports that ultimately lead to any rule-making changes,” said Rohit Chopra, a former FTC commissioner who is now head of California’s new Business and Consumer Protection Agency.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Was Ralph Nader right about (almost) everything? His challenge to Democrats ahead of the midterm elections
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Heather Timmons in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
‘Really change things for the working class,’ the ex-presidential candidate says

A corporate plutocracy. A broken healthcare system. Massive and widening inequality. Cash-soaked elections. Angry people struggling to pay their bills and disgusted with lawmakers in Washington DC.

Nearly everything that pushed famed consumer-rights advocate Ralph Nader to launch the 2000 presidential run that made him a political pariah in Washington is front and center as the US gears up for the 2026 midterm elections. But this time, things are much, much worse.

Nader, now 92, has been seething from his home in northwest Washington as the Trump administration rips the guts out of the hard-fought consumer and safety protections he built in the 1960s and 1970s. He’s once again calling for a revolution in a Democratic party that still wants nothing to do with him.

“The best thing that could happen for the Democrats is for [Senator Chuck] Schumer and [Hakeem] Jeffries to be voted out in January,” Nader told the Guardian during one of several long phone calls, speaking of the Democratic leaders in both houses of Congress.

If Democrats win next week, they need to be bold to fix the country, Nader said: prosecute corruption, restore the federal agencies that have been destroyed, and really change things for the working class. He doubts Schumer and Jeffries will do it.

“You think they’re going to have that kind of energy and courage?” Nader said. “They have no stomach for that. They’re going to drag the Democratic party down. People want justice.”

As Democrats and their allies seek to defeat Trumpism and restore the US’s teetering democracy, it would be easy to dismiss Nader as a tragic footnote amid the current chaos: the man, although he and his allies vehemently disagree, whose run as a Green party presidential candidate cost Al Gore the presidency and left George W Bush in control.

But the ideas he’s preached for decades, rooted in the New Deal ideals that built the US into an economic powerhouse, are front and center in the midterms and beyond, after a failure to address the woes of working-class Americans opened the door to Trumpism.

For Nader, and many others, the central question is: does anyone in US politics have the fight to fix what’s wrong?

A series of progressive wins in the Democratic primaries and a flood of cash to Republicans has put everything on the table, from taxing billionaires to raising minimum wage to ‘Medicare for all’ to campaign finance reform. Even the left’s most moderating voices and a few Republicans agree it’s time to rein in the power and influence of big business.

Democrats “believe in regulated capitalism, and that we have overdone the capitalism and underdone the regulation”, said Matt Bennett, whose Third Way thinktank pushes moderate ideas. “The fact that we have a trillionaire who is trying to control American politics is pretty good evidence of that,” he added, speaking of Elon Musk’s Republican donations – now over $442m for the midterm elections.

“There’s a prairie fire rebellion taking place across America today,” said Barry Lynn, director of the Open Markets Institute, an anti-monopoly thinktank in Washington. “Tax policy is not enough,” he said. “People want revolutionary change.”

As a lawyer in his 30s working with political heavyweight Daniel Patrick Moynihan, then a labor department official, on auto safety, Nader was thrust into the national spotlight after he wrote “Unsafe At Any Speed” that blamed car design instead of what the industry used to call “the nut behind the wheel” for the high rate of US auto deaths.

After he appeared before a congressional hearing in 1966 to testify about his findings, General Motors hired private investigators to, as Nader later said, “obtain lurid details” about his private life.

When the sting was reported, the then GM’s president, James Roche, publicly apologized and Nader sued. He used the $425,000 invasion of privacy settlement as seed money to build a team of hundreds of lawyers, dubbed “Nader’s Raiders” who investigated everything from airline safety to air quality to the radiation being emitted from television sets, and left a trail of new laws and federal agencies in their wake.

Big business hasn’t faced as much pushback in the United States since, with the notable exception of the Consumer Finance Protection Bureau (CFPB) created by Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren after Wall Street created the 2008 financial crisis.

Republicans, led by the Trump administration, have been trying to destroy the CFPB for a decade and appear to be close to succeeding. After Joe Biden’s administration stepped up enforcement of predatory practices, reexamined monopolies, and championed labor rights, Trump’s White House has gone the opposite direction.

What Nader was able to do during the 1960s and 1970s isn’t going to work today. New rules for how businesses should act happened because of the energy in Congress then and Nader’s ability “to create an advocacy model and push through a lot of legislation and policy where business wasn’t ready for it and the times were demanding it”, explains Robert Weissman, the co-president of Public Citizen, one of groups Nader founded.

“The problem now is the times demand it and people want it but business is organized against it,” Weissman said. “It’s not that we’re not trying hard enough. There’s a different kind of pushback.” Federal lobbying, or money businesses and other groups spend trying to influence policy set in Washington hit a record of $5.13bn in 2025, a 250% increase from 1998. Trade groups representing industry, realtors and drug companies are top donors.

At the same time, “we’re dealing with an administration that’s both carrying water for corporations and wrecking regulatory agencies, against the backdrop of a hostile court system,” Weissman said.

Vermont senator Bernie Sanders ran presidential campaigns on these issues in 2016 and Sanders and Warren in 2020. But no one has become an effective national champion for them in the way Nader did at his zenith. He was plastered on magazine covers and topped most-trusted polls, appeared on Saturday Night Live and Phil Donahue’s talk show, and had the ear of presidents, Congress and major news organizations.

“It’s almost infuriating that we don’t have somebody helming a consumer movement in this country given how central these issues are to the national conversation,” said Lindsay Owens, the president of Groundwork Collaborative, a Washington research and policy group pushing new laws to curb algorithmic pricing and other pro-consumer moves.

And no, Sanders, 85, doesn’t want to talk to him either. “Bernie hasn’t called me back in 25 years,” Nader said.

Nader once cornered Sanders in the Senate barbershop while the senator was getting a shave. “He couldn’t run away,” Nader recalled, so he grilled him about why the senator wasn’t meeting with him or other public advocates and organizers. “Look, he doesn’t want to be associated with me because of the way they tainted me on 2000,” he said.

Nader remains undeterred. He backed an impeachment seminar in July and predicted Trump could step down this month. Recently, he has been dialing progressive candidates including Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Maine’s Troy Jackson directly, to present his policy plan he thinks would guarantee their midterm success even as money pours into Republican opponents. On the agenda: higher wages, universal health insurance, putting “corporate crooks” in jail and impeaching Trump. “The better their agenda, the less money they need” to win, he said.

Nader’s not optimistic about big changes if Democrats win both houses of Congress, however. “They’ll break open the champagne and go back to business as normal and start raising more money for 2028,” he predicts. “I can predict ‘em like you predict the sun coming up every morning,” he added.

The 2000 presidential election that unexpectedly put Bush into power catapulted the country into a fresh round of corporate tax cuts and deregulation, as well as the disastrous Iraq war. Some liberals point to it as a turning point, marking the death of bipartisanship and politicalization of the supreme court.

Nader was first recruited to run for president in 1996 by a Green party dismayed by, among other things, Democratic president Bill Clinton’s welfare reform. The goal was to capture enough of the popular vote to cross the 5% threshold for a public funding grant in the next election, ushering in a new era of three-party politics in a country dominated by two for over 130 years.

Republicans and Democrats had cozied up to corporate power so completely that citizens and citizens groups like the ones he founded couldn’t do much any more, Nader said. “King Corporation rules in Washington DC,” he said in a May 2000 speech. “We have a government of the Exxon’s, by the General Motors, for the DuPonts.”

“He wanted to get his message out but he also wanted to help the Green party get 5% of the vote so they could build as an organization,” said two-time former campaign manager Theresa Amato, a lawyer and public advocate.

A precursor to Sanders’ presidential campaign, Nader drew thousands of young people in massive rallies. He was joined onstage by celebrities including Susan Sarandon, Patti Smith, Ani DiFranco and Eddie Vedder.

He started his run promising not to campaign in swing states that could have cost Gore the election, but changed his mind after he was blocked from the presidential debate, filmmaker Michael Moore, a Nader supporter, recalled in a 2020 podcast. “That’s when things went awry for Ralph,” he believes.

Stepping aside wasn’t an option. “There was an immense amount of pressure” to exit the race in late 2000, Amato said. “Nader’s view was that we could not abandon our supporters, all the volunteers and donors, and the embryonic US Green party, that had mobilized for the campaign and just drop out at the last minute.”

While 2000 was its most successful year, the Green party eked out less than 3% of the popular vote. In Florida, Nader got nearly 100,000 votes. When a 5-4 supreme court decision halted a recount in the state, Bush had 537 more votes, giving him Florida’s 25 electoral college votes and the presidency.

Gore didn’t even win his home state, Tennessee (Bill Clinton won there twice). Other third party candidates and a faulty ballot likely played a role. Patrick Buchanan’s ‘Reform party’ got nearly 17,500 in Florida; Stanford University researchers found Palm Beach County’s confusingly designed “butterfly ballot” caused more than 2,000 Gore voters to vote by mistake for Buchanan there alone.

At one point, Gore sent him a letter, Nader recalls, absolving him of responsibility. Gore declined several requests for an interview. He is “overbooked”, a spokesperson said.

Nader was suddenly an outcast. “He was no longer invited onto talk shows, he wasn’t invited to anything. He was a pariah,” Moore explained.

That hasn’t changed as the economic red flags he warned about proved true. Nader “played a very steep reputational price for being the Cassandra” of the situation the US is in now, said Steve Skrovan, producer of “An Unreasonable Man,” a 2006 documentary about Nader and the 2000 presidential election.

Today’s corporate overreach “would not have happened had the so-called ‘opposition party’ not ceded the ground for this through their own neglect and corporatization,” Skrovan said.

Nader remains unapologetic. “The Democrats are scapegoaters on steroids,” he said. “They never look at themselves in the mirror and say ‘How can we not have landslided this bumbling governor from Texas with a horrible record who couldn’t string three sentences together?,’” he said, referring to Bush.

They did it again in 2016, he added, when Donald Trump beat Hillary Clinton. “Imagine blaming Jill Stein, who got a few votes in Pennsylvania,” he added, speaking of the Green party candidate who got 1% of the vote, running on a $15 minimum wage and guaranteed health care. “What if you picked up her agenda? You would have won in a landslide, you idiots.”

The 2000 election was a pivotal moment for the Democratic party’s finances too. That’s when Tony Coelho “revolutionized the party, placing fundraising above ideology as the Democratic credo”, the New York Times wrote in 1999, as he was placed at the head of Gore’s campaign.

In the years since, the amount of corporate donations for both Democrats and Republicans has skyrocketed. They got an extra boost from the 2010 Citizens United supreme court decision that allowed big business to openly back candidates.

Taxing the wealthy and making companies treat their workers and customers better are highly popular with voters. Republicans crafted a long-term plan to use non-economic ideas to drive wedges into the coalition that passed reforms supporting these ideas in the first half of the 1900s, Pat Buchanan, a consultant to Republican presidents Richard Nixon, Gerald Ford, and Ronald Reagan explained in “An Unreasonable Man”. “You did this with social, cultural issues. You carve off all their issues which do not conflict with your own…and keep hammering and hammering them,” Buchanan said.

To win votes on economic issues, Democrats are going to have to turn against their donors and brave an onslaught of lobbying and campaign cash against them. It’s about time, some progressive strategists believe.

“You spent a generation cozying up to these guys, and there’s no middle class anymore,” Dan Geldon, senator Warren’s former chief of staff, who worked on her 2020 campaign.

The Democratic party’s infighting and Trump’s recentering of the Republican party around white supremacy, a nationalist foreign policy and more power for companies and the wealthy come as fewer and fewer Americans want either party.

The percentage of US voters who consider themselves “independent” hit a record high of 45% in late 2025, Gallup polling shows. For gen Z voters, born between 1997 and 2007, that figure is a record 56%, up from 40% for the same-aged voters in 1992.

“Workers need rights and representation in this world,” Dan Osborn, who is running for Senate from Nebraska as an independent, told the Guardian. “Otherwise, they’ll work you to death and not pay hardly anything,” he said. Osborn, a union leader, led a strike at Kellogg’s Nebraska plant after the company said it would offshore jobs and cut benefits while showering investors with stock buy-backs.

“To me, it’s all about standing up for the little guy, and I didn’t see anybody doing that,” he said, explaining why he is running. Osborn lost handily in 2024 to Republican incumbent Deb Fischer. Going into the midterm election, he’s trailing Pete Ricketts, a Republican whose father is a billionaire. Going into the midterm election, Ricketts has a slight lead in the polls.

For his part, Nader has some more uncomfortable predictions. “Someone asked me decades ago, ‘What’s going to cause the end of the world?’ And my answer was science and technology in the hands of giant corporations and dictatorships’ “ Nader said. “We’re right on track.”

Citizens still have the power to change everything, Nader said, by organizing themselves to demand Congress pass something revolutionary like universal healthcare. Maybe a popular podcaster like Joe Rogan could jumpstart the movement, he said. He hasn’t been able to get through to Rogan, though.

“It’s still ‘We the people’ in the Constitution. It’s not ‘We the Congress’ or ‘We the Corporation,’” Nader said. All we need is “the people to just get off their ass.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: New Mexico megachurch endorses Republican candidates, testing federal ban
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Cecilia Nowell
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Legacy Church’s endorsements violate law banning tax-exempt nonprofits from endorsing political candidates

A megachurch in New Mexico has endorsed two Republican candidates running in this year’s midterms, including a Donald Trump-backed candidate running in one of the blue state’s few competitive races. The church’s endorsements, which violate federal law banning tax-exempt nonprofits from endorsing political candidates, come as the Trump administration is challenging that ban in federal court.

In mid-August, pastor Steve Smothermon of Legacy Church, a nondenominational church with nine locations across the state, told his congregation about one of the candidates: “Greg Cunningham has faithfully served our church for 14 years and shares our biblical values. Let’s pray for him, support his campaign, get registered, and vote to flip this seat for someone who will stand for God, our Constitution, and a better New Mexico!”

Greg Cunningham, a Republican, is currently running to unseat Democratic Representative Gabriel Vasquez. Recent polling shows Vasquez receiving 48% of the vote to Cunningham’s 44%. In 2024, Vasquez was one of 13 Democrats across the country who won his House race in a district that voted for Donald Trump.

In hopes of maintaining their narrow majorities, Republican congressional leaders have traveled to New Mexico to campaign for Cunningham. House speaker Mike Johnson has stumped for Cunningham twice, and Senate Majority Leader Steve Scalise campaigned in southern New Mexico in late October. Trump endorsed Cunningham, the only candidate from New Mexico he has weighed in on, in a Truth Social post in April.

Two months after endorsing Cunningham, Smothermon also endorsed Gregg Hull, the Republican candidate for governor. In a 6 October social media post, Smothermon wrote, “Gregg Hull should be the next governor of New Mexico,” and encouraged his followers to “Stand up and vote your biblical worldview.”

Smothermon has drawn criticism for years for endorsing candidates in state and local elections. His disputes with local politicians have made headlines since at least 2011, and in 2014 the church gave parishioners sample ballots with the names of the candidates it supported highlighted. In 2021, Smothermon told parishioners who to vote for in a city council race, and in 2022, he told members of his church to vote for Republican gubernatorial candidate Mark Ronchetti, calling the current Democratic governor “demonic”. The Freedom from Religion Foundation, a nonprofit focused on the separation of church and state, later filed a complaint with the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) over Legacy’s involvement in the 2022 election.

That year, Legacy Church made headlines when Smothermon told his congregation that Ronchetti had confided in him that, if elected, he would ban abortion in the state. After the 2022 election, it emerged that Solomon Peña, a state house candidate who hired hitmen to fire at the homes of several New Mexico Democratic leaders after he lost his race, had attended Legacy Church.

“For the last 2.5 centuries, resisting censorship has been a cornerstone of our republic, so we knew laws curtailing it were unconstitutional and therefore null and void – especially for political speech,” Smothermon said in a statement to the Guardian. “Add to that a government manufactured health crisis as an excuse to shutter Churches and other institutions that rival or limit a pervasive overlord state and we realized very quickly that silence in the face of such tyranny was not an option. Further, in stark contrast to most government programs, we do social work that actually works rather than enabling social ills, so we earn every bit of our tax status.”

Legacy has been tied to several other scandals in the state. In 2020, Smothermon’s nephew was sentenced to 45-years in prison for abducting two men, mutilating and dismembering one of them, after he believed they stole money and drugs from his home. And in 2024, a patient of a residential drug treatment facility that the church operated sued the facility for sexual abuse. The facility and Legacy Church both deny the claims, saying the lawsuit was “riddled with spurious allegations”.

The church has otherwise made headlines for protesting against same-sex marriage, school bathroom policies and Covid-19 precautions. It hosted Charlie Kirk for one of his last public appearances in August 2025.

“I very literally would not be here if not for Charlie. He visited my church and he inspired me to take a stand and answer a call to serve on this new battlefield,” Cunningham said during a speech at the Republican National Convention in September. Cunningham saw Kirk speak at Legacy Church, which he called “a home away from home” in a campaign video.

Although still illegal, the Trump administration has tried to challenge the law banning churches from endorsing political candidates. In 2017, during his first term in office, Trump promised to “totally destroy” the Johnson amendment, the 1954 law barring tax-exempt nonprofits such as churches from making political endorsements. That year, he signed an executive order limiting the treasury department’s enforcement of the law.

After he was re-elected in 2024, Trump resumed efforts to chip away at the Johnson amendment. In 2025, the administration’s Internal Revenue Service issued a court filing saying churches could endorse political candidates to their congregations. Although a court blocked the IRS’s proposal, Trump’s justice department appealed the ruling in September.

Religious institutions, particularly evangelical churches, are increasingly testing the limits of federal laws barring electioneering. According to a recent analysis from researchers at the University of Notre Dame, Dartmouth and the University of Pennsylvania, 14.7% of churches engaged in direct political advocacy and endorsements during the three months surrounding the 2024 election.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Flávio Bolsonaro’s defeat is a major blow to Trump and his orange wave
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Tom Phillips in São Paulo
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
The far-right candidate was supposed to claim the presidency, but Brazilian voters had other ideas

For Donald Trump, Brazil’s presidential election was meant to represent the crest of the “orange wave” – a three-year surge of rightwing triumphs that has reshaped Latin American politics in the US president’s tangerine-hued image.

The far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, was supposed to claim the presidency on Sunday, bringing the region’s biggest democracy and economy into Trump’s orbit, after similar victories in Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Honduras, Ecuador and Peru – not to mention the capture of Venezuela’s government after the country was invaded in January.

But Brazilian voters had other ideas, turning out in huge numbers to vote against the pro-Trump populist and return the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, to power. On Tuesday, as Lula celebrated his 81st birthday to the sound of samba in Brasília, Bolsonaro fled to Miami on a private jet.

“This is a significant blow, indisputably, to Trump’s regional strategy,” Benjamin Gedan, the director of the Stimson Center’s Latin America programme, said of Bolsonaro’s defeat.

“[Trump] was perceived to be steamrolling over South America, having invaded Venezuela and seen close allies win elections in Argentina and Chile, in Bolivia and Colombia. That momentum had given the impression that he could determine political outcomes throughout Latin America – and he clearly enjoyed it,” added Gedan, a former White House South America adviser.

“This is a region where he was really perceived to have a successful foreign policy, and this just flies in the face of that image.”

The US setback was celebrated in China, whose rapidly growing influence in Latin America Trump has been trying to combat with his so-called “Donroe doctrine” of regional domination. “[Lula has] effectively thwarted Trump’s strategy for the region … Trump failed to bring Brazil, the largest nation in South America, under his sway,” Hu Xijin, a prominent Beijing propagandist, enthused on X.

Trump has responded to his ally’s failure by halfheartedly querying the election, which Lula won by 4.3m votes.

“I think the election was really strange … It’s so terrible to see,” he told reporters. “But I wasn’t involved,” Trump added, despite a months-long campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure apparently designed to boost Bolsonaro.

Despite Trump’s decision to offer shelter to Bolsonaro – who is facing several criminal investigations in Brazil – many observers suspect the US president is unlikely to pick a major fight with Lula over his rightwing ally’s plight.

“One of Trump’s good qualities - and I mean this sincerely, even though it sounds ironic – is that he can smell a loser, and he wants to be around winners,” said Michael Paarlberg, a former Latin America adviser to Bernie Sanders.

Paarlberg noted how Trump got along with leftist “winners” including Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani – and even Lula himself. “I like Lula, I get along with him very well,” Trump said this week.

“He will certainly favour his ideological co-partisans,” Paarlberg said of Trump, “but if the stink of loserdom starts to waft over them, he will drop them.”

The “stink of loserdom” certainly wafted over Bolsonaro as he fled into Argentina on Tuesday and caught a private jet to Florida, where he briefly declared himself Brazil’s “true president-elect” before apparently changing his mind.

Brazilian social networks filled with memes mocking the far-right politician who, only hours earlier, had vowed to stay in Brazil to lead opposition to Lula.

One particularly scathing internet joke featured a photo of Bolsonaro and a parody of his movement’s fascist-inspired slogan, which was: “God, Homeland, and Family.” “Goodbye, Homeland and Family,” it said.

Speaking at his birthday party, Lula said: “This is what the Bolsonaro family is like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US.”

Lula’s chief foreign policy adviser, Celso Amorim, claimed Bolsonaro’s movement – which was founded by his jailed father, former president Jair Bolsonaro – was dead in the water after Sunday’s defeat, although the losing candidate secured 59.8m votes.

“I think Bolsonarismo was defeated once and for all,” Amorim said, recalling how the movement had lost two successive elections to Lula, in 2022 and 2026.

Amorim predicted a more reasonable conservative movement would replace Bolsonaro’s “extremist” one and called his loss “the last gasp of a radical, irrational, lying right wing”.

Under Lula, Amorim indicated Brazil would not join Trump’s controversial Shield of the Americas “counter-cartel coalition” – as Bolsonaro had planned to do.

But Amorim also signalled Lula would pursue pragmatic ties with Washington. “[Trump] has a certain level of pragmatism. They know Brazil isn’t just any old country. So I think we’ll seek to have proper, balanced relations without failing to defend our interests, but without being needlessly hostile, as we’ve always tried to do,” he said, recalling Lula’s good rapport with George W Bush.

Amorim attributed Trump’s questioning of Brazil’s election to “incorrect things” that “rightwing radicals from the state department” had put on his desk.

On Monday, Trump’s former chief strategist, Steve Bannon, urged Trump and secretary of state Marco Rubio to sever diplomatic and trade relations and “shut down everything with Brazil” as a result of the election supposedly being “stolen up in your face”.

Paarlberg said Trump’s remarks – criticizing the election, but emphasising his fondness of Lula – suggested he would not take Bannon’s advice.

“I read that as: ‘I will give you [Bolsonaro] moral support, but nothing else’,” Paarlberg said. “He certainly wasn’t saying: ‘I’m going to call for further tariffs, or further visa sanctions or any further actual measures to try to punish the Lula government.”

Gedan was unsure about Trump’s next move. “Anything’s possible, and I’m certain he has no idea how he’s going to approach it either,” he said.

But Gedan believed Trump and Lula could patch things up – perhaps striking a deal involving Brazil’s massive critical mineral reserves - despite Trump’s hopes of a “glorious return” for the Bolsonaros being dashed.

“There’s actually quite a bit of space for a positive relationship, if Trump does not decide to explode US-Brazil relations,” he said. “I think you absolutely could see Trump finding a way to admire Lula’s political skills.”

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: A new wave of electric ferries is here in the US. Some even fly
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Ben Tracy of Climate Central
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Replacing diesel-powered ferries with electric vessels could reduce emissions and improve air quality

Cutting through New York Harbor in the shadow of the Statue of Liberty, the small white boat we were riding on caught the attention of passengers aboard a nearby sightseeing ferry.

“It’s quite a curiosity at the moment,” Eric Laakmann, the chief executive and co-founder of Vessev, said.

His company builds fully electric hydrofoil boats. These vessels use underwater “wings” to lift their hulls above the surface as they pick up speed. By raising the boat out of the water, the design dramatically reduces drag, one of the biggest obstacles to making boats more energy-efficient.

“We’re picking up speed. We’re going for a takeoff,” Laakmann said as the boat rapidly accelerated.

The hydrofoils lifted the hull about a foot and a half above the water. Almost immediately, the ride transformed. The familiar slap of the boat pushing through waves became a smooth, almost airborne glide.

The hydrofoil effect is more than a novelty. Water creates significant resistance, and overcoming it takes energy. Electrifying boats is a challenge because batteries are heavy, and that extra weight increases the power needed to move the vessel. Hydrofoils may offer a solution. By lifting much of the hull out of the water, they reduce drag, allowing a vessel to move more efficiently.

“We substantially reduce the drag that you feel and that’s really what makes electrification viable,” Laakmann said.

Vessev says its hydrofoil design cuts drag by about 66%. That greater efficiency allows the boats to carry smaller battery packs, reducing both weight and cost.

But efficiency is only part of the equation. Making a boat electric is not simply a matter of replacing a diesel engine with a motor and battery. Operators must also consider how far a vessel needs to travel, how many passengers it carries, how quickly it must recharge, and how much weight it can accommodate.

Vessev operates passenger services in New Zealand and is expanding to Australia. In the US, its first service is planned for Lake Tahoe. Laakmann sees a future in which electric vessels become a routine part of public transportation, rather than a niche attraction.

“More like subways, more like buses, more like Ubers, more like taxis but on the water,” he said.

Waterways can connect communities and move passengers without adding more vehicles to crowded roads. When powered by increasingly clean electricity, electric ferries can also cut the pollution associated with diesel engines.

Transportation remains the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the United States, according to federal environmental data. Road vehicles account for much of that pollution, but ships and other watercraft also burn fossil fuels. Replacing diesel-powered ferries with electric vessels could reduce emissions and improve air quality around busy waterfronts.

Vessev is not alone in pursuing the technology. In Stockholm, commuters are already riding electric hydrofoil ferries built by the Swedish company Candela. The company says its design can reduce energy use by as much as 80% compared with conventional vessels of a similar type. Norway has ordered 20 of its electric hydrofoil boats for coastal service.

For ferry operators, the attraction is not simply environmental. More efficient designs and advances in battery technology are opening up routes for electric boats that might once have been impractical. There is also the potential for lower operating costs as fuel prices soar.

“I think in a more sustainable future we’re likely to see more and more vessels like this around the world,” Laakmann said.

In San Francisco, the city’s largest ferry operator carries about 3.5 million passengers a year, according to Seamus Murphy, who leads the agency. The network serves a region shaped by water, with commuters relying on boats to cross the bay and reach the city.

Yet the fleet runs entirely on fossil fuels. All 18 vessels in the system are powered by diesel. That is set to change as the agency prepares to add four battery-powered ferries over the next two years. It is part of an electric overhaul worth about half a billion dollars that also includes charging infrastructure at docks.

Unlike a car that can be plugged in at home overnight, a ferry may need to complete repeated trips on a fixed timetable. Its batteries must provide enough energy for the route, while shore-side chargers deliver enough power during the time the vessel spends at the terminal.

Making that work requires more than the right boat. Operators must coordinate vessel range, timetables and charging capacity to keep passengers moving without disrupting service. San Francisco won’t initially be using hydrofoil boats, but the agency says its new vessels will make it the first ferry operator in the United States to run high-speed, all-electric ferries.

For transit agencies, climate goals alone rarely justify a major fleet overhaul. The numbers have to add up.

Battery-powered ferries generally require a larger initial investment in vessels and charging equipment. But electric motors can be more efficient than diesel engines, and operators may save money over time on fuel and maintenance. Murphy said rising diesel costs and improvements in battery technology strengthened the case for making the switch.

“You make the upfront investment at the beginning and then you save over time and at the end of the day you’re going to have lower costs in the long term,” he said.

The financial case depends a lot on the route. Batteries remain heavy and expensive, charging infrastructure can be costly, and not every route is suited to a fully electric vessel. Long distances, tight schedules and limited opportunities to recharge can all complicate the transition.

The shift could create opportunities well beyond the water. For San Francisco’s expansion, the boats and their batteries are being built in the United States. This could create opportunities for domestic manufacturing jobs.

For Murphy, the transition is a chance to cut pollution while helping develop new business for shipbuilders and battery manufacturers.

“These jobs are going to get created in other countries and we have an ability to create them here if we manage this in the right way,” Murphy said. “We don’t want to be left behind,” he added.

Climate Central is an independent group of scientists and communicators who research and report the facts about our changing climate and how it affects people’s lives.

https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.title: The secret life of the scream park: fear, fainting, clowns – and ‘code brown’
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.author: Elle Hunt. Photographs and video by Ali Smith
https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2026/.text:
At Norfolk’s ‘premier scare attraction’ there are ghouls, chainsaws, satanic cults and a haunted hospital. But what goes on behind the scenes?

‘We always say to the scare actors, you’re going to think the boys will be the worst. They are not.” Backstage at PrimEvil, billed as “Norfolk’s premier scare attraction”, park director Ben Francis is sharing the advice he gives each year to his new crop of performers, before they set out to give punters the fright of their lives – or at least their Saturday night. As Francis covers each demographic, he ticks them off on his fingers. Teenage boys “scream like banshees, and run in packs”. Teenage girls tend towards being unimpressed: “Do your scare and move on, because they will get nasty.” And mixed groups? “There will be an alpha and he’ll be wearing a North Face top.” Francis’s advice is to not waste time. “He will not react to anything … Aim for the weaker one at the back.”

This is part of the workplace induction at PrimEvil, one of many immersive “scream parks” that pop up across the UK in the lead up to Halloween. For about £40 a ticket, groups of all ages spend the night roaming themed attractions and being terrorised by actors and special effects. Though the risks are minimal, the spikes in heart rate are very real.

For Francis and the rest of the team, PrimEvil is months in the making. The nightly production involves more than 100 actors and dozens of crew, spread across six themed attractions, each drawing from familiar horror tropes – the scary clowns at the Circus of Terror, the cannibalistic trailer-dwellers over at Route 666, the satanic cult of The Offering. The winding routes are designed to disorient you with strobe lights, smoke machines, mirrored walls, hidden doors, false exits and unstable floors. But it’s down to the performers to bring the nightmare to life.

‘It’s the best form of therapy and you get paid to do it’ … park director Ben Francis

“I think people who don’t know what to expect think it’s just a nice little walk round, where you see the odd actor, they have a chat with you, then you carry on,” says Francis. “Actually, what the industry does now is completely immerse you in the theme of this world for 10 minutes.”

PrimEvil is the special Halloween event of ROARR!, a dinosaur-themed adventure park a half-hour drive from central Norwich. That family-friendly attraction remains open in the day during PrimEvil’s run. Now, coming up to 5pm, an hour before the gates open, the transition from theme park to scream park is under way.

It’s Saturday, the second night of PrimEvil’s nearly two-week run. Yesterday, 1,400 people spent the evening here, despite steady drizzle; the same number are expected later.

At PrimEvil HQ, a purpose-built warehouse, actors start flooding in for wardrobe and makeup. For our interview, Francis and I hole up in the laundry room, out of their way. Still, we’re intermittently interrupted by performers, partway through changing into costume, looking for plastic gloves or spray-on blood. Francis himself is in high demand, not just as PrimEvil’s boss of operations but also as an old hand. This is the 17th year he’s been involved, having attended the very first event in 2009. Though there were UK scare attractions then – notably Tulleys Shocktoberfest, now 30 years old, and Fright Night at Thorpe Park – they were still fringe.

Francis didn’t know what to expect, he says. “I remember being absolutely terrified.” The following year, he applied to be an actor, and discovered a passion for scaring people. It’s not as sinister as it sounds, he insists. “It’s the best form of therapy, and you get paid to do it.” Francis was cast as a clown, “apart from one year where I was a hillbilly”. He found venting in character to be effective stress relief from his day job in the charities sector. “You shout at people, and they love it.” One evening in 2016, Francis arrived at PrimEvil in a foul mood after a board meeting had left him feeling disillusioned about his purpose. Martin Goymour, ROARR!’s founder and managing director, offered him a job. Both were in costume at the time, Francis confirms. “I was a clown, and he was in lederhosen.”

A familiar sight … Martin Goymour, ROARR!’s founder and managing director, dressed as Skullmore

Goymour joins us in the laundry room now, looking for face paint. We met earlier, at ROARR!’s offices across the park; I don’t immediately recognise him in his brocade suit and top hat, his face white and bloody. To PrimEvil regulars, Goymour is a familiar sight as “Skullmore”, the dark Victorian ringmaster, sweeping the park on his Segway.

Goymour was inspired to start PrimEvil in the mid-00s, after visiting Hollywood and one of Universal Studios’ legendary Halloween Horror events. The first PrimEvil, in 2009, was a single maze, built within the steel frame of ROARR!’s office building, after construction was paused by the recession. The idea was to draw a new crowd to the park after dark, and “have some fun” themselves. It was half a decade before the event broke even.

Now PrimEvil attracts 20,000 visitors annually (Tulleys, the largest in Europe, boasts 150,000), while most theme parks stage spooky-season events. Their popularity has grown alongside the mainstreaming of Halloween and horror in the UK, driving up the standard. There is even a trade show, ScareCON, and industry awards, the SCARs; PrimEvil won the top prize in 2024.

‘We say to the actors you can’t all be jump scares. You can be someone who just stands and stares …’

Francis and Goymour tweak the attractions every year and regularly travel to the US to scope out new tech and props. There, a single scare attraction can gross nearly $1m per season, though that’s offset by mounting costs. Goymour told me he spent “quite a bit” on “gory bodies” last year – about £10,000. According to IT manager Richard Colsell, responsible for the technical aspects of PrimEvil, the innovation is focused on electronic control systems. These trigger features such as animatronics or lighting changes; increasingly, the industry is using AI to read and respond to visitors in real-time, and even track their gaze.

Wherever possible, Colsell prefers to leave control in the hands of the actors. “Sometimes less is more.” With each performance typically lasting less than 30 seconds (then repeated for hours), theatrical chops are less important than dynamic range across the cast. “We say to the actors, ‘You can’t all be jump scares,’” Francis says. “That’s what gets the reaction, and the adrenaline – but actually, you can be a creeper scare, a stalker, someone who just stands and stares …”

‘More than once, catching someone’s eye, I’m startled by their red or white irises’

This year PrimEvil received an unprecedented 230 applications for about 132 paid spots. They were selected at a group audition, starting with a dance-off, then testing their improv skills. “The more of a prat you feel, the better you will be coming across,” says Francis. A self-avowed control freak, this year he “granted the gift” of assessment to his six team leaders, one for each attraction, who could also call dibs on performers. One man in his 70s was sought after by all six. “I had to shake a dice,” says Francis. The man wound up in Mayhem Manor, the haunted residential hospital where guests are chased by doctors and nurses wanting to violently uncover their “inner beauty”.

There are strict rules in place to protect actors and visitors, chiefly: no touching. Older women on a girls’ night can struggle with that one, says Francis. “They can get very touchy-feely.” Contracted security patrol the park for disruptive or intoxicated visitors. Performers are likewise instructed “no rude, lewd or crude” behaviour. People do strike out in terror, but actors are taught to distinguish between dodgy reflexes and ill intentions – and to watch visitors’ hands, which can suddenly spring up.

Still, accidents happen. “We have had code browns,” says Francis, though “not as often as you might think”. He estimates there are two each year, with more “code yellows”, though he assumes both are underreported. “Sometimes we’ll lend them trousers from our wardrobe, if they come and tell us.” Last night there were four panic attacks (about average, Francis says) plus two girls who fainted, and another who broke her finger. “She fell over while running away.” Most often, the on-site welfare team assists those wanting some quiet time-out.

‘My boyfriend kept jumping while watching Insidious, while I was literally taking notes’ … Courteney Dunn, head of makeup at PrimEvil

As Francis and I talk, actors emerge from the wardrobe transformed. A young man has traded his trackies for a boilersuit; there’s an increasing number of nuns. Francis admits to feeling a little wistful. “I used to love being a scare actor.” When he took the job at PrimEvil, nearly 10 years ago, he was “adamant” he wouldn’t give up performing. Now, due to the demands of his job as park director across ROARR!, he’s had to quit the Circus. His costume is still stored in wardrobe. From a wall lined with grotesque masks, Francis pulls down one with demonic arched eyebrows and crazed red curls, and introduces me to Lofty the clown: his longtime alter ego. “No one’s allowed to touch my clown costume,” he says, fingering the satin sleeve. He declines to don it for a photo – soon, it will be showtime.

Across the hall, the makeup team is finishing up the final few actors with brisk efficiency. Kara Field is applying brown and purple shadows to a Route 666 cannibal, to create sunken-looking eyes. “If you do it wrong, they look like drag queens,” she warns. Taped to the mirrors are print-outs with guide images and keywords for each attraction. This year the clowns’ makeup is monochrome for greater impact under the Circus’ UV lights. “We decided to go a lot darker, with more depth, shadows and contours,” says Courteney Dunn, 28, head of makeup and props.

Most of Dunn’s team of eight makeup artists are “obsessed” with horror. Watching the new Insidious film with her partner, “he kept jumping, while all I was doing was looking at the makeup, literally taking notes.” Where possible, makeup artists work with the actors’ style: unnatural hair colours or facial piercings might suit workers at the toxic Werehouse 51, but not the plague-time nuns of The Crypt. Dunn appraises me: “I feel like I could put you in Route 666.”

With 20 minutes before the gates open, actors are applying finishing touches to their looks, bloodying blond wigs or blackening their teeth. The scene is less nightmare than fever dream. There’s a nun, texting intently; two pilgrims at the sink, filling up their vapour-powered torches; a clown juggling a can of Monster, a vape and a sausage roll. More than once, catching someone’s eye, I’m startled by their red or white irises.

An estimated 50% of this year’s cast are returning, motivated by the experience as much as the work. “It’s a good way to make money, but it’s also really fun,” says Mia McConnell, 19, hanging out the front of the warehouse, vaping with friends. A shop worker by day, tonight McConnell is a mutant nurse. “The best way to scare people is to hide in the smoke. They don’t see you coming.” Sometimes the shock is mutual. Last night a trainee drama teacher (who requests anonymity) came face to face with some of her pupils, “super-excited to see Miss outside school,” she tells me, wincing beneath her bloody head bandages. Yesterday’s costume offered less coverage. “If I’d looked like this, I’d have been fine.”

‘It’s a good way to make money, but it’s also really fun’ … Mia McConnell in costume

A slowly clanging bell gathers everyone to the front of PrimEvil HQ for Goymour’s pre-curtain pep talk. In character as Skullmore, he greets his “children of the fright” and urges them to “speak up, entertain” – and stick to their assigned spots. Then, after a team chant of “PrimEvil”, the horde is released into the park, grabbing a fortifying Mars bar from the box Francis is shaking.

Scarlett Morris, 23, a barista and musician, is playing a ditzy sheriff at Route 666. In ordinary life, Morris tells me, she can be self-conscious and never leaves the house without makeup. “PrimEvil is the place to go to leave everything behind … it’s good for your confidence, dressing up and doing something you’d never do in real life.”

That might also explain the draw for punters. Research into “recreational fear” suggests it’s not just thrill-seeking but also a form of play, offering people a safe way to engage with difficult emotions. A 2025 study found that groups who went to a haunted house attraction reported feeling closer to each other, the “collective storytelling” solidifying their bonds.

For some actors it seems akin to a calling. This is Neville Everett’s 10th PrimEvil, and at the moment his only gig. “I’m a man of leisure,” he says, eyes mischievous beneath his evil-clown makeup. Everett sticks largely to the same playbook, loitering by the Circus’s exit and jumping out just when people think they’re safe. “Then I chase them,” he says. Usually he has a chainsaw going.

He struggles to articulate the precise appeal. “It’s just something I like doing … You get rid of your frustrations on people.”

Watching Everett in action, however, this sells him short: his dance with the public seems both conscious and two-way. A group of teenage girls literally plead for his attention (“Hi! Hi! Shalom!”), squealing in delight when he duly revs his chainsaw. When a pair of boys pass by, studiedly aloof and above the game, Everett calls their bluff and ignores them; they can’t hide their disappointment.

Judging by the screams coming from the nearby Werehouse 51 and the whacks reverberating along the corrugated-iron walls, PrimEvil is in full flow. In the now-quiet warehouse HQ, Francis settles in for the late evening, keeping things ticking over until the gates close at 11pm, and beyond. One of his tasks is doing “constant” loads of laundry, washing and drying the black bags that go over visitors’ heads for The Offering.

For all the hard work that goes into designing a frightening night out, ultimately it’s all about the visitors’ imaginations, Francis says. A sign hangs in his office, gifted to him by Goymour: “The biggest fear is the fear of the unknown.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Trump’s plea – ‘pretend I’m on the ballot’ – deserves to backfire | Margaret Sullivan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Margaret Sullivan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
With his poll numbers tanking and his behavior getting odder, the remark seems more appealing to himself than to voters

As he criss-crosses the nation, stumping for Republican candidates, Donald Trump keeps asking voters to use their imaginations.

“In this election, I’m asking you to pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just pretend,” he urged at a Kansas rally as he campaigned for the incumbent senator Roger Marshall and gubernatorial challenger Ty Masterson last month.

“Pretend I’m on the ballot” has become a regular rallying cry as Trump tries to fend off a Democratic “blue wave” in Congress.

Given his own lack of popularity and weird behavior, it’s an egotistical notion – more appealing to himself than to voters.

After all, his approval ratings are in the basement. Gas prices are higher, on average, than at any time during the Biden years. People feel like they need to float a loan before heading to the supermarket.

In that Kansas rally, he referred to the opposition as “Dumocrats”, which is typical of the level of presidential discourse to which the nation has become accustomed.

In his rallies, he appears “increasingly detached from reality”, as one campaign analysis in the Independent put it, as he “vacillates between topics to the point where his remarks border on the nonsensical and he ends every appearance by awkwardly dancing to the Village People’s well-known gay anthem YMCA”.

Stranger still, as the Guardian’s Adam Gabbatt reported recently, Trump has been offering “unsolicited and increasingly unhinged assessments of men’s bodies” over the past few weeks.

“I examined his ass,” the president said in Kentucky, speaking about Republican senator Jon Husted. “And then I looked at his shoulders … I looked at his jawline … I then patted him on the shoulder, and it was like a piece of steel. I’m still recovering.”

Trump has also been – to put it mildly – stretching the truth on the campaign trail, sometimes merely misleading in his remarks, sometimes straight-up lying.

For example, he promised a North Carolina rally that gas and oil prices would tumble soon and he claimed: “I had it down to the lowest level in years,” apparently speaking about the price of filling up a gas tank at the pump. A PolitiFact examination disputed this, noting that when Trump took office at the beginning of last year, the average gas price was $3.23 a gallon, but by late September of this year, it was $4.61.

But it’s not just what he says at rallies that may backfire on the candidates he hopes to help.

Much of what’s happened in Trump’s second term is working against Republican candidates. That includes the widespread self-dealing that, as the historian Garrett Graff wrote recently, “is so endemic and so obvious that it has broken through to voters”.

It’s also his misguided war, his rants on social media, his disparagement of longtime allies, including Canada. It’s also his obvious plan to declare the election rigged should it not go his way.

“Even Maga die-hards and GOP allies in Congress have grown weary of his erratic behavior,” as the Wall Street Journal’s Jason Riley noted.

And Democrats, including Barack Obama, are only too happy to campaign by associating Republican candidates with Trump.

These midterm elections, Obama told a crowd in Ohio, “is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration. It’s the circuit breaker in the system.”

That blast of sanity and good sense seems far more likely to resonate with potential voters than Trump’s unhinged rants and dangerous threats.

Maybe that’s effective with Trump’s remaining cult-like base. And maybe it will bring some of those loyalists out to vote next week if they had been thinking of sitting out this election.

But more likely, the imagined association with Trump will serve to remind most voters that Trump’s malfeasance must be rebuked and rejected. Certainly not encouraged.

Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.title: Trump and Obama trade barbs on campaign trail in final days before midterm election  – US politics live
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.author: Tom Ambrose
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text:
Former president says ‘these are not serious people’ as Trump holds rallies for Republican candidates

President Trump and the former president Barack Obama have continued to trade barbs on the campaign trail, with less than a week to go before congressional races that could shift the balance of power in Washington.

While Donald Trump has been on a weeks-long campaign blitz ⁠that has exposed Republican concerns about losing control of ⁠Congress for the final two years of his presidency, ​Obama had kept a relatively low public profile until the past week.

However, the former Democratic president has taken a more prominent role in recent days, delivering speeches criticizing Trump, which appear to have got under the skin of the current occupant of the White House.

“These are not serious people,” he said of Donald Trump and the Republican party, speaking at a Wednesday campaign rally in suburban Atlanta. “And we’re all paying the price for their lack of seriousness.”

Obama has offered pointed criticism of Republican candidates and Donald Trump in a style that has been unusual for the former president.

He continued to do so on Wednesday, again invoking the image of Trump’s gilded renovations of the White House and noting Trump’s strident reaction to his crack last week likening it to Saddam Hussein decorating a Cheesecake Factory.

“The Saddam Hussein thing didn’t bother him. But he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory,” Obama said. “I mean, it’s all crazy, but this is the crazy part: they mobilized a whole government response to that joke.

“The White House even called the secretary of the treasury,” the former president continued. “The guy who is trying to figure out how to lower inflation … they told him he should hold a press conference in front of the Cheesecake Factory.”

Trump, meanwhile, defended his White House decor and said Obama left the property deteriorated.

“The White House, I think, is the number one symbol of our country, and we can’t have a White House with broken windows, with broken stone that hasn’t been painted in 30 years,” ⁠he said at a rally in Ohio.

Thirty-five of the 100 Senate seats and all 435 seats in the House of Representatives are being contested next Tuesday. Nonpartisan analysts generally favor Democrats’ chances of capturing a majority in the House, with the contest ⁠for the Senate seen as very close.

A federal judge declined to order California election officials to segregate ballots from people the Trump administration claimed were non-citizens, rebuffing a legally thin request from the justice department that appeared designed to cast doubt over the results of the midterms.

Jason Turkish, who is engaged to Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens, appeared at a campaign event for Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan and told reporters he was voting for the Republican, not Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who narrowly defeated Stevens in the Democratic primary.

A heckler disrupted Trump’s speech in Ohio by shouting “Trump went on the Jeffrey Epstein plane!” The president then congratulated himself for banning his friend of at least 17 years from his beach club. “I threw Jeffrey Epstein out of a club like 20 years ago, because I thought he was a whack job,” Trump said.

Around lunchtime on Tuesday, a Rolls-Royce stopped at the intersection of Beverly Drive and Dayton Way in Beverly Hills, California. Local people in athleisure walked past Balenciaga, Dior and Prada boutiques, as visitors on Hollywood bus tours ogled nearby Rodeo Drive, where Burberry and Louis Vuitton shops meet at a celebrated street corner.

Up the street, across from the upmarket Erewhon grocery store – home to $21 smoothies – a few diners sat outside an American landmark: the Cheesecake Factory.

The beloved restaurant chain began here in Beverly Hills in 1978; now it has hundreds of locations across the US and Canada. And this week, it’s become the US’s latest surreal culture-war touchstone.

It started when Barack Obama, campaigning for Democrats in Ohio, made a joke that hit Donald Trump right in the real estate. Referring to his successor’s remodeling obsession, the former president said: “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere.”

The joke was about maximalism: Saddam had 100 palaces and loved gold plating, and the Cheesecake Factory, while affordable for many, offers swanky surroundings that a curmudgeon might describe as over the top. While the Beverly Hills restaurant has a fairly staid interior, a nearby location at Los Angeles’s Grove mall has a grand staircase, floral paintings on the ceilings and an ornate balcony.

Obama’s comments got a laugh at the rally – which surely contained many Cheesecake Factory customers – and went viral. It’s likely the former president knew he would touch a nerve, given Trump’s twin fixations on remodeling and on Obama himself.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Solidarity among young people’: four lessons the US can learn from the youth protests in France
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Claire Lampen
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Despite structural differences between countries, protests are a reminder of what makes demonstrations so powerful

Since mid-September, students in metropolitan France have been mobilizing against poor conditions in public high schools. The mouvement lycéen has spread from a single campus in a Parisian suburb to include high schoolers and university students nationwide, with public sector workers, climate activists, labor unions and everyday people joining in solidarity. The unifying concerns have largely centered on the climbing costs of daily life, shrinking funds for social services and general anxiety about the future.

For two weekends running, France has seen hundreds of thousands of people take to the streets: first on 17 October, when a day of largely peaceful gatherings ended in looting and vandalism; then on 24 October, as the state met the movement with aggressive policing and protest bans intended to keep people at home.

But curfews, teargas and sweeping arrests have not been enough to deter the students. On Monday, they won their first government concessions: $4.45bn in government loans for the renovation of rundown buildings, more university spaces, more teachers and other administrative changes.

Protesters remain unsatisfied. Calling these “crumbs”, a spokesperson for the l’Union Étudiante, a national university student union, vowed to keep fighting. More actions are scheduled for 31 October, with a national strike called for 5 November.

Their resolve highlights how ingrained protest culture is in France. “There’s this idea, very deeply rooted in France, that expressing yourself by demonstrating is a democratic right,” said Quentin Deluermoz, a historian at the University of Cambridge and Université Paris Cité who studies social movements. “When something truly problematic is felt on a large scale, people will demonstrate to make their voices heard and demand a change or adjustment in policy.”

While fundamental structural differences between France and the US complicate easy comparisons, the French student movement is nonetheless a useful reminder of what makes demonstrations powerful on both sides of the Atlantic.

The mouvement lycéen has been bolstered by a strong network of unions across French society. In France, unions provide organizing power within the public sector, responsible for calling strikes and filing the paperwork that makes them legal, in addition to consolidating worker demands and negotiating with the state.

But the right to strike, enshrined in the constitution, belongs to individuals: once a work stoppage is called, anyone can join it, whether they’re unionized or not. As long as they obey protocol, workers generally can’t be fired for walking off the job (though they do lose pay).

Not so in the US, where “going on strike is a very risky activity”, said Eric Blanc, assistant professor of labor studies at Rutgers and author of the Labor Politics Substack. “If you have to pay rent and make sure your kids have food next week, you’re going to think twice about taking action even if you know it could benefit you.”

Still, the US has seen what an effective action can look like, namely the 2018 teachers’ strikes that spread from West Virginia to Kentucky and Arizona. By walking out of their classrooms for more than a week, public school educators “created a crisis” that forced politicians to pay attention, Blanc said, and they did so knowing it would spark anger at either the state or the teachers.

To head off the latter outcome, teachers “were really conscious about winning over parents and community members”, Blanc said. They rallied bus drivers, custodians and other support staff. They coordinated childcare at local community centers and food donations for families affected by missed school meals. The West Virginia strike also “broke with the rules and practice and went straight to the [state] capitol to demand more money”, Blanc noted, ultimately winning a 5% pay raise for all public sector employees in the state.

So far, the French student protests have drawn a broad coalition without diluting demonstrators’ demands. That owes in part to the unions and activist groups that have piled onto the cause: the gilets jaunes, or yellow vests, a leaderless movement that came together in 2018 to protest fuel-tax increases and eventually the cost of living, set the date for the 17 October action in early September. After the student movement took off, it put out a call on their website inviting “Gen Z, Indignés [anti-austerity activists], farmers, firefighters, workers, teachers, healthcare workers, climate activists, residents of disadvantaged neighborhoods and retirees” to join them. The unions then called for protests on the same day.

On 24 October in Paris, the situation went further: multiple groups merged into one march, along one route. “It wasn’t just the numbers that mattered – it’s that we had a single demonstration with everyone,” explained Robi Morder, a jurist and political scientist specializing in student movements.

That solidarity is important for the students because it lends legitimacy to a more vulnerable group, and because workers have leverage high schoolers lack. While high school and university students do have their own unions, which represent them in talks with the government, their walkouts don’t have the legal standing that workers’ do. After all, when the lycéens boycott their classes, it “doesn’t bother anyone except the high school students, since stopping work isn’t like in a factory”, Morder said. Teachers’ unions have already organized walkouts in support of the students, and a general strike is coming next week.

To get the government’s attention, Morder said, “we have to be very strong and very numerous, that’s the idea: strength in unity”.

That idea has taken hold at the local level in the US, too: in Minneapolis this winter, unions, community leaders, mutual aid networks and everyday people pulled together to push back ICE; and in Cascade Locks, Oregon, voters banded together to recall their elected officials and cancel plans for the construction of a datacenter.

Earlier this month, the students drew up a list of 10 emergency measures they’d like to see implemented, including the need for “clean and functional sanitary facilities”, staffed classrooms and buildings adapted to extreme heat and cold.

For many workers in France, those complaints are reasonable and relatable. “What’s happening in the high schools is the same situation as in the hospitals and in all the public services,” said Deluermoz.

According to Blanc, mobilizing around grievances that are “really widely and deeply felt” tends to be a productive avenue for organizing. “One of the exciting things about the French movement is that it’s focusing on these core issues of economic redistribution,” he said. “It’s oriented not just to making the point, but towards winning something” – which “necessarily obliges a higher degree of sustained participation”.

In the US, recent large-scale protests at the national level have often been less about making demands and more about voicing dissent. No Kings, for example, may mobilize parts of the population not previously involved in activism, but its most immediate impact is showing that many people are upset about a certain thing – in this case, authoritarianism.

Dana R Fisher, professor and director of the Center for Environment, Community and Equity at American University, said that the US protests generating immediate effects tend to revolve around specific community threats at the state and local levels. Often, these efforts are catalyzed by “a moral shock”, she said: “Someone murdered by ICE, families being targeted at schools by immigration agents.”

More or less since the lycéen movement began, law enforcement has responded with a heavy hand, using military-grade weapons that have cost teenagers eyes, hands and teeth. Online, Deluermoz now sees a “war of images”: protesters and some media have circulated “shocking scenes of police violence inflicted on people under 18, with very childlike faces”. The government has countered by advancing the narrative “of the casseur, of looters, to give the impression of anarchy and justify a use of force that legal experts … consider disproportionate”, Deluermoz said.

While photos of shattered Parisian storefronts and Limoges’s flaming city hall may have consumed international headlines, the local story has unfolded a bit differently on social media. The teens have filmed themselves doing viral dances and “aura battles” (a trend in which two people face off in competing displays of charisma) in front of the police. The injection of meme culture into the manifs draws a line under the inherent absurdity of riot police facing off against kids who are asking for more chairs in their classrooms; it also reflects a gen Z-specific sense of humor that translates across borders.

Take the now-viral phrase “bismillah, c’est les ténèbres”, which entered the lexicon in early October when a screenshot from Snapchat circulated online, apparently showing a request to access an organizer group. “Hi, in the name of God, it’s the darkness. When’s the blockade, wallah, bro?” the message said, followed by a string of Algerian flag emojis, according to Al Jazeera. Students quickly blamed undercover cops, reading the nonsensical mashup of Arabic and French slang as an example of racial stereotyping by police. They co-opted the line as a slogan, which has now popped up on protest signs in France as well as Belgium and Italy.

While several experts said organizing via social media can prove difficult and ephemeral in the long term, it undeniably catalyzes people to get out into the street. In the US, arguably the clearest example is the Black Lives Matter movement, which sprang from a Facebook post in 2013 after George Zimmerman was acquitted in the shooting death of Trayvon Martin, a Black teenager in Florida, and has leveraged social media as an organizing tool ever since. In May 2020, footage of George Floyd’s murder shared on social media triggered protests against racially motivated police brutality all around the world.

In France and now beyond, the footage of young people in the streets has created “solidarity among young people”, as Morder put it. “They recognize each other; they face more or less the same problems.”

None of this guarantees the students will get their way – France faces a dire budget crisis and is poised to elect a new president next spring, meaning candidates on both sides of the political spectrum are spinning the protests to serve their own agendas. But the movement has nonetheless surfaced popular concerns that apply not only across France but around the world, putting a point on what people want from their governments.

“There’s something deeper at play here,” Morder said. “It’s seeping into society. We see reactions here from adults, parents, grandparents, employees, who say: ‘We’re very proud of the young people, because they’re moving, they’re acting.’”

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.title: Computerized clairvoyance: psychics push back against AI-generated readings
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.author: Kari Paul
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.text:
Human practitioners warn computer-generated offerings lack the empathy and connection central to divination

“This journey isn’t just about algorithms or data,” an AI psychic named Urban Mystic recently told me. The chatbot, featuring an AI-generated profile photo of a smiling woman surrounded by palm trees, also said I will get married soon, that I have a pink aura and that I may have been an herbalist in a past life.

Urban Mystic is one of more than a dozen bots on the mobile app Your AI Psychic, which offers live, allegedly psychic readings via chat, video and voice calls as well as palm reading, astrology chart analysis and daily horoscopes. The app works on a coin system: each question costs 4.06 coins to ask. Users can purchase packages ranging from $9.99 for “a quick question” (82 coins) to $99.99 (1,180 coins) for “ongoing guidance and clarity” from an AI psychic of their choice.

Your AI Psychic joins an increasingly crowded space of mobile apps and websites promising users algorithmically generated spiritual insight and knowledge of their futures. The divination industry, like mathematics research, copywriting, software engineering, and a host of other professions, is facing upheaval amid the AI boom – and human practitioners are scrambling to respond. The rise of AI is particularly fraught in a profession offering spiritual products that are not well-regulated.

“Our industry has, unfortunately, been associated with scams for hundreds of years, and we have to constantly be ahead of that,” said Lauryn Kellett, an intuitive coach and a professional psychic of 10 years. “So in some ways, this is not new to us: we always have to find ways to show we are real, authentic and have good integrity.”

In addition to chatbots and apps, AI-generated psychics are a growing presence on TikTok Live, racking up dozens of views. Professional human psychics, who frequently make use of the social network’s live features, have expressed consternation and warned that computer-generated readings lack the empathy and human connection they say are central to psychic communication, especially Elon Musk’s Grok. Meanwhile, according to human spiritual practitioners, AI-generated horoscope readings and spells have been flooding Etsy, which serves as a popular marketplace for divination products.

Psychic practitioners have begun adding “no AI” clauses to their advertisements to combat a market being saturated with computer-generated offerings. In a recent vlog on the topic, Kellett said, “ignoring AI and how it could impact our industry is irresponsible … AI is here to stay, and it’s going to change our industry, and maybe not in the ways we think.”

Kellett, who coaches new practitioners on accessing their psychic abilities, said she has shifted her teaching toward how to best distinguish human-offered services from AI, as AI readings passed off as human work have become “rampant” online, encouraging clients to post videos and photos of themselves to prove they are not bots.

As the rise of users turning to AI chatbots for therapy underscores, many people feel more comfortable sharing personal problems with a faceless entity. But as with turning to AI for therapy, using AI psychics to process difficult situations may worsen mental health crises, practitioners warn. Studies have shown that large language models (LLMs) can amplify paranoia in users vulnerable to psychosis. On TikTok Live, many human psychics, as a rule, refuse to answer questions about health or finances, arguing that high-stakes decisions should not be made in these contexts.

Ahna Hendrix is a psychic who, instead of channeling entities such as spirits from other realms, works with the Akashic Records – an extra-dimensional “database” of energy and human knowledge. She said her practice is centered on empowering clients rather than making decisions or recommendations for them – something that AI chatbots are less inclined to do.

“One of the cornerstones of my work is really helping people to remember who they are and to come back to their own internal guidance system that is within all of us,” she said. “When we begin leaning on AI too much for validation or for decision making, we stop using those mechanisms within us that are really important. If we start outsourcing that, what are we left with?”

A chatbot does not have to be branded as a psychic to serve a divination function, noted Sally Applin, a consultant and anthropologist who researches human agency, AI and automation in the context of human systems. People ask ChatGPT about life decisions such as whether to get a new job or leave their partner. In their book chapter, External Intelligence: Oracles, Divination and Animism, and the Use of LLMs/Generative AI, Applin and co-author Michael D Fischer argue that even prior to the explosion of LLMs, people turned to Google search with questions about their fates and choices.

“Some interaction with LLMs can be seen as a modern iteration of the oracular consultation,” they wrote. As with traditional divination, users must interpret the answers they receive, and sometimes ask the same question repeatedly until they are satisfied with the response. “The meaning is always coming from the inside of the person’s head,” Applin said.

Critically, however, she said LLMs work from statistical patterns learned in training and lack the cultural and personal context that historically inform human-led divinatory processes. The sense that a chatbot is a knowing entity is a projection of human expectations, she said, reflecting an enduring desire for connection and guidance rather than a metaphysical resource.

“What is also missing is contextual awareness, the ‘there there’ of human social relationships,” she said.

The models behind AI psychic chatbots offered on the app store are, as is often the case with LLMs, black boxes.
