One web and phone-based platform, MystiCall, markets itself as having been trained on “three generations of clairvoyants”. In a statement, co-founder Laurie-Anne Bernard said this wording refers to clairvoyance practiced in one of the co-founders’ families. The company also consulted with a human psychic who helped shape the app’s “conversational experience”.

Mysticall uses technology from AI audio technology company ElevenLabs for processing live voice conversations and OpenAI for post-call summaries. Bernard said in a statement that Mysticall does not sell private conversations, use them for targeted advertising or train proprietary AI models on them. She added that the company has disabled the use of conversation data for model training by its partner companies ElevenLabs and OpenAI.

Mysticall began as a human phone-reading service, but pivoted to AI as a means of “removing barriers” to such consultations, like cost and availability, Bernard said. The goal of Mysticall, Bernard added, is to offer a more accessible means of processing emotions through personalized consultations, not to offer explicit – and potentially harmful – predictions or mental health diagnoses.

“We do not claim that our technology possesses supernatural abilities or can reliably predict the future,” she said. “Instead, we see tarot, astrology and other symbolic traditions as ways of exploring questions, emotions and different perspectives. AI allows us to make these experiences more interactive, personalized and accessible.”

It is often difficult to obtain an answer from companies producing AI psychics about how their products work. I asked my own AI psychic, Urban Mystic, where she gets her divination abilities, but chatbots are often not reliable narrators of their own construction. She told me she was trained on a “wide range of information”, dating up until October 2023, including “spiritual practices, psychology, and various belief systems”, but could not offer more details. The app’s privacy policy makes no mention of AI, referring only to “psychic advisors”, and names no AI providers. The company listed as the publisher on the app store, RF Master Group Ltd, did not respond to repeated requests for comment. Its privacy policy lists a different entity, “Expert Center”, as the app’s holding company, which also did not respond to requests for comment.

The opaqueness of chatbots can be particularly fraught when users share sensitive information. MystiCall’s privacy policy acknowledges conversations may touch on users’ “relationships, mental state, health, sexuality, beliefs, finances”. The policy for Your AI Psychic does not address sensitive information at all.

Kellett said this lack of transparency around how data is handled makes her particularly wary of AI apps. She said a number of platforms have contacted her for help training their LLMs, but when she pushes for more details, they tend to disappear.

Unlike many workers who fear they will someday be replaced by AI, Kellett said she does not believe her ability can be replicated by chatbots. Even if she were to hand over all of her training courses for developing psychic ability to an LLM, she does not think AI is yet at a point where it could make the leap to intuition.

“Psychic ability itself is the ability to connect to a divine source, and AI cannot do that,” she said. “AI can’t pull information from somewhere else. It can only derive information from what you give it. If you ask it to meditate, to sit down, to clear its mind, and connect to a psychic source, how would it do that? It’s just a computer.”

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Shell profits double to $10.8bn as Iran war pushes up margin on oil
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Energy firm to return $5bn to shareholders as climate campaigners criticise high profits

Shell has doubled its profits in the last quarter after the Middle East conflict drove up the price of oil and gas and created shortages in the global market.

Shell reported on Thursday morning that it made an adjusted profit of $10.8bn (£8.1bn) in the July-September quarter, up from $5.432bn in the third quarter of 2025. The results beat analyst expectations for a rise to $10.33bn.

The company also raised its share buyback programme – it plans to return $5bn to investors for the next three months, up from $3bn in the last quarter.

“Shell’s relentless focus on operational performance enabled very strong results in a quarter with continued severe disruption to the global energy system,” the Shell chief executive, Wael Sawan, said.

Climate campaigners criticised the jump in profits, which pushed Shell’s shares up by 3% in early trading on Thursday morning.

“As fossil-fuelled storms, floods, and soaring costs wreck communities, oil executives like Shell’s Wael Sawan are popping champagne on the deck of a sinking planet. We are paying with our lives and pay-cheques while they cash in on our misery,” said Philip Evans, a senior campaigner at Greenpeace.

Shell’s profits were also higher than in the second quarter of this year, when it made $9.836bn.

Shell told investors earlier this month that it expected the profit margins at its refineries to climb to $42 for each barrel of fuel produced in the July to September period, far above the margins of $24 a barrel in the second quarter of this year.

These margins are also significantly higher than the previous record for petroleum products of about $28 a barrel, set in the early months of the Russia-Ukraine war, due to shortages in the global market caused by severe damage to refineries in the Middle East and Russia.

Shell’s gas production has been hard hit by the Middle East crisis, which led to severe damage to one of its key gas processing facilities in the Gulf. The company’s prewar gas production of 900,000 barrels ⁠of oil ​equivalent ‌per day fell by a third as the Middle East war unfolded.

Europe’s benchmark gas price index reached an average of almost €64 per megawatt-hour in the third quarter, up from more than €48 a megawatt-hour in the second quarter. Meanwhile, the global oil price benchmark averaged $94.90 a barrel, up from $69.10 a barrel in the same quarter last year.

The steadily rising commodity prices helped lift the market value of Europe’s biggest oil and gas company, now the largest company on the UK’s FTSE 100 index. Shell’s share price rose to a record high of more than £40 a share earlier this month as the global oil price climbed towards $117 a barrel, the highest price in six months.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Rare love letters to French aristocrat shed light on Louis XVI maritime mystery
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Kim Willsher in Paris
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
‘Miracle’ cache of letters written by French scientist who died in ill-fated La Pérouse mission give personal account of 1785 voyage

As he prepared to climb the scaffolding to be publicly executed by guillotine on 21 January 1793, Louis XVI is reported to have asked: “Is there news of Monsieur de la Pérouse?”

He was referring to Jean-François de Galaup, the count of Pérouse, a naval officer and navigator whom the French king had dispatched in 1785 on a round-the-world scientific mission to rival discoveries made by the English explorer Captain James Cook.

The two ships under La Pérouse’s command, La Boussole and L’Astrolabe, disappeared three years later after leaving Botany Bay in Australia. The wrecks were only formally identified in 2005 and exactly what happened to them remains a mystery to this day.

Now rare letters written by an illustrious scientist who perished in 1788 have resurfaced, giving a new and personal account of the voyage. They are described as veiled love letters addressed to the married daughter of an aristocratic family, and were discovered hidden in a book of engravings being examined in preparation for auction.

Ludovic Miran, a book and manuscript expert for the auctioneers selling the letters next month, described the find as “a miracle”.

“We have a certain number of documents from the expedition but they are almost all scientific, so these personal letters are extremely rare,” Miran told the Guardian. “They throw a completely new light on what is in France an extraordinary scientific and historical event.”

The La Pérouse expedition was launched at a time when Britain and France were in a period of intense rivalry over colonial expansion. La Pérouse was a great admirer of Cook and his maritime mapping and scientific discoveries, but Louis XVI had more political and trade ambitions. The French wanted to create trade routes and discover whether the secret information they had that Britain was planning to establish a permanent base at Botany Bay, giving it access to unexplored areas of the Pacific region, was correct.

La Pérouse’s ships, carrying 225 crew, officers and scientists, sailed from Brest on France’s Atlantic coast on 1 August 1785 and for almost three years sent reports during stopovers including from Alaska, California, Asia, Russia and Samoa, where the captain of the Astrolabe and 11 men were killed.

At the time of Louis XVI’s execution, there had been no news of the frigates since their departure from Botany Bay in March 1788. To La Pérouse’s dismay, Captain Arthur Phillip and Britain’s First Fleet had beaten him to the Australian coast – inhabited by an Indigenous population for tens of thousands of years – by just six days.

La Boussole and L’Astrolabe are believed to have foundered on coral reefs at Vanikoro east of the Solomon Islands during a tornado a few months later. Wreckage was discovered in 1826 and 1964 but only formally identified in 2005.

The letters were written by Jean-André Mongez, a brilliant scientist, director of an illustrious science revue and church canon who was with the expedition, to Louise Victoria Le Cloustier, the daughter of a minor noble family from Rouen, Normandy.

Miran said Mongez used the letters to express his unhappiness at her marriage and appears to repent for previous bad behaviour. “He writes several times: ‘I will be back, I will be another man, a better man’,” Miran said. “One has the impression he has not behaved well towards her and she has put him in his place.”

This may, he added, have been behind Mongez’s decision to undertake such a long and perilous journey. “The references are often veiled, but they seem to have had a very close relationship but he seems to have caused some offence at some point. They are intimate, very personal letters,” he said.

“He tells her he is leaving ‘a bit for the love of fame and the desire to acquire new knowledge’, but he already had scientific glory and a good career and they would have all read James Cook’s works before leaving so they knew about the dangers.

“We will never know why he decided to join this perilous journey, but it is clear he was leaving in part because of this emotional relationship.”

Miran added: “The correspondence also provides answers as to how these young men endured three years of navigation around the world, a completely new and unimaginable experience. We learn how they withstood the shock of such a crazy journey and horrible conditions.

“He recounts how his friend and others were massacred on one stop. In his last letter he tells her the expedition has taken a sad turn and he now only wants to come home because such unhappiness is not compensated for by the meagre scientific results they have.

Le Cloustier died in 1821, like the rest of the world unaware of the fate of Mongez or the expedition. “But she kept the letters and we can tell they have been read, and reread. I would imagine she had to hide them from her husband,” Miran said.

The auctioneer Benoît Derouineau said he had discovered the letters in an “unremarkable” 19th-century book of engravings being prepared for sale.

“I didn’t realise what they were at first. They had clearly been carefully saved and hidden. Perhaps because they were a kind of love letter and the recipient didn’t want them seen. But she hadn’t thrown them away or burned them,” he said.

“That Louis XVI is said to have asked about La Pérouse shows how much was invested in this expedition. It was a very important event in France.”

The letters, valued at €30,000-€50,000, are being sold as one lot by Daguerre at the Hôtel Drouot, Paris, on 17 November.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Cambodian police and soldiers helped guard abusive scam compounds, Amnesty alleges
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Oliver Holmes in Bangkok
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Survivors tell rights group that serving officers who worked as guards administered electric shocks and beatings

Cambodian police and military officers worked as private security guards in scam compounds where thousands were forced to work in the online fraud industry, according to a report by Amnesty International.

The global rights group alleged they worked for security companies as part of a system that enabled slavery and rape in the compounds, with some guards using electric batons to keep people trapped.

“For years, survivors of these nightmarish compounds described encountering members of the Cambodian military or police inside. These accounts could not be independently verified – until now,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s secretary general.

Based on 151 survivor interviews, visits to 82 scam compounds and social media videos from dozens of guard accounts showing them in company uniform, the investigation said it could link illicit operations with five well-connected private security companies.

“Our findings begin to expose the long-suspected links between Cambodia’s billion-dollar criminal scamming networks and politically connected figures who have remained largely beyond scrutiny,” Callamard said.

“At the heart of these connections are security companies whose guards controlled compound exits, hunted down people who escaped and enforced compliance through fear and violence. Without them, this system of mass exploitation could not have functioned.”

Hundreds of thousands of people have been trafficked into south-east Asia from across the world, according to the UN. In many cases, they have been lured by the promise of an office job and then forced to carry out online scams, targeting victims globally.

Among these is so-called pig butchering, a type of romance fraud where criminals build a fake relationship with a victim, slowly “fattening them up” before stealing their money.

The Amnesty report, titled Official Business: Security companies and authorities at scamming compounds in Cambodia, alleges that a company called Leap Somnang had the largest footprint and was linked to at least 15 compounds across eight provinces. Twelve survivors identified the company’s guards, uniforms or logo, the report says.

Amnesty alleges that Leap Somnang is believed to be controlled by Ban Sophat, who publicly served as its chair while also being a colonel in the armed forces. It provided photos it claimed showed him alongside Leap Somnang guards at two scamming compounds.

The rights group quoted a letter from Ban Sophat denying holding any ownership, director or management role in Leap Somnang, stating that he had “served as an adviser to the company owner”.

“The fact that I may appear in a photograph taken at a particular location does not mean that I have knowledge of, or involvement in, the activities or operations conducted there,” it cited him as saying.

Scam site survivors have described guards administering electric shocks and beatings, detaining people in “dark rooms” and standing guard while compound managers raped women.

Amnesty said it had identified more than 20 members of the military and police who were seen to have an active presence at the compounds, including working openly as guards.

With annual losses estimated at about $100bn – a sum that outstrips the GDP of several countries in the region – international pressure has grown on countries such as Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar to crack down. There are signs that some parts of the industry are moving to South Asia.

In July 2025, Cambodia launched its largest-ever crackdown on scam operations, promising to wipe out the criminal networks. Authorities claim to have shut down hundreds of scam centres, and Amnesty said the industry there was now “dormant”.

“Even if scamming compounds are dormant, our findings clearly show that the infrastructure of impunity has not been dismantled,” Callamard said. “Cambodia will not have ended this abusive industry until it has held to account those who staffed, managed, financed and protected this abusive system.”

Amnesty said it presented its findings to Cambodian authorities, and cited a response from the ministry of interior stating that it had, as part of its ongoing crackdowns, already disciplined 77 police officers, prosecuted six private security guards for using stun batons illegally and detained 17 military, police, and civil officials for colluding with criminals.

Authorities had sent 3,477 suspects to court, the letter says, citing a policy of “no tolerance, no exemption, and no retreat” to ensure Cambodia did not become a “haven or operating base for transnational criminal networks”.

The Guardian has contacted Cambodia’s interior ministry, Ban Sophat and Leap Somnang for comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Hello Kitty company cuts ties with Japanese spy show after China outcry
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Justin McCurry in Tokyo
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Sanrio ends association with TV drama Vivant after China says portrayal of ruthless Chinese agents is ‘deliberate smear’

The company behind the successful Hello Kitty franchise has apologised and ended its commercial tie-up with a Japanese TV drama after Chinese state media and netizens condemned the show’s “deliberate smears” against China.

Sanrio, a Japanese firm whose characters are popular around the world, said in a post on the Chinese social media site Weibo that it had decided to end its association with the TV drama Vivant after concluding that it “contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio’s core values”.

In the second season of the popular spy thriller, produced by the Japanese TBS network, Masato Sakai plays a salaryman who is drawn into a web of international crime and espionage.

The backlash began this week when Chinese state media blasted the portrayal of Chinese agents using “ruthless violence” to torture members of a secret unit of Japan’s self-defence forces, calling it a “deliberate smear” against Beijing.

Chinese media said that some of the torture methods were similar to those Japanese troops used against Chinese civilians during the second world war.

The state-run tabloid Global Times said the acts shown in the episode “bear striking similarities to the torture inflicted on Chinese nationals by invading Japanese troops” during the war, adding that the drama “distorts the truth by attributing these atrocities to modern Chinese characters”.

In the 4 October episode, a Chinese agent is seen cutting off the fingers of the Japanese intelligence officer and stabbing him in the abdomen.

Sanrio said in a statement: “Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people.

“We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects.”

The drama’s first season, set in a fictional central Asian country, avoided controversy, but its latest season is being shown at a time of increasingly fractious relations between Beijing and Tokyo.

Japan’s conservative prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, set off a diplomatic row in November last year when she told MPs that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger the deployment of her country’s self-defence forces if the conflict posed an existential threat to Japan.

Takaichi said earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and hoped to watch them over the year-end and new year holidays.

China is a crucial overseas market for Sanrio, whose cast of characters includes My Melody and Cinnamoroll – both featured in Vivant-themed merchandise.

The Tokyo-based company racked up 781m yuan ($117m) in revenue from the Chinese market in the first half of this year, according to Chinese media, up more than 40% from the same period last year.

The backlash against Sanrio comes days after the French international footballer Kylian Mbappé was dropped by several Chinese brands after he jokingly referred to Mao Zedong as a “dictator”. The Real Madrid forward, who is nicknamed the “dictator” for his influence on the game, later apologised for his “ill-judged” remarks.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Minnesota officials surveilled activists urging closure of waste incinerator, emails show
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Tom Perkins
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Local officials tried to grow close to activist groups and collected information that was then shared with industry

Newly released emails show local government officials in Minneapolis have quietly surveilled environmental justice activists who are working to close a controversial waste incinerator that is emitting pollution into low-income neighborhoods around it, activist groups allege.

County officials sent an employee who is also an environmental justice activist to collect intelligence, among other tactics, emails show. The information was then used to help successfully kill state-level environmental legislation opposed by the incinerator’s leadership, and try to stay one step ahead of activist campaigns and protests. In another instance, a county employee presenting himself as an ally allegedly tried to obtain the identity of a whistleblower, a recording shows.

The county allegedly sent other employees to try to grow close to activist groups for the purpose of collecting information, and developed reports and dossiers on local environmental justice leaders.

The operation is laid out in emails that the Zero Burn Coalition, Minnesota Environmental Justice Table (MNEJT), and other advocacy groups and leaders obtained via a Freedom of Information Act request. The groups published some of those emails in a report to support their allegations.

The emails reveal how information collected was shared among top county environmental officials, who then in some instances sent information to industry, including the company that owns the controversial trash incinerator.

“Why are public resources and county staff time being directed toward monitoring community members who are simply organizing to shut down an aging, outdated trash burner that should have been closed nearly a decade ago?” Minneapolis organizer Audua Pugh, who was among those surveilled, asked county political leadership during a board meeting this week.

Hennepin county via a spokesperson told the Guardian in a statement that the allegations “mischaracterize the county’s community engagement work and staff responsibilities”. It added that officials “routinely attend public community meetings, stakeholder discussions and participate in social media to listen, learn, share information, and understand different perspectives on issues affecting the county and our residents”.

The north Minneapolis trash incinerator, called Hennepin Energy Recovery Center (HERC), incinerates 365,000 tons of trash annually. Nearly 100 municipal or hazardous waste incinerators operate nationally, including seven in Minnesota.

They have drawn increased scrutiny in part because they are known to release high levels of Pfas “forever chemicals” that are widely used across the economy and concentrate in municipal waste, but cannot be fully destroyed by the incineration process. They are also to emit high levels of other pollutants, but the powerful waste management industry markets them as recycling or “green” operations.

Similar battles to close polluting facilities are playing out in cities like Baltimore and Miami.

Emails show much of the county’s alleged surveillance operation ran through Joe Vital, who was considered by many in environmental justice leadership to be an ally and associate, according to the report. He was previously chair of the Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party Native Peoples Caucus; has worked with members of MNEJT to oppose Line 3, a controversial Enbridge fossil fuel pipeline proposal; and has helped lead fights against other area polluters.

Vital was hired by the county in 2021 and serves as its environmental engagement coordinator.

In June 2023, advocates held a Zoom meeting to discuss their next steps in their campaign to shut down the incinerator. Though the meetings are open to the public, organizers vet who is on the call to determine whether industry or political opponents are present.

The information obtained via Foia revealed that Vital had been on the call and developed a dossier that he sent to his superiors. He had gone unnoticed in the advocates’ screening process, Nazir Khan, executive director of the MNEJT, told the Guardian.

He said the environmental groups screen for potential county or industry employees, and greet people who they do not know, so they would have noticed Vital’s name had it been displayed. The emails show that Angie Timmons, a county environmental department manager, saw the invite for the advocates’ meeting, and asked Vital to attend.

The dossier included notes on who attended, including a sitting state representative and a former city council member, and each of the groups’ and individual’s planned activities.

Among those who received Vital’s dossier was Hennepin county’s energy and environment department director, Rosemary Lavin. A series of county emails show the supervisors planning to meet to discuss Vital’s findings, and report them to “Lisa”, who advocates say is almost certainly Lisa Cerney, a top county public works official who reports directly to political leadership. Cerney then made public media statements in support of the incinerator.

The emails revealed other similar instances of Vital developing reports about advocates’ activities and sending them to supervisors, and Vital during a conversation with Khan also tried to confirm the identity of a whistleblower, a recording shows.

Vital did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian, but Khan said activists confronted him over the county’s information-gathering operation detailed in the Foia emails. In recordings of a conversation provided to the Guardian, Vital suggested that advocates had it wrong – Vital was actually working for the activists.

Vital said his activity was part of a ploy to gain intelligence on the county officials, Khan said, and described the tradeoff this way: “You have to offer a pound of flesh to maintain inside the room,” Khan claims Vital said to him. Khan told the Guardian that Vital provided very little information of value to advocates, and they do not believe his claim that he is on their side.

A county spokesperson told the Guardian the actions were “ordinary functions of government”.

“The county seeks to find alignment, when possible, but working together does not mean agreement on every issue,” the spokesperson said.

Among county officials to whom Vital provided information was David McNary, who also sits on the board for the Minnesota Resource Recovery Association industry trade group which describes itself as a “private-public membership organization that supports the utilization of today’s waste as a local, renewable, and sustainable source for tomorrow’s energy”. It represents the interests of companies like the incinerator’s owners.

In one instance in 2024, McNary passed on advocates’ emails about organizing plans to industry as the latter mobilized to kill an environmental justice community-backed bill that proposed to let cities phase out polluting land uses. The emails were initially obtained by a county employee, Mallory Anderson, who had gotten on advocates’ email list without the advocates’ realization.

On 12 March 2024, Anderson sent the emails to McNary. McNary wrote that he feared the bill “could impact [incinerator] facilities as well as every other production, processing and industrial facility in the state”.

McNary sent emails on 13 March from advocates to an industry trade group attorney, HERC operator president Tim Steinbeck, and other industry representatives.

“The following email is from the EJ groups trying to get people to testify in favor of the bill,” he wrote. He asked the attorney: “Have you been able to get any information on who is opposing this bill?”

Steinbeck responded that the bill would be “detrimental” to the incinerator industry and urged everyone on the email thread to testify against it. Their efforts to help kill the bill were successful.

The emails reveal other instances of the county passing on emails to industry, and the situations illustrate how Hennepin county, which has 9,000 employees, dispatches staff to work in roles to gather information, Khan claimed.

Advocates “let down their defenses because the county is using people who are seen as part of the community to get in the door and build a relationship, then gather intelligence”, Khan added. “[Advocates] assume [the county employees] are an ally, but they’re trying to cultivate these relationships so that they can then share information up the chain.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: It’s easy to see through Trump’s Ukraine ploy | Kenneth Roth
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Kenneth Roth
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
In advance of the midterms, Trump is blaming Kyiv for high gas prices while making clear moves to support Russia

As the US midterms approach, Donald Trump is abandoning Ukraine’s democracy in a desperate effort to deny responsibility for worsening inflation. Yet this past weekend’s dramatic elections in Brazil and Serbia show that voters can see through such subterfuge.

There is nothing like a political party’s corrupt indifference to the plight of ordinary people to galvanize voter turnout. If US voters follow in the footsteps of their Brazilian and Serbian counterparts, a Democratic landslide is likely.

If that happens, Democrats in Congress must act quickly to rein in Trump before he does more damage to the US’s economy and global stature.

Any objective observer would see that Trump’s war of choice against Iran has inflated energy prices, because Iran predictably responded by restricting shipments in the strait of Hormuz, through which much of the Middle East’s oil and gas flows. But Trump, never one to admit error, needed a scapegoat. Enter Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

While holding off Russian troops on the front lines in the Donbas region of eastern Ukraine, Zelenskyy’s forces have been damaging the Russian economy by attacking its oil refineries. That has finally brought the war home to ordinary Russians in the form of long lines at gasoline stations. It has also disrupted oil production, putting pressure on a major source of revenue for Putin to fund his invasion.

Trump is trying to blame the inflationary surge in US gasoline and diesel prices on these attacks, even though their effect on the global market is small compared to the diminished flow through the strait of Hormuz.

Meanwhile, with Russia making only limited progress in eastern Ukraine despite losing hundreds of thousands of troops, Putin has taken, as is his wont, to attacking Ukrainian civilians. He has bombed their cities and attacked their energy infrastructure to deprive them of heat for their homes this coming winter.

He seems to hope that a freezing populace will pressure Zelensky to capitulate. Yet many Ukrainians remain determined to defend their country’s democracy from Putin’s dictatorship.

So Putin has turned to his ace-in-the-hole, Trump. The naive American president, with his inattention to detail, craving for flattery, and disturbing admiration for autocrats, was easily won over.

Trump has now openly sided with Russia. He has authorized the purchase of diesel fuel from Russia, financing Putin’s attacks on Ukrainian cities. The gesture will not noticeably reduce market prices before the midterms, but it allows Trump to make a nod of acknowledgment toward the affordability crisis that he normally derides.

He has waived new sanctions on Russia which had just been adopted by overwhelming Congressional majorities in the name of the late senator Lindsey Graham, a purported friend of Trump whose devotion to Ukraine’s democracy Trump now betrays.

The Trump administration suspended delivery of defensive missiles to Ukraine and early-warning intelligence of Russian attacks just as Putin was intensifying his bombing of Ukrainian cities, leaving civilian residents to their fate.

And it reportedly greenlit a decision by Trump’s buddy Elon Musk to slow Starshield, the version of the Starlink satellite internet service that Ukraine’s military depends on for its drones to defend the front line against a vastly larger Russian military.

Finally, Trump called for an “energy ceasefire”, by which he effectively meant only an end to Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries (Ukraine has only one badly damaged refinery), not an end of Putin’s efforts to force Ukrainians to freeze this winter. Ukraine is attacking what are arguably legitimate military targets. Putin is committing war crimes. Yet Trump condemned only Ukraine’s attacks, not Russia’s.

The Ukrainian government would have welcomed a real energy ceasefire but rejected this selective one.

Trump claims his embrace of Putin is an effort to build a relationship with him so he will negotiate peace. But offering him enormous benefits in return for nothing won’t force him to the bargaining table. The former German chancellor Angela Merkel believed that tying Russia to Europe economically would preserve peace with Russia. Instead, Putin acquired the means to invade Ukraine.

Trump’s amateur diplomats – Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner – are hardly primed to do better. Witkoff embarrassingly dubbed Putin a “humanitarian” for releasing one elderly American held in prison on concocted charges while Putin kept up the indiscriminate attacks on Ukrainian cities.

The envoys still seem to think that Putin aspires for only a chunk of Ukrainian territory rather than the destruction of Ukraine’s democracy.

Trump hopes his blame-Ukraine campaign will prevent a Republican midterm debacle. It should only reinforce voter sentiment that Trump is indifferent to their plight, that he would rather deploy smoke and mirrors than alter his corrupt, self-serving reign.

Will a Democratic midterm victory make a difference? The American presidency largely runs foreign policy, with little input from Congress. However, there are some things that the Democrats might do if they take the reins in January.

I would begin with sanctions on Russia. The latest round of sanctions won overwhelming bipartisan support, yet the legislation contained the traditional national-interest waiver that Trump invoked to ignore them.

The Democrats should re-enact the legislation without the waiver. They might even name the bill again after Graham. Outrage against Trump’s betrayal of Ukraine is widespread among Congressional members of both parties in Washington. If the legislation can secure a veto-proof two-thirds majority, Trump would be stuck with it.

That might also break his aura of being beyond restraint. A successful rectification of US policy toward Ukraine might be followed by bills that limit Trump’s tariff authority or curtail the funds he needs to keep fighting Iran – as he is considering doing after the midterms.

There is nothing normal about the current Republican Congress’s abdication of its foreign policy role to Trump’s self-promoting priorities. Ukraine is on the frontline of the global defense of democracy. The American people see that. So does Congress. Trump may be oblivious, but under Democratic leadership, Congress should take matters into its own hands.

Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: England’s Ivan Toney to stand trial during Euro 2028 after denying assault charge
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Sam Cunningham
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Ivan Toney has in effect been ruled out of Euro 2028 after his trial for assault occasioning actual bodily harm was scheduled for 12 June 2028.

Toney appeared at Southwark crown court and stood in the dock to confirm a not guilty plea. The striker is accused of head-butting and punching Saber Da Silva at a Soho nightclub on 6 December last year.

Setting the trial date for 20 months’ time, Judge Hehir apologised to Toney for the delay. “That’s a long way, I’m sorry about that,” he said. “As you may know, the crown courts are operating under a great deal of pressure.” Toney – wearing a black button-up cardigan, white shirt and tie – was told he was in a queue of defendants awaiting crown court trials.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

Toney was part of Thomas Tuchel’s England squad for the 2026 World Cup, coming on against Argentina in the semi-final and starting the third-place playoff victory against France. Toney, who plays for the Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, was charged by the Metropolitan police three weeks after the tournament. He was not part of Tuchel’s next squad for the Nations League fixtures at the end of September and early October.

It appears inconceivable the England manager would select a player for Euro 2028, which is due to be held in the UK and Ireland, while the player faces a criminal trial during the group stage.

Toney was released on unconditional bail and told it was “very important” and “a matter of common sense” that he stayed in regular contact with his solicitors while awaiting trial.

Judge Hehir told Toney that the law obliged him to give the footballer a formal warning, as with any defendant on bail awaiting trial, about the consequences of failing to attend court. “It’s a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment,” he said. The case would likely be tried in his absence if he did not appear, the judge added.

When Toney appeared at Westminster magistrates court to enter his plea at the start of October, the court was told by the prosecutor, Tom Heslop, that Toney and Da Silva exchanged words that resulted in them “squaring up” to one another before Toney “lunged forward and head-butted the complainant, followed by a few punches”. Da Silva sustained injuries to his nose and fingers, it was alleged. After pleading not guilty, Toney requested that his trial be heard at a crown court.

After the Metropolitan police announced Toney had been charged, a spokesperson for the player said: “Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court.”

Toney, who has 10 England caps, started his career at Northampton before moving to Newcastle and Peterborough. His career took off at Brentford, where his goals helped them win promotion to the Premier League in 2021 before he established himself as one of the leading top-flight strikers. He moved to Al-Ahli for £40m in 2024.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: US economy grows faster than expected in report out just ahead of elections
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Reuters
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Growth is in sharp contrast to ​households’ assessment, reflected in ‌Trump’s record-low approval ratings

The US economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter as resilient consumer spending and AI-driven ⁠business investment more than ⁠offset the impact ​of higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East.

Gross domestic product (GDP) increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the commerce department’s ⁠bureau of economic analysis said in its advance estimate of the third quarter GDP on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2% pace.

The strength in growth is in stark contrast to ​households’ downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in ‌Donald Trump’s record-low approval ratings ‌and a sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment. The report was published less than a week before Tuesday’s midterm ‌elections, which will determine control of Congress.

The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Federal Reserve officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of around 2%. The US central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75%-4% range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated”.

Economists expected the Fed to raise rates in December. The Fed chairman, Kevin Warsh, told reporters “economic activity is expanding ‌at a strong pace,” noting that “while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.”

Given the increasing dominance of AI-related spending, some economists said the ​strong GDP growth was probably not a true picture of the economy. Investors are increasingly focusing on the rising costs of long-term AI projects, in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending. Still, economists did expect ⁠this pillar of support to weaken, though a pullback in spending was likely.

Consumer spending, ​which accounts for more ​than two-thirds of the economy, increased at ​a 3.8% pace in the July-September quarter after growing at a 3.8% rate in ​the second quarter. Historically low ‌layoffs and moderate ​hiring are helping ​to underpin spending, though wage gains have at times lagged inflation.

But households also have been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending. With average gasoline prices still above $4 a gallon as the US-Israel war on Iran drags on, economists anticipated a slowdown in consumer spending.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17bn in major grocery delivery consolidation
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Acquisition will supercharge DoorDash’s grocery delivery, ‘one of the hardest things to get right online’, CEO says

DoorDash is gobbling up Instacart in a $17bn acquisition that will supercharge its grocery delivery business.

DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app will remain, and Instacart shoppers can continue fulfilling orders for Instacart. Grocers can also choose to work with Instacart or DoorDash. Instacart customers will now have access to 50,000 additional stores covered by DoorDash, the company said.

Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the US and Canada. Its 600,000 “shoppers” – who are independent contractors – completed 338m orders last year, according to company filings. Instacart has a market value of $14bn.

DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food and electronics. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3bn orders last year using a network of 9m independent delivery workers. It has a market value of $73bn.

DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores.

The partnership with one of the nation’s largest grocery chains expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 US Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco .

Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash, said the acquisition will combine Instacart’s expertise in grocery with DoorDash’s expertise in logistics and delivery.

“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts,” Xu said in a statement. “Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery.”

DoorDash’s aggressive market-share gains have hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on US delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company. DoorDash’s share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats’ share held steady at just under 20%.

It’s not yet clear what the deal will mean for some partnerships. Instacart offers delivery from Walmart, for example, but DoorDash stopped providing Walmart delivery in 2022.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Two Colorado college students found dead after going missing during hike
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Kaden Matsuda and Jackson Donlon were on a trip in Rocky Mountains last weekend when heavy snowstorm hit

Two Colorado college students have been found dead after going missing during a hiking trip in the Rocky Mountains last weekend when a heavy snowstorm hit, authorities said.

The bodies of Kaden Matsuda, 19, of Ridgway, Colorado, and Jackson Donlon, 20, of New York, were found on Wednesday afternoon in a basin of West Apostle Mountain, about 100 miles (160km) south-east of Aspen, the Chaffee county sheriff’s office said in a statement posted on social media.

The pair left Colorado Mountain College’s Leadville campus on Friday, telling family and friends they planned to hike up Ice Mountain, a nearly 14,000ft (4,270-meter) peak near West Apostle Mountain that requires technical climbing, the sheriff’s office said. They were expected back by Sunday, but college staff reported them missing on Monday morning.

The sheriff’s office said the causes of their deaths were under investigation, but foul play was not suspected. Authorities said they would not offer theories on what may have happened until autopsies are completed.

“Our heart aches for Kaden and Jackson’s family and friends,” Chaffee county’s sheriff, Andy Rohrich, said in the statement on Wednesday night. “We are very proud of our team’s efforts to find them before this weekend’s coming storm. Although this is a gut punch, our prayers were answered that we would find Kaden and Jackson, allowing some closure for the family.”

About 60 search and rescue volunteers, aided by helicopters, drones and dogs, searched for the two men.

The helicopter crew on Tuesday discovered a tent collapsed under the snow with their sleeping bags, a stove and clothing near a lake north-west of Ice Mountain, but the students were nowhere to be found.

Based on the tent’s location, officials said they were aiming for the 13,597ft West Apostle Mountain.

The sheriff’s office said their climbing equipment was not in their dorms, tent or vehicle, suggesting they left their tent prepared for a technical climb. Trash inside the tent indicated they had eaten before starting their hike, officials said.

Matsuda was studying to become a wildland firefighter, and Donlon was studying to become a mountain guide, Rohrich said.

Authorities had been concerned that aerial searches could be limited later this week because of poor weather that is expected to begin on Friday.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: A Mississippi Democrat is unexpectedly threatening Republicans’ grip on the state
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Adria R Walker
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
As Scott Colom challenges incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith for Senate, one of the country’s most reliably Republican states may be in play in the midterms

On Tuesday, with just one week until the election, Scott Colom’s headquarters was buzzing. Volunteers arrived for phone-banking, while staffers prepared for another day of campaigning. Colom, a Democrat who is challenging incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith for US Senate, had just held a press conference in Corinth, Mississippi.

Trump campaigned for Hyde-Smith in Corinth, a small city near the Tennessee border that typically leans Republican on Tuesday, too. He told attendees that he was there “because Cindy’s doing great, but I just got to make sure. I can’t take a chance.”

Other prominent Republicans in the state attended and spoke at the rally, including the governor, Tate Reeves, who told attendees in the nearly full arena that “this is the most important election of our lives”.

But the fact that Republicans viewed it necessary to call in Trump has been seen by many as an admission of their vulnerability: Mississippi, one of the country’s most reliably Republican states, may be in play in next week’s midterm elections, which will determine which party controls Congress for the last two years of the president’s term. The race has attracted national attention in recent weeks as national Democrats suddenly have poured new money into a seat that had seemed out of reach. In August, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, the fundraising arm of the Senate Democrats, left Colom out of a $40m investment into battleground states. Since October, many national Democrats have stumped across the state in support of Colom.

But that wasn’t always the case. “The Democrats just basically conceded the state,” Colom said, describing the previous view of national Democrats towards Mississippi. In doing so, he said, the party was signaling indifference to loyal Black and white Democrats in the state who continued to support the party even if the relationship did not seem reciprocal: “For too long, we weren’t willing to challenge that. For me, I’m ready to challenge. I want to show the people I have courage. And that’s what it takes in this moment. We cannot be afraid to call out the lies. We cannot be afraid to call out the betrayal.”

Colom’s press conference in Corinth attracted about 100 attendees, despite the short notice. He also spoke to people who had lined up outside Crossroads Arena to see Trump.

“[Trump voters] are getting betrayed,” he said. “They voted for America first. They’re getting Mississippi last. They were voting for lower grocery prices on day one. Well, the only thing that happened on day one is we got the greatest increase in sales tax in decades. They voted for no more endless wars. We’re back at war with no end in sight. They voted for the release of the Epstein files.

“I wanted to make sure I go to the lines there and listen to what matters to them. And tell them: ‘I’m just trying to make sure you get what you voted for. I agree with you. We need lower grocery prices. I agree with you. We need to get out of stupid wars. And I agree with you that we can’t protect pedophiles without a prosecutor.’”

Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982. It’s been much longer – not since 1875 – that the state elected a Black person to that office. Without the party label, Colom’s bonafides might make him a shoo-in for a win: in 2015, he unseated a nearly 30-year incumbent when he was elected the first Black district attorney for the 16th circuit. As district attorney, he had a 94% success rate for convictions. He’s a seventh-generation Mississippian, whose father was a longtime Republican who campaigned for Ronald Reagan and was friends with Thad Cochran, a longtime state politician.

Yet Colom is fighting an uphill battle to unseat Hyde-Smith, a senator for eight years who has not sponsored any legislation during her tenure (she has co-sponsored 32 bills that became law).

When Colom walked back into his office the morning after Trump’s visit, volunteers were exuberant. They hugged and offered words of encouragement and support.

Barack Obama campaigned in Mississippi in 2008, speaking at Jackson State University. But neither Hillary Clinton nor Kamala Harris visited during their presidential campaigns. Bernie Sanders had a scheduled appearance in the state in 2020, but canceled it at the last minute to go to Michigan instead.

The state has largely been ceded to Republicans, said Marvin King, an associate professor of political science and African American studies at the University of Mississippi.

“National Democrats do historically ignore Mississippi. They ignore plenty of red states, so Mississippi’s not alone,” he said. “The problem for Mississippi Democrats is that their voter base, the base that they rely on for votes, is quite frankly a lower income base, so it’s hard for Democrats here to raise the money internally.’”

The walls of Colom’s office are adorned with photos of him at campaign stops, him with volunteers, supporters and staffers. At his first town hall in Jackson, Colom said, he had four people show up. He knew he had to build his own momentum, doing town halls and going to festivals, housing projects and homecomings.

Bennie Thompson, currently Mississippi’s lone Black and only Democratic congressional representative, told him that he’d have to campaign all across the state.

“I put these pictures up to remind myself of the joy in it,” Colom said. “It takes a lot of endurance, but these photos remind me of why I’m doing it. It feels like the people of Mississippi are finally getting the attention they deserve. The potential of our state is getting the recognition it deserves and I’m proud to be fighting for the people in this moment.”

Also prominent in the office are signs that bear one of the main mottos of the campaign: “Mississippi matters.” It’s a guiding light for the campaign, and something that Democrats are starting to consider on a national level, too.

On 14 October, Georgia senator Raphael Warnock, a Democrat, campaigned in Jackson for Colom. He raised more than $500,000 for Colom’s campaign committee, according to Politico.

“I am here because I am tired of the South being overlooked or diminished in terms of its electoral importance,” Warnock told the Gulf States Newsroom. “We ignore the South at our own peril. Democrats are investing here. I would like to see more, for the sake of the country.”

Colom said that senators Lisa Blunt Rochester and Angela Alsobrooks were all early national supporters of his campaign. Other notable Democrats – Cory Booker, Pete Buttigieg and Harris – have also recently visited the state to stump for Colom. Barack Obama released an advertisement in support of Colom, telling voters: “Mississippi, it’s time for a change.”

“If I’m Colom, I’m only upset that the Democrats waited so late,” King said. “If the national Democrats had entered this race in June or July, it’s a very different story.”

Mississippi has the largest percentage of Black voters, a voting bloc that largely votes Democratic. To win, Colom will need both Black voter turnout and to win about a quarter of the white – otherwise Republican – vote. In 2018, Mike Espy, Mississippi’s first Black congressman since Reconstruction and a former US agriculture secretary, lost a special election to Hyde-Smith by just seven points. But Reeves won his 2023 re-election bid by just a three percentage-point margin and finished less than one percentage point above the majority threshold required to avoid a runoff.

Mikel Bolden, executive director of the Mississippi Democratic party, said that the voters themselves are why national Democrats are taking notice of the state.

“You cannot take voters for granted simply because of how they voted in the past,” she said. “People are paying attention. Voters are speaking out a little bit more. Nationals really sees that not only are we pushing for them, but the voters are pushing for them.”

Though Mississippi doesn’t have early voting, the state does offer absentee voting to older adults and those with qualifying excuses. As of 27 October, more than 56,000 absentee ballots were cast in Mississippi, up from 22,221 in 2022. During the last midterm election, however, the Senate race was not on the ballot. The number is lower from where it was during the 2024 presidential election.

“I feel like I need to do everything I can to represent the values and vision of the people of Mississippi,” Colom said. “For too long, Mississippi hasn’t been a lost cause, it’s been a betrayed cause.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ​Pragmatic or pointless? Europe’s rift over whether to pick up the phone to Putin
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Pjotr Sauer
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
With no single European representative negotiating directly with Moscow, some leaders are establishing their own channels – with messy results

The Nordic countries rarely fall out in public over foreign policy, least of all over Russia.

But a 90-minute phone call this week to Vladimir Putin by the leaders of Finland and Norway drew an unusual rebuke from their Danish and Swedish neighbours.

On Tuesday, Finland’s president, Alexander Stubb, and Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, spoke with Putin, in a rare high-level conversation between the Russian leader and Ukraine’s European allies. The two Nordic leaders stressed that the call had been conducted on Ukraine’s behalf and that allies had been informed in advance.

“I am very sceptical about this independent initiative by Norway and Finland,” said Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, who complained that the call had not been coordinated with Copenhagen. “I honestly don’t know what they think they can achieve by this.”

Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, also criticised the initiative, saying he had not been informed beforehand.

The friction offered a glimpse of the divisions threatening to complicate Europe’s attempts to establish its own channel to Moscow, as governments struggle to agree not only on whether to engage Putin but also on who should speak on their behalf.

“Instead of looking like a firmly united, homogeneous group, we see a rift,” said Arkady Moshes, director of the Russia programme at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs. “By the standards of the Nordic world, it’s pretty serious.”

Since the summer, European leaders have been discussing, without much progress, whether to appoint a representative to negotiate directly with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine. The debate has grown more urgent as Donald Trump has moved closer to Moscow in recent weeks at Ukraine’s expense.

A new round of peace talks is expected to take place in Abu Dhabi next month, leaving European governments anxious about being sidelined in negotiations that could shape the continent’s security for decades.

“There is an agreement overall that we need to talk to Putin, but the outreach is starting to feel like a free-for-all,” said a senior European diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity. “Too many leaders believe they can be the one to get Putin to negotiate.”

This year, British, French and German ambassadors have held talks with Russian officials, Emmanuel Macron’s senior diplomatic adviser has travelled to Moscow, and the office of the European Council president, António Costa, has pursued its own engagement with the Kremlin.

It is a far cry from the diplomatic isolation imposed on Putin after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, when most European leaders largely shunned direct contact with the Kremlin. Stubb himself said during his 2024 presidential campaign that he would not pick up the phone if Putin called.

Analysts this week blamed some of the fallout from the Stubb/Støre call on mixed messages about what it was actually for. Initially framed as an effort to convey Ukrainian messages to Putin, the call appeared to have broader aims.

Støre later defended Norway’s decision to engage directly with Putin, citing the need to manage shared fish stocks in the Barents Sea and maintain security along the countries’ common border. Stubb, meanwhile, said the conversation was also intended to prevent misunderstandings between Russia and its Nordic neighbours.

“Stubb and Støre can’t seem to get their message straight on whether this was about Ukraine or also about their own security concerns,” said Joel Linnainmäki, a former Finnish diplomat and analyst in Helsinki.

The confusion reflects a wider disagreement across Europe over how to approach Putin, even as governments remain broadly united in their support for Ukraine.

“On substance there is actually quite a good level of unity in Europe, but then there are different views on how to approach Russia, when is the right time to reopen dialogue at the highest level and who should be doing it,” said Kristi Raik, director of ICDS, a leading Estonian thinktank.

France has long advocated keeping a channel to Putin open, while Germany and Britain have been more cautious. The Baltic states and Kaja Kallas, the EU’s foreign policy chief, fear that renewed high-level engagement could ease pressure on Moscow without securing concessions.

The question of who should lead any European outreach has proved contentious.

Xavier Bettel, Luxembourg’s foreign minister and one of the few European leaders to have maintained telephone contact with Putin after the full-scale invasion, recalled facing criticism from European colleagues for taking the initiative.

“Some colleagues told me: who is the Luxembourgish prime minister to speak to the president of Russia and the president of Ukraine? You are such a small country,” he said at a conference in Prague in May.

“That’s also a problem of the state of mind of some countries who think only France, Germany or the USA can lead discussions.”

For now, no single figure has a clear mandate to negotiate on behalf of the EU’s 27 member states.

In theory, the task of speaking to Moscow could fall to Kallas. But she lacks the independent authority to negotiate on behalf of the bloc without a mandate from its member states, and there has been growing frustration in European capitals over the EU’s diplomatic service, which she leads.

Kallas, a former Estonian prime minister and one of the EU’s most vehement Kremlin critics, is also seen by many as an unlikely interlocutor for Putin. Moscow has placed her on a wanted list, while Russian officials have made clear they have little appetite for engaging with her.

Reinier van Lanschot, a Dutch member of the European parliament, has called on EU leaders to convene a summit and agree on a single representative to engage with Putin.

He said: “The EU must speak with one voice, and Ukraine must always be involved. If you take those two things into account, then I think it makes perfect sense for Europe to engage in talks.”

But he acknowledged that reaching a unanimous agreement would be difficult, with any proposed appointment potentially vulnerable to a veto by a single member state.

In the meantime, this week’s Nordic initiative could encourage more European politicians to establish their own channels to Moscow, said Linnainmäki.

“It’s inevitable that politicians around Europe will now raise the question: if the Finns and Norwegians are calling Putin, why should our country not do it?” he said.

Beyond the question of who should speak to Putin lies a more basic question: whether there is any point in Europe talking to him at all.

Raik warned that Putin might interpret Europe’s sudden interest in reopening dialogue as a sign that Ukraine and its allies were growing desperate, with Kyiv facing a difficult winter.

“My concern is that the way the Kremlin is reading this step now is that the Europeans are in trouble, the Ukrainians are in trouble,” she said. “Knowing how Putin looks at Europe, I think he’s always keen to try to use opportunities to create divisions, or at least appearances of division,.”

The Kremlin’s account of Tuesday’s conversation offered little indication of any change in Putin’s maximalist demands for ending the war.

According to the Financial Times, Putin spent part of the conversation lecturing the Nordic leaders on medieval Slavic history, repeating pseudo-historical arguments that have long been used to question Ukraine’s right to exist as an independent state.

Still, Moscow has appeared more willing to entertain European involvement in diplomacy since US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Putin in St Petersburg last week.

Moshes suggested that Moscow was tiring of Trump’s unpredictability and looking to Europe as an alternative, calculating that the US midterms could leave the president politically weakened.

But Putin’s willingness to take the call should not be mistaken for a readiness to compromise, Moshes cautioned.

“It doesn’t mean we are moving anywhere towards a ceasefire, let alone peace, because it’s clear that Putin’s plan A is a military defeat of Ukraine.”

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: South Park turns to America’s beef shortage – and explodes in diarrhea
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Jesse Hassenger
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
The 29th season has begun to slightly spin its wheels, but this poo-splattered episode suggests an imminent story arc: the release of Grand Theft Auto VI

Are record beef shortages simply not that rich a topic for South Park to riff off? The show’s 29th season had its first outright middling episode this week with a zigzaggy outing that gestured vaguely toward the performative eating of particular foods, nodded slightly at a father-son story development, and wound it all up by repeating and amplifying a funny season-long running gag that increasingly seems like it will actually serve as a makeshift story arc.

But let’s jump back to the beginning, perhaps the most laugh-out-loud moment of the episode: Cartman in a fugue of delight over the impending meal of sloppy joes at the school cafeteria, to which he forms a tribute in the form of a sloppy-joe-themed version of Gary Glitter’s Rock and Roll Part Two – a music clearance reaffirming that Trey Parker and Matt Stone don’t care if a song choice might make people tut-tut (because the singer is a serial sex offender) or just annoyed (because that song sucks). Cartman’s infectious glee is short-lived, however, when he’s informed that the lunch special for the day isn’t a sloppy joe after all, or anything beef-related, but cuy – Guinea Pig on a stick.

This is an actual Peruvian dish, to match with South Park’s season-long rechristening as South America. And thanks to its patriotic (if confusingly so) bona fides, beef farmed in South, uh, America is in higher demand than ever in the rest of the country. So while it’s a beef town, no one who lives there can actually get a reasonably priced cut of meat. This despite the fact that frequent cutaways, usually to Ruth’s Chris Steakhouse, reveal that South Park beef, rich and buttery as it is, gives people who eat it literally explosive diarrhea after one bite (and yes, obviously this is shown in great cartoonish detail.) This side-effect does not sate demand for the beef; consuming it is seen as a patriotic act.

This seems like both a commentary on the actual beef shortage in the United States, as well as the MAHA-driven desire for stuff like beef tallow. This week’s South Park – “Guinea Pig on a Stick” is the episode title – doesn’t get into all that, but there are certainly undertones in the way it depicts demand for larded-up beef from faraway elites. The steakhouse clientele are all drawn to look like the show’s celebrity caricatures, even though none of them are quite an exact match for any real figure that I could recognize. It’s a metaphor for the episode at large, which perpetually feels like it’s satirizing something bigger and more direct but doesn’t quite come into focus.

Part of the problem is that the beef shortage dilemma only lightly dovetails with the episode’s wispy kid plot, which is that Stan’s dad Randy, still in a miniaturized child’s body after the previous episode’s Sephora looksmaxxing mishap, wants to be one of the gang. Kyle and Cartman both seem willing to shrug him off, but Stan keeps snapping at him. It’s understandable; it’s annoying that Randy oscillates between off-trend kid obsessions (laughing about Italian brainrot) and his own dad-aged references (he simply refuses to shut up about the Goonies). But he does sincerely want to connect with Stan, and eventually everyone kinda tells Stan he’s being a jerk. Stan softens in the face of his dad’s sincerity.

The kids do come up with a solution to the beef shortage after a violent showdown between Ruth Chris herself (not her actual name; that would be Ruth Fertel, the founder of the confoundingly named chain) and the fake cowboys who run the Sizzler. Sizzler runs away with all of the cows in town, even the ones that might have been consigned to the cattle farm’s champagne room (a funny idea that turns out to be a momentary gag), and like everyone else in the South Park universe this season, Ruth Chris says issues like this will be massively affected by a big change that’s on deck for November.

Unlike in previous episodes, this joke is finally elaborated upon: Ruth Chris shows a top-secret video of GTA gameplay, opening the kids’ (and Randy’s) eyes to just how much things could indeed change in November. Maybe this will remain a running gag, but the way it’s brought to the foreground now, almost in lieu of an actual resolution, makes it seem like it will figure into the season finale (which does, after all, air not too long after the game’s release). So, wait, is this a piece-moving episode? Of South Park?! It sounds absurd, like a recapper reading an irreverent animated comedy like it’s a self-serious serialized show – but it does feel like the endgame.

In the meantime, the kids do figure out what to do about the beef shortage. They rebrand Guinea Pig on a stick as a particularly patriotic delicacy; it turns out the steakhouse customers don’t care what they’re eating so long as it’s got that American branding and is larded up with plenty of rich butter. With the right preparation, Guinea Pig on a stick can provide the exact same explosive diarrhea – and so we’re treated to the episode-closing sight of diners exploding into fecal matter, now with an extra hue of red and blue fireworks in accompaniment. Again, a pretty funny gross-out sight gag, but no moreso than the first dozen times. Weirdly, this episode of South Park made me look forward to Grand Theft Auto VI, too, assuming there’s now a fun storyline building up to it.

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.title: ‘Algorithms make everything predictable’: why the CD is making a comeback
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.author: Alfie Packham
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.text:
As John Lewis reports a 96% rise in searches for CD players, music fans share their reasons for ditching streaming

CDs appear to be having a resurgence. John Lewis said searches for CD players are up 96% since July, while another report on trends in music and film this year found that CD sales are up 16%.

With this in mind, we asked music fans why they favour discs over other formats, and if it is a new preference or a lifetime habit.

Andrew Wales, 67, from London, owns “well over 10,000” CDs. “My wife’s very considerate,” he says over the phone. “There’s quite a few in this room where I’m speaking.” They have also spilt into the next bedroom and into the corridor.

“I don’t need Spotify,” says Wales. “The fact is, I like listening to music and I have always preferred owning it in a physical form. The [size of the] CD format allows me to own the number I own despite living in a two-bedroom flat and not a country mansion, so that’s another bonus.”

Much of the classical music Wales buys and listens to is available only on CD. “I bought my first CD in 1991 – John Scofield, Meant to Be – around the same time that I bought my first CD player. LPs were becoming increasingly shoddy, both in terms of pressing and presentation, and their limitations meant that often or not songs or tracks were included on the CD release, but not on LP. There are still cases where that happens today.”

That said, Wales also owns “about 2,000 LPs”, “a few hundred cassettes” and an increasing number of Blu-rays. “I’m not always wedded to a single format.”

Unlike Wales, Gabriela Crowley, 32, from San Jose, California, started listening to CDs only over the last year. “Growing up, my parents had a tonne of them,” she says. “My dad played them in the car and everywhere. And then he got an iPod. By the time I was like 18, everything had started to shift away from physical media.”

Her return to physical records started with the vinyl trend a few years ago. “I met my husband, who also had a large record collection, and we enjoyed that hobby together for a while. But after having a baby, we found we really weren’t listening to our records much any more – they were too bulky and inconvenient. My father-in-law gave us one of his old CD players and now we use that every day.”

A CD collection helps with the “paradox of choice” that streaming brings, she says. “Instead of being paralysed by the endless options, you become more intimately familiar with what you have. I find it a much more satisfying way to engage with music. Plus, no autoplay or AI-generated playlists are being forced on me.”

“I bought my first CD in 1988 and have been collecting ever since,” says Neil Cumming, 53, from Gloucester. “I have several hundred of them. Everything from classical, folk, rock, blues …”

Cumming buys CDs mostly to support musicians. “I like a lot of small indie and folk bands, who are not making a lot of money. I buy CDs directly from them when I can, which means they get a bigger share of my money than they would if I streamed their music.

“And it means I own the CD for ever,” he says. “Streaming means you are basically renting the music, and it can disappear from the streaming sites. I enjoy the ritual of selecting a CD and putting it in the machine – it is a nicer experience than just pressing play on an app.”

Not that he’s anti-streaming. “It’s quite good for trying music before you buy CDs or finding new acts. But in the evening, with a mug of tea or a glass of whisky, I find the experience of a CD more satisfying.”

“I am drawn to the narrative and aesthetic arc of an album,” says Asha Varadharajan, 65, from Toronto. “It’s the antithesis of scrolling. I’ve never been a fan of music as white noise in the background, unless I’m boogying while vacuuming.”

Varadharajan has owned her CD player since 1999, “which allows me to listen to five CDs at a time in any order I choose, building my own narrative arc as I listen.

“I’m grateful to friends who introduced me to artists I may never have listened to,” she says. “The patience and persistence required in listening to a CD makes songs memorable. Streaming makes music ephemeral. I think algorithms make everything predictable, but everybody’s taste is kind of random.”

It helps that CDs are hard to damage, she says. “I’m a klutz and was terrified of scratching albums as a child because I never could place the needle accurately without my hand shaking.”

Ed, 63, from London, bought his first CDs in 1986 – “Genesis, Invisible Touch, and Level 42, World Machine, if you must know” – and has “never stopped”, he says. “But my interest in the format has waxed and waned.

“When they first came out, CDs were very much positioned as: they’ll last for ever, you can drill holes in them, you can put jam on them and they still play. But I got put off CDs because they sounded too bright and shiny compared to vinyl.”

But over the past two years, Ed has bought more CDs owing to their “almost throwaway prices against the excessive costs of vinyl”. Having music on CD “gives me something tactile and tangible”, Ed says. “A good digital source is now every bit as engaging as a good record player.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Could Abdul El-Sayed’s plan for AI companies stave off catastrophe? | Jerel Ezell
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Jerel Ezell
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The Michigan Senate candidate is calling for public ownership and other reforms, offering a potential antidote to ideological gridlock

The Michigan senatorial candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, occupies a strange but increasingly common place in modern American politics. He’s praised by progressives, begrudgingly tolerated by moderate Democrats and largely demonized by Republicans.

He’s also uniquely positioned to forge an all-too-elusive thread of political kinship between these perpetually-at-odds groups with his bold but contentious plan for reining in AI, called AI Under Democracy.

And it couldn’t come at a better time. According to a poll conducted this summer by NBC News, 70% of Americans said that they were more worried than excited about AI, a shocking reversal from just a couple of years ago. Another poll from Quinnipiac several weeks ago found that 73% of Americans are concerned about AI posing a threat to human existence.

AI Under Democracy was revealed several weeks before the Michigan Democratic primary. At the time, El-Sayed was still a relative underdog, a physician with threadbare political credentials and views that – it seemed – were woefully misaligned with the moderate, blue-collar sensibilities of Michiganders.

When it comes to his AI plan, and a companion proposal called AI Under Control that he released this month, that may no longer be the case. In fact, it could be a potential antidote to our ideological gridlock over the promise and peril of AI.

Back in 2023, I was invited to be a guest on Abdul El-Sayed’s podcast, America Dissected. Both Michigan natives with backgrounds in public health, El-Sayed and I commiserated over global leaders’ glaring lack of relatability and, by extension, the grating way they dismiss – and often increase –the struggles of everyday people. It all seems quite prescient now.

Barack Obama recently urged Democrats to rally around AI regulation in the midterms, but El-Sayed and many progressive Democrats have already been leading the charge.

El-Sayed’s AI ethos is deeply shaped by his history as a healthcare provider – not as a politician. His maxim for AI development is “first, do no harm,” a transposition of the Hippocratic oath into this new wild west of technology, as AI companies face pressure to balance profit against the public interest.
