To this end, El-Sayed’s proposal calls for corporate divestiture from AI’s largest companies, recognizing that legacy companies such as Google, Microsoft, Meta and Amazon simply have too much controlling interest in frontier AI ventures like OpenAI and Anthropic, creating untenable friction between their revenue-generation prerogatives and our public safety.

For example, Microsoft has an estimated 27% stake in OpenAI, and Google owns 14% of Anthropic, giving each a sizable say in how the companies operate. Under El-Sayed’s proposal, the tech giants would have to divest or abandon those investments within a defined transitional period.

The plan also calls for the regulation of datacenters: slowing the volume of developments, facilitating local job creation, freezing residential utility costs, and addressing the public health and quality of life issues that datacenters produce in terms of noise and pollution. He has been especially vocal about the colossal OpenAI-Oracle datacenter being erected just outside of Ann Arbor, Michigan, where he attended the University of Michigan.

Today, there’s a groundswell of resistance towards datacenters. An August poll found that only one in 9 Americans would support the construction of a datacenter in their local community. El-Sayed’s plan dovetails with the public’s clear and growing opposition: keep AI’s footprint and its environmental and socioeconomic consequences – those known and as yet unknown – contained.

Far and away the most controversial – but essential – part of El-Sayed’s plan to thwart an AI-fueled catastrophe is his call for 50% + one of board seats (a simple majority) at influential AI companies to be publicly appointed or democratically elected. This would in theory foster transparency around AI companies’ plans and give Americans the power to veto decisions – on matters like datacenter development and biological weapons manufacturing – that could undermine the public interest.

While both Democrats and Republicans may come to support heavier regulation and moratoriums on AI, public control may be an entirely different can of worms. For many, the idea of transferring ownership of a private enterprise to a public trust smacks of socialism. And this narrative certainly feeds into the common Republican critique of El-Sayed, as well as his Republican challenger Mike Rogers’ even more aggressive attempt to tar him as a feckless communist.

However, communities across the US have long embraced public ownership of essential resources such as water, natural gas, and electricity. And according to a June report, roughly 69% of American adults support AI companies transferring 50% of their stock to public sovereign wealth fund, a pot of money used to support public interests.

This is a paradigm which Bernie Sanders, El-Sayed’s most prominent booster on Capitol Hill, has legislatively proposed. There’s a good chance that Americans will continue warming up to this idea.

It’s not a coincidence that, as we approach the midterms, feverish debates are now erupting over how – or even whether – AI’s soaring risks can now be tempered via federal policy.

Naturally, in the US, people are looking to their political leaders for answers – even though a whopping 78% of Americans disapprove of how Congressional members are handling their job and Donald Trump’s approval ratings are underwater.

Many of these politicians seem unaware of or ambivalent about the state of AI and its mushrooming perils. That’s where younger, tech-savvy candidates like El-Sayed – who has called for a pause on AI’s most potent releases, a ban on artificial superintelligence, and an AI kill switch – shine and can provide leadership and restraint as we confront a future where AI is ubiquitous.

Exhibit A of the opposite: Trump and other administration officials who have been aggressively poo-poohing demands to slow AI’s rapid ascension, saying the uproar is a “hoax” while continuing to insist on the US’s AI dominance at essentially any cost.

To be sure, some – including leaders in the White House and Silicon Valley investors beholden to the sunken cost principle – will remain bullish on AI.

But calls for regulation from everyday people on both sides of aisle should be the ultimate shot across the bow. And AI’s top plutocrats, such as OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, rallying around the idea of “pacing the frontier” are a big, red flag being waved right in society’s face.

All this can be addressed through a deliberate, balanced public ownership policy.

Jerel Ezell is executive director of the Center for AI and Everybody and an assistant professor at the University of Chicago

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Rodman rule has been revised but the fight to keep stars in the NWSL goes on | Moving the Goalposts
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Megan Swanick
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Gone are the eight criteria to be a High Impact Player so clubs can spend their money on whichever player they want – and the solution makes sense

When Washington plays Chicago this Sunday in DC, “Rowdy Audi” will probably be full. It will also be full when the post-season starts, should they lock up their top-four position with a positive result on Decision Day. Equipped with an accessible stadium in a big city, a proud fanbase, and a formidable roster rife with players qualifying for the High Impact Player (HIP) rule’s initial criteria (including Trinity Rodman, who gave the rule its moniker), the Spirit hold sway in the attendance charts.

But starting next season, everyone on the Spirit will qualify for the “Rodman Rule”. So will every player in NWSL. Announced Friday, NWSL settled a grievance with the league’s Players Association, who argued that the initial criteria violated federal labor law.

Admittedly, when the new policy arrived on the scene last winter, it appeared half-baked, a somewhat frantic attempt to keep Rodman from floating across the Atlantic and doing something terrible, like playing for Michele Kang’s London City Lionesses instead of Michele Kang’s Washington Spirit.

A rule was born to prevent that. It allocated added funds beyond the salary cap for players who met league-set criteria which clearly prioritized international name recognition in a global market. Qualifying players needed to meet one of eight categories including SportsPro Media’s top 150 Most Marketable Athletes (only Alessia Russo and Aitana Bonmatí placed in 2026, though 16 female football players did in 2025, including three in the NWSL at the time – Trinity Rodman, Sophia Wilson and Marta, in that order). It also included ESPN’s Top 50, the Guardian’s top 100, top minutes on the US National Team, the Ballon d’Or’s 30-player list, or NWSL’s MVP and Best XI awards.

Some measure of umbrage followed, as invested onlookers argued for a more simple solution: just raise the salary cap. And perhaps they should, but keeping an American-style sports league competitive in a global football landscape is less straightforward. The looming spectre of Europe’s super-teams, who have attracted key members of the USWNT starting XI, is ever present, waiting to take Croix Bethune away for the right amount of money. No doubt, the NWSL’s appeal is evident in its expansion and growth, in the success of its spine of stateside stalwarts, in its rapidly expanding dedicated facilities, and in the international talents such as Esme Morgan or Ann-Katrin Berger that choose to sharpen their skills in the US.

However, the domestic sporting culture of the NWSL is somewhat at odds, in some ways a disadvantage, when it comes to maintaining its margins, with a stand-alone team structure in a parity-driven league, while competing for international glory with teams such as Chelsea, Lyon or Barcelona, who spend three times or more the amount that some NWSL teams do. While competing for status as the world’s go-to destination, for players and fans, glory hunting and name recognition do matter.

Just look at the Ballon d’Or: Barcelona’s women took all but one of the awards available to them, though Alexia Putellas, who collected her third main prize, now plays in London. That Putellas deserves her trophy is not in dispute, though the inequitable factors contributing to international accolades were manifest. Putellas starred for two super-teams: Barcelona and Spain. Ewa Pajor, Barcelona’s Polish striker, fell just short, perhaps edged out by only having one super-team to play for.

Subtly, it seemed, the original criteria for the HIP rule flirted with the idea of fostering a super-team in the US. Prior to the update, there was no cap on the number of players who could access the extra million if the salary cap was already met. For a team like Kang’s in Washington, the door felt open, possibly, to building a team even more ready to contend with the heavy spenders in Europe (including those also funded by Kang), and the international accolades that go with it. If a NWSL player lifted the NWSL trophy, helped win January’s inaugural Club World Cup, then performed well at the World Cup, could a second NWSL (active) player win the Ballon d’Or?

The structure of the HIP rule remains in place. Teams that have met 2027’s salary cap of $4.4m (£3.3m) in 2027 can spend an additional $1.257m (as reported by ESPN) on a player. The post-grievance difference is that teams can spend that additional sum on any player. Gone are the stipulations mandating adherence to that eight-criteria list of global recognition.

The change is a win for players that did not meet it, which includes elite players who fell short in previous seasons (such Ashley Sanchez) or star players with long-lasting or recurring injuries (Catarina Macario). It gives the NWSL’s individual teams the autonomy to decide which players are worthy, based on whatever criteria they see fit. And, with a cap on the number of players that can access it, it gives cash-strapped teams the theoretical ability to reign in teams with already-stacked rosters.

But the spirit of NWSL’s original criteria has more merit than many suggest. The NWSL is responsible for securing overhead issues such as an improved media rights deal, marketing marquee names to broadcasters, ensuring the league is seen as the go-to destination ahead of a World Cup and performing well in global cup competitions such as the Concacaf W Champions Cup (Mexico’s Club América prevailed in the most recent final) or the upcoming Club World Cup. With that in mind – plus the ever-pressing desire to keep USWNT players in the US – the original HIP criteria had its eye on awarding stardom as it’s seen in the global market.

Stardom is imprecise. It’s hard to measure, but impossible to miss. Rodman did not make the Ballon d’Or shortlist and is not leading the Golden Boot race. But Rodman and her closest national team peers (including “Triple Espresso” compadres Mallory Swanson and Wilson) are the presumed stars of the NWSL. Rodman, alongside Wilson (who clocked the Michael Jordan “shrug” celebration after scoring in the 2022 Championship final) have not just the skill but the personality flourishes reminiscent of Alex Morgan sipping the tea in Lyon.

The NWSL has yet to replicate the Morgan effect (think default attendance records and adoring away fans), but requiring that teams reward players with a certain je ne sais quoi in their international football fame was baked into the league’s original attempt at the HIP criteria.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Russell Brand’s wife tells court he is ‘amazingly attentive husband’
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Emine Sinmaz
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Giving evidence at her husband’s rape trial, Laura Brand says couple previously split up over his promiscuity

Russell Brand’s wife has told a court that they previously split up over his promiscuity but that he was a “wonderful father” and an “amazingly attentive husband”.

Giving evidence at her husband’s rape trial, Laura Brand, 39, said they fell in love after meeting in 2006 but that the comedian found monogamy difficult.

“I wasn’t interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people,” she said.

Brand, 51, is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.

Giving evidence at Southwark crown court on Wednesday, Laura told the court she met Brand at the Edinburgh festival in 2006 after his show Shame, which was “very, very, very funny”, “extremely entertaining” and sexually explicit.

She said they met in the foyer of the Assembly Rooms, where Brand complimented her friend, who had a boyfriend. Laura recalled: “And he said to me: ‘But tell me you don’t have a boyfriend,’ and I said: ‘No, I don’t.’”

Laura recalled that Brand contacted her the next day and they had oral sex. Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, asked: “Did he want to have penetrative sex?” to which Laura replied: “I didn’t want to, but I don’t remember it even being a topic. I didn’t intend to and I don’t remember him asking.”

They began dating in September 2006 and Brand “absolutely” respected her wishes sexually, Laura said. Describing his treatment of her, she said: “Very caring, totally at my pace. I was not experienced, I had only had one partner before Russell and I felt entirely cared for, and looked after by Russell.”

But the court heard their relationship broke down over his cheating. Winter asked: “Did you become aware shortly thereafter that he was promiscuous and engaging in sexually activity with others?” Laura replied: “I was aware when I met him that he liked women and I was aware towards the latter part of that year that he was engaging with other women, yes.”

Laura said the couple split up in February 2007 because of his infidelity. “I was invested, we both had told each other we loved each other but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous. We talked about it. I did find that difficult,” she said.

Laura said she was “heartbroken” after the breakup but that the pair resumed contact as friends in summer 2007. She said she became friendly again with Brand when his marriage to the US pop star Katy Perry ended, and that they rekindled their romance in 2015, married two years later, and they now have three children together.

When asked if she was aware of Brand’s promiscuity during their time apart, Laura said: “I was very aware of it and I would read about regularly in the papers and he also told me, we talked about it.”

But both the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, and the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, objected when Winter asked Laura what her view was “as to the truth” of the criminal allegations her husband faces.

Winter then asked Laura to describe Brand, to which Laura replied: “Russell, my husband, is caring, he’s kind, he’s a wonderful father to our children, he’s an amazingly attentive husband.

“He’s got an eye for detail I’ve never known before. The way he treats me is to really know me, I feel very seen by him, in a way I’ve never experienced before. I love him very much.”

She continued: “We have a very frank, honest and clear relationship and marriage. It is one of the most important parts of our marriage, and our relationship has always been honest.”

In cross-examination Karmy-Jones noted that Laura had been present throughout most of the trial and had taken notes. She also challenged Laura about how much contact she had had with Brand after their break up in 2007.

Laura said she had spoken to Brand after his marriage to Perry ended. “He called me after his marriage and gifted me meditation for me and my boyfriend at the time,” she said.

Brand nodded and smiled as Laura insisted that while they had not had a sexual relationship in the years before they got back together in 2015, they had spent time together by going to the theatre and watching box sets.

The prosecutor said that in 2017, shortly after the couple had their first child, Brand was a guest on the US talkshow, The Wendy Williams Show. She said the comedian had said of his relationship with Laura: “When we went out with each other we loved each other very much but I was in a phase where I thought the world was an amusement park made out of orgasms.”

Earlier, statements from two of Brand’s ex-girlfriends were read to the court, as they gave good accounts of his character. They also said he had cheated on them and they had supported him financially.

Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Alaska governor orders investigation into Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ariana Baio
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Republican Mike Dunleavy plans search after Peltola accused of recruiting Dan Sullivan to confuse voters

The Republican governor of Alaska announced plans to launch a criminal investigation after a report accused the campaign of the Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola of trying to confuse voters by recruiting a candidate with the same name as her opponent.

Governor Mike Dunleavy wrote on social media that he was “directing the department of public safety to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted”.

It came after the New York Times published a damning report in which one of Peltola’s former staffers said that the Democrat’s campaign recruited people named Dan Sullivan to run for office against the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan, to deliberately confuse voters.

Donald Trump also called for Peltola to be “removed from the Ballot and prosecuted” after the report. The US president previously condemned the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan and accused Democrats of putting an “imposter” on the ballot.

Peltola’s campaign had denied involvement in encouraging or soliciting Dan J Sullivan, a former educator with no political experience, to run against Dan S Sullivan, according to an Anchorage Daily News report from May.

But Dunleavy said the report “reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections” and that “Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support.”

“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections. Anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable,” Dunleavy wrote.

The New York Times report relied on interviews with Peltola’s former campaign manager and longtime aide, as well as several other people who participated in or were told about the plan.

Text messages and documents seen by the New York Times also shed light on the plan that Peltola’s campaign staff and senior aides in the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) hatched to encourage other people named Dan Sullivan to run.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Cornell faculty press ahead with no-confidence vote in handling of gang-rape case
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Richard Luscombe and agency
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
A recording of a closed-door meeting revealed some faculty sought to delay the vote, but others urged immediacy

Faculty members at Cornell University are pressing ahead with a no-confidence vote in campus leadership over its handling of a gang-rape scandal involving students at a fraternity at the Ivy League institution.

Cornell professors on Wednesday discussed, at an emotional faculty meeting, how the school’s leadership tackled a woman’s report that she was raped by at least seven male students at a fraternity house in 2024.

The Associated Press, which obtained a recording of the closed-door meeting, reported that some faculty urged patience and sought to delay the vote, while others argued that years of institutional failures required more immediate action.

Faculty will vote electronically on a proposed no-confidence resolution in Cornell’s administration through 6 November, a largely symbolic move that at least could put pressure on the university trustees that choose the university’s leadership, the AP said.

Prosecutors in New York said last month they were reopening the case after the woman, a then 20-year-old Cornell student who said she was forced to leave the university after the incident, filed a civil lawsuit naming her alleged attackers.

University leaders faced a backlash, including mass campus protests, when it was revealed that their inquiry into the woman’s original complaint resulted in only two expulsions. Others among the alleged rapists were ordered to write essays, attend workshops, or serve short suspensions as part of their punishment, following the review by Cornell, an elite, private sector university based in Ithaca, in upstate New York.

The woman accusing the men recently wrote a letter to the campus faculty senate saying she felt “unsupported and disbelieved” by Cornell’s president. And in a separate development at the weekend, a New York state judge ruled that she could continue to be identified by the pseudonym Jane Doe in the ongoing lawsuit, citing concerns for her safety.

Earlier this month, Kathy Hochul, the Democratic governor of New York state, appointed the state’s attorney general Letitia James as a special counsel to investigate the case.

At Wednesday’s faculty meeting, some faculty struggled with whether they should speak out publicly, sharing painful experiences of harassment and fears of professional retaliation, the AP said.

Beth Frances Milles, a performing arts professor, Cornell graduate and parent, pleaded for civility after describing receiving messages from women who experienced sexual assault, including former classmates.

“I understand we have to take action,” she said. “There are so many things to talk about. Please, let’s talk about it together and not sneer at each other when we disagree.”

After at least an hour of debate, members voted down an attempt to delay voting on the resolution until an independent investigation into Cornell’s handling of the sexual assault allegations was completed.

The resolution co-sponsor, Anne Marie Brady, said she was encouraged by the breadth of faculty who spoke, despite fears of retaliation. As a contingent faculty member, she said, speaking publicly carried professional risks.

“The more people who speak out, the more we protect each other,” Brady said in a phone interview after the meeting.

Music professor Ariana Kim said she unexpectedly found herself sharing her own experience of sexual harassment and bullying after hearing suggestions that faculty did not do enough to address such misconduct.

She described how the harassment affected her tenure case and how her efforts to get help from administrators, including Cornell’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, when he was provost, went nowhere.

“It’s hard to get up and do that on a number of levels,” Kim said, describing a sense of relief and pride that she had spoken.

During the meeting, economics professor Seth Sanders agreed that sexual assault was a serious problem at Cornell but said faculty did not yet know enough to judge the administration’s response.

He said about 80% of his department opposed the resolution for now, with many awaiting the independent investigation.

“I don’t think setting it up as having confidence in the administration or supporting the administration is right,” Sanders said. “I think it’s legitimate to think that you don’t know whether to have confidence because you don’t know what happened or why in the Jane Doe case.”

Wednesday’s meeting came a day after 20 female science and engineering faculty members called on Kotlikoff to resign in a letter to trustees that was obtained by AP.

The woman in the ongoing case about the fraternity incident claims she was drugged and repeatedly raped in October 2024 at a house belonging to Cornell’s since-closed chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity. All seven of the alleged attackers deny the claims against them.

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: My sister-in-law is nearly 40 but cannot handle losing at board games. What can I do? | Leading questions
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
A game is not a moral exemption to your usual self. Sometimes the best way to puncture ‘it’s just a game’ is to show people that you’re judging them in reality

My sister-in-law is nearly 40 but cannot handle losing at board games. No matter how high or low the stakes, she has to win. When she doesn’t, she becomes explosive with rage, and often upends the game, sweeps dice off the table, or storms off in a rage. She is otherwise a normal and lovely person, with whom I get on very well. Seeing this side of her makes me deeply uncomfortable and it feels really childish and inappropriate. Will she behave that way with me if I say or do something she doesn’t like?

I think in an effort to smooth the tension, my husband’s family always laughs and teases her about her reaction. It’s like her “special little characteristic” that everyone pretends to love. I wish there was a way to address it but everyone seems to just sweep it under the rug. My husband is aware of how I feel about this.

Recently, she’s started dating a new partner, who is absolutely lovely. When she has a big reaction after board games I can also sense him tensing up, so I know this is affecting more than just me. Ultimately, I’m worried for my sister-in-law that if she continues this behaviour, and the family continues to indulge it, she will suffer personal and professional consequences. I also don’t enjoy being around the dynamic, and think it is likely we’ll spend less time with her as a result. What can I do?

Eleanor says: I know someone who ended a relationship because their partner too gleefully teamed up with an ex to lie in a game of wink murder. I know someone who decided not to have kids with their then partner because when he played with kids, he got a kick out of really scaring them. I know someone whose friendship never recovered after one shouted the c-word in a card game.

It’s not that the way you behave in a game is a straightforward guide to the kind of person you are. The whole reason games are fun is that that isn’t true. Games let you experiment with being a different kind of person; they let you explore different kinds of agency. They are fun and absorbing precisely because you focus on a single goal or way of reasoning. A game is a vacation from the rules and goals of normal life, and an excursion into new ones.

But games aren’t meant to be a moral exemption to your usual self. They’re meant to let you play with and develop your usual self by putting it in unusual circumstances. Treating games as a forum for exorcising the worst parts of yourself with the petulant excuse “it’s just a game” misunderstands the whole enterprise.

You’re astute to notice that the family going along with it doesn’t help. And you’re astute to notice that their laughter might be a bid to make things less awkward – not a sign that they actually enjoy it. Like how we laugh after an off-colour comment, hoping to social magic it into counting as a joke. They might hope that if they applaud, make this “her thing”, that transforms her behaviour into a fun bit – not just an adult having a tantrum.

Their approach might make things less awkward, but it doesn’t give the disruptive person evidence of how disruptive they are. As always, the more you paper over the cracks someone’s created, the less you can be surprised when they don’t notice them.

Sometimes the best way to puncture “it’s just a game” is to show people that you’re judging them in reality.

You don’t have to say “don’t do that” or “why are you so mad” while they’re heated. (In fact, if it’s a real anger management thing, it’s better not to). You can just let your sincere attitude show in a moment they presumed would be structured by the fiction. A long look without a smile or a laugh. Silence. A hint of the ick it’s giving you in real life. In the same way that laughing along is a bid to turn a tantrum into a joke, reacting as you would in other circumstances can be a bid to separate her behaviour from the game.

Awkward, yes; socially costly, yes. But as with all things, if you want her to know you’d prefer she stopped this, you have to endure the discomfort of her learning how you feel.

The boyfriend who lied in wink murder, the man who scared the kids and the friend who shouted in the card game didn’t realise that the way they acted in games would affect how people saw them in real life, until it was too late. A long look across the table now – or even a quiet word from a relative once she’s calmed down – is a much kinder way for her to find out.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The tabloids that used Thomas Markle to attack Meghan should now reflect. I bet they won’t | Zoe Willliams
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Zoe Williams
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday plundered Meghan’s estranged father for clicks. But soul searching or remorse would be institutionally impossible

As the allegations mount against Thomas Markle Sr, his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, has released a statement describing her deep distress, and saying her priority is the protection of children. Is this the point at which Thomas Markle will cease to be an acceptable source for the Sussex character attacks that have become a tabloid staple? The Daily Mail and its sister paper, the Mail on Sunday, have been utterly brazen in their cultivation of the embittered Thomas Snr, using him as a weapon against his daughter since she first married into the royal family. Now, they’ll cut loose from him and describe the charges laid against him with the same outrage as everyone else. It would be institutionally impossible for them to discuss or reflect on their prior relationship with Markle without admitting a long-range and vindictive grudge against his daughter.

Markle denies all allegations against him. His son, Meghan’s half-brother Thomas Markle Jr, described in a video for the Sun the material he claims to have found on his father’s spare mobile phone, after Markle Sr had gone back to the US to have his leg amputated. Markle Jr was in the Philippines, where both men had moved in 2025. He said the material included “the most horrific video of a very young Asian girl … couldn’t have been more than 10 years old”. He almost threw up; he almost dropped the phone. His immediate fear was for what else he might be inadvertently in possession of. “I’m on the hook for this, now,” he said.

As he made contact with the FBI, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children and the Pennsylvania state police, he reportedly found more and more material: “the most obscene, disgusting, lowest-of-the-low images … thousands and thousands of them.” He said he started to question every aspect of his family history, all the times his father had hastily snapped shut his laptop, “all the locked rooms in all the houses we’ve ever lived in”.

Meghan Markle has been estranged from her father since 2018. In 2019, she was passed a letter alleging that he had sexually abused a child, which she says had been sent to the Metropolitan police. The Met took no action on that letter and it has been reported that they subsequently misplaced it – whether that’s because they could believe no ill of Thomas Markle, or simply because they lose things, is unknown.

But until now, the Daily Mail and the Mail on Sunday’s trust in Markle Sr and solidarity with him have been without question.

In 2018, he handed the Mail on Sunday a five-page letter that his daughter had written to him after her wedding, which he had declined to attend, citing health reasons. Meghan successfully sued Associated Newspapers for printing part of the letter, though “printing” doesn’t really encompass the torrent of coverage and insinuation they wrung from its contents. It was the start of a relationship between the newspaper and the now alleged sex offender that was so close by last year that when Thomas Markle learned about his amputation, the first person he told was Caroline Graham, the Mail on Sunday’s US editor (and previously a biographer of Queen Camilla). In photos of the pair together, the emotions are almost laughably legible: Markle looks pugnacious and triumphant, like the guy who’s managed to get public opinion on speed dial. Graham looks serene and also victorious, the first reporter on to Goose Green in the tabloids’ favourite war.

A free press is essential and sometimes it is scabrous. But is this what a free press is for? To groom an estranged parent or other former intimate of someone in public life in order to undermine the latter person’s credibility and standing, seems sadistic. That’s a large word, particularly in the context of the allegations against Thomas Markle, and I use it advisedly. One of the hideous things about family estrangement is the feeling that everyone involved has had their character besmirched. The accused fight back with counter-claims. Nobody’s probity survives unscathed (although most of us could tell that Meghan’s father was exploiting her lovelessly for attention, and probably cash, long before these charges surfaced).

A political or media enemy plundering that dynamic for an easy win, for clicks, for a vendetta, does not even have the fog of emotionality as a defence. Everybody recoils from it. When the Republican gubernatorial candidate in Ohio, Vivek Ramaswamy, made an attack ad featuring his opponent’s mother calling her daughter, Amy Acton, a liar, most people didn’t know the history. They didn’t know that Donna Arthur had lost custody of her children decades previously, after her husband, their stepfather, was indicted on charges of child rape. People could nevertheless see how low it was to air a view that was poisonous by definition under the fig leaf of hearing from both sides.

Ramaswamy lost a major endorsement and had venue cancellations within a day of that attack ad. What the Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday would have to lose to even reflect on their allegiances in this episode is impossible to guess.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: My phone thinks my boyfriend is my ‘best friend’. It’s not alone | Patrick Lenton
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Patrick Lenton
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Being in a same-sex relationship can make you weirdly invisible. Queer identity shouldn’t be treated as abnormal

My boyfriend and I invented a game on our recent trip to Italy. We called it “invisible gays”, which might have been an attempt at some kind of word play around “gays” and “gaze” – but I was on holiday and feeling lazy, so I didn’t push it.

The game began when one night he took me out to a little trattoria to celebrate my birthday. It was a warm night, and fairy lights were entangled in the fragrant blooming flowers over our heads, and we drank good wine and ate bowls of perfect pasta, and there was candlelight, and it was so romantic I wouldn’t have blinked if two dogs had started smooching over a strand of spaghetti. Che bello!

We were one of four tables, all couples of various ages looking at each other with disgusting wet amorous eyes. During the evening a man selling roses approached the other tables. One young guy even bought one, presenting the blossom with a flourish to his girlfriend, earning applause from other patrons and a round of toothy photos. Caught up in the moment, my partner pulled out his wallet to buy a rose for me too, despite my wildly insincere protestations – but the rose man didn’t even clock us as a couple and wandered off into the night.

I briefly wondered if it was because my outfit wasn’t chic enough for Rome. Then I realised we were the only couple who weren’t the societal default setting of a man and a woman, having instead made the dire mistake of being two beautiful men dining together. I wonder if he thought we were some kind of complicated interracial brothers?

This continued all around Italy, with more than seven episodes of being passed over at romantic tourist traps marked on our scorecard. When I organised a fancy dinner for my boyfriend’s birthday weeks later, one of the servers said I was a “good friend” for doing so.

I’m used to the way that being in a same-sex couple can make you hyper visible or put a homophobic spotlight on you, so that it feels like every time you kiss in public it’s like Frodo putting on the One Ring, drawing the attention of the Dark Lord and his screeching Nazgûl. I’m used to muttered comments from people you walk by on the streets when you’re holding hands, or of making out with a tall guy outside a bar after our first date only for a car full of men to stop and yell slurs at us. I’m used to holding the hand of a boyfriend as we were chased down the backstreets of Newtown late at night by three silent men.

I’ve also dated enough women to know that there’s a contrast – no woman I’ve ever dated has flinched away from a kiss on the cheek and whispered: “Maybe not in public.” I’ve had men I’ve dated comment on how “openly affectionate” I am, because I haven’t had to learn to self-censor my public love languages. Women I date usually just comment on how clean my legs are and how many Gilmore Girls references I make.

Obviously being hyper visible and therefore at risk of overt and violent homophobia is worse than not being able to buy an overpriced street flower. Over the past year in Australia, hate crimes against gay and bisexual men have been making headlines. As someone who has suffered a hate crime or two, I can confirm that dealing with this should be the authorities’ priority instead of cracking down on the rose men of Rome.

But with the 10-year anniversary of the marriage equality win coming up next year, it’s worth looking at all the ways being in a same-sex relationship can still make you weirdly invisible. It’s another argument for why Mardi Gras, pride flags and Idahobit days in schools are still so necessary – because, when love between queer people goes unseen, it makes it seem as though it isn’t “normal”. And when queer identity is treated as abnormal, it fertilises the ground necessary to justify violence against queer people.

We all know the little “collections” of photos and videos our smartphones occasionally create. This can be anything from “Your trip in Italy 2026” to “Furry pals throughout the years”. It’s been a source of constant amusement to me that it sorts all the photos of my boyfriend and me into a collection called “best friends”. These are photos of two men kissing and, without oversharing, sometimes photos of two men doing things even more intimate than kissing (kayaking).

It shows you that homosexual invisibility is so hardwired into aspects of society that a phone short-circuits and decides that two men in love are just good bros. I’ve never had any of the women I’ve dated put into a folder called “best friends”. In fact, none of the women who are my actual best friends have made it into those folders either. My dog does get filed there, which, when its alongside my boyfriend, feels a little like one of those slippery slope arguments made by the Australian Christian Lobby during the plebiscite.

It seems as though we have a Goldilocks problem with queer relationship visibility: there’s too much visibility or there’s not enough. Make up your mind!

Not only do I simply want to express my love for my boyfriend publicly and without risk of violence, and for it to be recognised for what it is; I also don’t want my sexuality to be the only thing that people notice me for. I want to be noticed for my abnormally good looks and sex appeal.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: The low-budget Brewers won the World Series – and exposed baseball’s biggest lie
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Howard Bryant
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Milwaukee’s first World Series championship is a rebuke to baseball’s oligarch class, whose insistence that small-market teams cannot compete has been laid bare as fiction

For the entirety of the 2026 baseball season, the overlords of the game have stood on the single position that what has now happened could not happen, and the result was a year that has been treated like an appetizer for the main course of the offseason: the shutting down of the game until the players, after 40 years of resistance, finally agree to a salary cap. The insistence that the game had been predetermined undermined the Milwaukee Brewers, who spent 149 days this season atop the standings.

Baseball dismissed Milwaukee’s 22-0 demolition of Seattle on 18 August, the 20-0 waxing of Cincinnati a month later, and the comprehensive dusting of their division – their fourth consecutive National League Central title and fifth in six years – by 14 games. Baseball’s owners, at their persuasive best, would have their paying customers believe that the Brewers’ franchise-record 103 regular-season wins also were an illusion, or worse, the dreaded outlier, even though Milwaukee have won 770 games since 2018, the fourth-most in all of baseball. Even when Milwaukee exhaled and made the Dodgers look old in a stirring four-game sweep, ESPN’s Jeff Passan reported the owners’ position remained unchanged.

The Brewers to that point had not helped dispel the notion. They had sputtered badly in recent postseasons, giving life to the thought that maybe their summer wins really were empty. Only one thing could ever change that perception: winning in the playoffs.

Fri 23 Oct Game 1: Milwaukee 3, Tampa Bay 2Sat 24 Oct Game 2: Milwaukee 5, Tampa Bay 4Mon 26 Oct Game 3: Milwaukee 10, Tampa Bay 1Tue 27 Oct Game 4: Tampa Bay 4, Milwaukee 3 (12 innings)Wed 28 Oct Game 5: Milwaukee 4, Tampa Bay 1

In the US, all World Series games will air on Fox and Fox Deportes, with streaming available through Fox One. In the UK, the series will be carried by TNT Sports. In Australia, fans can watch on ESPN, with streaming available through Disney+ and Kayo Sports.

Surrounded by so many friends that a Wednesday evening at Tropicana Field in St Petersburg felt like a home game – the good folks of Milwaukee and points beyond will remember the date specifically as 28 October 2026 – the Brewers rejected the notion they could not win both because of the economic forces against them and the intangibles champions possess but seemed to go missing from their group when the clocks fall back. They did so by winning the World Series for the first time in their 58-year history, and doing so resoundingly, destroying the Tampa Bay Rays in five games.

The final score was 4-1, ending a month that will be played and replayed in the minds and DVRs of Milwaukeeans. Few teams have ever been better. Few moments have exposed the hypocrisy of baseball’s oligarchs. Few teams so emphatically demanded so much of themselves.

What had been accepted as fact has always been decidedly fiction – but fiction can live as truth until it is exposed, killed once and for all on the ballfield. No matter the argument to concede the season to the inevitability of money and not having it, the truth is the Brewers have been an elite team for the better part of the decade, and the signature joy of this World Series run has been the joyous, ruthless attention this team paid to the task of not merely believing they were championship level, but proving it, to every team that opposed them this season, but more thrillingly, to themselves.

Nothing else mattered but emerging from this month as champions – not the payroll or the labor battles that will almost certainly shut the game down over the coming weeks and quite likely wipe out spring training and at least a portion of the 2027 season and the Brewers’ title defense, or the mystique and riches of the two-time defending champion Dodgers; not the twin histories of having never won the whole thing since that long-ago day near the end of spring training in 1970 when the Seattle Pilots’ equipment truck loaded in Tempe, Arizona, but the team didn’t know where home would be as a court order determined if the truck was headed back to Seattle or to a new home in Milwaukee, or the Dodgers’ long record of torturing Milwaukee baseball. That torture dated back to losses to Brooklyn in 1956, Los Angeles in 1959 before the Braves left town for Atlanta, and to the recent postseason defeats to the Dodgers in 2018, 2020 and 2025, when the Brewers began their second decade in the National League by being as good as the franchise had been since the big American League years of Yount and Cooper, Molitor and Fingers, only to suffer the familiar NL fate of being good, but not good enough to beat the Dodgers when it counted.

The Brewers were nowhere men – only the World Series would heal the past wounds that have stayed with them, highlighted by last year’s humiliating four-game sweep in the NLCS by the Dodgers – and they played with a buoyant and calm desperation, a gorgeous certainty that could not last, but did. The Brewers won the requisite 11 games to claim the trophy and needed only 13 games to do it, but trailed in eight of them. Yet, as an example of their belief, none of their series this postseason was tied after two games. Both Brewers losses in these playoffs were by one run.

When they faltered, they did not panic as desperate teams too close to the prize do; they got tougher. Jake Bauers’ soul-snatching at-bats against the Dodgers offered a sign, the youthful charges of Series MVP catcher William Contreras, Jackson Chourio, and the too-young-to-care stardom of Cooper Pratt was another, coming back from down 4-0 against the Dodgers and Rays was still another, and the two-out, eight-run fifth in Game 3 seemed to end the Series – except that it didn’t. Most impressively, responding to losing Game 4 three outs from the title in the bottom of the 12th not with the doubts that create suspense and pave the way to epic collapse, but by returning the next night unfazed and champagne-ready, demanding they be taken not as a cute story but a hard-edged team ready, at long last, for its close-up.

Neither the doomsday rhetoric of an unnecessary work stoppage or the fearsome reputation of the former champions, nor the feisty underdog spirit of an admirable Tampa Bay could block the sunlight, too long in arriving, of this Brewers team. They played pure, determined baseball and responded to the insult – and it is an insult – that the decimal points on the balance sheet meant more than winning 103 games and 90-plus so many times before that, meant that once it was time to deal the cards they couldn’t win. The Brewers won 114 games in 2026, finished the regular season 15-3, and then went 11-2 in the playoffs for a grand total of 26-5 since 7 September.

Baseball’s finances need addressing, but they don’t require shuttering the place. Even with the game the owners are playing in their quest to increase franchise values, their words speak an untruth – Brewers owner Mark Attanasio purchased the team from Bud Selig in 2005 for $223m and the team that supposedly cannot win (but did) has a valuation by Forbes at $1.9bn. The game that matters, however, is the one on the field, the one that belongs to the players, and this October, there was absolutely nobody better.

Howard Bryant is the author of 11 books, including Full Dissidence: Notes from an Uneven Playing Field, and Kings and Pawns: Jackie Robinson and Paul Robeson in America. He also writes on Substack

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: How did the Spain train crash happen and what will investigators be asking?
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Audio file appears to point finger at control centre, but there are questions around signalling and technical issues

At least 69 people died when a high-speed train from Madrid to Seville hit another train on the same track from behind near Toledo on Wednesday morning.

Both trains had been brought to a halt earlier when the signalling system failed. The driver of the state-owned Spanish train, a Renfe AVE service, was told by controllers to restart the journey, but crashed into the train in front, run by the private operator Iryo. The front carriages of the AVE train and rear of the Iryo train were destroyed and others derailed.

The nature of this disaster, as well as its human toll, seems particularly shocking. There are multiple safeguards on high-speed lines, including different types of automatic train operation, which should ensure trains are never able to come close on the same track.

The audio file released to Spanish media by the government appears to point the finger at the control centre, with a controller in Madrid telling the driver of the halted AVE train to proceed “con marcha normale” – under normal operations – rather than at low speed. The instruction was described by the transport minister, Óscar Puente, as an “inexplicable decision”.

Rear-end collisions are rare, as are any kind of crash between trains on international high-speed networks. The closest comparator occurred in China in 2011, when a high-speed train hit a stationary express in front of it in Wenzhou, killing 46 people. The rear-end collision between two East Midlands trains in Bedford this year was the first fatal crash of that kind in 40 years in the UK, and occurred on a stretch of railway without automatic train operation, after the driver apparently failed to slow despite the danger signal.

While the audio appears to indicate human error played a central role, there are other elements that remain unclear, such as what caused the initial failure of the signalling system. Investigators will be looking at the sequence of events and technical issues that allowed the Renfe train to proceed but the Iryo train to stay put.

Signallers, or track controllers, are increasingly based in remote computer centres but are acutely aware of the risk and responsibility their job entails. Any investigation will want to establish what circumstances or pressures could have led to that instruction.

In all modern hi-tech transport, whether air or rail, known safety risks are eradicated as far as possible. Accident investigations typically yield rare, if not unprecedented, combinations of technical failure and human error.

The Spanish government will want to demonstrate that this latest disaster is completely unconnected to the head-on crash between two trains that occurred on the same line in Adamuz in January after one derailed, apparently due to a small section of faulty or missing rail.

Train drivers were due to strike, even before this week’s crash, in protest against under-investment in the railway and its people, which unions say is directly connected to safety.

The success of Spain’s high-speed railway, linking Madrid to Seville and Barcelona, was the envy of British rail planners. It was modern and had cut journeys from the capital to Andalusia to two and a half hours; a car takes twice that, and the public transport alternative of the coach, three times as long. Good public transportation links bring jobs and growth; losing them could mean the opposite.

The long-term trend since 2010 has been fewer fatalities of any sort on the railway. Most years, in most countries, no passenger is killed in any type of train crash, a world away from the death toll on the roads. However, worries about under-investment in the railways, particularly after costs and subsidy soared as fare revenue dried up in the pandemic, are not unique to Spain.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Nvidia CEO reportedly targeted by Chinese spy
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Johana Bhuiyan
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China

US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by a Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to a new report by the New York Times.

Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.

In the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.

White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he’s developed with Trump, according to the New York Times.

The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.

In a statement to the New York Times, Nvidia said there was nothing out of the ordinary about the Nvidia CEO’s interactions with Alice Huang.

“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in a statement. Megaspeed and customers like it “receive ordinary business information – not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets – and zero information relevant to national security”.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Finland launches criminal investigation into Google’s clearing of forest for datacentre site
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Jon Henley
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Authorities allege company may have breached Finnish environmental laws by forgoing required impact assessment

‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentre

Finnish ⁠police have launched a criminal investigation into possible breaches ⁠of the country’s environmental ⁠laws ​at the site of a planned Google datacentre in rural northern Finland.

Authorities allege that Tuike Finland, a Google subsidiary, cleared and drained 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest at the planned site in Muhos before environmental impact assessments required by Finnish law had been completed.

Like other Nordic countries, Finland is attractive to tech companies seeking to build datacentres because of its relative geopolitical stability and abundance of land, but also because its cool climate should allow them to cut energy costs.

“Based on preliminary information, there have been ambiguities and ‌shortcomings in the drainage and water management at the construction site of Tuike Finland ​Oy’s datacentre project,” Finnish police said in a statement on Thursday.

“The criminal investigation will examine, among other things, circumstances related to these issues,” they added.

Finnish authorities are considering applications for a total of 145 new datacentres at various stages of planning, including a €13bn (£11bn) artificial intelligence infrastructure project by Google that the US company has called its largest ‌investment in Europe.

Earlier this month Finnish authorities ordered Google to suspend work at two sites – Muhos and Otanmäki, about 100km to the south-east – after the company failed to complete environmental impact assessments before clearcutting the land.

The Supervisory ⁠Agency, which oversees environmental permits and assessments, told Google to halt “preparatory ​measures altering the environment”. Campaigners estimate 250,000 trees have been felled at Muhos and 150,000 at Otanmäki.

Google’s Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, has apologised for the forest clearings, but argued that the company had acted according to “the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time”.

The Finnish government has encouraged the projects. In September, when Google’s plans were announced, the prime minister, Petteri Orpo, said attracting investment was a “top priority” and the deal would “deliver lasting benefits”.

But the revelations over Google’s alleged misconduct have sparked a national debate over what datacentre deals mean for communities, the environment and energy prices. The issue could impact parliamentary elections due in April.

More than 93,000 people have signed a petition demanding more datacentre regulation and compensation for environmental damage. Experts say datacentres bring a limited number of local jobs, and benefits on a national level are minimal.

“Really, for Finland, there are no benefits,” said Jussi Kangasharju, professor of computer science at University of Helsinki. “They are international companies serving international customers. Datacentres ultimately have little benefit for others except the datacentre operator.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘Strength of matriarchs’: New Mexico’s Deb Haaland poised to be first female Native American governor
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Cecilia Nowell in Albuquerque, New Mexico
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Ex-congresswoman is connecting with young people and Native voters with promise to expand the social safety net

The road to Isleta Pueblo, a Native American tribal community just 20 minutes south of downtown Albuquerque, New Mexico, is peppered with campaign signs. Among the many names of candidates running in next week’s midterm elections and tribal elections later in November, there’s one that is poised to make history.

Deb Haaland is set to become the first Native American female governor in the US when voters cast their ballots on 3 November. Recent polling shows her with a comfortable lead over her opponent, Republican Gregg Hull, a businessman and the longtime mayor of the city of Rio Rancho. Her bid for office also signals the growing power of the Democratic party in the state, where Democrats control the legislature, hold all top offices and have enacted progressive policies, such as universal childcare, that have been heralded across the country.

Haaland, who is a member of Laguna Pueblo, has been a rising star in national politics since 2018, when she was elected to Congress alongside a wave of progressive freshmen lawmakers, including Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib. In the House of Representatives, Haaland sponsored legislation such as the Not Invisible Act, which focused on the epidemic of missing and murdered Native Americans. After Joe Biden was elected president in 2020, he named Haaland to lead the interior department, making her the first Native American to lead a cabinet agency. In that role, Haaland oversaw the formation of a missing and murdered unit within the Bureau of Indian Affairs and advocated for protecting culturally significant lands, including Chaco Canyon and Bears Ears.

After years in Washington, she’s returned to her home state, running for governor with promises to expand the social safety net, improve healthcare access in rural communities, and protect natural resources and sacred lands. In recent weeks, she’s secured endorsements from prominent Democrats including Barack Obama, while Michigan’s governor, Gretchen Whitmer, and the former transportation secretary Pete Buttigieg traveled to the state to stump for her.

Her campaign has sparked excitement among New Mexico’s sizable Indigenous community, who make up more than 12% of the state. Many see themselves reflected in her, and voice enthusiasm for a candidate who’s promised to protect the state’s water, investigate the legacy of New Mexico’s Native American boarding schools, and prioritize missing and murdered Indigenous persons cases.

For Haaland, the historic nature of the election isn’t lost on her – but the final weeks of campaigning have been so hectic she sometimes forgets she’s on the brink of a milestone.

“Sometimes I forget about the fact that I would be the first Native woman. We’re in the throes of this statewide campaign and it’s so busy and we’re trying to be everywhere all at once,” she said in a recent interview. “But I recognize that for some people who feel like they haven’t ever been represented – I really, I’m grateful that I have this opportunity … I just hope that I can help folks to see that hard work still means something. That anyone can be a leader regardless of where you come from or how much money you do or don’t have.”

Haaland has throughout her campaign invoked her experience as a single mother navigating the Medicaid, WIC and Snap programs before attending law school in her 30s. Early in her career she ran a small business selling salsa, and when she was appointed secretary of the interior, Haaland was still paying off student loans. At a recent panel conversation on housing with the Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren, Haaland described trying to apply for a special home loan available to Native Americans while raising her young child.

“I think that there is a lot of excitement,” Janice Lucero, who is a member of the Isleta Pueblo and a co-founder of the Isleta Pueblo Voters Alliance, said, speaking from her farm on the Isleta reservation. “I think Deb actually has a lot of influence on the younger generation. She’s able to really reach those folks and really hear the concerns as well in a lot of the communities.”

Jade Begay, who is Tesuque Pueblo/Diné, lives in New Mexico and served as the Native American engagement director for Kamala Harris’s 2024 presidential campaign, agrees.

“I think that Native women are especially excited – and young Native people,” she said. “They know that she’s qualified for this job. They know that we can trust her as a leader of New Mexico. And we know we can trust her as someone who will be on the frontlines for New Mexico and defend us from the Trump administration.”

Haaland is running in an election cycle that is uniquely significant for Native candidates. According to Advance Native Political Leadership, a record-setting 358 Indigenous candidates have or are running for office in local, state and federal elections across the country this year.

Alongside seeing the first Native woman elected governor of a US state, the country could see its first Indigenous woman elected to Senate, if either former Alaska congresswoman Mary Peltola or Minnesota’s lieutenant governor, Peggy Flanagan, win their race.

“The first thing that made it feel really possible was seeing Deb Haaland, was seeing Sharice Davids [the Native American congresswoman from Kansas] on a national level,” said state senator Angel Charley, who is Laguna/Zuni/Diné and entered politics in 2024 when she ran to represent a district that includes Laguna and Acoma Pueblos but had never previously been filled by a Native woman.

“I am a strong believer in the strength of the matriarchs,” said Ahtza Dawn Chavez, who is Diné/Kewa Pueblo and the executive director of NM Native Vote, a Native-led group focused on getting out the vote, which endorsed Haaland soon after she announced her candidacy. “We felt very strongly about having an Indigenous governor, and in particular an Indigenous female governor.”

Although Native Americans have made significant gains in political power in recent years, it’s been a long road to get here. Native Americans have only been allowed to vote across the entire United States since the 1960s.

In New Mexico, Native Americans won the right to vote in 1948, when Miguel Trujillo, a second world war veteran and an Isleta Pueblo tribal member, sued the state.

“My mother was a registered Republican for the longest time, believe it or not,” Haaland said. “There was a Republican candidate who came around to the Indian camp in Winslow, where they all lived, my grandparents working on the railroad because they were part of the assimilation policies,” she explained, referencing federal policies that forcibly relocated Native Americans and aimed to assimilate many into white society through jobs. That candidate, she said, “registered all the Laguna people in the Indian camp as Republicans”.

When Haaland ran for lieutenant governor in 2014, in a race Republicans ultimately won, her mother switched her registration. “I’ve worked really hard to help people like my mom understand that our values as Native people align with the Democrats,” Haaland said. “When I think about who’s in the White House right now and the horrible policies that are coming out that are making New Mexicans sicker, poorer and hungrier, those values don’t align with us.”

Across the country, many Indigenous voters continue to face challenges casting their ballots due to vast distances between polling sites on rural reservations, a lack of addresses served by the postal service from which to mail in ballots and provisions in some states preventing Native people from using tribal IDs to register to vote.

In 2023, New Mexico became the first and only state in the country to implement an updated Native American Voting Rights Act, which gave tribes greater input on polling locations and redistricting.

Charley adds that, particularly since the Covid-19 pandemic, many tribes and Native organizers have adopted new measures to help voters get to the polls – including sending out text alerts sharing when poll sites are open, coordinating rides to the polls and hosting community events, rather than door-knocking in rural areas.

While local groups such as the Isleta Pueblo Voters Alliance and NM Native Vote have focused on getting out the Native vote in New Mexico, national coalitions such as the Native Organizers Alliance and Advance Native Political Leadership have aimed to organize Indigenous voters nationwide.

Haaland herself got involved in national politics in 2012 when she served as the Native American vote director in New Mexico for Barack Obama’s campaign. “I’ve been a voter activist for the longest time. And I was always trying to help my grandma and my aunties and my mom get out to vote,” Haaland said.

That organizing work saw remarkable success in 2020, when an outpouring of voters from the Navajo and Hopi reservations in Arizona saw the long-red state vote for Biden.

Despite that win, Begay says working on the Harris/Walz campaign in 2024 underscored for her “just how deeply under-resourced and overlooked Native voter engagement is”.

She also adds that, although she’s seen deep support for Haaland among Native women, “my criticism and my observation is that Native men are not as excited”.

At the Isleta Pueblo Voters Alliance, Lucero and her colleagues have published a voting workbook that includes worksheets for thinking through a candidates’ platform – including by ranking issues such as housing and healthcare, but also a candidates’ approach to land and water, language and culture, and the crisis of missing and murdered Indigenous people.

“We have to think about the future and what’s at stake,” said Lucero. “How are we going to keep sustaining our ways of life?”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: How Laura Loomer and Trump allies amplified ‘Muslim Brotherhood’ lie dogging Abdul El-Sayed
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Robert Mackey
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Michigan US Senate candidate signaled support for Egypt’s pro-democracy movement in 2012, not Islamist group

The Republican campaign to defeat Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate race by casting him as an Islamic extremist is based on a false claim first made by the conspiracy theorist Laura Loomer eight years ago, a Guardian review of the evidence reveals.

Loomer, an influential outside adviser to Donald Trump who calls herself “a proud Islamophobe”, has claimed since El-Sayed entered politics in 2018 that an open letter he signed in support of democracy in Egypt in 2012 was a public endorsement of the Muslim Brotherhood. The text of the letter, however, does not even mention the Muslim Brotherhood, and is not, as Loomer maintains, “a pledge” of support for the Egyptian Islamist group.

Because the letter was only published in Arabic, in the chaotic aftermath of the Arab Spring uprising that toppled a dictator, El-Sayed’s opponent, former congressman Mike Rogers, has been able to mischaracterize it without much scrutiny from US political journalists unfamiliar with Egypt’s brief experiment in democracy, which was snuffed out in a 2013 military coup.

Rogers began his campaign against El-Sayed in August by restating the false claim first made by Loomer about the letter: that the Michigan-born son of Egyptian immigrants had “pledged his support to the Muslim Brotherhood”.

That false account of the letter, in which prominent Egyptian Americans had urged Egypt’s first elected president, Mohamed Morsi, a former member of the Muslim Brotherhood supported by secular activists, to defend their nascent democracy, has been amplified in bigoted remarks about El-Sayed from Trump, Ted Cruz and Robert F Kennedy Jr in recent days.

The allegation went viral two weeks ago, when a Republican operative posing as an ordinary voter asked El-Sayed if he would “disavow the Muslim Brotherhood”, and the candidate replied, “Sure, yeah, absolutely,” before comparing the fearmongering about his faith to fears about John F Kennedy’s Catholicism in 1960.

In Michigan’s final Senate debate last week, Rogers claimed that El-Sayed was so “passionate about defunding the police” that he even “asked the new brother – Muslim Brotherhood, excuse me, head, Morrissey [sic], in Egypt – to defund the police there too”.

The Egyptian revolution that toppled dictator Hosni Mubarak in 2011 began with widespread demonstrations on Police Day, a national holiday dedicated the repressive dictatorship’s police force.

The falsehood about the letter is at the center of Rogers’ closing message too. In a television ad released last week, Rogers said that the Democrat “has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood” and “publicly supported these terrorists”, as images of El-Sayed superimposed over footage of Hamas militants in Gaza appear on the screen behind him. The ad closes with Rogers warning: “Abdul El-Sayed’s radical ideology is a threat to our national security.”

In fact, as the Egyptian journalist Hossam el-Hamalawy confirmed to the Guardian this week, the actual text of the letter El-Sayed signed, as a medical student at Columbia University, “makes no reference to the Muslim Brotherhood” and simply “called on Morsi to pursue the goals of the revolution by purging the state institutions, particularly the police and state media, of officials loyal to the former regime”.

While the headline published above the letter by the editors of the Egyptian state newspaper Al-Ahram, which was still controlled at the time by loyalists to the deposed Mubarak, did call it a plea from “Morsi’s supporters in America”, Hamalawy notes: “The signatories themselves did not use that description.”

Asked to comment on the attempt to mislead American voters about El-Sayed’s support for democracy in Egypt, Hamalawy observed: “I see the American right wing borrowing directly from the playbook of Arab authoritarian regimes before, during and after the Arab Spring. These regimes have consistently sought to portray demands for democratic change as inherently Islamist-driven, suggesting that any challenge to authoritarian rule would inevitably pave the way for reactionary Islamist forces or even terrorism.”

“It is particularly ironic given that many of these same regimes have long enjoyed the political and military backing of western governments,” he added.

The depiction of the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist group is also misleading, since it is a political and social group with no armed wing that is not on the US state department’s list of designated Foreign Terrorist Groups. The group was officially banned but tolerated as the main opposition force to Mubarak’s government before the 2011 uprising.

After Morsi was elected president in 2012, Rogers himself, then the chair of the House intelligence committee, told Reuters that the US government should be wary of the group Morsi had previously helped lead but could engage with some members of the group. “Do I think there are moderate Muslim Brotherhood individuals we are going to have to reach out to and talk to? Yes,” Rogers said.

The tentative US engagement with members of the Brotherhood appointed to Morsi’s short-lived government in 2012 gave birth to a sprawling conspiracy theory that Huma Abedin – a Muslim aide to Hillary Clinton, who was the US secretary of state at the time –was a secret agent of the Muslim Brotherhood.

As Abedin explained later, a letter from then Republican congresswoman Michele Bachmann, asking the state department’s inspector general to investigate the false claims that Abedin’s family was “connected” to the Muslim Brotherhood, and the Obama administration was secretly funding the Islamists, was even raised by leaders of Egypt’s Christian community during Clinton’s tumultuous visit in 2012, as a conspiracy theory developed in Washington spread to Cairo.

Those unfounded allegations, which closely echo the false accusations against El-Sayed now, were raised during the 2016 presidential campaign by Donald Trump and his supporters. “Why aren’t we talking about Huma and her ties to the Muslim Brotherhood?” Sean Duffy, a Republican congressman at the time, said in a CNN interview in August 2016.

Beyond the letter first surfaced by Loomer, Republicans have tried to claim that El-Sayed’s mother and members of her family in Egypt might have once had sympathy for the Brotherhood, based on tweets posted in 2012 and 2013 by the candidate’s half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi.

Like the open letter signed by her half-brother, the social media posts from El-Sayed’s half-sister, which have been seized on by rightwing outlets, came in response to political developments in Egypt at the time.

On 24 June 2012, the day that Morsi, a former Muslim Brotherhood leader, was elected Egypt’s president, with the support of secular pro-democracy activists who celebrated in Cairo’s Tahrir Square, Abdelhadi posted criticism of the Islamist group while saying that her family had supported it during its long years of opposition to the ousted dictator.

The same day, as secular supporters of the revolution that deposed Mubarak expressed relief that Morsi had defeated a military-backed candidate, Abdelhadi also posted: “Had an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early 70s while she was in college.”

On 3 July 2013, when Morsi was deposed in a military coup by Gen Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, starting a bloody crackdown on Islamists and secular activists that lasts to this day, El-Sayed’s half-sister posted that she was praying for family members in Egypt who supported the Muslim Brotherhood.

El-Sayed, who was raised by his father, stepmother and grandparents – told NBC News that his half-sister’s tweets did not contradict his repeated statement that he has no ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. “I wasn’t raised by my mother,” El-Sayed said, adding that he has never talked to his mother about her days as a student activist in Egypt a decade before his birth in the US.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: What is it like to work when your co-workers are AI agents?
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Arielle Pardes
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Using AI for roles from executive assistants to chiefs of staff, companies are boasting about doing more with less, creating tension with their human workers

On an average workday, Dhruv Amin chats with dozens of colleagues to get things done at his AI startup Anything. He might ask Gwen, his executive assistant, to schedule a meeting, then troubleshoot a technical problem with Cody, his coding partner. Then he might check in with Betsy for search engine optimization, or Juno for onboarding customers. If the office runs out of snacks, he sends a Slack message to Justin, the office manager charged with stocking the kitchen.

But none of these co-workers are people. They’re artificial intelligence agents, software that handles tasks without human intervention. Anything is one of several startups building them, and betting on a future where workplaces will increasingly turn over their sales, marketing, coding and other tasks to semi-autonomous AI. At Anything, there are 15 human employees and roughly 150 agents – a ratio that Amin believes will soon be the norm.

“I think in a year, every company will have more AI co-workers than human co-workers,” he said.

In the San Francisco tech scene, agents have quickly become a new status symbol, showing that a company can do more with less, several startup employees said. It’s common for workers to brag about how well their agents can handle common office drudgery like answering emails or help with essential business operations such as giving sales pitches.

But agents are also creating tension. They are alienating customers and colleagues who seek human interaction, eliminating roles and forcing employees to become overnight managers of the bots that often make mistakes.

While startup techies such as Amin are some of the early adopters, corporate America may not be far behind. About 40% of large organizations used AI agents in some capacity between May 2025 and June 2026, up from 27% the year before, according to McKinsey’s State of AI Global Survey. Companies also expect to scale back their workforce by 10% to 15% over the next few years as they delegate more work to AI, a recent report from Boston Consulting Group found. In the present moment, companies are not seeing major productivity gains from AI, MIT research shows.

A wave of startups and big tech companies are fueling the push toward AI agents, selling companies on automated co-workers.

There’s Viktor, a company that lets companies create their own “AI chief of staff”, and Lindy, which makes customizable agents for sales, customer support or admin work. OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Claude Cowork and Microsoft’s Scout can each integrate with thousands of other tools to handle projects after employees leave for the day.
