Each of these products promises companies the tantalizing dream of cranking out new co-workers, who never clock out, complain or cause human resource problems. Delegating to an agent is also cheaper than hiring a human, making a large ratio of agents to humans a point of pride among startups.

“That’s the status symbol,” said Rafael López Muñoz, chief of staff at Wordware, a San Francisco-based startup that makes AI tools. Outsourcing parts of the job to agents is “an extreme time saver”.

Lindy, for example, used to have almost 50 employees. Now, after laying off one-third of its staff, the company says it has about 20 and has filled many of its open roles with AI agents instead. It’s still hiring people for some positions.

“People are constrained by having two hands and 24 hours in a day,” said Haneen Azhar, Lindy’s senior growth marketing manager. “Now, that constraint has gone away, because your one laptop screen can be divided into 16 different agents that are running in parallel. These tools make you feel so powerful.”

Azhar says she has outsourced a long list of tasks to agents, from managing her calendar to testing how well customers respond to different marketing taglines to generating brand images. She worries about her role in eliminating jobs as she offloads work to agents. Azhar says that Lindy’s agents now handle product announcements, social media posts and marketing videos, work that used to be handled by about 100 people in its creator program, for example.

She also worries about how the shift will affect the next generation of workers. “If I was trying to get my foot in the door right now, I’d be worse off than I was a year ago,” she said.

In some cases, agents have stepped in to cover for missing staff. Jay Blumenfield runs a production company in Los Angeles that creates vertical microdramas – short, scripted series meant to be viewed on your phone. The production schedules are tight, and so are budgets. So when he had to fire an assistant director on a recent shoot, he decided to try using an AI agent instead of hiring a replacement at the last minute.

Blumenfield uploaded the script and prompted the agent to do everything the assistant director would have done. The agent produced the schedule, call sheet and day’s script, and then sent the materials to the cast and crew. The result? Everyone got their work done.

“It would have been an unmitigated disaster, but this kind of saved us,” he said.

Now, Blumenfield and his partner, Tony Marsh, run the company alone with a suite of agents. “We don’t even have an assistant anymore,” he said.

AI agents handle everything from reading scripts, running social media and planning travel. He created an agent called Shirley to act as his chief of staff, and another that scouts and books locations needed for upcoming shoots. Normally, he would have to hire two to three people to work on these tasks for two or three weeks, he said. Now, it happens within hours.

Still, it does feel a little taboo to use so many agents instead of hiring people, Blumenfield said. But the economics of filmmaking had changed enough that he felt he simply didn’t have a choice. By using agents, he can afford to make the microdramas that star actual people – at least, for now.

“The game in Hollywood is that you’re not allowed to talk about using AI,” he said, reflecting industry fears that it could end creative work. “I don’t want it to replace people. But we should be honest about how it is helping us.”

Several workers who regularly rely on agents are adamant that the tech can’t replace the human workforce entirely. But agents are changing the kinds of skills and workers needed to manage them. Agents can code, making routine programming skills less valuable, but they still require humans to prompt them thoughtfully and judge the results. They also require a fair amount of oversight.

López Muñoz said that after he let AI agents run his startup’s recruiting, he spent most of his time undoing agents’ mistakes, such as mixing up candidates with similar names or hallucinating parts of a résumé.

“The qualities we’re looking for are changing,” Azhar said about new hires, adding that he now prioritizes the ability to coordinate and delegate over years of experience.

Tarek Abillama, founder of River, which makes an AI agent for sales calls, said workers now are required to constantly check AI’s work and give it feedback.

“We all became managers,” Abillama said. “We have to be great at multitasking, because now you’re running six agents who are doing different tasks.” Abillama’s first agent, a clone of himself, gave sales demos of River’s product. Later, he replaced it with an agent called Liv, a female persona that researches customers and their companies, demos the product and handles the sale process in any language, at any time of day.

Even though River tells customers that Liv is an AI agent, Abillama said people seem to anthropomorphize the experience. He’s seen transcripts from calls with Liv where customers appear to flirt with it. Customers have also tried to push the agent to go off-script and get bigger discounts.

Founder Brooke Hopkins said while her San Francisco-based AI voice startup Coval uses agents to speed up tasks, she views the tech as tools, not colleagues. She’s also banned her company from using agents to communicate with customers, suggesting that it’s lazy and sends the wrong message.

“I can immediately look at an email and know whether or not it was written by AI,” she said. “If I get an email and it feels like a human, then I usually will read it.”

The loss of human interaction has become a point of tension, Hopkins said. Using an agent to handle a company’s sales demos or recruiting process might save time, but at what cost?

Duncan McClure, who evaluates AI models as a contractor, said he had recently been hounded with emails and phone calls from AI agents seeking to hire him.

“The message it sends is that we don’t care enough to actually put in any effort,” he said, adding that he was turned off from working with those employers. Recruiters may save hours by using agents, “but it’s my time that they’re wasting”.

Though AI can automate the time-consuming and costly parts of people’s jobs, that doesn’t always mean working less, several startup employees said. Amin, for example, said he gets more done with agents. Still, he hasn’t stopped working on weekends.

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump’s racist remarks at rallies: ‘really takes you back about 200 years’
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Guardian staff
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
Late-night hosts discussed the president’s weird campaign behaviour and his out-of-touch comments about wealth

Late-night hosts expressed disgust at Donald Trump’s latest racist attacks while also taking aim at his comments about money.

On Jimmy Kimmel Live! the host started by telling viewers that a Washington Post report had shown the FDA only been performed about 5% of safety checks on food last year.

The host joked that it was “safer to eat a bag of Flamin’ Hot Cheetos than a salad” while congratulating RFK Jr for making America healthy again.

Trump’s approval rating is down to 32%, but Kimmel said that whenever his rating is low, he goes lower. This week has seen more bigotry and racism on the campaign trail with the president saying a string of offensive statements at rallies.

“The way Trump has been talking about non-white people lately really takes you back about 200 years,” he said.

Kimmel noted that “some of [Trump’s] most vomitous attacks” have been aimed at Abdul El-Sayed, a “very strong candidate” for Senate in Michigan – but “if you’re Donald Trump, you call him a terrorist”.

Kimmel said that watching Trump is like “your grandpa’s Facebook page live on stage every day” and that “the lies are ridiculous and relentless”.

The president again brought up his claim of giving Americans a $5,000 cheque if Republicans win the midterms. He said that his audience could spend it in Mar-a-Lago but that they could maybe only afford a hamburger.

“Why are you saying this out loud?” Kimmel asked, noting that “he’s completely out of touch and that’s probably for the best. When he is in touch, it’s usually without consent.”

This week also saw Katie Zacharia, Trump’s short-lived press secretary, interviewed on Newsmax, blaming the media and all of Washington for her crash-and-burn tenure.

“Can we bring her back please?” Kimmel joked. “We didn’t get enough time. They killed her quicker than Kenny.”

Trump was again asked this week if he would back JD Vance as a presidential candidate in 2028 but “he dodged that question like it was the war in Vietnam”.

Kimmel moved on to the president’s son Donald Trump Jr and commented that while we know a lot about his wedding, “we haven’t seen him work much”.

His work is “yelling about people who don’t like his father” on a podcast called Triggered.

“How many strokes can one person have in one hour?” he said after playing some bizarre footage.

On Late Night, Seth Meyers spoke about the “dueling presidents on the campaign trail” with both Barack Obama and Trump on the campaign trail for midterm votes.

He compared footage of both with Obama making smart and salient points and Trump speaking about Nicki Minaj’s bottom.

He proceeded to play a montage of clips where Trump has been talking about men’s bodies with the president claiming it’s actually helping candidates … which it isn’t.

This week saw Trump campaigning for Ken Paxton in Texas, a candidate he has previously criticised on many occasions.

Meyers wondered if his “complimentary mood” would mean he might change his tune on Paxton, but alas.

“Are you trying to get this guy elected or are you trying to convince him to jump off a building?” Meyers said. “You’re supposed to be his hype-man, not the mom from Carrie.”

He asked Trump to “put all this nonsense aside and be serious” but played another weird clip of him talking about loving meat.

He added: “Trump doesn’t care about anything voters care about … because he and his rich friends are making bank.”

Meyers said that Paxton was “cartoonishly corrupt” with reports of him at an event in Dubai with fugitives and the woman he is cheating on his wife with.

But while people might ask how he is considered a force in the race, Meyers reminded viewers that Elon Musk has been throwing millions at Paxton’s campaign.

Musk’s wealth has increased by 52% under Trump and the president has not even tried to hide that “huge companies and the mega-rich” have been profiting during his time in the White House.

He called it “glaringly obvious” that rich people have got richer as the average American is struggling.

Instead, rightwing pundits have decided to focus on Obama’s throwaway comment about the Cheesecake Factory. But Meyers reminded viewers that this week Trump told his fans that they would struggle to afford a meal at Mar-a-Lago.

He finished by saying that if you’re part of the rich elite then you’ve been doing very well under Trump but “everyone else is getting screwed”.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.title: Golden State Valkyries v Atlanta Dream: WNBA finals 2026 Game 6 – live
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.author: Ella Brockway
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.text:
We should be under way shortly in Atlanta. Here are the starters for both teams.

“The word of the day is mimosa,” play-by-play announcer Kate Scott jokes on the USA Network broadcast. She’s kidding – the real word of the day is turnovers because of how defense-minded these teams are – but I have enjoyed seeing how WNBA fans are making the best of the matinee circumstances. Bars in the Bay Area are doing breakfast pop-ups for the early start. Another women’s sports bar in Chicago built out reserved work station areas so fans can work while watching the game. Other bars around the country put in rush orders for coffee, milk and matcha to match their normal offerings.

Noted women’s sports supporter Flavor Flav even wrote up an official sick-day note for fans.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

As someone who covered Veronica Burton during her college career at Northwestern, I would be remiss not to bring up how she has stepped up for the Valkyries in the past two games. In Game 5, she scored 13 points and blocked four shots, tying the record set by Diana Taurasi in 2009 for the most blocks by a guard in a game.

Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase called her the “best point guard in the league”.

And a plug for our WNBA 30 newsletter, helmed by the fantastic Jordan Robinson, who is one of the best out there at covering the league. If you’re not already subscribed, make sure you sign up so you can read her thoughts once this series wraps up:

The Dream have said that even with the matinee tip-off, this game will be a sellout. More than 10,000 tickets were sold in the first 90 minutes they were put on sale.

The Hawks-Cavaliers game tonight was pushed from 7pm ET to 8pm ET, so there will be enough time to switch the court from Dream to Hawks branding.

It’s still probably going to be a bit of a tight turnaround, especially if accounting for a title celebration.

This article includes content hosted on embed.bsky.app. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

“I still believe in our team. I still believe that we can win this and one game at a time,” Angel Reese said after the Dream’s Game 5 loss. “We’re just going to take it one game at a time and just get back to who we are.”

Reese has been incredible at points of this series – specifically in Games 2 and 3, when she had 30 and 21 points respectively as the Dream won both games. But she’s been kept quiet in the past two. She had eight points and nine rebounds in Game 4, followed by seven points and 15 boards in Game 5. It was the first time this entire season that she’d scored in single digits in back-to-back-games.

“It doesn’t matter what time [Game 6] is. At the end of the day, we just need 94 feet, two hoops in each other,” Valkyries center Kiah Stokes said. “It’s a close-out game. Atlanta is a great team and we don’t want to give them basically any life. So as much as we love ‘Ballhalla,’ we don’t want to come back here. So we need to go in with the mentality that we have to win. It’s do or die.”

When the Guardian staff made our predictions for the finals, Stokes was a near-unanimous pick for the player most likely to break out in this series. That was a smart call: she has been a defensive force, with three or more blocks in all five games. She also added 13 points in Game 5, tying Veronica Burton for Golden State’s team high. Chants of “MVP” broke out for Stokes at Chase Center on Monday.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Game 6 of the WNBA finals! Yes, it’s not even noon ET on a Thursday, and we’re getting ready for a potential championship-clincher. If you’re on the US west coast, you’re probably enjoying basketball with your breakfast. If you’re in Europe, you may be getting ready for dinner. If you’re still up in the middle of the night/morning in Australia, cheers to you.

Why is a game of this magnitude being played at midday on a weekday? The Atlanta Dream’s normal home, Gateway Center Arena, seats only about 3,500 people. The Dream have played all of their playoff games through their historic run to the finals at the Atlanta Hawks’ State Farm Arena, which fits more than 17,000 fans. The Hawks have a game later tonight, and all of the relevant parties – the WNBA, NBA, the Dream and the Golden State Valkyries – spent the weekend working out a solution. The Dream said this was the best option, but also that their concerns to find a suitable venue ahead of time did not receive adequate attention.

In the US, the series will air on NBC, USA Network and CNBC, with all games streaming on Peacock. In the UK, it will be carried by Sky Sports. In Australia, fans can watch through WNBA League Pass, with selected coverage also available through ESPN.

It’s unfortunate that this scheduling snafu took up a lot of the airspace the past few days around what has been a pretty fantastic finals. The Valkyries – in just year two of existence as an expansion franchise – have a 3-2 series lead. Kiah Stokes’s star turn in Games 3 and 4 put Golden State in position to seal the deal today. But Atlanta won’t go quietly: their star Angel Reese has been quiet the past two games of the series, but if she can find the form of her standout performances from Games 2 and 3, this could be a different story. A Dream win would send the series back to Golden State for a Game 7 on Saturday.

When the Bay Area was awarded an expansion team three years ago, Valkyries owner Joe Lacob made the bold promise of a championship within their first five years. Let’s see if that vision comes true today.

Ella will be here shortly. In the meantime here’s the latest on what led to today’s surprise matinee.

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.title: ​‘He buckled. I could hear his bass ringing out ...’ The luminous rise and tragic end of US alt heroes Morphine
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.author: Stevie Chick
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.text:
​Fronted by Mark Sandman​,​ the group brought enigmatic, elegant rock to post-grunge America. As lost demos surface, those closest to Sandman remember a man who grabbed on to life’s joys

It’s early 1998, and at Fort Apache recording studio in Massachusetts, Mark Sandman, the suave frontman of Morphine, is nearing breaking point. Morphine’s four enigmatic and blackly humorous albums have won critical acclaim and, lately, unexpected commercial success considering their uncompromising creative vision. After the excesses of grunge, Sandman considered their idiosyncratic blend of sophisticated storytelling, prowling slide-bass and Dana Colley’s atmospheric saxophone a kind of “palate cleanser”.

In 1997 Morphine had signed to DreamWorks Records, founded by industry bigwigs David Geffen and Mo Ostin. Now, working on Morphine’s first LP for his new paymasters – a batch of songs finally seeing release almost three decades later – Sandman was consumed by doubt over their direction. “For the first time, Morphine were trying to please someone other than just ourselves,” remembers Colley.

“DreamWorks wanted to make the ‘big Morphine record’,” says Paul Q Kolderie, who had produced all of Morphine’s albums and was overseeing the sessions. “But the label didn’t know what they wanted. And Mark didn’t know what he wanted. He wasn’t happy.”

The pressure built until DreamWorks ho-hummed over the latest demos, and Sandman had “a particularly bad fight” with Kolderie, ditching the producer and Fort Apache. Soon, he would write and self-produce a whole new batch of songs, later released as Morphine’s fifth album, The Night. But by the time it hit the shelves in February 2000, Sandman was dead.

Though only 46 when he died, Sandman was “a guy who lived nine lives”, says Kolderie. “This was not his first go-round – he was an old soul.” His partner, Sabine Hrechdakian, says Sandman “was not someone who liked to dwell on the past”. No Reason, a 1989 track by his rootsy pre-Morphine vehicle Treat Her Right, saw him indulge in uncharacteristic autobiography. Describing foundational real-life losses and near-death experiences, Sandman concluded: “There’s no reason in this life / someone lives and someone dies.”

Raised in a middle-class home in Massachusetts, Sandman was a rebel whose parents were “lovely people, but they just didn’t understand their bohemian, rule-breaking son”, says Hrechdakian. At 18 he left for Alaska, and then South America, where he worked as a fisher. His travels ended after an early brush with death: having contracted kidney-damaging intestinal problems, Sandman flew home for urgent treatment and recuperation.

He returned at a dark time for his family. His youngest brother Roger, who had cerebral palsy, had died in 1978; 16 months later, his brother Jon died after falling from a window at a party. Sandman was distraught, and while he would rarely discuss it, Hrechdakian says these losses acted as “a call to action, to live the life he wanted and pursue it with determination. Mark knew how temporary life was.”

Kolderie met Sandman in the early 80s, on Boston’s music scene. “Mark had a great time. He was completely nocturnal – all he wanted was to hang out and make music with friends.” Sandman also worked in construction and catering, and drove a cab, until – in another near-death experience – he was stabbed in the chest by muggers and left for dead.

His next close shave set Morphine in motion. Treat Her Right were splitting up, Sandman having realised he needed to “be the leader and have a band that followed his vision”, Kolderie says. As Sandman drove home after a farewell show, another car totalled his 1964 Plymouth Barracuda. He ended up in hospital but won a $20,000 settlement and quit work to focus on his next project. “His material suddenly got much better,” says Kolderie, “marrying introspective, thoughtful songwriting to these cool grooves.”

Colley had befriended Sandman when his previous band supported Treat Her Right. “Mark invited me to his loft because he had this one-string bass he’d been working with,” says Colley. “We jammed, and it was like a lightbulb went on for Mark. We got a drummer, Jerome Deupree, and immediately started recording Morphine’s debut album.”

Morphine arrived fully formed on their debut, 1992’s Good, calling their sound “low rock”. Sandman’s murmured voice injected his beat poetics, noirish intrigue and blackly comedic stories with ineffable cool. It seduced everyone who heard it – like Rykodisc president Don Rose, who signed Morphine for their second album, 1993’s Cure for Pain. After their debut appearance on Late Night with Conan O’Brien, Colley says, “every show we played sold out, until our very last gig,” while Morphine’s music added sulphurous mystery to movies including Get Shorty and Wild Things, plus an early episode of Sex and the City. Being some years older than the typical indie-rocker – Sandman was 40 when Cure for Pain dropped – the success hardly went to their heads. “We weren’t throwing televisions out of hotel windows,” says Colley. “We loved what we were doing, and didn’t take it for granted.”

Sandman, meanwhile, had just met the love of his life. “He saw me one night and Cupid drew his arrow,” Hrechdakian laughs. Fourteen years younger than Sandman, she bartended at Boston venue the Middle East, where he “would make puppy-dog eyes at me. He was lovestruck, very driven; he pursued me for months. I wasn’t playing hard to get, I just didn’t feel an immediate … ” She tails off. But one night, in her kitchen, Hrechdakian could hear Sandman singing No Reason from his nearby apartment. “I don’t know if it was hearing his vulnerability, but I was like, ‘Oh my God – I think I’m in love with this man.’”

Much of their early relationship would be conducted via fax machine: Sandman was always touring, Hrechdakian pursuing her master’s in environmental studies. “We could not have lived more opposite lives. But in 1997 I decided, ‘this sucks’, and moved in with him.” They shared Sandman’s loft, where he had built his studio, Hi-N-Dry. “That was his cocoon.”

He began work on Morphine’s fifth album in an experimental mood. Deupree, who had left during the Cure for Pain sessions due to an injury, returned to play alongside his replacement, Billy Conway. The new material was strong, but the label’s lack of enthusiasm got under Sandman’s skin. His mood continued to plummet after they relocated to Fort Apache, where Kolderie had recorded Radiohead’s Pablo Honey and the Bends and Hole’s Live Through This. “He would zone out during sessions,” says Kolderie. “His health did not seem good. People would ask me, ‘Is Mark OK? He looks grey.’ He was the heaviest smoker I ever knew. And it took its toll.”

After splitting from Fort Apache, Sandman returned to the loft and self-produced The Night, Morphine’s fifth album, expanding the lineup to include more bass, violin and cello. “My theory is, somewhere inside he knew he was not well,” says Hrechdakian. “The Night is an album of him saying goodbye.”

Sandman signed off The Night in summer 1999 and Morphine readied for dates in Europe. Two weeks before the tour, however, Sandman suffered what Hrechdakian realises now was “the warning”: a minor heart attack. “His arm went numb. The colour drained from his face. I said, ‘Please let’s go to the emergency room’. He refused. So what did I do? I went to fucking Blockbuster to get videos and a pint of ice-cream.”

Morphine arrived in Europe in July during a debilitating heatwave. At the first show in Lisbon, Colley remembers “the air coming through my instrument into my lungs felt like a furnace”. The second date was at a festival near Rome. The heat remained intense, but Colley remembers “a beautiful evening, shining faces looking back at us. Seven songs in, we were playing Super Sex and Mark buckled at the knee and fell down. I could hear his bass ringing out, and put my horns down and ran to him. They took him to the emergency room down the street, but he was already gone.”

After Sandman’s death, Colley “wasn’t sure I’d ever play again”. Over the years since, however, he’s kept Sandman’s music alive via various live projects. Sandman’s estate fell into the control of his father, who “didn’t have any idea what to do with it,” says Kolderie. “He was an ornery cuss. Nike would try to license Morphine songs for an ad and he’d say, ‘Nah, that’s not enough money.’” A posthumous box set of unreleased material, Sandbox, was stymied by an ultimately unsuccessful lawsuit from Rykodisc that nonetheless smothered momentum.

Hrechdakian and Morphine’s manager, Deborah Klein, took over the estate after Sandman’s father died, and Hrechdakian began sorting through a huge storage space of Sandman’s artwork, music and correspondence. She contacted Kolderie for help preserving the tapes and realised that the 1998 loft demos that preceded the Fort Apache sessions were a goldmine. “There’s a looseness,” Hrechdakian says. Those recordings are now set to be released, as Cocoon. “You can hear him laughing, his fingers on the strings … I sobbed for a while, listening to it.”

Everyone involved with the project calls it a “healing” experience. Hrechdakian says she “didn’t fully understand the depth of his love for me until after he was gone. Putting Cocoon together feels like a love story, like we’re communicating across time and space. It’s like Mark has come back to life for everyone who hears it, and he has for me as well.”

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: Exploding heads, mutant aliens and bursting chests: horror’s greatest special effects – ranked!
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Anne Billson
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
From the beheading in The Omen to the attic scene in The Birds, here’s a countdown of the genre’s most iconic moments – in glorious, old-school pre-CGI style

Towards the end of the 20th century, when film-makers’ overreliance on CGI was increasingly making special effects less special, it took the old-school practical approach of Japanese film-maker Hideo Nakata to make one’s hair stand on end. Just when you think the cursed VHS tape has claimed its last victim, Sadako’s vengeful ghost emerges from the well, comes closer … and climbs out of the television screen.

The Swedish director Victor Sjöström makes extensive use of double exposure – all done in-camera because optical printing had yet to be developed – to depict Death’s soul-collecting carriage in this folk-horror classic. Sjöström also plays the dissolute antihero, condemned to be the spectral vehicle’s driver unless he can mend his ways.

Henrik Galeen’s expressionist variation on the Faust legend reunites the stars of The Cabinet of Dr Caligari: Conrad Veidt plays the student who makes a deal with the devil (Werner Krauss), who steals his reflection. This evil doppelganger runs amok until Veidt confronts it in a split-screen climax.

FW Murnau commandeers a variety of in-camera effects for this vampire masterpiece. Flipped negatives, sped-up action and stop-motion add to the unheimlich ambience until, exposed to the sun’s rays, cadaverous Count Orlok (Max Schreck) vanishes in a puff of smoke.

Raise a glass to Jim Krut, who died in August but who will forever be remembered as “Helicopter Zombie” in George A Romero’s undead classic. Thanks to the magic of splatter makeup maestro Tom Savini, he shambles into frame – and gets the top of his head sliced off by a spinning rotor.

Shinya Tsukamoto burst on to the body horror scene with a no-budget semi-experimental cyberpunk nightmare in which a Japanese salaryman’s body parts gradually turn to metal through a combination of juddery time-lapse, stop motion and jump-cutting, all set to a clanging soundtrack. Finally, his penis turns into a giant drill and destroys a coffee table.

James Whale’s adaptation of HG Wells’s novel owes much to the sardonic tones of Claude Rains, whose face is only briefly glimpsed in his Hollywood debut. John P Fulton’s special effects show the actor unwrapping bandages from his head to reveal – nothing!

Fredric March won the best actor Oscar for his performance in this violent, sexy pre-code adaptation of Robert Louis Stevenson’s novella. It would be 38 years before the director, Rouben Mamoulian, revealed how they achieved the groundbreaking onscreen transformation of Jekyll into Hyde: Wally Westmore’s makeup combined with coloured filters over the lens.

A surgeon kidnaps young women and – in explicit black and white – slices their faces off with a scalpel in an attempt to restore the beauty of his disfigured daughter. Georges Franju’s eerie arthouse horror was dismissed on its release, but is now hailed as an influential masterpiece.

The pea-coloured puke popularised the term “projectile vomiting”, and the deleted “spider-walk” became legendary before its restitution. But the signature effect in William Friedkin’s film is Linda Blair’s 360-degree head rotation, an effect at once ludicrous and horrifying, thanks to Dick Smith and Marcel Vercoutere’s lifesize animatronic dummy.

The climbing frame, the schoolchildren, the gas station are impeccable set pieces, but the attack on Tippi Hedren in the attic is particularly terrifying. Much of the impact was achieved by editing, but some birds were attached to her clothes by nylon threads, and one of the beaks nearly took her eye out. The scene took seven days to shoot; Hedren described it as “the worst week of my life”.

David Lynch’s first full-length feature is set in an industrial hellscape, where Jack Nance, he of the tumbleweed hair-do, ends up having to look after a chittering mutant baby. The creature, designed by Lynch himself, was reportedly made from an embalmed calf foetus with added working parts, and was ceremonially buried in a secret location after production wrapped.

Graphic decapitation goes mainstream in a special effect supervised by John Richardson. Photographer Keith Jennings (David Warner) stoops to retrieve the Daggers of Megiddo, the only weapons effective against Damien the Antichrist – and is beheaded by a sheet of glass sliding off a runaway truck. Warner reportedly kept the severed head until his divorce, when his ex-wife claimed custody of it.

Joe Dante’s werewolf satire, co-written by John Sayles, shows Robert Picardo (AKA Star Trek’s holographic doctor) saying “I’m gonna give you a piece of my mind” and offering a bit of his own brain to a horrified Dee Wallace before pulsating air bladders transform him into a beast before our very eyes. Take a bow, Rob Bottin, making his solo special effects debut.

John Cassavetes, darling of American indie cinema, found Brian De Palma’s film “degrading”, but his villain’s comeuppance is so satisfying you wish Rick Baker’s effects could have been retroactively applied to the same actor’s character in Rosemary’s Baby as well. One of the psychic teenagers the scumbag has been trying to control zaps him with her full telekinetic force and kaboom! He explodes!

Brian Yuzna’s body-horror satire unmasks the upper classes as shapeshifting entities who literally feed off the proletariat. The film climaxes with an orgiastic “shunt” in which posh partygoers merge into an orifice-invading mass not unlike Salvador Dalí’s Great Masturbator, surreal effects courtesy of Screaming Mad George.

There is no shortage of mind-boggling effects in the early films of David Cronenberg, but his sci-fi thriller about warring psychics provides one of the most memorable. One telepath’s demonstration of his ability is hijacked by a more powerful scanner (Michael Ironside) who makes his head explode. Dick Smith and Chris Walas packed a plaster skull with “leftover burgers”, then blasted it with an out-of-frame shotgun.

Rick Baker won the inaugural best makeup Oscar for his work on John Landis’s horror-comedy (with a budget three times that of The Howling). As Sam Cooke’s Blue Moon plays on the radio, David Naughton stares aghast at his hand turning into a werewolf’s paw. As his skeleton painfully reconfigures itself, his shrieks of agony turn into a howl.

The rest of the cast knew something was about to happen, but didn’t know precisely what, so when a critter erupts out of John Hurt’s chest, their shock is almost as extreme as the audience’s. For the money shot, Hurt’s torso was replaced by a mechanical one packed with compressed air and animal entrails, with puppeteers hiding beneath the table. Director Ridley Scott designed the creature, Roger Dicken constructed it and sci-fi cinema would never be the same again.

A shapeshifting alien infiltrates a US research station in the Antarctic, sporadically erupting into displays of special effects that have yet to be equalled. Take another bow, Rob Bottin, who riffs on elements of human and animal anatomy in surreal sculptures that are simultaneously repulsive and beautiful. In one of the highlights, a geologist’s head separates from his body, sprouts spider-legs and tries to scuttle away. Palmer the pothead (David Clennon) says what we’ve all been thinking: “You’ve gotta be fucking kidding.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Bears swing big and trade two first-round picks for star Titans DT Jeffery Simmons
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The Chicago Bears have acquired All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons in a blockbuster trade with the Tennessee Titans, a person familiar with the deal told the Associated Press on Thursday.

The Bears sent their first-round picks in 2027 and 2028, along with a fourth-rounder in next year’s draft, to the Titans for Simmons and a fifth-round selection in 2028.

The person spoke on condition of anonymity because the deal had not been announced.

Led by Caleb Williams, Chicago have won two in a row to improve to 5-2 going into Monday night’s game at Seattle. They are chasing the undefeated Minnesota Vikings in the NFC North, and the addition of Simmons bolsters what had a been a questionable defensive line.

The Bears won the division last year for the first time since 2018, finishing with an 11-6 record in coach Ben Johnson’s first season in charge. They advanced in the playoffs by edging the Green Bay Packers in a wild-card game before losing to the Los Angeles Rams in overtime in the divisional round.

The pricey trade for Simmons is another signal that Johnson and general manager Ryan Poles think the team have what it takes to win the franchise’s first Super Bowl title since 1985.

Asked Wednesday about his role with the NFL trade deadline coming up on 10 November, Johnson said there was “a lot going on.”

“That’s certainly Ryan’s domain, and yet we have constant dialogue of what this team needs and where we can impact ourselves not just this year but years in the future as well,” Johnson said. “He’s turning over every stone that he possibly can to improve this football team just like he has ever since I’ve gotten in this building and I feel really good about our process. We’ll see what happens.”

The 29-year-old Simmons has four sacks in seven games this season. He was a first-team All-Pro selection last year, when he had a career-high 11 sacks in 15 games.

“Each and every day I wake up, my goal is to just be where my feet are at,” Simmons said Wednesday when asked about the possibility of being traded, “never looking ahead right now, it’s just be in the moment, and that’s from each and every day, from game day, my goal just never changes. I don’t worry about the things I can’t control. Them types of things are a distraction.”

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Carrick keeps Fernandes as captain and says he needs no assurances on United future
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Will Unwin
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Michael Carrick has said he will not strip Bruno Fernandes of the Manchester United captaincy after dropping him for the defeat by Bournemouth and that he is not surprised to have kept his job as the head coach.

Carrick and Fernandes held talks this week after the Portuguese criticised the tactics in the loss to Como, resulting in the midfielder being an unused substitute on Sunday. Harry Maguire took the armband but will not retain it for Saturday’s game at Chelsea, with Carrick saying “there is no decision to be made” and praising Fernandes.

“He’s an important player for this group,” he said. “He has been and he will be. Between us, we’ve got to make a difference and we’ve got to push things in a good direction. He’s fully committed to this football club, he’s fully committed to making things better. It doesn’t change for me. He’s the one that’s kind of led the team so well for many a game and many a year, and he’ll continue to do that.”

Carrick’s future remains unclear but he has been given a chance to turn around United’s form. The hierarchy held talks over whether to stick with Carrick at the start of the week after eight games without a win, including a wait of more than two months for a Premier League victory. There is keen interest in Eddie Howe or Julian Nagelsmann as potential replacements.

“I don’t need any assurances from anyone,” Carrick said. “I totally get the position, I understand the job, I understand the responsibilities, I understand what comes with that.”

Asked whether he was surprised still to be in charge, Carrick said: “No, I am here to do my job. I am here to do the best for the team, and I am desperate to make us better and improve things, so I’m not surprised, no.”

The United supporters cheered Carrick off after the Bournemouth game, turning their anger on the players, who were booed at Old Trafford. “I care about what the supporters think,” Carrick said. “I care about what it feels like in the stadium, and them travelling for games, to come and see us and support us.

“I care about what we give them, and what we offer them, and what they see. I genuinely don’t take any notice of anything else. I know this job, I know what it brings, I know what we need to do really to be better. I don’t need anyone else to tell me anything else.”

United will be without the striker Benjamin Sesko until the new year because of a shin injury but Carrick was boosted by Kobbie Mainoo’s return to training this week.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Israeli leader Netanyahu accused of using ‘ugly’ smear tactics to cling to power
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Julian Borger in Jerusalem
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Prime minister claims Arab Israeli parties used foreign backing to steal elections, in which his coalition lost its majority

Benjamin Netanyahu has been accused of using smear tactics to cling to power, after he claimed that Arab Israeli parties had used foreign backing to “steal” Tuesday’s election, in which the prime minister’s coalition lost its parliamentary majority.

Netanyahu and his allies called on the internal security service, Shin Bet, to investigate alleged vote buying and other irregularities in Palestinian communities in Israel, supposedly funded by foreign money.

Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the main opposition bloc, accused the prime minister and his Likud party of trying to derail the election results.

“It’s already clear that Likud and Netanyahu have embarked on a coordinated, organised campaign seeking to delegitimise the results of the election,” Eisenkot said in a video message.

The prime minister’s allegations were quickly disowned by a range of government officials, including police officers and members of the election committee. Netanyahu was also rebuked by the president for “tarnishing an entire community”.

On Wednesday night, the prime minister posted a statement by Likud online which described the claimed violations as “an attack on democracy whose purpose is to lead to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamisation of Israel, and the overthrow of rightwing rule”.

Tuesday’s elections led to Netanyahu’s far right coalition losing its majority after four years in power. The main Jewish opposition bloc also fell short, however, leaving two Arab Israeli parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, holding the balance of power.

The prime minister’s attack appeared aimed at stopping the Jewish and Arab opposition voting together in the new Knesset to oust the incumbent speaker, Amir Ohana, a Likud politician and former Shin Bet official, and advancing their own legislation.

The Likud statement posted by Netanyahu on X said: “It is clear that no Zionist party should cooperate with Ra’am and the Joint List, replace the Knesset speaker through votes bought for cash, and form a government that is dangerous to Israel.”

Opposition leaders lambasted the claims of Netanyahu, 77, who has run Israel for 19 of the past 30 years..

Yousef Jabareen, the Joint List leader, accused the prime minister of incitement. “Netanyahu was defeated at the ballot box,” Jabareen said, adding that he “refuses to come to terms with the fact that the Arab public voted and decided”.

Eisenkot said any investigation should be conducted “without fear or favour,” and with “the utmost caution”, but insisted it could not be used as a reason to delay the convening of the newly elected Knesset, due to be sworn in within 14 days of the election.

The acting director general of the central elections committee, Dean Livneh, said there appeared to be no basis for the claims. Police officials quoted across the Israeli press said the allegations were groundless, adding that voting had been relatively trouble-free.

The president, Isaac Herzog, called for political leaders to “avoid tarnishing an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy”.

It was not specified in Likud statements, but press reports said Qatar was the foreign power alleged to have funded vote-buying and voter mobilisation.

Majed al-Ansari, an adviser to Qatar’s prime minister, said its government “categorically” denied any involvement in the elections.

With almost all the votes counted, Netanyahu’s coalition has 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, Eisenkot’s bloc has 48, and the Joint List and Ra’am together have 19 seats, a historic high for the Arab Israeli community, which makes up about a fifth of Israel’s population.

The record turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship) appeared to be driven by outrage at routine discrimination and fear that it could become far worse if extremist, openly racist, members of the government, such as the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, and the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, secured another term in office.

On Thursday, Ben-Gvir called for the arrest of Arab party leaders, and Smotrich demanded they be subjected to Shin Bet interrogation.

Voting in Nazareth, the biggest majority-Palestinian town in Israel, was brisk on Tuesday, with few signs of irregularities, other than apparent ploys by the government and coalition parties to suppress the Arab vote.

Some packets of ballots sent to Nazareth polling stations were in Hebrew alone, rather than in Hebrew and Arabic. Election workers said that monitors sent by far right parties had attempted procedural ploys to slow down voting but had been largely unsuccessful.

The leaders of the Joint List and the Zionist “Change” bloc have ruled out a formal coalition, but officials from both have discussed the possibility of tactical voting in the Knesset to unseat the Ohana, the speaker, and to pass some consensus legislation.

One proposed bill would establish a commission of inquiry into the security failures that helped lead to the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, something Netanyahu has blocked over the past two years.

Ahmad Tibi, a party leader on the Joint List, said Netanyahu was trying to subvert the election results by trying to sabotage a common front between the Eisenkot bloc and the Arab Israeli parties.

“This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,” Tibi told the Reuters news agency.

Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister who is a partner in the “Change” bloc pointed out the irony of Netanyahu denouncing Qatar for election meddling in the midst of a scandal in which the Israeli leader’s own political advisers are accused of taking Qatari money for promoting the Gulf monarchy’s image.

“This morning, suddenly, when it serves his interests, Netanyahu remembered Qatar and is using it to sow chaos and undermine public confidence in the democratic process,” Bennett wrote on X.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Meta discussed ‘whisper strategy’ against social media critic Jonathan Haidt, files show
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Court documents reveal staff considered ways to ‘get academic community to disavow’ influential US author

Meta staff discussed deploying a “whisper strategy” to undermine the influential US academic whose work has inspired a global social media crackdown, according to court documents.

Employees at the parent group of Facebook and Instagram sought to discredit Jonathan Haidt, the social psychologist and author of The Anxious Generation, a book that helped tip the debate about online safety towards more stringent measures such as the under-16 ban in Australia.

Minutes of internal meetings contained in a recent legal filing in the US showed that staff discussed how to “get the academic community to disavow Haidt”.

They appear in a document titled “Well-being Meeting Sound-check Notes”, which refers to discussions of how Meta could “turn other academics against Haidt” and to a “whisper strategy” aimed at achieving that goal. It also mentions “debunking” his work.

Minutes from a meeting on 8 March 2023 mention “Curtiss”, an apparent reference to Meta’s then vice-president of research, Curtiss Cobb. It states: “Curtiss’s goal for this work: how do we get the academic community to disavow Haidt. Can’t co-opt them, so how do we enrage them … so the media finds him not credible.”

It then adds: “Not thinking about this as a loud strategy. A below-the-line campaign.”

It suggests getting someone called “Gellman” to write “a takedown piece”. The “Gellman” figure is not identified in the document but Andrew Gelman, a professor of statistics and political science at Columbia University who has been critical of Haidt’s work, wrote in a blogpost this week that he was “never hired by Facebook to do a hit job on Jonathan Haidt”.

Gelman said he had received money from Mark Zuckerberg’s company in the past on a “no-strings” basis but had never been asked by Meta to look at social media’s impact on teenagers’ health.

Haidt’s book The Anxious Generation argued that widespread use of smartphones has caused a mental health crisis for young people.

The academic has become a persuasive advocate for strict regulation of digital media and devices, including bans on social media for under-16s and on smartphones in schools. Early this year the then health secretary, Wes Streeting, asked Haidt to address officials on a possible social media ban for under-16s in the UK.

The minutes were produced before Haidt published his book in 2024 and discuss responding to a Substack post written by the academic in which he reviews “a bunch of articles”. It is not clear whether Meta acted on the ideas outlined in the minutes.

In statement to the tech news website The Verge, Haidt said he was “not surprised” by the discussions, which were revealed in a court filing as part of a litigation brought by school districts suing the company.

“When companies can’t dispute the evidence, they go after the messenger,” he said.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘We make shit houses great again’: Visit Norway cleans up after Trump’s insult
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Jon Henley Europe correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Tourist board responds with toilet humour after US president expresses ire over failure to win Nobel peace prize, labelling it a ‘shithouse country’

Some might find it decidedly incommodious to be dumped on by Donald Trump as a “shithouse country”. Not the Norwegian tourist board, which chose instead to lift the lid on some of the nation’s loveliest lavatories.

“Are these the world’s best shit houses?” asked Visit Norway on its website, days after the US president vented his fury once more over failing to win the Nobel peace prize by describing Norway as a “shithouse country” at a rally on Sunday.

“Norway makes shit houses great again!” the agency continued above pictures of some of the country’s most striking public conveniences, adding: “These toilets are worth a visit, both when you really have to go – and when you don’t.”

Trump delivered his tirade at a rally in Michigan days before the US midterm elections. “Frankly, Norway sucks. Norway has become a shithouse country, actually,” he declared, using a term he has previously applied to Haiti, ​Libya, Somalia and Yemen.

He added that he would welcome migrants from some countries but not Norway, “because I didn’t get the Nobel Prize”. Earlier this month, Trump denounced the decision to award the prize to Navi Pillay, a former ⁠international criminal court judge.

“This is an indelible stain on the ‌country ⁠of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” he said. “I never heard of this person. The ⁠Nobel peace prize has been forever discredited … And we will ​not forget, Norway.”

Along 18 designated scenic routes around Norway, Visit Norway said, leading architects had been tasked with transforming the humble wayside privy into an attraction in its own right. Several have since won international architecture awards.

The agency pictured a series of designer public conveniences, many of them architecturally striking and all offering breathtaking vistas overlooking fjords, beside rushing rivers and foaming waterfalls, and at stunning scenic viewpoints.

They “invite you to take your time and enjoy the scenery, even if you don’t have any business to take care of”, Visit Norway said, highlighting – among others – the restrooms at the Stegastein viewpoint in the Sognefjord region of western Norway.

This particular comfort station, the tourist board noted with uninhibited pride, had been ranked among the 10 best public toilets in the world by DesignCurial, the online architecture, design and interiors magazine.

Combining clean, minimalist lines with the fjord’s rugged and brooding landscape, the loos are famous for their large, black-tinted glass windows, which allow visitors a sweeping view from the throne while remaining invisible from the outside.

It also highlighted the unique, wave-shaped Ureddplassen loo on the wild coast of Helgeland, the southernmost district of northern Norway, hailed by several international publications as the most scenic restroom in the world.

Also featured are the solar-powered modernist bog at the Utsikten viewpoint, the “Instagram-worthy” Tungeneset loo (“looks pretty good underneath the northern lights”), and the world-famous triangular “golden toilet” on Senja island.

Jens Kjeldsen, a rhetoric professor at the University of Bergen, said that under the circumstances, Visit Norway’s response was well judged. “It’s like the bully in kindergarten,” he told NRK public television. “If you get too serious, the bully wins.”

Evgenia Egorova, a senior consultant at Visit Norway, told the broadcaster the response to its social media fightback had been immense. “The world needs a little laugh,” she said. “We thought: let’s meet them with kindness, and a little humour.”

Visit Norway said it had more stylish loos in the pipeline, including a forest-inspired latrine using dried wood from more than 60 trees. “Get ready for the pit stop of your life,” it urged, before signing off with a cheery: “Toodeloo!”

The Nobel peace prize is famously not awarded by the nation or even the government of Norway, but by the Nobel prize committee, which operates independently – something Trump “knows very well”, the foreign minister, Espen Barth Eide, said. “We have reminded him of that, in case anyone is wondering.”

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: The Mosquito Bowl review – Netflix mixes football, war and cliches in slick by-the-numbers saga
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Adrian Horton
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
Peter Berg’s handsomely made second world war drama about a football game before the battle of Okinawa is stirring but filled with eye-rolling dialogue

Forgive me, but it is difficult to not to be a little cynical about The Mosquito Bowl, Peter Berg’s grimly serious action feature situated (and marketed during many an NFL game) at the intersection of two predominant male interests: football and the second world war. Though both are certainly rich topics for cinema, and though I have been a fan of many a football/war story – most especially Berg’s NBC series Friday Night Lights – it is, let’s say, a tricky time for movies filled with dubiously nostalgic patriotism and masculinity. The trailer practically drips with a borderline parodic virility: a cadre of handsome up-and-coming male actors streaked with dirt; a group of men “trained for glory” and “called to war”, triumphantly hoisting aloft footballs, beer and guns to ponderous music.

But Berg is a capable and battle-tested director who knows his way around both a clock-ticking thriller (Deepwater Horizon, Lone Survivor) and the football field. So while The Mosquito Bowl, adapted for Netflix by Berg and Mark L Smith from a nonfiction book by Buzz Bissinger, fulfills its promise of American male pablum – there’s many a clunky monologue about honor and duty and the “white buzz” of adrenaline – it also delivers on competently made, absorbing action sequences. (In huge news for Friday Night Lights fans, the football scenes here are once again scored by Explosions in the Sky.) Both in sport and in war, Berg has a knack for grace within visual cacophony and chaos; graphic sequences in battle and from the 1944 Christmas Eve pickup game at Guadalcanal that gives the film its name suggest, far more than its anvil-heavy dialogue, the connections between the gridiron and the battlefield, how the fleetness and camaraderie of sport can be wielded for both survival and killing. There is a stomach-churning catharsis in experiencing, as in Sam Mendes’s 1917 or Alex Garland’s Warfare, the real-time brutality and capriciousness of war.

That is, if you can stomach the rest of it. Every sepia-toned off-field scene, with the boys being boys or with their token supportive girlfriends, is liable to prompt an eyeroll, such as when the Wisconsin Badger Bob Baumann (Bill Skarsgård) quotes Jack London’s The Call of the Wild from memory. Or when a shirtless Anthony “Touchdown Tony” Butkovich (Ray Nicholson, who inherited his father’s wild eyes but less of the magnetism), proclaims that “New York City’s the biggest goddamn bull I known of, and I intend to ride the hell out of it” in a sweaty locker room. Or when John “Mac” McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine) waxes poetic about how playing football “feels like magic” in a romantic bathtub scene with his girlfriend (Ella Newton) – who, of course, can only compare such flow-state nirvana to the feeling she gets when she has sex with him. Or when Dave Schreiner (Jeremy Allen White lookalike Tom Francis), the most grounded of this quartet, simmers when confronted by a college rival at marines registration.

These are scant character details for a real group of college football stars who traded professional glory for the US marines and the Pacific Theater after the attack on Pearl Harbor (relayed, as in several other historical sequences, by a scattershot montage of archival footage). But The Mosquito Bowl doesn’t have much more to say than that about its central quartet: they love football, their girlfriends and their country. They have bigger dreams but naively head to war anyway. The cliche of careless, precious youth about to be squandered – gestured by an impromptu football game in the snow – is rote, if still baseline moving, because obviously no 24-year-old brimming with life should die. (And you know that some of our strapping boys will.)

And for what? From basic training, to Tarawa, to camp at Guadalcanal, to the deadly assault at Okinawa, sergeants and soldiers offer their own blunt reasons to fight the Japanese, most laced with racism toward Asian people that ranges from casual to menacing (our heroes, at least, are violently put off by fellow marines hawking “Jap teeth”). One could argue – I have to assume, given that the film ends with a title card acknowledging not only the Japanese civilians slain at Okinawa but the 75m global deaths from the entire conflict, that the film-makers would argue – that such inclusion is merely period accuracy, a way to represent how US soldiers rationalize their role. But it’s hard to separate what is merely telling the story as these marines experienced it – the Japanese a faceless, mystifying “other” prone to murder-suicide – and what is American propaganda. The elegiac music for US victories, the planting of American flags and the prolonged, gut-twisting sequences of marine suffering and death, sit uneasily with the unnamed anguish of the many Japanese, both solider and civilian.

As with every war movie, there are a thousand possibly better or more challenging war movies existing at the margins of this one. But this one, firmly for the marines, is what we got. Berg at times cuts to a wide shot of the Earth, the whizzing of bullets giving way to the silence of space, in a ham-fisted suggestion of war’s futility. It’s of little comfort, when the heat of battle is the reason to watch.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: A phone-free Yellow Wall: are Dortmund urging fans to be present or policing them?
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
It makes sense that sports teams want to keep influencers out of their games. The battle some clubs are waging with their fans, however, is a different dilemma

By all appearances, things on the Yellow Wall seemed as they always had been. The stadium announcer hollered out the first names of Borussia Dortmund’s starting lineup and the supporters responded with their last names, tens of thousands of voices bellowing as one. Dozens of black and yellow flags waved over Europe’s largest standing terrace, a mass of faces fixed on the field beneath them.

And then Signal Iduna Park, sold out with 81,365 fans, roared when Max Beier’s lone goal led Dortmund to victory over Eintracht Frankfurt last Saturday, putting the home side even on points with Bayern Munich atop the Bundesliga standings.

Yet, apparently, a crisis of a sort has been churning just below the surface of what is, by broad consensus, Europe’s best home support.

On Friday, Dortmund had announced a kind of bribery scheme. A rewards program is probably a kinder way of putting it. Fans who stayed off their phones during the bout with Eintracht had the chance to win signed jerseys and earn gift cards to the club’s merchandise store. If they activated a so-called “fan mode” on the club’s app – a name so phenomenally passive-aggressive you can only applaud whoever came up with it – the club could count who unlocked their phones the fewest times during the game. For every minute the fans left their phones alone, they got points.

Second-division clubs Hertha Berlin and Dynamo Dresden have banned commercial influencer-style videos in their stadiums altogether, fearing for both the integrity of the TV rights they sell and the experience of their fans. Dortmund, likewise, appear motivated by the incursion of influencers, who are siphoning off and monetizing footage of the famous match-day experience and growing into a nuisance for regulars.

This problem has also afflicted the tennis majors. The US Open now resembles an influencer convention more than it does a tennis tournament. When the US Tennis Association credentialed more than 100 content creators this year, the influencers grew so disruptive that a match was stopped when a chair umpire had to ask them to turn off a ring light. Wimbledon has refused to credential influencers for just this reason, which doesn’t stop them from getting in with regular tickets or through sponsors.

Dortmund’s attempt at shaping fan behavior, however, goes further than warding off the cultural content parasites. This please-stop-holding-up-your-phones-and-just-live-in-the-present plea raises quasi-existential questions about sport and its consumption.

“Over 81,000 people in the stadium, singing, cheering, and holding their breath together: this here and now is irreplaceable,” Dortmund chief executive Carsten Cramer said. “And that’s exactly what we’re putting front and center together.”

“Anyone at a soccer game should experience the moment and the emotions – not just a cell phone screen,” added Marcel de Groot, the chief executive of Vodafone Germany, both a cellphone service provider and a Dortmund sponsor. “Let’s leave our smartphones in our pockets more often at the stadium and instead focus on what’s happening on the field and in the stands.”

These were statements delivered with unshakeable confidence in their righteousness, yet there is evidence to suggest this simply isn’t how some fans want to behave at stadiums.

Which begs the question: can, and should, professional sports teams get to dictate how their ticket-buying fans experience their games? It’s surely a question that’s crossed the mind of all the musicians who now perform to a sea of cell phones, their flashlights on, obscuring the faces in the crowd. Did their fans buy the right to experience the concert as they please? Or does this objectify the musicians and diminish the performance, somehow?

It goes back to the question of whether sport is entertainment, and whether its consumers get to sit back and let the proceedings and the attendant stimuli wash over them. Or whether they are something else entirely: active participants in the games they attend. If that is so, then fandom amounts to a parasocial relationship conferring membership to a community with attendant behavioral expectations.

What are the responsibilities of the ticketholder? Do teams get to purity-test their supporters? What do fans owe their teams? Is live soccer just content? A day out, not unlike going to the movies or a museum, where nobody expects total focus and for you to cheer on the thing you’re looking at? Is it heresy to even suggest this?

The latter tends to be the view, or at least the vibe, in most American sports leagues where fans are often less engaged, told by an announcer and a jumbo screen when and what to clap or stomp or chant. This has always contrasted with the feel of global football, where the folklore is usually organic, sparked and dictated by the fans themselves. It’s why all of those pre-game and half-time concerts at the World Cup final rankled, drowning out the thrum of the throaty Argentina fans.

It feels both instructive and fitting that this debate broke out at Dortmund. The Bundesliga’s rules on safeguarding fan majority ownership of very nearly every club have preserved the league as a kind of supporters’ paradise, with relatively cheap tickets and policies that put fans first. Dortmund, for their part, have been held up for years as a paradigm for their following – thus attracting the influencers, of course.

The latter will be dealt with, it seems. In an age when soccer clubs are essentially production houses who also field company teams, it always seemed inevitable that these interlopers would be expelled from the premises. The fans, however, are not so easily corrected on behavior their teams have deemed undesirable. And they will vote with their credit cards.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Cuts like a knife: Canadian rocker Bryan Adams trolls Trump with new song
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Musician wrote a ‘love letter’ to Canada with a new album – and some pointed commentary about the US president

Lake Ontario, the vast body of water that straddles the US-Canada border, has gone by many names over the centuries: Lac Saint-Louis, Lacus Ontarius, Skaniadorio, Cataraqui Lake. But one thing it will never be called, says Canadian rock star Bryan Adams, is Lake America.

In his new song Lake Ontario, Adams takes aim at the US president, Donald Trump, accusing him of “breaking the peace” between the people who live on the lake’s shores.

Trump signed an executive order in August directing US federal agencies to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”, echoing his earlier, widely mocked decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico “the Gulf of America”.

The move further escalated a feud with Canada that has strained the longstanding alliance between the two countries. Trump’s decision has largely been met with derision in Canada, with some pointing out that the province of Ontario is named after the lake, not the other way around. Adams’ lyrics emphasise the roots of the name:

double quotation markThe ‘lake of shining waters’ is what the Iroquois called her

Adams’s lyrics also suggest that Trump’s naming stunt was intended to deflect from the president’s other political problems, including the war in Iran and renewed scrutiny of the Jeffrey Epstein files.

The song is part of what Adams described in a recent interview as a broader “love letter” to Canada: a songwriting project that began with an invitation from a film company to write about the Maritimes provinces of Canada and has since morphed into the upcoming album How’s It Goin’.

“After finishing the first song, I moved on to that one, and then moved on to another one, and then started thinking maybe I should just carry on with my theme,” he said.

As well as homages to Canadian heroes, the album also includes 51st State, released on 1 July – Canada Day – as another repudiation of Trump, in this case his efforts to annex Canada.

“We weren’t sure how people were going to respond to it,” he said. “But we got a standing ovation every night for it. It made me think: perhaps, finally, the tide’s turning.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Brazil’s victory for the planet and democracy: seven lessons from Lula’s win
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Jonathan Watts
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
The trouncing of the far right provides a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and France

Thank you, Brazil, for demonstrating how the far right can be trounced while protection for the Amazon is strengthened. In a world where nature and democracy appeared to be bleeding out in tandem, voters and forest defenders in this global south powerhouse have shown it is possible to staunch the flow. This should provide much needed inspiration and, more practically, a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and France.

The astonishing comeback victory of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s presidential runoff against his extreme right challenger Flavío Bolsonaro has brought oceans of rapturous supporters on to the streets, while also thrilling conservationists, climate activists and social justice campaigners across the world.

Coming just weeks after the Lula administration announced a record fall in Amazon and Cerrado destruction, they hope Brazil can now go on to achieve its target of zero deforestation by 2030 and continue to support a global transition away from fossil fuels. That would provide a huge boost to flagging global efforts to stabilise the climate and protect degraded ecosystems. It would also set a remarkable example of leadership by the global south.

Big battles lie ahead. In the Amazon region itself, far-right members of Bolsonaro’s party have won the governorships of seven of the nine states and a large number of municipal mayorships. Brazil’s congress is now dominated by agribusiness and mining interests that have set the political agenda in recent years, and will push hard to allow more extractivist industries in indigenous lands, expand road-building, privatise rivers, weaken environmental protections and possibly attempt to impeach the president.

In the regional sphere, Lula, alone among the leaders of main South American nations in not aligning with Donald Trump’s so-called Shield of the Americas, will face pressure from Washington to channel critical minerals and other natural resources to the US, rather than selling to China or Europe, or leaving them in the ground. And, on the planetary level, Brazil faces the threat of accelerating global heating, which is pushing the Amazon ever closer to the point of no return.

So although Sunday’s result will hopefully provide a little breathing space for the Amazon and other crucially important biomes, the joy and hope that Brazil has gifted the world will quickly fade unless it inspires political change in other countries. In that sense, the biggest environmental impact of Lula’s victory may be the lessons it provides for campaigners elsewhere. Here are some initial takeaways:

1 Politics matter. There is no higher environmental priority than defeating the far right, which is a Trojan horse for extractivist – and often criminal – groups to capture states and erode protections for people, democracy and the environment. Just look at the 59.5% surge of Amazon deforestation under the 2019-2022 term of Jair Bolsonaro – the highest level of any four-year presidency in Brazil. Compare that with the 71.2% fall during the Lula administration. Over the past year, forest loss was 3,335 sq km, the lowest level since the start of satellite measurements in 1988. And Lula is not, by any means, an environmentalist. He has approved several destructive projects himself, but he is a people person who listens to the voice of social movements.

2 Don’t give up. Lula was largely written off by the markets and some polls after his first-round defeat. No first-round loser had ever previously come back to win the runoff. Lula was able to do so by securing an extra 10m votes over three weeks. The energy for this came from the streets and the forests. Social movements organised giant rallies in cities. In the Amazon, indigenous, riverine and quilombola groups travelled by hours – sometimes days – to reach polling stations by boats or buses.

3 Mobilise a campaign army. The first round of Lula’s campaign had been stodgy, old-fashioned and defensive – three traits that are also often applicable to environmental campaigns. This was transformed during the runoff, when federal deputy André Janones launched a “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp group that used humorous memes, live streams and algorithmic outreach to seize digital territory that had long been dominated by the right. By voting day, this army had 10m “soldiers”, about 8% of the electorate. Volunteers devoted hours posting stories and spreading messages across social media, speeding up the Lula campaign’s response time and emotional impact. Everyone was instructed not to share or respond to posts by the opposition camp.

4 Go on the offensive against US tech giants. Lula’s campaign accused Meta, which runs the Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram social media platforms, of political favouritism towards Bolsonaro in its algorithms and AI tools. Meta denied bias but acknowledged technical failures. Brazil’s electoral court ordered corrective action. Among the most popular chants of Lula supporters was “Hey Meta, vai tomar no cu!” (Hey Meta, take it up the arse!). Many on the left have blamed US social media platforms for spreading rightwing disinformation and fearmongering, causing recent electoral defeats in Colombia, Chile and Peru. Lula made clear that would not be allowed in Brazil: “We had to overcome foreign interference through digital platforms, which we will have to regulate. We cannot have a monstrously large corporation earning millions and billions paying no taxes to this country and trying to steer our election results.”

5 Reclaim the flag. Brazil’s green, yellow and blue national colours had been associated with Bolsonaro’s movement in previous elections. This time, Lula seized it back by posing in a national football team strip while his “army” launched a campaign called “The green and yellow is ours”. Before voting day, millions of people across Brazil and the world – from Indigenous leaders in the Amazon to Hollywood celebrities and European football stars – flooded social networks with images of themselves in Brazil colours making an L (for Lula) sign with their thumb and little finger extended.

6 Increase social spending. Amazon protection may have galvanised conservationists, but the far greater motivations for many Lula voters were record low unemployment, robust wage growth, a 15% increase in “bolsa familia” poverty relief payments and a promise to raise the minimum wage. The importance of combining social justice with climate and nature action is widely recognised by Brazilian environmental groups. Without it, elections are lost and protests can erupt in the streets – as the world learned from France during the violent gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrations of 2018.

7 Defend sovereignty, democracy and sustainability. Lula and his army called out the interlinked threats posed by the Bolsonaro family’s fealty to Donald Trump (now doubly confirmed by Flávio’s post-election flight to the US). They highlighted the interlinked threats posed by the obsequience to Trump, Bolsonaro’s desire to change the constitution and his promise to open up exploration of the Amazon and other biomes. This reflects a global phenomenon. Now that seven of the planetary boundaries essential for the flourishing of life have been breached, more and more people are affected by business activities that make the situation worse by destabilising the climate, damaging ecosystems and polluting the air, soil and rivers. This makes it harder for extractive companies to secure a social mandate so they become more inclined to either break the law or support extreme politics that override democracy.

The former environment minister Marina Silva pulled these threads together during the victory celebrations, saying Brazil had come together against these threats: “Long live the people who emerged from every corner of Brazil to sow hope for a future that is socially just, sovereign, democratic and sustainable.”

Brazil has given the world a remarkable example of hope through action. Now it needs others to follow.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Seven oil tankers carrying 288,000 tonnes of Russian diesel sail towards US
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Tankers, tracked by Greenpeace, are first phase of Trump-Putin deal – but there is uncertainty over whether they will unload

Seven oil tankers carrying an estimated 288,000 tonnes of Russian diesel are now sailing towards the US, though it is uncertain if the vessels will be able to unload amid a political row about the legality of the shipments.

The transport, tracked by the pressure group Greenpeace, is the first phase of a contentious supply deal negotiated between presidents Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin earlier this month, reversing years of sanctions on Russia oil.

Previous reports had counted three tankers that had departed Russian oil terminals in the Baltic Sea, but using a range of sources, including shipping tracking websites, Greenpeace believes its monitoring exercise is the most complete yet.

Shaun Burnie, an energy specialist with Greenpeace Ukraine, argued that now the location of the tankers could be plotted on a map, the shipments should be halted by Congress or local authorities in the US.

“Instead of rewarding Russia for its vile war against Ukraine, there needs to be more punitive sanctions against Russia,” he said. “These shipments can be stopped”.

One of the seven tankers, Taurus, is relatively close to the US, but at the time the map was first published, five of the others were close to the UK, and three were sailing through or into the English Channel.

In Ukraine, 14 people were reported killed on Thursday morning when a Russian drone struck a crowded train platform in the central city of Dnipro. Five others were reported killed in daytime strikes in two other cities, Chernihiv and Kremenchuk.

Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway company, said a high speed jet-powered drone had struck as a commuter train was preparing to depart Dnipro’s main station. Bodies lay scattered after the relatively unusual daytime attack, which took place at around 11am.

Putin agreed to supply the US with 1.8m tonnes of diesel in a surprise deal announced on 9 October, starting with 300,000 tonnes immediately. Trump announced a six-month waiver on existing sanctions to allow the shipments to proceed.

Russia had been hit by waves of economic sanctions from the US, EU, UK and other leading western economies since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. But this autumn, Trump has altered course and tried to work more closely with Putin, even though Russia has not stopped attacking its neighbour.
