Earlier this week, a group of US lawmakers, led by a handful of Democratic senators, warned banks and port authorities that they could face congressional investigations and other legal action if they handled the Russian diesel.

Mikie Sherrill, the Democratic governor of New Jersey, said she was looking at how to prevent the diesel from being unloaded, if an attempt was made to do so in her state. She described the deal as “corrupt and illegal”.

There have been reports that the White House has been trying to encourage US firms to take the oil, though it is not clear buyers are forthcoming, given the legal risks so close to next Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Trump’s popularity has waned as fuel prices in the US have soared since he attacked Iran in the spring. Polling suggests a high likelihood that control of the House of Representatives could pass to the Democrats in the elections, while the battle over the Senate is considered too close to call.

The US president had argued that the Russia deal would help lower diesel prices, though the price per gallon has risen from $6.28 at the time the agreement was announced to $6.33, according to the American Automobile Association.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, denounced the agreement because the money raised would help the Kremlin fund the ongoing war. “Backroom deals” gave Putin more chances on the battlefield, he said.

The Kremlin has been trying to keep information about the latest oil exports secret. A presidential decree from the end of September restricted the publication of information about oil exports in an effort to evade international sanctions.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Dream serve up lunchtime rout of Valkyries to force historic WNBA finals Game 7
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Bryan Armen Graham
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The Atlanta Dream had no intention of letting a matinee become their curtain call.

Facing elimination at a lunchtime tipoff, the Dream overwhelmed the Golden State Valkyries 80-69 on Thursday afternoon to force a decisive seventh game in the WNBA finals, rediscovering their offensive touch just as their championship hopes were threatening to slip away.

Atlanta buried six three-pointers and shot 73.3% from the floor in a blistering opening quarter at State Farm Arena, built a lead that ballooned to 25 points before half-time and held on to send a series that had swung sharply towards Golden State back to San Francisco for Saturday night’s winner-take-all finale. Both teams are seeking their first championship.

In the US, the series will air on NBC, USA Network and CNBC, with all games streaming on Peacock. In the UK, it will be carried by Sky Sports. In Australia, fans can watch through WNBA League Pass, with selected coverage also available through ESPN.

Allisha Gray scored a team-high 23 points including five threes, Rhyne Howard added 21 while Angel Reese notched her fourth double-double of the series with 15 points and 14 rebounds to go with six assists.

Gabby Williams finished with a game-high 26 points for the Valkyries after being held to four in the first half. Tiffany Hayes added 15, but Golden State shot just 31.4% from the field and 25.9% from three-point range. Veronica Burton endured a particularly difficult afternoon, making just two of her 13 shots from the floor and missing all six three-point attempts.

“It’s do or die. It’s win or go home,” Howard said. “I knew that coming in, we had to be aggressive from the jump, and that starts with me. You know, I have to be a good leader for this team. I have to set the tone early, and I feel like that’s what I did today.”

The Dream had managed only 62 and 55 points in back-to-back defeats that erased their 2-1 series lead. On Thursday, they scored 32 in the first quarter alone, making 11 of their first 15 shots and moving the ball with a fluidity Golden State had largely disrupted over the previous two contests.

Golden State cut the deficit to 13 early in the fourth quarter, but Gray hit a three-pointer and Reese followed with another to restore a 74-55 advantage with 5:43 remaining.

The Valkyries made one final push, getting as close as 77-69 on Williams’s three-point play with 75 seconds left, which founded out Howard. But Gray answered with her fifth three-pointer off a Reese assist to remove all doubt with 56 seconds left.

“We needed the opportunity. That’s all we needed, and we maximized it today,” Reese said. “I’m just really proud of this group. The job is not done, and I’m looking forward to it. One more. Job’s not done.”

The performance came amid the controversy surrounding a 12.30pm tipoff, a scheduling compromise that placed the biggest home game of Atlanta’s season in the middle of a work day. The Dream nevertheless announced a sellout crowd of 17,099 for Thursday’s game.

“I had no doubt that they would show up,” Howard said. “Everybody kept asking me about 12:30, 12:30.”

She added: “Now they can leave with a better taste in their mouths, go get the bottomless mimosas, you know, enjoy the rest of the day, ’cause I know nobody’s going back to work.”

For Golden State, the start was equivalent to 9.30am on their normal California clock, although Nakase dismissed concerns beforehand.

“We prepared for this,” she said. “We knew when they announced it. We’re good.”

The WNBA adopted a best-of-seven finals last year, only for the series to end in a four-game sweep. This time, the extended format has delivered the ultimate decider.

Six games have left nothing to separate the Dream and Valkyries. On Halloween night, the first Game 7 in WNBA history will decide it all.

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: The best water filter pitchers and dispensers in the US, tested in a lab – and none are Brita
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Mikita Hill-Cashaw, Rachel Sherman, Alessandra Mora and Jonathan Deutsch
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
If your Brita is looking tired or your water tastes icky, consider one of these well-tested (and reviewed) options

We have all had the experience of drinking water and thinking, “Oh ... that’s not right.” A water filter can help with the taste and much more – and a better understanding of them can help you pick the right one for daily use.

Water quality can be affected by plumbing, geography, mineral buildup, weather events and emerging contaminants such as Pfas, pharmaceuticals and disinfection byproducts. Many filters on the market claim to remove impurities, but that doesn’t mean the technology is reducing the contaminants that you should be most concerned about.

We decided to put these claims to the test. We tested nine different water filters for taste and ease of use, then third-party tested them in labs to evaluate their efficacy. Fascinatingly, the household-favorite Brita was beaten by many other brands.

We are students, professors and researchers from the Drexel Food Lab at Drexel University, a food product design and culinary innovation lab. For the Filter US, we have previously tested the best air fryers, the best nontoxic cookware and the best instant coffee, and answered common questions about food safety.

We talked to public health experts and water quality engineers about how to choose the best water filter systems. After setting up each individual water filter using manufacturer instructions, we organized a blind taste test.

Between 67 testers, we managed three rounds of tests in an elimination method. Winners move on; losers are left behind. We tested nine separate filters against a control sample from our lab’s kitchen sink. Each filter was assigned a randomized number, and participants were asked to smell and taste each sample in a random order

Last, we sent samples to third-party labs facilitated by the water testing company Tap Score, using their Essential City Water Test and VOC Water Test, which were tested in labs in Pennsylvania and New Jersey, respectively. VOC stands for volatile organic compounds, or the toxic chemicals you don’t want in your water.

We tested these water filters in our food lab in a commercial building on Drexel’s campus and our plumbing and water system is different from a residential setup. After sending our water to Tap Score for testing, we learned that our regular tap water has high quantities of chloroform and other water disinfection byproducts. These contaminants are a result of the chlorination process used to reduce bacteria in our drinking water. Your residential water should not be testing nearly as high as ours, but it does make you think about water quality for those who work from an office or industrial building.

Water filter with longest lifeAlexaPure Pro Water Filtration System (2.5 Gallon)

Why we love it: This filter produced some of the best-tasting water, according to testers. The Larq uses a two-step filtration with a carbon-based filter and a secondary UV light to kill bacteria. Its easy setup included washing all parts (minus the UV-C wand), soaking the filter for 10 minutes, then flushing the first batch of water.

As a “smart” filter, it offers the Larq app to track your hydration needs and filter replacement times. We asked a student to take the filter home and report back about her experience after using it for about two weeks. Tester Dr DeAndra Forde especially liked how the Larq app connected with Apple Health to “assess based on [data] how much water or liquid intake I need daily”.

It’s a shame that … It is the most expensive pitcher we tested, with a base price of $168 plus $32.50 for replacements every two months. At that price point, you could spend a bit more and go for the brand’s Under Sink Filter at $199. This attaches to the pipe under your sink (no plumber required), filtering the water before it comes out of the faucet, and can filter 1,453 gallons of water over six months. The PureVis pitcher can only filter 180 gallons in the same time and will require three replacement filters to do so.

Why we love it: Culligan’s pitcher offering is simple enough to use. This slender seven-cup pitcher is designed with an ergonomic handle for easy pouring and could fit in a refrigerator door. At $24.99, it’s a few dollars more than a comparable Brita, but you get much more contaminant reduction, including lead and Pfas.

The standout feature is the integrated total dissolved solids (TDS) reader. The TDS puts a visual on when you need to replace the filter. The tool is actively measuring TDS with every refill. When the number reads higher than six, that’s your cue to replace. A little over half of the respondents said there was no aftertaste, but written feedback was mixed. While some people said this pitcher was “very clean tasting”, one more ambiguous (and poetic response) was that it reminded them of a “3am random wake up in the winter”.

It’s a shame that … The filters cost almost as much as the pitcher itself, but we appreciate its high quality for the overall low price.

Why we love it: This countertop filter system was easily integrated into our lab setup. With a detachable water chamber, it allows for rapidly filtered water at the press of a button. Unlike other systems, where you have to wait for the water to drip through, the Aquasana filters water as it pours, so you can quench your thirst immediately.

The chamber’s 64oz capacity is enough to fill the alleged day’s worth of water for one person or two emotional support water bottles. It does require a plug, so it has to live on the counter, and at about 10x8in and a foot tall, it may not work if you have a small kitchen area at home.

It’s a shame that … Since the filter is on the counter, the water isn’t chilled. If you prefer cold water, this may not be the best option for you.

Why we love it: The Culligan MaxClear has a unique stainless steel aesthetic, so it will look beautiful anywhere, indoors or out. And 11 out of 15 respondents agreed there is no aftertaste and one commented on how “smooth” the taste was.

The MaxClear uses a dual carbon and ceramic filter to reduce microplastics, total Pfas, lead and 15 other contaminants. It comes with one filter that you insert into the top section, and for the Scout size you have the option of using two filters, which allows them to last longer together. Unlike traditional water pitchers, this is a multigallon gravity filter system (using natural gravity to pull water down through a filter). If you’ve had your eye on the famous Berkey, but are not ready to drop the cash, this could be the pick for you. It’s a shame that … This system has a slow drip (6.4oz per minute after setup) and may take more than 24 hours to get the three discard batches of water through during setup. So, don’t do your first setup at the campgrounds, or you may not have water for a few days! Finally, this is not meant to be used “adventurously” with untreated water. The best use case is a campground with a plumbing system.

Also made from durable stainless steel, AlexaPure has the same large capacity as the MaxClear, but claims to filter up to 200 gallons with each replacement – four times more than the MaxClear and much more than any other filter on this list. While both gravity systems did have similar lab reports, the AlexaPure ended up ranking in the middle among the nine filters based on the Tap Score reports (84 out of 99). The real ding is the overall cost. The initial system comes in at a whopping $279.95 including one filter, and each filter replacement is $119.95 (though, again, 200 gallons).

Tap Score generates a score from 1 to 99 for every water sample based on a proprietary algorithm. It takes into account health factors such as the presence of arsenic, aesthetic factors like smell, and even factors that could affect your plumbing, including pH. The health factors are weighed the highest.

In order to understand water filters and their technology we dived into the research and spoke with our colleague Nicole Weber, MPH, an affiliate faculty member at Dornsife School of Public Health at Drexel University and a certified health education specialist. When asked about common misconceptions regarding water filters, Weber had two main takeaways. The first, the misconception that filters can remove everything. She said: “Filters are specific, so it’s important to choose the right one for your particular water quality issues.” Jessica Goddard, PhD and chief science officer, and John Pujol, CEO and water quality engineer for Tap Score, a company that connects people to labs for third-party water testing, agree. Testing your water before buying a filter ensures you pick the right filter, which means you get the right filter for your needs, they said.

You should still review your annual water utility report to find out which contaminants (and levels) are present in your water before buying a filter. “[When] you know your risks, you can identify which water treatment or filtration solution would be most appropriate,” said Weber. Her second point emphasized the importance of maintenance for the filter. “Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions for cleaning, changing and maintaining the filter,” she said, “otherwise you can introduce bacteria or mold in this process, potentially making your water less safe.”

Learning about water filter technology can be eye-opening and seriously overwhelming. The main takeaway is that different technologies have different efficacy on different contaminants. For example, the tap water in our lab tested for high levels of nickel, copper, and magnesium. A carbon block filter is effective for reducing nickel, but not for the other two. A more effective filter would be reverse osmosis or an ion exchange. But these technologies can vary in price, up-front and in maintenance costs. To pick the best option, consider your budget and who will take responsibility for cleaning and changing the filters.

Every filter that makes a claim to reduce a contaminant should have the certification to match. Certifications aren’t everything, but it is the best way to ensure that the filter targets your contaminants of concern. It is best to go directly to the producer’s website to review their certification documents.

If we didn’t say it enough already – proper maintenance is important to ensure the filter keeps working over time. Some of our filters said to boil weekly; others had no cleaning instructions. All the filters had different guidance for replacement, and you’ll typically see two suggestions: a set timeline or water usage. Consider your household size, your municipal water report results and how much water is consumed daily. With a little calculation, you will be able to determine how often to replace your filter and how many filters are needed for a year. (Tip: if you buy from companies directly, they often have discounts for bulk or subscription orders.) If you know you won’t replace the filters, save your money and keep drinking tap.

Yes. Tap Score offers a variety of tests for different needs. After you buy the test online, in the mail you’ll get a sample tube and details about how to take your sample. You will need to ship it on the same day you take the sample, so plan to take it early in the day so you have time to drop it in the mail.

Tap Score also has a lot of educational resources about water, water testing, regulation and how to read your water report. On their website they have examples of water test reports so you can click through the resources offered for a sample test. They have even conducted peer-reviewed research about bottled water toxicity compared with average residential tap water. In case you’re tired of lugging cases of water on a weekly basis, you might check it out.

MaxClear Scout 2.25-Gallon Gravity Countertop System with Gravity Water Filter
