Thirty-three months after it was announced, the grime legend’s new album is coming out. He explains how skinheads, fatherhood and rap history came to bear on its socially conscious contents

‘I can’t be perfect,” Skepta says, pulling a black Arc’tyrex beanie down over a furrowed brow with both hands. “But I can be conscious.” The self-proclaimed king of grime has always been a serious person, wary of fools and time-wasters. Focus is important to him, perhaps because he’s often multitasking: balancing his music career, his fashion label Mains, film-making and acting (his debut short, Tribal Mark, came out in 2024), his Big Smoke festival and a house music project, Más Tiempo.

He coordinates them all from the scruffy but functional studio in London’s West End where we meet. At one point, he picks up a Rubik’s Cube from the cluttered coffee table, and, over the course of five minutes of conversation, solves it. “This album has been winding me up,” he admits, referring to The Fork and Knife, which is out next week, 33 months after it was first announced. “But I think I’ve actually made something here that is what the people want from me.”

Now 44, Skepta isn’t just grappling with the rap elder’s struggle of how to stay relevant in middle age, but also the impact his words carry, and his responsibility to say and do the right thing. He seems newly attached to the idea of being a “conscious” rapper, and more mindful than ever of his past missteps. The mums of his children’s friends are going to hear what he’s spitting about on the radio while they’re all doing the school run, he says – there’s no room for loose talk any more.

“Don’t get me wrong,” he says. “I’m human. I’ve made ignorant songs, I’ve made ‘turn up’ [ie party] songs, there’s still that side of me. I’m still Joseph from Tottenham. But I’m growing and I’m learning.”

In person, Skepta is wary about not being seen as preachy, a stance bolstered by his experience of talking about politics to his two young children. “They don’t like getting into the isms and schisms,” he says. “That’s some adult shit to them.”

The task for the new album, then, is to “deliver these conscious messages, but still have a vibe”, he says. “I’m like, damn Skep, you’ve used your voice for grime, but what’s happened over time is your voice has become something that people believe in and follow – so what are you gonna use your voice for now?”

He chose his recent single Innocent Smile, featuring a guest spot from Suggs and hectic breakbeats from Chase and Status, to answer that question. “Don’t ask what happened to my innocent smile,” he spits. “Ain’t no love for an immigrant child.” In the first verse alone he references lyrics by Oasis, J Hus and Mobb Deep, criticises MPs’ scapegoating of immigrants, and celebrates his parents’ resilience, and the journey they made “from Nigeria to Meridian” – Meridian Walk, the Tottenham estate he grew up on.

The choice of Suggs for this grandstanding defence of multicultural Britain is no accident. Skepta pulls his collar aside to show me the two-tone neck tattoo he got 14 years ago. “I’ve always loved that movement,” he says. “That was the time when my dad came to the UK, and he was a DJ, so he was always playing ska tunes in the house. I’d see skinheads in my house when I was younger. My dad would come home with his friends from work and start playing his vinyl, and my mum would have her white friends round, Auntie Elaine and Auntie Susannah.”

Skepta sees multiculturalism not as an abstract idea, but as something that’s “second nature to me”. It is, he says, at the root of what he does – ska couldn’t have come from anywhere else but the UK’s unique cultural mix, and nor could grime. “A British outlook is a universal one,” he says. “All our kids are mixes of different cultures. Even my parents: my mum’s Igbo, my dad’s Yoruba, and in Nigeria, they’re not supposed to mix, they’ve had wars together. But they came to England, met each other, fell in love and had me. This whole ignorance towards immigration at the moment is horrible. It’s not British. We know who it is when we open the door to the Uber: it’s just people here trying to work.”

Skepta’s ongoing reckoning with his personal responsibility is why it has taken him seven years to make his sixth album, and it’s the source of his pride in it, he says. The Fork and Knife, his first full solo record since 2019’s Ignorance Is Bliss, was announced on 1 January 2024, and now it’s complete, it’s not a full-on conscious manifesto but features a fuller sound enhanced by the wisdom of age.

Its 15 tracks range from the smooth Chippie, a zouk-flavoured R&B collaboration with French-Malian star Aya Nakamura, to Belly, a fierce eight minutes of grime packed with guest verses from a younger generation of MCs: north-west Londoner Kibo in particular shines through. The new stars are given the opening verses, and, in a clever nod to their roles as elder statesmen, the closing verses by Boy Better Know members JME, Frisco and Skepta himself balance new lyrics with classic old-school punchlines.

For two decades, Skepta’s rap style has prioritised sounding clear and direct on the mic over sound effects, gimmicks or skippy flows, but the decades’ battle scars have leant his distinctive voice the authority of experience. The rap swagger is still there on The Fork and Knife, but the sheer bravado of his earlier material (his 2007 debut was called Greatest Hits) has been tempered with epiphanies and reflection. Perhaps the clearest window into his state of mind is the poignant Revenge, a memoir of his mid-career missteps, his subsequent redemption and his resilience after 20 years in music. “It was 2008 when I lost my way … I fucked up the greatest run,” he spits, referring to a time when his reputation as king of the grime underground was clouded by a string of ill-advised mainstream dalliances.

Skepta is the rare artist who acknowledges his mistakes head-on: his infamous pornographic music video for 2011 single All Over the House, the playground transphobia of 2009’s Disguise, wearing Gucci and Louis Vuitton in a way that was not him, doing the Rolex Sweep with Timmy Mallet. As a result, these gaffes have become understood as part of his redemption arc – the awards, magazine covers and sold-out shows that have flooded his way since 2016’s Mercury-winning Konnichiwa and its hit singles That’s Not Me and Shutdown.

He apologised again in January 2024, when the artwork for the new album’s first single, Gas Me Up (Diligent), showed a group of men with shaved heads, one of whom had “GAS ME UP” (slang for “hype me up”) tattooed on his skull. There was consternation over its – inadvertent – evocation of the Holocaust; Skepta had intended to draw on the same interest in 1980s British youth culture as the Suggs collaboration. At the time, Skepta vowed “to be more mindful going forward”.

Today, he says the issue left him frustrated. He was trying to celebrate the unity found through youth culture that existed in his childhood, in spite of the racism in wider society; his dad would DJ at east London parties “where Black people and skinheads used to link up”. While he acknowledges the misinterpretation, his message hasn’t changed at all: “We’re still definitely British, definitely multicultural, definitely two-tone. This is an important part of my British story.”

Also in 2024, he apologised for the contract he signed with Puma in 2022. The sports brand has been on the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions campaign’s boycott list for their sponsorship of the Israel Football Association (IFA). Challenged by fans on social media, Skepta noted that Puma would soon be severing their ties with the IFA, and said that in hindsight he wished he had stayed independent. “I’ve realised it’s a lot more than reading the small print,” he wrote at the time. “[You’ve] gotta do your due diligence … I am forever a student.”

“I’m from Nigeria, innit,” he replies when I ask about the Puma spat. “I’ve spoken about injustices in Nigeria all my career; we see injustices in Sudan, Congo, Palestine, everywhere. And I’m not at the point where I’m doing it for money – I don’t think I’ve ever done it for money.”

During the album’s long gestation, Skepta has been thinking a lot about rap’s history, as well as his own. “People like Run-DMC, Public Enemy and Tupac made their rap at a point when Black people were looked at as degenerate, and they made it sophisticated, they had messages,” he says. “But over the years, we’ve been paid – and bought – to start talking about twerking and drugs and foolishness.”

Skepta’s engagement with public criticism is perhaps one reason he has more than once managed to recoup lost credibility, and moved forwards where so many of his peers have fallen by the wayside. The other is his unusual self-belief and persistence. It is 19 years since I first interviewed Skepta. On that occasion I arranged the interview by messaging him on MySpace – a few years into underground stardom, he still didn’t have a manager, a PR or a record label – and spoke to him at 2am after he played a small gig in east London. It was 2007, and after a few years of frantic energy, almost everyone had given up on grime. That night, Skepta told me he had had major label prospects, and a collaboration with Mike Skinner, dangled and then withdrawn again.

The Black British club scene was moving rapidly on to funky house, dubstep was beginning to take the international language of “wub-wub” bass to global dancefloors, and Dizzee Rascal had just met Calvin Harris. The received wisdom went that the arcane style and bright flame of grime was quickly burning out.

Implausibly, pigheadedly, Skepta disagreed. “I believe that we don’t have to change grime to make anyone buy it,” he told me then. “People are running away from grime thinking it’s not working, but they’re sellouts, man. That’s why Boy Better Know is easily going to be the best thing in grime.”

Nineteen years later, this August, he played to vast, raucous crowds on the main stages of the Reading and Leeds festivals. I tell him that the same festival I’d attended as a teenager in the 90s was so guitar-heavy that it would have had at most two rap acts on the bill each year. He smiles. “That’s the journey we’ve been on.”

Even back in 2007, when Skepta was one of the last men standing in a flailing grime scene being shut out by the British music industry and shut down by the Metropolitan police’s notorious risk-assessment Form 696, he told me he wanted to write and perform for as wide an audience as possible. In the mid-2020s, pulling in primetime audiences at Glastonbury, that hasn’t changed.

“I love the way rock bands can write,” he says. “I love the way they can write songs that are almost like nursery rhymes, but they’re so impactful, and they mean so much.” He references the unlikely trio of Jamiroquai, the Bee Gees and Oasis. “My aim every time I go into the studio is to make songs that are as big as Wonderwall. I even think about things that Shakespeare wrote that we still use now. It’s always been my mission to make classics.”

He recalls touring Europe playing clubs in the late 2000s with dubstep DJs Plastician, Mala, Benga and Skream, when something clicked. At a show in Prague, Skepta found that the London slang and references that were getting acclaim back home weren’t “really hitting. It wasn’t making sense.” It was time to write for an audience beyond the world he grew up in. “If you want to be a world rapper, you need to think of words that the world can say with you, and rap in a way that the world can sing with you,” he says. “Maybe I’ll get Liam Gallagher to come in on the next album and play some maracas.”

The fact this is a plausible option is not lost on an MC who grew up in Tottenham. “I’ll never forget the junior that used to sit on the wall in Meridian, swinging his legs,” he says, as if reminding himself as much as anyone else. “I won’t do him dirty.”

Not long ago Skepta moved out of London for a quieter life, and recently took his son back to the estate where he grew up. “Going to Tottenham brings up a lot of trauma,” he says. “If I ever go to Tottenham, it’s generally to process some trauma.” He wanted his son to understand his dad’s humble origins and the distance between their childhoods: what it means to have a garden, a nice house, financial stability, the humble immigrant dream.

What was his son’s response, I ask. “He didn’t give a fuck,” says Skepta immediately, and laughs harder than he has all afternoon. “He’s only four! He’s looking at me like, ‘Dad, can we go and get ice-cream?’” It’s been a long road from there to here, says Skepta. “But I knew it was only a matter of time until people were singing along with me.”

Bruno Fernandes owes Manchester United a performance, Mathys Tel has arrived at Spurs and Liverpool are improving

Michael Carrick and Bruno Fernandes held clear-the-air talks this week. Fernandes was an unused substitute against Bournemouth after criticising Carrick’s tactics during the Champions League defeat by Como but it seems the situation has been resolved – for now. Dropping Fernandes did not do United any good against Bournemouth, who ran riot at Old Trafford, and the captain is expected to return to the starting lineup for the trip to Chelsea. If that happens, he owes Carrick a performance. Fernandes has been poor this season and it is time he did his talking on the pitch. Jacob Steinberg

Since Manchester City were found guilty of serially breaching Premier League financial rules, Enzo Maresca’s team have won four games (including Wednesday’s Carabao Cup shootout victory over Brighton) and lost two. Saturday’s 2-1 reverse at Aston Villa was their first Premier League defeat and should another follow in their rematch with the Seagulls, the manager may start to fear the guilty verdict and possible sanction (demotion to the Championship, for example) may become a distraction to his players. There is a precedent for City initially responding well to adversity, before it then affected results. After Rodri sustained a serious knee injury against Arsenal in September 2024, Pep Guardiola’s team went undefeated in seven matches, winning six. But then the wheels clattered off, with one victory and 10 defeats in the next 13. Jamie Jackson

The last time north-east opposition visited the CBS Arena, Frank Lampard’s side had no trouble finding the net, but their four goals against Newcastle on 12 October make up two-thirds of their league total for the season. Perhaps the most creative player at the club has spent most of this campaign watching from the bench. Gustavo Hamer, who created 12 goals for his Sheffield United teammates in the Championship last season, has asked to play for the under-21s to get his minutes up. “Myself and the staff have been really, really impressed by his approach, his training, his ethic,” Lampard said before Hamer came on as an 86th-minute substitute in last weekend’s defeat by Fulham. Will he get more than four minutes off the bench against the only team beneath Coventry in the table? Billy Munday

Beating Milan and then Manchester United made for a halcyon week in Bournemouth’s history. Winning at Old Trafford and defeating Aston Villa in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday all followed Marco Rose’s first Premier League win, against Sunderland on 18 October, which came as a great relief. The project is back on course. Eli Junior Kroupi, a late substitute last Sunday, has returned to the squad. In the Frenchman’s absence Evanilson has been on his best run of form since joining the club. He has four goals from five matches, and a tight-angled finish to make it 3-0 at United belied his reputation as a player who could score more. The Brazilian is a capable line leader, with Kroupi able to work the space his partner’s tireless running creates. When Sturm Graz were defeated in the Europa League, Evanilson served as support striker for the raw Álvaro Rodríguez. There is little starry about a club-record signing whose work ethic has been important to Rose’s early weeks in charge. John Brewin

Brentford’s early-season charge has slowed. No wins from their last three, and a disappointing draw at Hull last week – although only Liverpool have beaten Keith Andrews’ team this season in the Premier League. A 1-1 draw at Ipswich last Friday heightened frustrations at Nottingham Forest, Liam Delap’s scoring touch continuing to desert him, an unmarked Murillo missing a free header the best of a host of unconverted chances. The better opportunities tended to arrive from the flanks, with Daniel Muñoz overlapping from wing-back as the supplier for Neco Williams’ goal. After a decent start to the season for Morgan Gibbs-White in terms of chance creation, he was crowded out by Ipswich’s packed midfield. Oliver Glasner’s formation, founded on a defensive trio, seeks to bring the best from playmakers and ball-players. It brought results from Eberechi Eze and Adam Wharton at Crystal Palace but Gibbs-White and Forest are yet to prosper. Better finishing would certainly help a team stuck in the bottom three. JB

Two promoted teams and two positive managers meet at MKM Stadium on Saturday. “There will be ups and downs, this is normal,” said Hull’s Sergej Jakirovic last week. “We showed already that we can compete.” Ipswich’s Gary O’Neil is similarly enthusiastic: “They’re an incredible group,” he said of his players this week. “We’re not carrying anybody in that, there’s no one getting dragged along by this group.” Both teams kick off in mid-table, though with the awareness of the importance of defeating an opponent with similar ambitions. While other Championship graduates have been too readily accepting of their fate, both have grasped the nettle and shown off their survival instincts. Manchester City’s potential punishment could create an opportunity, leaving just two relegation spots to avoid. Hull’s initial hot streak has cooled, though last week’s draw with Brentford was useful. Against Forest, Ipswich made up for their lack of fluidity by showing the staying power to claim a point. JB

Despite landing in the Premier League in January last year, Mathys Tel’s goal against Chelsea felt like an arrival of sorts. The 21-year-old was highly rated as a youngster at Bayern Munich but has found the net just seven times in 50 league games since joining Spurs, initially on loan. Against Chelsea he picked the ball up in his own half and drove forwards 40 yards before finding the bottom corner from the edge of the box. Spurs fans will want more from Tel who, unlike many of his teammates, is rarely injured. “I think I can still do better,” he said after the 2-0 win at Chelsea that made it two on the spin for Spurs. “I can always do better. I need to work, work, work, work.” Crystal Palace come off the back of victory over Fulham in the Carabao Cup – the head coach, Pierre Sage, has been backed by the board after a tricky spell in the league. BM

Álvaro Arbeloa is at last getting somewhere with Fulham. After going without a win in his first six league matches, the Spaniard has collected six points against Hull and Coventry. Goals remain in short supply, though, and the form of the £40m striker Gonzalo García – seven games without scoring – is concerning. Arbeloa’s past relationship with García at Real Madrid is not proving as beneficial as Unai Emery’s knowledge of Nicolas Jackson’s game. That pair worked together at Villarreal, where Emery gave Jackson his La Liga debut. “Unai taught me everything about football,” Jackson said on signing from Chelsea in the summer. With four goals in five Premier League games, including a double against Manchester City last Saturday, Jackson is one of the form strikers in the country. “He was shooting a lot of balls over the crossbar,” Emery said. “Now he’s getting better.” BM

“Let’s try to finish this four-in-a-row in the best way,” said Andoni Iraola on Wednesday as thoughts turned from the Carabao Cup penalty shootout win over Chelsea to Arsenal’s impending visit to Anfield. Three consecutive home wins in different competitions, and in quick succession, have helped build momentum at Liverpool, although seven wins from the last eight (including Chelsea) shows the process had already begun. Iraola has handled his first intensive run of Champions League, Premier League and Carabao Cup fixtures expertly, rotating in every game while continuing to produce results. Noticeably, there has been no drop-off in Liverpool’s physical intensity either. The manner of Arsenal’s title triumph last season – and the general shift towards more aggressive, urgent football in the Premier League – were factors in Liverpool’s decision to change head coaches in the summer, and the results are paying off quickly. Iraola will be facing questions about a title challenge should four-in-a-row finish as he hopes on Sunday. Andy Hunter

David Moyes described it as “out of this world”, Alan Shearer talked about a world-class intervention, and Jordan Pickford agreed it ranked as “up there with my very best.” Rewind to March and Everton are beating Newcastle 3-2 on Tyneside when, in the 94th minute, Sandro Tonali unleashes a vicious and technically perfect volley. To the astonishment of everyone inside St James’ Park, Everton’s goalkeeper throws out his right hand and tips the ball over the crossbar. Pickford’s teammate Jarrad Branthwaite said it was “the best save I’ve ever seen” and Moyes can only hope his England goalkeeper proves in similarly defiant mood at a time when his international place is under a little pressure from the Leeds goalkeeper, James Trafford. Not that Pickford will lack inspiration; the lifelong Sunderland fan always enjoys frustrating Newcastle, as he did again in Thursday’s Carabao Cup victory. Matthias Jaissle’s team, and their midfield, are still adapting to life after Tonali and face a testing rematch at St James’ Park on Monday. Louise Taylor

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Could 2026 be the year that democracy fought back? | David Van Reybrouck
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: David Van Reybrouck
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Elections are never enough by themselves, but the stunning results from Serbia, Brazil and Hungary have given us hope in dark times

It is undoubtedly too early to declare victory, but the recent electoral defeats of Viktor Orbán, Aleksandar Vučić and Flávio Bolsonaro make me wonder: is 2026 turning out to be the year democracy slowly, but surely, fought back?

Even in Israel, prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s reigning bloc lost its parliamentary majority and saw the spectacular rise of Arab parties. Though the opposition may not be able to form a government yet, it does have the larger parliamentary bloc.

The shift began with an astonishing election result in Hungary in April. Against all odds, Orbán, the EU’s most deeply entrenched autocrat, was unseated by challenger Péter Magyar. Over his long years in office, Orbán had done everything possible to consolidate and perpetuate his authoritarian grip on power. The media were in his pocket, the judiciary ate from his hand and academic freedom was systematically curtailed. Yet a broad civic movement coalesced around Magyar’s party and succeeded in ousting him. The banks of the Danube witnessed their most exuberant night of celebration this century.

Joy was equally palpable last Sunday night, 300km down the river in Belgrade. There in Serbia, the Student List, a bottom-up alliance of students, academics and angry citizens, unexpectedly sent Vučić packing. Vučić had held a tight grip on power since 2014, first as prime minister, then president, relying on a familiar cocktail of far-right bravado, financial scandals and contempt for the rule of law: the winning formula of recent years. But there seems to be a limit to what citizens are ready to accept. Vučić’s fate was sealed after the newly constructed roof canopy of the Novi Sad train station collapsed in 2024, killing 16 people and triggering widespread public fury against systemic corruption.

Then came the biggest news of all on Monday morning, when Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defied expectations to emerge victorious in Brazil’s presidential election. In the first round, Flávio Bolsonaro had been in the lead, and almost every poll predicted he would win the run-off. Many Brazilians braced themselves for an administration at least as radical-right as his father’s. Instead, Lula, the son of poor, illiterate farmers and a former factory worker himself, surprised friend and foe alike by winning the presidency of Latin America’s largest economy for the fourth time.

Commentators were quick to point out that Lula’s victory halted a winning streak for rightwing populists across Latin America. That is certainly true, but zooming out reveals a broader pattern. This is not primarily a story of left v right, but rather of democrats v post-democrats. Hungary’s Magyar is by no means a leftist; he is a centre-right leader who was once a member of Orbán’s own party. In Serbia, the Student List was headed by Ilija Srdanović, a cardiologist and university professor with no pronounced ideological profile. While he champions liberal values such as press freedom and the rule of law, his stance on Kosovo aligns with traditional Serbian nationalism: it should not be independent.

What Magyar, Srdanović and Lula share – despite significant political differences – is a fundamental belief that the rules of the democratic game must be respected. Elections must be fair, judges and journalists must work independently, and checks and balances exist for a reason.

Post-democrats, by contrast, treat laws and international agreements as mere suggestions, a convenient menu of policy options from which they can cherrypick. They use elections to gain power, only to hollow out democratic institutions once they are in office and maximise their private business profits. As corruption is key, they have to remain in power to stay out of jail. Opposing voices must be muzzled and critical media prosecuted. Post-democrats only keep the outer shell of democracy. Bolsonaro Jr took a page from Donald Trump’s playbook: election results are declared unimpeachable when he wins, and rigged when he loses. Similarly, Netanyahu is now attempting to discredit the Israeli election outcome, by suggesting Qatar interfered on behalf of the Palestinian parties.

Post-democrats have been on the rise for years, and it is terrifying. Since 2000, we have witnessed a steady, deliberate dismantling of democratic achievements across every continent. Anyone reading the latest international Democracy Report, produced by the V-Dem Institute, could easily despair. In terms of overall democratic health, it finds that we have effectively regressed to the levels of 1978. Only 7% of the world’s population live in liberal democracies.

Yet after years of alarming headlines about global democratic backsliding, the news from Budapest, Belgrade and Brasília offers rays of hope in dark times. So does the massive wave of Gen Z protests this year, from India and the Philippines to Albania, Argentina and Chile. Huge crowds of young people have taken to the streets to challenge autocratic power and corruption in their countries.

Could liberal democracy be finding its second wind? Is it actually possible to defeat autocrats and authoritarian regimes after all? Could this mark the beginning of a democratic revival that might extend to the US next week? Most polls suggest that the Democrats stand a strong chance of reclaiming at least the House of Representatives in the upcoming US midterms.

Meanwhile, the delegitimisation of Arab voters in Israel this week reminds us of the limitations of change via the ballot box. Elections can help us get rid of post-democrats, but in deeply divided societies they are not enough to heal. The individual, silent act of voting must be complemented with collective processes of deliberation.

Nonetheless, globally, 2026 may come to rank as the best year for democracy in more than a quarter of a century. Could this be the turning point?

What this tell us ahead of critical elections in some of the EU’s largest member states in the year ahead – France, Spain, Germany and Poland – remains anyone’s guess. Looking at the momentum of the AfD in Germany, rightwing populist parties with post-democratic tendencies remain very much alive in Europe. And Vox could be part of a People’s party-led government in Spain in a matter of weeks. But Hungary, Serbia and Brazil have delivered a vital reminder: the rise of autocrats and their permanence in power are not immutable laws of nature. Soon enough, post-democracies may start to feel passé.

David Van Reybrouck is a Belgian author and philosopher laureate for the Low Countries. He is the author of Against Elections: The Case for Democracy, and the initiator of Democracy27

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.title: Attention Seeking Behaviour by Aea Varfis-van Warmelo review – a slippery liar’s tale
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.author: Aimée Walsh
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.text:
Shortlisted for the Goldsmiths prize, this compelling interrogation of memory, justice and truth offers no easy answers

The Goldsmiths prize-shortlisted debut from British-Greek author Aea Varfis-van Warmelo opens with a confession: “I have never told this story before.” The narrator, who bears the author’s name, goes on to tell the reader that she is a liar. From Humbert Humbert’s self-justifying account of abuse in Lolita to the devastating misinterpretation at the heart of Ian McEwan’s Atonement, the trope of the unreliable narrator exposes the dangerous gap between the stories we tell and the truths they obscure. In Attention Seeking Behaviour, the reader is asked to examine their own capacity for trust.

A young woman aspires to be a writer – yet she has paused her postgraduate degree in poetry. She works unfulfilling jobs that demand little from her and has a lot of sex, which she describes as offering her “solitude”. She does all this while lying compulsively. She lies for fun, to flirt, to steal, for sympathy. She lies out of a desire to hurt others, but also to preserve her own privacy. Lying is, as the narrator claims, universal, though success at lying is not. She regards fraudsters and scammers with derision: they are “divorced from reality” and give her “second hand embarrassment”. In her eyes, her own lies are somehow purer.

Grief and trauma pulse beneath the story, as the narrator is haunted by the dead bodies she sees in parks and floating in canals. She says she has called emergency services, but her account is slippery: the harder we try to grasp it, the more it slips through our fingers. Can we believe a word she says?

Attention Seeking Behaviour draws the reader through personal confession and a gripping narrative of misadventures while dating, but the novel loses some of its momentum in its discussions of deceit. An essay on Paul Ekman’s Facial Action Coding System for classifying facial movements to determine deception disrupts the narrative drive. When this bleeds into the narrative, her boyfriend says: “No more. Please.” These sections interrupt the flow and lack the immediacy achieved elsewhere.

In the book’s second part, questions of credibility become more acute. Acting on behalf of a journalist, the narrator copies files at a legal firm relating to a rape case in which a lecturer is accused of assaulting his student. The victim bares her soul, giving first her phone over to the police, then her laptop. Eventually, after police question her for signs of deception, she withdraws her participation in the investigation. The case is closed.

Complainants often anticipate the difficulties of a police investigation. Their testimony is the evidence, their body a crime scene. The narrator says: “We are ambiently aware of what is believable – of what people think is true, whether or not it is real.” Victims of sexual violence are judged in courts and beyond, for what they wore on the night in question, for what they did or did not do in the aftermath. Here lies the book’s genius: it turns the question of reliability back on the reader, exposing the expectations we place on women. Must an account of rape be consistent, coherent or complete to be worthy of belief? Should a woman’s past, including what she has said and done, have any bearing on whether she is believed? The reader may find their own response to the narrator’s story as unsettling as the story itself. The narrator cannot name the trauma that happened with her ex-boyfriend Isaac. Instead, she unravels it “like a police report”, recounting what she said (nothing) and what she felt (numb). The book asks, unflinchingly, do you believe her?

Brilliant and breathless, Attention Seeking Behaviour brings no easy resolutions to questions of memory, truth and justice. Yet, as the narrator tells us again and again, all she wants is to be believed.

High fashion looks without a big budget? Follow our frugal guide to pinch the biggest autumn/winter ‘26 catwalk trends for free

Dark mornings, darker evenings and the end of Celebrity Traitors. It’s easy to feel a bit meh at this time of year. However, without sounding too TikTok life coach, just as you are encouraged to winter-proof your morning routine (light a breakfast candle, make your favourite cup of tea) to start your day on a brighter note, the same approach could be applied to your wardrobe. An outfit you look forward to wearing to the office or an accessory update that can make a long-term favourite piece feel new again, can help put some much-needed pep in your step. That’s even when the forecast reads five days of rain in a row.

The autumn/winter 2026 collections shown on the catwalks way back in February (yes time works funny in fashion) have finally hit shop floors, and high-street brands have been quick to pay homage. But there are plenty of styling tips and tricks you can borrow for free. Here are nine to get you started … ***

In good news for those who struggle to make decisions, this season, collars come half tucked, half untucked this season. See Bottega Veneta (above), where shirt collars popped over knits and coats and Jil Sander where they half emerged over blazers. Yes, it will be annoying when someone tries to tell you your collar is only partly popped.

Love the Prada floral socks? Nearly fainted when you saw the £860 price tag? You’re not alone. DIY instead with a packet of satin ribbon rose buds and your favourite knee-highs. Haven’t picked up a needle and thread since textiles class? Don’t worry, a crash lesson on YouTube and some sheer determination will get you through it.

At Chloé, creative director Chemena Kamali tucked everything from jeans to leather trousers into over-the-knee boots in contrasting colours. Over at Celine and Bottega Veneta, tailored trousers were loosely stuffed into ankle boots. It’s one way to worry less about hems and puddles.

Still have a pile of rosettes from your sports day victories or pony club days? Pin them to a blazer or silky top a la Simone Rocha. For extra impact, try clustering them together. Top tip? Avoid sky blue unless you want to be mistaken for a Tory candidate on the election trail.

We all know how useful a white shirt is, and now, thanks to Givenchy, there’s even more mileage to it. Follow the lead of creative director, Sarah Burton, and style yours backwards. Very useful if you happen to spill tomato soup down the front of it too.

A jingly jangly necklace isn’t just for party season. At Celine, oversized versions were styled over formal coats and blazers. For affordable costume jewellery, secondhand sites and charity shops are a good bet.

Yes, by day 15 of rain, wind and cold, you will get bored of wearing your winter coat. Slow down this process by adding a pair of colourful gloves to your look. At Polo Ralph Lauren, emerald greens and marigold yellow brightened up charcoal coats and denim jackets, while leather opera gloves in cacao and teal popped up at Balenciaga. It’s similar to the great red sock trend of 2023. Easy yet surprisingly impactful.

Make your next secondhand search a cummerbund. The menswear black-tie accessory has now been reimagined by fashion brands including Kallmeyer, Dries van Noten and Valentino, the latter whose cinched top and dresses with contrasting coloured waist sashes. We’ve also seen formal cummerbunds wrapped around trench coats and striped ruby shirts which adds an unexpected edge.

Unless your daily screen time is a single digit, you will be well aware that a personality skirt is gearing up to be big in fashion. Think a leather midi skirt. An embellished pencil skirt. Or in the case of Tory Burch above, high-shine patent. This all sounds quite scary for real life, but follow Burch’s lead and pair it with something boring on top, such as a cotton sweatshirt or a cashmere jumper. For extra laid-back energy, roll up the sleeves. Main character who?

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: Trump’s foreign policy, from Ukraine to Iran, raised fears of world war three. Americans are about to have their say
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Robert Tait in Jenkintown, Pennsylvania
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Voters who backed the US president in the last election are saying they can’t vote for him today: ‘This is an abomination’

Outside the Ukrainian educational and cultural center in a quiet Pennsylvania suburb of Jenkintown, on the outskirts of Philadelphia, a banner expressed unqualified gratitude: “Thank you USA for supporting Ukraine.”

Inside, however, the sentiment was altogether different. Irene Skulsky, a retired teacher in her late 70s, voiced indignation at Donald Trump’s sudden turn against her ancestral homeland, which she believed had come close to killing her son, Darko, and a desire to punish his fellow Republicans at next week’s midterm elections.

“When we vote, we have to vote with Ukraine in our hearts,” she told her fellow retirees, gathered to hear a presentation by the Daughters of Knyahynya, a women’s group delivering military equipment to Ukrainian special forces on the frontline. “I know many people here are Republicans, but we can’t go according to party lines now. Ukraine needs us. They need our support. We need to shift the balance of power in Congress and in the Senate.”

Days earlier, Skulsky told fellow members at a meeting of the Ukrainian American Senior Citizens Association, Darko had been sitting in traffic en route to work in Kyiv when Russian drone missiles slammed into five cars immediately ahead of him.

There had been no prior alert, allegedly as a result of a decision by Washington to suspend its intelligence-sharing arrangement with Ukraine that has acted as an early warning system against missiles attacks since Russia invaded in February 2022.

In recent weeks, Trump – who pledged during his victorious 2024 presidential election campaign to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict within 24 hours of returning to office – appears to have abandoned Ukraine.

He struck a deal with the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, to buy nearly 5m tonnes of diesel, overriding US sanctions on Moscow. He called on Ukrainians to replace the country’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. His administration was accused of throttling the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service.

And while the Trump administration denied that it had stopped sharing intelligence this month, as relations with Ukraine nose-dived, Zelenskyy has said his country received no advance warning from US intelligence networks of two Russian missile attack waves.

Darko escaped injury, but several people in the vehicles in front were killed in the strikes, according to Skulsky. Her frustration spilled over to include Trump’s fellow Republicans, whom she said were “selling our souls” rather than standing up to the president.

“Republicans are afraid of Trump,” she said. “They’re afraid to lose their position. I think their heart is with Ukraine, but they’s sitting on their hands.”

Many American Ukrainians will express their outrage at the polls on 3 November, according to Eugene Luciw, a retired lawyer and local representative of the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America, an advocacy group.

“For [American] Ukrainians, I believe foreign policy is unquestionably the No 1 issue,” he said. “But I think even the average American without the added affinity of a homeland in Europe is going to see foreign policy as a very important issue.

“It’s beginning to reach people’s minds and hearts that something very important is brewing in Europe. If Ukraine loses this war, we have the beginnings of world war three.”

The most recent Ukraine development is the latest in a trio of Trump foreign policy decisions with the potential to hurt Republicans when Americans head to the polls next week.

More relevant to voters’ living costs – a key issue in this election, according to polls – has been Trump’s protracted war with Iran, and his determination to impose tariffs on imports from much of the world.

The Iran war, launched with Israel in February, shows no signs of ending despite Trump’s early claims that it would be a short-term “excursion” certain to end in the “unconditional surrender” of Tehran’s Islamic regime.

Instead, Trump has reportedly drawn up plans to launch renewed strikes against Iran after the midterms as he seeks to break Iran’s grip on the strait of Hormuz, an energy choke point that was the conduit for one-fifth of the world’s energy supplies before the Tehran regime closed it in response to being attacked.

The strait’s closure has resulted in soaring global oil prices, which have been passed on to US consumers in the form of higher prices for petrol and diesel, which is vital for supply chains and US farmers.

Polls have consistently shown voters’ disapproval of Trump’s handling of the war, and his management of the economy and inflation. Roughly 70% are now critical of both, according to a recent AP-Norc survey.

The war’s economic impact has compounded the inflationary effects of Trump’s tariffs, which has affected the prices of consumer goods and increased costs for manufacturers by increasing the costs of imported raw materials such as steel, copper and aluminum.

The tariff regime has also strained Washington’s relations with once-close allies – perhaps most visibly with Canada, the US’s second-biggest trading partner. Ties between the two neighbors plunged to a new low in August following the collapse of bilateral trade talks.

Following the collapse, the Trump administration imposed tariffs on $20bn of Canadian imports – including cars, forestry and dairy produce – triggering a retaliatory tit-for-tat response from Canada’s government, led by the prime minister, Mark Carney. In Michigan, which shares a border with Canada, even Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers released an ad calling on Trump to end the trade war and declared: “Canada is not our enemy.”

Trump has articulated his vision with characteristic bullishness. After January’s US attack on Venezuela, during which it ousted the country’s president, Nicolás Maduro, he dubbed his strategy the “Donroe doctrine” – a play on the Monroe doctrine, named after the 19th US president, which states that the western hemisphere should be Washington’s exclusive domain.

He bragged about extracting Venezuela’s oil resources and fantasized about making the country “the 51st state” in a speech this week in Corpus Christi, Texas, during which he showed off a tanker he claimed was carrying 1m barrels of oil and repeated a phrase – “to the victors belong the spoils” – that startled foreign leaders when he first uttered it at last month’s gathering of the United Nations general assembly.

There are fears that his neo-imperialist instincts could be applied after the midterms to Cuba, where he has repeatedly pledged to topple the communist regime that has ruled for the past 67 years.

Meanwhile, Trump’s fixation with autocratic leaders has been extended to China’s president, Xi Jinping. Having already met Xi at a summit in Beijing this year before hosting him at the White House, Trump will go to China again next month to meet the Chinese leader.

On a range of issues, he has shown disdain for diplomatic niceties – dispensing with seasoned diplomats to instead rely on Steve Witkoff, a real estate investor and attorney with no background in foreign policy, and Jared Kushner, his businessman son-in-law, as negotiators over matters as intricate as Iran, Gaza and Ukraine.

Yet Trump’s latest Ukraine turn carries special resonance, not least because it risks a dramatic rupture with Washington’s European Nato allies, who are heavily invested in Kyiv’s protection as a first line of defence.

It has highlighted once again Trump’s complex relationship with Putin, an autocratic leader for whom he has repeatedly voiced admiration. It is also a reminder of Trump’s failure to live up to his frequently expressed vow to swiftly end the Ukraine war during the 2024 presidential election campaign.

Trump has blown hot and cold towards Zelenskyy. At an explosive White House meeting in February 2025, he told the Ukrainian leader “you don’t have the cards” – but with a peace deal on terms acceptable to Russia seeming ever more distant, relations seemed to thaw, with Trump even publicly mooting giving Ukraine a license to build its own Patriot missiles.

In recent weeks, however, Trump appears to have definitively ditched the US’s putative ally and sided with Putin.

Economists argue that the volume of diesel covered by his deal with Moscow is too insignificant to reduce diesel prices, which have been inflated mainly by the effects of the Iran war, rather than by the actions of Ukraine.

Witkoff, Trump’s envoy, caused further consternation by praising Putin as a “humanitarian” after the Russian president agreed to release a 74-year-old US citizen, Stephen Hubbard, whom Russia had imprisoned for several years after falsely accusing him of fighting for Ukraine.

The Russia-friendly moves have stunned Ukrainian Americans, many of whom have pro-Republican sympathies dating back to the cold war, when staunchly anti-communist presidents like Ronald Reagan were seen as champions of self-determination for the constituent, so-called “captive nations” that comprised the Soviet Union, which included Ukraine.

“We are befuddled and upset by what’s going on,” said Andrij Chornodolsky, chair of the senior citizens association, who urged his fellow members to call the White House and leave comments criticizing the recent policy moves. “How can you be doing this to us?”

The US is “helping a country that wants to subjugate Ukraine back into a new empire, the Russian empire”, added Chornodolsky, who was equally angry with Republicans who have failed to criticize Trump over his abandonment of Ukraine.

“What are the comments coming out of Congress?” he said. “Silence speaks very loudly. If you do nothing, you agree with the person making the pronouncements.”

There are about 60,000 people of Ukrainian descent in Philadelphia’s metropolitan area, the second-largest such ethnic population in the US after New York. From 105,000 to 122,000 people are estimated to claim Ukrainian ancestry throughout Pennsylvania.

Peter and Orysia Hewuka, long-term Republicans who had both previously voted for Trump, said they were likely to vote for a local Democrat because of Ukraine, even though it represented a psychological hurdle.

“I am very hesitant to vote Democrat. I’m a lifelong Republican,” said Peter, 88, a retired nuclear physicist. “But I can’t vote for people who support what Trump is doing. The Republican party has left us, we haven’t left the Republican party.

“It’s very difficult for me and for a lot of Ukrainian Americans to vote for the Republican party based on what they’ve been doing in the past months.”

Luciw, of the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America, said even Trump’s diehard supporters in the Ukrainian community had been alienated by the diesel deal with Putin.

“From my interactions on social media and elsewhere, I would say more than 75% of those who supported him have now abandoned him because it’s now clear where this is headed,” said Luciw, 68, who described himself as a Reagan Republican, but now also intends to vote Democrat.

“Until the last few weeks, there was a hope that Trump’s swinging back-and-forth on Ukraine was a kind of negotiation … that maybe he would come to terms with things because it looked liked Ukraine was going to win and he would support a winner,” he said. “But the diesel deal reversed all that.”

Mykola Hryckowian, director of the Center for US-Ukrainian Relations, said he voted for Trump three times and been active in an ad hoc group called Ukrainian Americans for Trump – but has since severed his last vestiges of support.

“I went to the polling booth in the last election not knowing who to vote for, thinking I might write in Zelenskyy, but in the end voted for Trump, because I couldn’t vote for Kamala Harris,” he recalled. “Today, I could not vote for Trump.

“But a lot of my colleagues [on the committee] were very staunch, holding onto Trump until the very end. But in these last two weeks, they have turned around and said: ‘This is an abomination’.”

Not all Ukrainians are surprised by Trump’s actions. Mark Andryczyk, a Ukrainian studies scholar at Columbia University and board member of the Ukrainian League of Philadelphia – a cultural group that hosts performances by writers and musicians from the country – said the president’s actions were predictable.

“I never thought Trump would be a good idea for Ukraine,” he said. “You just have to look at how happy Russia was each time he was elected.”

“All his information on the war is basically Russian talking points,” added Andryczyk. “I can’t imagine why anybody would think he was pulling for Ukraine. Perhaps people somehow thought that he wouldn’t be doing this. I would think that their eyes are open now.”

A clear-eyed view of Trump’s foreign policy could reap an electoral whirlwind for Trump’s Republican allies on 3 November, with the pocket-book effects of his tariffs and the war on Iran looming large as voters head to the polls.

Yet such an outcome could be a double-edged sword. Should Trump become hemmed in at home by a Democrat-controlled Congress in the final two years of his presidency, where better to assert his power than the rest of the world?

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Mary Peltola made a mistake. But her Republican opponent would be a disaster for Alaska | Kim Heacox
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Kim Heacox
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Trump and Senator Dan Sullivan have put my home state on the chopping block. But Peltola understands Alaskans

Should I be surprised? The previous time he visited my home state, in August 2025, he ordered the US military to roll out a red carpet for Russia’s Vladimir Putin. The two billionaire oligarchs chummed it up and posed for cameras, then talked about the war in Ukraine and achieved no formal ceasefire and no peace agreement.

I was curious to see what Trump would do this time. If our economy is so good, as he says it is, and if Republicans are so superior to Democrats, as he says they are, then why fly 3,400 miles to hold a rally for Dan Sullivan, Alaska’s junior Republican senator running for his third term?

Sullivan is in a tight race with his Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola. That’s why. Control of the US Senate for the next two years could come down to Alaska.

A week ago, Trump made a desperate move. He directed the US Department of Justice to file a lawsuit against the state of Alaska because a second Dan Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher from the coastal fishing town of Petersburg, is also on the ballot.

On Wednesday, the plot thickened when the New York Times reported that back in the summer of 2025, Democratic operatives began to engineer ways to get a spoiler on the Alaska ballot, according to interviews with Peltola’s former campaign manager and longtime aide, Elisa Rios, who was fired in a staff shake-up in August. Other sources included texts.

Rios said Peltola was not directly involved in the operation but was aware of it. Last week, Rios contacted the Times and retracted all statements “made regarding the 2026 Alaska Senate Race”. She added: “I am not willing to be a source for any story in any capacity.”

A spokesperson for the Democratic Senate campaign arm told the Guardian: “Republicans have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns.”

Trump’s justice department lawsuit, however, is unprecedented. It seeks to block a Peltola win “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan”. Meanwhile, the justice department has reportedly issued subpoenas over the matter.

Four months ago, the Alaska supreme court approved both Sullivans on the ballot. The Alaska division of elections lists the Petersburg candidate as “Sullivan, Daniel J Jr” without a party affiliation, and the senator, Dan S Sullivan, as the incumbent Republican.

Criticism of the lawsuit has been deep and wide. “Attention Alaska,” wrote Libby Bakalar, the municipal attorney for Bethel and a former assistant attorney general. “Donald Trump is abusing the judicial system in an attempt to personally appoint your next United States senator. Don’t let him.” (Following the Times story, she told KTOO: “Not a single illegal thing happened here.”)

Which brings us back to the rally on 13 October. The Wasilla sports center – not so large but easy to fill – thrummed with excitement as Trump and Sullivan shared the stage and appeared to have a good time, playing to all the flags and phones and red hats.

Sullivan said nothing about Alaska’s federal employees who lost their jobs due to government cuts, many of them highly educated scientists. He also made no appeal to the many Alaskans in remote villages who struggle with some of the highest prices in the state’s history: home heating fuel at $7-$9/gallon, milk at $25-$30/gallon.

And if that weren’t enough, he said nothing about the estimated 30,000 Alaskans who have lost, or will soon lose, their medical coverage.

Instead, Sullivan stood with the man responsible for those problems and told the crowd what he had said to Trump privately: “Mr President, I just really want to thank you for all that you’re doing for Alaska.”

Was I missing something? I’ve lived in Alaska for nearly 50 years – have been charged by bears, surrounded by caribou, charmed by whales and inspired by glaciers.

I can’t imagine my heart and soul thriving anywhere else. A young ranger with the US National Park Service back in the 1970s, I came north for adventure and beauty and found both. The wild America I was born too late to see down south, awaited me up north. For that, I will always be grateful.

Blame it on Henry David Thoreau, Edward Abbey and Rachel Carson, American authors who convinced me that nothing is more valuable than wildness, curiosity and a sense of wonder.

As such, it’s not bears that frighten me. It’s men like Sullivan and Trump who can hear a dollar bill fall on the tundra. Men who get excited by 1) drilling for oil in the Arctic national wildlife refuge 2) reducing the western Brooks Range to a massive mining district and reaching those mines by slicing a cut-and-fill road through Gates of the Arctic national park, and 3) repealing the US Forest Service’s Roadless Rule that will enable clearcut logging in the Tongass national forest – a temperate rainforest, one of the rarest biomes on Earth – where massive, ancient trees and a thick understory store more carbon than any other national forest in the country. Of the roughly 1.6m responses, more than 99% opposed the repeal. Americans appreciate the life-giving value of their trees.

Trump and Sullivan make a destructive bromance. Sullivan has voted with Trump’s stated positions more than 95% of the time, including, more recently, 14 votes against resolutions aimed at curtailing the president’s military authority or against removing US forces from Iran. No wonder Trump wants to keep him around. Drill, dig, fill and kill.

Off the road system, listening to village Alaskans express their concerns about, well … everything. The cost of fuel and food, their warming world and declining numbers of caribou and fish; the northern rivers turning rustic orange-yellow, laced with toxic metals leached from thawing permafrost. Their homes sinking into swamps or falling into the sea that no longer freezes in autumn, which allows ocean storms to tear down protective bluffs and eat away their villages.

“Bring on the pardons,” he announced, and the beneficiaries stepped forward: two Anchorage mechanics who had pleaded guilty to violating the Clean Air Act through a business that disabled pollution control devices on diesel engines. “They want to put them in jail for 10 years because they fixed an engine,” Trump told the crowd. “How sick.” He proceeded to talk about trucking and “all of the environmental crap” that allegedly makes vehicles expensive and inefficient.

This is where we find ourselves. In a landscape and ecosystem butcher shop run by Trump and Sullivan and other Republicans doing their best to defeat “environmental crap”.

Come clean with the people she seeks to represent. Stand strong and promise to take the high ground. She’s a lifelong Alaskan who knows how to listen and who understands what she calls “kitchen table issues”.

Sullivan, by stark contrast, is a corporate shill. If re-elected, he will continue to bend the knee to our wannabe king. The choice is clear.

Can Peltola unseat Sullivan on 3 November? Yes. Alaska will be counted last, but don’t count us out. My forecast from the land of caribou, whales and bears: cloudy with a chance of better days ahead.

Kim Heacox is the author of many books, including The Only Kayak and Jimmy Bluefeather, both winners of the National Outdoor Book Award. He is a former ranger at Alaska’s Glacier Bay, Denali and Katmai national parks

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Everyone is thin and we’re not allowed to say so: the toxic legacy of body positivity
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Hannah Marriott
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
In the late 2010s, a movement argued that no one body type is superior than another. Now in the GLP-1 age, people are still pursuing thinness - and just not talking about it

Vogue World Milano was held beneath the vaulted glass domes of Italy’s oldest shopping arcade, featuring Gigi Hadid in archival Valentino couture and robots dancing on the catwalk while Miuccia Prada scowled at them. A splashy event staged in the midst of a month of fashion shows in New York, London, Milan and Paris, in which 97.5% of models were a size four or under, what ticked people off most was the presence of trillion-dollar pharma company Eli Lilly on the list of sponsors.

Eating disorder advocates spoke out against the association between an aspirational fashion show and the manufacturer of the weight-loss drugs Zepbound and Mounjaro.

Fans of doublespeak, however, would have found much to enjoy in the language an Eli Lilly spokesperson used to defend the partnership, saying it collaborates with “cultural platforms like Vogue … because that is where conversations about bodies and health take place. Lilly is working to shift the conversation about weight from aesthetics to health and to challenge the stigma people with obesity face every day.”

So to summarise, Eli Lilly is partnering with Vogue – a byword for fashion, glamour and thinness for more than a century – in order to shift the conversation away from aesthetics.

But Eli Lilly is not alone in serving word salad in this bewildering moment.

We are living through a strange time in the language around bodies. Body positivity – a movement which peaked in the late 2010s, and argued that no one body type is morally, sexually or aesthetically superior to any other – has all but vanished within mainstream visual culture. At the same time, much of its social training lingers.

During the body positivity movement’s peak, of the late 2010s, many of us learned to try to think differently about bodies – our own, and other people’s. All bodies are beautiful, we were told, first by activists, then by brands which used those ideas to sell deodorant. At the same time, phrases such as “fat shaming” and “body shaming” went viral as high-profile women revealed the pain wrought by relentless objectification by industry gatekeepers, trolls, fans and the media in the previous decade. We learned, too, that casual body chat could be actively damaging for people suffering from eating disorders. Diet chat became taboo. Self-acceptance, not skinniness, was the prize, we learned – or, at least, we tried to.

We are now in a very different moment, with ideals shaped by a very different set of cultural and economic forces. Self-improvement strategies are pushed at us near-constantly. Social media feeds are thick with thin fitness influencers, GLP-1 before and afters, and injector-influencers advising us how we can jab our way to our best ever faces. A million GLP-1, Botox and plastic surgery adverts stare down at us from billboards and in doctor’s offices. The dominant narrative suggests we can have near-perfect control over our bodies, if we just have the time, taste and budget. Self-acceptance feels like a relic from the pre-Covid era.

Still, in many circles, it remains socially frowned on to talk about weight loss as an aesthetic goal – even as weight loss could scarcely be more high profile, with many GLP-1 drug adverts citing average pounds lost, and telehealth companies targeting slim people who want to lose the “last 10lb” on social media.

It remains taboo to overtly venerate thinness – particularly within the sanctioned spaces of media interviews or marketing for large corporations – or even to admit to noticing thinness in other people, yet slimness has never been more culturally rewarded. It’s hard to ignore the reality that so many high-profile people, now, from actors playing cops on TV, to Instagram chefs to musicians selling us beauty products, appear to be shrinking. What we’re left with is a world in which skinny bodies are lionized in fashion, culture and daily life, but to either admit a desire to conform, or express concern about it, feels socially verboten.

Body positivity has radical roots, said Tigress Osborn, chair of the National Association to Advance Fat Acceptance (NAAFA). The phrase has been used by eating disorder therapists, and “especially fat liberation and fat activists”, she said, since at least the 1990s. Osborn views the phrase in tandem with other “body liberation” movements, including Health at Every Size, which argues that higher bodyweight should not be pathologised, and also “bodily autonomy”, not only in terms of sexual freedom or reproduction, but meaning “you own yourself and you get to do what you want” with your body.

Its mainstream adoption began with plus-sized people, who posted pictures, on Tumblr and Instagram, along with captions of self-love and self-acceptance along with the hashtag #BoPo. Gradually, those ideas went viral.

What followed was heralded as a golden age of body inclusivity. In 2015, the model Tess Holliday was billed as “the world’s first size 22 supermodel” on the cover of People magazine. The rise of celebrities who didn’t fit the usual skinny celebrity mould like Meghan Trainor, with her 2014 body positivity anthem All About that Bass, and plus-sized superstar Lizzo, who rapped joyfully about “getting thicker” became part of a cultural narrative. Mainstream brands soon jumped on board, with campaigns urging body positivity through the purchase of self-tan and leggings. Luxury fashion tentatively followed suit, with US Vogue featuring a plus-sized model, Ashley Graham, on its cover for the first time in 2017, though the composition of the shot – wedged between straight-sized models, so that the contours of her body were not visible – raised immediate questions about the authenticity of this apparent milestone. Though, by the time Lizzo covered US Vogue in 2020, as the first Black plus-sized woman to do so, presented in a full-body shot wearing tomato red Valentino chiffon, the movement’s impact on the highest echelons of fashion felt more certain.

The way body positivity was embraced by the fashion industry could sometimes feel hollow. Osborn describes peak body positivity as: “you go, girl!” She said that it was still “radical to declare that you love yourself in a world that is constantly telling you that you should hate yourself” but said the industry’s focus was only on the “personal and individual” and not about trying to “change or dismantle systems”.

Others said it glorified obesity. One plus-sized influencer, Gabriella Lascano, said that the cultural movement ignored health concerns and encouraged her to put her own wellbeing at risk. (The CDC links obesity to an increased risk of many serious diseases and conditions, though fitness is a better indicator of health than BMI and it is a misconception that better health always means a smaller body.)

What most people agreed on was that its adoption by companies wishing to sell products often felt inauthentic.

In mainstream consumer spaces, brands from Dove to Aerie to Lane Bryant were using body positivity slogans, and more diverse models and influencer-ambassadors, to try to sell products.

The more mainstream things got, said former body-positivity activist Matthew Diaz, the more the same beauty standards it was supposedly railing against came into play. Those being “lifted up”, he said, were only “slightly outside what would be considered acceptable by the norm, but by no means representative of the biggest swaths of the community”.

As a consequence, Diaz grew to question the term itself which, he said, “still focuses a lot on appearances, but just allows for more diversification”. He is now a “body neutrality advocate” a concept which, “decentres your appearance. The issue isn’t that my body isn’t right. The issue is that I am deriving all of my value from it.”

Within luxury fashion, body positivity did have a limited impact. In the late 1990s and 2000s, plus-sized models were virtually nonexistent on luxury catwalks. Extreme catwalk skinniness, on the other hand, was so ubiquitous that it prompted frequent public outcries, and industry initiatives were established to protect models, particularly after two models died from complications of anorexia in 2006.

During the body-positivity era, according to online publication the Fashion Spot, which tracked catwalk diversity between 2015 and 2022, there was a trend towards diversity: only six plus-sized models walked in the fall 2016 season, but there were 50 in fall 2020, and a record 103, or 2.34% of all castings, in fall 2022. Since then, though, according to Vogue Business, which uses slightly different metrics and began tracking shows in 2023, size diversity has decreased. Ninety-five per cent of looks were shown on straight-size models in 2023 and 2024. That has risen to 97% in the two years since.

Many household name brands didn’t do body positivity at all (one academic study found that Calvin Klein, Versace and Chanel did not use a single plus-sized model between 2013 and 2018.) Even so – from a very low bar – the presence of even a couple of plus-sized models in, say, every third or fourth fashion week show felt like progress.

Behind the scenes, though, inclusivity wasn’t really part of the business model, said Michaela Stark, an artist, model and couturier who worked in fashion at the peak of body positivity. Brands often didn’t actually make clothes in plus sizes, even when they modelled them on plus-sized models (as was the case with Paloma Elsesser’s 2022 I-D cover, on which she later commented: “I am not just going to wear a stretchy dress. I’m wearing the Miu Miu” – when Miu Miu did not make clothes in her size in reality.)

For hundreds of years, said Stark, “every single micro level of fashion has catered to creating clothes for an ultra-thin body. Brands would have to invest a whole lot of money and expertise into reinventing that.” That didn’t happen.

She would sometimes help cast diverse models for brands, and the process could be painful. At one shoot for a magazine in Paris, a creative director asked her to cast models as though from a shopping list, she said: “It was like: one Black, one Asian, one old, one fat. You’re not casting these people because of who they are. You’re just trying to tick every box,” she said. She modelled herself and remembers a stylist telling her: “You look like a squished sausage!” Her own artistic work – she creates corsets which accentuate rolls of flesh – was branded as “body positivity” which did not sit right with her, “not because I don’t strongly believe in the ethos, but because, in the peak, you could feel people doing it for cultural validation”.

The impacts of body positivity, even at its peak, remain contested. Several studies found viewing body positive imagery beneficial for individuals’ mood and body satisfaction in the short term; others claim otherwise. But it was this inauthenticity that put off the next generation of young fashion fans, said Anastasia Vartanian, who writes as @FatAnnaWintour – a name wittily capturing the tension she felt as a curvy, teenage Tumblr fashion obsessive. They found the worthiness “cringy”, she says, and overcorrected. Among young people now, “it’s almost now cool to be problematic,” she says. As the Y2K trend infiltrated young people’s wardrobes, she started noticing “a lot of worship of old 2000s runways” online, featuring pictures of very thin models posted with captions along the lines of: “bring back real models!” and “fashion’s not the same any more!”

Vartanian said what has happened since “is really wild. It’s unsettling how a lot of people in the public eye are so very thin. And it feels as though we’re living in a twilight zone where you can’t comment on something that’s clearly unhealthy without sounding mean. But some people are using the language of body positivity, even body neutrality, towards what is clearly anorexia, and I’m finding that such a headfuck.”

What body positivity has changed, and profoundly, is language. In the 00s it was commonplace for objectively slender celebrities to be labelled “porky” in the tabloids, acceptable for Victoria Beckham to be weighed on live TV, for Karl Lagerfeld to say “no one wants to see curvy women” or blame “the hole in social security” on “all the diseases caught by people who are too fat” (Lagerfeld lost 90lb himself in the early 2000s. Perhaps he was hungry.)

It was normalized, too, for Victoria’s Secret models to detail their grueling preshow routines. In 2011, for example, model Adriana Lima said she did not eat solid food for nine days before walking the catwalk in her undies. And who could blame her? Because, during this time, famous women were constantly told they were too fat by producers and impresarios. It was so normalised that when, in 2004, Simon Cowell told a 19-year-old X Factor auditionee she was too overweight to be a pop star, Sharon Osbourne – the good cop in this scenario – invited her to the next round by saying, with a kind smile: “Mrs, go on a diet.”

Much of the pushback against this kind of talk came from high-profile women themselves, who spoke out against the scrutiny they had faced for decades. Ashley Graham, for one, wrote a viral essay declaring: “The cycle of body-shaming needs to end. I’m over it.” Jessica Simpson, Keira Knightley, Hayley Atwell, Jennifer Lawrence all made similar comments. In a receptive, peak #MeToo era, the tide turned.

Then came Ozempic. Even body-positivity icons including Trainor and Lizzo lost weight with semaglutides. Oprah, whose yo-yo diets and weight struggles had been watched like a soap opera for decades by the public, spent most of 2023 talking about her GLP-1 weight loss experiences while promoting a book she co-authored, Enough: Your Weight, Your Health, and What It’s Like to Be Free.

Fans expressed disappointment as these women became icons for something else entirely: the idea that, deep down, we had all wanted to be thin anyway. As ever, individual women were taken to task, and were understandably annoyed about it. As Adele said: “It’s not my job to validate how people feel about their bodies – I feel bad that it’s made people feel horrible about themselves but it’s not my job. I’m trying to sort my own life out.”

The average GLP-1 weight loss is 10-20% within one year, meaning many plus-sized people who take GLP-1s remain plus-sized afterwards, Lizzo included. Yet the narrative about fatness has shifted profoundly.

Now, talking about weight loss for aesthetics remains taboo – but talking about weight and health is a different story. For people in larger bodies, whom others believe would be healthier if slimmer, “it emboldens literally everyone,” said Osborn. “People get to tell themselves that they’re being kind to you by telling you that you should be using it.” This pressure, she feels, is at odds with bodily autonomy: “If you want to lose weight with these drugs that’s your business. But you shouldn’t be sociopolitically coerced into it.”

In June 2021, at the same time the first GLP-1, Wegovy, was approved for weight loss, social media was shifting profoundly. TikTok was booming; it became the world’s most-downloaded app in 2022. The workings of its algorithm, though notoriously opaque, were very different from what had come before. It’s For You page apparently served content based on demographics and engagement, rather than prioritizing content from accounts users had chosen to follow.

This seemed to skew thin: studies found that TikTok perpetuated “toxic diet culture” and promoted the misconception that “weight is the most important measure of a person’s health”. Instagram’s feed changed accordingly. The idea that our better selves could “curate our feed” – a frequent refrain in the body positivity era, when campaigners urged us to follow accounts representing a variety of different bodies – no longer felt possible.

Many women reported feeds flooded with GLP-1 content, fitness chat and plastic surgery before-and-afters. Eating disorders had mushroomed during Covid and, for some, this contributed to very serious mental health issues. In 2025, TikTok announced that it had banned a hashtag – #SkinnyTok – which promoted disordered eating. But much worrying content still remains, and is very easily accessed. Amanda Raffoul, a University of Toronto assistant professor, explains that “the particular unique danger of the modern age of social media is the algorithmic funneling”, because content is pushed “to people who might not have been seeking it out in the first place”. The apps are doing better, she said, in banning “blatantly pro-eating disorder” content. But there is so much “grey area content that platforms are either not succeeding, or maybe don’t care to do a good job in eliminating, because it reaches larger audiences and is more profit-generating”.

Images of certain celebrities have fuelled week-long churn cycles, as when Ariana Grande appeared looking desperately thin in her Petal music video. The debates about whether it was OK to comment about her appearance fuelled the story for days. And there isn’t a right answer, said Raffoul, adding that even those working to combat eating disorders struggle. If you were worried about a person in your real life circle, she said, the advice would be straightforward: “you ask them about how they’re feeling. But we can’t ask a celebrity, ‘Hey, girl, how you doing?’ And those people have social capital.” Picking apart an individual is counterproductive, but also: “what message are we relaying if we say nothing?”

There is no right answer, so debates abound, which appears to be how the algorithm likes it.

And still, for all of the noise in the comments, in the legitimized spaces of school gates and red carpet interviews and offices, the idea that we might want to be skinny is only ever uttered in a whisper.

Fitness does a lot of heavy lifting. As one nutritionist, Hadlee Garrison, put it in a recently posted video liked by 40,000 people, titled “Girl from 2006 meets girl from 2026”, we have developed a new lexicon. Influencers talk about macros, not calories. Looking snatched or toned, not looking skinny. Our feeds are full of advice on eating more protein, achieving calorie deficits, but never diets.

As 2026 girl explains, she never weighs herself. “The scale is such a flawed metric,” she said. “I do a body-composition scan. It tells your fat percentage, visceral fat, lean mass, water weight, metabolic age.”

This week’s Victoria Secret show demonstrated the shift. Preparation, in 2026, is not about avoiding food, said Rosie Huntington-Whiteley. It’s “a mindset more than anything” it’s about “feeling strong and fit, as opposed to thinking about a number on the scales or on a measuring tape”. Yes, there is strength training, rest, hydration and protein, lymphatic drainage, cold plunges and facials, but “nothing is off the table for me ever with my diet”.

Fashion magazines that would never openly applaud skinniness run galleries titled: “Abs Are the Best Beauty Flex at the 2026 Grammys”. Influencer-injectors claim they would never comment on, for example, Susan Dell’s face – before unpicking “why this look can happen and what you can do if you feel like it’s happening to you”, and asking, amusingly, while pointing at a picture of Dell’s face: “now, what are the key features that stand out that look human?”

Demi Moore, who looks about 25 in her 60s, stars in People magazine’s World’s Most Beautiful People issue, while saying her appearance “doesn’t define my value or who I am”, then promotes Lancome’s Absolue Longevity MD range which, she said, is “moving away from this idea that we’re fighting something through anti-ageing”. The product’s aim, rather, is to “reverse the skin’s visible biological age at every life stage”, which sounds quite similar.

What we are left with is doublespeak – as the rhetoric popularised in the body positivity era is skewed to fit a very different purpose – or silence, as friends shrink before our eyes and we don’t say a word, or celebrities become stick-thin and it feels unsisterly to notice. In many real-life circles, weight becomes the great unsaid, an issue that is too grave to look at directly. Only in the anonymity of the comment section, are bodies truly discussed – ad nauseam and for hours.

Recently, though, when the Practical Magic 2 star Joey King responded to speculation that she had had a facelift at 26 – after the internet described her as “snatched” on the Met Gala red carpet – she revealed her actual pregame tactics. A 36-hour fast – “No food, nothing but water … I don’t promote that,” she said – and lymphatic drainage. There was remarkably little pushback or handwringing about that online – rather it was presented in some headlines using the body-positivity era language of her “shutting down” facelift rumours.
