Perhaps, finally, there was nothing to argue about. At least she was being honest.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: Patrick Stewart brought gravitas and complexity to the screen, from Star Trek to X-Men
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Peter Bradshaw
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
From Jean-Luc Picard to Charles Xavier, the actor’s Shakespearean training – and that sonorous voice – made him a unique charismatic force in Hollywood

O Captain, our Captain: on Star Trek, Patrick Stewart could make anyone feel hopeful for humanity

No actor showed the commercial potential of blue-chip British classical training like Patrick Stewart. With style, technique and the most minutely self-aware, almost vaudevillian sense of mimicry, Shakespearean thesps can turn their hand to American movies and high-end American television and show the American method actors how it’s done – sometimes, even, at the beginning of their screen careers, at a competitively low wage.

Stewart was one of the thoroughbreds of the Royal Shakespeare Company’s 1970s stage generation who had also had classy small screen roles, such as his intimidating Sejanus in I, Claudius opposite Derek Jacobi. But he effected a warp-speed leap to pop culture stardom by getting the role of Jean-Luc Picard, captain of the Federation starship USS Enterprise, in TV’s Star Trek: The Next Generation, the hugely successful reboot of Star Trek that ran from 1987 to 1994, spawning four separate feature films and then another series, Star Trek: Picard.

Stewart was athletic, commanding, sonorous – and bald (though in a distinctively virile way). William Shatner’s Captain James Kirk had been a more clean-cut JFK of the space-exploration world, an action-romantic lead, but Stewart’s Picard was a more complex figure, slightly nearer in spirit – with that exotic name of his and the hairless head – to the alien figures and indigenous planet-dwellers who were now a regular feature of intergalactically diverse Star Trek cast. (Alan Rickman’s haughty actor turned sci-fi icon Alexander Dane in the 1999 space comedy Galaxy Quest was perhaps a little inspired by Stewart.) A whole new generation of Trekkers found a charismatic new leader to rally round.

And with that remarkable coup in the bag, Stewart went on to conquer the world of superhero-dom; he transferred the pop-culture capital he had amassed in Star Trek to the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Stewart became a character-actor-slash-star of the multiplex as the wheelchair-using eminence Professor Charles Xavier, or Professor X, in the X-Men franchise at the beginning of the 00s as the Marvel brand began its colossal box-office dominance. As Xavier, Stewart played opposite Ian McKellen as Magneto, that other RSC Galactico who good-humouredly wore the Lycra and delivered the lines with resounding conviction. And in fact the role of Professor Xavier, the mentor and tutor to the mutants, probably allowed Stewart to draw even more on his Shakespearean background: he often had a wise and kingly mien as Xavier, especially when the franchise showed him as a kind of exiled monarch.

It should be said that Stewart had some form in sci-fi and fantasy way before this. He was Guenevere’s father, King Leodegrance, in John Boorman’s visionary Excalibur in 1981 and the adviser to Paul Atreides, Gurney Halleck, in David Lynch’s distinctive version of Frank Herbert’s Dune in 1984.

But for me his most satisfying non-franchise movie role, and the one that allowed him to be vehemently and compellingly bad in a way Star Trek and Marvel didn’t, was Jeremy Saulnier’s horror-thriller Green Room, in which Stewart plays a neo-Nazi leader who, along with his brutish rank and file, tries to attack a rock band who have barricaded themselves into the green room of the scuzzy bar they’ve just played and where they have discovered something awful.

Stewart’s face could transform into a threatening mask: he could look handsome and refined but also leonine and aggressive, and the mellifluous voice could deliver a nasal edge of threat. Stewart was a unique charismatic force on screen.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: ‘I left shellshocked’: writers on their scariest non-horror movies
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Radheyan Simonpillai, Morgan Jerkins, Alaina Demopoulos, Veronica Esposito, Andrew Lawrence,Juan A Ramírez, Jesse Hassenger, Shrai Popat,Rafaela Bassili, Benjamin Lee, Adrian Horton and Andrew Pulver
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
For Halloween, Guardian writers have picked the most efficiently terrifying films outside of the horror genre from How to Have Sex to The Hunchback of Notre Dame

Hiding in plain sight throughout Lee Chang-dong’s deliciously enigmatic Burning, in which a spirited young woman (Jeon Jong-seo) disappears, and a wealthy playboy (Steven Yeun) gives serial killer vibes, is a disaffected male rage. That’s perhaps the most commonplace horror of our times, whether on the internet or politics, and you feel the tremors of it steadily breaking the surface in Yoo Ah-in’s performance. He plays Jong-su, an aspiring writer, quietly frustrated with his lot in life. Jong-su works odd jobs and tends to his incarcerated father’s dilapidated farm, growing more desperate to grasp some sense of control over the world around him, which is where the scary part comes in. Chang-dong is the master dramatist who with Burning tilts violently into thriller territory, navigating elements from Taxi Driver, The Vanishing and Michael Haneke’s Caché, using the language of horror movies to conjure up a creeping anxiety and dread that erupts into pure existential fear. Radheyan Simonpillai

Burning is available to watch on Mubi and Tubi in the US, to rent digitally in the UK, and on Netflix in Australia

The scariest non-horror movie for me is Disney’s The Hunchback of Notre Dame. The scene where Quasimodo is bound to a pillory where the townspeople throw food and jeer at him because of his appearance and disability will for ever be seared into my brain since I first watched it as a six-year-old child. To this day, I still believe that I was far too young to witness that particular depth of human cruelty even though it’s very real. Not to mention that the story deals with xenophobia and bigotry towards the Romani people and sexual predation from a religious leader that takes the basic idea of good versus evil to a whole new level. The Hunchback of Notre Dame reminds me that you don’t need jumpscares and gore to frighten someone. Sometimes, the real monsters are human beings with a bit of social standing over someone else due to money, beauty, authority or all of the above. Morgan Jerkins

An insane loner motivated by his all-consuming misogyny perches beside his bedroom window, methodically shooting women on the street below. He writes of his compulsion to kill in a series of letters to police and begs the authorities to hurry up and catch him. This grimly prescient noir from 1952 feels all too familiar for modern viewers who are numb to stories of gun violence and incel culture. It’s a disturbingly acute portrait of urban alienation and the destructive nature of obsession, released more than two decades before Taxi Driver epitomized those themes. Equally haunting is The Sniper’s backstory. Director Edward Dmytryk was one of the blacklisted Hollywood Ten who refused to testify in front of Joseph McCarthy. He later reversed course after a six-month prison sentence, ghoulishly ratting on his contemporaries and ending countless careers. Alaina Demopoulos

The Sniper is available on YouTube in the US and to rent digitally in the UK and Australia

In Stanley Kubrick’s magisterial 2001, human creativity is such a mysterious and foreboding thing that it isn’t even couched as of this world – rather, an eerie alien monolith gives it to the primates who later evolve to be human beings. The film will for ever be remembered for its visionary jump cut from a bone spinning in slow motion – tossed triumphantly into the air by a primate in a fit of conquering rage – to an orbiting space satellite carrying nuclear weapons: in one deft motion Kubrick encapsulates the history of creativity as a carrier of our liberation, but also our destructive potential. From there, what unfolds is a carefully choreographed dance of death between humanity’s ability to responsibly discharge its ever-growing technological powers and the devices that become more and more dangerous to our survival as a species. Although Kubrick ends the movie on a note of hope and transcendence, what sticks with me more is the existential terror that one of our greatest strengths as beings will ultimately lead to our collapse. In an age of extremes where we are regularly reminded of the many technologically fueled threats to global civilization, it’s hard not to feel that fear. In 2001, astronaut-protagonist Dave Bowman manages to save himself – and thus take the next leap in human evolution – by simply disconnecting the runaway AI known as HAL 9000, but in our world we’ve already passed the point where that would have been possible. Veronica Esposito

There’s so much I loved about growing up in the 80s: the funny pages, the power ballads, going for a drive, malls of genuine value – entertainment and otherwise. But one thing I did not love and still don’t was the era’s obsession with animatronic realism, of stuffed animals come disturbingly to life. And by far the worst offender was Howard the Duck. Here was a human adult-sized mallard foisted from his alien nest on to the unwitting citizens of Cleveland, Ohio, looking for all the world like a Donald Duck mascot who had fallen into a vat of primordial ooze (with those golf ball eyes screaming Help!). That Howard also happens to be a martial arts-wielding feminist with an appreciation for hair bands never endeared him to me more than the Dark Overlord who’s also summoned from deep space to … fuck with him? With us? (His true goals still remain somewhat unclear.) My nine-year-old mind was not prepared to see him in bed with Lea Thompson, and rarely does a Halloween go by when some part of me isn’t bracing for a surprise reunion with this quack at a backwoods haunted house. You simply cannot release a movie like this two years after Child’s Play and expect people not to mistake it for a horror. I wonder if the comics company that spawned this duck ever recovered … Andrew Lawrence

Howard the Duck is available to rent digitally in the US, on YouTube in the UK and to rent digitally in Australia

Remember the backseat scene in Bo Burnham’s excellent Eighth Grade, where a horny teen tries to seduce its young lead through a coercive game of truth or dare until her guilelessness catches up to his intentions? How to Have Sex is that unbearable, all-too-recognizable dread blown up to 91 minutes. In an extraordinary breakout performance, Mia McKenna-Bruce plays a 16-year-old on holiday in Greece with two more developed girlfriends. As they flirt with boys and party endlessly, she realizes that keeping up with a shot count might not equal sexual maturity. What’s brilliant about writer-director Molly Manning Walker’s debut is that the worst rarely ever happens: the girls can stumble home down a dark alley and make it back all right, but the threat of the worst-case scenario suffuses every single frame. It’s a queasy, unforgettable viewing experience, activating both parental and innocent impulses as we hope for the best for McKenna-Bruce’s fully realized heroine. Juan A Ramirez

How to Have Sex is available on Netflix and Mubi in the US, on Mubi in the UK and on SBS on Demand in Australia

The horror movie my friends and I were supposed to see that day was The Rage: Carrie 2, a little-seen sequel to the 1976 masterpiece. We did see it – I’d even call it mildly underrated! – and it was indeed a horror film, albeit not the scariest one. But the movie that sent us off into the night so rattled that my buddy briefly drove down the wrong direction of a one-way street was what we casually ducked into afterward: 8mm, a thriller starring Nicolas Cage. Cage was the draw there, so I didn’t think much either way about the subject matter, which was snuff films; Cage plays a private investigator hired to find out if such a film, starring a teenage runaway, is real. I understand why critics at the time mostly shrugged the Joel Schumacher movie off as exploitative, histrionic and even cheesy, but screenwriter Andrew Kevin Walker knows his way around bringing rococo horrors into a stylized version of the real world (he also wrote Seven), sneaking horror into more quasi-respectable genres. The movie’s detective-thriller trappings are probably what ultimately made its more over-the-top elements, including multiple gruesome deaths, an extended confrontation between Cage and a creep played by James Gandolfini, and Cage tracking down a mysterious snuff-film performer called Machine, so viscerally upsetting. My two buddies and I left shellshocked. I like to pretend that I haven’t revisited 8mm since its 1999 release because I’d be embarrassed by how affected I was by such shlock, but the truth is, I’m still a little afraid of the damn thing. Jesse Hassenger

There are many reasons why Awake – the melodramatic thriller in which Hayden Christensen plays a wealthy finance bro who undergoes a heart transplant but remains conscious for the entire operation – continues to scare me the more I think about it. First, the idea of anesthesia failing is terrifying enough. But being paralyzed and unable to communicate that it’s not working? That feels unnecessary. Then there are the film’s many competing plot points. Christensen’s billionaire protagonist, Clay (a name I’ve yet to encounter in nearly a decade in the US), is apparently saint-like. While awake on the operating table, he gleans that his friend and cardiac surgeon (Terrence Howard) is in cahoots with his new wife (Jessica Alba) to kill him. The film is largely confined to a New York hospital, which sounds like a compelling chamber drama? Well, you’d be wrong. Because there apparently isn’t enough anxiety in Joby Harold’s directorial debut, we also get Clay’s hallucinations, including memories of his abusive father. It becomes a race against time for Clay’s mother (Lena Olin), another benevolent billionaire, to stop the plot. Somehow, it only gets more unbelievable. Still, Awake is weirdly exhilarating. Everyone commits fully to the madness, acting with a capital A. Shrai Popat

Awake is available on Tubi in the US, to rent digitally in the UK and on Netflix in Australia

Todd Haynes’s 2019 legal drama, Dark Waters, tells a familiar American story: a principled lawyer goes up against a massive, unscrupulous corporation and loses. But there is a lot in this film, which was based on Nathaniel Rich’s 2016 New York Times profile of former corporate defense lawyer Robert Bilott, to make this duel terrifying. Throughout his career, Haynes has looked at how external forces contaminate the domestic sphere, and here, it’s no different: the obsessive spiral that sweeps Mark Ruffalo’s Bilott is nearly as scary as the complete indifference with which DuPont, the chemical corporation responsible for knowingly poisoning West Virginians with “forever chemicals”, regards human life. One image in the film haunts me more than others: Bilott kneels among stacks of paper that tower over him as menacingly as Nosferatu’s shadow. It’s a terror of scale – all that work won’t kill Bilott, but it will whittle him down to a wisp. To DuPont, crushing Bilott is as simple as swatting a fly. Once you see the horror, you can’t unsee it. Rafaela Bassili

Dark Waters is available to rent digitally in the US and the UK and on SBS on Demand in Australia

There’s something uniquely, nightmarishly terrifying about trying to defend yourself against a false accusation. It’s what makes documentaries about particularly egregious examples of injustice not just enraging but seriously scary – how mechanically efficient the system can be when it’s focused on destroying you, often as the result of something as random as bad luck. In Thomas Vinterberg’s almost unbearably clammy drama The Hunt, a claim is made and believed and it’s cleverly one we’re never kept in the dark about. We know instantly that Mads Mikkelsen’s kindly kindergarten teacher didn’t sexually abuse the young daughter of a friend who, through a confused blur of emotions, makes a comment that is seen as proof of something devastating. With every small decision then made by those around her, some initially understandable and some maddeningly ill-advised, a tight-knit community turns on someone they had previously embraced. It’s horrifying to watch for so many reasons, exposing just how incredibly fragile the trust and acceptance of others can be and how so many are happy to rely on grim preconceptions about men who work with children. What’s chilling is how unstoppable the spiral can often seem and, in a disquieting final scene, how unfathomable it can be to move on from even if the crime has been disproved. In The Hunt, a pitchfork is far scarier than a knife. Benjamin Lee

The Hunt is available on Tubi in the US and to rent digitally in the UK and Australia

There are many reasons why Zodiac, David Fincher’s 2007 film on the infamous serial killer, is considered one of the best detective movies of all time: its precise detail, its masterclass escalation of suspense, its immersive and unsettling mood. But the legacy of Zodiac, to me, isn’t Jake Gyllenhaal’s obsessive spiral, or the vexatious unsolved cryptograms, or even Guillermo del Toro’s viral tweet thread on the movie’s perfection. It is the unnerving re-enactment, about 20 minutes in, of a black-clad man striding in broad daylight toward a picnicking couple. At first he appears to be just another park visitor; only after a few paces can you see that he is masked, marked by an ominous symbol and carrying a gun. Fincher mostly keeps the camera trained on the female victim’s face, as her initial curiosity morphs to concern, then fear, then terror. That shift – when she knows something is off, but can’t yet tell it’s dire – pops into my mind when, say, a stranger approaches on an empty sidewalk, or when I am alone in a park. My dread has yet to ever be substantiated, but that scene is a pathway to panic: sometimes, as in this actual 1969 murder, your fear was right. Adrian Horton

Zodiac is available on YouTube and Paramount+ in the US, on Netflix and Amazon Prime in the UK, and on Netflix in Australia

As a committed avoider of actual horror movies, my most scary experiences at the cinema tend to sneak up on me when I’m not really expecting them. Both the original Vanishing and Jonathan Glazer’s Under the Skin contained scenes that temporarily put the fear of God into me, but I think for cumulative dread and general misery, Darren Aronofsky’s mighty adaptation of Hubert Selby Jr’s junkie novel stands supreme. As its title indicates, Requiem is a nightmare inversion of the American dream: after attempting to go into business with a “pound of pure”, the three youthful protagonists, played by Jared Leto, Marlon Wayans and Jennifer Connelly in manifestly career-high performances, end up having an arm amputated, being battered by prison guards and being forced into gruesome sex work, respectively. In this film, heroin is the equivalent of the creepy killer doll, or hulking monster no one else can see; it’s the silent, remorseless slayer THAT CAN’T BE STOPPED. And that’s not even counting the fourth protag, Ellen Burstyn’s gameshow wannabe, so hopped up on speed-laced diet pills that she goes into amphetamine psychosis. This isn’t a tale of terror, as such, but their collective descent into abject misery is as profoundly disturbing an experience as cinema has ever recorded. Andrew Pulver

Requiem for a Dream is available on Peacock and Tubi in the US and to rent digitally in the UK and Australia

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: Serial killers, set designers, and hordes of skeletons: welcome to the Halloween capital of America
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Lois Beckett in Burbank, California
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
In the placid LA suburb of Burbank, residents spend months – and thousands of dollars – turning their homes into Disney-style attractions. Why does it go so hard for Halloween – and is it becoming too popular for its own good?

Every night, starting in mid-September, Diego Linares puts on a serial killer costume and stands in his front yard for three hours. The 40-year-old alternates outfits: some nights he’s Michael Myers, the masked murderer from the Halloween films. Other nights he’s Jason Voorhees, from the Friday the 13th franchise.

His family’s modest suburban yard in Burbank, California, has been transformed into a slasher movie set. Fake mist leaks out of the door of a cabin labeled “Crystal Lake”. Jack-o-lanterns, monsters, corpses and illuminated gravestones jostle for space across the ground. From the roof above the front door, a giant skeleton blinks its digital eyes.

“All this started because I wanted more trick-or-treaters,” said Linares, who describes himself as an introvert.

Burbank, a placid city of 100,000 in Los Angeles county, has become known as the “Halloween capital” of America. Here, the holiday isn’t just one night, or even a week, but a spooky, ecstatic, intensely competitive celebration that can last a month or longer.

Linares is just one of dozens of enthusiastic locals who have turned their homes into DIY haunted houses – transforming Burbank into a destination for Halloween tourism. Residents here spend months – and sometimes thousands of dollars – turning their front yards into miniature Disney-style attractions, complete with elaborate sets, music, lights, animatronic figures, and sometimes even costumed human actors. Some houses accept donations to support their decorations, but none of them charge a fee.

Linares, who puts on his front-yard haunted spectacle non-stop for 42 nights, starting on 19 September and running through Halloween, is particularly hardcore.

On Tuesday, Linares, standing 6ft 6in, and wearing Jason’s characteristic hockey mask, repeatedly emerged from the cabin door holding a bloody axe, which he used to menace visitors standing close to the front fence. He worked the crowd easily – swinging the axe with a gentle swoosh, complimenting family costumes, coaxing high fives from wide-eyed toddlers, even taking off his mask to reassure a tiny girl: “It’s fake – it’s pretend!”

On this relatively slow work night before Halloween, the house still attracted about 500 visitors. The whole experience – photographs, hand-designed stickers, a short walk through a haunted tunnel, hours of crowd-control work from Linares’ sisters – was free.

“We didn’t have a car growing up. I never got to go to Disneyland or Universal Studios. I never got a picture with Santa Claus. I know what it’s like,” Linares said. “This is my making the world a better place.”

It’s no surprise that all of Los Angeles – a city of underemployed actors, stylists and special effects experts – goes hard for Halloween. Griffith Park, Los Angeles’s wilder, craggier version of Central Park, hosts a collection of haunted houses so massive that their fake mist regularly drifts out on to Interstate 5, impeding visibility on the highway.

But Burbank operates on an even higher Halloween level – displaying the kind of skill and ambition that emerges when the neighbor coming to look at your decor is a Disney Imagineer.

“We get people from everywhere. We get international tourists,” said Burbank resident Al Ritch, whose front-yard decor features two skeletons pointing the way to more famous Halloween houses on neighboring blocks: “Pirates” one way, “Pumpkins” another. Both of these houses – “Pirates of Burbank” and “The Pumpkin Cemetery” – have their own social media accounts with a few thousand followers, and fans who return to visit them year after year.

The subculture of Halloween fans who make their own “home haunts” is a phenomenon across the US, with enthusiastic “haunters” gathering for annual conventions on the east and west coasts, in the midwest, and in Texas. But the Los Angeles region “really is unlike anywhere else in the world”, and the city of Burbank “is probably the epicenter”, said Derek Young, the founder of SoCal Haunt List, a website that maps more than 200 elaborately decorated homes from Bakersfield to San Diego.

“This goes so far beyond just putting up lights and maybe carving some pumpkins and putting out candy,” Young said. “These are people who dedicate multiple months of their lives every year to creating these experiences for people to come and see, and a lot of them rival the big theme parks.”

Burbank’s mayor, Tamala Takahashi, said that the creativity and skill of local homeowners should come as no surprise. The 100,000-person Los Angeles suburb is the longtime home of many major Hollywood studios, including Disney and Warner Bros. While other towns might have more on-screen Hollywood talent, “most of Burbank is back of house”, Takahashi said. “We’re the set designers, the costumers, the production managers, the post-production, the special effects.”

Many of Burbank’s elaborate Halloween houses are “a celebration of movies and cinema”, Takahashi said – homages to shows such as Stranger Things or to the visionary horror director Tim Burton, who graduated from Burbank high school in 1976.

She said that the city’s taste for Halloween mania has blossomed over the past decade or so. “It’s gotten more and more elaborate and exciting. I think we’re at our peak right now,” Takahashi said.

The mayor, unfortunately, is not a big Halloween fan. “It’s a little scary for me, personally,” she said. “I like to watch from afar.”

Many of the United States’ longtime Halloween destinations – like Salem Massachusetts, home of the Salem witch trials, or Sleepy Hollow, New York, home of Washington Irving’s Headless Horseman – are on the east coast. Their versions of Halloween tend towards the stuffy and colonial: ghosts, witches, Puritan repression.

The west coast’s Halloween capital is much more contemporary – offering an unabashed celebration of Hollywood gore and horror. Burbank’s rise to prominence is just a few years old, driven by TikTok and Instagram influencers posting about their visits to local houses, but also fueled by local creative ferment. Like the artists of the Harlem Renaissance in the 1920s, or the Beat poets in San Francisco in the 1950s, Burbank now has a critical mass of Halloween artists who are inspiring and competing with each other, pushing their collective creative output to new heights.

Homeowners behind some of the most fantastical local decorations – think full pirate ship sails and rigging atop a roof, or an elaborate animatronic recreation of the Tim Burton horror-comedy film Beetlejuice – say that their ties to the Hollywood set and prop industry are overstated, and that what’s driving the trend is mostly a fanatical level of hobbyist enthusiasm.

Just a few years ago, John Pouncey, whose family has lived in Burbank for 18 years, decorated his house with a modest spooky cemetery in the front yard. Year after year, his family failed to secure even an honorable mention in Burbank’s official city Halloween decorating contest, which has been running for the past decade. So, inspired by the houses that won prizes, he decided to pick a more elaborate theme: Burton’s Beetlejuice, about a ghost couple trying to exorcise the living family who has taken over their home.

“Now, I don’t even care about the competition,” he said. “This just became kind of an obsession.”

Pouncey and his wife, Misty, work in the entertainment industry: she as a costume supervisor, he as a camera operator – a job, Pouncey said, that has very little to do with the elaborate set he has constructed in his front yard, which takes a full six weeks to set up.

His yard is now crowded with animatronic skeletons, some of them powered by small motors, others by pressurized air. Everything is handmade, he said, although “obviously we bought store-bought skeletons”.

The massive skeleton on the roof, which came from Costco, is dressed in a plaid-shirt Misty made from several shower-curtains. Pouncey made its head spin.

“I’m a handy guy” who has watched Beetlejuice “a million times”, he said, and “I see things in the movie that I think would be funny as a prop. And I just, like, immediately know how to do it.”

Another major Burbank Halloween house, “Holiday Fantasies Come to Life”, has rotating, often Disney-inspired themes, and is the home of Arnulfo Padilla, a professional chef. This year, there are pirate sails on his roof, and a Jack Sparrow statue outside his front door. Padilla said he worked through an entire night to arrange the gold loot around Sparrow’s chair.

He enjoyed seeing adult visitors shriek and gasp and point at their favorite details.

“Why not make other people happy, and spread the joy, and make them feel like little kids again?” Padilla said.

Another fan favorite, the Pirates of Burbank, is run by Susan and Dan Hoy. They’re also enthusiasts from outside the industry: she’s a retired member of the Burbank public school district, and he’s a professor of graphic design at ArtCenter College in Pasadena.

“It’s very funny because people think we’re all in the business, and we’re not,” Susan Hoy said. “Some rumors started last year on TikTok, I think, that we’re all prop makers. We’re not.”

Preparations for the Hoy’s pirates display, which is essentially a yard-sized version of Disneyland’s Pirates of the Caribbean ride, started this April, when she started building the skeleton-filled grotto and fountain in her driveway, Hoy said.

While Halloween decorating can easily become expensive, Hoy prides herself on pulling off her stunning display on a budget, using donated wood and paint, costumes bought from thrift stores and objects found on the street. Her grotto is mostly discarded boxes and cardboard. Her kraken tentacles are decorated with slices of pool noodle. The most expensive item in the display is a ship’s wheel, purchased for $100 on Craigslist. Her animatronic skeletons are powered by several windshield wiper motors, and one rotisserie chicken motor.

“We discovered motors three years ago and we haven’t looked back,” she said.

Young, the SoCal Haunt List founder, said the “haunter” community does a lot of skill-sharing and DIY tutorials to help keep down the costs of their over-the-top decor. Still, the costs of costumes and props quickly add up.

Linares estimated that he spends at least $1,000 a year on candy, and another $1,000 to make hand-designed themed stickers to hand out to visitors. A quality full-body costume with a molded character mask can easily total $1,500, he said. “But I love doing it. It makes me feel good,” he said. “I’m not into sports or cars. I’d rather do this.”

Linares’s sisters said their brother can’t stop buying new props, no matter how many he already has. A pile of fresh-from-the-store skeletons and new plastic pumpkins were stacked next to his living room couch. The skeletons were originally $45, Linares said, but he got them on sale for just $15.

With their Halloween fame only continuing to grow, homeowners and city officials in Burbank said they are feeling some of the strain of viral success. Popular Halloween houses are drawing so many visitors to Burbank that they’re causing snarls of traffic in quiet residential streets, making local parking a nightmare, and leaving behind significant quantities of trash. The houses with the biggest lines are now attracting street vendors selling hot dogs and churros from the sidewalks.

Last year, one of the city’s most famous viral haunts, the Burbank Clown House, attracted an estimated 15,000 visitors on Halloween night alone – an unsustainable level of attention, according to Gary Lane, one of the house’s creators, even though the city had started providing police officers to help with crowd control.

The Clown House, co-created by Lane and his twin brother Larry, both 51, and designer Michael Bowen, 52, became famous online and on local television news for its stylish mixture of horror and dark comedy, and for its live costumed clowns – including on the roof. Lane recalls turning off the house’s lights at 10pm on Halloween last year, and watching visitors stay outside for hours: “You saw a sea of dark shadow heads until 1am,” he said. When the crowds finally left, they spent another two hours picking up garbage along the street. The total amount visitors donated that night, he said, was just $89.

This year, after multiple attempts to find an alternative commercial venue fell through, the Clown House has gone dark for the season – with only a single symbolic clown decorating its lawn, and promising a return in 2027, Lane said.

Linares, the serial killer impersonator, said the continual growth of the crowds outside his house worried him. “It’s getting out of hand now,” he said. “This is getting nuts with social media.”

Burbank’s biggest Halloween houses have formed a group chat to share information, which allows them to share tips and give each other a heads-up about badly behaved visitors. “It’s so tea. I love it,” Susan Hoy said.

My own recent tours of Burbank’s Halloween houses, on the Sunday and Tuesday nights before Halloween, were dazzling, disorienting, and frankly overstimulating. There was a Burbank witch trial, a skeleton Mardi Gras, a papier-mache Alice in Wonderland, an X-Files spaceship dangling from a tree. The positivity on the crowded sidewalks was overwhelming: adults gasping and cheering at each new effect, and eager to offer praise and ask the homeowners questions. Children dashed by in costume: couples posed for photos together. As I approached a third hour of touring on Tuesday night, wandering through the fake mist drifting through Burbank’s suburban streets, I found myself staring at a skeleton riding a dinosaur, which was spitting a stream of real water towards a fake giant spider.

“This Halloween theme is a little confusing to me, too,” I heard a nearby skeleton say in a recorded voice.

Alissa Carroll, who lives 45 minutes away in Simi Valley, brought her boyfriend and his visiting parents to Burbank for the night on Tuesday, where they toured nine different houses, finishing up at Sherill Watts’s popular Circus of Nightmares house just before 10pm.

Carroll, who is from New Jersey, argued that her home state “had more of the Halloween spirit”, and said she thought more houses put up some kind of Halloween decorations there. But for the intensity of Halloween decor, there was no competing with southern California.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.title: Trump cancels rallies in Iowa and Kansas in shift of Republican strategy – live
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.author: Chris Hippensteel (now) and Tom Ambrose (earlier)
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text:
The president has been on a campaign blitz in key Republican strongholds, including a stop in Florida this evening

Two scheduled campaign appearances by Donald Trump – one in Kansas, another in Iowa – that Trump had reportedly backed out of are now back on, the Associated Press reported.

Trump had initially planned to campaign in Kansas on Saturday and Iowa on Sunday. Now, both Trump rallies are slated to happen back-to-back on Sunday.

Pollsters from The Washington Post and George Mason University, seeking to shed light on a closely-watched Senate race in Kansas, found themselves with an issue.

Democrats, the poll found, were overwhelmingly more likely than Republicans to engage with poll-takers on the issue. And while partisan differences in participants’ likelihood to answer polls is common, the scale of the problem was exceptional in Kansas.

Even after tailoring the poll to net more responses from hesitant would-be voters, the poll still received participation from a wide gap of 32 percent of Democrats compared to 12 percent by Republicans.

The poll’s result shows Adam Hamilton, the Democratic candidate for Senate who is leading a surprisingly tight campaign against Republican Roger Marshall, by 52 percent to 43 percent. But the Post felt it necessary to caution that the poll likely overestimates Democrat support.

The results of that poll may temper Democratic optimism for next week’s midterm elections, which has been buoyed by a series of polls showing Democrats leading or closely contesting key races, including some for normally deep-red Senate seats.

In a series of posts to his personal social media platform this morning, Trump appeared to back Pete Hegseth’s firing of the Pentagon’s top military planner, as well as his referral for prosecution in connection with an alleged leak of information.

Hegseth dismissed Gen Brett Sylvia, a high-ranking army strategist serving on the Pentagon’s joint staff, on Thursday following allegations that he shared classified information.

On Friday, Trump shared a pair of screenshots to Truth Social of conservative commentators applauding Hegseth’s decision and calling for the general’s prosecution.

One of those posts refererred to Sylvia as a “traitor” and said he should be “sent to Leavenworth,” the prison for military personnel convicted in a court-martial.

Speaking to a Kansas City radio host this morning, Donald Trump said – as he has many times before – that an end to the Iran war is imminent.

The wary, Trump said, “is going to get wrapped up soon,” Trump said ‌in an interview with Kansas City ​radio host Pete Mundo.

Trump said the conflict’s resolution would require “a guarantee there’ll never be ⁠a nuclear weapon” in Iran.

Since launching the war in February with hopes for a quick capitulation from Iran’s decimated leadership, Trump has consistently expressed the belief that the war would end, even as fighting has escalated and economic shocks from the conflict have multiplied. On the campaign trail, he has asserted that fighting will end soon after the US midterms, so long as Republicans maintain a majority in Congress.

Recent reporting indicates that the President may be preparing another round of intense military action on Iran, in the event the country’s leadership doesn’t agree to a deal.

Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola has denied that she knew anything about an effort to put another candidate on the Alaska ballot with the same name as the Republican incumbent as the Justice Department escalated a criminal investigation with new grand jury subpoenas.

“I just want to clear the air,” she said at the top of a speech in a downtown bar in Juneau, Alaska’s capital.

“I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters.”

Peltola is running against senator Dan Sullivan. A person familiar with the matter told the Associated Press that subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony or documents, along with records preservation demands, were issued after The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J Sullivan Jr as part of an alleged effort to confuse voters.

Members of Congress sent a scathing letter to federal immigration officials this week demanding answers about conditions inside a Texas immigration jail, as detained immigrants on a prolonged hunger strike claim officials are retaliating against them and threatening them with force-feeding.

A group of seven congressional Democrats sent the letter earlier this week to Markwayne Mullin, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) secretary, and David Venturella, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) acting director, protesting about the treatment of hunger strikers.

The El Valle detention facility in Raymondville, Texas, detaining men and women, has fallen under scrutiny in recent weeks for allegations of harsh conditions. Detained immigrants on hunger strike say the facility has substandard medical care, undrinkable water and guards that mistreat them.

Some hunger strikers are also protesting against their prolonged detention and are asking for their cases to move more quickly or to be transferred closer to loved ones in other parts of the country.

“It is abundantly clear that DHS continues to demonstrate gross disregard for the health, dignity, personhood, and safety of our communities,” the group of lawmakers, led by the Illinois representative Delia Ramirez, said in their letter to the DHS and ICE. “However, we remain committed to conducting oversight, advocating for our constituents, and pursuing accountability.”

The representatives “unequivocally condemn” conditions reported at the facility.

Donald Trump has cancelled weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas, instead opting to support Republican candidates with tele-rallies as midterm campaigning reaches its final days ahead of the midterms.

Trump was scheduled to hold in-person rallies on Saturday and Sunday but the Republican National Committee (RNC) announced that he would instead spend a “72-hour sprint” doing rallies by phone rather than in person.

It is a move the RNC said would maximize Trump’s ability to speak to voters nationwide, adding that telerallies are planned for nearly 20 states and more may be announced.

It marks an abrupt shift in Trump’s pledge to push through the final days of the campaign doing rally after rally to galvanize his supporters. As of Thursday, he had done 25 rallies during the month of October, falling short of a goal he had once placed north of 30.

The president travelled to South Carolina yesterday for the second time in a month, a sign of Republican anxiety about Darline Graham’s ability to fend off a robust challenge from Democratic candidate Annie Andrews for a critical US Senate seat.

Voters in South Carolina have not sent a Democrat to the Senate in nearly three decades. But Andrews, a pediatrician who previously ran unsuccessfully for Congress , is urging voters seeking change to “try something new for once.”

Beyond South Carolina, Republicans are entering the final days of this year’s midterm elections navigating tight contests in Texas, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska. Both parties are also closely following developments in the Mississippi Senate race, AP reported.

Trump lashed out at a Reuters reporter who asked him why he cancelled the planned appearance at a rally in Kansas on Saturday in support of a embattled Republican senator, Dr Roger Marshall. “You’re sick to ask that question,” the president said.

Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for Ohio governor, confirmed on Thursday that his campaign is no longer airing an attack ad that features the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Dr Amy Acton.

Donald Trump called again for Democrat Mary Peltola to be criminally prosecuted and disqualified from the Alaska Senate race for her campaign allegedly recruiting a man named Dan Sullivan to run against Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed will campaign on Sunday in Detroit with Haley Stevens, the congresswoman he narrowly defeated to win the Democratic party’s nomination in August.

Tom Hoyle, who achieved instant viral fame on Thursday by comparing Trump supporters to a cult in a live interview with Fox News before the president’s rally in South Carolina, was removed from the venue by three Secret Service agents.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘Amateur morons’: Flávio Bolsonaro’s short-lived ‘president-elect’ claim met with mockery
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Brazilian media ridicule defeated candidate over ‘shameful’ absconsion to US and bizarre letter with wrong coat of arms

Flávio Bolsonaro had hoped that by Sunday night people would be calling him the next president of Brazil.

Instead, the far-right politician’s decision to flee to the United States after losing the election and – for 58 minutes – declare himself “Brazil’s true president-elect”, has made him a laughing stock, with Brazilian newspapers and commentators raining a barrage of scornful adjectives down on the conquered candidate.

“If it served any purpose at all, Flávio’s foolishness liberated the democratic right from a family of coup-mongers, which for far too long held it hostage to their reckless folly and irremediable disdain for Brazil,” the conservative Estado de São Paulo newspaper thundered on Friday.

Bolsonaro fled to Miami on Tuesday, 48 hours after being beaten by his leftwing adversary, the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, by 4.4m votes. Lula’s victory has been recognised by rightwing leaders from around the world, including El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, not to mention Bolsonaro’s own party and many key allies.

But on Wednesday after landing in the US, Bolsonaro published an outlandish letter – reportedly produced with the help of ChatGPT – in which he declared himself “the true president-elect of Brazil” and made phoney claims about election fraud.

Perhaps most bizarrely, the far-right absconder claimed he would continue to lead Brazil’s opposition from abroad, comparing himself to Charles de Gaulle, who in the 1940s led a French government-in-exile against the Nazis from London, and the Cuban independence hero José Martí, who challenged the Spanish empire from New York.

“They were all treated as criminals by the regimes they confronted. History called them something else,” Bolsonaro said, also likening himself to Venezuela’s Nobel laureate María Corina Machado and Rui Barbosa, a Brazilian politician who went into exile in London in the late 19th century after challenging an authoritarian president known as “the Iron Marshal”.

Just under an hour after Bolsonaro’s proclamation was first published on social media, a corrected version was issued, altering his claimed status to “leader of Brazil” – reportedly after he was upbraided by Trump administration officials keen to avoid a full-blown diplomatic split with Brazil’s actual leaders.

The amended letter also updated the out-of-date Brazilian coat of arms that had been used erroneously in the letterhead of the first version referring to the “United States of Brazil” – a name the South American country has not used since 1967.

Bolsonaro’s flight – and his brief but bogus claim to be “president-elect” of one of the world’s largest democracies – prompted a ferocious outpouring of opprobrium and ridicule.

“[This letter] seems to have been written by a foolhardy, loony halfwit,” Flávia Oliveira, a prominent political commentator, told the network GloboNews.

The Estado de São Paulo’s leader writers said: “Flávio’s letter isn’t worth the ink of this newspaper, but there’s no way the embarrassment can be ignored,” before savaging a man they called “a con artist of the highest order”.

The Rio broadsheet O Globo said Bolsonaro’s “shameful and sneaky” decision to abscond laid bare the “pathetic” nature of his political movement, Bolsonarismo, while the Folha de São Paulo said it exposed the true nature of the “authoritarian, ignorant, incompetent” Bolsonaro family.

José Casado, a columnist for the conservative magazine Veja, wrote: “The comedy storyline has already guaranteed him a spot in the pages of political satire.”

Merval Pereira, a conservative columnist for O Globo, called Bolsonaro “a madhouse Napoleon”.

Even Silas Malafaia, a pugnacious televangelist who is close to Bolsonaro’s jailed father, Jair Bolsonaro, had harsh words. “Bolsonaro’s kids are jackasses … A bunch of amateur morons,” Malafaia was quoted as saying by O Globo.

Some observers see Bolsonaro’s post-defeat getaway as proof that his dispirited movement is dead. “I think Bolsonarismo was defeated once and for all,” Lula’s chief foreign policy adviser, Celso Amorim, said this week, calling the result “the last gasp of a radical, irrational, lying rightwing”.

The Estado de São Paulo’s editorial board agreed. “Flávio belongs to the past and will soon vanish into the basement of political irrelevance from which he should never have emerged,” they predicted, urging conservatives to ditch Bolsonaro and throw their weight behind his ally Tarcísio de Freitas, the São Paulo governor.

Others warn Bolsonarismo will remain a powerful political force, even if the Bolsonaro family’s leadership of the far-right movement is now in doubt.

Social media users were also merciless in their reaction to Bolsonaro’s short-lived claim to be “president-elect”. One meme invited supporters to attend his January inauguration – at Cinderella Castle in Walt Disney World, Orlando. Another parodied his movement’s fascist-inspired slogan “God, Homeland and Family”, which became “Goodbye, Homeland and Family”.

Donald Trump has declined to publicly recognise the result of an election he has called “a very great embarrassment to the people of Brazil”. But a US diplomatic cable obtained by the Folha de São Paulo called Lula’s victory “surprising but definitive”.

Asked if he saw Bolsonaro as Brazil’s “rightful” leader, Trump replied: “I won’t get involved.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Gulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says report
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
IISS study questions overreliance on American support and ‘overdependence on expensive, high-end systems’

Gulf states are going to have to reconfigure their trillion-dollar defences given the damage inflicted on their economies and the questionable continued value of US bases in the face of Iranian attack, according to a study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

The report says that in the weeks before the 8 April ceasefire, 12 regional states, overwhelmingly in the Gulf, faced 4,670 Iranian one-way attack drones and more than 1,400 ballistic missiles. Nearly half were aimed at the United Arab Emirates. Although the vast majority were repelled, one estimate of the damage to energy infrastructure cited by the report is put as high as $58bn (£43bn).

Iran would portray either a reduction or complete withdrawal of US forces from the region as “a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness, but also use it to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection”.

The report says the war also highlights another “uncomfortable truth for the Gulf states: not only has their trillion-dollar acquisition of US weapons not translated into US protection at the crucial time, but their respective militaries are also not adequately prepared for the new kind of attritional air war to which they are being exposed”.

Despite huge investment in mainly US armaments, the report identified significant shortcomings: “overwhelming reliance on US-supplied air- and missile-defence systems and munitions; a failure to achieve regional defence integration; a shortage of minesweeping capability; limited retaliatory options; and the prohibitive costs stemming from an overdependence on expensive, high-end systems to take down relatively inexpensive drones and missiles”.

The report is neutral on whether the divided Gulf states should seek a new non-aggression pact with Iran, but notes that the US-Iran war has shown longstanding defence and security partnerships with the US “have failed to ensure adequate protection against Iranian aggression”.

It adds: “If anything, US military bases and defence partnerships with the US have provided Iran with another pretext for attacks against the Gulf states.”

Public opinion on the US in the Gulf has also been shifting, it says, “from security provider to strategic liability”.

Any reduction or withdrawal of US forces from the Gulf region would be portrayed by Iran “as a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness” and would also be used “to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection,” the report notes.

The study comes after Chris Murphy, the Democrat senator and member of the senate foreign relations committee, said a debate was under way in the US military about the value of seeking to rebuild the damaged US bases in the Gulf.

Murphy said the Gulf state leadership “want us to rebuild” and “to keep a presence in the region”, but asked: “What good is it to have a base in the region to protect American interests if within 24 hours of a hot war starting, it is wiped off the map?

“We would be criminally incompetent as stewards of taxpayer dollars if we were to rebuild bases that are blown up within hours of the next war starting.

“So clearly, we are going to have to have a smaller footprint in the region, and the limiting principle on the footprint that we rebuild will be ‘what can we protect?’ because we clearly cannot protect the scope of our footprint today and if we can’t protect it, it is useless.”

Murphy suggested that, at the very least, the US may need to relocate its bases in the eastern Mediterranean further away from Iranian missiles.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: James Comey lawyers seek to have third criminal case dismissed
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Guardian staff and agency
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Federal judge to hear arguments on Friday over leak case that was twice previously investigated with no action taken

Lawyers for the former FBI director James Comey will ask a federal judge on Friday to block the US justice department from pursuing its third criminal case against him.

Comey is an outspoken critic of Donald Trump, in open feud since the US president fired him from that post early in his first term, and he is a frequent target of Republican outrage.

Court documents unsealed on Monday showed that the Trump administration this month bypassed a grand jury and filed a charging document known as a “criminal information” over allegations of a decade-old and previously investigated news media leak.

The justice department defended the maneuver as an effort to extend the legal time limit for seeking a grand jury indictment, but Comey’s lawyers have called the case legally invalid.

US district judge Trevor McFadden in Washington, DC was expected to hear arguments on that question on Friday. He was appointed by Trump.

The latest effort to prosecute Comey, who says he is innocent of the allegations, is part of a series of politically charged investigative actions the department has undertaken in the run-up to next week’s midterm elections.

Comey was FBI director when Trump first took office, having been appointed to that role in 2013 by Barack Obama. He oversaw an investigation into whether Trump’s presidential campaign conspired with Russia to tip the 2016 election in the Republican’s favor over the Democratic party nominee, Hillary Clinton. The two men have been bitterly at odds since, with Comey likening Trump to a corrupt mafia don “untethered to the truth” in a book he published, and the president accusing him of treason and calling for his imprisonment.

The first criminal case against Comey, filed in federal court in Virginia, accused him of lying to Congress in 2020 but was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who brought the charges was illegally appointed.

A separate, pending indictment charges Comey with threatening Trump via a snapshot posted on Instagram of seashells in the numerical arrangement of “86 47” – 86 is slang meaning “to throw out”, “to get rid of” or “to refuse service to”, and Trump is the 47th president. The former FBI director has sought to dismiss the case.

The latest allegation concerns an October 2016 New York Times story related to a secret court order that required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. The story cited two government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity about the order from a judge on the foreign intelligence surveillance court that Yahoo was barred from publicly disclosing.

Federal authorities, including prosecutor John Durham, began investigating the disclosure in early 2017. Durham, who later investigated the FBI’s conduct as it scrutinized potential ties between Russia and Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, wrote a classified memo in December 2018 recommending no criminal charges against anyone in connection with the disclosure, Comey’s attorneys said in a recent court filing.

In 2019, the US attorney’s office for the District of Columbia, the federal prosecutors in that district, opened a second investigation of the same matter under the code name Tropical Vortex. But that investigation was closed without any charges filed in early 2020.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: British student pilot among three dead after two helicopters collide in Oregon
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Anna Betts
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Flight instructor, 22, and pilot, 38, among other fatalities after mid-air collision occurs near small airport

Three people have been killed after two helicopters collided in mid-air near a small airport in Oregon on Thursday, authorities have confirmed.

The Yamhill county sheriff’s office said on Thursday that it received reports at about 2.10pm local time about an aircraft incident involving two helicopters that had crashed south-east of McMinnville, near McMinnville municipal airport.

“We located two crashed helicopters in a private farm field,” the Yamhill county sheriff, Sam Elliott, said at a news conference.

Elliott confirmed that the crash involved a 1995 Robinson R22 helicopter and a 2018 Airbus AS 350B3 helicopter. He said two people were onboard the Robinson and one onboard the Airbus.

The sheriff identified one of the victims onboard the Robinson helicopter as a student pilot from the United Kingdom, and said that local authorities were working with the British consulate and the FBI to notify the individual’s family.

The second occupant of the Robinson helicopter was identified as Maddie Aasbo, 22, a flight instructor from Texas.

The sole occupant of the Airbus helicopter was its pilot, 38-year-old Tyler Sturdevant from Newberg, Oregon.

Elliott said that the crash site had since been “turned over to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the National Transportation Safety Board (NSTB)”, which will investigate the collision.

In a statement on Thursday, the FAA confirmed that “a Robinson R22 helicopter and an Airbus H125 helicopter collided in mid-air near McMinnville Municipal Airport in Oregon around 2:15 pm local time on Thursday”.

“The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board will investigate,” the agency said, adding that the NTSB would take charge “of the investigation and will provide further updates”.

Meanwhile, local aviation school Jerry Trimble Helicopters, located in McMinnville, said in a statement shared on social media it was “deeply saddened to confirm that one of our aircraft was involved in an aviation incident this afternoon” near the McMinnville municipal airport.

“Our hearts and thoughts are with the individuals involved, their families and everyone affected by this event,” they said. The company added that it was “fully cooperating” with local and federal authorities “to secure the site and determine the cause of the incident”.

https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/o.title: Ousted 60 Minutes correspondent Cecilia Vega on overhaul at CBS News: ‘It hurts to watch’
https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/o.author: Jeremy Barr in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/o.text:
Vega said she still doesn’t know why she was fired from the show, which has experienced a slump in ratings

Cecilia Vega, the 60 Minutes correspondent fired as part of a dramatic overhaul of the CBS News show this spring, said it “hurts” to see what has happened to the storied newsmagazine and other segments of the network, and repeated allegations that she was told to insert “factually untrue” information into her work.

“It pains me. It hurts to watch, from afar. It hurts to talk to my colleagues who are still there. It hurts to see the ratings slump that is happening right now,” Vega said during a Thursday evening talk for students at American University in Washington DC.

Vega was among several correspondents and producers fired in May as part of a revamp of the show by CBS News’ editor-in-chief, Bari Weiss, who hired the tech journalist Nick Bilton as executive producer. Her contract as a 60 Minutes correspondent was not due to expire until March 2027, leading to – still unresolved – confusion about why she was targeted for termination.

“I still don’t know why I was fired,” she said. “I was not given a reason. I was fired without cause. I just find it exceptionally disturbing.”

CBS News management also parted ways with correspondent Scott Pelley “for cause”, after he clashed with Bilton, and declined to renew correspondent Sharyn Alfonsi’s contract. The show’s executive producer Tanya Simon was also fired, along with several other top producers.

Weiss opted to upend the show despite industry-leading ratings. The 58th season of the show averaged 9.1 million viewers, up 9% compared with the previous season. This season has seen softer ratings – the show’s most recent episode drew just 5.64 million viewers, the smallest audience this century for the sixth episode of a 60 Minutes season. Weiss said during an industry conference on Wednesday that she was not “focused” on the show’s ratings and was instead focused on building the network.

“I still don’t know why the overhaul, and it’s hard to watch,” Vega said. “It’s really hard to watch what’s happened.” As for the broader corporate strategy for the network, which is now owned by David Ellison’s Skydance, she said: “I don’t know what the endgame is. I think it’s a real mystery.”

During her talk, Vega repeated her contention that newsroom managers attempted to insert political bias into her stories for the show, efforts she resisted.

“I felt like people had to know what was happening in there, that the news that they are seeing, in my experience, had become compromised,” she said on Thursday. “Some of the stories I did, and some of the things that I was asked to do. I held the line, and Scott held the line, and Sharyn held the line, and I think people are still holding the line over there. But what they are having to go through, or what we had to go through, should never happen in a newsroom.”

Vega said she was “told to put information that is just factually untrue in a piece of journalism”, though she said she “can’t prescribe a motive” as to why she was told to do so.

CBS News has denied Vega’s claims of political bias, which she expressed during an appearance at the National Association of Hispanic Journalists Conference & Expo this summer.

“We respect Ms Vega and her contributions, but her claims are not based in reality,” a network spokesperson said in late May.

Vega, who was wearing a shirt honoring the late labor leader Dolores Huerta, was interviewed by Antoine Sanfuentes, a former NBC News and CNN executive who serves as an adjunct professor at the university.

Vega was hired as a 60 Minutes correspondent in early 2023, after serving as chief White House correspondent and an anchor at ABC News. She was brought on by the show’s then-executive producer, Bill Owens, who resigned from CBS News in protest in April 2025. She was the show’s first Latina correspondent.

Pelley has continued to speak publicly about his time at 60 Minutes, asserting that political pressure was applied to make stories more palatable to the Trump administration.

“In my experience, and having talked to my colleagues as well, there was an imperative to move our coverage in the direction of the president. To put a thumb on the scale, if you will, in terms of the president’s viewpoint,” he said during a panel discussion on Wednesday.

“I had never seen anything like this. This was corporate influence coming into the news division saying, ‘We want you to report stories with this particular bent, in terms of politics.’ It was anathema to all of us who had worked at 60 Minutes for so many years, and we fought the battle against it. We pushed back against it.”

Like Pelley, Vega expressed concerns about what might happen to the journalists who work at CBS News and CNN now that they are owned by the same company – and could merge. “I’m fearful for job security. I’m fearful for editorial independence. I hope folks can hold the line, but I don’t have a crystal ball and I’m not going to predict what happens. It makes me nervous for sure.”

Speaking to a room of students, the 49-year-old Vega said she “has no idea” if she will join another legacy media outlet – or do something independently.

Acknowledging uncertainty in the media industry, she told the students: “I don’t know what it’s going to look like when you’re going to get a job. I don’t even know what it’s going to look like when I get a job. Hopefully.”

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: Basketweavers get in a twist over Alexander Skarsgård’s Wicker Husband
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Chloe Mac Donnell
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
Why is he not made of willow? Why is he plaited and not woven? World’s basket makers have plenty of questions

Hollywood heart-throbs are known for their good looks and charisma. But in a classic plot twist, the latest big-screen dreamboat causing viewers to get hot and bothered isn’t even human.

Alexander Skarsgård’s Wicker Husband character in the romcom Wicker has sent the internet into a frenzy.

“Never looking at my patio furniture the same again,” says one Instagram comment. Ikea captioned a picture of its wicker furniture with the term “husband material”.

The basketweaving community, however, is getting worked up for very different reasons. The fact the Wicker Husband isn’t made of willow, and he appears to be plaited rather than woven, has angered some makers.

Deborah Needleman, former editor of the New York Times’s T magazine turned basket maker, was one of the first to question it. Writing on Instagram, she said: “I’m excited that the basketweaving community now has our own hot, woven leading man, but I’ve also got issues. Why is a dude woven in an English fishing village not made of willow – or even rush?!” More than 100 fellow basket makers have since weighed in.

The Oxford English dictionary defines wicker as “thin sticks of wood twisted together to make baskets, furniture etc”.

Eleanor Morgan, trade adviser to the Worshipful Company of Basketmakers in London, says that while willow has commonly been used to denote wicker, it is less popular today. “Historically wicker could have meant any pliant twig or osier,” she says.

Joe Dunckley, a prosthetic designer at Wētā workshop, the special effects studio in New Zealand that created the upper body of the Wicker Husband, says it was a “big challenge” to create a costume for a character that is sentient but made of wicker. “Most prosthetic materials are soft to mimic skin. But he’s not flesh and bone.”

To get the wicker effect, Dunckley and his team of 80 specialists created 50 interlocking body pieces for Skarsgård to wear. Using a rubber-like thermoplastic elastomer, they were able to 3D print a bespoke weave coded by the studio that was then attached to a spandex suit. During the 18-month process they also created 10 facial appliances.

Dunckley says willow wasn’t a viable option for what they needed the suit to be able to do. “It is a similar reason to why, in film, we don’t make armour out of actual steel or use real swords. This is a fantasy film.”

Lewis Prosser, a basket maker from Cardiff, says every maker is thinking about how they would have approached the task. “It certainly isn’t the way I would have done it, but that doesn’t mean that it is bad,” he says.

Prosser says his understanding of wicker is that it is “an object that is woven but one that is specifically not textile”, adding that “some will disagree with me”. Some basket makers, including Needleman, argue that wicker refers to a type of weave rather than a material.

For Prosser, who creates wicker costumes using techniques traditionally found in Wales and the south-west of England, there are three main ways to make a basket. Coiling, where threads of plant materials are wound together in a spiral, braiding, or stake and stand basketry whereby vertical rods are woven through horizontal strands. “What we would traditionally call ‘wicker items’ would usually have that latter aspect,” Prosser says. The Wicker Husband does not.

Although the actor Olivia Colman and her fellow villagers in the film speak in a range of British dialects, the film is not set in England. Dunckley suggests the basket maker character played by Peter Dinklage has travelled the world, learning skills from other makers.

Prosser says that if the film had been set in a specific location, it would be more authentic for the costume to reflect the plants that grow there. In the UK, willow would be apt, whereas in Spain, Esparto grass would be fitting.

Dunckley and his team worked using a 3D cast of Skarsgård to ensure the “audience would be able to recognise Alexander in basket form”. Key to this is what Dunckley calls the “Skarsgård smoulder”, which they captured by ensuring the weave could furrow at the brow. His hair, beard and lashes were made from muka, fibres from New Zealand flax.

Describing the interest and criticism from the weaving community as “really cool”, Dunckley says: “I don’t blame anyone. True artists of the craft have dedicated years to it. I would expect them to look at a fantasy version of their art form and see failings in it.”

For the willow purists, Morgan says “there is no lack of osier-related eye candy” in the film, pointing to a plethora of basket scenes. Prosser says he is thrilled the film has drawn attention to basket making, especially as some skills and traditional techniques are now endangered. TikTok is rife with wicker costume making guides, including nipple tutorials which Skarsgård has said was the “best part” of his suit. He gave his own pair to the TV host Graham Norton describing them as “extraordinary craftsmanship”.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: A rare red line in deeply cynical times
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Lauren Gambino
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
It’s been a particularly brutal cycle for attack ads, but voters are responding with humanity. Plus: on the campaign trail with a Democrat in Kansas

This was originally published in the Stakes 2026, a newsletter about the midterm elections. Sign up to get it in your inbox

There’s a campaign moment I can’t stop thinking about. It happened shortly after the campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio, released a shocking attack ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.

In the ad, as many readers will know by now, Acton’s mother accuses her daughter of lying and tells Ohioans not to vote for her. Acton, 60, says she has not spoken to her mother since she was 12, when she and her brother were removed from their mother’s custody after their stepfather was arrested and charged with raping her. Acton says she last saw her mother at the courthouse, where her mother came to support her husband as her daughter testified against him.

The moment that captured my attention took place at a campaign event on a farm in Wharton, Ohio, and it was much less newsy. Acton was speaking to a group of supporters and a woman asked: “Can I give you a hug?”

“Of course you can,” the candidate replied, walking over and allowing herself to be embraced. After watching the ad, the woman told Acton: “All I wanted to do was cry and hug you and tell you it’ll be OK.”

It was a small moment of humanity in what has otherwise been a particularly vicious campaign season, even by the standards of the Trump era. After weeks of wondering ‘how much lower can they go’, particularly on the right, Ramaswamy pulled out a shovel and dug deeper.

In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate, has faced a barrage of ads attacking his religion (he is Muslim) and claiming, baselessly, that he has ties to Islamic terrorist organizations. As Donald Trump barnstorms the country trying to salvage Republicans’ majorities in Congress, he has hurled Islamophobic invectives at El-Sayed.

In Texas, the Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and his allies have pumped out controversial ads – many of them AI-generated – that attack his opponent James Talarico as effeminate and misstate his position on transgender rights. JD Vance doubled down on that line of attack, baselessly musing that Talarico was gay.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, both Trump and Vance have defended Ramaswamy’s ad. “Stop whining,” the vice-president told Republicans who had called for the ad to come down. Ramaswamy, a billionaire entrepreneur who has embraced the president’s never-back-down, politics-as-bloodsport ethos, was defiant.

Many Republicans, including the state’s outgoing governor, Mike DeWine, have condemned the ad alongside Acton. “It’s wrong to run this ad,” said DeWine, who has endorsed Ramaswamy. On Thursday, amid mounting pressure and polling that found the ad backfiring, Ramaswamy said that his campaign had discontinued it.

Politics has never been for the faint of heart. Attack ads have long been a tool of political combat. In 1964, Lyndon Johnson’s presidential campaign pulled the so-called “Daisy” ad from TV amid fierce public criticism over its suggestion that the Republican nominee, Barry Goldwater, would wage nuclear war if elected.

The “Daisy” ad seems almost quaint now, from the vantage point of 2026, a year in which the US president threatened to “annihilate” Iran in a speech before the United Nations general assembly.

Trump has crossed so many red lines since he emerged as a presidential candidate in 2015 – gleefully breaking political, legal and constitutional norms – that it can be hard to tell what the rules of engagement are any more. He has mocked world leaders, flattered dictators, disparaged political opponents as the “enemy within”, encouraged violence against protesters, called a female journalist “piggy”, declared that undocumented immigrants were “poisoning the blood” of the country, and on and on.

So it took me by surprise that the Ramaswamy ad was met with such strong bipartisan condemnation – the rare red line in deeply cynical times.

The ruthless ad aired in Ohio, a one-time presidential battleground that has shifted toward Republicans in recent election cycles but is home this year to several competitive races. Will the ad have a blast radius that hurts other Republicans in the state, like Jon Husted, the incumbent Ohio senator whose posterior Trump can’t stop raving about?

Acton must have known when she decided to run that the campaign would be ugly. She first rose to prominence in early 2020 as the director of the Ohio department of health. She became an early face of the pandemic response and, in the beginning, was roundly praised for her clearly communicated daily briefings, inspiring bobblehead dolls and little girls’ Halloween costumes. But as backlash brewed against the state’s lockdown measures, she also became a high-profile target of armed protests outside her home, antisemitic slurs (Acton is Jewish) and misinformation campaigns.

At a campaign event earlier this fall, an armed man was arrested after lunging at Acton as she spoke at a county fair. She was not injured, and Acton, a physician, stayed on site to treat one of the onlookers injured in the episode.

For many disgusted voters in Ohio, the choice on Tuesday is now between a woman who at 12 took the stand in court to testify against her mother’s husband – the man charged with raping her, while her mother stood by his side – and a man who allowed that dark story to be twisted into a political attack ad.

Kansas hasn’t elected a Democrat to the US Senate in nearly 100 years. Adam Hamilton is running to change that.

Hamilton, a United Methodist pastor, is challenging the Republican incumbent, Senator Roger Marshall, who was elected in 2020.

My colleague, Rachel Leingang, was recently in the unexpected battleground state to catch Hamilton on the campaign trail.

Hamilton, a former Republican who had considered running as an independent, regularly points to one of his state’s most famous residents: Dorothy from The Wizard of Oz. Recalling a visit he made to Liberal, Kansas, and its Oz museum, he asks the audience to recall what Dorothy’s companions on her journey need. The lion needed courage, the scarecrow a brain and the tin man a heart.

Read more: Kansas Democrat’s pitch to voters amid historic Senate bid: ‘I’m gonna just fight like hell’

double quotation markWe’re watching a bit of a political revolution play out in slow motion.

– Stan Barnes, a political consultant and former Republican state senator in Arizona, referring to his party’s eroding support in the suburbs around Maricopa county, which has powered a slate of Democratic victories in the years since Trump was first elected to the White House

This year, Arizona Democrats believe they can finally flip congressional district 1, where Democrat Amish Shah – an emergency room doctor who narrowly lost the seat in 2024 – and Republican Jay Feely – a former National Football League kicker backed by Donald Trump – are battling for the House seat left open by Republican congressman David Schweikert.

Read more: ‘A revolution in slow motion’: is Arizona’s wealthiest district finally done with Trump?

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: As Trump escalates extreme attacks, Democrats – finally – rally round El-Sayed
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Joseph Gedeon in Detroit
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Endorsement not always full-throated but party backing marks major turn after bitter split over nomination

Facing a barrage of extreme attacks from Donald Trump and his allies, the Democratic establishment is finally rallying around progressive Abdul El-Sayed, the party’s candidate in the closely watched US Senate election in Michigan. But the endorsement is not always full-throated, and often even omits his name.

At a rally in Port Huron on Sunday, the US president launched the latest in a wave of Islamophobic rants against El-Sayed, erroneously branding him a “jihadist” and “Muslim Brotherhood member” while invoking 9/11.

But prominent Democrats have lined up to support El-Sayed. That same weekend, the independent senator Bernie Sanders rallied with him in Grand Rapids, and former president Barack Obama stood beside him in Detroit. Days earlier, the New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez toured the state with him.

This last-ditch show of solidarity marks a turn for a party that split bitterly over El-Sayed’s nomination in August, which he narrowly clinched by beating a moderate pro-Israel candidate backed by much of the central party machine.
