The Michigan Senate race – which could help decide which party controls the entire chamber – is close, according to polls, which have typically given El-Sayed a small lead over his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.

Senior Democrats have increasingly traveled to Michigan to back a nominee who many of the party’s leaders did not back in the primary – while making clear they are not fully aligned.

In an effort to close the gap, Republicans have doubled down on their incendiary attacks. Trump has repeatedly called him “Mohammed” this month, and the National Republican Senatorial Committee has aired ads using his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.

El-Sayed, who was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrants, has dismissed such attacks as a distraction. “He knows my name is Abdul. He says it every day,” he said in a statement, accusing the president of trying to “use my name and my faith to distract us” from the cost of gas, groceries and healthcare.

A former Detroit and Wayne county health official, El-Sayed is running on a platform that endorses the Medicare for All proposed system of universal healthcare, and calls for taking corporate money out of politics, taxing billionaires and corporations and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). He has also called for ending US military aid to Israel, while calling its war in Gaza a genocide.

A Marist poll last week put El-Sayed at 50% and Rogers at 48% among likely voters. He was trailing by nearly two to one in ad spending as of early October.

Obama’s Saturday appearance in Detroit was the clearest sign of the shift by the Democrat party heirarchy. He joined El-Sayed on stage on the first day of early voting – his first public show of support for El-Sayed since the August primary – while a protest held by the white nationalist and 6 January rioter Jake Lang took place outside.

The former president likened the attacks on El-Sayed’s name to those he faced himself. “I remind them his name was Barack,” El-Sayed said.

Obama, whose 57% favorable rating in a CNN poll conducted in May is the highest of any living president, also rejected the idea that El-Sayed is radical. “What is so radical about wanting everybody to have healthcare?” he asked, saying El-Sayed would “finish the job we started” with the Affordable Care Act.

But Obama acknowledged that he did not agree with El-Sayed, who has criticized some of his decisions as president, all the time. “We are not going to agree on every detail of every issue,” he said. “You know who else doesn’t agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama.”

Both Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders have transferred $1m to the El-Sayed campaign. Former vice-president Kamala Harris appeared with him in Detroit last month.

Senator Elissa Slotkin, who spoke at the same rally, told the crowd she was counting on El-Sayed as a partner in confronting Trump’s agenda in Congress. Yet she has also said she and El-Sayed “don’t agree on everything — and that’s OK”, and previously argued that condemning the leftwing streamer Hasan Piker, with whom El-Sayed has campaigned, should not be hard.

Others have been more guarded. The Senate Democratic leader,Chuck Schumer, who has now endorsed El-Sayed, said his views on Israel were “much different than mine”, while the former congressman Sander Levin endorsed him despite what he called “significant disagreement” on the same subject. Representative Hillary Scholten said she would not campaign with anyone who associates with Piker.

Senator Cory Booker of New Jersey, who has historically been pro-Israel, gave a similarly noncommittal answer on CNN on Wednesday, when anchor Boris Sanchez played a clip of a Black pastor saying some voters fear that El-Sayed would prioritize issues abroad such as Gaza over Michigan’s needs.

Booker spoke about his family roots in Michigan and about “winning back the Senate” without mentioning El-Sayed by name. When Sanchez pointed out to him this was not “a ringing endorsement”, Booker remained stone-faced, and the segment continued.

But the coolest response came from Haley Stevens, the pro-Israel congresswoman El-Sayed beat in August by less than a point. She had been backed by groups including the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) , which spent close to $30m backing her – the lobby’s largest investment in a single race.

Asked by CNN’s Dana Bash on Sunday whether she was still fully behind him, she said she was “on the team”. “You didn’t mention Abdul El-Sayed in that last answer,” Bash noted. Stevens replied that she had urged El-Sayed to give a speech addressing Black voters’ concerns, and that it had not happened.

In the primary, Stevens beat El-Sayed in Wayne county, home to majority-Black Detroit, taking about 51% of the Democratic vote to his 45%. Obama urged Saturday’s crowd to back the full ticket.

El-Sayed and Stevens are set to campaign together on Sunday – two days before election day – it emerged last night, in what would be their first joint public appearance in months.

Rogers, meanwhile, is courting Jewish voters, traditionally more likely to back Democrats, by telling the Jewish Telegraphic Agency that El-Sayed is “anti-Jew”, a charge El-Sayed rejects.

Whether a cautious and caveated embrace by the Democratic establishment is enough for El-Sayed will be settled on Tuesday, in a state Trump won by less than two points in 2024.

If El-Sayed wins, he would be the first Muslim US senator. To get there, he has already pulled a skeptical party machine toward his side.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Five reasons why the US midterms matter for the climate – and your energy bill
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Hilary Beaumont
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Voters are feeling the pinch of Trump’s anti-climate agenda as energy costs rise, but a shake-up in Congress could shift things

If the polls can be believed, the US could see a blue wave in the midterms, giving Democrats a chance to take back the House and Senate, and gaining up to four governor’s seats.

These wins could give Democrats new power to resist Donald Trump’s anti-climate agenda, and to push forward climate policies at the state level. But if Republicans maintain power, it could further embolden Trump’s “drill, baby, drill” agenda and leave intact his administration’s latitude to continue dismantling regulatory measures his critics say protect public health and the planet.

The election will also be a test of how voters respond to Democratic candidates tying the biggest issue of the election – affordability – to the climate crisis.

If Democrats take control of the House or Senate, they won’t be able to overturn previous Republican actions like gutting the Inflation Reduction Act, and they can’t pass new legislation that Trump would veto, but they will have more cards to play to oppose Trump’s pro-fossil fuel agenda going forward.

If Democrats take back the House, it will mean the White House has to compromise with Democrats in order to pass budgets. This would give Democrats the power to add climate provisions into appropriations legislation, said Michael Gerrard, founder and director of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law. “Many appropriations begin in the House, and these are huge bills that have to pass, so it’s possible that some pro-climate provisions could be put in some of the appropriations legislation,” he said. “Often presidents sign appropriation bills that have provisions they don’t like because they need to get the budget passed.”

Democrats could also use their power in the House to launch investigations and subpoena witnesses and documents. Dan Farber, a law professor at the University of California, Berkeley, suggested they could investigate possible conflicts of interest or corruption, like the Trump administration intervening in a federal lawsuit to allow Elon Musk to continue using portable gas generators in his Mississippi datacenter, which the suit alleges is a violation of the Clean Air Act.

If Democrats win the Senate, they could oppose further confirmations of federal judges, cabinet officers and sub-cabinet positions. “That gives [Democratic] senators some leverage to stop appointments they don’t want,” Farber said. “But you can also hold appointments hostage in return for other things.”

Preventing appointments of anti-climate judges would leave more vacancies for the next president to fill, he added. “That can have a big long-term effect on the environment.”

Gerrard said a power shift in the House and Senate could change negotiations around the permitting bill which could clear hurdles for both clean energy and fossil fuels projects. The bill would significantly weaken the National Environmental Policy Act, making it impossible for a court to halt a project due to a Nepa violation, he said. “But if the Democrats are in charge of both the House and the Senate, that bill might look different.”

Farber and Gerrard said state climate policy was also hanging in the balance this November. The Cook Political Report found that Democrats could gain two-to-four governor’s seats this cycle. “If some of the governor’s offices flip from Republican to Democrat, that could yield a profound change in state climate policy,” Gerrard said.

If the Republicans buck polling predictions and manage to keep control of the House and Senate, it would embolden Trump to continue his anti-climate agenda.

Trump could continue his favoritism toward polluting companies, because Democrats would lack the investigative and subpoena powers to hold him accountable.

And he could continue appointing conservative justices: “Trump has been packing the lower courts with anti-regulatory, super-conservative judges,” Farber said.

Under this administration, Republican lawmakers have backed Trump on policies that were unfavorable to their constituents – such as voting to repeal clean energy tax credits that created jobs in their districts. If Republicans win in the midterms, Republicans would continue to vote in support of Trump. “Maybe even more so, because I think this would be seen as a big win for him personally,” Farber said.

“They have not just been sitting on the sidelines – they have helped Trump, in terms of repealing the Inflation Reduction Act from Biden, and overturning some specific regulations by Congress. We could see more of that kind of thing coming from them. So it would be another big step backwards,” Farber said.

“I keep thinking, how much worse could they do? But they always find something,” he added.

The administration’s constraints on renewables are forcing consumers to spend more on energy. A study by Nera predicted that between 2027 and 2033, economy-wide household energy costs would increase on average by $11.6bn annually from constraining the deployment of solar and wind. The region hardest hit by these constraints is Texas, where rates are forecast to rise as much as 22%, the study found.

Trump’s attacks on clean energy have also led to mass job losses, including many in battleground states. The US’s clean energy workforce lost nearly 37,000 jobs last year – the first annual job loss in America’s clean energy economy since the pandemic, according to a September report from E2, a business advocacy group for the clean economy that analyzed Department of Energy data.

A report from Climate Power puts that number even higher, with 173,000 clean energy jobs either cut or delayed since Trump took office. The report found that Texas saw the most jobs lost from Trump’s war on clean energy.

The Nera report found that increased reliance on natural gas capacity and generation raises reliability risks and increases exposure to price volatility. According to Climate Power, since Trump took office, gas and electric utilities have raised or sought to increase bills by more than $92bn, affecting more than 100 million customers across the country.

Polling shows that Democrats and Republicans in battleground states want candidates to talk more about the climate crisis. And even though one in three US adults have been directly affected by extreme weather, midterm candidates are avoiding talking directly about climate change in what’s known as “climate hushing”.

But researchers from the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability have found that there are three groups of Democratic candidates and officeholders who are talking about the climate crisis in subtle instead of direct ways: energy populists like Democrat Sherrod Brown in Ohio are using datacenters and utility bills to connect the issues of climate and affordability, climate champions like Arizona Democratic candidate JoAnna Mendoza are promising bold action like investing in clean energy, and candidates who are advocating for an “all-of-the-above” approach to energy, like Amy Acton in the Ohio governor’s race.

“The one thing that they all have in common is a focus on affordability … and talking about energy issues in the context of affordability,” said Geoffrey Henderson, an assistant environmental policy and planning professor at the University of Michigan.

He noted that a few candidates, like Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa, were emphasizing how extreme weather events worsened by the climate crisis are driving up the cost of insurance.

With various quiet climate messages being tested in battleground states, this election could be a test of how voters respond to these messages. Henderson expects political analysts will study the data after the election to draw lessons from it. “The climate message has in a number of ways been brought into alignment with the affordability question, and so I think this is a test of whether that combination resonates,” he said.

The issue of climate hushing has come up election after election, but Henderson believes it’s a positive thing that candidates are still finding ways to talk about climate, even indirectly. “It’s better that candidates are tying climate to affordability than not mentioning it at all, and I do see how different parts of the country lend themselves to different strategies.”

Environmental laws are being tested in US courts like never before. “We’re now at a stage where every significant environmental regulation is challenged in court by one side or the other,” Gerrard said.

The Trump administration has set out to weaken and revoke environmental regulations, triggering a wave of litigation attempting to undo those actions. If a future Democratic president tries to restore those regulations or issue new ones, they would also be challenged in court, Gerrard said.

Gerrard is closely watching the fight over Trump’s repeal of the endangerment finding, which stated that the buildup of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere endangers public health, allowing the Environmental Protection Agency to limit greenhouse gas pollution from various sources. “There’s a case before the DC circuit on Trump’s revocation of the endangerment finding – that’s a very big case,” he noted.

Gerrard is also looking ahead to the supreme court’s decision in the Suncor v Boulder case that will decide whether local officials in Boulder, Colorado, can force fossil fuel companies to pay for their share of damages from the climate crisis. If the justices rule against Boulder, it could block future climate damages cases, removing a vital method of accountability.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘The status quo sucks’: affordability and Trump loom over final stretch of Maine’s tight Senate race
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Shrai Popat in Portland, Maine
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Key contest between incumbent Republican Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson will gauge how voters feel about Trump 2.0 and rising costs

The 27-year-old fisher spends longer on the water when out hauling traps in Casco Bay, but the trade-off helps him save fuel at a time when costs have surged. Before the US war with Iran began in late February, filling his tank cost about $350 a week. Now it’s doubled to nearly $700.

“Last year at this time I had to go out and catch 40 lobsters to fill up my tank, this year it’s over 104,” LaMontagne said at Widgery Wharf in Portland, where his 34ft Wayne Beal boat is docked just steps away from the hum of tourists in the city’s Old Port.

Practically every part of Maine’s billion-dollar lobster industry has been squeezed by Trump administration policies like the Iran war and sweeping tariffs. Despite the economic pressures shaping his vote, LaMontagne remains undecided in the state’s tight Senate race.

One of the most closely watched contests of this midterm cycle pits Troy Jackson, the progressive lumberjack who mounted a breakneck 101-day campaign, against Susan Collins, the entrenched Republican incumbent seeking a sixth term. Democrats see Maine as critical to their effort to retake the upper chamber, though recent polling shows the nominees neck-and-neck heading into 3 November.

The race was beset by turmoil early on after the former Democratic nominee, Graham Platner, withdrew after a series of controversies, culminating in a sexual assault and rape allegation that he denied.

Now with less than a week to go, pocketbook concerns increasingly blend into a broader judgment of Donald Trump’s second administration. And Maine’s conflicted voters may decide the election.

In the final stretch of this often-acrimonious Senate competition, Jackson has cast himself as the working-class alternative to Collins’s three decades in Washington, arguing that her reputation for independence masks a voting record that ultimately benefits Trump.

The federal funding that she has brought in is “a pittance compared to what we’re losing”, Jackson said at a recent campaign event for Maine veterans in Brunswick, adding that Collins “takes credit for an awful lot” but won’t take credit for helping pass Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which he said is “crushing” the state.

Jackson has also worked to yoke Collins more closely to Trump after a ProPublica report in September that revealed the FBI had investigated the senator over an alleged pay-to-play scheme involving a campaign donor. The inquiry reportedly withered after Trump dismantled the justice department division handling the case.

He called the episode “corruption of the highest order”, while Collins’s office dismissed the report as “categorically false” and noted there were never any allegations of wrongdoing by the senator’s campaign.

“The reality is that 100% of the time, when Donald Trump needs her, Susan Collins is going to be there,” Jackson said during one of four televised debates this month, while also invoking the senator’s vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the supreme court, which later helped overturn the constitutional right to abortion in 2022.

Collins, whom Trump once derided as “absolutely atrocious”, argues that her willingness to break with the president and her party sets her apart from most Republicans. “I decide my votes on what I believe is best for Maine and for America, not on whether or not any president, and I’ve worked with five, is for it or against it,” she said at a recent campaign stop.

On the trail, the senator points to her vote against repealing the Affordable Care Act, her vote to impeach Trump after the January 6 insurrection, her opposition to Pete Hegseth’s nomination as defense secretary and her support for a war powers resolution limiting military action against Iran without congressional approval. (The Collins campaign did not respond to the Guardian’s request for an interview.)

However, a New York Times analysis found that while Collins has broken with her party 17% of the time during the current Congress, roughly in line with her rate of defections during Trump’s first term, those breaks have rarely slowed the president’s agenda since his return to the White House last year.

One example was Trump’s signature domestic policy package that imposed steep Medicaid cuts, including billions affecting Maine. Although Collins opposed the bill’s final passage, she supported a key procedural vote that allowed it to reach the Senate floor.

Collins is also the only Republican senator up for re-election in a state Trump lost in 2024, leaving her exposed to the broader backlash against the administration. A recent Marist poll found that only 42% of likely Maine voters approve of Trump’s job performance, while 41% say their congressional vote is primarily a vote against him.

“Jackson, in some ways, seems almost irrelevant,” said Dan Shea, a professor of government at Colby College. “I think it’s about whether or not [voters] can tolerate giving Trump one more vote in the Senate.”

Meanwhile, Collins’s ability to secure concessions from the Trump administration may be her greatest boon on the campaign trail, and Jackson’s biggest disadvantage.

In recent weeks, she has touted a major Pentagon contract for the Bath Iron Works shipyard, the release of more than 300,000 barrels of heating oil to ease costs across New England and Trump tariff exemptions benefiting Maine industries caught in the US-Canada trade war.

As a freshman senator, Jackson would face a steeper climb in directing federal resources to the state, particularly if Democrats remain in the minority.

Faced with the reality of rising costs and an unpopular president, Collins’s former supporters are weighing their options. Beyond gas, heating oil has emerged as another flashpoint in Maine, where nearly half of households rely on it to make it through the winter. The average price of a gallon now exceeds $6, a record high, according to the state’s department of energy resources.

“I put in 131 gallons of oil. It wasn’t even filling the tank, and it was $729,” said Cheryl Clukey, 77, a retired school principal from Augusta. “I’ve never had that before, and I’m scared.”

Clukey, who has voted for Collins in the past and was raised Republican, said the senator’s 30 years in Congress are “enough”.

At Jackson’s campaign events in the final week before election day, enthusiasm is palpable. Yet many supporters appear motivated less by Jackson himself than by opposition to the president.

“I would have voted for anybody who could put brakes on Trump. If I’m honest, Troy [Jackson] would not have been my first pick,” said Susan Cellucci, 64, of Scarborough. “But I would’ve voted for pretty much anybody who is a Democrat because I think that this guy in the White House and his administration needs to be brought back to earth.”

In Biddeford that anger remains particularly acute, after a federal immigration agent shot and killed 26-year-old Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian man and father, at a traffic stop in July.

“This is not something that happens here in a small seaside town,” said David Kurtz, a Biddeford city councilor and local attorney backing Jackson. “We’re seeing those chickens come home to roost for people … There are people who are never going to vote Republican again, no matter who that person is.”

Still “no result will surprise me,” Kurtz added, noting that Collins has repeatedly outrun the political odds in the past, including her nine-point 2020 victory over former Maine house speaker Sara Gideon despite trailing in most polls.

In 2020, Collins won re-election with the help of ticket-splitters who backed her for Senate while sending Joe Biden to the White House. One of them was Rick Dolliver, a registered Democrat and seafood restaurant owner in Ogunquit, who plans to support her again this year.

“She’s given Maine a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to bring more federal resources to our state,” he said. “She’s proved that she’s the only member of the delegation who can effectively push back against [Trump’s] bad policies.”

Dolliver pointed to Collins’s role in creating the Paycheck Protection Program during the Covid pandemic, which he says helped keep employees on payroll while his restaurant was shuttered. He described Jackson as a “rookie” with “no chance of getting anything done” if elected.

For undecided voters like LaMontagne, the question is whether Jackson, a former state senate president, can match the influence that comes with Collins’s seniority and longstanding relationships on Capitol Hill.

“Do I agree with her on a lot of stuff? Probably not. Do I agree with her on some stuff? Yeah, maybe. Is she an ally of the lobster fishery right now? Absolutely,” LaMontagne said, pointing to funding Collins has secured and regulations she has helped ease for his industry.

“The status quo sucks,” he said. “Frankly, it just kind of sucks when your business makes less money every year and there’s no change in sight.”

While Collins benefited from the turmoil that engulfed Democrats after Platner’s implosion, she may now be more vulnerable than at any point in the campaign, as some independent voters who have backed her in the past weigh Jackson as their clearest option for checking Trump.

Democrats also appear more energized this cycle. Many in the party will likely “crawl over broken glass to get to the polls”, whereas Republicans are “sort of hanging their head as they drive by the gas station and turning off the news”, Shea said. Jackson could also benefit from strength in the state’s gubernatorial race. Hannah Pingree, a former state representative, is leading Republican Bobby Charles by double digits in several polls.

That includes voters like LaMontagne, who said he was “excited” to vote for Pingree.

As he considers his options ahead of Tuesday, however, LaMontagne said backing Jackson would still require something many Mainers are wrestling with: a leap of faith.

“Taking some trust that he has pivoted the campaign enough to have a good vision for the country, and that the people around him will help lift him up to do a good job,” LaMontagne said.

“I give a shit about people’s families,” he said. “If you think that you want to vote for somebody that backs the billionaires, well, God bless you. That isn’t me.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Battle lines redrawn in Spain’s snap election after latest train disaster
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Sam Jones in Madrid
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Next month’s poll no longer the contest it was, as Pedro Sánchez finds himself forced to defend government’s safety record

One of the most dependable cliches of contemporary Spanish politics is that it never pays to bet against Pedro Sánchez. Time and time again – as leader of the Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE) and as prime minister – Sánchez has shown an almost preternatural ability to profit from adversity, and to confound expectations and wrongfoot his opponents.

But next month’s snap general election, called by Sánchez after rightwing and far-right parties voted down the housing reforms his coalition government had announced in response to angry protests, may suddenly not be the contest it once was.

Wednesday’s deadly rail collision, in which at least 69 people died, has, for the moment at least, subdued much of the vicious language and posturing that has come to characterise recent elections. The crash could sap Sánchez’s recently resurgent momentum and the issue of rail safety now threatens to overshadow his attempts to defend his record and remain in the Moncloa palace.

The poll the left had billed as a last chance to stop the conservative People’s party (PP) joining forces with the rightwing Vox party to roll back decades of social progress – and which the right had billed as an opportunity to end eight years of what it disdainfully calls sanchismo – will now take place in a country deep in shock and grief.

Not only has Spain’s extensive high-speed railway long been a source of national pride, it is also a transport network that millions of Spaniards depend on for work, holidays and family visits. This week’s crash, after another on the same line that killed 46 people in January, has left people angry, bewildered and worried.

Thursday’s headlines spoke for themselves. El Mundo’s front page lamented “Another massacre on the trains”; ABC’s noted “At least 68 dead nine months on”, while El País mourned the “Second high-speed catastrophe in less than a year.”

Even before Wednesday’s terrible events on the outskirts of Urda, Sánchez and his allies were facing a battle. As well as the housing protests, the prime minister has had to contend with a slew of corruption allegations surrounding his family and inner circle, while his government’s handling of the mass crossing into Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta over the summer had been fiercely criticised at home and abroad.

Pablo Simón, a political scientist at the Carlos III University of Madrid, stressed the delicacy of the moment, saying that people across Spain were still struggling to come to terms with what had happened this week.

“There are a lot of fronts [for the government] here, and I think this accident has a twofold impact,” he said. “First, it draws attention to the state of railway infrastructure, suggesting that the problem is structural, and pointing to a broader decline in public services in Spain, specifically regarding infrastructure.”

Simón said that Sánchez’s government, which has been in power since 2018, could not blame the state of things on its PP predecessor, which carried out austerity cuts. “That’s simply not credible,” he said.

“But there’s also a second issue: even before this, the government faced an uphill battle; it was already highly unlikely that they could secure the necessary support.”

Sánchez has said it is “unacceptable” for the country to experience two high-speed rail disasters in less than a year, and promised to strengthen safety measures “so that something like this never happens again”, but his opponents say that is simply not good enough.

The PP leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said on Thursday that any politician found to be responsible for the crash would be held to account, adding: “We can’t go on like this; this kind of management just can’t carry on.” According to the PP, Spaniards are not asking for “miracles; they’re just asking for a Spain where things work again”.

Vox, on the other hand, is going all out, accusing the government of “killing” the train crash victims and of systemic mismanagement and cronyism. It has also urged the supreme court to investigate Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, on suspicion of manslaughter and causing bodily harm through gross negligence. Puente has rejected allegations of mismanagement, insisting that Spain’s railway system is “safe and reliable”.

Simón said the contrasting reactions of the PP and Vox reflected splits on the right, as both parties compete to put an end to Sánchez’s government: “The question becomes what tone should one adopt: a more institutional one, which is what the PP is currently attempting, or a tougher, more aggressive one, which is what Vox is doing?”

He also suggested the sombre national mood could make it very hard for Sánchez to rally as many as 1.2 million “politically dormant” but PSOE-leaning voters, on whom he had been counting. The electoral event the prime minister had hoped to portray as a Manichean clash between progressives and reactionaries, fought over issues of housing and equality, has morphed into something else.

“An election campaign relies on high spirits and a sense of optimism,” Simón said. “But how can that exist when the entire country is in mourning over this tragedy?”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘Swift justice’: Student List supporters focus on cleaning up Serbia’s rotten institutions
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Guy de Launey in Belgrade
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
After improbable election victory, the unconventional grassroots movement says it will prioritise dismissal of corrupt officials

In Belgrade’s Pioneers Park, just across from the national assembly, a small crowd craned their necks to listen. One woman held aloft a placard reading “Love prevailed for the people and Serbia”. With a bouquet of media microphones in front of them, members of the Student List, the direct democracy movement that won an improbable but decisive victory in Sunday’s election, gathered under the trees.

Having spent days bathing in the euphoria of their unexpected triumph, the candidates’ focus was now clear: the cleaning up of the rotten institutions that had increasingly blighted the lives of Serbs over the 14 years of government by the populist leader Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS). They called for the dismissal of many senior law enforcement officials, among them the chiefs of the criminal police, the paramilitary gendarmerie and an anti-terrorism unit.

Student List candidate Svetlana Stanarević was applauded when she accused the officials of violating the law. She also called for the director of Serbia’s internal intelligence agency to resign, accusing him of running the organisation as “a party security service, not a state security service”.

There was approval, too, for the “reopening or expediting of cases” related to the disaster that sparked the student protest movement. Sunday will mark the second anniversary of the canopy collapse that killed 16 people at a renovated railway station in Serbia’s second city, Novi Sad. There have yet to be any convictions.

The announcements on Thursday were the Student List’s way of stressing they intended to put anti-corruption efforts at the heart of government.

“For years, for decades, people have been really frustrated,” said Iva Marković, a Student List candidate and political ecologist who founded the Right to Water initiative. “We see this as a time where everyone who was honestly and credibly working within [public] institutions can do their jobs. They are no longer under political pressure, and we ask them to do their jobs, which also means for prosecutors to prosecute, and police to investigate.”

Reinforcing the student movement’s key principles is also a way, perhaps, to allay concerns that the Student List might not know how to handle its stunning victory over Vučić and the SNS. The movement is not a traditional party. It does not have a hierarchy or leader – and although the students selected the list of candidates, they will not have any direct control over the people who have been elected, once they have been sworn in as MPs.

Marković said the common commitment the students and their parliamentary candidates had made should not be underestimated.

“The process didn’t start with the elections,” she noted, adding that preventing “individualism” from undermining core goals had been key to the student movement’s success. “When you dream together with some people, it’s very hard to forget this dream, even if you are in parliament.”

Borko Stefanović’s choice of a pizzeria themed around ’Allo ’Allo! as a meeting place reflects Serbia’s enthusiasm for British sitcoms of a certain vintage. Only Fools and Horses is a particular favourite, with its tales of thwarted schemes and broken dreams chiming strongly in a country that has been through turbulent times since the early 1990s.

Stefanović knows this better than most. He was part of the political movement opposed to Slobodan Milošević – and saw the democratic coalition that emerged from the overthrow of Serbia’s notorious former president fritter away its early promise. It is not a film he cares to watch a second time.

“There is this almost legendary saying in Serbia that we won on the 5th of October [2000] over Milošević, but we never had the 6th of October,” he said, adding that the Student List was correct to prioritise the dismissal of corrupt officials.

“Get the right people in the right places, bring swift legal justice, liberate institutions and the media, and allow the prosecutor’s office to arrest criminals. Everyone who wants to contribute to the reforms needs to get on board and to do everything we can to make this excellent example in Europe a lasting one.”

Perched on a sofa in a coffee roastery in Belgrade’s old town, Tara Blagojević was convinced the movement she has been a part of already had the right people in place. With the elections over, she said it was down to the successful candidates to form a government. The student assemblies will take a less active role, acting as “advisers or kind of supervisors”.

“Everything’s going to be fine,” Blagojević insisted, adding that although the Student List was “kind of a political experiment”, the people who will soon be sworn in as MPs “recognise each other’s strengths and are able to project who can be suitable to do certain things within the new government”.

Slobodan Tomić is optimistic about the Student List’s prospects. The Belgrade-born political scientist at the University of York has been following the student movement since its inception. “It is an extraordinary change,” he said of the party’s unconventional structure. “I couldn’t find any example across the world of anything similar happening.

“The MPs had to sign a pledge that they would follow through the programme that the Student List had created. So on paper, there isn’t much space for drift.”

The organisers of the famous Exit music festival are also convinced. They moved the event out of the country this year in protest at the policies of Vučić and the SNS. They confirmed that Exit would return to its home in Novi Sad next year.

The news further energised the crowd at Belgrade’s first big gig since the election, where the euphoria showed no sign of subsiding. Chants of “Victory!” welcomed Fontaines DC on stage among the shipping containers at the port of Belgrade. “Congratulations,” responded the Irish singer Grian Chatten. “This is your moment, not ours.”

A former punk rock bassist himself, Stefanović is sure that assessment is correct. “These wonderful, wonderful people from the Student List and the student movement, they know exactly what needs to be done,” he said. He added just one caveat from experience: “Don’t blow it.”

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Raccoons at the ready! 20 Halloween costumes for 2026 – from Erling Haaland to Kate in Widow’s Bay
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Morwenna Ferrier
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Do you want to channel a cult horror film, steamy ice hockey show, disgraced political operative, or one of the stand-out stars of the Bayeux tapestry? Here’s how to do it

Why not go as Man City’s most likable player, Erling Haaland? Specifically him emerging from a plane in Oslo with a taxidermied raccoon holding an empty bottle of Greenall’s wild berry gin, and a Dolce & Gabbana tote slung over one shoulder, after Norway’s 2026 World Cup run. Why did he have a taxidermied raccoon holding an empty bottle of booze, you might ask? It was a keepsake, of course, bought at Wild Bill’s Western Store in Dallas, Texas. For those wanting to recreate the look on a budget: a blond ponytail wig, black hoodie, LL Bean tote, raccoon plushie and empty bottle of something would do the job nicely.

An easy one to start with: take a traditional lightweight plastic bin, cut a slit for your eyes and a square for your mouth, add a Batman costume, cape, purple sash and some heavy-duty boots. Nigel Farage may be the real villain, but Count Binface has been a key political talking point this year – and wearing a bin on your head is never not funny.

We lost some great artists this year, but the man who launched a thousand coulrophobes is surely up there as horror’s greatest character actor. There are plenty of Curry roles to choose from, but for clarity it’s best to go with either The Rocky Horror Show’s Frank-N-Furter (stockings, pearls, wig and a fake tattoo), or Pennywise, the shape-shifting murderous clown with the Bronx accent. You just need some face paint, a clown costume and a copy of Georgie’s paper boat.

It’s always useful when a Halloween costume doubles up as an icebreaker, especially when said costume is a football club recently found guilty of more than 100 charges of rule-breaking in what is the biggest financial scandal in football history! It’s perfectly achievable: just wear a Man City shirt.

You could go as Bad Bunny himself in a cream Zara suit complete with a football jersey with the name Ocasio and number 64, but do you really want to give the Spanish brand any more publicity? A better option perhaps is one of the sugarcane “bush people” who formed the backdrop of the singer’s Super Bowl half-time show performance. Start with a green tracksuit, add some synthetic raffia grass, or perhaps a plastic hula skirt and, if possible, add green goggles. One for the crafters.

Haven’t seen Backrooms, the cult psychological horror film about a disillusioned furniture store owner who discovers a secret door in his basement? No matter. If you’ve been to any large centre of commerce – an Ikea or Big Yellow storage perhaps – you can well imagine how easy it might be to pass through solid walls, out of reality and into a maze of rooms with no clear exit. It’s fairly easy to pull off this look: cut a piece of cardboard, paint it yellow and strap it to your back. Bonus points if you bring your own chair to suggest an eerie human presence in an otherwise uninhabited world.

It wouldn’t be Halloween without some kind of Trump-adjacent costume. If you’re feeling a bit lazy and happen to be blond, going as the former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is an easy win. Lots to work with here: Zacharia stepping down from her role after five days, Zacharia referring to herself as a lawyer, Zacharia answering a question about where she passed her bar exam with: “When I moved to China.” (She later said she misheard the question; in fact she never passed any bar exam.) Keep it simple: navy business suit, mobile podium and a sign with “I did it in China” would probably do it.

Obsession is a horror film about what happens when an “incel” gets their one true wish – the reciprocal love of his hot best friend without her consent! Already a frontrunner for most popular costume of 2026 is Nikki, said victim, from the now infamous party scene in which she smashes a bottle into her own face for reasons unclear. This is partly because the scene involves lots of blood, and partly because a replica of her red zebra bandeau top seems to be widely available online. On a separate note, it feels like a pertinent costume choice anyway, given the film’s message that non-consensual love is more terrifying than any bogeyman. Do bring a foam brick to fake-murder your rival love interest if you can source one.

A little recap: earlier this month, the singer Kelly Clarkson got into a public quarrel with a shop in Brooklyn who she claimed treated her as though she couldn’t afford its merchandise, which was Molly, a clockwork bird. The store claimed it wasn’t for sale, and that it offered her another singing bird for about $2,000 (£1,500). Clarkson apparently left and the whole dispute played out on social media. Did anyone care? Not a jot. Which is why this is the perfect costume for Halloween 2026: tongue in cheek, topical and symbolic of the vapidity of celebrity. It’s also perfect for couples. One of you can dress as Clarkson as per the CCTV footage in a baseball hat and yellow T-shirt, and the other can dress as a giant mockingbird with a price tag around your neck.

The British-Canadian writer is on this year’s Halloween moodboard thanks to her new book, Life of M, which – according to rumours – is based on the actor Natalie Portman, and isn’t terribly flattering. Low effort, this one: long dark wig, natty suit, a copy of the book. Or go as Portman herself – as above, just adding something “thinly veiled” like a piece of gauze.

It has been a solid year for fictional bourgeois couples squabbling in films (see also: The Invite), but my top pick would be Zendaya in The Drama, in which she and her husband, played by Robert Pattinson, end up in a diner on their wedding night. She – for reasons that would spoil the film – is bedraggled in a white wedding dress and orange puffer coat, an ideal look to copy.

Couples only here, and no, it doesn’t matter if you haven’t seen Nathan Fielder’s smash hit documentary about disgraced US entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes because good luck getting tickets when it comes out later next month in the UK. The most meme’d scene – therefore easiest to borrow from – is a shot of Fielder and Holmes eyeball-to-eyeball discussing integrity. He could wear a salt and pepper wig, earphones and a thin film of sweat. She just needs those fancy-dress glasses with the wide-open eyes.

This is the year Justin Trudeau became more famous for dating Katy Perry than for being the former prime minister of Canada. It’s a great costume if you can’t be bothered, as there are lots of easy-to-parse Instagram moments to choose from. Top choice has to be the faux candid, behind-the-scenes shot of Trudeau at Coachella wearing a plain white T-shirt and a backward baseball hat while eating regular takeaway noodles. We’re happy for them, but let’s not pretend this celebrity statesman didn’t know what he was doing here. Add a red cup for the full divorcee frat-boy look.

Probably the easiest to cobble together if you have teenage sons, this costume takes inspiration from Swedish rapper Yung Lean’s seven-and-a-half-minute music video for his track Storm. Directed by Romain Gavras, it features an extraordinary 66 dancers dressed up like schoolboys dancing in fluid movements that have been compared to “dolphins”. It’s a particularly zeitgeisty choice since it became a cultural flashpoint after being described as the kind of music video AI could never create.

Didn’t get tickets for the Bayeux tapestry? Try dressing as the mysterious woman, Aelfgyva, depicted in the 11th-century wall hanging instead. You just need a green cloak, some sort of red hoodie underneath and (well, it is Halloween) a severed limb attached to your head.

The beloved late singer has been an evergreen presence at fancy dress parties, but given her death, you can expect to see multiple Partons on your doorstep or at parties this year. Don’t let that put you off: you just need a blond wig, a rhinestone jumpsuit with cape-like sleeves, acrylic nails and perhaps a guitar or a nine-to-five typewriter if you can be bothered to lug one around.

Halloween loves a nod to the monoculture, which is why this steamy TV show about a pair of closeted hockey players is a winning costume par deux for any couples this year. Ideally you’d have different colour wigs and ice hockey costumes, and would carry a Gatorade bottle and a hockey stick each. Failing that, just go for the preppy-shorts-and-T-shirts look as above, and keep whipping out Ilya Rozanov’s Zippo lighter from your top pocket.

Punch the macaque became a sensation in February after he was abandoned at birth by his mother at Ichikawa city zoo, and given an Ikea orangutan toy for comfort by zookeepers. The good news is he’s now recovering well, so it’s not in poor taste to capture the spirit of the young primate by dragging around a £19 Djungelskog toy, which is now thankfully back in stock at the Swedish megastore.

If you’re thinking the sentient but highly flammable “wicker husband” in this romantic fable starring Alexander Skarsgård and Olivia Colman might be hard to pull off without a full-body woven prosthesis, think again. You just need to wear head-to-toe brown, and pop a wicker paper basket (John Lewis do an affordable one in willow) over your head. You can reuse the bin, so it’s also the most eco choice.

Patricia is the breakout character from Widow’s Bay, the comedic horror series about a cursed coastal town in New England. Her most famous scene? Hosting a hellish “sunset cocktail” party in which she accidentally spikes her guests, hypnotising them into a trance and almost drowning them all while dressed in a crown of bloodied antlers. Think fever dream here: red floral dress, some sort of crown fashioned from bones, perhaps a taxidermied animal as its centrepiece. If you can’t get the above, just wear a tiara, which is what Patricia thinks she’s wearing.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: ‘I saw the script and went: oooh!’ Olivia Colman and Alexander Skårsgard on their steamy folk-horror movie Wicker
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Ryan Gilbey
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
She plays a depressed fisherwoman. He plays a man made of wicker who is solely dedicated to her pleasure. How did the actors feel about this strange, emotional connection – and what did Colman draw from her own marriage?

Another year, another raunchy comedy-drama in which Alexander Skarsgård is the answer to a social outcast’s erotic dreams. “I fucking loved Pillion so much!” says Olivia Colman, reliably sweary straight out of the gate, as she brings up last year’s British indie hit starring Skarsgård as a leather-clad dom with a timid traffic warden as his submissive. “And when they kissed at the end … Aww.” The 52-year-old Oscar-winner for The Favourite gives a mock-sniffle and a little shake of her frizzy grey locks, then pretends to dab her eyes.

Seated beside her in a London hotel room and wearing a bright orange “I’m With Stupid” T-shirt, Skarsgård tilts his head appreciatively. In Pillion, it was Harry Melling who had the privilege of being ravaged by the 50-year-old Swedish actor. Now it is Colman’s turn in Wicker, an earthy adult fairytale filmed in Budapest and set in a medieval village populated almost exclusively by British comic actors who converse in language both archaically formal (“Happy to transact with you”) and bluntly colloquial (“I’d better fuck off”). Among them is Phil Daniels as a leering butcher and Richard E Grant as a doctor who is even more inept at his job than Grant was as a Celebrity Traitor.

Colman plays the Fisherwoman, ridiculed by the other villagers for her pong and her general absence of allure. In the spirit of mocking the dominant patriarchal conventions, where men put metal collars on their wives when they get married, she asks the Basketmaker (Peter Dinklage) to fashion her a husband. A month later, she has a groom made entirely of wicker and dedicated solely to her pleasure and happiness. If the movie works, says Alex Huston Fischer, who wrote and directed Wicker with his wife, Eleanor Wilson, “you are essentially connecting emotionally to a basket”.

This is where Skarsgård comes in. His performance as the Wicker Husband was augmented by Weta Workshop, the New Zealand special-effects outfit behind the Lord of the Rings series. “I had a full bodysuit, a mask glued to my face, then added prosthetics for lips and eyelashes,” the actor says. “Oh, and hair made from flax. Highly flammable.” He tried out different accents but that felt “too removed from myself, what with the mask and everything else”. Colman gives an amused snort: “Might as well have got someone else in,” she says. Her co-star responds by puffing out his chest: “Hey, people pay big bucks to see Alexander Skarsgård on screen!”

In truth, he is humbler than all that. “Alex gets very awkward with compliments,” says Colman, then turns to him: “Well, tough. I don’t think there are many people who could have got quite so much across while acting within such restrictions. It’s a mark of how good you are. Sorry!” Is it fair to call his performance minimalist? “From my point of view, it was maximalist,” he says. “Because of the mask, I had to exaggerate everything and it felt like I was being hammy. Subtleties wouldn’t register. Underneath that beautifully crafted suit, I was like: ‘Aaah!’, ‘Grrr!’” His guttural sounds are accompanied by facial expressions which suggest a beginner’s guide to semaphore acting.

Skarsgård’s performance and the cross-hatched weave effect are magically textured. The impact of the creaking sound design should not be underestimated either, especially once the newlyweds get down to conjugal business. As one Letterboxd user put it: “Whoever chose the erection sound effect … you’re a genius and I love you.”

It turns out I’m not the only one amused by Wicker’s Letterboxd reviews. “As a director, you should never read the comments,” says Fischer. “But these ones are so entertaining.” Users have offered alternative titles (John Wicker, The Shape of Wicker, Fifty Shades of Hay), double entendres (“All my eggs are going in his basket”) and the witty suggestion that Etsy could become the new Hinge. One astute comment likened Elizabeth Debicki’s character, a jealous neighbour who tries to sabotage the Fisherwoman’s happiness, to the spiteful Emma, played by Mercedes McCambridge, in the classic western Johnny Guitar.

In any discussion of Wicker, the word “horny” is never far away. “We even included it when we pitched the movie,” says Fischer. “There’s something so human about it,” says Wilson. “We are these fleshy bodies with desires that are embarrassing and messy. It seemed like a great place for comedy.” Fischer notes that Colman’s goggle-eyed reactions were vital: “For someone to be surprised by incredible sex is very funny to us. Especially when it’s Olivia. She’s so good.”

Colman returns the compliment. “You get sent a lot of scripts that you feel you’ve seen before. But when I read this, I was like an octopus. I changed colour and went: ‘Oooh!’” A deft impression of a cephalopod follows, arms undulating. The Fisherwoman is the only female character with her own name, Colman points out, rather than being known as, say, The Bakerwoman or The Innkeeper’s Wife. “And she’s the only woman with agency. She’s perfectly happy with her life. It’s when pushed that she says, ‘I’m going to fuck this up and make a mockery of your beloved convention of marriage.’ Then she gets this kind, beautiful creature, and suddenly the world is even more joyous.”

Wicker is based on Ursula Wills’ short story The Wicker Husband, which has already been adapted as a stage musical combining actors and puppetry. Reviewing that version in 2020, the Guardian theatre critic Arifa Akbar saw it as a story about “insider parochialism, the demonising of outsiders and the tyranny of conformity” with “echoes of Brexit Britain”. All pertinent, the directors agree now. “Those things were in our heads when we were writing,” says Fischer. “Elizabeth’s character is trying to protect herself and the village from what she sees as this foreign element that is there to destroy them.”

Dev Patel was originally set to play Colman’s basket-case beau until a scheduling clash forced him to pull out. Never having quite shed his Slumdog Millionaire innocence, Patel seems a more natural choice for the part than Skarsgård, who even prior to Pillion was drawn to stone-cold alphas: a tech bro (Succession), a violent husband (Big Little Lies), a coke-snorting cop (War on Everyone). Even he admits that he is cast against type in Wicker. “I tend to play characters who are messed up or internally conflicted. That duality is something I’ve done a lot and still enjoy. That wasn’t there for this character: he has a purity to him that was different to what I’ve done in the past. It was about making him relatable and interesting without that inner struggle. So that was a bit of a departure, and slightly intimidating.” Wilson argues, though, that Skarsgård has “qualities that are very Wicker Husband: he has a stoicism, and such presence. We needed that. It’s the sweetness that is the big surprise.”

The Fisherwoman’s newfound fulfilment and her husband’s inherent goodness eventually have a destabilising effect on the other villagers, who realise how impoverished their own lives are by comparison. Trouble follows. Had the honeymoon period between the couple continued, however, would it not have got irritating eventually? Don’t relationships need a little creative friction to remain interesting? “Oh, I don’t know,” says Colman, thoroughly unconvinced. “I quite like a friction-free life. I don’t think I’d cope with a fighty relationship. I prefer to work things out gently.”

Her thoughts turn to her own marriage to writer and producer Ed Sinclair, with whom she has three children. “We’ve been together for 32 years and married for 25,” she says. They have also worked together several times, including on Wicker, which they co-produced. While their domestic life is harmonious, there have nevertheless been “moments with the odd little look” in a professional context. She gives an example of one such look. The narrowed eyes, the abrupt withdrawal of warmth: no one would want to be on the receiving end of that. All the cosy Olivia Colman-ness has drained away in an instant.

“But we’ve never had big fights,” she says, back in chirpy mode again. “Very early on, when we first started working together, there was a suggestion from him of an acting note.” Hearing this, Skarsgård lets out a wicked laugh, instantly spotting a taboo. “Strong side eye,” he says. She continues: “Or sometimes when I’ve needed to do a taped audition, I’d say: ‘Can you tape this for me?’ And he’d ask, ‘Have you thought of trying it like this … ?’” There’s that look again. “Then he’d say, ‘OK, point taken!’”

Where does she think Wicker ends up vis-a-vis marriage? “I’d say it’s pro equal relationships. It’s perfectly possible to do it nicely. If you’re planning to share your life with someone, be considerate. Ask yourself: Have I been a good partner this week?” She draws a tick in the air with her finger. “Check!”

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: ‘I felt bad for my exes’: Awkwafina on making deeply personal TV – with her grandma
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Coco Khan
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
The star takes on her biggest challenge yet: resurrecting her family’s Cantonese restaurant. She discusses the stress of rewatching her sitcom, nearly becoming a meat inspector … and her beloved matriarch, who passed away after filming

I’m embarrassed I didn’t bring anything. It’s 10-something in the morning, and I’m meeting Nora Lum, 38 – best known as rapper, comic actor and writer Awkwafina – the morning after the Bafta TV awards. I feel that I should have brought her a pastry pick-me-up. Yet here I am empty-handed. “It could have been Chinese buns,” she playfully suggests.

Yes, it could have been. Especially because we are meeting to discuss her new series on Apple TV, Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook. It sees the star of box-office hits Crazy Rich Asians and Marvel’s Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings travel across the US to learn from a new generation of Asian American chefs, in the hope that she might revive her own family’s long-closed Cantonese restaurant. But there’s one problem: she can’t cook.

Or so she says. “Unlikely” cook? There’s nothing unlikely about it, I wager. Sure, in the first episode, Lum looks genuinely alarmed by the triple threat of hot oil, high heat and sharp knives in wok cooking. But she does very well. She clearly has a knack for food.

“Well, I think it was the easiest knack to develop, because all it really takes is to eat at a ton of restaurants and order food constantly,” she pushes back.

“But look, I was raised by immigrant Chinese people – I did eat all the weird Chinese stuff,” she says, understating her family’s impressive culinary credentials. The full story is thus: back in the 50s, Lum’s great-grandfather Jimmy opened one of New York’s first Chinese-American restaurants in Flushing, Queens. Called Lum’s, it became something of an institution, helping to popularise the Chinese-American food beloved today (think: orange chicken and BBQ ribs).

“The restaurant is how we came to this country,” she explains. “It closed in 1982, so I wasn’t born. But it was so important. The way they talk about it is like a family member that passed away.”

Lum’s new TV show about it is pleasingly warm and personal, with much of its gentle humour coming less from the supposedly awkward personality that inspired Lum’s stage name than her deep appreciation for food and hospitality. Have you ever seen someone scream “Oh my God, not the cilantro!” in ecstatic anticipation of a herb? I have, and it’s charming. But ultimately, Unlikely Cook is a love letter to Lum’s magnetic, occasionally foul-mouthed, paternal grandmother; the woman who raised her when she lost her mother at just four years old.

Several months after I meet Lum, I see the Instagram post announcing her grandmother’s death. But, for now, I ask about the woman who has loomed so large over her creative work, and regularly steals the show in Unlikely Cook. How easy is it working with your own grandma?

“It’s crazy. I’ve been asking my grandma to be in things since my first [TV] job, which was on MTV’s Girl Code,” Lum explains. Grandma obliged, starring in the brilliantly named episode Bad Sex, Grandparents, Eating Habits.

“I’m always a little worried, thinking: ‘Oh my God, what are you going to say?’ But she has such a lovely on-camera affect. It just kind of clicks.”

“With this [project], she’s calling me at all hours of the night, we’re staying up talking. Actually, she called me a week ago and was like, ‘I’m just thinking about the menu, and we should put a pu pu platter – but we shouldn’t call it pu pu, because, you know, it means shit so we should call it the volcano platter.’ It’s giving her excitement again.”

Between the family appearances and actor Jimmy O Yang’s star turn (Lum’s real-life best friend) Unlikely Cook may be Lum’s most biographical work yet. Which is saying something given her hit 2020 comedy television show was literally called Awkwafina Is Nora from Queens, and starred her as directionless, awkward Nora living in – you guessed it – Flushing, with her widowed father and boisterous grandmother.

For fans of Nora from Queens, there may be a particular, parasocial joy in watching Unlikely Cook. The sitcom could be absurd (Nora’s grandma accidentally growing cannabis, for instance), but you always sensed some emotional truth beneath it. Now we get the real Nora Lum.

“Oh my God, yeah,” she exclaims. She refers to an episode where she is stressed. “That episode was bizarre to watch. Because I have never seen myself be serious, be panicked. That’s never been recorded.”

“There was something about it where I actually felt bad. I felt bad for my exes, my friends. I was watching myself back like, ‘Chill out, girl!’”

I didn’t have her pegged as the self-conscious type, I say, what with working so frequently from her real life. “I’ve never been documentarised in quite this way,” she explains. “There’s a part of me that’s like, oh my God, you let people see this crazy, unbridled version of you?! I still don’t know how to deal with that. But I do feel that whatever is honest, it can’t be the worst.”

To be fair, food is emotional stuff, and so often bound up in questions of identity, history and, especially in the immigrant context, family sacrifice. I ask Lum about her observation in the documentary that a generation of elders grafted in restaurants so their kids didn’t have to. They could be lawyers instead.

“The truth is that a lot of the [older] people we met didn’t want their children to go back into the restaurant business. For my great-grandpa’s generation, when they came over they were relegated to either laundromats or restaurants, cooking food that has historically been demonised,” Lum says. “But then again, it’s also something that people love. There are more Chinese restaurants in America than there are McDonald’s, KFC, Burger King, all of that.”

But while the restaurant business gave Lum’s family life, it also took a lot of it. Her grandmother had her own restaurant for a time, but when it failed, Lum’s grandparents were forced to file for bankruptcy, losing both their business and home. For a while, the whole family lived in a one-bedroom apartment.

“I think her business failing was really hard on her. She would fold the napkins in the back. She would launder napkins in our home. And she would be the most amazing maître d’ that the whole town knew. I don’t think she ever really recovered from it.”

“I think giving back – if I’m in a position to do that – does feel like this full-circle moment where I could still make my family proud in that way. It would definitely be something for her.”

All this talk of making family proud and honouring their sacrifices is something I know well, having also been raised in an immigrant household. Did Lum agonise over her choice of a creative career as much as I did when I chose English lit over law – something I loved over something that might more reliably make good on what my family gave me?

“No, because I don’t think I was smart enough to get into law school,” she laughs.

“I’m actually not a good student. I went to summer school for gym. For gym. If you fail a class during the year, you can make it up over the summer. But it’s like a punishment, right? Every day I was taking two periods of gym, because I had failed so many times.”

She continues: “Do you know what Earth science is? The rock one? It’s the easy rock one. It’s not even chemistry. I had to take the Earth science [exam] five times, dude.

“So I think my family were just thinking, well, she has nothing to lose. Besides I wasn’t doing it off their dime, so I think maybe they were just happy I was doing something. But my dad really wanted me to be a meat inspector. I’m still on those government job registries that he signed me up for. He’s like, “Meat inspector, that’s a really good job.”

“It is! Great entry level salary. And you always, always need a meat inspector,” she says.

“I know, I know” she laughs, and I wonder if she has the same idea I have. Awkwafina is the Meat Inspector, coming soon to Apple TV.

OK, back to business. Watching Unlikely Cook, I couldn’t help thinking about the politics of America right now. After all, a show celebrating the work of immigrants feels significant in the age of Trump and ICE. Was that intentional?

“No, not at all. But if you want to tell the story of Chinese-American food, immigrant culture is something you can’t ignore. It’s also a deep part of our identity as second-generation Asian Americans, it’s part of how we see the world. And it’s a hard thing to see right now in America.”

Our time is nearly up. But wait, I’m still not sure, does this mean someday there will be a permanent Lum’s? “It’s still in the works of being figured out,” she says.

But clearly, in Nora Lum herself, something has stuck. “After this show, I did start dabbling a little,” she says. While shooting a film in Kentucky, she took to cooking her own breakfast, “a four-egg omelette with spinach and cheese”, she says with faint pride. It’s not quite as impressive as Chinese buns. But maybe they’ll come soon.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Iran war is deepening the US energy crisis. A bad winter is ahead | Mark Wolfe
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Mark Wolfe
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Congress must act to ensure that families are able to heat their homes before the start of the season

Heating oil may be the clearest warning yet of how the war in Iran is deepening the US’s energy affordability crisis. Families who heat their homes with oil are facing bills that could be 50% higher this winter, adding nearly $900 to the cost of keeping their homes warm. These families were already struggling before the war began.

As the Guardian recently reported, research by my organization found that electricity shutoffs in 10 states had increased 28% over the past two years. Millions of Americans were already falling behind on their utility bills, forced to choose between paying for energy, food, medicine and rent. Now they face another round of increases in gasoline, electricity and home heating costs.

The war didn’t create America’s energy affordability crisis. But it is making a bad situation much worse.

For families living on social security, minimum-wage workers and others with little room in their budgets, higher energy prices are taking an especially heavy toll. Even middle-class families are struggling to absorb another $100 or $150 a month for gasoline, groceries and home heating.

Heating oil is the canary in the coalmine for the broader affordability crisis.

Heating oil and diesel are essentially the same petroleum product, and both have been hit hard by the disruption to global energy markets. Higher diesel prices increase the cost of moving food, delivering goods and operating farms and construction equipment. Those costs eventually find their way into the prices families pay.

But for the millions of households that rely on heating oil, the impact is much more immediate. Unlike gasoline, which families can sometimes conserve by driving less, heating oil is essential for keeping homes warm. Families cannot simply stop filling their tanks when prices rise.

Trump described higher oil prices resulting from the war as “a very small price to pay for USA, and world, safety and peace”. But there is nothing small about an additional $878 in heating costs for a family living on social security or working for minimum wage. The president has also said that fuel prices will fall “like a rock” when the war ends. I hope he is right.

Even if the war ended tomorrow, energy prices would not necessarily return to their previous levels. Damaged refineries need repairs, shipping routes must reopen, and depleted petroleum inventories need to be replenished. That could take months. Families cannot postpone paying their heating bills while the oil market recovers.

Congress needs to act when it returns after the midterm elections and before winter arrives. We are calling on lawmakers to add $3bn to the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (Liheap), which helps low-income families pay their heating bills.

This would allow states to provide families with supplemental assistance to cover rising heating oil and electricity prices before the start of the winter heating season.

The problem extends beyond the poorest families. Many working families earn too much to qualify for assistance but still struggle to pay their energy bills. Congress should consider temporarily expanding eligibility for Liheap to struggling middle class families, with additional funding to ensure that assistance to the lowest-income households is not reduced.

A recent survey conducted by Consumer Reports found that more than a quarter of all families reported reduced the heating and cooling in their homes to uncomfortable levels to save money and 19% cutback on groceries or switched to less expensive food options.

Without additional energy assistance, families will fall further behind, and some will face the possibility of losing heat during the coldest months of the year.

But Congress also needs to address the larger problem. For too long, we’ve measured America’s energy security by how much oil and natural gas we produce. Yet producing more energy at home hasn’t protected the US families from price shocks caused by wars overseas.

We need to think about energy security differently. That means expanding energy sources, including wind and solar, whose fuel costs cannot be driven up by a war. There is no strait of Hormuz for solar power.

That is the longer-term challenge. Right now, millions of families are heading into winter facing energy bills they cannot afford.

At some point, the war in Iran will end, but the affordability crisis will not end with it. Washington needs to help families get through this winter and make sure the next war thousands of miles away doesn’t once again determine whether they can afford to heat their homes.

Mark Wolfe is an energy economist and serves as the executive director of the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (Neada) representing the state directors of the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program and the co-director of the Center on Energy Poverty and Climate (CEPC). He also serves as an adjunct professor at the George Washington University public policy school

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: This is the hard lesson from Israel’s election: to stop national populists, you can’t play by gentlemen’s rules | Jonathan Freedland
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Jonathan Freedland in Tel Aviv
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The opposition can’t win unless they join forces with Arab parties. Benjamin Netanyahu knows this, and will use every ruse to stay in power

It’s less an election result than a philosophical puzzle: what happens when a win contains a loss, a loss contains a win and the two collide? That’s the question posed by the confused and confusing outcome of this week’s Israeli election, one that, despite its murky uncertainty, offers clear, sharp lessons – both for that country and for those locked in combat with nationalist populists across the globe.

Start with the result that has simultaneously handed Benjamin Netanyahu a devastating defeat and a strong chance of staying on as prime minister, extending a run that has seen him lead Israel, on and off, for more than 19 of the past 30 years. The defeat is clear enough. At a stroke, his parliamentary majority was wiped out. Before Tuesday, the parties that together comprised his ruling coalition controlled 68 of the Knesset’s 120 seats: that tally has now shrunk to just 53, far short of the 61 seats needed for power. That’s a loss in anybody’s language.

And yet, Netanyahu does not look or sound like a man defeated. That’s because he knows that while the parties arrayed against him won many more seats than he did – 67 to his 53 – their chances of forming a government are slim. If they fail, one or two of them might peel away and enter a so-called national-unity government – under Netanyahu as PM – or there will have to be fresh elections, ones from which, most analysts agree, Netanyahu would emerge stronger.

The opposition’s problem is not arithmetical. It goes much deeper. Put simply, a big chunk of the anti-Netanyahu seats were won by parties that chiefly represent the one in five Israeli citizens who are Palestinian. This was the big twist of Tuesday’s election, a huge surge in turnout for what Israelis refer to as the Arab parties. Usually, far more Jewish than Arab Israelis participate in the country’s elections, but this year that pattern was flipped: turnout in Palestinian communities inside Israel hit 80%. The result is a record total of 19 seats for Arab-led parties. The anti-Netanyahu bloc cannot form a government without them. In today’s Israel, Palestinian politicians are the kingmakers.

On paper, the next step might look straightforward enough. All Netanyahu’s Jewish opponents need do is team up with their Arab colleagues and they can send the PM packing. But such an alliance would mark a watershed in Israeli history. It would mean breaking a taboo that has endured, with only fleeting exceptions, since the founding of the state, a taboo rooted in mutual suspicion.

On the one hand, Israel’s Jewish-led parties have long shunned the mainly Arab parties because the latter identify as anti- or non-Zionist, meaning they reject Israel’s self-definition as a Jewish state. For that same reason, Arab-led parties have maintained a boycott, refusing to legitimate the Israeli state by participating in its government.

In 2021, a short-lived “government of change” broke the taboo by including in its ranks Ra’am, an Islamist party regarded, improbably enough, as the most moderate of the Arab groupings. But after the Hamas massacres of 7 October 2023, the taboo was restored – and hardened. Netanyahu cast Palestinian-Israeli politicians as an enemy within, as tacit allies of the Hamas killers, a framing buttressed by a crude anti-Arab racism voiced most explicitly by his coalition allies – the likes of Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich – and which sought to delegitimise Israel’s entire Arab minority.

This was Netanyahu’s core message throughout the campaign: you can’t trust my opponents because, when the moment comes, they will sit with “the Arabs”. In recent days, he and his allies have doubled down on that message, claiming high Palestinian turnout means that “the Arabs are stealing the election” – rather than merely exercising their democratic rights – and, on Thursday, alleging that Qatar paid Palestinian-Israeli citizens to vote, thereby rendering the entire result void.

Instead of challenging Netanyahu’s framing, and insisting that the vote of every citizen, Arab or Jewish, is of equal worth, most of the main opposition parties – Yair Golan’s Democrats were the exception – bowed to it, pledging that they would not forge a coalition with the largely Arab parties, and certainly not with any group more radical than Ra’am. Now they find themselves in a bind. On their own, the Jewish-led opposition cannot form a government. Unless they somehow manage to lure defectors from Netanyahu’s bloc – perhaps one or both of the ultra-Orthodox parties – even Ra’am’s support won’t be enough to reach the magic number of 61. They need Arab partners – and probably several of them.

This, then, is the big lesson for Israel. That group that has long opposed Netanyahu – Jewish-Israelis who despise a PM on trial for corruption, who has mounted serial assaults on Israel’s institutions, including the supreme court, and brought isolation, if not pariah status, upon the country – are now confronted with a fact that has long been true but which they have preferred not to see: that they are a minority in the land they once dominated. As Aluf Benn, editor of the liberal daily Haaretz, told me: “The Jewish vote is predominantly rightwing in Israel and has been for decades.”

That means the Jewish Israeli opposition cannot win alone. This week stands as proof, because this was their perfect opportunity. Netanyahu was at his lowest ebb, the leader on whose watch the most calamitous day in Israeli history took place, the leader who promised to destroy Hamas in Gaza, but who succeeded only in turning that place into a ruin, killing tens of thousands and, in the process, destroying Israel’s standing in the world. He faced in Gadi Eisenkot, his lead challenger, a decorated former general rooted in the Mizrahi working class, a man universally regarded as honest and decent, a bereaved father whose own son fell in the Gaza war – a man, in other words, who might have been designed to appeal to the very voters who for so long have been beyond the opposition’s reach. And yet none of that was enough to win.

The only way the opposition can succeed is by making common cause with their Palestinian fellow citizens, just as Democrats in the US – who have not won a majority of the white vote since 1964 – could never win the presidency without the support of Black Americans. No one should underestimate the scale of the task, which requires a deep cultural shift as much as a political one. It should have been the work of decades, rather than a panicked scramble in a few rushed weeks of coalition horse-trading. It demands a reshaping of Israeli society, breaking a pattern of systemic discrimination and inequality within the country that has existed since the founding of the state (to say nothing of the post-1967 occupied territories where, of course, millions of Palestinians have no vote at all in Israeli elections).
