That task was always essential, but this week has confirmed that, if the right’s lock on power is ever to be broken, it can be delayed no longer.

Much of this is peculiar to the unique political terrain of Israel. But there are broader lessons for all those fighting nationalist populism, whether that be Donald Trump in next week’s US midterms, Marine Le Pen in France or Nigel Farage in Britain. First, don’t accept the terms laid down by the other side: that was the cardinal error made by Netanyahu’s challengers. Second, mere opposition and criticism is not enough. The nationalist populists will always tell a compelling story; you have to tell an equally compelling one of your own. And, last, you need to be every bit as determined as they are. Too often you play by gentlemen’s rules, when those you are fighting are anything but gentlemen. Netanyahu is without shame and will do anything – cross every line, cut any deal – to keep power. The opponents of such a man will prevail only if they show an equal resolve in seizing it.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: Billionaire tax: how a union leader’s ‘crazy’ idea became the defining issue of California’s midterms
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Dara Kerr
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
It was an ambitious notion – now Californians will vote on a one-time 5% billionaire tax, and state’s super rich have pulled out all the stops in opposition

One year ago, the idea of a billionaire tax in California was still in its infancy.

It wasn’t yet one of the most contentious ballot measure fights in state history – pitting Democrats against Democrats, drawing national attention from political heavyweights, and netting hundreds of millions of Silicon Valley dollars to fight it. Back then, it was a bold and desperate answer to Donald Trump’s healthcare cuts.

Trump had just signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which dictated a trillion dollars of Medicaid, Affordable Care Act and other healthcare funding be cut over the next decade to offset sweeping tax cuts. When the bill goes into effect in January, that could mean more than 3.4m Californians will lose their coverage, including millions of children.

“That’s why we were willing to do something that lots of people said was crazy,” said Dave Regan, the divisive architect of the billionaire tax and president of the healthcare union SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW). “To us, what’s crazy is doing nothing and watching millions of people lose coverage.”

Now, with the midterms less than a week away, California voters will decide on whether to pass the ballot measure known as Proposition 40. The proposal would levy a one-time 5% tax on billionaires living in the state as of 1 January 2026, the proceeds of which would fund healthcare programs, along with some education and food assistance.

The initiative has its critics, even among Democrats, who point at its structure as a one-off tax that would only fund certain healthcare programs. But its most vocal critics have been billionaires.

The idea of taxing the Golden State’s ultra-wealthy has snowballed into a messy brawl over the last year. Progressive politicians have become bedfellows with tech billionaires, opposition ballot measure campaigns have been mounted, Signal chats leaked, and boatloads of money have been spent.

Tech billionaires have treated the proposal as an existential threat, dumping upwards of $356m into “independent expenditure-only” political action committees (Super Pacs) to stop it. In the first two weeks of October, according to the most recent campaign filings, the opposition campaign spent more than $42.8m – surpassing $2.5m per day. That money went to an army of consultants, who have been tasked with lobbying politicians, blanketing the airwaves with ads and placing op-eds in Latino newspapers across the state.

“This looks like it’s going to be the most expensive ballot measure ever,” said David McCuan, a political science professor at Sonoma State University. “Not in California history, but in the history of the world.”

Meanwhile, the far-less-funded pro-Prop 40 camp has relied on viral social media campaigns from influencers and actors, including the artist Shepard Fairey and actor Mark Ruffalo, and raucous rallies headlined by leftwing politicians. During one packed event in San Francisco earlier this month, Vermont’s Bernie Sanders said: “The whole country, and frankly people from around the world, are paying attention to what is happening here.”

While Prop 40 is just one ballot measure election in one state, it is causing ripple effects nationwide. It comes at a time when affordability is top of mind and the disparity of wealth in the US hasn’t been so stark since the Great Depression. McCuan said the billionaires’ big spend was partially due to a fear of contagion to other states. Likewise, supporters say they hope the proposed tax is a harbinger for referendums on wealth inequality across the country.

Regan and his union got started on their endeavor last summer. After Trump signed his bill on 4 July, Regan’s team began making calls. They put together a working group of policy experts, economists, lawyers, researchers and political consultants, who came up with the one-time 5% tax to keep hospitals open and union healthcare workers in their jobs.

Regan is known for using the ballot measure process as a political tool to strongarm deals with lawmakers and push causes important to the SEIU-UHW. Since 2012, the union has sponsored 48 initiatives. The strategy with the billionaire tax was to sharpen the focus on inequality.

“We worked to come up with something that could draw enough support from voters, and that could avoid a catastrophe,” Regan said. “We just bore down on that.”

When their plan became public after the October 2025 filing deadline, the billionaires hatched a working group of their own.

Chris Larsen, a cryptocurrency mogul, hosted a Christmas party in northern California’s swanky Marin county last December, according to Bloomberg. It was in a treehouse tucked into a grove of towering redwood trees. The singer Janelle Monáe performed and California governor Gavin Newsom was there, along with Google co-founder Sergey Brin.

Newsom’s relationship with Brin goes back decades to when he was mayor of San Francisco. The governor, now a presumed presidential candidate, had flown on Google’s jet with Brin, and the two men attended each other’s weddings. But a lengthy exchange they reportedly had at Larsen’s party was far from collegial.

Brin confronted Newsom about the proposed billionaire tax, according to people who spoke with Newsom, Bloomberg reported. The Google co-founder, currently worth about $245bn, told the governor it was forcing him to leave California.

Newsom and Brin did not respond to the Guardian’s detailed list of questions.

By that point, more than a dozen tech executives and prominent Silicon Valley venture capitalists had reportedly already joined an encrypted Signal group chat expressly dedicated to burying the billionaire tax, the San Francisco Standard reported. Brin and Larsen were members, along with venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, PayPal co-founder Max Levchin, Stripe chief executive Patrick Collison and investor Ron Conway, according to people who saw the chats.

Larsen and Levchin declined to comment. Brin, Andreessen, Collison and Conway did not return requests for comment.

The group brainstormed ideas for fighting the tax. They reportedly met every Tuesday for months via video call, debated fleeing the state, and tussled over how much to trust Newsom because of his position as a Democratic governor of a blue state. Newsom has long opposed state wealth taxes and quickly came out against the billionaire tax, repeatedly saying it would “drive a race to the bottom” and stifle innovation as the ultra-wealthy leave.

While a handful of those ultra-wealthy have left, the vast majority of the state’s 200-plus billionaires have remained – including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who said he’s “perfectly fine” with the tax. Initially, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg threatened to leave California, but filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission last week revealed he struck a deal with his company’s board to help him foot the bill if Prop 40 passes in exchange for staying in the state.

Among others who indicated they’re departing are Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, Trump’s former AI and crypto czar David Sacks, and Google co-founders Larry Page and Brin. Last December, Brin moved to a $42m mega-mansion on the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe, just steps from California’s border.

Brin is the de facto ringleader of the Prop 40 opposition campaign. Through a Super Pac called Building a Better California, he’s contributed at least $102m to the cause – more than any other donor. Brin worked with political operatives and had his family office map out plans to trounce the tax, according to the New York Times. Brin is also a frequent guest at the White House and was awarded the National Medal of Science by Trump earlier this month.

Abby Lunardini, a spokesperson for Building a Better California, said: “Californians deserve to know the facts about a measure that would permanently gut the state’s budget, tax base, and economic advantage, all while making the problem it’s supposed to be fixing – healthcare funding – worse.”

Another major early donor to the opposition campaign was Thiel, who gave $3m to the California Business Roundtable Super Pac at the end of December. Larsen has donated more than $23m through various Super Pacs, and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt has given more than $42m, according to campaign finance filings.

At least some of the donations were in cryptocurrency, which had to be converted to dollars under state rules, documents show. Campaign expenditure filings for the tech Super Pacs reveal more than $40,000 has been spent on crypto processing fees alone. Company stock shares given by founders like DoorDash’s Tony Xu reportedly comprised another significant chunk.

The opposition campaign’s initial goal was to ensure Prop 40 didn’t make the ballot. They already had Newsom publicly vowing to defeat the proposal. The next step was to go after the signature-gathering process. Anyone can put forward a ballot measure in California if they can gather enough signatures by the filing deadline. Signature-collection firms charge per signature, and the price fluctuates each election based on demand.

Opponents to the billionaire tax came up with a strategy to kneecap SEIU-UHW’s signature-gathering process by introducing several ballot measures of their own to boost the price of each signature – the going rate went from $4 per signature to a record-breaking $36.

The venture capitalist Conway spelled it out in a podcast in March: “Our job is to get Gavin to negotiate this so that it doesn’t get to the ballot. So maybe they don’t get the signatures.”

When the SEIU-UHW used mostly volunteers to amass their signatures, the opposition campaign reportedly attempted another plan – purchase the firm the union used for signature-collection, so that those signatures couldn’t be used, according to Regan. The same idea was floated in the Signal chat, according to the San Francisco Standard, with one participant reportedly messaging: “That’s what you would do in business: If there’s an impediment, just buy it.”

Fred Kimball is the president of the signature-gathering firm Kimball Petition Management, which worked with the SEIU-UHW and pioneered this type of business. He said that not only did his company endure denial-of-service cyberattacks, which stalled their signature validation process, but he received two calls from unnamed individuals inquiring about a sale.

“It never got any further than that,” Kimball said. “The requirement would be that I’d have to turn over the signatures. Once you do that, it’s all over … My dad started this industry, there’s no way I’d do that.”

By the end of April, well before the signature filing deadline in June, the SEIU-UHW took a victory lap, announcing they’d gathered 1.55m signatures – nearly double the necessary amount to qualify for the ballot.

“This is a David versus Goliath battle,” Mayra Castaneda, an executive member of SEIU-UHW, said at a press conference at the time. “David has just won the first round.”

After the union’s signature-gathering triumph, the responsibility to kill the billionaire tax rested with Newsom, at least in the eyes of billionaires. Newsom’s objective was to reach a compromise with the SEIU-UHW to withdraw its proposal before the June deadline. The governor and Regan had been in talks since December, Regan said, but they remained at odds in finding a solution to the impending healthcare crisis.

Newsom had brought together a coalition to negotiate a deal, enlisting other unions and interest groups to oppose the tax. The governor also tried to get Regan to his side, according to Regan. He said Newsom’s chief of staff invited the union boss to a press conference, in which the governor would credit Regan for a national wealth tax proposal. Regan said Newsom’s national plan lacked teeth, so he declined.

SEIU-UHW offered a counter proposal: they’d drop the one-time tax from 5% to 2% if Newsom endorsed it. In a letter to the governor, the union wrote: “Let’s save patient lives together.”

“But that was a non-starter,” Regan said. So SEIU-UHW announced in late June that it was advancing to the ballot, saying: “David won the second round against Goliath”.

Two billionaire-backed countermeasures also made the ballot, however: Proposition 41 and 42. Prop 41 directly targets the billionaire tax, while Prop 42 is a general proposal on limiting certain new taxes and would ban any taxation on billionaire wealth. If either measure receives more yes votes than Prop 40, it will stop the billionaire tax from taking effect – even if it passes. Regan calls them “poison pills”.

After that, the battle entrenched. Flush with tech money, which kept rolling in, the opposition side grew quickly, landing dozens of endorsements. Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, the lobbying branch of the healthcare group, joined the cause, as did the influential California Teachers Association, the California Medical Association, and a host of building and trade unions and public safety associations.

The newly formed coalition launched an ad campaign calling Prop 40 a “dangerous wealth tax” and “reckless experiment”. The campaign received endorsements from several prominent Democrats, including Xavier Becerra, the gubernatorial candidate; Katie Porter, a former congresswoman; and Daniel Lurie, the mayor of San Francisco. While Porter contends the tax doesn’t fix the underlying system, Lurie argues the tax would drive revenue out of California. Becerra says billionaires should pay their fair share, but Prop 40 isn’t how to do it.

When asked about No on 40’s campaign strategy, a spokesperson for the campaign instead shared a comment from Jack Chou, the president of the California Medical Association, who said the cause has gained endorsements because the measure “permanently damages our economy and budget while failing to fix our healthcare system, improve care, or lower costs.”

The Prop 40 campaign looked doomed as its core allies, Democrats and unions, were jumping ship. But then things took a turn.

In August, the California Democratic party held a board meeting in San Diego, where they voted on endorsing Prop 40. At first, the measure lost. But, according to people familiar with the matter, Congresswoman Maxine Waters stepped in and condemned her colleagues for not supporting the tax. A reconsideration was introduced and the votes swung in favor of Prop 40.

State filings show that the opposition campaign had donated tens of thousands of dollars to the California Democratic party, along with the Democratic parties of San Diego, Orange county and Los Angeles county. Despite the donations, all of these Democratic parties have endorsed the billionaire tax.

Ro Khanna, the Democratic congressman who represents the district that includes Silicon Valley, has been a staunch supporter of Prop 40. “It makes no sense to me why any democratically elected official or traditional Democratic allies wouldn’t be supporting this,” he said during a June press conference. “People want folks who are going to stand up to the billionaires and the trillionaires.”

Another turning point was the endorsement of the powerful California Federation of Labor Unions AFL-CIO, which lists 1,300 unions in its roster. During its biennial convention in August, its members voted overwhelmingly to endorse Prop 40.

Lorena Gonzalez, the president of the federation, described the scene on the floor of the convention center that day. One-by-one, union healthcare workers stood up and spoke passionately about the need to fund hospitals, maternity wards and emergency rooms to ensure they don’t close in the wake of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, she said.

“Once you heard that, and heard that billionaires got tax breaks from the big BS bill and that Medi-Cal got cut, it just became a no-brainer,” Gonzalez said. “I’m not going to be a labor movement that bows down to the establishment and is scared of taking on billionaires.”

As the election nears, California residents have witnessed the two campaigns vie for attention and relentlessly demonize each other.

Last week, after Newsom endorsed the billionaire’s Prop 42 countermeasure, which would stop the state from ever passing a wealth tax, the Prop 40 campaign released an attack ad on the governor. Likewise, the opposition campaign sent voters across the state a glossy four-page mailer that read: “You’re Next.”

Since July, the tech Super Pacs have upped their donations to the committees opposing Prop 40 and supporting Props 41 and 42. The three campaigns have received a total of more than $379.5m – making it the most expensive opposition campaign in state history. “We’ve said for months we’re going to get carpet-bombed by these guys,” Regan said. “Their so-called strategy, there’s only one prong to it: we can buy anything we want.”

Along with the flood of spending and negative ads, accusations and personal attacks have been flying in all directions. Much of this has been focused on Regan, who’s been criticized in Democratic and union circles for being an aggressive bulldog and spending his union’s resources to push ballot measures.

In one specific instance, Courtni Pugh, a former executive director at the SEIU, accused Regan of physically assaulting her in 2009, according to the Los Angeles Times. She said he kicked open her office door, pinned her against a wall and screamed that she was a “dumb ass”. The SEIU investigated the allegations this year and wrote in a report that Pugh’s claim was substantiated. Regan denied the alleged abuse, claiming that the allegations against him are retaliatory for his support of Prop 40. (The union investigation did not substantiate Regan’s retaliation claim.) Law enforcement did not investigate the abuse allegations and no charges were brought.

Pugh is now serving as a senior advisor to Becerra and working as a consultant for the No on 40 campaign. Regan told the Guardian: “Courtni Pugh, at Hilltop Solutions, wants to invent accusations about me from 17 years ago on the payroll of the billionaires.”

Pugh said Regan’s response “is offensive to the people – especially the women and women of color – who have had to endure his threatening behavior”. A spokesperson for Becerra said Pugh has not advised him on his position on the wealth tax.

The newest Democrat to vocally oppose Prop 40 is former congresswoman Porter, who’s known for taking corporate executives to task. She has written op-eds in local papers, posted videos on social media, and is quoted in ads and mailers saying: “Prop 40 does nothing to reform our healthcare system.” After losing a gubernatorial bid to Becerra earlier this year, she said she was retiring from politics. But she’s waded back into the fray with Prop 40. Late last month, Newsom also appointed her to a paid position on the board of governors for the state’s community colleges.

Despite the controversy and criticism, the SEIU-UHW has brought notable figures to its side. Last month, six Nobel prize-winning economists wrote an open letter endorsing Prop 40. Doing the math, they wrote that the combined wealth of California’s billionaires is $2.3tn, equal to the entire annual income of all 20m taxpayers in the state. They pointed out that billionaires’ net worth has grown nearly 150% over the past couple of years, fueled by the AI boom. “This tax only partially plays catch-up, but it is a move in the right direction,” the economists wrote.

Now it’s up to the voters, who appear to be unswayed by the onslaught of messaging. A Politico poll last week showed that 84% of registered voters said they’d seen campaign ads involving Prop 40 and the majority of them weren’t persuaded into changing their positions. Despite that, the measure has fallen in the polls. While it enjoyed a seven-point lead over the summer, it’s since fallen to a one-point lead.

For Regan, win or lose, he said the idea of taxing billionaires isn’t going away.

“I think this campaign has already put this issue on the national agenda in a very significant way,” he said. “This issue is going to be at the center of the nominating process for a Democratic candidate in 2028.”

https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/ng-.title: I wrote a book about death. Here’s what people really think about dying
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/ng-.author: Suzy Hopkins
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/ng-.text:
In the eight years since my graphic novel on death published, I’ve learned readers of all ages want to talk about loss and preserve their family’s stories

Becoming an author in my late 50s was unexpected, the result of my daughter Hallie’s own existential anxiety in her early 20s.

Fearing my untimely demise, she begged me to write down advice that would cover all of life’s bases going forward. I agreed, but put the project off for years; it wasn’t until she cornered me with a laptop on vacation that I gave in. She asked countless questions, and I found, to my surprise, that I had plenty to say. Hallie helped shape the manuscript, and then spent a year painting its warmly emotional gouache illustrations.

Our graphic novel, What to Do When I’m Gone: A Mother’s Wisdom to Her Daughter, was published in 2018. Though marketed for mothers and daughters, it holds my advice to all three of my children on moving forward after I die. Included are notes on grief and loss and life, plus a few recipes – not because I’m a great cook, but because food is so integral to family heritage. The book is a lighthearted, emotional and highly illustrated ode to moving forward and living life fully while grieving the loss of a parent or, really, anyone you love.

What we’ve learned in the eight years since its release is that readers of all ages have a deep hunger to know more about their parents’ backgrounds, beliefs and values, including around grief and loss.

Gone wasn’t exactly a hot property. All but one publisher rejected it, uncertain who would buy a book on death and grief. But Bloomsbury editor Nancy Miller saw potential for broad readership. Eight years later, it has been published in seven languages and continues to find new readers.

I lost a parent (or other loved one, including spouse or beloved pet) and your book helped me through.

I can’t bear the thought of my mom or dad dying, but they don’t want to talk about it. I’m hoping that sharing the book with them will start some conversations.

But the most frequent sentiment we hear is: My mom or dad died, and I wish they had left me something like this.

In book events in New York and on the west coast, invariably, someone in the audience was crying. Sometimes, it was because of the person’s fractured relationship with their mother, and grieving the loss that represents. Most often, it was because they missed their mom or dad, and did not have a record of their unique voice and wisdom to lean on.

There is science behind this hunger to know more, to deepen this vital connection between the generations. Studies have shown that knowing more about family history, including weathering hard times, is good for mental health and identity formation.

I understand that hunger to know more, both as a longtime journalist and as a daughter. Years before Hallie coaxed me into doing our book, I wanted to capture my own mother’s story and did a series of interviews with her. Two decades after her death at 85, the slim memoir that resulted preserves her voice, wit and love for family.

At the moment she died, I was at her bedside holding her frail hand when, suddenly, I was swept into an invisible cyclone of memories and feelings that lasted for several minutes – and left me stunned.

Years later, that otherworldly experience helped me pen the closing pages of our book.

But this isn’t an ad for Gone. You, like some readers, might even hate it: “It just rambles on about recipes and driving a car off a cliff and being trampled in a Black Friday sale and replacing your mother with someone else,” wrote one Amazon customer called Christine. “Is there even a point to the book?”

Talk about your beliefs, history and values with the people you love while you’re alive; share the stories that are yours, and in turn, theirs.

Thankfully most readers seemed to understand, given all the feedback we’ve received. Some found themselves “ugly crying” in bookstores (though the book is funnier than it sounds) and many sent notes or wrote emotional reactions online.

“As someone who has lost their mom, it’s something I reach for often when I need a hug from her,” Dara wrote. Natsu shared the book with her mother, who then wrote her own book – each section named after a favorite song – which Natsu spent a year illustrating. Some readers acknowledged that their parents would have very different advice from mine, but echoed that universal desire for help finding their way forward.

At two and a half, they are little human yardsticks by which I measure my remaining years. I may be around for their high school and perhaps college graduations, but clearly, the first decades of their lives will be the last decades of mine. And the older I get, the more I appreciate simple days, simple problems: hangry toddlers, high grass that needs mowing.

I can fix these, unlike the world’s larger problems: the climate crisis, injustice, greed, the othering and abuse and killing of entire populations.

These children, and their children, will need help making their way through chaos we cannot yet fully imagine.

In it, they will see the sense of humor and worldview Hallie and I share, and perhaps better understand their own. When they hit hard times, I hope they will find comfort in its pages.

So, Christine, the underlying message is this: Think about what you will leave behind.

Hallie and I always intended that Gone would encourage other families to have these deeper conversations: why you chose the paths you did, what you truly care about and why, how you think about death and grief and what’s beyond. The only real requirement is willingness to examine what you believe.

Each person’s life leaves an imprint, and that imprint most affects the people we love – those who are here and those yet to come. Tell them what really matters.

Because, as many people around the world have told us, it all matters more than you will ever know.

Suzy Hopkins, a former newspaper reporter and magazine editor, is the author of What to Do When I’m Gone and What to Do When You Get Dumped. She lives in Cincinnati, Ohio. She previously wrote about the unique grief of divorce for the Guardian.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.title: Ghost in the machine: how AI is haunting the search for the supernatural
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.author: AW Ohlheiser
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/n.text:
Ghost hunting has changed in recent years due to AI chatbots, and paranormal enthusiasts are concerned

Ghost hunting is a tech-heavy pursuit. When Amy Waine and Jarrad Cutting investigate haunted locations, they’re loaded up with software of their own design, such as an app that assigns signals from a phone’s sensors to different words in a database. In the age of ChatGPT, the ghost-hunting pair is probing the world of AI. They describe one of their latest inventions, an app called GhostTube Seer, as “the world’s first AI Ghost Hunting tool”. In the hands of paranormal investigators, scientific tools like EMF meters (used to detect electromagnetic fields) are repurposed to identify changes and anomalies that they believe indicate supernatural activity. Seer is, in many ways, simply an expansion of that practice, another way to scan an empty room and believe that something may be there. The app, which requires a paid monthly subscription, has more than 1m downloads, according to its Google Play store listing.

But for others in the ghost hunting world, AI is an unwelcome presence. Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, AI-generated ghost stories and images of the supernatural have flooded online spaces, so much so that popular forums like the r/Nosleep subreddit, meant for scary stories, have implemented a strict policy against AI-generated material.

Waine and Cutting claim their app can generate images depicting the supernatural, using signals from a phone’s built-in magnetometer, identifying words and phrases in those signals, and then running them through an image generator.

Fellow paranormal enthusiasts can post the images they generate to a feed and comment on other users’ pictures. Since its release in 2023, Seer has become a regular part of their onscreen work. In a recent video on their Amy’s Crypt YouTube channel, the pair sat in a carefully selected location in the Winchester Mystery House while running GhostTube Seer.

“Can you show us what used to go on in this room?” Cutting asked. The app generated an abstract compilation of wooden walls and golden curtains that the pair suggested could be one of the home’s bedrooms. Seer also generated images of humans and animals while running: a woman reading, another woman with a black shawl, and a flock of white birds flying. Each was interpreted by the pair to have some relevance to the history of the home. The pursuit of ghosts has historically been relatively niche and personal, even after early 2000s TV shows like Ghost Hunters prompted a surge of interest in the hobby. That’s changed in recent years. Ghost stories and sightings, once they find their way online, can become training material for large language models like ChatGPT or Google Gemini, just like any other content.

New technologies have always been a part of paranormal history, says Alex Matsuo, a paranormal researcher and author whose day job is in the technology industry. Thomas Edison’s attempt at a “spirit phone” to contact the dead is an early example, one with an ambition not dissimilar to today’s AI-powered “deathbots”. The history of spirit photographs, a hotly debated phenomenon of the 19th and early 20th century, parallels advances in new photography techniques.

Some paranormal enthusiasts, though, are concerned that generative AI is more than just another new technology to play with and instead threatens the soul of what they do. “I’m not surprised that AI has been embraced by a lot of people in the ghost hunting community,” said Matsuo.

When GhostTube Seer was first released, she tried it out. She is skeptical of what she’s seen so far.

“Any time someone’s coming out with a ghost hunting tool using AI, my big question has always been: ‘OK if you’re using AI, you’re using some sort of large language model, what data are you training it on to [determine] what’s a ghost?’” Matsuo said. She also noted that there are ethical concerns: is a generative image tool using copyrighted art to create its own spectres? Are ghost hunting chatbots sending users into their own “paranormal echo chambers”?

Other paranormal enthusiasts are embracing the proverbial ghost in the machine. Seer isn’t the only generative AI app designed for ghost hunters. Sean Austin, a paranormal investigator who was featured on a Travel Channel series about ghost hunting, launched an app called Spirit Phone Innovations that uses “advanced AI” to analyze audio signals to detect EVP – electronic voice phenomena – a mainstay of ghost hunting.

“A lot of us come into the ghost hunting world because we’ve gone through some trauma or grief,” she said. Ghost hunting is, for many, a form of processing loss, she said. “Everyone’s trying to find the next big thing that could give us an answer into the unknown or validating the existence of ghosts.”

As AI’s physical footprint expands with the rapid construction of datacenters across the US, ghostly locations are likewise facing the threat of change. A former asylum in Pennsylvania that became a beloved haunted house was sold to a datacenter developer in late 2025 to be torn down. However, local residents banded together and successfully blocked it in May.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Christa Pike makes first public comments since failed execution: ‘There is pain in my mind and in my soul’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ed Pilkington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Pike is facing death penalty for 1995 murder of classmate, despite surviving a botched execution last month

Christa Pike has marked a month since her failed execution by Tennessee and released a statement in which she laments the “incompetence” that has led to this moment, adding that despite ongoing healing she remains in constant physical pain and mental anguish.

In comments released by her legal team on Friday, the prisoner said that there had not been a moment since she was injected with a massive dose of the sedative pentobarbital that she had not been in pain. “My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul,” she said.

Though she does not mention the state authorities who tried to kill her a month ago by injecting a full 5g of pentobarbital into her arms, she does make a pointed criticism clearly targeted at them. “I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position,” she said.

Pike was strapped to a gurney in the Tennessee execution chamber on 30 September, facing death for the 1995 murder of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, when she was 18. Members of the execution team spent almost an hour trying to establish an intravenous line through which to pump the sedative, but the procedure was botched and the prisoner survived.

Medical experts told the Guardian they were shocked by the apparent level of incompetence displayed in the execution chamber, after a blow-by-blow account of events was released by Pike’s lawyer, who was present in the room.

Pike is being held in the infirmary at the Debra Johnson rehabilitation center in Nashville, where she was returned after 10 days of intensive hospital treatment. She is being kept largely in solitary confinement, she said, “away from other people and the human connections that mean so much to me”.

Such isolation was its own form of pain, she said, given that she spent the first 28 years on death row in solitary confinement.

The events of 30 September have roiled Tennessee and sent shock waves across the US. The Republican governor of the state, Bill Lee, has ordered a pause on further executions until an outside review is conducted.

It is not clear what Tennessee intends to do with Pike. Earlier this week, Lee said he expected her death sentence to remain the same unless the courts determine otherwise.

Pike, dictating her statement to her lawyers, said that she had been prepared to die that night. “I had made my peace.”

Since she awoke, “alone in a hospital confused and in pain”, she has been searching for meaning about what happened to her. “I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time.”

She said in her slow road to recovery she drew sustenance from the “extraordinary love and support I have received from people around the world. To know that so many people care about me, that they see me as a human being whose life matters, is humbling.”

She thanked the first responders, doctors and nurses who cared for her in hospital, as well as her attorneys and those who “fought for me, stood beside me and refused to give up on me”.

She added: “I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone.”

Agent Mario Alberto Morale charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon over incident in Houston

A federal immigration agent who drove into and seriously injured a Texas man on 10 October after a botched traffic stop was indicted Friday on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

Mario Alberto Morales, 33, an agent with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), deliberately veered his SUV into Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, causing multiple leg fractures and a hip injury, journalists at a news conference in Houston were told.

In announcing the charge against Morales, Harris county district attorney Sean Teare questioned the training that Morales, a recent appointment by ICE, had received – and denounced the activities and conduct of the agency in support of the frequently violent immigration crackdown during Donald Trump’s second presidency.

His office is also investigating the fatal shooting by ICE in Houston in July of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, an immigrant who, like Parra Hernandez, was not the intended target of an enforcement operation.

Friday’s indictment came little more than five months after Christian Castro, an ICE officer who shot and wounded a Venezuelan man in an operation in Minnesota in January, was charged with assault and falsely reporting a crime.

“Their behavior and the fear that’s being instilled in such a big, vibrant group of people, of Harris county residents, is objectively making us all less safe,” Teare told reporters, citing what he said was a documented drop-off in reports of domestic violence, aggravated robberies and sexual assaults by victims who feared deportation.

“One of the most insidious things about these tactics and the way that ICE is behaving in our community is the fear that a large percentage of our population has right now. An ICE badge does not give you free rein to injure, kill, or violate the constitutional rights of anyone.”

A grand jury empanelled to investigate the case involving Morales returned the indictment on Friday morning after hearing evidence that Teare said was “as clear as any that I’ve ever prosecuted or investigated”.

Morales was driving an unmarked Jeep Cherokee and attempted to stop a pickup truck containing two men who jumped out and fled. Surveillance video played at the news conference showed Parra Hernandez, a Mexican construction worker with no criminal record or active deportation order, running across a restaurant parking lot when the pursuing SUV swerved into him and ran him over.

In an audio recording of a 911 call Morales made requesting the assistance of paramedics and the Harris county sheriff’s office, he is heard telling the dispatcher that Parra Hernandez ran in front of his vehicle and was hit, an assertion repeated in an official ICE account of the case released the following day.

In a statement on Friday, an ICE spokesperson said: “Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra Hernandez intentionally are reckless and false. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct.”

The spokesperson said the indictment was “nothing more than a political stunt by Houston sanctuary politicians”, using a term meant to describe local officials who don’t cooperate with federal immigration authorities.

“Federal officers acting in the course of their duties can only be investigated by other federal agencies,” the spokesperson also said. “Local governments do not have the authority to run such an investigation.”

Harris county sheriff Ed Gonzalez told the press conference his investigators later found out that, at the time it struck Parra Hernandez, Morales’s SUV also contained two handcuffed detainees from a previous, unrelated operation.

“I know of no law enforcement agency that would deem that to be acceptable,” he said. “To the contrary, it’s very unsafe. If some other crash could have occurred with them being handcuffed and shackled inside the vehicle it would have been a maybe even worse situation because they were very limited in their movement and in the backseat of the vehicle.”

Teare said that ICE deported at least two “material witnesses” within a week of Parra being struck over the prosecutor’s objection and with no opportunity to interview them. Parra Hernandez, he said, “is not even able to leave the rehab facility, and they are having court dates to try to deport him”.

The district attorney said he had collected “a significant amount of information” on Morales’s background – and said he was hired by ICE in August 2025 as part of the agency’s aggressive immigration “surge” into a number of US cities.

He declined to give details of any previous employers and said he had not received any of Morales’s training records.

“Whether or not he has those, we don’t know, but I can unequivocally tell you that I’ve reviewed thousands of job applications and resumes for law enforcement officers from around this state, and I’m not familiar with a single agency that would have hired this person based on his past,” Teare said.

Lawyers for Parra Hernandez, who remains in ICE custody, have said he would need numerous operations to recover from his injuries.

The whereabouts of the person that ICE said it was pursuing when Parra Hernandez was hurt are unknown. The agency identified a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes as their target, and released an image of someone they said was him.

The person in the photo, however, was Jose Hector Jimenez, who died in 2017 while being pursued by federal immigration authorities as he was trying to re-enter the US, said the Houston-based immigration advocacy group FIEL, which produced a Mexican death certificate provided by his family.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘Deepest possible partnership’: Canada and EU announce new alliance
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Alliance for the Future, unveiled at Montreal summit and open to other countries, conceived for world ‘shaken by new storms’

Canada and Europe have announced a new alliance of like-minded nations to serve as both a “protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive” and a powerful hedge against the unpredictable nature of geopolitics, while welcoming other countries to join.

Speaking to reporters on Friday from Montreal, the prime minister, Mark Carney, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, called the new partnership the Alliance for the Future and said the “deepest possible partnership between Canada and the 27-member bloc had the potential to offer unprecedented stability and opportunity”.

“Our societies have been shaken by new storms,” Carney told reporters, referring to the damaging effects of the climate emergency but also the “erosion of democratic norms” and “the weaponization of trade”.

As they concluded their two-day summit, Canada agreed to contribute to a €90bn support loan for Ukraine. Leaders also said future discussions would lead to a more integrated market worth tens of billions of dollars, reduced trade and travel restrictions, and new educational opportunities for both sides.

While a trade war between Canada and the United States has seen Carney go hunting for new geopolitical partners, an over-reliance on American companies – especially for defence – has also given Canada pause.

Last week, Elon Musk throttled the speeds of Starlink and Starshield over Ukraine in mid-October, severely disrupting Ukrainian military and defense operations.

Carney has repeatedly raised the concern that Canada’s defense technologies could be at the whim of political actors or companies with opposing interests. Musk, a dual Canadian citizen, is a critic of Canada’s governing Liberal party and has advocated for provinces to separate.

Carney pointed to a planned merger between the Canadian artificial intelligence company Cohere Inc and Germany’s Aleph Alpha GmbH as a step to lessening reliance on American AI giants. The tie-up will see the newly formed company have dual headquarters in Berlin and Toronto, and Canada’s federal government has announced a stake in Cohere worth up to C$1.6bn.

“We are not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don’t know, or by whom we don’t trust,” Carney said on Thursday.

Brussels and Ottawa also announced an agreement on Friday that would bringing Canada into Europe’s supercomputing network, giving Canadian access to European machines to train AI models.

In addition to lofty promises of helping to reshape the global order, or giving safe harbour to like-minded nations looking to weather uncertainty, Canadian and EU leaders also pitched their new, deeper relationship as one that addressed key sources of anxiety for residents, including the cost of living.

“When trade becomes a tool of economic pressure, it’s the families that pay the price, from the supermarket shelf to the cost of a new car,” Von der Leyen said, noting that previously trusted trusted suppliers of energy, critical minerals or semiconductors “are increasingly turned into instruments of pressure”.

“More competition, more choice,” Carney said earlier in the day, suggesting the alliance could find ways to build certainty around supply chains and “withstand shocks, together”.

The leaders once again brought up the prospect of Canada becoming an associate member. The designation is uncharted territory, said Von der Leyen, who added: “We have the ambition, trust, and creativity to shape it together.

“This [associate membership] is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength.”

While the leaders committed to the idea of associate membership, they said a clearer scope of the role would come at a 2027 summit. Some EU members had bristled at the idea of Canada being given a legally meaningless designation that they fear confuses other nations looking for membership. Germany and other states had worked behind the scenes to remove the phrase from a draft of the summit statement. But Von der Leyen, who first floated the term, and Carney both again referred to “associate membership” at the summit.

European Council president Antonio Costa, meanwhile, said earlier that Canada was “by far the most European of the non-European countries”, a sentiment that reflected a belief that despite geography, there was a collective sense of shared values.

Costa said the two sides would pursue “the most closer, the most deepest, the most stronger association ever between European Union and a non-European country”.

Still, the mere fact of the summit has caused friction in the province of Quebec, where the separatist Parti Québécois was recently elected to a minority government. The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, skipped the event after Ottawa’s refusal to let him speak publicly at it.

“The federal government would have us believe that the premier of Quebec being granted permission to serve shrimp cocktails at a reception constitutes an acceptable and sufficient form of influence for representing Quebec’s interests,” St-Pierre Plamondon wrote in a social media post earlier in the week.

He said an invitation to sit at the head table was the federal government asking Quebec “to get back in line, with the vassalization and invisibilization of Quebec which that implies, in exchange for obtaining better seats to watch the party”.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Charges dropped against man arrested in mass shooting at Ohio festival that wounded 12
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Eljay Crisp-Carr, 20, spent five months behind bars before prosecutors asked to dismiss charges

Ohio prosecutors on Friday dropped charges against a man arrested in connection with the 6 June shooting at Toledo’s Old West End festival that injured 12 people.

Eljay Crisp-Carr, 20, had faced more than 50 felony charges stemming from the shooting, including 25 counts of attempted murder. He was released after spending about five months behind bars.

But during a hearing Friday before the judge Lori Olender of the Lucas county court of common pleas, prosecutors requested that the charges against Crisp-Carr be dismissed.

His mother, April Carr, told news outlet WKYC she was “ecstatic” about the outcome.

“I’m beyond excited because what mother wants their child to be broadcast across the world for something they didn’t do?” she said.

Crisp-Carr’s defense team believes another person involved in the shooting remains at large.

“Now we’re still concerned that there is still somebody out here who actually did do the shooting, and as far as we’re concerned, that guy might be still out here still shooting,” defense attorney Alex Bodiford told WKYC.

The local news outlet WTVG reported that attorneys for Crisp-Carr had said he was not even at the festival when the shooting occurred. Lawyers for Crisp-Carr said they had video and cellphone evidence that supported his alibi, according to WTVG.

The Lucas county prosecutor’s office issued a statement to the media Friday morning explaining its decision, noting the dismissal was without prejudice – meaning charges can be refiled if necessary – though also acknowledging that it had found evidence apparently supporting Crisp-Carr’s defense.

“Due to new and developing evidence, the state of Ohio asked the court to dismiss the charges against Eljay Crisp-Carr without prejudice, and the court granted the request,” the prosecutor’s office said. “In September 2026, the Lucas county prosecutor’s office informed Mr Crisp-Carr’s attorney of discovery that may support his defense.”

The statement also addressed the status of the investigation, saying it was ongoing.

“The Toledo Police Department continues its investigation,” the statement said. “Both the department and our office remain committed to following the evidence and getting it right, just as we are in every case. As we said after the shooting in June, we will try this case in a courtroom, not in a court of public opinion.”

Speaking with WTVG after the charges against him were dropped, Crisp-Carr said: “God is good.”

He maintained that he had always known he was innocent and believed authorities had mistaken him for someone else.

When asked whether he believed the mistaken identification came from photographs, Crisp-Carr responded: “Yes, sir. Just picking with me.”

He also said he had attempted to explain to authorities that he was not the individual shown in the photograph. “They told me I was a monster,” Crisp-Carr said. “They just incriminated me.”

The Old West End festival mass shooting erupted when a fight between rival groups apparently escalated into two people shooting at each other, although they were not among the wounded.

Hundreds of people were attending the annual festival in a historic district of Toledo, a city on the western edge of Lake Erie. Organizers canceled the event’s second day because of the shooting.

As of Friday, there had been more than 385 mass shootings in the US so far for the year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, a nonpartisan resource which defines such cases as those in which four or more victims are wounded or killed.

The US perennially has had high rates of mass shootings, prompting many to call on the federal government to implement more substantial gun control. But Congress has not implemented such measures.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Florida prosecutors drop felony charge against Rick Ross in domestic violence case
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Miami-Dade officials drop charge of battery by strangulation against rapper due to ‘insufficient evidence’

Florida prosecutors on Thursday dropped a felony charge against rapper Rick Ross nearly a month after he was arrested in Miami Beach when a woman he was living with told police he hit her, court records said.

The Miami-Dade state attorney’s office filed paperwork on Thursday to drop a felony charge of battery by strangulation because of “insufficient evidence”. Ross, whose legal name is William Roberts II, still faces a misdemeanor charge of battery domestic violence.

Ross, 50, has pleaded not guilty to all charges, and his attorney said on Friday that his client would continue to defend himself against the allegations.

Ross surrendered at the Miami Beach police station on 1 October, two days after the woman filed a report with police, officials said. He was freed on bail several hours later.

According to an arrest report, a woman told Miami Beach detectives that she had been living with Ross when he accused her of cheating on him and struck her multiple times on 28 August. She said Ross also choked her with the collar of her shirt and slammed her into a wall. The woman said she was eventually able to leave the home and returned later – after Ross left – to collect her belongings.

Ross previously pleaded no contest to aggravated assault in 2017 after he was accused of forcing a man into a guesthouse at his suburban Atlanta mansion in 2015 and beating him with a handgun, according to Georgia court records. Under a Georgia first-time offender program, the court issued an order exonerating Ross of guilt on that felony count.

Ross is a longtime south Florida resident who gained prominence in 2006 with his debut single Hustlin’.

The rapper and entrepreneur helped put Miami on the musical map in the early 2000s, when most hip-hop fans looked to Atlanta and Houston as the southern rap headquarters. Hustlin’ was certified platinum twice by the Recording Industry Association of America and sparked a bidding war for Ross.

Ross’s debut album, Port of Miami, also went platinum, debuting at No 1 on the Billboard 200 chart. It was the first in a series of chart-toppers, including 2008’s Trilla and 2009’s Deeper Than Rap. He has been nominated for nine Grammy awards.

In 2008, he founded the Maybach Music Group label, boosting the careers of signees like Wale, Meek Mill and French Montana.
