https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Auzzy Byrdsell
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Daniel Jones held on $3m bail after studio art chair Pipo Nguyen-Duy and Tran Thi Phong found dead at home

Oberlin College was shaken on Friday after an award-winning professor of photography who had worked at the Ohio liberal arts college for nearly 30 years was found shot and killed on Wednesday, officials said.

Pipo Nguyen-Duy, 64, and his wife, Tran Thi Phong, 56, were found shot to death in their home.

The professor’s son, Daniel Jones, 31, was arrested on Wednesday in connection with the deadly shooting.

Officials said they were investigating a motive for the killing. Jones was charged with six counts of murder, four counts of felonious assault and one count of tampering with evidence, the authorities said. He was being held on $3m bail after an initial court appearance on Thursday. He did not enter a plea.

Nguyen-Duy was the studio art chair at Oberlin College, in north Ohio close to Lake Erie, where officers had responded to a car fire in a parking lot that morning.

The investigators found a Toyota hatchback with Oregon license plates registered to Jones.

Officers searched his father and stepmother’s home for a wellness check after the arrest. After a forced entry, Nguyen-Duy and Thi Phong were found shot to death, the authorities said.

Oberlin police have been in contact with Jones’s mother in Oregon, ABC News reported. Her name was not released, but Oberlin police report she told officials Jones had a mental illness and required medication.

Investigators also discovered Jones’s wallet and passport along with ammunition in the car before finding Jones about a mile away more than an hour later, the police said. The officers responded to a call from a resident reporting a “wet, disheveled man” at her front door and the authorities took him into custody without incident.

Officials said Jones had cuts to his face and injuries to his hand and arm at the time of the arrest. His lawyer, Jenifer Berki Merrill, said he preferred to go by his birth name, Asia Nguyen-Duy.

Pipo Nguyen-Duy migrated to the US from Vietnam in 1975 as a political refugee. He was considered highly respected at Oberlin College and had been honored for his photography and been named a Guggenheim fellow.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: A working-class Alaskan Native takes on a ‘multimillionaire’ Republican for seat in Congress
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Michael Sainato
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Independent candidate Bill Hill is threatening to unseat Trump ally Nick Begich with a message of affordability

As Republicans fight to maintain their narrow majority in Congress, they face a unique challenge in Alaska – not from a Democrat, but from an independent commercial fisher and first-time candidate running to flip the state’s lone House seat.

Bill Hill, who is an Alaska Native and has worked in education and construction, has positioned himself as a working-class candidate who will fight to make life more affordable for people like himself and his family.

Like voters across the country, Alaskans are deeply worried about affordability and the rising cost of basic necessities. Hill counts himself among the voters who have felt squeezed by high fuel prices driven up by Donald Trump’s war on Iran.

“When the spring fuel barge showed up in my home town of Naknek this spring, I went from paying $118 to fill my truck up to over $200,” Hill said. “Our gas went from $6.70 a gallon to almost $9 a gallon.”

Hill’s campaign to unseat the Republican congressman Nick Begich has gained momentum in the final weeks before the 3 November election, as national Democrats line up behind him and ad spending ramps up. The non-partisan Cook Political Report recently shifted the race from “likely Republican” to “leans Republican”, with the district favoring Republicans by six percentage points.

Recent polls showed Hill trailing Begich by single digits, but Hill’s support grows when voters learn more about his background, as he works to boost his name recognition. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added the race to its coveted “red to blue” program in September.

Hill has not specified whether he would caucus with Democrats if elected. This cycle, he is among several independents challenging Republicans in red states, including Senate candidates Dan Osborn in Nebraska and Todd Achilles in Idaho.

In Alaska, Begich may benefit from being the only Republican in the four-way general election contest run under the state’s ranked-choice system. Polls suggest support for Democrat Eric Hafner, who is serving time in a federal prison in New York and has no apparent links to the state, could complicate Hill’s path.

Hill has staked his campaign on his ability to personally relate to the economic pain and frustrations of his fellow Alaskans.

“I have spent a life being in the ditches, in the school hallways, on the back decks of fishing boats with hard-working people, running a small business like so many Alaskans do, and I know what the struggles and challenges that we face are,” Hill said. “I also know what our hopes and dreams are.”

He noted the cost of heating fuel nearly doubled, from $4.50 a gallon to $8.30, while price increases in some of Alaska’s more remote villages have soared even higher. In places such as Ambler and Shungnak, Indigenous villages that sit along the Kobuk River near the Arctic circle, the price of a gallon of gas has surpassed $25.

“This is crushing Alaskans,” Hill said. “We are feeling the crunch every single day.”

More than one in three Alaskan households aren’t earning enough income to cover housing, food, childcare and other essential expenses, according to a report by the United Way of Anchorage and Alaska 211 published earlier this month.

In 2024, Begich, the conservative son of a prominent Democratic family in Alaska, narrowly ousted the incumbent Democrat, Mary Peltola, who is currently running for US Senate. Though Trump won the state by a resounding 13%, Begich prevailed by just 2.4%.

Like Peltola, Hill is a supporter of gun rights, in line with Alaska’s strong hunting tradition, and is a supporter of both the oil industry and the renewable energy industry.

Hill cited the impacts on Alaskans of cuts to the Snap nutrition-assistance program and Medicaid, the expiration of Affordable Care Act tax credits, Trump’s tariffs, federal job losses in Alaska, and the cancellation of several Alaskan renewable energy projects by the Trump administration as contributing factors to added costs facing Alaskans, with many of the cuts enacted by the president’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act set to go into effect in 2027.

“It is getting very, very difficult for working people in Alaska to get by,” Hill said, charging that his opponent was a “multimillionaire working for billionaires”.

With his reported assets valued at $119,000, Hill has sought to highlight the vast wealth gap between himself and his opponent, who is worth at least $7.4m. “He’s somebody who doesn’t represent the everyday Alaskan in his work,” Hill added.

Begich’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment, but previously denied his wealth affects his voting record.

“Congressman Begich’s personal finances have no impact on his legislative decisionmaking process,” Silver Prout, a spokesperson for Begich’s congressional office, told the Anchorage Press in an email.

Begich praised the passage of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, calling it a “transformative victory”, and has continued supporting Trump’s war in Iran.

Hill, a Dena’ina Athabascan Native Alaskan, has worked as a commercial fisher since he was eight years old and continues to do so. He has also worked union construction jobs with Laborers’ Local 341, and worked for 25 years in education as a union member teacher, principal and school district superintendent.

Alaska has one of the highest union density rates in the US. As of 2025, 18.1% of all workers in the state were union members, the third highest rate in the US, behind Hawaii and New York.

More than 20 labor organizations, including the Alaska AFL-CIO, have endorsed Hill’s campaign. Begich, meanwhile, has signed on to the National Right to Work Act and has a 0% lifetime voting score by the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the US.

“Unions need more support in Congress, and we see attacks on trying to tear down their power in this nation,” Hill said. “At the end of the day, unions built the middle class of this country, and they’re the ones who can do it again.”

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: Seth Meyers on Trump and Vance’s tactics: ‘No one’s buying your fake folksy bullshit’
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Guardian staff
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
Late-night hosts criticised ‘cosplaying as everyday folks’ and mocked the president’s latest attack on a reporter

Late-night hosts ridiculed Donald Trump and JD Vance for their hollow attempts to appeal to working-class voters while also detailing the president’s latest unhinged attack on a reporter.

On Late Night, Seth Meyers said that Republicans had been “cosplaying as regular, everyday folks” for a while, showing clips of Donald Trump working at McDonald’s and the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, claiming to be a soybean farmer.

This week the right continued to lose their minds over a joke made by Barack Obama, comparing Trump’s White House to Saddam Hussein decorating a Cheesecake Factory.

They were less bothered about the comparison to a “violent oppressive dictator” and more about a perceived slight towards a popular restaurant chain, organising an unsuccessful press opportunity outside one that Bessent was visiting.

Obama responded with more jabs, leading Meyers to say that “standup comedy Obama is back” and joked that his next special will be called Hussein in the Membrane.

Meyers also quipped that Rudy Guiliani “missed it because he showed up at the Cheesecake Factory Total Landscaping”.

Meyers called it “rightwing fan fiction” that Trump was a “true man of the people”, a claim that was “such obvious bullshit”.

This week also saw JD Vance claim that he can’t pronounce the names of countries in the Middle East when talking to audience members at a rally.

“No one’s buying your fake folksy bullshit,” Meyers said, reminding his viewers how rich and entitled Vance is.

He did joke that “if Trump said he couldn’t pronounce the names then I would believe that” then playing a clip of him stumbling over countries.

The right has also been obsessing over James Talarico, the Democratic candidate in Texas who “isn’t a real American because he secretly doesn’t like meat” with Trump claiming he is a vegan yet mispronouncing the word.

“Trump’s just gone full goblin now,” he said after playing a strange clip of him talking about meat.

Yet it was “not the most bizarre insult” from the right, with Ted Cruz saying that if you picked 1,000 adjectives for Talarico, the list wouldn’t include the word masculine.

“Do you think you’re masculine just because you grew 65% of a beard?” he asked.

There have also been some “truly revolting attacks” on the Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, with Republicans calling him many things including a jihadist.

“It’s disgusting how nakedly racist this is,” Meyers said before adding that it “seems like these tactics are backfiring” given poll numbers.

On Jimmy Kimmel Live! the host spoke about Trump having a tantrum after a reporter asked him if he was feeling well given a last-minute change in his schedule.

“Natalie, baby’s cranky again, we need a diaper change on runway two,” he said before adding “imagine him calling someone else out of shape”.

Kimmel suggested someone taking “him out to that reflecting pool” so he can see himself, adding that it was the “pot calling the belly fat”.

His rallies “used to be Team Trump through and through” yet more and more interlopers have found their way in. This week saw an Ohio heckler shout that Trump went on “the Jeffrey Epstein plane” and his fans responded with boos.

Trump has continued to brag about passing his cognitive tests, something “they give old people to make sure they can wipe themselves”.

He also played clips of Obama responding to the outrage over the Cheesecake Factory joke saying that we “traded in a Ferrari for a folding chair”.

Kimmel joked that, for Trump, the Cheesecake Factory menu was the “closest he gets to reading a book”.

This week has also seen Trump’s infamously terrible ex-press secretary Katie Zacharia “trying to repair her image” with a string of interviews, including a disastrous one with Piers Morgan.

Kimmel played footage of her “glitching” when trying to avoid a question, saying that someone should “maybe unplug her and plug her back in”.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Trump vowed to reduce prices, but his policies have fueled US inflation  | Steven Greenhouse
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Steven Greenhouse in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
‘Even though economists warned that tariffs would be inflationary, Trump has enthusiastically embraced them’

Donald Trump successfully campaigned for his second term two years ago promising to reduce prices on day one, but ever since he returned to the White House, he has done little to fight inflation or reduce prices. Instead, some of his most important policy decisions – most notably his war against Iran and his tariff wars – have increased inflation instead of reducing it. This helps explain why more than one in five Americans who voted for Trump now disapprove of the job he’s doing.

Even though economists warned that tariffs would be inflationary, Trump has enthusiastically embraced them during his second term. Indeed, the “liberation day” tariffs he imposed soon after returning to office increased the price of hundreds of goods, including citrus fruits, steel, bananas, beef and auto parts. When the supreme court overturned those tariffs as illegal, Trump immediately imposed new 10% across-the-board tariffs that again helped push up prices (a lower court found those tariffs unlawful, too). Time and again, Trump has slapped on new tariffs even though they inherently push up prices because tariffs are a tax on imported goods. Little wonder that a Fox News poll this month found that 77% of Americans disapprove of how Trump has handled tariffs.

Candidate Trump pledged to slash “energy and electricity prices by half”, to get “gasoline below $2 a gallon”, and to bring down “airfares and housing costs”. He has failed to do any of those things. Gas now averages $4.28 a gallon nationally, according to AAA. Yale Budget Lab says Trump’s tariffs will cost the average household $1,100 this year, while Moody’s Analytics says the war with Iran has already cost US households about $2,000 from higher energy, fuel and transportation costs and from higher interest rates.

Worsening Americans’ affordability problems, prices have been rising faster than workers’ wages in recent months. As a result, Americans have seen no real wage growth on average since Trump returned to office – both average hourly pay and prices have risen by 5.4% since January 2025.

Matthew Middleton, a White House spokesman, defended Trump’s record on inflation and critiqued Joe Biden’s, saying: “President Trump has implemented an aggressive, pro-growth economic agenda that has blunted Biden’s historic 40-year high inflation crisis, driven economic growth, increased wages and created private-sector jobs in areas that had been hollowed out and shipped overseas.”

After returning to the White House, Trump helped push up electricity prices by ending federal subsidies for low-cost renewable energy. His gung-ho cheerleading for datacenters, along with his speeding up of federal permitting to build them, has helped fuel a datacenter construction boom that is expected to increase electricity costs to consumers by more than $6bn. Trump and the Republican-led Congress further hit consumers by raising the cost of many electric vehicles by $7,500 when they ended EV subsidies.

When Trump plunged into war against Iran eight months ago, he showed little concern about what that war would mean for inflation back home. He ignored warnings that the war would cause Iran to close the strait of Hormuz, which in turn would cause oil and gas prices to soar. Since the war began, US gas prices have risen by over 40%, diesel prices by nearly 70%, and some fertilizer prices by 20%. Record diesel prices have pushed airfares skyward, while soaring diesel and fertilizer prices have created a sea of red ink for US farmers.

In one tiff over inflation, after Trump said last June “I love the inflation,” Senator Bernie Sanders responded, “You know who doesn’t love inflation, Mr President? Working families struggling to afford gas, groceries and other necessities because of your disastrous actions.”

Further defending Trump’s record on inflation, White House spokesman Middleton said: “The President has always been clear about temporary disruptions as a result of the Iran conflict, but this administration will continue to deliver economic wins for the American people over the next two years. While Democrats pretend to care about ‘affordability’, this administration has delivered tangible wins to make life more affordable for American families: President Trump signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, locked in nearly 20 trade deals and will continue to put American workers first.”

A White House official added that Trump’s policies “have created an environment for sustained increase in energy supply and lower costs for American households and businesses”. Those policies have included making it easier to drill for oil and reducing business and environmental regulations.

Trump’s moves have further worsened Americans’ affordability woes by pushing up interest rates. By the time Biden left office, inflation, which had soared to a painful 9% during the pandemic, had slid to 3.0% and was heading lower. But Trump’s policies have played a major role in pushing inflation back up to 3.7%. That has caused the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, while also pushing mortgage rates higher. Thirty-year fixed mortgage rates have climbed to 7.4%, making it considerably harder for young and non-affluent Americans to buy homes. (As for Trump’s 2024 promise to reduce housing costs, he refused to sign a bipartisan bill that sought to speed housing construction with the aim of making housing more affordable.)

Under Trump, not only has the national debt climbed above $40tn, but this year’s federal budget deficit will reach $2tn. That worsening fiscal picture has worried bond investors and pushed up interest rates. (In 2019, Trump promised to eliminate the entire national debt within eight years.)

Trump’s policies have increased healthcare costs for millions of Americans. By pushing Congress to cut Medicaid by $1tn and to not extend Obamacare subsidies, Trump helped cause more than 20 million people to lose health coverage or pay more out-of-pocket for healthcare. Americans who pay for their own health insurance saw their premiums jump by 25% this year, with many households paying not just hundreds of dollars more, but thousands more.

To be sure, Trump has taken several steps to fight inflation, but most have been minor. His TrumpRX program has offered many drugs at lower prices, and that was one factor among many that contributed to the 4.5% drop in prescription drug prices over the past year. In August, Trump announced he would import 660m pounds of ground beef from Latin America to reduce beef prices – that move (which angered ranchers) was a direct response to the public outcry over the higher beef prices resulting from his tariffs. Last November, in a sharp about-face aimed at reducing prices, Trump rescinded his tariffs on coffee and tropical fruits after consumers had grown angry that coffee and citrus prices had soared due to Trump’s tariffs.

With his promise to pay $5,000 to every adult if Republicans retain control of Congress, Trump is essentially saying he will make it up to voters for pushing up prices and worsening affordability problems. Trump says the money for those payments could come from tariff revenues, but guess where those tariffs revenues come from? They come from the money that US consumers have had to pay on Trump’s tariffs – on his taxes on imports. Some might say that Trump wants to pay Peter by first robbing Peter.

Trump keeps saying that affordability problems are “a hoax”. But whenever average Americans go to a supermarket or gas station, they know that the affordability squeeze is real and a big issue in their lives. Many can see that Trump, despite his campaign promises, has done precious little to reduce inflation. Indeed, in very bad news for Republicans in the midterm elections, a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 78% of Americans blame Trump’s policies for pushing up prices.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: I’m a gen Z voter. Content creators have far less power than politicians think | Alex Bronzini-Vender
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Alex Bronzini-Vender
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Both US parties scramble to win young voters via influencer operations. The evidence doesn’t support their efforts

In tight races, any group that shifts a few points can be called decisive. In 2024, however, gen Z voters actually earned the spotlight.

Take Michigan, where Donald Trump won by about 1.4 points: he and Kamala Harris evenly split the youth vote, a 24-point collapse in the Democratic edge since 2020. If young voters made up just 15% of the state’s electorate, their swing toward the president would be worth roughly 3.6 points, larger than Trump’s entire margin of victory.

Ever since, both parties have scrambled to court the tastemakers who seem to have gen Z’s ear.

At her debut briefing, the former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt reserved a “new media seat” in the briefing room, inviting podcasters, influencers and content creators to apply for credentials. The NRCC, House Republicans’ campaign arm, has paid more than $120,000 to a network of conservative influencers, listing the expense simply as “media”.

Not to be outdone, the Democratic National Committee has partnered with more than 500 online personalities through its “Influencer & Creative” operation – and has lately floated the idea of a creator-hosted debate during the 2028 primaries.

The same wishful theory undergirds all these efforts: both parties seem to think online creators can simply upload political opinions straight into our heads.

As a zoomer myself, I find this theory rather patronizing. More to the point, it isn’t true: there’s little evidence that online creators play much of a role in how zoomers actually vote. And if young voters decide these midterms, influencers shouldn’t get the credit.

In a survey this year by the Media Insight Project, 63% of 18-to-34-year-olds said they get news from influencers “at least sometimes”. Yet among teens and adults who actually receive news from these people, just 9% report having a great deal of confidence in what they are being told. (AI chatbots enjoy a nearly identical rate of trust, at 10%.)

Other polls have found much the same thing: when YouGov surveyed young voters across eight battleground states in September on whom they actually turn to for political advice, half named a family member and three in 10 named a friend. Just 6% named an influencer.

In another survey of young people released this spring by Circle, a civic-engagement research center at Tufts, just 9% of respondents said they got political information from social media posts by influencers and celebrities. Another 14% pointed to podcasts hosted by influencers, artists, comedians or other celebrities.

By contrast, 45% of respondents – the largest share – got their information from political, advocacy or community organizations they follow, while nearly a third cited conversations with family and friends.

To whatever extent that internet personalities actually persuade people, their powers rest entirely on the illusion that they speak for themselves. Naturally, both parties have responded by shattering that illusion.

Campaigns and their allies increasingly pay for those voices, often at exorbitant prices. In this year’s race for California governor, Tom Steyer paid at least 17 influencers $5,000 or more apiece, while Katie Porter’s campaign paid one lifestyle creator $25,000 for what appeared to be a single post. A TikTok creator with 1.7 million followers said a Republican-affiliated group had offered her $36,000 for a video, and a company with deep Republican ties once paid a squad of gen Z creators to defend Ken Paxton, now Texas’s Republican Senate nominee, on X.

Some influencers attempt to keep these “partnerships” hidden. The New York Times found that Josh Greene, a progressive creator with nearly 800,000 followers, had not always disclosed the fact that he’d taken money from at least seven candidates and allied groups this cycle.

And when the payments do come to light – as they tend to – they risk destroying the very credibility that campaigns were trying to buy. As the Rainey Center for Public Policy found this summer, 47% of voters said they’d trust a creator less after learning a political post had been paid for by a campaign; only 11% said they’d trust them more.

Obviously, the internet matters. Zohran Mamdani, who won young men by roughly 40 points in last year’s New York mayoral race, has said many New Yorkers he met knew him only from his appearances on podcasts such as Flagrant, hosted by the comedian Andrew Schulz. (As Mamdani put it, Democrats should “stop treating young people and young men with the condescension that we often see and hear in our politics”.) And Trump’s tour of the podcasting sphere in 2024 had racked up more than 100m YouTube views by the day after the election that year.

Still, both appearances were interviews, not simply paid content. Even if the questioning is friendly, the candidates still do most of the talking. And the podcast-interview format itself isn’t magic: Kamala Harris’s appearance on Call Her Daddy seems to have done little to move young voters.

Every older generation finds the next one inscrutable, and gen Z is an especially tough read. Older Americans can be forgiven for struggling to grasp what it means to come of age in the era of social media. (Our memes are, admittedly, really weird.)

Still, if you ignore our screen time, we’re pretty normal after all. Like swing voters twice our age, we’ve ditched the Republican party because prices remain stubbornly high. For all the money Washington is spending to decode our political decision-making, the most surprising thing about gen Z voters may be just how boringly ordinary we are.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The world needs the United Nations more than ever. It needs a new lease on life | Alex Rondos and Mark Medish
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Alex Rondos and Mark Medish
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
We need neither ‘peace in our time’ nor ‘perpetual peace’ – but enough peace to keep civilization

To save the United Nations from the irrelevance in which it now wallows, the next secretary general will require the concerted backing of the few powers that govern the security council.

The paradox is that the great powers who created the institution in the 1940s and recently treat it with a cavalier cynicism are now the ones who need it most, as does the rest of the world.

This is not about nostalgia for what was created after the second world war. That world has changed. We are no longer in the cold war. But it is carelessness of high order to assume that some mystical process will create a world while, in the meantime, the most powerful give license to some dangerous pathologies that have brought us to ruin in the past.

The resort to war over dialogue and diplomacy has reared its head again. Restraint has given way to calculated recklessness. Changing facts on the ground before talking now creates leverage, and that is why we see an unprecedented multiplication of centers of violence. Militias and mercenaries abound.

Collective security to which all commit to be effective is now supplanted by a petulant isolationism. Revolutionary new technologies have spurred a rush to secure minerals and supply routes upending traditional notions of sovereignty. Drone warfare has made violence much more affordable. Frontiers are now up for grabs.

The permanent members of the security council, anachronistically still composed of the victors of the second world war, have a tall order. Quarrels that are as old as tribes, communities and nations now have new, more lethal weapons.

Civil wars, border wars and the return of imperial ambition are not relics. They drive the war in Ukraine, the drift toward conflict in the Horn of Africa, the instability around the Gulf and the Red Sea, and the standoff over Taiwan.

These conflicts are now multiplying at a scale and speed in a time when global regulatory arrangements over existential threats are denigrated. Proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, pandemics, climate change will either be fueled or managed by artificial intelligence.

As AI is woven into military planning, early warning and command systems, it compresses the time leaders have to think before they act, and it multiplies the tools of deception and destabilization. A world that learned, slowly and at great risk, to live with nuclear weapons must now learn to live with machines that may shape decisions about using them.

These dangers can only be contained if we dispense with some misplaced assumptions.

The first is that the UN is a club of the like-minded. It was never meant to be. The UN exists so that states that distrust or even detest one another have somewhere to meet – a place that offers hospitality to adversaries.

If the hard conversations about war and technology do not happen there, where else will they happen in a way that protects the rest of humanity? It is about co-existence, not convergence.

The second assumption is that power can be evenly distributed. It cannot. Pretending otherwise is idealism to the point of fault. A handful of states possess the disproportionate capacity to contain these dangers or to unleash them. In practice, today this means the United States, China and Russia.

But there is no reason to exclude India or a better-integrated European Union. Even if they do not trust one another, they need only recognize a shared interest in a world that remains manageable.

This harsh reality should temper the fashionable faith in “middle powers”. Their activism is understandable, even admirable: they see the great powers changing character and are trying to respond. But they are called middle powers for a reason. They cannot, on their own, end a major war or govern a technology developed mostly elsewhere.

This does not mean that might makes right. Neither does it mean that complicated times need simple answers which would be a repudiation of politics at the international level. Power checked by reasonable deliberation, negotiation and diplomacy is a core principle that inspired the charter of the United Nations. This moment calls for a rededication to principled pragmatism.

History has much to teach. When the plague swept Europe in the 14th century, the city states of Italy established the practice of quarantines and an early form of health certification. The science may have been wrong and the system imperfect. But it worked well enough, and it rested on self-interest, not virtue.

Since the mid-20th century, in a radically different technological era, nuclear proliferation and the risk of nuclear war have been contained, so far, through a lengthy process of negotiation and agreements.

Imagine a renewed UN that is a problem-solver rather than a bystander, a credible forum rather than a costly talking shop, and the prime instrument for collective action.

None of this happens unless the great powers want it to. Choosing a secretary general is one of the few moments when they must agree on a qualified person and a timely agenda. The superpowers, middle powers and emerging powers of the global south may each have reasons for skepticism. But they share a stronger reason to make this effort.

We need neither “peace in our time” nor “perpetual peace” – but enough peace to keep civilization.

Alex Rondos is a former envoy of the European Union. Mark Medish is a former senior US national security and treasury official

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on 50 years of The Selfish Gene: flawed, outdated, yet still a model of truly popular science writing | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Richard Dawkins’ first work has thrilled fans and frustrated critics for five decades. The science has moved on, but any writer looking to supplant its place must learn its lessons

Richard Dawkins’ The Selfish Gene was not predicted to be a success. Its initial print run, published this week in 1976, was just 5,000. It went on to sell millions, and is perhaps the most influential work of pop-science ever. For 50 years, it has been the go-to resource for the layperson seeking to understand evolution.

What accounts for its enduring power? Prof Dawkins’ central claim, that “we are survival machines – robot vehicles blindly programmed to preserve the selfish molecules known as genes” was provocative, stripping the messy stuff of human and other life down to a simple law. And yet the book is primarily concerned with proving that complex, selfless behaviour such as altruism in animals can emerge from these basic “selfish” drives, satisfyingly resolving an apparent paradox. Prof Dawkins – a zoologist by training – also succeeded in conjuring entertaining, vividly drawn vignettes of the lives of animals, from lions and ants to hawks and honeybees, to make his points.

Nevertheless, 50th anniversary celebrations have been somewhat muted. In an essay in the journal Nature, the historian of science Nathaniel Comfort suggests there is something almost malign about The Selfish Gene’s commitment to a simple kind of determinism.

There is certainly that and more to take issue with. Prof Dawkins fought publicly with eminent biologists such as Stephen Jay Gould about whether genes were the primary target of natural selection, rather than the individual organism or group – a legitimate clash between differing theories that was mirrored in the scientific literature. More quietly and damningly, many biologists bemoan the way the book seems to assume every trait is some kind of adaptation – hardly the textbook view, which has long recognised the role of randomness and chance in evolution. It also focuses almost exclusively on animals. And it is hard to read Prof Dawkins fresh, without the knowledge that the later books are repetitive and that his comments outside his field – including on feminism, disability and describing Islam as “the greatest force for evil in the world today” in 2013 – don’t suggest a great or sensitive thinker.

Perhaps the best way to read The Selfish Gene is alongside its critics. Prof Dawkins’ Oxford tutor Arthur Cain called it a young man’s book, pointedly suggesting that the author would come to regret or recant his most bombastic claims. Prof Dawkins never really did, but his intransigence brought out the best in his critics, from Prof Gould to Richard Lewontin or Hilary and Steven Rose. Read all together, it makes for a full and rollicking picture of modern evolutionary debate

It also remains a model of style. The philosopher John Dupré, no fan of Prof Dawkins’ scientific thought, nonetheless calls it a paradigmatic example of successful popular science writing. The book works on this level because it takes a point of view in a live scientific debate, and argues its side with engaging dash and zeal. Prof Dawkins is often too polemical, but most science writing tends to be heavily didactic, with little argument or rhetorical flourish. And it is possible to both inform and persuade: Sean Carroll’s Endless Forms Most Beautiful and Nick Lane’s The Vital Question take a similarly clear, provocative line.

The science has moved on, and The Selfish Gene has flaws. But any writer looking to supplant its place in the public imagination with a more capacious vision of evolution must reckon with the reasons for its long-running success. For all its problems, it remains a model of its genre.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: ‘We are not in Disneyland’: Arteta warns Dowman of Arsenal’s demands
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Ed Aarons
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Mikel Arteta has warned Max Dowman that he “is not in Disneyland” and must learn from his red card against Fleetwood after Arsenal’s appeal against his three-match suspension was rejected.

The 16-year-old became the youngest player ever to be sent off in the League Cup on Tuesday as the Premier League champions crashed out to the League Two side Fleetwood. Arteta said he was “very disappointed” that the Football Association rejected the appeal against his red card and felt Dowman was lucky not to suffer a broken foot from “reckless tackles”.

But despite describing his reaction as “minimal”, the Arsenal manager revealed he had spoken to Dowman this week to underline his responsibilities after he was also sent off this month playing for England Under 19s.

“I’ve done it, so I try to prevent that [in future]. That’s why I’m so protective of these things and especially with young players, because we have made those mistakes. You know how much you can get punished and how much it can change what happens next, and it’s not the first time, so obviously we need to put an end to it very, very quickly,” Arteta said.

Arteta said he had not seen the criticism of his angry reaction to Dowman’s red card, when he appeared to aim a few choice words towards the forward as he headed down the tunnel. But he defended his actions after warning Dowman he was likely to be targeted before the game. “It’s something that we discussed just before we went out, because it’s not the first time that happened,” he said.

“For me, it was the best reaction ever to be able to be who I am. You want to see the reaction of his teammates? When they have to play with 10, you want to see that? That’s the level, and that’s the reaction. But the reaction when I don’t win, you know what the reaction is? I’m pissed off, big time.

“So we need to be ready for that. This is the environment and this is the reality. Otherwise, we are in Disneyland. We are not in Disneyland. We are in the Premier League at this level and we look after him so much that you cannot imagine. But at the same time, we’re going to demand [from] him like anybody else because he needs to earn the right to play.”

Dowman will be suspended for Sunday’s trip to Liverpool and the games against Hull and Newcastle, while Noni Madueke faces a late test to see if he has recovered from an ankle problem that kept him out of the game against Fleetwood. Arteta also revealed that Bukayo Saka is not expected back until at least after the international break as Arsenal await more news on his thigh injury.

Arteta said they had “put every argument on the table” in an attempt to clear Dowman’s name but to no avail. “Very disappointed,” he said. “Especially with the reckless tackles that he received, and then his reaction is minimal in relation to the action.

“I think you have to read the context of the player, the age, and what happened previously. It could have been really bad. And we are lucky today that he hasn’t had a broken foot. That’s clear.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.title: Breeders’ Cup 2026: Folsom Blues set to go off as favourite in Juvenile Turf, day one – live
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.author: Greg Wood
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.text:
🐎 Updates from Keeneland. First race 6.55pm GMT (2.55pm ET) 🐎 Full race card | Thoughts? Get in touch with Greg via email

Two minutes to post time for the Juvenile Fillies, and Emphatic is the one for money on-course. She’s down to 3-1 on the tote, with Miss Monica steady at 2-1.

Miss Monica has opened as the 2-1 favourite on the US tote, with Emphatic next at 7-2 and Domain Expansion on 9-2.

The unbeaten Manuka Honey deserves a mention too, she is unbeaten in three and showed plenty of determination to get to the lead in the stretch in the Grade Three Pocahontas at Churchill last time.

Libertango went off as a very warm favourite for the opener, paying $5 for the win to a $2 stake, which is 6-4 in British terms.

News on the objection – Harper’s Corner has been disqualified from third place, and Mussab moves up to take his place with Final Objective in fourth

Harper’s Corner was placed behind Moonrise after being found to have caused inteference to Andrew Balding’s filly.

News on that objection when it arrives, but for now we need to look ahead to the next race on the card, the Breeders’ Cup Juvenile Fillies.

The market for the first of the two dirt events is headed by two unbeaten fillies, Emphatic and Miss Monica, while Domain Expansion was an impressive winner switching from turf to dirt last time out.

Emphatic is three-from-three for trainer Brendan Walsh, and her prep includes a win in the Grade One Alcibiades Stakes over track and trip last time out, when she made all the running from the inside stall.

Miss Monica is unbeaten in two for Bob Baffert, both at Del Mar and including the Grade One Debutante Stakes last time, which she won by six-and-a-quarter lengths.

Domain Expansion was an outsider for the Grade Two Oak Leaf Stakes at Santa Anita but went clear to register an easy seven-length success.

It promises to be a tight contest between the three market leaders, but there was a lot to like about Miss Monica’s latest win and she appeals as the likeliest winner.

There is, though, an objection, although it concerns Harper’s Corner, in third. David Egan, who rode Force Noir, has lodged it.

Fairytale stuff from Billy Loughnane. He broke in mid-division and was forced to wait behind horses before starting to thread his way through, and still had five lengths to make on the leader turning in.

He launched Libertango down the middle of the track and as Ruiva dropped away, he started to make ground relentlessly and then reeled in Hell Of A Spin with a stride to spare.

They are down at the start before the Breeders’ Cup Juvenile Turf Sprint, Libertango remains a solid favourite at 2-1. And they’re loading now …

I can’t be entirely certain about this as I don’t have a Kentucky rulebook to hand, but a commentator on the track feed suggests that if Libertango wins, Flavien Prat will still be due his cut of the prize money because the switch was so late.

George Boughey is chatting to a track reporter about Billy Loughnane’s unexpected appearance on Libertango.

double quotation markI feel a little bit guilty as Flavien has ridden a Graded winner for us out here and I had to send him a message apologising. It’s a strange scenario but Billy is our retained rider.

2-1 Libertango 4-1 Brickyard Belle, Harper’s Corner 8-1 Mussab 10-1 Moonrise 13-1 bar

I was torn between Libertango and Brickyard Belle as the pick for this race, but the Billy Loughnane news has persuaded me to come down on Libertango’s side. What a story that would be to launch the 2026 Breeders’ Cup.

Now there’s a surprise – Flavien Prat was expected to be aboard Libertango in the opener but Billy Loughnane has somehow managed to get himself down to 8st 5lb and will be a late replacement on George Boughey’s filly. She’s opened up as the 2-1 favourite in the on-course betting.

A deep European challenge for the opener also includes Andrew Balding’s Moonrise, fourth of six in the Cheveley Park, and Richard and Peter Fahey’s Mussab, the winner of his last three starts including the Cornwallis Stakes.

Force Noir, in the purple colours of Kia Joorabchian’s Amo Racing, deserves a mention too. He was a blowout when fancied for the Norfolk Stakes at Royal Ascot but back to form when second in the Group One Middle Park Stakes last time.

Ruiva was a late addition to the field for the opener and could well add more pace to what was already likely to be a fierce gallop. She will do well to get to the turn in front of Harper’s Corner, though, while Libertango will likely be tracking the main US-trained hope, Brickyard Belle, in the early stages.

Flavien Prat takes over from Billy Loughnane in Libertango’s saddle as the new champion jockey on the Flat cannot do the weight. She was no match for Sun Princess, the favourite for the Juvenile Fillies Turf, in the Cheveley Park Stakes last time but there is nothing of that quality in this field and she is a worthy favourite.

Brickyard Belle, meanwhile, is unbeaten in two starts and made up plenty of ground to catch Harper’s Corner in the Grade Three Matron Stakes last time, having been shuffled back earlier in the race.

Hello racing fans wherever in the world you happen to be, and welcome to the Guardian’s liveblog coverage of the 2026 Breeders’ Cup meeting at Keeneland in Kentucky.

As is now traditional at the self-styled “World Championships” of Flat racing, Friday is for the juveniles, with a total of $7m (£5.2m) up for grabs, while tomorrow’s nine-race card, worth $27m (£20.3m) will include the Turf and the Classic, featuring many of the best middle-distance runners in the game.

The last time that the Breeders’ Cup was staged at Keeneland in 2022, European-trained horses took all three of Friday’s turf events and the visitors will be hoping for the same again this time around. Europe fields the favourite in all three, including Aidan O’Brien’s outstanding filly Sun Goddess in the Juvenile Fillies’ Turf at 20.15, and while O’Brien has scratched two from the Juvenile Turf at 21.35, he still has the second-favourite, Haffner, and his son, Joseph, will saddle the market leader, Folsom Blues.

On the dirt, there’s a somewhat disappointing turnout of just half a dozen for the Juvenile, and USS Valor, quite possibly the best two-year-old seen out in the States this year, is not among them, as Barry Irwin, his owner, wants to focus on next year’s Kentucky Derby instead. In his absence, Bob Baffert’s Hughes will be a strong favourite, and Baffert will have high hopes of a big-race double as his unbeaten Miss Monica is fancied for the Juvenile Fillies.

The action is underway in Kentucky at 18.55 with the Juvenile Turf Sprint, and there will be previews, pace maps, quotes, betting news, results and more to enjoy here on the blog as the the card unfolds.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: NCAA basketball 2026-27 predictions: from JuJu Watkins to Tyran Stokes, the names you’ll know by March
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Ella Brockway, Bryan Armen Graham, Stephanie Kaloi and Nicholas Levine
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Can Florida’s continuity trump the transfer portal? Will JuJu Watkins pick up where she left off? And who will survive an expanded March Madness? Our writers weigh in

Lots of stuff. The return of JuJu Watkins at USC after her 19-month injury layoff, the debut of Tyran Stokes at Kansas, the potential turnaround of the Big East on the men’s side, and the stacked ACC on the women’s side. Ella Brockway

JuJu Watkins’ return from injury, obviously, but also the question of whether college hoops can maintain any sense of continuity in the transfer portal era. Michigan won the men’s natty in April, then lost their coach to the NBA and watched much of their roster disintegrate. Florida, meanwhile, have managed to keep the majority of the core from their 2025 title team together. Which model wins out? Bryan Armen Graham

Multiple things, but top of mind: Like many fans of women’s college basketball, I’m already excited by what JuJu Watkins has shown in the preseason. She’s been away from the court for a long time, and it will be thrilling to see the presumptive No 1 draft pick take over again. Stephanie Kaloi

The new-look Pac-12 Conference. This nine-team league has only two schools that were previously in the Pac-12 and adds five schools from the Mountain West, plus powerhouse Gonzaga from the WCC and Texas State from the Sun Belt. An interesting mix of playing styles, from one of the nation’s best defenses in San Diego State to one of the most efficient offenses year in and year out in Gonzaga. Nicholas Levine

… not good nor necessary nor something that I think will affect most people’s consumption of March Madness. If the tournament is going to expand, I think we should full-send it and go to 128 with first-round games on campus. EB

… a solution in search of a problem. When the deadline for most office pools is still Thursday at 12pm Eastern, the games on Tuesday and Wednesday have always felt like the tournament’s waiting room. Now we’re just making that waiting room bigger. BAG

… potentially cool! I’m cautiously optimistic that this is more than just another money grab for the NCAA. Hopefully, it means more surprise wins from underdog programs that might not otherwise get a shot at the tournament. SK

… fine. Like most people, I’m a “64 just feels so clean and right” guy. I like seeing more quality teams get a chance to compete, but expansion also hurts more of the lower-seeded automatic qualifiers, who now have to play in the First 12 on Tuesday and Wednesday. NL

The Miami men won 26 games last season but were knocked out in the second round of the tournament. With 6ft 9in forward Malik Reneau back for a fifth year, they’re a top-10 team and a Final Four contender. I’m also excited about Jasmine Bascoe, one of the best point guards in the country last season, running it back for year three with the Villanova women. EB

The Michigan women have never reached a Final Four, but they return their top six scorers from an Elite Eight team. Olivia Olson, Syla Swords and Mila Holloway have grown up together and the Big Ten could be there for the taking with defending champions UCLA in a rebuild. BAG

I think the Michigan women will make more noise than they have in recent years. They finished third in their conference last season, and beyond the usual suspects like South Carolina and UConn, the women’s game feels less predictable than it has in some time. SK

The Arizona State men. Randy Bennett spent 25 seasons building Saint Mary’s into one of the country’s most consistent programs, winning 20-plus games 19 times and reaching 12 NCAA Tournaments. An early adopter of the ball-screen-heavy offense now commonplace across the sport, Bennett brings his tactical acumen and attention to detail to a Sun Devils roster loaded with size and skill. Look for ASU to shake up the Big 12. NL

In a world where 76 (seventy-six!) teams make the NCAA Tournament, all of these teams should be safe. For the sake of the exercise, I’ll pick the Tennessee men. Of the top teams in the SEC, they probably have the lowest possible floor. EB

The Michigan men lost four starters, coach Dusty May to the NBA’s Mavericks and blue-chip recruit Brandon McCoy to a season-ending knee injury. Elliot Cadeau and Trey McKenney give them an elite backcourt, but expecting the Wolverines to remain among the top flight of contenders after so much upheaval feels optimistic. BAG

The Notre Dame women are in an interesting position. Missing the tournament entirely feels like a stretch, but they’re relying on a lot of young talent this season. UCLA are also rebuilding after losing several seniors to graduation, though the defending champions have earned some breathing room as they put together their next contender. SK

Texas Tech men. There is no one in the country more reliant on their fifth-year players remaining eligible than the Red Raiders. If they don’t go three-for-three in their eligibility lawsuits, they simply won’t have enough talent to earn a high seed in the NCAA Tournament. NL

Jeremy Fears Jr, Michigan State. Last season’s national assists leader takes a step up – and maybe even takes the Spartans to their first Final Four since 2019. EB

Thomas Haugh, Florida. The 6ft 9in forward could already be earning an NBA paycheck, but instead he’s back in Gainesville alongside Alex Condon and Rueben Chinyelu. His versatility and experience make him the centerpiece of a team with legitimate title ambitions. BAG

Thomas Haugh, Florida. He’s a player I’m watching closely. Passing up strong NBA draft prospects to stick with the program is already a compelling storyline. SK

David Mirković, Illinois. The 6ft 9in forward from Montenegro suffered a foot injury over the summer and has yet to be cleared to play. Once healthy, the skilled big man will be the best player on one of the best teams in the country. Coach Brad Underwood gives his players the freedom to play to their strengths, and Mirković should be highly productive on both ends of the court. NL

JuJu Watkins, USC. The four-way race between Watkins, Sarah Strong, Hannah Hidalgo and Mikayla Blakes will be the highlight of the season. I’m picking JuJu. EB

Sarah Strong, UConn. With Azzi Fudd having moved on to the WNBA, the reigning national player of the year becomes the undisputed centerpiece of Geno Auriemma’s offense. Strong’s cocktail of scoring, rebounding, passing and defensive instincts is almost unfair. Watkins will generate more headlines, but Strong could put together the more complete season. BAG

JuJu Watkins, USC. Sarah Strong is a close second, and I think we’ll see these two battle it out all season. Vanderbilt’s Mikayla Blakes is another to keep an eye on. SK

Juju Watkins, USC. Not only could the consensus 2024-25 All-American win national player of the year honors, but she could go down as one of the greatest college players of all time. If her supporting cast can take some of the offensive pressure off her, look for Watkins to lead the Trojans on a deep tournament run. NL

Tyran Stokes, Kansas. The 6ft 7in freshman is the front-runner among the standout freshman prospects. On the older end, Motiejus Krivas could boost himself into the top-five pick conversation with another year at Arizona. EB

Tyran Stokes, Kansas. He looks like he was designed in a lab for maximum appeal to professional scouts: explosive, versatile, capable of creating his own shot and jumping out of the gym. His jump shot and decision-making remain works in progress, but the physical tools appear to have no ceiling. BAG

Everyone is very excited about Tyran Stokes at Kansas, so I’ll hop on the bandwagon. But he’s got a lot to learn in just a handful of months. Caleb Holt is another dynamic player who should cause a ruckus at Arizona this season. SK

Tyran Stokes, Kansas. The best high school player in the country last season should follow in Darryn Peterson’s footsteps as a one-and-done Jayhawk. The 6ft 7in wing has an NBA-ready body and the athleticism to guard almost any position. Early signs suggest he can get into the paint and be productive once he’s there. If he continues to develop his perimeter game, he could be the first player taken in the 2027 NBA draft. NL

Watkins will go No 1 in 2027, but the No 2 pick should be Madison Booker of Texas. The pro scouts will be watching to see what jump her already well-rounded game can take. EB

Hannah Hidalgo, Notre Dame. At 5ft 6in, she defies the prototype of a modern professional guard. But few players in the country can match her combination of scoring, defensive disruption and sheer competitive motor. The question is whether her diminutive frame limits her professional prospects. I’m betting her talent and tenacity win out. BAG

I’m going to stick with JuJu Watkins, but Madison Booker cannot and should not be ignored. Ultimately, this may come down to what each team needs most. SK

JuJu Watkins, USC. She appears to be a no-brainer as the best WNBA prospect. Not only does she have great size and athleticism, but she also checks the “smart, tough, skilled” boxes all coaches are looking for. NL

The expanded tournament won’t generate much of a reaction. Expansion is the way of the future, from the World Cup to tennis majors to leagues themselves, because more teams means more games means more money. This year’s tournaments will probably feel bloated and include a few more lopsided results, but I suspect most fans will either begrudgingly enjoy an extra upset or two – or just skip the play-in round entirely and tune in starting Thursday. EB

Rick Pitino takes St John’s to the Final Four. The Red Storm have won 61 games and two Big East tournament titles over the past two seasons, but haven’t advanced beyond the Sweet 16. With a formidable NIL war chest and a 74-year-old Hall of Fame coach who cannot go on forever, the urgency is palpable. This is the year Pitino delivers the program’s first Final Four appearance since 1985 – an outcome that suddenly feels natural with the Liberty and Knicks having primed the pump by ending decades-long droughts of their own in recent years. BAG

After an OK first season and an absolutely brutal second under head coach Kim Caldwell, I think Tennessee’s women will surprise a lot of people. They’ve brought in a strong, enthusiastic group, and there’s something powerful about rebuilding a roster from scratch. Caldwell is such a unique force in college basketball. I think they’ll make a serious push come tournament time. SK

The New Mexico men win the new-look Mountain West and make a tournament run. Eric Olen is in his second year in Albuquerque and has retained All-Mountain West first-teamer Jake Hall, the preseason conference player of the year, along with backcourt partner Uriah Tenette. The Lobos have also added a mix of European pros and transfers. The last time Olen had this much skill and positional size, he led UC San Diego to 31 wins and an NCAA tournament appearance. Grand Canyon will provide the stiffest competition in the conference, but look for Olen and the Lobos not only to secure the automatic bid but also to reach the Sweet 16. NL

Duke. I’ve spent too much of my life watching the Blue Devils (albeit from the other side of the Tobacco Road rivalry) to believe they’ll let a third straight NCAA Tournament heartbreak happen. They have a deep roster, but their biggest threats will be from Florida and Illinois, who also spent the offseason retaining and retooling. EB

Florida. In a sport increasingly defined by roster turnover, Todd Golden has achieved something remarkable: keeping much of his 2025 championship core together. Haugh, Condon and Chinyelu give the Gators the kind of experienced, physically imposing frontcourt that grinds out wins in March. Duke may have more individual talent, but the Gators have something harder to manufacture: continuity. BAG

UConn. That loss to the Wolverines was a tough pill to swallow, and I expect they’ll come back laser-focused on getting the biggest win of all this season. There’s plenty of motivation to go one better. SK

Illinois. The Fighting Illini have experienced returners who are proven winners. With an international-heavy roster and great size and skill at every position, they’re a matchup nightmare for opponents. At one point last season, they had the highest offensive efficiency rating of the KenPom era. The health of David Mirković and Andrej Stojaković will be critical, but their combination of skill and winning experience gives them the edge over powers like Duke and Florida for me. NL

South Carolina were embarrassed in the national title game against UCLA last season. Dawn Staley and co will use that as fuel. The Gamecocks have a gauntlet of a schedule, but they also have valuable depth that will pay off in November and in March. EB

South Carolina. Dawn Staley has enough frontcourt talent to field two formidable teams, with Joyce Edwards, Chloe Kitts and Ashlyn Watkins headlining an embarrassment of riches. Add Tessa Johnson’s experience and a promising collection of newcomers and the Gamecocks look built to withstand just about anything. Last April’s title-game humiliation against UCLA should provide all the motivation they need. BAG

South Carolina, probably, and I’m making my peace with it, despite always enjoying the possibility of a surprise. Dawn Staley continues to build teams that are light years ahead of the rest. And after losing last season’s championship, I suppose the Gamecocks are underdogs in a way. Their talented freshmen should fit in nicely alongside the veterans. SK

USC. I’m sticking with the JuJu theme and predicting she’ll lead the Trojans past their crosstown rivals UCLA. The generational star will most likely turn pro after this season, but not before cutting down the nets in Columbus. NL

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Fifa to miss equal Women’s World Cup prize money ambition set by Infantino
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Tom Garry
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Fifa is to fall short of gender equality with the prize money on offer at next year’s Women’s World Cup, despite making a record $15bn (£11.2bn) in revenue from this summer’s men’s tournament.

Gianni Infantino, the Fifa president, said in 2023 that the organisation’s ambition was to have equality for the prize pot for 2027, saying: “Fifa is stepping up with actions, not just with words.” There had, therefore, been widespread hope across the women’s game that 2027’s prize pot would match the men’s on at least a per-team basis.

There were 48 teams at the men’s event and 32 women’s teams will participate in Brazil next summer, so a women’s pot two-thirds the size of the men’s $655m would have been regarded as parity, but it is understood the women’s prize money will be about a third of the men’s.

That does mark a substantial increase. Some sources with knowledge of the extensive negotiations that have taken place in recent weeks are privately praising the rise, but one senior female source described the news as a “huge missed open goal” by Fifa. No decision is expected to be confirmed until December’s Fifa council meeting.

Sky News, which revealed that Fifa would not match the men’s prize fund, has reported that the women’s pot is being targeted to double from $110m in 2023 to $220m, which would be a more than seven-fold increase on the 2019 women’s finals in France. Fifa prize money to the men’s teams this year included $50m for the winners, Spain.

Senior Fifa officials are understood to have spoken to some leading female players to outline its wider investments in the women’s game and explain the decision, which is believed to be related to the commercial income the 2027 event will generate.

Infantino has previously criticised broadcasters for not paying more for the television rights for the women’s tournament, which in 2023 reached 933 million viewers on linear television and 895 million on streaming platforms, according to Fifa. The final between England and Spain in Sydney had a global live audience of 67 million and reached 222 million people overall, Fifa said.

Fifa did not comment when contacted by the Guardian but sources at the governing body said there would be further enhancements to the women’s club benefits programme and additional money ringfenced for the players who take part in the tournament.

It was confirmed this month that 2027’s Women’s World Cup teams will receive the same preparation money from Fifa as those who played at the men’s tournament. The preparation money has been more than doubled to $2.5m each.

Every player will be guaranteed business class or chartered flights, and their own hotel room rather than having to share, which Fifa says brings the provisions in line with the men’s World Cup.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Teen boy from Ghana chased and fatally shot on way to school in New York City
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Javits Frimpong, 15, was being bullied at school before he was shot and killed in the Bronx on Thursday, his father says

A teenage boy from Ghana was chased down and fatally shot Thursday morning on his way to school in the Bronx.

The New York City police department (NYPD) received a report on Thursday morning about a shooting near Corona Park in the Bronx, a police spokesperson said on Friday. At about 9.24am, responding officers found Javits Frimpong, 15, with a gunshot wound to his stomach.

Javits was transported to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead. Police have not made any arrests and an investigation is ongoing as authorities search for three teenage boys in connection to the shooting.

Surveillance footage reportedly captured Javits running, as a person wearing all black trailed behind. Another angle of video footage appeared to show masked individuals in dark clothing fleeing the site of the shooting.

The deadly attack has rocked the Bronx’s Claremont neighborhood and the city’s west African community.

“I lost him,” the teenager’s father, Thomas Frimpong, told reporters on Thursday. “I don’t know what to do now.”

The fatal shooting came as Javits marked one year of being in New York after arriving from Ghana, Frimpong said. Frimpong described his son as “clever” and “quiet”. Javits was being bullied at the DreamYard preparatory school, according to Frimpong.

Frimpong said the high school’s principal, who could not be reached for comment by phone or email, informed him recently that two students were suspended for harassing Javits, he said.

An NYPD spokesperson declined to comment Friday on whether the reports of bullying were related to the attack.

Ghana’s minister of foreign affairs, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, condemned the attack in a Friday statement. “We will pursue justice and we will make sure that those who did this do not get away with it.”

“Just one year ago, Javits arrived in the United States from Ghana to reunite with his father and begin a new chapter of his life. Like so many Ghanaian immigrant families, his family came together in America with hopes of greater opportunity, security, and a promising future,” the Ghana diaspora public affairs collective, a US-based non-profit, also said in a Friday statement.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Five Great Reads: Elections, eugenics and high school reunions
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Jacqui Housden and Miles Herbert
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqui Housden and Miles Herbert

Hello and welcome to the weekend. It’s been a big week around the world, with results of three major elections taking many people by surprise. And away from the news cycle, our journalists have been asking some big questions – about birth, death, cocaine and why on earth anyone wants to go to a high school reunion.

At a time when populist leaders and the far right appear to be on the rise, Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s extraordinary victory on Sunday offered more than a glimmer of hope. As Jonathan Watts writes: it “should provide much needed inspiration and, more practically, a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections”.

So what do we do? Many analysts have put Lula’s win down to galvanising the streets and social media, and that campaign group – in particular the WhatsApp group ‘“Lula’s Army” – gathered up about 8% of the electorate by voting day. But that’s far from the only mechanism – political messaging, challenging tech giants, standing up for the environment and sheer determination are among some of the big takeaways here.

Notable quote: “Brazil has given the world a remarkable example of hope through action.”

Further reading: How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback; In Serbia, a new type of democracy is taking hold, and Europe is watching closely.

You may have noticed it – at the pub, with friends at dinner, or maybe even brazenly, out in the open – people shamelessly snorting cocaine. Journalist Robyn Vinter had been observing the uptick in drug use for some time and wanted to know “how did cocaine conquer Britain?” Here, she lays out some sobering findings.

From the middle class to the far right: “It is just staggering the amount and the accessibility of it,” a West Ham pub owner says. Wastewater analysis suggests people in England consumed 123,000kg of cocaine in 2024-25, a rise of 26% since 2021. And the class A drug, once firmly associated with middle classes, has moved around the demographics, including now appearing to be a drug of choice for the far right.

Fuelling crime: The Guardian’s investigation found a 10% rise in recorded crimes where the drug was mentioned since 2019, and Home Office figures sent to the Guardian show nearly six in 10 police drug tests carried out on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse were positive for cocaine between July 2025 and June this year.

Further reading: ‘I thought the baby would change him’: the women whose pregnancies are blighted by domestic abuse.

Most people do their best to avoid talking about death. But as of now, science has yet to find a cure for the affliction that comes for us all. So why the social taboo? In the final instalment of the Guardian’s series about death – Memento mori – Meaghan O’Connell documents the journey her mother took after deciding she wanted to donate her body to science. O’Connell wasn’t prepared for what came next but says, “In some ways, it was absolutely perfect”.

Why would you donate your body to science? Demand for medical cadavers far outstrips supply. More than 25,000 Americans donate their bodies for research purposes after their death but, according to Tamara Ostervoss, director of Oregon Health & Science University’s (OHSU) body donation program, “it remains an unpopular choice”. For medical students, the ability to practise procedures on the real thing versus a human model is like “the difference between a flight simulator and piloting an airplane”.

The emotional cost: Not knowing exactly what happened to her mother’s body weighed on O’Connell’s mind. But she says going down the donation route also offered an element of simplicity. No being upsold by funeral directors, no grief-stricken decisions about embalming, or what goes on the gravestone. Just a quick phone call and a short physical assessment, then “voilà, off my mom went to fulfil her destiny”, O’Connell says.

Notable quote: “Was it odd to feel jubilant on the same day I watched my mother take her final breath”? – O’Connell, after learning her mother’s body was accepted as a medical cadaver.

A memorial of sorts: After fulfilling her mother’s posthumous wishes, O’Connell was invited to a “body ceremony”, a 25-year tradition where students from OHSU memorialise body donors and their families. Two students offered their thanks through an aerial yoga routine; others sang Taylor Swift. O’Connell was looking for closure but all this offered was amusement.

It may be Greek for “good birth” but the term eugenics has, for the past century at least, been seen as a racist and repulsive movement. But whether you like it or not, eugenics is back in a new guise, this time by companies offering prospective parents the problematic promise of delivering the “best baby”. Jan Grue, who has a form of spinal muscular atrophy, considers the ethical implications.

What is ‘the best’? Adverts on the New York City subway offer embryo scans for every genetic disorder under the sun, eye and hair colour, and for traits ranging from strength and longevity to insomnia and male pattern baldness. Whether the promises are credible is one thing but a more important one might be: what is “valuable and worthless in a human life?”

Notable quote: “I think it is crucial to acknowledge disability as part of human variation. In treating ever more traits and qualities as things to be measured, ranked and diagnosed, we are doing the opposite – turning variation itself into something like disability.”

Further reading: The girl with a will to live: the love, hope and pain of raising Elsie – my one in 163 million daughter.

High school reunions are notoriously awkward; just ask Romy and Michele. While some look forward to reconnecting with friends, others see reliving the past as “a potential hellscape”. But can you go in prepared? The Guardian asked a mix of experts and reunion-goers for their advice on tackling one of life’s most fraught social situations.

Should you even go? Psychologist and author Amberley Meredith says it is normal to ruminate over reunions, and you should expect to not be the only one with existential questions about your place in life. If you are on the fence, experts say avoid making a pros and cons list – instead, just focus on the potential positives.

The dos and don’ts: Still feeling nervous before the big day? Etiquette expert Jodie Bache-Mclean says you can come prepared with a few conversation starters and a bit of background on your past classmates, but while “a little homework is helpful; a full social media investigation is not”. What about alcohol? Should you drink to calm your nerves? “A glass of wine may help, four may not!” Bache-Mclean says.

Further reading: Why are class reunions so terrifying? And are they even good for us?

If you would like to receive these Five Great Reads to your email inbox every weekend, sign up here. And check out out the full list of our local and international newsletters.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: British people can’t be made to pay for the wrongs of slavery – but we must confront our complicated history | Andy Burnham
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Andy Burnham
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Financial reparations are not the answer. Working together with our Commonwealth family is the best way to ensure prosperity for us all

Andy Burnham open to calls for formal apology for Britain’s role in slave trade

On 28 October 1787, Thomas Clarkson pushed through the crowds to reach the pulpit of Manchester Cathedral. A campaigner for abolishing slavery, he spoke urgently about the horrors of the slave trade and the humanity of enslaved people. “He drinks the cup of sorrow,” Clarkson said. “And he drinks it at our hands.”

During Black History Month, these are the stories it is important to remember. They show us the complicated truth of our history. Thousands of people in Manchester signed a petition against slavery after Clarkson’s sermon. And yet Manchester’s cotton industry was built on the labour of enslaved people. There are similar stories up and down the nation. We are a country where brave people led the way in abolishing slavery, but we are also a country that participated in the trade in human lives.

The transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of those people. They were denied their humanity. They were separated from their families, treated as property and worked to their deaths. I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today.

Our history is intertwined with countries that are now our allies, particularly in the Commonwealth. Next week, I will attend the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm). In an increasingly divided and dangerous world, our family of nations in the Commonwealth is vital to our interests: a beacon of stability, strength and security. Together we can face down shared challenges. We can seize opportunities for trade and economic collaboration. We can strengthen our respective countries and share our values to build a safer world for us all.

But facing a changing world together requires us to stand on firm foundations. To meet those challenges of the future, we need to face up to the past. For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery. By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function.

Having these difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future is the right thing to do. It is also the patriotic thing to do. Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.

So we are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade. Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.

Some have called for financial reparations for the slave trade. I do not believe that is the right answer. I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.

My focus is on building a future where people at home and abroad live in greater peace and prosperity.

So we will bring to the Chogm our determination to tackle the issues that affect people across our Commonwealth family and beyond.

Today, debt-servicing costs in the poorest and most vulnerable countries are at their highest in more than 25 years. More than 40% of these countries spend more on interest repayments than on health. I want to launch a new drive on debt, working with our global partners to help those countries repay over a longer time period and with better rates. That is why the chancellor, foreign secretary and I have asked Gordon Brown, who will join us at the Chogm, to help with this work.

We will also support the energy transition in the face of the climate crisis. And we will build on the incredible work being done to educate women and girls, give smaller countries a louder voice on the world stage, and end global poverty and inequality.

I want us to build stronger relationships with each other and renew the relevance of the Commonwealth in a new era. We do that by facing our past together and focusing on a future where every person living within it has equality, security and hope.

We stand on the shoulders of those such as Thomas Clarkson and the many ordinary people who spoke out for justice and humanity.

In 1862, at the height of the American civil war, Manchester was the cotton capital of the world. In a vote at the Free Trade Hall, the humble cotton workers resolved that they would no longer handle slave-picked cotton. Their actions helped end the civil war, prompting Abraham Lincoln to write to them praising their “sublime Christian heroism”.

It is so often the case in British history that huge injustices ignored by the powers-that-be are eventually overturned by ordinary people. Those Manchester cotton workers represent that proud British tradition, and I will take inspiration from them as we go forward into our new dialogue.
