https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Arteta can take inspiration from George Graham to expunge painful Anfield memories
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Ed Aarons
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Arsenal have not won at Liverpool for 13 league games but Gunners’ win in 1989 remains one of club’s greatest nights

Mikel Arteta used a Spanish word to describe what it felt like to be helpless at Anfield while playing for Everton in 2011: bajar. “It’s when a cyclist is going up and looks amazing, then in one kilometre he goes ‘boom’ and he’s struggling again,” he said in Amazon’s All or Nothing documentary. “The game was going well and then suddenly I could only see red shirts flying around. The game is passing all over me and I cannot react. I only had that feeling in my career once, and it was at Anfield.”

Given Arteta’s record at Liverpool, Sunday’s showdown with his childhood friend Andoni Iraola – five days after Arsenal were dumped out of the Carabao Cup by Fleetwood – could be expected to fill him with dread. Arteta finally tasted victory there as a player with Arsenal in September 2012, after five failed attempts in the Merseyside derby, but ended up spending the night in hospital with concussion after colliding with Jordan Henderson in an incident he has described as “the biggest fear of my life”.

Arteta was part of the Arsenal side that won at Anfield again six months later thanks to goals from the new signings Lukas Podolski and Santi Cazorla. That was the last time the club triumphed there in the Premier League. They have not won at Anfield for 13 league matches, equalling the club’s worst run at Liverpool. Arsenal’s one victory at Liverpool in the interim came in the League Cup on penalties in 2020 on Arteta’s second visit as a manager.

The Spaniard tried to prepare his players for a trip to Anfield in November 2021 by playing You’ll Never Walk Alone over the training ground speakers but that ended in a 4-0 defeat. He was criticised after last season’s loss in late August, when Dominik Szoboszlai’s late free-kick ended a sequence of three Arsenal draws at Liverpool, for a perceived failure to take off the handbrake, having started Mikel Merino as his No 10. Gary Neville went as far as to say Arsenal lacked “the mentality to go and win big matches at big away grounds”, an assertion that will have hurt Arteta but does have credence: they have not beaten Manchester City in the Premier League at the Etihad since 2015 under Arsène Wenger.

Arteta will be keen to disprove such perceptions, especially after Arsenal struggled so badly against a team 84 places below them in the pyramid in a stadium that holds fewer than 6,000 people. The strikers Kai Havertz and Viktor Gyökeres surprisingly started in tandem at Fleetwood, presumably in an attempt to lighten the load on Martin Ødegaard, although both look badly out of form. Bukayo Saka is out with a thigh injury, there are concerns over Noni Madueke’s ankle and Arsenal’s failed appeal over Max Dowman’s red card rules out the teenager for three matches.

With that in mind, Arteta’s best chance of beating Liverpool is probably by taking the cautious approach that has served him so well and was the cornerstone of last season’s Premier League title triumph. He can take inspiration from one of the most famous nights in Arsenal’s history 37 years ago when George Graham’s side arrived at Anfield needing a 2-0 victory to be champions.

“I told my players to keep things tight in the first half – it was imperative we did not concede,” said Graham in an interview to mark the 20th anniversary of that dramatic finale to the 1988-89 season, when Michael Thomas scored in stoppage time to end Arsenal’s 18-year wait for the title. “The papers were saying we’d have to attack from the off, but I was adamant that was wrong. If Liverpool had scored an early goal it would have been over. But they did very little attacking and played into our hands.”

Before the 1989 game, Arsenal’s players ran to all four corners of the ground to hand flowers to Liverpool fans as a show of sympathy after the Hillsborough disaster the previous month – an idea proposed by their longstanding director Ken Friar, who died this month.

Graham and Arteta were 44 when they won their first league titles and the similarities do not end there. The former Scotland midfielder, who scored almost 80 goals for Arsenal and helped them win the Double in 1971, was known for his emphasis on defending as a manager and “1-0 to the Arsenal” became synonymous with Graham, especially towards the end of his reign. Arteta has revived that tradition since he took over in December 2019, recording 1-0 victories 32 times in the Premier League, more than any club apart from Everton.

Arsenal scored their first set-piece goal of the season in a routine 2-0 win at home to Everton last Saturday and targeting Liverpool’s weakness from set plays while keeping things tight at the other end could be the most effective tactic against a team who have been finding their feet under Iraola in recent weeks.

“Collectively, we acknowledge the importance of defending,” said Arteta last year when asked about comparisons between his team and Graham’s. “We know that if we excel in that part of the game, the chances and the probabilities to win more matches is going to be very, very high.”

Arsenal flew back to London after losing to Fleetwood on penalties in a shootout that will have revived bad memories of May’s Champions League final defeat by Paris Saint-Germain.

The Carabao Cup has stretched Arteta’s squad in the past two seasons, when they reached first the semi-finals then the final, so that is one potential positive from their elimination – not that the ultra-competitive Spaniard would agree. For him, the only way to respond to the most embarrassing night of his managerial career will be to follow in Graham’s footsteps on Sunday.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Fiesta awaits in Mexico City as Kimi Antonelli speeds towards F1 history
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Giles Richards in Mexico City
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Italian 20-year-old is on the verge of becoming the youngest world champion with the Mexican Grand Prix ready for a carnival coronation atmosphere

An undeniable highlight of this Formula One season, marked by discontent at the new regulations, has been getting swept along by the sheer joy that the world champion-in-waiting, Kimi Antonelli, has displayed on his way to a title he will almost surely secure this weekend at the Mexican Grand Prix.

Antonelli was still a teenager for the first half of the year and it seemed fitting to describe him as such. His exuberant embrace of competing for Mercedes at the sharp end of F1 in just his second season was that of any 19-year-old. Like discovering a life-changing new band or how much fun can be had with a cold beer, a wide grin was barely off his face.

He is 20 now, still but a stripling and on Sunday at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez if he finishes in ninth place or better he will be F1’s youngest world champion, and the first Italian to win the title since Alberto Ascari in 1953.

Antonelli has confessed that as a four-year-old he did not recall when Sebastian Vettel became the previous youngest title winner in 2010. “I remember I was playing with Hot Wheels, but I don’t remember him clinching it,” he said.

This weekend he will likely embrace an unforgettable moment. Antonelli has shone on track, at home with the complex requirements of the new energy-managed cars, extracting a pace and control such that even his more experienced Mercedes teammate George Russell has been left flailing in his wake. To which traits he has allied a sharp and incisive driving style that has been extraordinary at times and a judgment that has belied his years.

That he has done so with such alacrity, especially after a difficult rookie season last year, has surprised many. Not least those team principal Toto Wolff pointedly observed had been questioning whether Antonelli should even be in F1 after his debut season. Doubts now assuredly consigned to the dustbin of history, in the city where Leon Trotsky, who coined the phrase, was killed in 1940.

It has been clear how much the Italian loves what he does and how that has informed his performances. At his shoulder through the trials of last season and the triumphs of this, has been Peter Bonnington. Bono, as he is known, was Lewis Hamilton’s engineer across the British driver’s six titles with Mercedes. He and Antonelli have established a close relationship, a friendship, with the Italian taking on board his colleague’s experience and cool head, often referencing him and the importance of their interaction.

During Antonelli’s run of five successive victories in the opening period of the season, the last of them was a striking performance in Monaco. Taking an exceptional pole position to deny Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, who was in fearsome form on the streets of the principality, he then delivered a remarkable race win, including seeing off two restarts.

After this, Bono, who often has the avuncular air of an older brother with his young charge, gave an almost disarmingly straightforward explanation of what made his driver so quick.

“As soon as he’s happy in the car: happy driver, fast lap time,” he said. The team have adopted an approach to allow Antonelli the opportunity to ensure he could drive in a way that allowed him to truly embrace being himself and in so doing, taking the pressure off.

Bonningham described this as “giving him the freedom to do what he enjoys, giving him the freedom to enjoy driving the car, that’s a real big thing and not stressing too much. He’s just a joy to work with.”

To trust the youngster’s instincts and talent, when the temptation to micromanage him must have been overwhelming, has worked brilliantly. Even as the opposition caught and at times surpassed Mercedes, Antonelli was able to deliver when a win was off the table. When it was, as at the last round in Austin, he stepped up to sweep it away with a nonchalance that typified why he is world champion elect.

This makes the atmosphere in Mexico City all the more febrile in what is already one of the most vibrant venues on the calendar. Antonelli could barely have chosen a better location to enjoy the celebration of his childhood dream. The fans here embrace F1 with the same passion the Italian has for his trade.

With the race coinciding with Mexico’s Day of the Dead, the city and the paddock are adorned with the bright orange Mexican marigolds, the “flor de muerto”. Skulls and skeletons, candles and colour are plentiful to welcome the return of the departed in a joyful, festival lending the weekend an already celebratory air.

The F1 faithful are also in good cheer in welcoming home hero Sergio Pérez back to the grid, with Cadillac and his image everywhere in Mexico City. On occasion he appears as a lifesize cardboard cut-out, rather incongruously in a line of fabulously-dressed skeletons. Yet fans will also doubtless revel in having this marvellous venue celebrate F1’s youngest champion in the heady atmosphere of the stadium section of Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.

Hamilton has experienced it twice, when he sealed the title here in 2017 and 2018, and the seven-time champion’s assessment of Antonelli’s season was as telling as that of his former race engineer.

“You never know how anyone’s going to do under pressure until you see them,” he said. “I could assume that he was going to be fine with the weight you have on you. When you have to do all these appearances and all these things, pulled left, right and centre. But he’s taken it in his stride. He’s a relatively old soul in that young body.”

Antonelli was withdrawn from his media duties on Thursday, with Mercedes saying he was unwell and needing to recover properly, but the Italian has stated he would like to finish the job in style and be able to relax for the remaining four races. There is no reason to believe he will suffer from any yips, certainly. He has demonstrated no such weakness thus far, even under the most intense pressure, with team principal Wolff sharing a further insight into why the 20-year-old stands ready to make history.

“In Austin, he came to my office sat down on the sofa and said: ‘I’m going to enjoy this one. Isn’t it funny? I’m not thinking at all about the championship,’” Wolff recalled. “I said: ‘Stick to that attitude. You have the best job in the world. Don’t forget that.’ He has the right mindset.”

The best job in the world and one he has, admirably, embraced with that irrepressible joy. The right mindset indeed. A deserved champion awaiting his coronation. On this form, not for the last time.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: How can playing for Manchester City fit into Marc Guéhi’s moral universe? | Barney Ronay
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Barney Ronay
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Club’s predicament raises interesting questions about principles, both for individuals and the Premier League

I felt unbelievably ponderous. My head was made of Aztec stone. I realised I didn’t want to be with all these people. Somebody came at me, a huge individual in silver and blue. I fell at his feet and grabbed one shoe. I started untying the lace. He kicked away from me. I got up and walked off. I was exceedingly hungry.

Not my words. Also not the words of the Manchester City centre-back Marc Guéhi, despite what you were thinking there. This is instead a condensed quote from the mind of Gary Harkness, existentially curious college running-back and the narrator of Don DeLillo’s great American football novel End Zone.

This passage describes a moment where Gary plays a game having been urged by his friends to smoke pot beforehand to discover whether it improves his understanding of time and space, or just makes him want to lie down and untie someone’s laces. It marks a turning point for Gary. To this point football has been a comforting world. He sees clarity in its militaristic rituals, finds in sport “the illusion that order is possible”, hears hidden truths in the coaches’ shouted instructions. Button up. Get fetal. Get fetal. Get fetal. Run with reckless abandon.

Now the illusion has collapsed. Gary walks off the football field and begins instead to fixate on cold war fears and nuclear apocalypse. Death and political power have entered the chat.

Now, I’m not saying Marc Guéhi is Gary Harkness. You might be saying that. That’s your choice. But Guéhi has seemed a bit distracted in the last few weeks. Oddly for an agile and technically sound centre-back, he has seemed brittle and absent, vulnerable to being pressed.

There have been a couple of things said about City’s players in this regard. The first is that their minds might not be wholly on the game, that in the middle of a game against Croatia, for example, concerned only with manoeuvring through tiny pockets of space, Nico O’Reilly is also thinking: “Hmm, but how is it possible even by omission to honestly contravene rules E.3 and E.4 which state clearly that …oh. Wait, no. Oh dear.”

Football doesn’t work like this. The physical game is a place of total focus. But still, nothing is watertight. And this speaks to the second thing people have said, repeated like an absolute truth, that the players are entirely separate from all this. They cannot be questioned here, or indeed expected to ask questions of their own. The players are simply avatars, employees, free from any kind of agency. Players don’t have access to Google. They cannot make moral judgments. And yes, this may not be true of any other human in any other field. It may be the case that elite footballers are in fact unusually empowered, free to do whatever they want. But the consensus is clear. It is not a footballer’s business to have opinions on their employers, or what happens out of their line of vision.

This does help to avoid some tricky conundrums. Guéhi, for example, is a man of absolute public principle. Fair enough. I respect his willingness to resist popular pressure and personalise his support for the rainbow armband by writing things about Jesus on top of it. This is living your values. It’s free speech, figuring out your own moral universe. Doing so by following the absolute tenets of his religion. Go for it.

At the same time, Guéhi is playing for a club that has been convicted of cheating and lying. People are free to disagree with the rules. But if others are sticking to them, this amounts to deceit, stolen win bonuses, stolen glory. And the Bible is very clear on this. Thessalonians 4:6: “No one should transgress and defraud his brother.” Proverbs 20:17: “Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel.” Now, I don’t believe these words to be divinely ordained. They’re great words. Totally dig the vibe. But Guéhi does believe these things to be an absolute instruction. How does this fit together in his head? How does that gravel (pending appeal) taste right now?

Again, fine if you can square it. It’s a personal journey. Park the apparent moral dilemma. See if your legal team can come up with a better final outcome. But things have changed in one significant way since the verdict dropped, an element that is now unchallenged, and which has been largely unremarked in the middle of the chaos. Understandably so. This stuff is gruelling. Everyone just wants to watch some football in the brief lull between legal rage events. But there are two points worth making in the interim. The second of which is an admission that affects many other things.

The first issue is: do you actually understand the basis of the Manchester City appeal? That evidence has seemingly been leaked. The irrefutable body of evidence, Body Of Evidence 2, the long-awaited tribunal-based Madonna erotic thriller vehicle, contains a vital detail: the additional money in City’s coffers, almost a billion, did not come from the owners, the Abu Dhabi United Group, which is owned, like City, by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan. This would be against the rules. It came instead from the Abu Dhabi government, which is essentially the Abu Dhabi royal family, of which Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan is a member; as he is also, wearing a different hat, of the Abu Dhabi government.

And maybe this means it’s fine. It seems the government often tops up the sponsor companies like a benevolent uncle. In the period the charges relate to there was no need for sponsor deals to be of market value, as there is now. So if we accept all this, if we can establish a binding principle of wearing different hats in different rooms, this may be a way out. Maybe.

This is a familiar concept in the high court, in an age of shell companies and tricky fiscal flows. Mega-million cases hang on whether ownership really is separate, or whether this is, to echo a phrase, a sham process. The person on the Clapham omnibus might not buy any of this. Do these really seem like separate entities? Or a bit like adopting a French accent when the bailiffs ring up and maintaining that, no, Monsieur Ronay is not here, and he definitely doesn’t run this dry cleaners. That, instead, is me.

If you make the case you win the case. This is all in the end about the application of rules, and that is a good thing. But the key point here is the secondary issue derived from this. City’s leaked defence, in making their case, is also saying, without pretence or mucking about, that the club is indeed funded by the Abu Dhabi government. This is something City’s fans have at times weirdly denied. But we have it in plain sight now, not just admitted but insisted on. The ultimate source of the dizzying success of the club that has defined a Premier League era is the government. Guéhi is, in effect, an Abu Dhabi civil servant. Perhaps the United Arab Emirates national team should have six stars on their jersey, one for each Premier League won. But there is no way of covering your ears now. City actively want us to accept this.

What are the consequences of this new fact? It comes with two urgent questions. The first is the moral one. Back again to Guéhi as the best example. This is what he is promoting here. And Guéhi is a man entirely guided by the principles of his faith. A private matter perhaps, except that it’s not, because Guéhi’s church explicitly orders its members to go out and proselytise. Guéhi is a member of Ballers in God, which actively tries to awaken Christian faith in the dressing room. He plays with Christian messages on his matchday kit intended to make you, the reader, think yes, maybe I too should follow this evangelical church.

And here is the key thing. This is a criminal offence in Abu Dhabi. Under UAE penal code, giving out Christian leaflets will get you arrested. A Christian pastor in the UAE was sentenced to a year in prison for giving a Muslim a Bible. Some Americans were deported for giving out Christian literature in the Dubai shopping district. Spreading the gospel, which Guéhi is morally bound to do, is illegal in the place that pays his direct employers.

Are players just avatars, empty shells? How much do you really believe in this? These are, more than ever, very interesting questions. And they don’t just apply to issues of personal principle.

The regulator now has this information, too. Abu Dhabi funded the purchase of Nolito. Abu Dhabi dictated the flow of English football finance. The same pocket that paid for this is also funding at arm’s length the civil war in Sudan, the hospital massacres, the piles of bodies so high they can be seen from satellite imaging. Abu Dhabi, which criminalises homosexuality, which crushes dissent, is openly identifying itself as the mega-funder of a Premier League club. Is this a fit and proper influence?

There are very obvious reasons why this is not desirable. Governments spy and wage war and break rules. They have a sacred trust to promote their own interests by any means necessary. It is hard to see how this kind of owner fits the regulatory framework. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund had to twirl through semantic hoops when buying Newcastle to establish it was an entity at one remove from a government, as opposed to a government entity. In making the opposite case for their funding City have not only exposed their own live-your-values central defender, they have put themselves in a place where, even if you win on one front, you’ve started to look like a very strange presence.

This deserves to be unravelled in all its wider implications. It may be the biggest issue here, whatever the final verdict. How can this be the right thing? How can City’s fans look their own autocratic government-funded club in the eye? The quiet thing has been said out loud. And its implications are bigger than the game, bigger than legal opinion. Enough, perhaps to make you question the existential point of this thing, where the best course of action really might be to walk off and look for the nearest cheeseburger.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Ben Doherty and Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Marco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycott

The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.

Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.

“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”

About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.

European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.

The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.

During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in front of Lavrov and said Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.

A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.

“Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”

The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.

Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.

Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.

That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.

“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.

Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success.

Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support.

But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.

“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Retired Michigan teacher released from Russian prison believed he would never be freed
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Guardian staff and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Stephen Hubbard said that only when he was being taken from Moscow to St Petersburg did he believe he was ‘going somewhere’

In his first comments since recently being released from a Russian prison, a retired Michigan teacher said he only believed he would be freed when he got new clothes.

Stephen Hubbard, 74, remarked on Friday that he had heard many times previously that he would be released – but never really trusted what he was told, adopting a philosophy of “seeing is believing” and “actions speak louder than words”.

“Only when they started giving me new clothes and leading me to the exit of the prison,” Hubbard said in his first public remarks since his 21 October release, which came during a visit at the White House with Donald Trump, “I went out and I saw the car, and I was accompanied by a couple of Russians, then I believed, finally believed, on the drive from Moscow to St Petersburg, ‘I’m really going somewhere.’”

Hubbard had been behind bars for more than four years on charges that he fought as a mercenary in Ukraine, which Russia invaded in February 2022. His legal team has denied the Russian accusations and said he was not involved in any military activity.

Trump has previously said that he had asked Russian leader Vladimir Putin to free Hubbard – and that the US did not have to release anyone in return.

“He was somebody I wanted to get back,” the US president said as he hosted Hubbard on Friday in the Oval Office.

The White House allowed a limited pool of journalists into Trump’s meeting with Hubbard, allowing primarily news photographers and a television crew.

Many in the international community perceived Hubbard’s release to be Russia’s latest maneuver to bring Trump closer to Putin’s position on the war in Ukraine. It also offered Trump a diplomatic victory ahead of the 3 November midterm elections, when his Republican party is expected to lose seats in Congress.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘We’re not freaks’: police raid sparks concern for Taiwan’s LGBT-friendly image
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Yu-chen Li in Taipei
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
The rounding up of customers at a gay bar weeks before Saturday’s Pride festival has some questioning the island’s progressive image

Josh was having a drink at Commander D, a popular gay bar in Taipei, on a Saturday afternoon when several police officers suddenly burst in. “Squat down and don’t move,” they shouted. Bewildered, he looked around to see the bar owner being handcuffed and forced to his knees.

The 28-year-old was among 51 customers to be rounded up and taken away for questioning over suspected breaches of public decency rules.

“I didn’t expect something like this to still happen these days. It definitely made me feel a lot less safe,” says Josh, a gay man from Taiwan whose name has been changed due to the sensitivity of the incident. The police operation was criticised by rights groups as heavy-handed, and has unsettled LGBTQ+ communities in Taiwan.

On Saturday the island hosts one of the region’s largest Pride parades, and some say the police operation is emblematic of a persistent, wider stigma that risks jeopardising its global image as a LGBTQ-friendly destination.

The raid took place on 3 October at a bar that is billed as Taipei’s first and only BDSM-themed bar and features in several international travel guides. Commander D has operated for more than a decade in the Ximending area – a hub for LGBTQ+ tourists where gay bars and sex shops can be easily spotted.

The bar’s owner was arrested and referred to prosecutors on suspicion of profiting from facilitating sexual or indecent acts, a charge that carries a maximum sentence of five years in prison.

In the days after the raid, the police department said that it had received 13 complaints this year alleging public decency violations at the bar.

In an interview with Taiwanese media on 7 October, the bar owner accused the police of using excessive force and said that any intimate encounters between customers were a matter of personal choice. He has not yet been formally charged with any offences. His lawyer declined to comment on the case, citing the ongoing investigation.

Videos posted on social media showed the police mocking a disabled customer and preventing some people from putting their clothes back on. Some had taken their shirts off because it was a warm day. Police said they had reviewed 41 body cam recordings and acknowledged inappropriate language had been used by its officers.

“There was an element of sexual humiliation,” says Victoria Hsu, a human rights lawyer specialising in LGBTQ+ rights. As police refused to let the patrons get dressed, “they weren’t allowed to go to the police station with dignity”.

The police department said their actions were intended to bring the scene under control and the court-authorised search had not targeted any particular group or sexual orientation. Yet after a strong public backlash, Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an apologised and six police officers were disciplined for inappropriate remarks and failing to supervise their juniors properly. Rights groups are calling for an independent investigation.

Wanhua police division said rights groups filed a criminal complaint with prosecutors on 7 October. “The matter has entered the judicial process, and we await the outcome of the investigation and any subsequent court proceedings.”

Midnight Poonkasetwattana, executive director of the Bangkok-based LGBTQ+ advocacy network APCOM, told Taiwan’s Central news agency that the raid “could undermine the gay-friendly image Taiwan has built”.

Hung Yan-an, a gay man living in Taipei, says he received messages from overseas friends about the incident. “A gay friend of mine in Spain has been asking me: ‘Is everything OK? If I visit, will it be safe to hold hands with my partner in the street?’”

The episode stands in stark contrast to a recent survey that found public support for gay marriage has increased from 42% to 54% since Taiwan legalised same-sex marriage in 2019, the first place in Asia to do so.

“But inclusion is not only about marriage equality, Pride or international recognition. It is also about how public institutions treat LGBTQI+ people when exercising state power,” Poonkasetwattana said in a formal letter of protest to Taiwan’s representative in Thailand over the decision to raid Commander D.

Local campaigners say the raid exposes a persistent stigma around queer venues, as well as “homophobia, discrimination and abuse of power that have long been embedded in the police system”.

A spokesperson for the Wanhua police division did not directly address the allegations of longstanding institutional homophobia but said it “fully respects social and cultural diversity and people’s rights” and would continue to combat crime and enforce the law to maintain public order.

Other gay venues have also faced scrutiny. In April, a gay bathhouse in the central city of Taichung closed after a police raid over suspected public-decency offences and subsequent inspections. In a Facebook statement announcing the closure, its owner accused police of discriminatory treatment. A gay gym in Taipei, which closed in 2021, had reportedly been inspected 186 times over three years.

“Some police officers assume that gay people are more likely to have drugs on them,” lawyer Hsu says. “I’ve had quite a few LGBTQ+ people come to me for legal advice, for example, some of them were subjected to improper police searches.”

For Chien Shih-han, a Taiwanese drag queen who performs as Hannah, discrimination is not always easy to identify. He recalls gay venues facing repeated noise complaints and a pre-booked taxi driving away after the driver saw a friend in drag.

“It could all come down to this subtle sense of discomfort or anxiety towards sexual minorities,” Chien says.

In his view, gay venues such as Commander D have offered a refuge to people who do not fit the mainstream, even within the LGBTQ+ community. “It was a kind of safety net,” Chien says. “Now it feels as though someone is setting fire to that net.”

Weeks later, Josh says he still feels “a little scared” when thinking back to the raid, but that it would not stop him taking to the streets for Taiwan Pride.

“I want to express my anger at being taken to the police station that day,” he says, “I want to go with the message that we’re not strange, we’re not freaks.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Packers’ Josh Jacobs says hands-behind-back TD celebration was not mocking recent arrest
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs says he was paying homage to a gospel song rather than making light of his recent arrest when he briefly had his hands behind his back while celebrating a touchdown Thursday night.

This was Jacobs’s second game of the season after coming off the commissioner’s exempt list. He was placed on that list after charges were filed against him in August stemming from a May altercation with his then-girlfriend during which she said he threw her to the ground.

Jacobs pleaded no contest last month to misdemeanor charges of battery and criminal damage to property.

Jacobs had just scored on a one-yard run in the second quarter of the Packers’ 27-19 victory over the Carolina Panthers when he put his hands behind his back for a moment while accepting congratulations from teammates. The video garnered attention on social media as some who watched on television believed Jacobs was simulating getting handcuffed.

Jacobs said he instead was modeling his celebration after a gospel song called Break Every Chain.

“The guys did it with me,” Jacobs said. “I didn’t think it was going to be a thing that can be perceived a certain type of way. But it’s 2026, and it is what it is.”

Jacobs said he had spoken with teammate Savion Williams and other receivers before making his season debut, and they came up with the idea that he would do a celebration thanking God after his first touchdown of the season. That celebration happened Sunday, as he went to his knees and raised his arms aloft after scoring in a 20-17 loss at Detroit.

They also had planned this Break Every Chain celebration after his second touchdown of the season. When Jacobs was asked about putting his hands behind his back as part of the celebration, he noted that the telecast only showed a brief portion of what he did.

“It was more to it than that,” Jacobs said. “They stopped showing the celebration after that. Like I said, it is what it is.”

Jacobs hadn’t been able to play or practice while he was on the commissioner’s exempt list. He was removed from that list last week, enabling him to play again even though the NFL’s investigation of him remains ongoing.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Alaska prosecutor investigates alleged Democratic plot to confuse voters with second Dan Sullivan
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Lucy Campbell, Robert Mackey and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Mary Peltola denies knowledge as party accused of recruiting spoiler candidate with same name as sitting Republican

Alaska Senate race: what to know about Democrats’ alleged ballot-stacking effort

The top federal prosecutor in Alaska confirmed on Friday the existence of a criminal and a civil investigation into an alleged scheme by Democrats to confuse voters by recruiting a spoiler candidate on the ballot for US Senate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent, senator Dan Sullivan.

Speaking at a news conference in Anchorage on Friday, US attorney Michael Heyman cited reporting by the New York Times which suggested that the Senate campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola and national Democrats had, in his words, “orchestrated a sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up Daniel J Sullivan as a sham candidate”.

Both Dan Sullivans – one a Republican senator and the other a retired schoolteacher with no prior political experience – qualified for the ballot.

“This new information has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska,” he added. “As we speak, law enforcement around the country are taking investigative steps with respect to a criminal investigation on these matters.”

In a separate filing, the Department of Justice asked a federal judge to order state elections officials to isolate ballots ranking Dan J Sullivan to investigate potential voter “confusion” with the incumbent Dan Sullivan.

E. Bryan Wilson, an assistant US attorney in Alaska, in a filing, said the government “seeks to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary”.

The justice department on Friday also asked a federal judge to issue a preliminary ⁠injunction ​that would ‌block ‌Alaska from ‌certifying its Senate election result if the incumbent senator loses to Peltola due to the presence of Daniel J Sullivan on the ballot.

Heyman would not say what potential crimes authorities are looking into. It is highly unusual for federal prosecutors to confirm the existence of an open criminal investigation, much less discuss it publicly.

“The civil lawsuit is publicly faced, and is focused on preserving the ballots,” Heyman said, referring to a Department of Justice suit filed last week.

A day earlier, Peltola denied any prior knowledge of the alleged effort, telling supporters in Juneau, Alaska’s capital: “I am not interested in tricking voters.”

“I just want to clear the air,” the Democratic Senate candidate said on Thursday at the top of a speech in a downtown bar in Juneau, Alaska’s capital. “I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about.”

Peltola is running against Dan Sullivan, the two-term US senator. A person familiar with the matter told the Associated Press that subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony or documents, along with records preservation demands, were issued after the New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J Sullivan Jr as part of an alleged effort to confuse voters.

The race is considered one of the most important contests of next week’s midterm elections, and will be key to determining control of the Senate. Alaska is one of a handful of states with Senate races this year that Democrats are targeting as they try to win back a majority in the chamber, where they hold 47 seats to the Republican party’s 53, and recent polls have shown Peltola in the lead.

More subpoenas were expected, according to the person who spoke to the Associated Press. Neither the recipients of the subpoenas nor the number of them were immediately clear.

Republicans have condemned the presence in the race of two candidates named Dan Sullivan, calling the newcomer a ploy by Democrats to cost the incumbent re-election by splitting the GOP candidate’s supporters.

Before the August primary, election authorities in the state attempted to disqualify the other Dan Sullivan, but the state supreme court ruled that he could appear on the ballot. Together with Sullivan and Peltola, the challenger was one of the top four vote-getters in the non-partisan primary.

On the general election ballot, the senator will be listed as “Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent” and the challenger “Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.”

Since the New York Times published its report, Mike Dunleavy, Alaska’s Republican governor, separately announced plans to launch a criminal investigation, saying the story revealed “disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates – including one with the same name as an incumbent US senator – to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes”.

“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Dunleavy added, noting that the report “substantially supports” earlier findings by the state’s elections board into the matter.

Donald Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate if she won the election.

“Well, you’re going to have to see what happens,” the president told reporters on his way to a rally in South Carolina. “It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”

Later, as he rallied for Darline Graham, a Republican senator, Trump said he felt Peltola “actually should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted”.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy praises US over $2.1bn Patriot missile deal but warns it could take years
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Guardian staff and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
The Ukrainian president called the US decision strong, but added that delivery of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles ⁠could take years

The US has approved the sale ⁠of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles ⁠to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1bn, but Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned deliveries could take years and stockpiles were needed now to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.

“The proposed sale will improve Ukraine’s capability to meet current and future threats by improving its integrated air and missile defense capabilities,” the US state department said in a statement on Friday.

The statement did not provide an estimate for when the weapons could be delivered to Ukraine.

Zelenskyy praised the “strong decision by the US state department” but said in a post on X early on Saturday: “However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS. We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors.

“Right now, the Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day.”

Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves ⁠of missiles Russia’s military fires at the country. The Patriot missile system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.

On Thursday, a Russian drone ​strike killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform ‌in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, while five ‌died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a late-evening missile strike killed 1 person in the capital Kyiv, officials said.

Zelenskyy said US and European allies had sufficient stockpiles of Patriot interceptors to provide to Ukraine now, which could be replenished in the coming years through contracts already paid for by Ukraine and its partners.

Delayed missile deliveries have added to Kyiv’s tensions with Washington ⁠after US president Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Zelenskyy for Ukraine’s unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.

But despite Ukraine’s urgency, it will probably not receive the missile interceptors quickly. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfil, and two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles – which are yet to be manufactured – are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.

One of the people said Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense was encouraging the Pentagon to bring ‌forward the delivery date, possibly by giving Kyiv missiles already in the US arsenal and backfilling with the new Patriot interceptors.

Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through a program called US Jumpstart, ​along with national funds financed by the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan, the state department said in a statement.

The programme uses donations from allies to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine to support its self-defence following Russia’s invasion, according to a Pentagon website.

Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors.

The US has ⁠supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, ​raising concerns about inventories of key air defense ​and precision-guided weapons.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Government corruption a top issue for US midterm voters, exclusive poll finds
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Lauren Aratani in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Harris poll for Guardian finds 76% believe officials care more about self-enrichment than helping everyday Americans

Government corruption has emerged as a top issue in the upcoming US midterm elections, with an overwhelming majority of Americans saying US government officials use their public office for personal financial gain, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian.

Nearly nine out of 10 Americans said that government corruption, as defined as elected officials putting their own or their donors’ financial interests ahead of the public’s, is a problem, according to the survey.

Three-quarters (76%) of voters said that elected officials care more about enriching themselves than improving the economy for ordinary people. Voters were more likely to say that government corruption (65%) is more concerning than corporate power (29%). Just under 10% said that neither concerns them.

The rising cost of living is still expected to drive the election, with 36% of voters saying it is the single most important issue to how they plan to vote in the midterms. But in a slate of other issues including immigration, housing costs, abortion, crime and safety and AI, corruption was the next top issue.

The results come after nearly two years of Donald Trump’s second term, where the president has both figuratively and literally reshaped Washington.

The president demolished the historic East Wing of the White House to make way for a $400m ballroom – $335m of which he said is coming from private donors, including companies such as Apple and Nvidia. The federal government is down more than 420,000 workers after Elon Musk was given the power to introduce huge jobs cuts after donating nearly $300m to Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign. Meanwhile, Trump’s sons are running the family’s lucrative cryptocurrency business that has made Trump $1bn since returning to the White House. And Trump himself accepted a $400m private jet as a gift from the Qatari royal family.

These actions have not gone unnoticed. Voters in the Harris poll were twice as likely to say that Republicans have a bigger corruption problem than Democrats. Forty per cent of voters, including 29% of Republicans, said the GOP has a bigger corruption problem. A third (32%) of voters said that both parties have the problem equally, while 21% said that Democrats have the bigger problem.

Independents, whose votes will be key in swing races across the country, were much more likely to say that Republicans have more of a corruption problem, with 34% saying that Republicans have the bigger issue and 13% pointing to Democrats. Most Independents (42%) said that both parties share the problem equally.

The economy as experienced by everyday Americans has been vastly different from the portrait painted by Wall Street. The stock market has been soaring on the back of never-ending AI spending. In early October, both the S&P 500 and tech-heavy Nasdaq stock indices hit record highs.

The gains have been a boon for a relatively small group of Americans. Americans in the top 1% of wealth own half of the stock market while the bottom 50% own just over 1% of the market.

Armed with more funds than ever, America’s wealthiest people have been driving even more donations into elections. After the supreme court’s 2010 Citizens United case removed limits on campaign contributions, each election year has brought in new records of cash. The midterms have already cost $11.2bn in ads, according to NBC News, the most ever for a midterm cycle.

A chunk of these donations are coming from the ultra-rich. Just 40 donors have already contributed $2.5bn to races this year, according to the Brennan Center for Justice. Last week, billionaire Michael Bloomberg announced he was contributing $80m in last-minute funding for Democratic candidates, while Donald Trump said his political action committee was contributing a total of $400m to Republicans.

For everyday Americans, this flood of cash has changed the motivations of elected officials, who many believe will ultimately prioritize themselves and their donors over their constituents. A majority of voters (78%) in the Harris poll agreed that “elected officials care more about enriching themselves than helping people like me”.

“Government corruption has shot up to become the second most important issue in the midterms after cost of living. Americans are triggered by leaders they now see as both responsible for and profiting off their growing economic hardship,” said John Gerzema, CEO of Harris Poll.

Regardless of who ends up controlling Congress after the midterms, voters across the political spectrum are expecting solutions to address the ongoing affordability crisis that is affecting their lives.

Out of a slate of policies to address the cost of living, a third (32%) of voters said that there should be limits on the influence of companies and lobbyists on government decisions. The second most popular policy was removing tariffs (29%), followed by limiting how much companies raise prices on goods (24%).

On Tuesday, voters in California will decide on a ballot measure that could place a one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires in the state. Tech billionaires have been spending an estimated $1m a day, altogether more than $340m, to fight the measure. Half (50%) of voters in the new poll, including 56% of independents, said that billionaires do not pay their fair share of taxes. Just 28% of Republicans said the same.

Some in corporate America are catching on to the discontent. Last week, the United Airlines CEO, Scott Kirby, said in an interview that he supports a national wealth tax, a comment that got him backlash from some Republicans.

“We should have a national wealth tax – it won’t work by state because people will just move,” he said. “And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them.”

This survey was conducted online within the US by The Harris Poll from 22 October to 24 October 2026 among a nationally representative sample of 2,065 US adults, among whom 1,481 are likely to vote in the 2026 midterm elections.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Luigi Mangione’s lawyers file to dismiss state charges, citing double jeopardy law
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Victoria Bekiempis
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Mangione pleaded guilty in August in federal case in the killing of UnitedHealthcare executive Brian Thompson

Luigi Mangione’s lawyers filed paperwork on Friday once again pushing for dismissal of his state-level case in the killing of UnitedHealthcare executive Brian Thompson following his federal guilty plea.

Mangione pleaded guilty on 14 August to federal charges in Thompson’s grisly death outside a Manhattan hotel on 4 December 2024. The shocking plea came less than a month before his state murder and weapons trial, which had been scheduled for 8 September.

Thompson’s death spurred a sprawling search for his killer. The incident simultaneously elicited an onslaught of anger against the for-profit US healthcare industry, which has long been decried for putting their bottom line ahead of patients, to the latter’s detriment.

About an hour after Mangione admitted to two federal stalking charges, his lawyers filed paperwork to dismiss his state case. They have contended that New York state’s double jeopardy laws bar him from being prosecuted by the Manhattan district attorney.

Double-jeopardy protection under the US constitution does not bar state prosecution for the same crimes as a federal case, and vice-versa. However, New York state statute maintains that “a person may not be twice prosecuted for the same offense” and “a person may not be separately prosecuted for two offenses based upon the same act or criminal transaction”.

In their new filing, Mangione’s lawyers reiterated their double-jeopardy arguments.

“The core misconduct of the federal and state prosecutions is the same: the intent to kill and the killing of Brian Thompson. Yes, stalking can also, in some circumstances, apply to conduct different and less extreme than intending to kill someone. But this has nothing to do with whether it also applies to intentional killing,” they wrote.

“One of the harms clearly addressed by the expansive federal stalking statute is stalking with the intent to kill and resulting in the killing of the person stalked,” they also said. “It is a statute that, like a state murder statute, is intended to keep people safe from being murdered—the oldest crime there is. That the stalking statute also criminalizes stalking conduct that does not result in death does not change that analysis.”

Manhattan prosecutors oppose Mangione’s push for dismissal. In paperwork filed on 9 October, they insisted his state proceedings can proceed “under an exception” of this state’s double-jeopardy provisions.

They have argued that federal stalking crimes, and state murder offenses, do not overlap in such a manner that state double-jeopardy protections would come into play.

“Statutory double jeopardy applies only when a defendant has been ‘separately prosecuted’ for the same misconduct, and dismissed federal charges do not constitute a separate prosecution,” they said.

The judge presiding over Mangione’s state case, Gregory Carro, pushed back these proceedings after the unexpected plea. Carro calendared the next court date for 10 December.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: Selma Blair says she is ‘so sorry’ to those she alarmed following alleged air incident
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Press Association
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
Actor pleaded not guilty to allegedly kicking a nurse and a police officer after an incident on flight from Los Angeles to New York

Selma Blair has spoken for the first time since being charged with assault after a mid-air assault incident, saying she is “so sorry” to anyone “that I hurt, I frightened, that I alarmed”.

Blair pleaded not guilty to state assault charges over allegations she kicked a nurse and a police officer after an incident involving crew members on a flight from Los Angeles to New York earlier this month.

At the time, her representatives said her alleged behaviour had been brought on by a severe medical emergency.

In a video posted to Instagram, Blair said: “I know I’ve been quiet for a couple weeks since October 11. And you deserve to hear from me directly, and I’m sorry that it’s taken this long.

“There is a legal matter going on, and my lawyers have asked me to not say anything about that day, and I’m listening to them.”

The actor said she took the matter “very seriously” and that the “very simple and the truest thing I know about myself is that not one day ever have I intended to hurt or frighten anyone”.

“And so to the people that I disappointed, that I hurt, I frightened, that I alarmed, I am so sorry,” she said, adding that she appreciated everyone who had reached out to her in support since the incidents.

Blair then assured fans that her service dog Scout, who accompanied her on the flight, was doing well. She was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2018 and got the Labrador as a service dog five years ago.

The actor concluded: “So, right now I’m going to be taking care of my health. And my son. And thinking of you all with my gratitude and love.”

Blair, 54, was detained by police when the Delta flight landed in New York and was taken to hospital for evaluation.

A police officer taking her to Jamaica hospital medical centre alleged in charging documents that while securing Blair to a stretcher, the actor pulled one of her legs from the straps and kicked her repeatedly around the face, neck and chest, causing serious pain and substantial swelling.

She was arraigned on two counts of second-degree assault late the following day at a court in Queens, where a judge set her bail at $20,000 (£15,141) cash or $60,000 dollars bond and set the next hearing for January.

Her lawyer Shawn Barnes told the judge that her actions were not intentional.

He said the actor missed several doses of “a powerful medication that controls severe neurological symptoms,” according to the New York Daily News and New York Post.

Mr Barnes said she boarded the flight in Los Angeles amid a heavy workload and hit her head during the flight.

He said these factors, along with the altitude, led to “a state of severe confusion and disorientation”.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: ‘We’re looking at a 30-year run’: UK pair aim to complete world’s most complex board game
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Mark Brown North of England correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Decades from now, friends may become first people known to have finished The Campaign for North Africa

“We have had a six-turn practice run. It took about 18 months,” said Andy Taeger, with what seemed like a chuckle as he contemplated playing the world’s most complicated board game.

“Based on that, we are looking at a 20- to 30-year run for the full game,” said his gaming partner James Purcell. “We’ve come to terms with it.”

The Guardian joined the pair in a Newcastle front room on Friday as they prepared to start an insane odyssey, playing the legendarily knotty war game The Campaign for North Africa.

If they finish it – and that, subject to the events of the next two to three decades, is the intention – they will become the first people known to have completed a game so vast, detailed and time-consuming that it has achieved mythical status in board gaming communities. It is a holy grail.

Purcell, 29, is a mental health worker from Wallsend, Taeger, 30, a software developer from Gosforth. They’re happy to be called geeks. They met about 10 years ago and realised straight away that they had a connection.

“We were at a house party with a mutual friend and I was singing James Blunt’s Wisemen in one of the bedrooms, quite drunk,” said Purcell. “Andy happened to pass by the bedroom door, heard me singing and decided to join in. So we became fast friends from there.”

Their shared love of Dungeons & Dragons and phases playing Yu-Gi-Oh!, a trading card game, and Carcassonne, a board game, have kept the friendship going. When another friend mentioned The Campaign For North Africa, a 1979 game designed by Richard Berg simulating the desert war of 1940-43, they set out to discover more.

They watched a few videos, read up about it and went to the pub. “We both realised that we’d been thinking about the game for two weeks. By the end of the night, we were committed to giving it a try,” said Purcell.

Along with buying the game – £970 from eBay – they decided to chronicle their journey on a weekly podcast, War With a Mate. “We knew there was no reason to keep playing unless we’re held accountable,” said Purcell. “Otherwise we knew we’d buy the game, we’d give up inside two weeks and we’d have a thousand-pound board game that we can do nothing with.

“With a podcast, people can follow along and if we back out we’ve got the shame of everyone calling us out on it.”

The pair have spent 99 podcast episodes chronicling their prep and practice for the game before starting it at 7.30pm on Friday for episode 100. It could take 20 years, but “originally it was looking like 50,” said Purcell, not wanting to contemplate the idea of still playing as they approached 80.

On Friday afternoon, they were setting up in a friend’s house because they will livestream day one. It will normally be played at Taeger’s flat.

The game comes with a 10ft map, which they have divided up into five picture frames and 1,600 pieces, which they will magnetise. “We haven’t punched the German pieces out yet because we won’t need them for about five years,” said Purcell.

They will have to keep track of aircraft, truck convoys, land units, supply dumps, water use, fuel evaporation and so, so much more, including not to do anything that could be deemed a war crime.

It comes with a history book as well as seven rule books with a dizzying list. One of the best known is the “pasta rule” about Italian forces needing more water in order to boil their pasta rations. It’s assumed to be a joke – but who knows?

Berg does seem to be “poking fun” at the players, said Purcell. At the same time, he clearly also has a thorough knowledge of the campaign. “The amount of research behind this must have been insane,” said Taeger.

Purcell is playing as the Axis forces and Taeger as the Commonwealth. It remains to be seen if the game will be so historically accurate that Purcell is destined to lose. He doesn’t think so.

“I think we’ve seen already, through the practice run, you can very much change the fate of the campaign through better decision-making,” he said.

Both think the game could very well end up a draw, which would be gutting. “I think, honestly, a loss might even be better than a draw because at least it’s a definitive result,” said Taeger. There is also the chance they’ll find that the game is simply not finishable, but thanks to the podcast, they will have plenty of people cheering them on.

“The reaction has been surprisingly positive,” said Purcell, with many boardgamers thankful that someone is doing it so they don’t have to. “We’ve not really had many people decry it as the stupid thing that it is, which would be the natural reaction.”

The players are determined, but they also intend to take it seriously – and tread very carefully.

“You don’t want to make a mistake because you were in a bit of a rush,” said Taeger, definitely laughing now. “You might have to be dealing with it for the next 10 years.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: As Trump fans the flames of a world on fire, can diplomacy take back control?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Amid the chaos, havoc and war caused by a capricious and amoral US president, countries are waking up to the dangers of being excluded and abused by America

Never has there been a time when the world has been more interconnected than now. What happens in the secretive inner councils in Tehran, the mountains of south-west Yemen, the steppe of the Donbas, the still bloody wasteland that is Gaza and even the elegant boulevards of Paris and Milan have a common thread.

One cannot understand one set of conflicts without weaving them into another, and it is this very interdependence that is making each problem so contagious, layered and difficult to resolve, leaving the world to live as if trapped inside a pressure cooker on the brink of an explosion.

Each night it seems the world has reached a collective rock bottom, only to wake in the morning to the sound of knocking from below.

In this great age of noncooperation and lawlessness, the need for one crisis to be resolved before another can be addressed leads to a collective paralysis, especially in the total absence of clear leadership by the world’s leading power.

Speaking this week, the Indian external affairs minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, said: “The indivisibility of our existence permeates every aspect of human activity and it has deepened as globalisation has advanced. The fact now is that war anywhere threatens peace everywhere.”

Tom Barrack, Donald Trump’s envoy to Turkey and wider counsellor to the president on the Middle East, in remarks in Doha last week highlighted these threads, admitting the war on Iran launched by his president and Israel in late February had brought unexpected consequences, turning “camp fires into forest fires”.

He likened the Middle East to a Rubik’s Cube, whereby a single move can inadvertently affect the whole picture. “When you adjust one thing in the region what we have seen is everything then changes. Those unintended consequences, and the sequential pace of what is happening, is unexpected,” said Barrack.

He then admitted: “We started trying to do something with our allies in Iran that spread through Hamas, Hezbollah, to six Iranian militias, the Houthis and is now going to north Africa. So where does it stop? How much does this US intervention help or hurt?”

Without breaking from Trump, he answered his own question pretty unambiguously. “We have had 23 regime changes take place across the greater Middle East and Levant instituted one way or another by some American hand or influence, and none of them have worked.

“Every time we try to intervene and change the person or the regime, it seems to have been a mistake,” Barrack said, pointing to Iraq, Libya and Afghanistan, but discreetly omitting Iran.

So it is easy to blame what has gone wrong on excessive interventionism and failed multilateralism.

In his new book, the American international relations expert Charles Kupchan explains: “The world is experiencing deep tectonic transformations. Power is rapidly diffusing across the international system, decentering global politics and reawakening great power competition.

“At the same time the advance of the digital era is eroding the social contract of the industrial era producing massive socioeconomic disruption that is affecting political life inside nations as well as relations among them.”

But it is also hard not to believe that in this interconnected world the disruptive damage that a capricious, vain and amoral US president can inflict has grown tenfold, and that is what we are experiencing. World disorder meets personality disorder.

The Iran war, for instance, as Barrack implied, remains Trump’s most consequential and most mysterious mistake, and its repercussions reverberate across the world. Any US president would have had to address the Iran issue, itself a product of system failure, the inability of the multilateral system to incorporate and change Iran. But the way in which the Iran issue was addressed is down to Trump, and his psyche.

The Democratic candidate for senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, put it simply: “Everybody could have told you this is a dumb idea. There was really only one person in the whole world who had a 40-year project to get us to fight this war. He’s a prime minister of another government [Netanyahu]. And he finally found the dumbass who was willing to do it.”

The foreign minister of Oman, and mediator in the February Iran-US talks, speaking in Cambridge this week reminded his audience an agreement on the core issue – Iran’s nuclear programme – had been within reach before the bombing started.

On every test the war has been a catastrophic failure, whose consequence keeps spreading beyond its initial boundaries, pushing worldwide inflation to 4%. The strait of Hormuz, a waterway open to commercial traffic for centuries, has become an Iranian bargaining chip. Less than a fortnight before the midterms, the price of Brent oil per barrel reached $117 – 50% higher than prewar levels.

The GDP of Saudi Arabia, the Middle East’s economic powerhouse, is forecast by the IMF to contract 3.3%, a five percentage-point downgrade from the 1.7% growth forecast issued only in July.

As the House of Saud analysis explains: “The country’s Vision 2030 plan was constructed as a hedge against oil-price volatility. It assumed open sea lanes, functioning airports, and a US security umbrella that would deter kinetic threats to the kingdom’s export infrastructure. Every one of those assumptions has failed since February.”

On 30 September, Saudi Arabia’s government felt forced to raise its 2026 budget deficit projection to $65.3bn, 48% above the original forecast.

Nor did the conflict lead to a more stable Iran. The Iranian with most strategic nous, Ali Larijani, was blown up on the first day of the war. Hardliners around the new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, are more entrenched than ever. If anything the public debate inside Iran leans towards ending the fatwa on possessing nuclear weapons.

Regardless of the nuclear issue, after being attacked twice mid-negotiation, the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps has already adjusted its defence doctrine to allow for preemptive strikes not just against US bases, but across the globe. “People can hurt us from a distance, and it doesn’t cost a fortune to be able to do so,” Tony Radakin, the UK chief of the defence staff, admitted.

Then there is the incoherence and lawlessness of the US-Israeli actions in Iran. Benjamin Netanyahu, spoiling to attack Iran for a third time in two years, wanted to order “the IDF, Mossad, and the security services” to “overthrow the regime in Iran”. The Americans focus was on nuclear weapons.

The chaos has left Trump’s domestic popularity in ruins. Yet as Dean Acheson, Harry S Truman’s secretary of state, asserted: “80% of the job of foreign policy is the management of your domestic ability to have a policy.”

Henry Kissinger said: “The acid test of policy is its ability to obtain domestic support.” A foreign policy has to be constructed to win popular backing and this one was not. As a result Trump feels entrapped, circling around solutions that failed before, making him ever more irascible and random.

The Republican pollster Karl Rove claimed Trump, as a result, “came across more as a heckler at a UFC match than as a reassuring wartime commander-in-chief. The more undisciplined the White House messages on war and the economy, the more at risk GOP candidates will be.”

Faced by the plunging poll numbers, incensed by Iran’s refusal to submit, incapable of self-criticism, Trump took the plunge and tried to deflect responsibility for high energy prices to a second theatre of war – Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries.

Trump flung open the floodgates of his hatred for Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy that he first released in 2025 only for European leaders, and domestic pressure, to force them shut again.

The pent-up bile has poured out as he demanded Zelenskyy stand down, describing him as the real impediment to peace, and a new era of Russian US business cooperation.

Trump first announced an entirely fictional 60-day “energy truce” that neither Zelensky or Putin had agreed. Then the deal to release Russian diesel emerged to be so small that no serious commentator said it would have a serious impact on the US prices.

As to why Ukrainian forces were suddenly deprived of their previous levels of access to the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink, the US administration gave conflicting accounts over the rules that govern such systems, and what actually happened.

Even after the decision was supposedly reversed, some blamed a freelancing Musk, the billionaire owner of the system, implying a private company could determine the conduct of a putative US ally. Others, including the vice-president, JD Vance, said contractually Musk would have required the permission of the White House or the military to act. Musk said the Ukrainians had breached the terms of the Starlink contract by using it to attack Iran.

The Ukrainian author Illia Ponomarenko wrote: “There have, of course, been times in human history that were even darker and more terrible. But never, it seems, have there been times so despicable and, above all, so stupid.”

Trump’s intervention and his intertwining of these two wars has given the Russians the chance to pounce by proposing a three-way China, Russia and US great power summit at an already scheduled meeting in Shenzhen, China, on 18 November.

To make this more appealing to Trump, Putin sent his veteran foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, on 19 October to Tehran for the first time since the Iran war broke out to see if he could bring the conflict to an end on terms Trump could tolerate.

“The more Putin can persuade Tehran to move closer to Trump’s demands, the more concessions he can extract from Trump on Ukraine,” the Russia affairs analyst Amir Chahaki said. The Russian ambition is to use Trump’s difficulties to end the two wars – Ukraine and Iran – together, largely on Russian terms.

Trump is taking steps to help Putin, including by shedding his status as an international pariah, overruling the objections of some in his own party by inviting Putin to this winter’s G20 summit, which the US is hosting at a Trump golf club just outside Miami.

Quite why Trump feels so certain of Putin’s good intentions is a mystery, one that no one can unravel. David Frum, a former speech writer for George W Bush, posits it is a function of Trump’s decline. Trump was “much more of a self-aware conman when he entered politics a decade ago than he is now. He now may be kind of lost: truly in a world of illusions, where he no longer himself knows what is true and what is a lie.”

But there is a consequence to all this. More and more countries are finally waking up to dangers of being excluded and abused by the US. The former Canadian foreign minister Chrystia Freeland admits it has taken a long time.

“There are leaders, thinking Trump is stupid, that decided: ‘I can win this guy over. I can give him the shiniest prize. I can give him a gold watch that’s encrusted with diamonds. I can flatter him in the most outrageous way.’”

For instance, Saudi Arabia offered gifts to Trump, and in return they have been left alone to fend off the attacks by Houthis that senior UN diplomats insist is entirely driven by a timetable that meets Iran’s needs.

In particular, Trump’s effort to deflect his Iranian disaster on to a largely innocent Ukraine has had a lethal effect inside Europe. The continent’s leaders are aghast at the gap between themselves and Trump on Russia.

Where Europe sees an existential threat, Trump sees a business opportunity. What is worse is that his pro-Russia rhetoric threatens the centre’s own political survival by feeding the populist narrative about the draining cost of Ukraine making lives unaffordable.

The torrent of propaganda about “peace with Russia” led the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, to exclaim: “My biggest concern at the moment is not our economy, not the USA or China, but Russia’s influence on our society.”

As a matter of self-protection, European leaders have no choice but to articulate their differences with Trump. As a result, they have had to become explicit in blaming the Iran war for the squeeze on living standards and to ask the rioters to criticise not them but Washington.

For instance, Emmanuel Macron, the French president, told the rioters that their anger about the cost of living was legitimate: “Demonstrators expressed concern about the cost of living and the price of fuel. Both are driven by the conflict launched in the Persian Gulf, a conflict in which France has taken no part but whose consequences we are suffering.”

The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, in his parliament admitted fuel prices for ordinary people were “devilishly expensive”, but added that the Donald responsible for this was not him but Trump, the hero of the Polish opposition.

The second knock-on impact is that Musk’s meddling with SpaceX has made it even more apparent to Europe that it has to end its debate on digital sovereignty and instead regulate to reduce its future dependence on US technology.
