Freeland predicts: “Countries are going to think really hard before they buy another F-35 controlled by the Pentagon. Why would you want a jet that Americans control?”

The European Commission in May proposed reserving 70% of the 2GHz frequency spectrum, which allows smartphones to connect directly to satellites, for European enterprises, thus restricting access for players such as Starlink. Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Vodafone and Telefónica are already lining up to make the bid, prompting US diplomatic protests.

The Polish foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, accused Musk of digging his own grave in Europe, asking why “a Ketamine-addicted trillionaire in bed with foreign powers should think he deserves regulatory privileges and frequency permissions”.

Similarly, some Middle Eastern powers are waking up to the threat to their sovereignty posed by a US system that consistently privileges Israel’s priorities.

It is early days, but for a Gulf state leader to call for a Gulf security pact that includes Iran, as Badr Albusaidi, Oman’s foreign minister, did this week, is a potential Berlin Wall moment. The implication is that the US should no longer be the security provider for the Gulf.

Iran is viewed with deep suspicion across the Gulf, and Albusaidi admits his proposal is counterintuitive. But, as his team says, “war sometimes just happens; peace is always caused”.

Either way, at a time when people have lost faith in the problem-solving capacity of postwar institutions, it’s critical that those who believe in the efficacy of collective action and diplomacy show they mean it.

After three years of havoc and war, they finally need to take back control from the demolition men.

https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.title: The cursed cruise: how the dream of never-ending luxury at sea became a nightmare
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.author: Oliver Holmes in Bangkok, Daniel Boffey in London and Adeshola Ore in Melbourne
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.text:
The MV Odyssey was billed as the ultimate escape from Donald Trump. Instead, the oil shock caused by his war has left passengers unceremoniously dumped in Cambodia

The idea was a never-ending retirement at sea, a continuous voyage around the globe. The promise to the passengers of the MV Odyssey cruise ship – many approaching the autumn of their lives – was that on the open seas they could cut loose from the troubles of the world. But the world had other ideas.

The end came in an announcement as stark as it was brief: they had seven hours to get off. They were going no further than Cambodia.

The Odyssey, owned by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, had first set sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024 with an explicit offer: Donald Trump had been re-elected to the White House, and this was a way for those ill-disposed to the president to enjoy a four-year “skip forward”.

For $319,998, a couple seeking such an escape could head off to the high seas for the length of a presidential term and come back from their journey to nowhere when the danger had passed – or not. For those who had simply had enough, there was a permanent residency option for a few hundred thousand more. Depending on the package, there were also monthly fees on top, which covered food, drinks, wifi, wellness programmes and room cleaning. They would have access to a pool, a pickleball court, a theatre, several bars and a gym. Exotic port destinations would be visited along the way.

It was by no means cheap – but the Odyssey was quite accurately billed as the “affordable” option for those interested in such a cocoon. The pioneer in the world of “residential ships”, a vessel called MS The World, offered apartments that typically ranged from $2m to $15m, with the pampered passengers getting to choose where it would go. For that experience, there was a waiting list.

The Odyssey was not in that league. Rather than built as a residential ship, it had previously been a traditional cruise liner named MS Braemar. Under that name, it had been turned away from several ports in the Caribbean during the pandemic when its passengers became ill. Cuba finally allowed it to dock, but the vessel never went into service as MS Braemar again. It was sold off by Fred Olsen cruises and adapted by its new owners. Villa Vie described the three-decade-old restructured vessel as “an intimate residential cruise ship offering a new way to live”.

At 642ft (196 metres) long, it was a relatively small ship, but at such prices, and with the world being held firmly at bay, what could go wrong? Neither the more than 200 passengers on the Odyssey nor its cruise operator foresaw the consequences of Trump’s war in Iran. The reality was, there was no escaping the US president.

On Tuesday, Villa Vie Residences issued a statement. It had run out of money owing to the soaring price of oil. Monthly fuel costs per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, placing it “under unsustainable financial pressure”, it announced.

“Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” the company said, explaining the slow death of its business model. “Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses.”

The Odyssey’s passengers were told to pack up their belongings before being transported on buses into the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand. “We are working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and temporary living arrangements, and are supporting residents, crew, and employees as we evaluate restructuring and recapitalisation alternatives over the next 60 days,” the company said.

“People were shell-shocked, numb, crying,” said one passenger, Kit Cassingham from the US, who spent two years on the ship with her husband, Randy. They had made their cabin into a home, putting down their own rugs and pictures on the wall. “People were angry. They were hysterical. They were sad … Disbelief,” she added. “I mean, that whole gamut of, what is it, the five stages of grief.”

Most of the passengers on the Odyssey were Americans, travelling with an international group of 156 crew members, including a ship’s doctor and two nurses. Many of the passengers were retired or digital nomads. One woman, Holly Hennessy, had been living happily with her cat, Captain, since the ship set sail two years ago.

One couple, Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin, who said they had bought a cabin with a 15-year guarantee, had been documenting their life at sea on YouTube, including the lead-up to the fateful announcement. The signs of financial distress had been apparent for weeks, they said.

“I’m Mr Super Positive, and I’ve felt really drained the last two months,” Bodin recounted in a video.

Footage from inside the ship’s lounge on the final night showed residents drinking, as rumours spread that their voyage might be over. Cruise ship staff had requested each passenger contribute $1,800 to ensure the ship had funds to travel to Bangkok.

The next day, the couple posted an update showing the inside of their cabin as a voice on the loudspeaker said the ship’s operator had “unfortunately” been “unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations”. An email was sent requesting that everyone disembark by 2pm.

“We knew the worst-case scenarios, but we didn’t think it would come to reality, which it did,” said Rina Cavazza, a pilates instructor from Brisbane, Australia.

Another passenger, Sherrie Cornett, wrote on Facebook that they were “dropped unceremoniously in the middle of town, left to our own devices”.

The company has not provided financial aid, passengers said, or even supplied a list of hotels in Cambodia. It later offered tickets for a charter flight to the US, although many passengers had already left. The company has been contacted for comment.

Kit and Randy Cassingham, now in a hotel in Cambodia, reflected on how life changed on the ship once the Iran war began, with ominous signs that the company was running out of money. The food quality began to deteriorate, and there was less of it; there were fewer excursions on shore, they said.

“I realised as soon as the strait of Hormuz incident came along, the energy of the ship changed,” Kit said. “I think it was because the ship management realised how much more this was going to cost. And then they were starting to do cutbacks that we weren’t aware of yet.”

Far from being a haven, the ship became a microcosm for the global economic turmoil. “I watched the world, and I don’t even pay attention to the news, but I’ve watched it just kind of crumble and shatter,” said Kit. “And I’m thinking, ‘it’s going to be difficult no matter what’.”

Randy said the writing had long been on the wall. They were, after all, on a ship that “drinks petrol by the metric tonne”. “You know, literally they’re buying 150 metric tonnes of fuel at a time,” he said. “We’re talking about $800,000 if we tried to get a full tank.”

While docked in Singapore in August, passengers had already been told the company did not have enough money to continue cruising, and several of the residents had contributed their own funds to get it moving again.

“Very few expect to get any money back because we know that they [the company] have been in terrible money problems from the beginning,” said Randy. Passengers had also passed a jar around for money for the crew, who are also stuck in Cambodia, he said.

Will the story of the Odyssey put people off cruises? It is unlikely, said Prof Andrew Coggins, an industry analyst, who pointed to an unprecedented boom since the end of the Covid pandemic, with global passengers reaching a historical high of 37.2 million in 2025.

Those numbers were in part because of “pent up demand” from those who had been unable to enjoy a cruise during the pandemic years, he said. But it was also the case, he said, that a cruise could offer good value for money. “You get to be pampered, you pack and unpack once, but you see different places, you eat better food than you would get at home, and then you have the romance of going to sea,” he said.

Residential ships such as the Odyssey were, though, in a very small category of their own, Coggins added. “The World is the only other one I know about and I think there are a couple that are trying to start up,” he said. But the finances are notoriously difficult. In 2023, a three-year cruise offered by Miray Cruises, with fares starting at $30,000 per person per year, including accommodation, food, drinks, laundry and even health care, was cancelled weeks before its due departure date owing to an inability to make the sums add up..

To survive choppy world markets, charges to the passengers have to be high, necessitating a concomitant level of luxury. “The World was actually built as a residential ship,” Coggins said. “The cabins or the state rooms are much bigger.”

Speaking earlier in the week, Mikael Petterson, who launched Villa Vie Residences in 2023, accepted that he was the “villain in the story” but said he was doing everything he could to help the stranded passengers. “Nobody that’s tried residential cruising has succeeded and we have gone further than anyone else,” he said. “But I think we would have been absolutely fine and we would have seen this through, if there was no Iran war.”

Back in Cambodia, Randy has been blogging to keep people updated while they work out what to do next. But he isn’t bitter. For all the promises, he said, all good things must come to an end. “Our message is that we’re not saying ‘poor me’. We know that people are having trouble, that they’re trying to put fuel in their cars, food in their mouths. And we’re very lucky. We’re not crying in our soup. So we are completely aware that we’re very lucky and that we’re going to land on our feet and be OK.”

Kit, a transformation coach, agreed. “This isn’t a pity party for us,” she said. “We actually want to say to people: ‘Live your dreams. Go for the gusto. Live life while you can because you don’t know how the adventure will turn out’.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘You need the power of all your votes’: Bedouin women secure success for Arab parties in Israeli election
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Emma Graham-Harrison in Azzarnug
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
With 180,000 eligible voters, Bedouin turnout was key in Palestinian-led parties winning unprecedented 19 seats

Last year, Umm Khaled Fatoum returned from volunteering in a Jewish-Arab support centre for victims of war to find bulldozers tearing into her son’s house in the Bedouin village of Azzarnug.

The demolition crew, who arrived under police escort, did not even allow them to remove furniture or solar panels before reducing the home and its contents to a pile of rubble.

This week, she took action of her own at the ballot box, targeting the extremist national security minister who ordered – and boasts about – the mass destruction of Palestinian and Arab homes.

“I had one goal, to send [Itamar] Ben-Gvir home,” Fatoum said. “There isn’t a single family in the Bedouin community that hasn’t been hurt by his campaign against us.”

In the weeks before election day, she joined a grassroots campaign to educate other Bedouin women about their rights and potential power.

It had spectacular results, with voting rates tripling in some Bedouin villages in the southern Negev region in Tuesday’s election, amid a broader surge in turnout among Bedouin voters.

Years of violent, racist government opened the door for change in conservative communities, said Hanan Alsanah, a lawyer and activist whose Alnashmiat network led the grassroots programme.

“We said that even if all the men go to vote, it is only half the community. You need the power of all your votes, because Ben-Gvir has a lot of power.”

The rise in Bedouin votes came amid historically high turnout among Arab citizens of Israel. Their votes secured an unprecedented 19 seats in the Knesset for Palestinian-led parties and were critical to stripping the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his allies of their governing majority.

This year, the lowest turnout in any Bedouin community was 62%. The highest was more than 93%. With an estimated 180,000 eligible voters, their turnout was key to the Islamist Ra’am party beating polling expectations.

Netanyahu has repeatedly used racist fearmongering to try to boost voter turnout among his own base. This year, his attacks included an AI-generated image purporting to show a crowded polling station in a Palestinian area and Bedouin female voters.

In an apparent attempt to undermine the surge in votes for Palestinian-led parties, Netanyahu accused them of fraud and foreign support.

“The increase in voter turnout in the Bedouin community in particular, and the Arab community in general, is unprecedented in the history of the state,” said Amit Segal, a pundit and close confidant of the prime minister.

The allegations have been rejected by opposition leaders, election organisers, and the activists in the Negev.

“I am very proud of our turnout. They are talking about ‘corruption’ [as the reason for high voter turnout]. The correct word is ‘awareness’,” said Amira Habdoubi, an organiser from the village of Abu Talul.

For a community whose civil rights are policed by racist authorities, the election was a rare opportunity for political expression, she added. “We can’t protest, because they will arrest us. Voting is the only opportunity we have to make a political protest.”

The Muslim Bedouin are part of a marginalised minority inside Israel. Before the state was created, they roamed widely across the Negev desert.

Now, although their villages take up only 2.5% of the land in the region, many are deemed “unrecognised”, targeted by the state for demolition and left without basic services including electricity and water supplies. The majority of the Negev has been designated as military training grounds and firing ranges.

More than 100,000 people live in about 30 unrecognised communities in the Negev. Another 200,000 live in official towns, or places with some level of recognition.

Netanyahu’s pursuit of open-ended regional conflicts also drove Bedouin turnout. War is particularly terrifying in unrecognised villages because the state does not provide them with bomb shelters or warning sirens ahead of rocket, drone and missile attacks.

Rockets that hit Bedouin villages without shelters killed six of the 36 child victims of the 7 October attacks. Several adults were also killed that day in the villages and at least four people have been seriously injured by Iranian missiles.

Organised crime is another concern, rising almost unchecked under the current government.

“We had clear goals. Stop the home demolitions, stop the hatred, stop the war. Ben-Gvir talks all the time about security, but we feel no security and no one cares about us,” said Mayada Abu Khweida.

The activists worked to help women understand their rights and tackle logistical and practical obstacles to voting, as well as cultural ones.

“Because [residents of unrecognised villages] can’t vote in the municipal elections, a lot of women don’t know they have a right to vote in national elections,” said Abu Khweida. “We told them: ‘There is a legal way to express your anger and raise your voice.’”

For similar bureaucratic reasons, there are no polling stations in unrecognised villages, so voters have to travel to nearby towns. Men went any way they could, including on camel, horse, donkey and bike, on journeys that took up to an hour in each direction.

Jewish women offered lifts to Bedouin women, but because in 2019 Israel’s election committee ruled that organising transport volunteers was illegal, voters and drivers connected individually.

“Hundreds of women volunteers went to help Bedouin women to access the polls, and at the same time about 150 men went to do protective presence at the polling stations,” said Raluca Ganea, the founding executive director of the Jewish-Arab community action group Zazim.

“We wanted to have Jewish men standing there to de-escalate, in case there was a rightwing provocation of some kind. So it would not be the Bedouin men in front of the provocateurs, because if the police come or there is violence, they are much more likely to be arrested or worse.”

Netanyahu’s racist get-out-the-vote campaign on social media included photos of Bedouin women with their faces covered.

Some of these women covered their faces to avoid being seen by strangers from outside their own community. In recognised towns, where women could vote in their communities, most did not cover their faces, Alsanah said.

Others hid themselves to avoid becoming fodder for Ben-Gvir’s extremist social media feed, which regularly features humiliation of Arab citizens.

“The women were worried the extremists would take photos at the polling stations and covered their faces to protect themselves from being exploited on social media,” Abu Khweida said, adding that his campaign of humiliation has affected all of Bedouin society.

The grassroots mobilisation of Bedouin voters aimed in part to give children back their dreams, one reason why women responded so strongly.

“In the last election in 2022, turnout among women was around 20%. Now in the unrecognised villages, informal data shows more than 60% turnout among women,” Alsanah said, adding that Israel does not break down voting statistics by gender.

The project built on more than a decade of work with Alnashmiat, based in Arab and Jewish solidarity, that could set an example for a new government, Alsanah said.

“We learned an important lesson from this election campaign. We should work together, men and women, Arab and Jewish citizens, and we should bring this approach to the Israeli parliament to rebuild the state.”

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Florid language and long silences: five things we learned from week three of Russell Brand’s rape trial
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Emine Sinmaz
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
The former comedian and his wife gave evidence in the case in which he denies all charges against him

Russell Brand’s trial at Southwark crown court began with widespread media coverage on 12 October. The former comedian and presenter faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges. Here are five things we learned in the third week of his trial.

Brand, 51, who was in the witness box for four hours on Wednesday, told the jury the criminal case had been a “deeply traumatic episode” in his life.

He blamed his public fall from grace on 2023 media reports, including a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary, about his alleged sexual misconduct. He said he had achieved “staggering fame” after his marriage to the US pop star Katy Perry but that now nobody would “touch [him] with a bargepole”.

The prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, suggested he hadn’t been “abandoned” by everyone he knows, and noted he had millions of followers online. “This is not the case of poor Mr Brand being taken apart by the media,” she said.

Brand denied her suggestion that consent had not been “uppermost” in his mind between 1999 and 2009, telling the court: “Consent is absolutely non-negotiable.” He said he was “innocent” of all the charges and added: “Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and, indeed, in many ways more important than sex itself.”

Brand admitted he was wrong to have used his fame and success to “facilitate” sexual activity with women. “I think I was in a position of fame, a successful person who was admired, and I misused that commodity very selfishly,” he said.

Brand’s wife, Laura, began her evidence on Thursday by confirming she is the TV presenter Kirsty Gallacher’s sister, and that they are the daughters of the Ryder Cup-winning golfer Bernard Gallacher.

She told the court she and Brand fell in love after meeting in 2006 but that the comedian had cheated on her early in their relationship.

“I wasn’t interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people. I was invested, we both had told each other we loved each other, but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous,” Laura Brand said.

They broke up in February 2007 but restarted their relationship in 2015 and married two years later. Laura Brand insisted he was a “wonderful father” and an “amazingly attentive husband”. “We have a very frank, honest and clear relationship and marriage,” she said.

During cross-examination by Karmy-Jones, Laura agreed that Brand has a channel on the video-sharing platform Rumble, presents at political conferences and was baptised in early 2024 after the sexual misconduct allegations emerged.

Brand has remained still during the trial, but he was animated during his wife’s evidence, and could be seen smiling and laughing at times. He appeared to be mouthing words towards her as she talked about his 2024 baptism and nodding when she spoke of their friendship.

He also showed more emotion during his evidence. With his hands behind his back, he began by giving confident answers in a booming voice to his barrister, Ian Winter KC. “Mr Brand, that is nice and loud,” the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, said. Brand also used florid language such as “badinage”, “loquacious” and “coquettishness”.

But there was a marked shift in the comedian’s demeanour during cross-examination, which was punctuated with pauses and long spells of silence. There was a long pause after the prosecution’s first question: “You blame Dispatches, don’t you?”, and again when Karmy-Jones repeated the question.

Brand was confronted with extracts from his 2007 book, My Booky Wook, and his comments in media appearances.

The first alleged rape victim had told the court she believed Brand was gay and effeminate when they first met at a 1999 Labour party conference fringe event, leading to her agreeing for him to come to her hotel room.

The prosecutor pointed out that in his book, Brand used a picture of himself as a seven-year-old and wrote the caption: “This is the exact moment when I decided to act gay to attract girls. It took 15 years to produce results.”

Karmy-Jones read out another in which Brand wrote: “My egotism and the single-mindedness with which I pursued potentially sexual conquests could often make me uneasy company.”

In another he set out: “Now if I want something – whether it’s a job or a woman – I will determinedly, resolutely, remove anything that’s in the way, until I possess the object of my desire.”

In the book, Brand referred to himself as a “fervid, febrile mass of sexual energy” towards the end of sex, adding: “I’ll do anything. I’m demonically sexy.”

The prosecutor gave her closing speech on Friday, telling jurors that the six women who had come forward to accuse Brand did not know one another and had nothing to gain.

“There is no benefit to them, apart from perhaps some closure by coming before you and telling you their accounts of what happened to them so long ago,” Karmy-Jones told the jury.

“What’s happened, we suggest, is these women have realised they’re not alone and they’ve bravely come before you to tell you the truth. The truth of what happened to them so many years ago. The truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years.”

Brand’s barrister is expected to make his closing speech when the trial resumes on Monday.

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: ‘Don’t worry about the leopard. It’s a man you don’t want to run into’: Delhi women reclaim the outdoors
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Romita Saluja in Delhi
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
On a wildlife walk in the Indian capital, a group of women share their stories of trying to enjoy nature in a city where strangers feel entitled to harass them

Vallari Sheel wishes she could carry a camera or a pair of binoculars without being asked what her father does for a living. Once, looking at a tree in her south Delhi neighbourhood, about 50 metres away from her home, a man in a car screamed at her: “You have been clicking photos here for 10 days. What are you going to do with them?”

Sheel, an urban ecologist, spends hours observing trees of all types in all seasons. She often travels by car for her own safety, worries about the impact of her work on her family, and has clear guidance for her female interns when they are, inevitably, approached: don’t engage, don’t respond.

“It’s the men who ask such intrusive questions: Who are you? Where are you from? What does your father do?” she says.

Sheel was recounting these experiences atop Delhi’s oldest fort inside Sanjay Van, a sprawling city forest overlooking a 12th-century minaret. She was one of about 20 women who had gathered on a crisp Sunday morning in October to enjoy nature, safely. Many had never experienced a forest before.

Among the group were a scientist who had stopped birding since she moved to Delhi, a psychiatrist who can’t find a safe place to run, and an environmental planner who cycles everywhere. For many women, simple pleasures such as enjoying nature have become beset by gender crimes.

“The city feels designed to crush any form of freedom, any form of exploration,” says Neha Sinha, who organised the walk. Author of My Wild City: Finding Nature, Meaning, and Hope in India’s Capital, Sinha has been organising these walks for two years.

During her own walks around the city’s forts, forests and wetlands to observe the diminishing number of fireflies, flying foxes, howling jackals, leopards and hyenas, civets and owls, and groves of 350-year-old trees, she has faced the wrath of men. She has changed her route countless times to mislead stalkers, and been asked by men on the street how much she would charge for sex.

“As has everybody else,” she says. “Nearly every woman I know has called a cop saying ‘I have a stalker.’ In a culture that tells you not to go out … how do you make nature your own?”

Two weeks before the women gathered on the walking trails of Sanjay Van, dotted with ruellias, vajradantis and jaal trees, hundreds of people had joined a protest in Delhi over the gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park.

Their demand was to make public spaces safer for women. The government’s response was to ban entry to public parks after sunset.

For Alankrita Narayan, a wildlife conservation student who often needs to work alone at night, that rule was unhelpful. During an internship, she recalls, her organisation trained her for worst-case scenarios in the jungle: What if something happens to your partner? What if you encounter a man carrying a weapon? What if you encounter a forest officer asking for sexual favours?

“And I was like, where did the animal come in here? What if I’m caught alone and a leopard comes in front of me? And they were like, ‘Oh, don’t worry about the leopard. It’s a man you don’t want to run into,” she says. Sinha agrees: “Animals have rules.”

Paroma Mukherjee, a photographer, recalls the advice she once got from a well-known photographer: be inconspicuous, wear clothes that blend in, keep your equipment small. “But then, he was a man. So he could blend in,” she adds.

“Men can pee on the road and we can’t even carry a camera,” another woman says. “You know, we had to take a detour today to avoid a lonely stretch on our way here,” says another. “I carry a pepper spray,” another adds.

On group walks, the women pick up and drop off each other at their homes, wait outside the forest gate until everyone has arrived, and stick together in isolated areas. “I always tell women, ‘Don’t go alone’,” Sinha says.

“We started the walk at 7am today, which is late for birdwatching, but everybody could not leave home while it was still dark,” she says.

However, the group agree that many of these measures might not work for women from less privileged backgrounds, who then miss out.

Walking as a woman is an act of resistance, as is observing nature. “Because you’re actually slowing down when you do that,” she says. “It’s so different from the instant gratification culture that we have today. It is more of an immersion, rather than conquering. Both are very political acts.”

In the heart of New Delhi, where India’s senior officials and dignitaries live, there are thousands of fruit bats that swarm out of their roosts every evening to feast on mahua trees.

“And on very clear wintry nights, when everything is silent, I even hear jackals crying and laughing from my home. It’s almost like a parallel city,” Sinha says.

Over three hours, the women collect cuttings, peer and marvel at speckle-like flowers through a pocket microscope, discuss the colonial concepts of wild plants labelled as weeds, chat about the drongo, black kite and tailorbird they spotted, and the next walk.

“Can we do it at night?” someone asks. “What would the forest look like at night?”

Sinha describes a previous night walk experience when frogs had put up an orchestral noise, fireflies lit the bushes and jackals were laughing. “It was the most eerie, magical, bewitching atmosphere I have ever experienced,” she says.

Men, she points out, can simply go ahead and enjoy such experiences, but women have to create an ecosystem around them to be able to.

But, she promises her enthusiastic group, she will try to arrange a night walk.

https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oc.title: Don’t make sugar a treat –or hide the broccoli: top chefs on how to make your kids happy eaters
https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oc.author: Mina Holland
https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oc.text:
I’m fairly certain every child is a picky eater. People who tell you their kids happily tuck into beetroot and feta salads? I don’t buy it. The majority of children are selective, and you just have to navigate it. If they see you eating vegetables often enough, eventually they come round.

Acey is 10, lifts weights and is seriously into rugby; he’s already training with boys older than him. He’s constantly burning energy, so my job is to get food into him before he realises he’s hungry. If I wait for him to ask, all he’ll want is whatever comes in the brightest wrapper.

He eats loads of meat and fish, loves cheese and salami, and we’ll make omelettes, burgers or cheese toasties with cured meat. He’s started making his own smoothies, too, blitzing frozen mango and pineapple with a mixture of coconut and cow’s milk. He’d never choose fruit, but if I put a chopped apple in front of him, he’ll eat it. This is also true of breakfast; he’ll say he’s not hungry, but if I put yoghurt, honey and granola in front of him, it’ll disappear.

Vegetables are still a work in progress. Sweetcorn, peas and carrots are fine, but anything greener needs a bit of encouragement. That’s where the old chef’s tricks come in. A tomato sauce packed with blended vegetables, a bolognese or stew cooked low and slow, or getting him to thread peppers on to kebabs or build his own pizza. If he’s involved, he’s more likely to eat it.

We don’t eat together enough during the week because of my work hours, but weekends are different. The barbecue goes on, everything gets dumped in the middle of the table – burgers, chicken, pitta, hummus, salad – and everyone helps themselves. He dodges the salad, but he’ll happily mop up the olive oil with warm bread, and that’s a start.

Tom Kerridge is a TV chef and founder of five restaurants including The Hand & Flowers in Marlow, Buckinghamshire.

As a mixed-race family, we cook boldly and eat widely. I cook from everywhere east of India and my husband, Hugh, loves Nigel Slater. That said, our children don’t automatically eat boldly, although they did both choose to be vegetarian.

Our eldest, Arya, only ate beige food until she was about six. Now she’ll out-eat all of us on the chilli front and that’s become her thing, it’s almost an identity. She even has a T-shirt with a bottle of sriracha on it (she first tried it age seven with some tofu nuggets I was experimenting with). Meanwhile, Yogi is becoming more open-minded; six to 12 months ago, she’d sometimes burst into tears if I put something new on the table. Now she eats most things, but I tend to have a backup – like fried eggs or bread and cheese.

Falafel is one of our go-to meals – I always keep some ready-made in the freezer. Everyone customises their own – with gherkins, pickled beetroot and chillies, hummus, cucumber, cherry tomatoes, grated carrot, mayonnaise, sriracha, cabbage, tahini and even mango chutney – which they find empowering. Egg fried rice was one of the first things we ate together and remains a favourite. We all love katsu curry, most dals, paneer in any form, and tofu, either in nuggets, or in a homespun poke bowl or, surprisingly, the silken kind with rice and a sweet and salty sesame sauce.

I’ve always found it works to introduce something new alongside something familiar. When I first made them my sticky mango and lime paneer naans, I explained they both loved all its ingredients – paneer, mango, naan. I’ve introduced spices gradually, too, making mild versions and then adding a quarter of a teaspoon more each time I make it.

I was labelled a fussy eater as a child, but I think I just had incredibly sensitive taste buds. We underestimate how differently kids experience flavour; a cumin seed can seem explosively bitter, and something like kimchi can be overwhelming. The biggest lesson for me has been not to label children. If you keep calling them fussy, they start believing that’s who they are. I used to tell Arya, “Just try one cherry tomato every year and see what happens.” The other day, she ate not one, but three.

Meera Sodha is a cook, author of four cookbooks and Guardian Feast columnist.

I’ve got two very different children, in temperament and in the way they eat. I’ve realised over time that the best way to tackle it is to find different ways to prepare the same thing.

Sam says he hates roast chicken, but what he actually doesn’t like is the fatty, “slimy” skin. If I slice up the breast and wrap it in a flour tortilla, he’s delighted. Jude, meanwhile, wants the chicken leg, skin and all. The same goes for broccoli. Sam likes it crisp and crunchy; Jude likes it cooked a minute longer until it’s soft. Once I started asking why they didn’t like something, instead of writing it off, feeding them became much easier.

They’ve always loved tuna macaroni, which I originally made with lots of sweetcorn. Over time, I’ve slowly built in more flavours – I’ll cook down onions, carrots and celery into a really delicious base, then grate in courgette until it melts away like butter, or finely slice green beans so they disappear into noodles. I’m wary of hiding vegetables, though. I tell them what’s in there because I don’t want food to become a trick. I’d rather they thought, “Actually, grated courgette is what makes this taste so good.”

When the boys were little, I couldn’t work out why they devoured my mum’s congee and omelettes but barely touched mine. Mum laughed and said, “Salt and sugar”, each of which she adds a pinch of when she cooks. As a new mother I was so focused on doing everything “right”, whereas she was focused on making it delicious.

They love chilli con carne and poke bowls. For the poke, I briefly marinate cubed salmon in mayo, soy, maple syrup, lemon and, more recently, wasabi. Grill it for two minutes and then put that on top of a rice bowl with edamame, corn and, if I’m feeling fancy, a pineapple and mango salsa. We also love ants climbing a tree, a Sichuan Chinese dish with glass noodles and minced pork.

Sometimes I think we put too much pressure on ourselves to produce the perfect balanced plate. The other night I was rushing out and just put prosciutto, halloumi, avocado and cucumber on the table. Sam texted me afterwards saying, “More of this, please.” It made me realise that a meal doesn’t have to look worthy to be balanced.

Helen Goh is a pastry chef and the author of Baking and the Meaning of Life. She co-writes the Sweet Spot column in Guardian Feast.

My eldest, Dylan, is 10 now and a brilliant eater, but it took a long time to get here. He always liked fruit and raw vegetables, which reassured me, but meals with sauces or lots of mixed flavours just weren’t his thing.

The big shift came when he was about six or seven and became obsessed with ninjas. All the stories featured ramen shops, gyoza and bowls of noodles, and I realised that food had become part of his imagination. We started making ramen at home, recreating the little trays of udon, vegetables and tofu he’d seen. Once Japanese food felt familiar through stories, it gave him the confidence to try other flavours, too.

Our younger son, Esca, is three, and he’s in his buttered toast and plain pasta era. We offer him a little of whatever we’re eating every night and most evenings he ignores it. I’ve tried not making alternatives, but I spend my life cooking to nourish people. I can’t send my child to bed hungry!

Having two boys at such different ages has made me much more relaxed. I know tastes change because I’ve watched it happen. In the meantime, I look for small wins. Smoothies packed with yoghurt, nut butter and seeds frozen into ice lollies have been a life-saver this summer. I think about protein in small ways, too, adding extra eggs and ground almonds to pancakes.

More than anything, I think children need ownership. Dylan loves tasting recipes I’ve been working on and giving me a verdict, but he’s just as inspired by seeing other children cook. He loves the Buddy Oliver and What’s Cooking Omari? shows on TV, and has been enjoying some of my old childhood recipe books – vintage Jane Asher and Jenny Chandler. It’s become a genuine interest.

Anna Jones is an award-winning food writer, author of four books about vegetarian home cooking.

This is a very long way from authentic ramen and is something I make with staple ingredients that my kids like to eat.

I cook the noodles separately as I find cooking them in the broth does not work. If you are using ready-to-cook noodles you can pop them straight in, though. I often use coconut aminos instead of soy sauce here as it adds umami with less salt; you can buy it from most supermarkets. I use a range of green veg, whatever I have to hand: broccoli, peas, edamame and sugar snaps all seem to go down well. I get extra points if I roast the broccoli.

For the quick broth A couple of coins of ginger A bunch of spring onions 1-2 tbsp white miso 1-2 tbsp veg stock powder 1 tsp soy sauce or coconut aminos 200g pack of udon noodles (you can also use ramen noodles or the straight-to-wok, ready-to-eat kind)

For the tofu Oil 400g block of firm tofu, chopped 2 tbsp sesame seeds 1 tbsp maple syrup 1 tbsp soy sauce or coconut aminos 4 big handfuls of green veg (broccoli, greens, sugar snaps, peas, edamame)

Put the ginger and the green tops of the spring onions into a deep pan and add a litre of cold water and bring to boil and simmer for a few minutes. Finely slice the white part of the spring onions.

In a separate pan, cook your noodles in boiling water according to packet instructions then drain and run under cold water. If any of your veg needs cooking (broccoli, frozen peas etc) you can add it for the relevant number of minutes with the noodles. Then drain and cool the lot.

Put a frying pan on the heat, add a little oil and the chopped tofu, and cook for a few minutes until it’s crisp and golden on all edges. Add the sesame seeds and cook for another few minutes until the seeds are toasted, turn off the heat and add the tablespoon of soy or coconut aminos and the tablespoon of maple syrup, and toss in the pan to coat.

Put the noodles into the bottom of four bowls, with enough room for your veg, tofu and broth. Put the broth into a jug and the tofu, vegetables and toppings into little bowls on the table so everyone can help themselves – little ones may need help with the warm broth. Slurp.

Weaning was such fun because Marcie ate everything. I probably drove myself mad trying to expose her to as much variety as possible. She’d be having adventurous home-cooked food while we were eating takeaway. Then she started nursery and the fussiness crept in.

I’ve never put pressure on what she has to eat. We decide what goes on the table, but once it’s there it’s up to her. If we give her agency, she’s more likely to try things. We’re quite strict about not making alternatives, though we always make sure there’s something she’ll enjoy. Usually that’s fruit.

I don’t like creating hierarchies around food. I don’t want food to become about rewards and punishments. I’m also not a fan of hiding vegetables. If she doesn’t know she’s eating something, she won’t know it’s something that she likes.

Family dinner isn’t always relaxing. But we still eat together almost every night because it’s an important pause in the day. Our classic meal is a slow‑cooked tomato sauce with lots of garlic, paprika and a little bit of sugar – that can go on pasta but I’ll often serve it with prawns. She’ll also eat tofu in any form – loves the stuff – and corn on the cob, crispy kale and any fish that isn’t breaded, which I serve with homemade chips. We get her involved, too – setting the table or perhaps rolling her own roti, if that’s what we’re having. I think children respond well when you don’t infantilise them. They’ll often surprise you.

Marie Mitchell is a cook and the author of the award‑winning Caribbean cookbook, Kin.

People are always telling me what a good eater Donnie is, but he’s only two and a half, so I know that could all change. I was such a fussy eater as a child – eating Indian food at home was non-negotiable, but I’d eat chips and a KitKat at school for lunch every day. Then I snapped out of it; when you learn about food and try some of the best produce, you can’t not love it. That’s what I’m trying to do for Donnie.

When we started weaning, I bought baby food pouches, probably out of fear of getting it wrong. Then I remember looking at them in the supermarket and thinking, “Hang on, I know how to cook.” So I started giving him bits of whatever we were eating – a lamb chop, a piece of salmon, a spoonful of rice. I’ve never really skimped on seasoning, either. He grew up eating cumin, coriander and proper home cooking; it’s only chilli he isn’t keen on.

We don’t make separate meals or “healthy” snacks. If we’re eating steak and chips, beef shin ragu or rotis, that’s what he’ll have. If we’re at the restaurant, I’ll let him have ice-cream or chocolate cake. I’ve tried not to frame sugar as a treat because I think that’s where things went wrong for me. Donnie knows he’s allowed it, so he doesn’t pine for it.

Of course, there are days when he barely touches a vegetable, and then the next he’ll eat a bowl of prawns or happily munch asparagus. I don’t fixate on it. The important thing is that food is around, we eat together, and he sees us enjoying it, too. That’s how I learned to love food, and I hope it’ll be the same for him.

Ravneet Gill is a pastry chef, food broadcaster and co‑owner of Gina restaurant in Chingford, London E4.

The difficulty with feeding four children is that there aren’t many points on the Venn diagram where all of their likes overlap. Just when you discover something they all eat, one of them decides they no longer like it. There are a few constants, though. A good ragu bolognese can usually carry the week. I’ll make a huge batch, then serve it with pasta one night, folded into tacos the next, over rice after that. I’m forever making chicken stock, too. Pasta is cooked in it, rice is cooked in it. It’s the easiest way I know to smuggle a bit of vitality into food in a form they find irresistible.

Beyond that, feeding children is much less a culinary challenge than a psychological one. They each cultivate their own impossible preferences. Breakfast is a perfect example: two insist on thick American-style pancakes, the other two will only eat crepes. I make one batter, then dilute half of it.

I used to take it personally. Eventually I realised that refusing food is one of the few forms of power children have. In a family where cooking matters, they understand that saying “Mum’s a better cook than you” lands exactly where it hurts.

I grew up surrounded by wonderful cooks and didn’t appreciate any of it because it was all I knew. That’s the great misfortune of childhood: you don’t value your parents’ cooking until you’re deprived of it. So I try not to take the ingratitude too seriously; it’s almost a happy inheritance.

Jackson Boxer is chef/owner of Brunswick House, Vesper and Dove, all in London, and culinary director of Cowley Manor near Cheltenham and Henri in London.

I don’t think of my kids as fussy eaters – but that wasn’t always the case. With my eldest, Aurelie, I took every rejection personally. I’d put something in front of her that she’d happily eaten a fortnight earlier and suddenly she’d refuse it. By the time Edwyn came along, I knew that if you keep exposing them to things, they often come back around. Pickiness is almost always a phase.

Being a food writer probably made it harder. I was trying to apply everything I know about making food exciting, when children often want the opposite: simple things. I’ll spend hours making something complex, only for them to reject it in favour of buttered pasta. I’ve had to separate my ego from what they’re asking for.

We’ve learned what meals work for us. They love slow-cooked food: chicken noodle soup, braised beef shin, lamb, pasta cooked in chicken stock, smoked fish chowder with sweetcorn, dal with spinach and cauliflower chopped up small. I usually try to introduce new things alongside foods they know, say aubergine or mushrooms with chicken and roast potatoes. We ask them to try it, applaud them for doing so, and offer it again another day if they don’t like it. If I’m introducing a new rice or pasta dish, I will usually hold back a couple of plain portions, to serve with butter or olive oil. The backup plan is always carbs and fat! Sometimes on holiday they’ll try something from my plate in a restaurant because it feels like a privilege rather than an obligation.

My expectations were too high in the beginning. Now I know it’s the pattern over weeks and months that counts. If all else fails, there’s always Greek yoghurt with fruit after dinner – and a glass of milk before bed.

Rosie Birkett is a food writer and cookbook author. She has a weekly Substack newsletter, A Lot on Her Plate.

I’ve been thinking a lot about the meals my kids grew up on recently – I’m working on a project about family food. The three of them always seemed to be eating, so I took the approach that if they didn’t eat one meal they weren’t going to starve.

We mostly gave them what we were eating. They loved pasta, roast chicken, brown rice, stir‑fries with broccoli, chard and Chinese vegetables, which they were used to because in those days we lived near Chinatown. We’d make rice balls, frittatas full of vegetables, tortellini with spinach, roast pumpkin. Apart from giving them the odd chicken bone to suck on, I kept them vegetarian until they were about two because I wanted to encourage a love of vegetables and for them to eat widely. It mostly worked, although none of them ever really took to fennel!

But they weren’t angels about food. Green vegetables were usually tricky, although they always loved peas. There was plenty of tomato pasta – I often say they were virtually made of the stuff – and we gave them fish fingers, too, which I’m rather against now, given the state of the oceans. I also used to make them “crusties”, just like my mum made for me. When our brown loaves were a few days old, I’d slice them thinly, spread them with butter and honey or Marmite, then pop them in a low oven until crisp. Perfect for packed lunches, and intriguing to the other kids.

The important thing was that food was always enjoyable. They grew up in restaurants – as babies they’d sleep under the tables, or join us in high chairs. Ours was a social house, people always coming for lunch or supper, so they were in an environment where food was a joyous, social thing. I don’t underestimate the power of that.

I once had a business making rice balls, and when I became a mum they became a go-to snack for my kids.

220g short-grain brown rice 500ml water 100g pumpkin, chopped up into 2cm pieces 1 tbsp wholemeal flour (optional) 2 tbsp sunflower seeds 2 tbsp sesame seeds ¼ cup flat parsley, roughly chopped ¼ cup coriander, leaves roughly chopped, stalks finely chopped 2 bunches of spring onions, finely chopped A pinch sea salt 1 tbsp soy sauce or tamari 1.5 litres of plain oil (rapeseed or sunflower)

Wash the rice several times until the water runs clear, cover in water and leave to soak for 30 minutes. Drain. You will need a saucepan big enough to hold the rice and water, with a tight-fitting lid. To this, add the rice, water and salt, and cover with the lid.

Place the pot over a high heat and bring to the boil; when you see steam coming out the side or hear the pan bubbling, turn the heat right down to very low and then cook for 45 minutes. Don’t take the lid off. Set aside for at least 15 minutes.

While the rice is cooking, prepare the other ingredients. The rice should have absorbed all the water and come together into a lovely sticky consistency. You should be able to squish it flat easily.

Once the rice has cooled down, mix in the rest of the ingredients with the exception of the oil. It should be a good sticky consistency and come together when squeezed. You can add the flour to help with the binding if needed. Roll into ping‑pong-sized balls.

In another deep pan, heat the oil to 180C. Drop the balls in and fry for three to five minutes, until golden brown. Once cooked, place on a plate lined with kitchen paper. Cook in batches so the oil temperature doesn’t drop too low.

There you have it! They can be eaten hot or cold. A minty yoghurt dip would be nice alongside.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Blind date: ‘He said: “If heaven is real, you’ll definitely be going there”, which might be the nicest thing anyone’s ever said to me’
