Nelson, 41, who works in legal services, meets Louise, 37, who works in marketing

First impressions? Louise is such a sweet, sincere person. With very interesting hobbies!

What did you talk about? All sorts of funny things, from feeding monkeys to the worst theatre shows and wooden toys.

Most awkward moment? When we met, I wanted to greet her with a friendly hug but she was seated and had to get up.

Best thing about Louise? She will laugh and think I’m taking the mick but I’m not: her dedication to the things she loves. So admirable! Passion and commitment. It’s infectious.

Blind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the UK) and online at theguardian.com every Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you can read all about how we put it together here.What questions will I be asked?We ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.

Can I choose who I match with?No, it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely to be.

Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.

How should I answer?Honestly but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.

Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.

Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.

Describe Louise in three words Energetic, passionate, excellent conversationalist (four I know!).

If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be? I wouldn’t change a thing! It was a very pleasant date overall.

What were you hoping for? Fun conversation with an interesting person and to discover a new restaurant.

First impressions? A gentleman, very polite, laughs very loudly (in a good way).

What did you talk about? London zoo volunteering – a typical day. Nelson growing up in Singapore. Covid – how I was in Singapore and Bali just as it started kicking off. Theatre shows we’ve been to – how perfect Oliver! is (this was mainly me). How we both go and see all the Oscar-nominated films every awards season. Nelson’s new startup.

Most awkward moment? The waitress thought a photographer would be joining us and we needed a table for three.

Good table manners? I was more conscious of my own, as I ate the tacos with my hands while he used cutlery.

Best thing about Nelson? He’s a very interesting and interested person – so many hobbies and passions. I liked that he shared my enthusiasm for all things cultural.

Would you introduce Nelson to your friends? Can’t think why not, he’s very interesting and sweet!

What do you think Nelson made of you? He said: “If heaven is real, you’ll definitely be going there”, which might just be the nicest thing anyone’s ever said to me. He also laughed very heartily all the way through so hopefully he thought I was funny.

Did you go on somewhere? No, but we were the last to leave on a Tuesday night, so pretty good going.

If you could change one thing about the evening, what would it be? The pineapple/lime/cinnamon ice-cream was incredible, we should’ve got one each.

Would you meet again? I think as friends – maybe at the cinema as Oscar season is approaching!

Nelson and Louise ate at Mirtala, London W4. Fancy a blind date? Email blind.date@theguardian.com

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: Yaga: chicken bones? Saltburn parties? This folk horror is so debauched, it’s hilarious
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Rhik Samadder
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams and Carrie-Anne Moss star in this audacious mystery about a Slavic witch. There’s supernatural weirdness, detective work … and a hero who looks a lot like Tim Key dressed in leather

Halloween was once a simpler time, when neighbourhood kids would dress up as mythical serial killers, the undead or bedsheet-wearing ghosts. At some point, following America’s lead, it became sexy and cat-forward. It has now become a sort of conceptual art show. I’ve heard people this year planning to go to parties dressed as Erling Haaland, Prom Carrie (Prime Video edition) and Bad Bunny’s half-time Super Bowl show. It’s horrifying.

The perception of witches has evolved, too. Once understood to be a malignant version of the crone archetype, sympathy for witches has grown. They have been embraced as a feminist image of the older woman, free of patriarchal command and possessed of a powerful rage. In recent years, Maleficent, Elphaba from Wicked and Marvel’s Scarlet Witch have given witches a pop edge. Some of my most intense friends proudly wear slogan T-shirts proclaiming themselves descended from the witches whom society failed to burn.

Now, in swoops Yaga (Sat, 9pm, Sky Atlantic), a quasi-horror mystery series from Canadian streamer Crave. They are known for making Heated Rivalry (matching oversized jerseys? Huge Halloween outfit this year). Yaga is another genre-bender. It opens with a cocky detective, Charlie Rapp, arriving in the quiet fishing town of Whittock, present day. He’s investigating the disappearance of Henry Park, son of a wealthy local family. As the case grows violent, it brings evidence of cult activity to light, and increasingly hints at the existence of a dark, supernatural figure behind events.

To those unfamiliar with Slavic folklore, Baba Yaga is a forest-dwelling hag who lives in a hut on chicken’s feet, flies around in a pestle and mortar, and eats children. It is her voice that bookends every episode in a taunting monologue, though her exact involvement with Henry’s disappearance is a grisly little puzzle. I’m a few episodes in, and it’s still unclear if she is a literal character in the play or the embodiment of its theme: women being sick of men’s shit.

The men are certainly a rum bunch. Charlie Rapp is our hero – yet his credentials are questionable, and he flirts with every woman in town, including his police partner Carson. Henry Park – played by Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams – is vain, adulterous and given to druggy parties. Williams also plays Henry’s slippery roommate Logan. The show has fun with the unlikely physical resemblance between them, as when Logan answers the door to the surprised detectives. “I have brown eyes and glasses,” he explains with a straight face. He’s also naked under his overalls, FYI.

The women are formidable, including Clark Backo’s drily unimpressed take on police detective Carson. She’s introduced as a fan of romantasy (or what her superior officer describes as “fairy smut”). Carson is unenthusiastic about pursuing the case of the missing rich kid. “Billionaires aren’t real people,” she shrugs. Even more no-nonsense is Carrie-Anne Moss as an older, morally ambiguous osteo-academic. When Charlie sits beside her at a bar and asks what excites her, she replies: “Sex. And bones.”

Given the bones, and the overalls, you may be thinking: “Stuff the spooky business, are there hella sexy shenanigans?” Yes and no … The theme of Henry’s parties, which take place Gatsby-like in his absence, is Dark Solstice. Expect masked ball eroticism, fetish wear and debauchery and, elsewhere, an erotic encounter that had me laughing at the audacity. But it’s never wholesome fun. There are chicken bones in unexpected places, and Rapp in particular is haunted by horror imagery. While sex is on the menu, the male gaze is under the microscope.

Playwright-creator Kat Sandler has, so far, found room on the broom to make Yaga pointed but playful, and fun while tackling the darkest of subject matter. There are Ukrainian covers of pop songs, a hero who looks like a leather-trouser version of Tim Key, and Saltburn-esque parties. But what I really want, whisper it, is for an actual witch to appear, rather than the political idea of one. I’m basic, and like pointy hats. Will this be another Blair Witch situation? How far will the witch-tease go? I’m crossing my fingers and burying the hair of a bat.

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: The Guide #267: Robert Pattinson embraced his inner low life and became one of the best actors of his era
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Gwilym Mumford
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
In this week’s newsletter: Sandra Hüller and Anne Hathaway might have been in more films this year – but Pattinson’s remarkable run confirms him as one of the best performers of his generation

For prolific actors, 2026 has been a banner year. The roles have kept piling up for a small cohort of stars, the roles have kept piling up, to the point where you wonder how they found the time to do vital things like sleep, shower or scarf down nuclear-fallout-covered chicken wings on YouTube interview shows.

Just look at Sandra Hüller, who by the time December ends will have racked up six projects in 2026, ranging from austere cold war road-trip movies to migraine-inducing Marvel blockbusters. Anne Hathaway, meanwhile, has since January appeared as – deep breath – a psychologically tormented fading pop star, a catatonic popular novelist, a suburbanite fending off hungry dinosaurs, an Ithacan queen fending off hungry suitors and reluctant fashion journo Andy in the belated Devil Wears Prada sequel. (Hathaway did also have time to go on the nuclear chicken wings show, but was unable to partake, due to being heavily pregnant.)

Robert Pattinson’s 2026 output looks almost leisurely compared to Hüller and Hathaway’s, though by normal standards the four films that he will have starred in by the end of year is an impressive haul. More impressive still is the quality of work, a remarkable run of roles that cements his status as one of the best performers of his era. And most certainly the best player of lowlifes: his 2026 has been a true rogues’ gallery, with every shade of scumbag accounted for.

This malcontent tendency is magnificently on display in Primetime, in UK and Irish cinemas now. Directed by Lance Oppenheim – film-maker wunderkind also behind the much-talked-about You Can See Everything – this clammy, queasy drama recalls the heyday (and ultimate demise) of To Catch a Predator, the US network reality show notorious for its stings on putative paedophiles. Pattinson plays the show’s preening host Chris Hansen, famous for his habit of sidling into the middle of an operation and casually confronting his target. Hansen’s slick, nightly news exterior disguises a grubby desire to bend the show’s ethics to breaking point, his motivations complicated by a trauma-inducing incident early in his career, and Pattinson does a great job at showing glimpses of the frayed, angry, fearful figure behind the squeaky-clean veneer. (Hansen, it should be noted, has declared the film “a completely made-up work of fiction” and “an insult to the thousands of men and women who work hard every day to protect children from predators”.)

Before Primetime came The Odyssey, and another oleaginous figure for Pattinson to ooze into. His alpha-suitor Antinous was, by design, a more two-dimensional character than Hansen; a crawling, craven antagonist primarily present for audiences to bristle at and Odysseus to dispatch with extreme prejudice. Still, Pattinson nails the assignment, with a performance that some critics saw as “stealing the show” – some achievement in a gargantuan three-hour epic featuring giants, men transforming into pigs and the like.

Compared to the lowlifes of Primetime and the Odyssey, Pattinson’s character in gleefully black comedy The Drama is positively well adjusted. Indeed, initially gentle art historian Charlie is the recipient of no little sympathy in the early stages of the movie, having been broadsided by a horrifying detail – which, six months after the film’s release, I’m still wary of revealing – from the past of his bride to be (played by Zendaya, another prolific 2026 star, and one who now shares three films with Pattinson). But as Charlie unravels, his cracked decision-making and general brittleness becomes deeply unlikeable. By the day of the wedding itself, you’re half-rooting him to fail miserably – a remarkable turnaround, and testament to Pattinson’s gift for unlikability.

There is of course one more performance to come this year and it’s a big onein Dune: Part Three. Pattinson plays Scytale, a shape-shifting manipulator set on usurping Timothée Chalamet’s space-messiah Paul Atreides. Another antagonist then – though Atreides’ slide into antihero-dom at the end of the previous Dune might complicate things. Still, with his dead eyes and general air of quiet menace in the film’s trailers, it’s hard to imagine Pattinson’s character will be handing out cupcakes and kittens.

But what is it that makes Pattinson so adept at playing sleazeballs? Certainly his playing against type, a former Twilight heart-throb gone to seed, seems effective. It helps too that he picks roles better than just about anyone, often working with auteurs who seem to understand his magnetic/repellent duality. It’s a shame that this sort of role tends to get sidelined for worthier, more outwardly heroic parts when it comes to awards season: no one seems to be including Pattinson in their Oscar best actor prognostications.

Perhaps that suits him fine – his choice of role hardly seems to be an impediment at the box office. The Odyssey is one of the highest-grossing films of the year, Dune: Part Three will probably join that bracket when it arrives in December, and both The Drama and Primetime have massively punched above their indie-film weight. And if you have had enough of him on the dark side, next year he reprises his role as the Dark Knight in the second of the latest Batman films. In the meantime, though, if you want a wrong’un played right, just call for R-Patz.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: ‘Apologies for any confusion!’: how to write the perfect passive-aggressive email
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Emma Beddington
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
In a survey, ‘just to be clear’ came out as the most loathed phrase. But I think I can do better

A new contender for the most passive-aggressive email phrase has emerged. “Just to be clear” was chosen by 52% of desk jockeys in a survey by email verification company ZeroBounce, closely followed by the perennial pass-ag fave, “per my last email” (40%), which tied with the identical-in-intent “as previously discussed”. Further down the list came “for future reference” and “kindly note”.

If you ask me, these all verge on actual aggressive. Imagine saying “just to be clear” out loud to another person: that’s a conversational poke in the ribs, isn’t it? It’s the kind of thing you unleash 10 minutes into an ill-tempered wrangle with your home insurance company about inflated renewal premiums. “Kindly note” is even worse – it’s a phrase from an angry message on the office kitchen wall about microwave abuse.

No, we can do better than that, or at least I – a person whose own spouse frequently describes her as unpleasantly passive-aggressive – can. Let me explain: an exchange of professional passive-aggressive emails is a ritual as intricately coded as a Belle Epoque duel and it demands the appearance of great politeness. Your message needs to read, on its surface, as exquisitely helpful and friendly, while leaving every cc and bcc on the thread in no doubt as to it what it really is: an epistolary shanking.

A good pass-agg email starts with a simulacrum of warmth and gratitude. I can usually generate the appearance of warmth by harnessing the dizzying rush of anger generated by whatever stupid message has prompted me to press “reply all”. “Hi X!” I usually start perkily, then I pause to hold up both middle fingers to the screen. Next comes gratitude: “Great to hear from you,” (it wasn’t) “and thank you so much for your message”. Thanks, that is, for giving me a chance to show everyone you’re out of line. I say “everyone”, because I like to deploy a cc on this kind of email.

I follow this Trojan Shetland pony of an intro with a selection of my preferred zingers:

I understood perfectly. I am correct. I am sorry for nothing. The question mark is a mere disingenuous flourish.

The import of this little phrase is clear: I have kept the receipts and I want you to know that. This email will be followed near-instantaneously by a second email, forwarding the evidence that I am right. The body of that second email will just read “FYI”, which is passive-aggressive for “checkmate, loser”.

It, and I, was entirely clear. I am only sorry you are a dolt. Some pass-ag practitioners drop in a bland, smiling emoji here, but I am a purist.

I hope this leaves you seething with the same fury your message inspired in me.

By saying I don’t expect you to respond it will make you look petty when you do; it also subtly implies you’ve already gone home. Your move.

Still, as much as I get satisfaction from the perfect turn of passive-aggressive phrase, I always realise later that it’s a hollow pleasure. What am I doing fighting, albeit with elegant restraint, a fellow worker when the real enemy is capitalism? Why are we emailing at all when we could be contemplating the beauty of a sunset, shoulder to shoulder? For future reference: I think we’d all be happier taking a deep breath, pressing backspace, and walking away.

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: From This City Is Ours to Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour: the week in rave reviews
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
The most fractious family in organised crime return while the US rapper embarks upon a series of benefit shows with some A-list guests. Here’s the pick of the week’s culture, taken from the Guardian’s best-rated reviews

Summed up in a sentence Four people share their shocking testimonies of what happened when the dictator gave Asians 90 days to leave Uganda.

What our reviewer said “There is a happy ending, of sorts. Bharti, Paresh, Harminder and Maz never stopped missing the country they were born in, but they made a new home in Britain, and they made Britain better: it would be hard, for example, to calculate the size of the debt we owe Bharti for her 40 years as a social worker safeguarding children in care. Every minute of Escaping Idi Amin contains an urgent lesson to learn.” Jack Seale

Summed up in a sentence James Nelson-Joyce returns in this terrifically acted, high-stakes crime drama in Liverpool – and it’s as lovable as it is bloody.

What our reviewer said “We can expect more of the following: convoluted drug deals conducted over congealing ragu; shouting; tiny-skulled henchmen with chests of astonishing bulbosity, as if someone had squeezed their legs like tubes of toothpaste and all the meat had been forced up to their armpits; beards.” Sarah Dempster

Summed up in a sentence The star’s friends and family celebrate his life – and give respectful insight into his troubles as well as his career triumphs.

What our reviewer said “It remains at heart a simple, sad story. But this unexpectedly candid, thoughtful, genuinely intimate film gives it nuance and depth, and a voice to wider sorrows – including what a shame it was that Perry could not enjoy his talent or appreciate the joy it gave as fully as his audiences always did.” Lucy Mangan

Further reading The hidden life of Matthew Perry: ‘He would say: I need to stop and get help’

Summed up in a sentence The French super-thief returns for a fourth series; the budget is bigger, the stakes are higher and there are lots of Houdini-style twists and thrills to be had.

What our reviewer said “Omar Sy, whose performance is magnetic as always, has graduated to co-showrunner and wants to lean harder into the show’s “superhero”-like qualities. These include tech and set pieces which undoubtedly add a sprinkling of Marvel.” Micha Frazer-Carroll

Further reading Lupin’s Omar Sy: ‘We wanted to show what the French are capable of’

Summed up in a sentence Disquieting drama with Léa Seydoux as a wife and mother whose life unravels when police arrive to investigate her husband.

What our reviewer said “This is a bleak, pessimistic film with two excellent lead performances.” Peter Bradshaw

Summed up in a sentence Supercool outlaw women go shoplifting in Boots Riley’s frantic caper in which Demi Moore’s haute-couture maven attracts the attention of a gang of Robin Hood style clothes robbers.

What our reviewer said “An entertaining, if very exhausting fantasy-caper about the fashion biz, a madcap mile-a-minute melee of unadulterated ker-aziness. You might need a couple of ibuprofen and a lie down afterwards.” Peter Bradshaw

Further reading Boots Riley: ‘Theft is not outside of capitalism, it’s what it was built on’

Summed up in a sentence Intriguing folk-horror romance with Olivia Colman as a depressed and bullied fisher who gets the answer to her dreams: an Alexander Skarsgård made of wicker.

What our reviewer said “It occupies a strange and intriguing Venn-diagram overlap between macabre horror and sentimentality. Yet devotees of bucolic British screen-scariness will note that it is, after all, about a wicker man.” Peter Bradshaw

Further reading ‘I saw the script and went: oooh!’ Olivia Colman and Alexander Skårsgard on their steamy folk-horror movie Wicker

Summed up in a sentence Backstory of modest music industry veteran Asher who started out as one half of pop duo Peter and Gordon, and went on to produce acts such as James Taylor and Linda Ronstadt.

What our reviewer said “Asher by any standards carved an amazing path through it all, making the absolute most of being in the right place at the right time.” Andrew Pulver

Summed up in a sentence Ken Russell’s 1971 possessed-nuns tale stars Oliver Reed and Vanessa Redgrave giving the performances of their lives in a film that highlights the violence of power.

What our reviewer said “It comes from an era when movies, playing in high-street cinemas, still had the power to shock, to position that shock in the polite cultural mainstream and to compel serious discussion about whether that shock – or, conversely, a ban – was justified.” Peter Bradshaw

Summed up in a sentence The extraordinary posthumous memoir of a Dutch poet.

What our reviewer said “Marsman’s language is so beautiful, and her textual references so original: she cites Leopardi, Pasolini, Alanis Morissette, Robert Musil, Spinoza, Euripides, Wittgenstein and William James.”

Summed up in a sentence The poet laureate takes on the ancient Mesopotamian epic about the adventures of a demigod king.

What our reviewer said “Armitage’s tactile, visceral version is a tour de force, combining careful scholarship with poetic verve and deft linguistic meldings.”

Summed up in a sentence Long thought untranslatable, a portrait of a breakdown by the man Karl Ove Knausgård considers Norway’s best living writer.

What our reviewer said “This is a universal story of modernity and its discontents, but Lund is at pains to give it a specifically Norwegian dimension.”

Summed up in a sentence The definitive biography of Seinfeld creator Larry David.

What our reviewer said “In 1992, just before it became the biggest show in America, he told friends, ‘Honestly, I would rather spend a year in prison than do another season of Seinfeld. It would be peaceful. Nobody would make me write anything.’ He was only half joking.”

Summed up in a sentence The former Scottish first minister on his family’s Gaza ordeal.

What our reviewer said “Under Fire is most powerful when Yousaf gives full vent to his anger at the unfolding genocide in Gaza and articulates not just the plight of his in-laws, but the barbarity of Israel’s actions.”

Summed up in a sentence This follow-up to the cult horror-satire Bunny has been shortlisted for the Wodehouse prize for comic fiction.

What our reviewer said “Awad is here to show us that romantasy can be serious literature, and nothing can really be too camp.”

Summed up in a sentence Collecting traditional songs of female struggle and strength, the Irish singer invests them with staggering power.

What our reviewer said “John ‘Spud’ Murphy’s production brilliantly brings out earthy, granular details, from the sucking-in of air through Peat’s concertina bellows on Cailín Deas to the disruptive thwack of Eleanor Myler’s drums.” Jude Rogers

Summed up in a sentence The US artist takes a newly compact approach to her craft, and trades technical composition methods for pure emotion on another sombre masterpiece.

What our reviewer said “The heavy opening notes of Map the Path are solemn yet startlingly direct for Malone, feeling for the first time as if she’s lifting her fingers from the keys and shaking the listener by the shoulders.” Laura Snapes

Summed up in a sentence The German pianist performs these works by Beethoven and Schoenberg – linked by Napoleon – with his characteristic exquisite touch, in interpretations full of poetry.

What our reviewer said “Levit rightly sees Liszt’s piano realisation as a masterwork in and of itself and his dramatic interpretation is full of poetry, often surprisingly gentle, and with breathtaking pianissimos … In a time of bullies and despots, this is essential listening.” Clive Paget

Summed up in a sentence After frontperson Juliette Jackson lost half her hearing, she wrote sad songs and felt frustrated. So she pivoted, writing herself a happy ending. The results are joyfully convincing.

What our reviewer said “The album’s sense of finding joy in sometimes difficult circumstances crystallises on the wonderfully titled You Remind Me That I’m Dying (And That It’s Good to Be Alive), those words providing what may well be this year’s most bittersweet euphoric chorus.” Dave Simpson

Summed up in a sentence Several unannounced guests feature on the first European date of the rapper’s sold-out benefit tour, including video messages from Mark Ruffalo and Cynthia Nixon.

What our reviewer said “There’s something very striking about the fact that the local artists who’ve heeded Macklemore’s call to help out are evidently committed to the cause behind it: you never get a sense of anyone rocking up in order to grab brownie points or reflected glory.” Alexis Petridis

Further reading If you really hate it when music and film stars do politics, here’s the answer: give us politics that works

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Tim Dowling: having a tortoise reminds you that life is long
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Tim Dowling
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
My wife got ours when she was eight, and he came to live with us soon after we got married. I don’t remember anything about that in the vows

It is the first truly bleak day of autumn – the sky is a deep grey and a steady drizzle is falling. Sitting in the unflattering light of a kitchen downlight and looking out the window, I think: this is it now, until spring.

Except it isn’t, quite, as a few hours later the cloud begins to break up and a shaft of watery sunlight reaches the brick step just outside my office shed. When I open the door to let in the warm afternoon air, I find the tortoise sitting there.

There aren’t many pets that allow you to forget their existence for any length of time. The cat reminds me that I have a cat twice a day. The dog will not let me forget I have a dog for half an hour. But it has been at least a week since it even occurred to me that I have a tortoise.

“All good?” I say. The tortoise winds its neck anticlockwise, so it can fix me with its right eye.

Certain experiences – raising children, say, or stepping into the path of a bus – remind you that life is short. But many other experiences remind you that it’s long – mostly things breaking, and then breaking again. I have measured out my life in dual-function push-button kitchen tap spray head replacements – they last, on average, about three years, and according to my order history, I’m on my fourth one.

Having a tortoise is definitely the latter sort of experience. My wife got ours when she was eight years old. At some point he escaped for a whole year, was found, went to live on a farm for 20 more years and then, when the farm was sold, was suddenly returned to us. By that point we’d been married for six years. There had been nothing about a tortoise in our wedding vows.

That was almost 30 years ago. Since then, the tortoise has outlived two dogs and three cats. Over the decades, I’ve spent countless hours searching the garden beds for him after dark. I’ve discovered him on his back and set him right about a dozen times. He’s bitten me at least as often. On occasion, when he was in a dormant period of reduced metabolic activity, I used him to prop open the kitchen door. And there were many years when I had to fish him out from the gap under the washing machine to tell him that spring was here.

I consult a weather app. “You know what?” I say. “I think it’s about that time.” According to the forecast, the tortoise could spend another night outside, but I will not find him this easily again.

I pick him up and carry him into the kitchen. He looks miserable, but that’s really his only look. I open the fridge, peel off a lettuce leaf and set it down in front of him. He sniffs it and then looks away disdainfully. When I check again an hour later, both the tortoise and the lettuce are in the same spot. An hour after that, both have disappeared.

That evening, a friend’s grown son drops by. As he looks around, I can see it dawn on him that he hasn’t been in our house since he was a child. In fact, the last time he was in our house, we lived somewhere else.

“Yeah, look, he’s right there,” I say, pointing to the spot next to the dog’s bed where the tortoise sits, legs and head withdrawn.

The dog comes running into the kitchen, to remind everyone that there is a dog in the house. The cat, a coward, hides somewhere until all non-family members have left the building. Many friends who visit our house regularly have never seen him. Some don’t believe we even have a cat, but we have pictures.

The next morning, the tortoise is standing in the middle of the square of sun coming through the skylight, awaiting more lettuce.

The morning after that I wake early, in the dark, oppressed by a heavy weight. The dog is standing on my chest, looking down at me. The cat is also there, squatting on the pillow alongside my head.

“What?” I say. The dog yawns theatrically. The cat presses a paw to my lips.

All this reminds me that I have a tortoise and that, thankfully, he doesn’t do stairs.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Relying on AI is rotting your brain. But here’s what you can do about it | Carly Dober
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Carly Dober
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Each new tech product is designed to make our lives easier and keep us mindlessly entertained. Switch off: embrace discomfort – and boredom

Ever longed for your own personal assistant? In the ever quickening tech race, Meta has recently launched Muse, a new AI personal agent. Unlike traditional chatbots, this little AI tool will be able to fill out forms for you, organise calendars, pay bills and make reservations. Meta describes Muse as a personal agent “built for everyone”. The launch comes at a time when AI agents have been making headlines for hacking into government websites, public agencies and businesses. However, my immediate concern is a little closer to home.

I work as a psychologist, and I’m often talking to clients about lifestyle habits that lead to short-term gain but incur long-term pain. Our brains have a beautiful way of preferring the path of least resistance, of doing what is easiest to preserve our resources. And with the demands of modern life feeling so overwhelming for so many people, the urge to scroll after a long week or defer to a chatbot because you are exhausted is incredibly seducing.

Tech bros pushing their products on to us is nothing new (we all remember the metaverse, right?), but the message is now seemingly at fever pitch for mass AI adoption and how integral it is for human development. It is helpful to remind ourselves what we are being asked to give up, to whom and why, and to consider the potential risks before we hand over our precious data.

Some technology, such as large language models (LLMs) and social media that has an infinite scroll algorithm, seem to have a dose effect: too much reliance on this technology can lead to particular cognitive biases being activated, brain chemistry being depleted, moods and mental health being affected, and even neurological skills being atrophied, to name but a few of the documented risks.

Overusing artificial intelligence affects the brain and learning by bypassing the mental effort required to build deep neural connections, a process known as cognitive offloading. Frequent AI use fosters a passive acceptance of information, reducing the internal friction and inquiry that drive genuine curiosity and problem-solving. The brain depends on mental struggle and overcoming failure to rewire and strengthen our neural pathways. Bypassing that friction reduces our overall cognitive reserve over time.

Our tendency to favour or give greater credence to information supplied by technology (such as ChatGPT or Claude), and to ignore a manual source of information that provides contradictory information (a textbook, for example) even if it is correct, illustrates the phenomenon of automation bias. Automation complacency is closely linked – an overlapping concept that refers to the monitoring of technology with less frequency or vigilance because of a lower suspicion of error and a stronger belief in its accuracy, even when we know that LLMs often generate inaccurate answers.

Social media is designed to be so addictive because its business model relies on maximising user attention, while people give up their privacy because the immediate psychological rewards outweigh the abstract risk of data exposure. Most people say they value their privacy, but their behaviour says otherwise. This contradiction is known in behavioural economics as the privacy paradox.

Digital tools make life incredibly convenient – you can order a car with the touch of a button, a hot meal can be delivered to your door, and you can order and return outfits without ever exchanging a word with another person. People gladly trade their location data, contacts and browsing history in exchange for free maps, personalised shopping recommendations and seamless communication. Many individuals falsely believe that because they aren’t committing crimes, their data isn’t valuable. They don’t realise that aggregate data is used to manipulate purchasing habits, influence political votes and predict private life events.

Privacy policies are also intentionally long and confusing, and written in dense legal language that is inaccessible to the vast majority of users. Users face “consent fatigue” and simply click “Accept all” whenever the pesky window pops up while they are browsing because they feel they have no real choice.

There is a way out of the muck, though. Become more discerning about what information you share online; consider turning your location off unless you’re using navigation apps; reject cookies tracking you; hell, even start to poison your data if you really want to engage in some online anarchy. Does the online store you bought a T-shirt from once really need to know your full legal name and date of birth?

To avoid AI overreliance, you need to start introducing “friction” into your days – deliberate obstacles that break the automatic loop of seeking instant gratification. From a psychological perspective, AI is highly addictive because it eliminates this friction, offering immediate rewards with zero cognitive effort – and our brains need cognitive effort to remain sharp. Every time you try to work out a problem or read a book instead of the comments section, that is your brain doing a push-up.

If you’re struggling to rein in your social media or AI usage, a good way to start is by logging out of online sessions. Forcing yourself to manually type your credentials every time creates a massive psychological barrier. Also, try restricting your AI usage strictly to a desktop or laptop computer: removing ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini from your phone eliminates the urge to use it while walking, lying in bed or waiting in line. Scrolling on our phones or talking to a chatbot impedes much of the necessary mind-wandering time that our brains need to function at their best.

When you feel the urge to ask an AI a question or have it write something for you, force yourself to wait about 30 minutes. Use this time to brainstorm, look at a book or simply sit with the problem. Often the urge passes or you solve the problem yourself. Commit to writing the first draft of any email, letter or presentation entirely by yourself. Embrace the discomfort of maybe getting things wrong. Instead of asking an AI for a recommendation or an explanation, ask a friend or colleague, or check a reputable website. The delay in waiting for a human response builds patience, and we need to practise this skill in order to retain it.

Dedicate specific hours of your day to completely screen-free activities. Read books, write with pen and paper or go for a walk without your phone and see how differently things feel for you after six weeks of consistent effort. Intentionally building friction into the frictionless online experience is hard – but I promise that your brain will thank you for it.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Massive Attack, Bob Marley, bell hooks and grime: the forces that shaped four generations of Black Britons | The panel
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arlo Parks, Eunice Olumide, Ade Adepitan and Vanley Burke
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
For Black History Month, figures from the arts, culture and sport reveal the people and ideas that made them who they are today

When you’re traduced, abused and gaslighted – believe me, Black History Month matters | Hugh Muir

What book has most inspired you? All about love by bell hooks taught me so much about the nuances of connection and desire; it helped me make sense of the world and embrace my sensitivity. She had such a compassionate and inspired approach to truth-telling that I try to carry with me wherever I go.

What albums or artists have most shaped your sense of self? British music has shaped me completely. In Rainbows by Radiohead taught me to yearn, bend genres and embrace minimalism. Blue Lines and Mezzanine by Massive Attack moulded my taste in drums and song structure. Dummy by Portishead encouraged me to be as vocally naked and unafraid as possible. [The song] Archangel by Burial taught me to embrace the grime and the magic and the grey of London.

What cultural moments have felt most significant to you? Radiohead headlining the Pyramid stage at Glastonbury. Tate Modern opening its programming into the late night. The founding of Notting Hill carnival, and Meltdown festival at the Southbank Centre.

If you were PM for the day, what would be your first priority? Protecting and advocating for young people’s health and education.

Which Black historical figure has most influenced you? It would have to be a cluster of figures for their fearlessness, vulnerability and dedication to their crafts: Zadie Smith, Steve McQueen and the painter Donald Rodney.

What political development in the UK has most disappointed or uplifted you? I’ve been most disappointed by the rise in anti-trans rhetoric and discrimination. I’ve been most uplifted by the Arts Everywhere fund and the general commitment to increasing public access to art.

What is most misunderstood between generations? That it’s impossible for generations to truly connect. I think that with some care and attention we could find common ground, grow and truly understand each other.

What would you change about your life? Nothing. I feel really lucky and am looking forward to seeing where life takes me.

What book has most inspired you? I really did enjoy the Loud Black Girls anthology. It’s a wonderful constellation of extraordinary voices, contradictions, ambitions and histories. As someone who has spent much of her life moving between different worlds, I’m interested in the people who refuse to be reduced to a single identity.

What albums or artists have most shaped your sense of self? Growing up in Edinburgh, my relationship with identity has always been layered. Music was one of the places where those layers could coexist without requiring an explanation. I have toured the world with artists from Lauryn Hill, the Roots and Skepta to Wu-Tang Clan and Roots Manuva. They have all in different ways challenged the idea that we must make ourselves smaller to fit into the world.

What cultural moments have felt most significant to you? The emergence of grime as a defining British sound. It brought the ingenuity, language and lived realities of young people from communities too often treated as peripheral into the centre of British culture. It was a reminder that culture does not need permission to become influential.

If you were PM for the day, what would be your first priority? I would bring education, culture and economic opportunity much closer together. I’d usher in properly funded creative education, meaningful careers guidance, paid routes into industries that have historically relied on unpaid internships, and a serious commitment to ensuring that young people from every background can participate in Britain’s cultural and economic life.

Which Black historical figure has most influenced you? Margaret Ekpo was an inspiring Nigerian women’s rights activist and politician who fought for equality and the empowerment of women. At a time when women were often denied a voice in politics, she bravely stood up for their rights and encouraged them to participate in decision making.

What political development in the UK has most disappointed or uplifted you? The repeated pressure on public services, education and the arts concerns me deeply. These are not peripheral concerns; they shape our ability to participate in society, develop our talents and understand one another. What has uplifted me is the progress made in recognising the breadth of Britain’s history and the people who have shaped it.

What is most misunderstood between generations? I think each generation underestimates the difficulty of the world the other has inherited. Older generations can sometimes mistake the language of younger people for a lack of resilience, when it may actually be a more sophisticated vocabulary for identifying problems that were previously endured in silence. Younger generations, meanwhile, can underestimate the ingenuity and sacrifices of those who navigated a world with fewer of the freedoms and resources we now take for granted.

What is a “good life”? To have been a source of utter joy and kindness to the world. To use my inspiration to help and heal. Loving my family, doing good and letting the rest be. In the end it’s not what you own or worry about, it’s who you loved and the good you left behind.

Presenter, disability advocate, former wheelchair basketball player and gold medal-winning Paralympian, 53

What book has most inspired you? King Leopold’s Ghost by Adam Hochschild opened my eyes to history. I have always had this craving for more knowledge about Africa, the world and why it is the way it is. It talks about the origins of racism and race theory, and where we are socially and politically in the world – you can see the roots of it from this book.

What albums or artists have most shaped your sense of self? I got Shut Up and Dance’s album Dance Before the Police Come when it came out in the 1990s. It is a seminal album from a time when British music was still trying to find itself. It is like a cross between hip-hop, breakbeat and dance – they were like the Prodigy before the Prodigy. I felt like the album had the right amount of anger and cultural references. Soul II Soul were pretty influential when I grew up, and Massive Attack were big for me as well.

What cultural moments have felt most significant to you? The London 2012 Olympics and Paralympics. The opening ceremony was a real celebration of Britishness, of who we are and who we had become. It talked about everything from Black culture to white British culture, and we all celebrated it.

If you were PM for the day, what would be your first priority? There are so many things like accessible housing and transport, but I just couldn’t get away from education. I get asked to go to a lot of schools to do talks and assemblies and I can’t understand how we can’t see that the difference between private and state education is so stark in terms of resources, facilities, everything. It is insane that we have a two-tier system with such a wide discrepancy. I would ringfence a certain percentage of GDP to go into state school education. Or introduce something like a kind of conscription for people who have been highly educated or have a degree to teach. I think everyone at some point should have to do a stint in teaching and put back into society.

What Black historical figure has most influenced you? James Baldwin, because he was so articulate and an incredible communicator. He grew up in probably the most divisive and dysfunctional country in the world: the US. In a country where you could literally get shot for stating those types of views, he was brave enough to make it look at itself.

What political development in the UK has most disappointed or uplifted you? What has most disappointed me is that a lot of our policies and political leaders have allowed their politics to be shaped by anger. Angry rhetoric about immigrants, about benefits; anger about taxes, or the country being overregulated. Arguably, if we hadn’t listened to some of these very vocal groups and allowed ourselves to be shaped by them, we may not have had Brexit. More appropriate regulation, rather than a focus on less regulation, might have avoided a tragedy such as Grenfell.

What has most uplifted me is people starting to take more notice of politics. I think when I was growing up there was a lot of apathy when it came to political ideas. We were not as aware of what was going on. But people now have been forced to [take notice], because we have been in a period of high political flux and [experiences] like Covid have made us examine who we are.

What is most misunderstood between generations? My generation thinks the millennials’ lives are really easy: “They are not as resilient as we were.” But then millennials will say: “You guys didn’t have to deal with the kind of world we had to.” We had 9/11 and that turned the world upside down. Then the next generation says: “Look at us; we are dealing with social media and cannot afford to buy a house.” We allow ourselves to be put into these groups and these groups are then put against each other.

What is a “good life”? It’s about feeling happy and fulfilled. If you manage to find your thing, no matter whatever else happens to you in life you will always be able to go back to that. For me, it’s sports and family – they anchor me.

What would you change about your life? What I regret is that a lot of my success came after my parents passed away or their health deteriorated, so we couldn’t enjoy as much. I would have loved my dad to have been a grandfather to [Ade’s children] Bolla and Zayla, and for my mum to have had more time while she was well with Bolla, and to have met Zayla. I would have liked things to have aligned when I was at my best and they were at their best. That would have been nice.

What book has most inspired you? The books by the Black photographers Gordon Parks and James Van Der Zee. They most influenced my visual style.

What albums or artists have most shaped your sense of self? Catch a Fireby Bob Marley and the Wailers undoubtedly had and continues to have an impact on me. His lyrics are so visual. Notable mentions: Burning Spear’s Marcus Garvey, Culture’s Two Sevens Clash, Stevie Wonder’s Songs in the Key of Life. The work of Nina Simone. So many great albums, it’s difficult to choose one.

What cultural moments have felt most significant to you? The release of Nelson Mandela, perhaps because I was in Africa for the first time when it happened. This significant moment offered hope not just for South Africa but also beyond the shores of the continent.

If you were PM for the day, what would be your first priority? Acknowledging the evils of the enslavement of African people over centuries, the teachings of colonial history and its impact on British society, and having serious plans about how we can pay reparations for the labour of enslaved Africans.

Which Black historical figure has most influenced you? The visionary Marcus Garvey offered hope for the Black people; he was not just a thinker but he also got things done. He was one of the most accomplished orators of all time. His thoughts and philosophy continue to reverberate throughout Africa and the diaspora.

What political development in the UK has most disappointed or uplifted you? No political development has uplifted me because we always return to the status quo, which is disappointing. Thatcher’s legacy and its continued legacy on the working classes, the selling of council houses, the dismantling of the manufacturing industry, privatisation and closing the coal mines. Her policies benefited a few but resulted in many of the issues that blight our communities today.

What is most misunderstood between generations? Most people – especially the younger generation – are plugged in and switched on to their own universe, leaving very little time to communicate with each other. Meanwhile, the bridging generation is having to deal with an ever-changing work-life balance, making it difficult for them to provide the necessary support bringing both sides together.

What is a “good life”? Not having to be conscious of race on a daily basis or even at all. But that isn’t going to be possible in my lifetime. And being able to pay your bills.

What would you change about your life? I’ve been quite happy with my life. I’m not sure I would change anything, perhaps tweak a few things. Changing one thing can have detrimental consequences on the rest of your life.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: When you’re traduced, abused and gaslighted – believe me, Black History Month matters  | Hugh Muir
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Hugh Muir
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
There is always debate about the concept’s necessity and efficacy. But with nativists in their pomp, it’s good to focus on who we are and why

Pity Black History Month UK, assailed on all sides. Those on the right seek to end the celebration on the basis that it amounts to special treatment for a group that doesn’t deserve it. History should be colour-blind: society should not differentiate, they say. We are not racist, we just want fairness. But often, they are – and they really don’t.

On the other side of the argument are the progressives, notably minority progressives, who say the idea of a month to consider Black history is demeaning because it should already have a year-round place in our teaching and consciousness. There is a further view that any beneficial effect the month once had has been diluted by unimaginative repetition and commercially motivated virtue signalling. Players taking the knee in the Premier League? Been there, done that: yawn!

I have long taken the glass-half-full approach. The ideal would be for Black history to be incorporated into the social and educational culture – and perhaps one day it will be. But in the meantime, I’ll take a mandated, month-long focus on the Black contribution to the way our society has evolved. And it seems very necessary this year, when the very notion of belonging in Britain and other major western countries has been so under attack.

A year in which we have clearly seen that a political party, with pretensions to lead the country, attracts activists with ugly racist and nativist views – at national and local level – with the same efficiency that magnets attract iron filings. Our expectations are different now. When transcripts of the things Reform folk say in private reach the public domain, the old-fashioned Tory dog-whistle seems comparatively quaint.

This is a year in which we have again seen the confidence and daring of those who cuddle close to pseudo-scientific theories asserting white superiority and black inferiority. The racial eugenicists are back from the fringes, championed down their venal path by Donald Trump, whose leadership of the free world gladhands nativists, targets Black officials and routinely belittles Black enemies as “low IQ”.

It’s been a year in which toxic politics and the mainstreaming of intolerance – against minorities of many categories – has led to racist unpleasantness on our streets and in the workplace. There is a snapshot from the Royal College of Nursing: racist abuse of NHS nurses – including use of the N-word – up 86% in the recent past. All part of what one NHS official called “a rising tide of racism”.

Another snapshot of the increasingly hostile environment is from parliament. What happened, via social media, when Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy posted a video in support of Black History Month? Vile abuse, of course: “Some of a kind that I had not necessarily seen in that volume before. I had people calling me the N-word, people telling me to eff-off and go back to where I came from, and people sending monkey photographs.”

Another snapshot from Chichester, Sussex, where a diverse group of actors recently went to perform A Midsummer Night’s Dream and were shamefully menaced. “I don’t know if I have witnessed and/or experienced as much racism, xenophobia and homophobia as I saw in those six weeks,” said the actor and comedian Munya Chawawa. Britain is a good place. The vast majority of our fellow citizens are decent and kind. But it’s now easy, far too easy, to unwittingly enter hostile territory.

So in years like this, when there are obvious, concerted, targeted, and well-funded attempts to undermine Black people and the Black experience – not least the targeting of books by Black authors by “anti woke” crusaders – it becomes more difficult to be sanguine about concepts such as Black History Month. It then becomes a good thing, perhaps an essential one, to remember and to highlight – if only over a calendar month – who we are, who has shaped us and how we have indisputably helped to shape Britain as a vibrant, diverse, first world power.

Today, at the end of this Black History Month, Guardian Opinion has asked Black Britons representing four generations to tell us how their own Black British identities have evolved, for we have been here long enough now to compare notes on the different stages of our lives on this island. A twentysomething sees the joy and pain of being here very differently to their elderly siblings, to their parents, to their grandparents.

Call it reflection with a purpose. In a time like this, it seems more vital than ever to know who we were, who we are – and the foundations on which we all stand.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: Election integrity, extremism and Pete Hegseth: nine voters on the US midterm election
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Rachel Leingang, George Chidi, David Smith, Fabiola Cineas, Dani Anguiano and Ed Pilkington, with graphics by Andrew Witherspoon
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Days away from a national verdict on Trump 2.0, we check in with nine midterm voters across the US and the political spectrum

US voters will soon deliver a national verdict on the second presidency of Donald Trump. On 3 November, millions of Americans will vote in midterm elections to decide control of the House of Representatives and Senate, as well as the governorships in 36 states and state legislatures across the country. The results could have a huge impact on Trump’s final two years in office.

Our reporters have interviewed nine voters across the country and the political spectrum about extremism in US politics, their confidence in the US voting system, what they hope Congress will tackle first and their views of the president’s secretary of defense, Pete Hegseth.

The answers – highlights of which are published below – offer insight into the national mood days before voters head to the polls. The Guardian will return to its voter panel after final votes are cast.

double quotation markThe times that we’re living through has created a certain extremism. My bias is that I see the extremism on the right. I see the extremism of Trump’s influence on the candidates, on the electorate and the people that I live with every day here in Taylor county. I’ve not been a fan of Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor in Wisconsin. He showed his extremism from the very start, seeking to undermine the 2020 election, voting for war, supporting tariffs, never swerving from the lockstep Maga extremist playbook, essentially.

double quotation markIt depends on what you mean by extreme. We have certainly seen way more candidates than usual making it out of the Democratic primaries who do not take billionaire or foreign lobby money, like Angie Nixon [in Florida] or Abdul El-Sayed [in Michigan]. While this shift is seen as electorally threatening to some, most of these candidates who are typically the ones labeled as “extreme” have policy prescriptions that are very close to the average American’s views, especially when it comes to topics like healthcare reform or participation in forever wars. Looking at the other side of the aisle, I do think there has been an emergence of candidates who display an “extreme” level of corruption and bigotry typically only seen coming from the White House these days. Mike Rogers [Republican Senate candidate for Michigan] comes to mind, with his main campaign strategy seemingly being a desperate bid to tie El-Sayed to anything radical or Islamist, and so does Vivek Ramaswamy’s notable doubling-down on a campaign ad implying his gubernatorial opponent [in Ohio] lied about her childhood sexual abuse.

double quotation markMost of the Democratic candidates are extreme. This political cycle has produced more extreme candidates than ever before. I’m 70 years old and I’ve never been involved in active politics. I’ve always voted since I was 18 and I’ve always voted conservative Republican but I’ve never seen anything that’s so extreme. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan is one that stands out and some have already been elected like the mayor of New York [Zohran Mamdani]. I never thought I would see someone that far left voted in.

double quotation markI believe that at the most local level, it will overwhelmingly be free and fair. And by that I mean that I have a great deal of faith in the town clerks and the county clerks, the people who, at the ground level, oversee elections and whose livelihoods, whose reputations are on the line. On the national level, I have every expectation that the extremists that are currently in power will do whatever they can to, well, to cheat, to break the law, to violate constitutional rights of the people, and to try to deny election results, as happened after the 2020 election.

double quotation markThe election itself will be free and fair as it’s conducted. However, we’re already seeing all the multiple attempts in the past two weeks of different types of intimidation from the justice department trying to interfere with elections. And we’ve seen that in California, we’ve seen it right now in Alaska, we’ve seen it here. So, they’re using the many tactics of intimidation and meddling and propaganda to interfere in the elections. But when I look at the amount of people that have already voted early, I think that’s the biggest guardrail that this election has.

double quotation markI can only hope. I’m thankful for the steps that the Republican party has followed with monitors and people watching the polls because, if an election is won fair and square, I am thrilled. That is the way of the people but, if there’s any cheating going on or one vote that is fraudulent, that vote should be thrown out because that’s not what this nation is based on. In some countries, people have died for fair elections and, unless we have fair elections, it’s to the good of no one.

double quotation markBeing a poll worker and observing what goes on, I think [elections] go on pretty well anywhere in the country. I think you will see a fair election. Unfortunately, maybe, delayed or not approved by the Trump administration. He’s saying if the GOP loses in Alaska, he’s not going to recognize it. [But] I think the Democrats have been anticipating this all along and have been putting together different ways of challenging him in the courts.

double quotation markI am hoping Democrats immediately reinstate and expand the ACA, [the Affordable Care Act], pass a war powers resolution to end engagement with Iran, pass an AI datacenter moratorium, end all military aid to Israel, reverse the White House’s cancellation of federally approved funding, undo the blanket tariffs, release the Epstein files, and scrutinize and impeach the cabinet and president. I also hope they fight to advance Medicare for All, a substantial increase in the federal minimum wage, and robust federal job and housing programs.

double quotation markWhichever party wins, I really hope they focus on doing the right thing and bring ICE under control. Right now, here in the Rio Grande valley, ICE is profiling individuals of a certain color, Hispanic people, and they are chasing them down, arresting and assaulting them. I’m not saying that they shouldn’t deport people, but it’s got to be done the right way, the legal way.

double quotation markI hope they will first [address] gas prices, food prices, medical costs and interest rates, and all of the things that are hurting the economy right now. I don’t think it’s time to talk about impeachment or anything like that. It would just cause more problems than necessary.

double quotation markBring civility back to society. It seems as though there’s something going on in society, and there’s a race to the bottom. Democrats had power before, and they spend so much time arguing amongst themselves. I think that when Democrats win, the speed of which society is collapsing will slow down, but it will not stop.

double quotation markIf the Republican party wins next week, I hope they will focus on bringing a swift and decisive victory in Iran. They seem to be allergic to winning, whether in individual races, a national agenda or geopolitics, and they need to grow a spine.

double quotation markStop ICE by any means necessary. Their harmful impact is threatening the lives of innocent people daily, and it makes us look like we’re run by a third world cartel. Obama deported just as many illegal immigrants, focusing on actual criminals and not using unchecked violence against families. No civilians were casually murdered on his watch.

Next, start impeachment proceedings and investigations into all the blatant and rampant corruption that the GOP has repeatedly ignored. If I had my choice, I would choose [Trump’s son-in-law Jared] Kushner as the first target and Trump’s sons to avoid the courts getting in the way with presidential privilege. If they do go after Trump, they should impeach both him and Vance simultaneously since they are in it together.

double quotation markI think Pete Hegseth is unfit for the job in almost every possible way. If you can look past his vitriolic attitude toward women and every minority – I find that difficult – he is clearly an incompetent buffoon chosen purely for his loyalty to the president over any real consideration of his capabilities. The livestreamed execution idea is just one of the latest in a series designed to propel America back into some of the darkest chapters of our history. As Jamelle Bouie of the New York Times succinctly put it: “That’s a lynching.”

double quotation markWe need a strong leader in any position that we have in the country. If my house is on fire, I wouldn’t want to follow someone who says: ‘Maybe we need to go this way, but I don’t know, let’s sit here and talk a minute and discuss it and find out what we need to do.’ I want somebody to get me by the hair of the head and say: ‘Let’s get the hell out of the house.’ I think that’s Hegseth. I was all for the livestreamed execution. When I first heard it I said: ‘Yeah, I’m going to watch it.’ I’m a mother of five children. Mothers look at things differently. People said, how are you going to protect the children? How many children watched Charlie Kirk get his neck blown out? Now, that wasn’t a choice but that is a part of this world and I believe if someone commits a crime, they should suffer the consequences.

double quotation markPete Hegseth is a force to be reckoned with. I appreciate his restoration of military culture away from the effeminate mockery of itself that it was under Levine [Admiral Rachel Levine, who is transgender and led the public health corps during the Joe Biden administration]. I’m equally pleased to see the war department retake its original, unashamed title. We’ve been sitting while everyone else pretends not to play the game for too long, and Pete Hegseth has called the world’s bluff. As to the public execution of the traitor that killed several American soldiers, I simply believe it should have been done a long time ago. America is a joke if it can’t execute justice.

double quotation markI think he’s the most inadequate person that has ever been in that position. I was in the Marine Corps for 15 years. I’ve seen different secretaries of war, as they like to put it, and he has come up with the most ridiculous things I’ve ever seen. No 1, he is prejudiced. He’s as prejudiced as Trump is about certain things, women in the military, minorities in the military. He’s gotten rid of many of the top generals and most of them are women, Black people or Latinos. He’s really downgraded the military, and he has no idea what he’s doing in terms of carrying out operations like the one in Iran. I think it was a very poor judgment on his part to even consider something like that. Because again, we’ve never done that in our history. I think it would just be another black mark on his ability to carry out his job.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Día de los Muertos celebrations rise from the dead as ICE arrests continue: ‘It’s important to bring joy in dark times’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Eric Berger
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
After canceling events in 2025, US cities including Henderson, Kentucky, are reviving public Day of the Dead events

Julia, a 19-year-old born in the US, and her parents, undocumented immigrants from Mexico, enjoyed attending the Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) celebration each year in Henderson, Kentucky, and selling aguas frescas, horchatas and a sweet bread traditionally eaten on the Mexican holiday.

Last year, her family also built an ofrenda, or altar, featuring flowers and a violin, to honor her grandfather, who played the instrument and died in 2023 in Mexico.

Unfortunately, organizers of the event in the town of 27,000 people canceled the party in 2025 because of concerns that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) would use it as an opportunity to arrest undocumented immigrants.

“The political climate around immigration was so difficult and controversial that we got a clear message from folks in the Latino community here” that “they would not come”, said Brad Schneider, the judge/executive of Henderson county, who co-founded the event.

This year, however, Henderson is among the US cities reviving public Day of the Dead celebrations after canceling last year. Meanwhile, some places that held events last year canceled because, in at least one case, of fears of ICE ramping up raids in their area.

The decisions over whether to hold a public Day of the Dead celebration reveal that while in some parts of the country, ICE does not incite the same worries as a year ago, the agency’s ongoing deportation efforts still unnerve many Latino immigrants across the US, and that is having a serious impact on community life.

“I trust in the leadership that we have in our community, and if they believe it’s safe to have it, then I trust in that,” said Julia, who is studying political science and secondary education in college.

Día de los Muertos, which takes place over several days, dates back thousands of years to the Aztecs, who believed that death was just part of a larger cycle of existence. The popular belief is that during the holiday, souls of the deceased can return to earth to be with their loved ones. As such, the living build ofrendas to welcome their spirits.

Millions attend celebrations in Mexico. In the United States, cities like Los Angeles and San Antonio have held Day of the Dead celebrations that can attract tens of thousands of people.

Schneider grew up in Arizona and California and developed deep connections to Latino people, food and culture. Almost 40 years ago, he moved to Henderson. He has since watched as more Latinos moved to the area; they now comprise about 5% of the local population, according to the Census Bureau.

After watching the 2015 James Bond film Spectre, which opens at a Day of the Dead celebration in Mexico City, Schneider asked Abraham Brown, owner of a Mexican restaurant in nearby Evansville, Indiana, whether they could hold such a celebration in Henderson.

Brown told him it was a great idea. In 2019, they held the inaugural event. The celebration has included mariachi bands, Mexican food, a faux graveyard where people decorate headstones, and face-painting.

But in 2025, local Latinos were “reading the newspaper reports and media accounts, children were separated from adults, and that was all very scary for people”, Schneider said.

This year, he and Brown again asked people at Mexican groceries and restaurants about holding a celebration, and “the overwhelming response was that they wanted it”, Schneider said.

In Long Beach, California, the local government also decided to hold its festival after canceling last year because of concerns over immigration enforcement.

“I think that it’s important to continue those traditions and be able to celebrate with family and friends, and so I wanted to give our city the opportunity to continue to do that,” city council member Mary Zendejas, who requested that organizers cancel the event in 2025, told the Long Beach Post.

In Worcester, Massachusetts, organizers canceled the city’s celebration last year. Instead, they held smaller events and did not announce them on social media.

“It had to be at a private location where not anyone could walk in, that wasn’t open to the general public, and we had to make sure that parking was close to the door, so people didn’t have to walk really far to get to their car,” said Raquel Castro, who runs the city’s division of youth opportunities and co-founded Casita Cultura Latina, which organizes the city’s Día de los Muertos celebration.

This year, they decided to again hold a public gathering on 24 October at a local park with a mariachi band, a DJ and art in honor of this year’s theme, “Amor como resiliencia”, which means: “Love as resilience.”

“It’s not easy to exist and to still bring joy in dark times, and we thought it was really important to do so,” said Castro, who immigrated from Ecuador, of why they held the party.

While some Latino residents have become more comfortable coming to public events, ICE has not gone anywhere. While the agency has avoided some of the negative publicity it generated during its operation in late 2025 and early 2026 in Minneapolis, its monthly arrests and detentions actually increased in June and July, according to the Deportation Data Project.

In San Antonio, ICE recently signed leases worth $51m for two office spaces and is preparing to open a detention center that can house 1,500 people per day, the San Antonio Express-News reported.

Amid the effort to expand its footprint, a local retailer, Planet K, canceled its annual Día de los Muertos celebration, which it started holding 20 years ago.

“This decision was not made lightly,” organizers posted on Facebook. “We refuse to bring people together under Ice terrorism.”

Marina Alderete Gavito, a San Antonio city council member, particularly enjoyed the event’s fireworks show and said it’s “just really sad that we are seeing these traditions” taken “away from us”.

Organizers also canceled Day of the Dead celebrations in Asbury Park, New Jersey, and Fresno, California.

The Guardian asked ICE’s public affairs office whether the agency planned to send officers to Day of the Dead celebrations but did not receive a response.

ICE has also appeared in Henderson. In July, federal agents arrested eight people there, the Hendersonian reported.

“He was the one that brought in the money, so it was a very difficult situation for them,” Julia said of her relative’s immediate family. “Julia” is a pseudonym, which the Guardian is using for her protection.

Julia’s mother recently obtained permanent residency; her father is still working on it. Still, they all plan to attend and sell food at the Día de los Muertos celebration Saturday.

“I love seeing the same customers come back, but with more people that they love” to celebrate “what a different culture looks like and what it can look like anywhere, like, for example, in Henderson”, Julia said. “It makes me happy to see that we are able to celebrate that again, hopefully in a peaceful manner.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Hear me out: maybe Norway should give Melania Trump the Nobel peace prize | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The first lady has been praised for ‘singlehandedly’ brokering a ceasefire in a Ukrainian city – though she might have had some help

Haters be damned: Donald Trump just keeps on winning. He won the inaugural Fifa peace prize last year and was presented with the completely real, totally not made-up “Man of the Century” award at a recent rally. The president has also spent the greater part of a decade claiming he was once crowned Michigan’s Man of the Year: a fantastic achievement considering there is no such award and Trump has never lived in Michigan.

But despite his many trophies, there is one honour that has proved elusive: the Nobel peace prize. Trump holds a bit of a grudge about that, recently terming Norway a “shithouse country” for passing him over for the award. In response, the country’s tourism board highlighted some of its nicest public lavatories with the tagline: “Norway makes shit houses great again!”

Speaking in my capacity as Philadelphia’s Woman of the Millennium, I’ve got a modest proposal for the people of Norway. The toilet gag was excellent, but if they want to do some top-tier trolling then I think next year’s Nobel peace prize needs to go to Melania Trump.

Some people would be thrilled for their spouse to be in the spotlight, but I’m not sure that’s the case with Donald. Indeed, the president has said: “You can only have … one star in a family; it doesn’t work with two.” If Melania got Trump’s coveted Nobel peace prize, it could spark a war in the White House.

But look, I’m not just suggesting the Norwegians honour Melania because it would raise Donald’s blood pressure. No, it seems Melania has become quite the diplomat. Last week, the White House announced that the first lady had “successfully secured a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, localized to the city of Oleshky”.

How on earth did she manage that? Apparently, Melania initiated discussions with Russia and Ukraine and “aligned the parties on the agreement’s objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary”.

Whatever all that means, it seems to have worked: the ceasefire went into effect on Tuesday in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city, which has been enduring a worsening humanitarian crisis. On Friday, hundreds of people were evacuated from the frontline town and emergency supplies were brought in for people who needed to stay.

Melania has been widely praised for brokering this ceasefire. Melania’s adviser has claimed she “singlehandedly” secured it, adding that no other first lady has ever achieved what Melania just pulled off, and she is “completely revamping the role of first lady … [and] saving lives.”

Perhaps. But if there is one thing that the Trumps are good at it, it is taking credit for other people’s work. So is the first lady really the great peacemaker that she’s making herself out to be?

To be fair, Melania has done some good work vis-à-vis Ukraine and certainly seems to be better at peacemaking than Jared Kushner is, who has made huge sums of money while operating as one of Trump’s top diplomatic envoys to the Middle East. Last year, for example, Melania wrote a letter to Vladimir Putin pleading for Ukrainian children seized by Russia to be returned to their families. Since then, her office has said she’s facilitated numerous rounds of family reunification.

However, despite the claim that Melania “singlehandedly” secured this ceasefire, it would appear she had a little help. Pope Leo XIV also personally appealed to Putin about the situation in Oleshky in early October. It’s unclear whether he had more or less sway than the first lady had, but the pope is certainly being rather more modest about his involvement.

So what’s next for Melania after her success in Oleshky? In an interview with Newsmax, her adviser Marc Beckman said Melania might help pave the way to “durable, everlasting peace” in Ukraine and Russia as a whole.

“She’s against war, she thinks it’s senseless … she wants to see peace all over the world,” Beckman added.

Does she indeed? In that case she might want to have a word with the president, who started a very bloody war against Iran and who is currently trying to use US taxpayer money to send 2,000lb bombs to Israel, a country accused of genocide.

Forget the Nobel peace prize. If Melania can do something about her husband, I’m crowning her Michigan’s Woman of the Year.

Last November, the FDA announced that menopausal hormone therapy medications would no longer require a scary “black-box” label on them, which is the highest safety-related warning a medication can have. This reassured a lot of women about the treatment and caused a surge in demand.
