Supply didn’t keep up, and there’s been a shortage of estrogen patches in the US all year because of an uptick in demand. Now Reuters reports that the shortage has spread beyond estrogen patches “with some injectable and vaginal estrogen products also in short supply”.

Huerta co-founded the United Farm Workers union (UFW), which improved conditions for agricultural workers in the 1960s and 1970s. She is also credited with coining the phrase “Sí, se puede!” (yes, we can), which was UFW’s slogan and then Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign rally cry.

“I think that going in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea,” Harris said in a MeidasTouch interview. “I was in the Senate for the last go-round, and the votes aren’t there.” In other words: don’t hold your breath that Trump will face immediate accountability if the Democrats dominate the midterms.

Attalah is the editor-in-chief of Madr Masar, an independent Egyptian news site that has frequently been critical of the Egyptian president Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi’s government. The government recently accused her of running a website without a license, detained her, and shut down Mada Masr. The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, one expert told the Guardian.

“We are living through a strange time in the language around bodies,” writes Hannah Marriott in the Guardian. The body positivity era is over, but “much of its social training lingers.” Thanks to the GLP-1 boom, everyone is shrinking, but it’s taboo to talk about it. “What we’re left with is a world in which skinny bodies are lionized in fashion, culture and daily life, but to either admit a desire to conform, or express concern about it, feels socially verboten.”

You may be familiar with this viral tweet: “I’m 50. All celebrity news looks like this: ‘Curtains for Zoosha? K-smog and Batboy caught flipping a grunt.’” I am still a mere 43, but I had my own curtains for Zoosha moment this week when I saw the headlines about G Flip, which I could have sworn was a watch. If you are similarly confused, Rebecca Shaw has an explainer as to why some of the queer community are in mourning.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: He was one of the NFL’s most feared runners. Now Larry Johnson fears what football did to his brain
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Andrew Lawrence
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Once among the NFL’s most punishing running backs, Larry Johnson opens up about memory loss, intrusive thoughts and his fears over football’s lasting toll

In his heyday, Larry Johnson was the NFL tailback you’d least want to line up against, the steamroller in pads who had defensive players and coaches questioning their life choices on every down. But since Johnson walked away from pro football in 2011, after seven seasons in the league and an All-Pro run with the Kansas City Chiefs, he’s the one doing the soul-searching, grappling with the toll all that gridiron glory has taken on his brain.

Johnson, who still cuts a fit and formidable figure at age 46, can scarcely recall his glittering career, much less its highlights. “I go up to maybe 2006, 2007,” he tells me. “Anything before or three years after, I really don’t remember.”

When Johnson was thriving as a pro in the mid 2000s, chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease associated with repeated head impacts, was not yet widely recognized as a risk of playing football. The NFL, however, had evidence that head injuries could cause lasting neurological damage, yet spent much of the decade publicly disputing the link as former players sought disability benefits for neurological problems – and were largely denied.

It wasn’t until Will Smith starred in the movie Concussion as Bennett Omalu – the forensic pathologist who sounded the alarm on CTE in American football players after examining the brain of Mike Webster, the Hall of Fame center who died in 2002 after years of cognitive decline and a range of behavioral problems – that Johnson began joining the dots between football and his own personality swings. Johnson has long suspected he suffers from CTE, even though the disease can only be diagnosed after death. A study published on Wednesday of former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 found that 74.5% had CTE. Of the nearly 400 players whose brains were donated for postmortem examination, 93.5% showed evidence of the disease.

Johnson’s NFL career was defined by physical punishment, and he was a violent runner who welcomed the blows. Ahead of the 2003 draft, Johnson seemed like everything a team could want in a franchise running back. He had size (6ft 1in, 230 lbs) and speed (4.45s 40-yard dash). He capped a four-year career at Penn State by sweeping the Doak Walker Award for the nation’s best running back and the Maxwell and Walter Camp awards for the nation’s best player after rushing for more than 2,000 yards on fewer carries than anyone in history. He had backing from Joe Paterno, when that still meant something, and more hands-on guidance from his father, Larry Johnson Sr – the former Nittany Lions defensive assistant who’s now Ohio State’s associate head coach.

But when the Chiefs selected Johnson 27th overall as insurance for franchise running back Priest Holmes, they did so over the objections of head coach Dick Vermeil, who had watched a parade of Penn State runners disappoint in the pros and figured Johnson would be no different. Vermeil singled out Johnson’s preparation habits and maturity, joking that he needed to “take the diapers off”. But Vermeil had to eat his words after Holmes went down with a season-ending neck injury midway through the 2005 season and Johnson stepped in to rack up 1,750 yards and 20 touchdowns in nine weeks. (“Well, he’s a talent,” the coach conceded later.)

The following season Vermeil retired and Herm Edwards took over, and the bombastic defensive guru made Johnson the centerpiece of the Chiefs offense. He ran for 1,789 yards on a whopping 416 carries – an NFL record that isn’t likely to be threatened in the current era of pass-happy offense and running by committee. Whenever Johnson publicly shares his CTE fears, fans often find themselves looking back at the season for answers. Was that the beginning? Too many blows? “People forget: I didn’t get hurt during those 416 carries,” he says. “I didn’t really start until 2006. I was in the league for three years – maybe the only first-round pick battling just to dress. If Herm had told me straight up, ‘I’m gonna run you 416 times.’ I would’ve been like, Why can’t we do 500?”

Johnson reveled in his star status, famously signing on as an ambassador for Jay-Z’s Roc-A-Fella record label as it was growing into a lifestyle brand. The Chiefs workhorse was frequently spotted partying with LeBron James and other members of Jay-Z’s inner circle at the rapper mogul’s bygone 40/40 Club in New York, helping get Jay-Z in the door with the NFL and paving the way for his later relationship with the league office and commissioner Roger Goodell. Johnson celebrated touchdowns by tenting his hands into a diamond, a gesture popularized by Jay-Z and his associates known as “throwing up the Roc”.

But the southern Maryland native never quite cottoned to the scrutiny that came with the spotlight. He was slammed in the press for demanding a trade and threatening to sit out as leverage for a new contract. He clashed with Chiefs coach Todd Haley – questioning his credentials to succeed Edwards – and disparaged fans and media with homophobic slurs, prompting suspensions before he was eventually released by the team.

Johnson drew more troubling headlines for his alleged assaults on women: a Kansas City nightclub patron accused him of spitting a drink in her face, and an ex-girlfriend accused him of beating and strangling her at the Bellagio in Las Vegas. Between 2003 and 2012, he was arrested five times in cases involving allegations of violence against women – resulting in convictions for disturbing the peace, domestic battery and assault, with penalties that stopped short of jail time. Johnson shies from blaming football for those incidents, but it’s hard not to wonder what the game left behind in a man so handsomely rewarded for violence – or how much the game messed with his head. Johnson began playing tackle football at age nine, taking helmet-to-helmet hits long before he reached the NFL.

Life after football was deeply unsettling for Johnson. “I couldn’t find anything that really will test your manhood and also test your character like football,” he says. “I enjoyed lining up eight in a box and then trying to get five or 10 yards – and then I’m getting 50. As twisted as it may sound, the thing I wanted to do was to die on the football field. I always felt like I had to go to war, like I had to fight even when I don’t have to fight.”

He had hoped to transition into nonprofit work, but found the 9-to-5 office environment stifling. A hair-trigger sensitivity to light, noise and group settings made it impossible for him to hold down a job. He fought with the mother of his young daughter, Jaylen, over school pickup schedules; during a two-year court fight, with Johnson’s own mother acting as a go-between, he finally realized he was the one misremembering the times. He enrolled in a master’s program with a cohort of NFL retirees, but says he quit after flipping out on a professor during a group project.

All the while, Johnson wrestled with intrusive thoughts and inner voices telling him to harm himself and others. The voices come in waves, he says, “almost like a suggestion. Certain things scare me. I can’t be close to balconies anymore. If I’m walking, I’ll think, What if something falls out of the sky? Just a constant state of paranoia.” To cope, he isolated himself for long stretches and self-medicated with drugs and alcohol – making matters far worse.

Johnson’s father had little idea of his son’s quiet suffering until the ex-Chiefs star went public in a 2017 Washington Post profile. Johnson feared that his father might not understand or relate to what he was going through; he went from checking in with his dad for any reason, even if it was just to say he was heading home after a game, to pulling away from his great mentor. The Post article, though, “gave my father new eyes,” Johnson says. “People would tell him, ‘That’s a really good thing your son did.’ I think that made him a little bit more accepting. [Now] we’re back to our relationship – as if I’m still in the house, you know?”

Johnson had another major breakthrough around the same time, when the NFL granted him lifetime disability benefits, giving him the financial security to focus on his health without worrying about making ends meet. In a league infamous for publicly denying former players’ claims and using race-norming to limit disability payouts (disputes that were ostensibly addressed in a revised league settlement), that victory shouldn’t be taken lightly. Johnson knows how fortunate he was to last seven years in a league where the average running back’s career is around 2½ years, leaving little time to build a safety net. He believes the modern trend of devaluing running backs only serves a league that’s “trying to lessen payments.”

Johnson’s daily life is still punctuated by bouts of confusion. Light and noise still bother him, and he gets irritated anytime he hears himself slurring words or otherwise struggling to put sentences together. But Johnson has better ways of coping. Jaylen is old enough to drive herself – and her dad – around now, sparing him the embarrassment of getting lost on routine trips or confusing the TV remote for a car key fob. Johnson spends a lot of time talking through his feelings with his wife, who knows when to prod and when to leave him be. All of it helps keep the voices at bay, but he still hears them. He likens the intrusive thoughts to a movie. “Yours might last for a scene,” he says. “Mine is like a sequel. Then there’s part three and hidden features. It’s like Marvel at the end of the movie. It engulfs me.”

Social media tends to be where Johnson gets in trouble these days, courting controversy with conspiracy theories about Jews, Kobe Bryant’s death and Jay-Z, with whom he has since fallen out. Away from the online fray, though, Johnson keeps a cool head in group chats with former teammates, even as it frustrates him that his peers never want to talk about what they’re really going through. “All they’re talking about is each other’s birthdays and going out and drinking,” he says. “We are in an era where if you admit you were hurt, you’re soft – you know what I mean?”

His new dream is to create an app that connects former pros struggling with their mental health with people who understand what they’re going through – former NFL clinicians like Susan Wilson, his team therapist at the Chiefs. “I would love to be able to have a symposium for retired guys,” Johnson says, “so they can hear not only the horror stories, but share their similar histories of how to deal with mental health. It’s been too hush-hush and taboo for such a long time because guys are embarrassed.”

CTE researchers are always keen to build relationships with former players, too. Last month, Emory University announced a partnership with the Concussion & CTE Foundation and Boston University on a medical study of former football players experiencing depressive and cognitive symptoms. The study is testing whether an FDA-approved drug that reduces inflammation can also improve those symptoms, recruiting men aged 30–55 in the Atlanta area who have played at least 11 years of tackle football.

Whether researchers are any closer to diagnosing and treating CTE in living patients remains an open question. “CTE is both a complex physiological and psychological issue,” says Concussion & CTE Foundation co-founder Chris Nowinski, a longtime advocate. “Learning you have CTE can have a positive mental impact for some, and a negative one for others. That’s why it’s critical to have a multi-pronged approach advancing diagnosis, treatment and mental health support.”

Johnson tries not to let his emotions get the better of him when watching football now. He appreciates the safety measures the league has introduced to protect players, but laments what they’ve taken away from the physical brand of football he once defined. It broke the ex-Chief’s heart to see his former AFC rival Chris Johnson opening up about his ALS battle. “To watch these players who could basically run 4.5, 4.4 40s be in wheelchairs, like, that haunts me,” he says. “If this could happen to Chris Johnson or Steve Gleason, it can happen to any of us, right?”

In an effort to keep tabs on his own neurological condition, Johnson has taken to posting videos of himself on social media and scrutinizing them for signs of decline – the ultimate mental health self-scout. Early replies describing his delivery as “mean” or “condescending” helped him modulate his behavior and even led to some online friendships. With a firmer handle on his general well-being, Johnson thinks differently about being tested for CTE now, while he’s alive.

“When I first said that, it was like, yeah, I would want to know,” he says. “But at the end of the day, I know I would obsess over it. I would be paying attention to every little micro movement and emotion. I would drive myself crazy thinking I don’t have much time, so let me act out. If there was a way we could figure out before then, at least I would know the damage. Whether I know it or whether I can feel it, I know something is there.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.title: Judge bars DoJ from threats to election workers as Trump to hold tele-rallies three days before elections – live
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.author: Chris Hippensteel (now)
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text:
With control of Congress on the line, next week’s midterms amount to a referendum on Trump, who has urged voters to pretend he is on the ballot

Donald Trump is tele-rallying from Mar-a-Lago with just three days to go before the midterm elections. On Sunday, he will make appearances at rallies in Iowa in Kansas in a reversal after he initially backed out.

With control of the US Congress on the line, next week’s midterm elections amount to a referendum on Trump, who has repeatedly urged voters to pretend he is himself on the ballot, as his approval ratings continue to decline.

Late on Friday, a federal judge barred Trump’s justice department from threatening or coercing election workers to stop processing ballots, the Associated Press reported. The decision also bars the department from demanding local election officials segregate or not count ballots that the federal government deems may have been cast by ineligible voters.

It marked another blow to the Trump administration’s efforts to assert control over local elections, after a federal appeals court on Friday rejected the Department of Justice’s request for California to sequester 20,000 disputed ballots.

The top federal prosecutor in Alaska confirmed on Friday the existence of a criminal and a civil investigation into an alleged scheme by Mary Peltola’s campaign and national Democrats to confuse voters in the closely watched Senate race by recruiting a spoiler candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan.

Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed resisted a demand from his defeated primary rival, congresswoman Haley Stevens, that he apologize for criticism of US military aid to Israel on Friday – two days before they were scheduled to campaign together in Detroit.

Early voting this cycle has set ‌a record. More than 49 million Americans have already cast ballots, either in person or by mail, the Associated Press reported.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Louisiana appeals court rejects lawsuit over suicide of boy expelled for shoving school bully
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Sara Brannon plans to continue legal bid against Catholic archdiocese of New Orleans, which governs high school

A Louisiana appellate court recently dismissed a wrongful death lawsuit being pursued by a woman whose teenaged son died by suicide hours after his Catholic school expelled him for what he had described as a shoving match with a campus bully.

One of the attorneys for plaintiff Sara Brannon on Friday said she intends to appeal that ruling from Louisiana’s fifth circuit appellate court in a case which characterized her son’s expulsion as unreasonable and arbitrary.

Brannon filed her state court lawsuit against the Roman Catholic archdiocese of New Orleans in March, a year after the death of her 17-year-old son Devon Shelton within hours of being expelled from one of the institution’s high schools.

She argued that Devon’s archdiocesan high school – Rummel, in the New Orleans suburb of Metairie – was negligent in its treatment of her son when it expelled him in the wake of what he termed a shoving match with a fellow student who had been bullying him.

Brannon maintained that Rummel had a duty to Devon to administer discipline in a commensurate, non-arbitrary way – and their failure to fulfill that obligation led to her son’s suicide at his former stepfather’s house. So, she said, the school owed her damages.

Lawyers for the archdiocese countered by contending that Louisiana law does not allow plaintiffs to recover damages for “off-campus acts of student self-harm following school disciplinary decisions,” as the fifth circuit court of appeal put in its ruling.

The archdiocese asked state district court judge Nancy Miller to dismiss the case, but she rejected that request in July. The archdiocese appealed – and fifth circuit judges Susan Chehardy, Jude Gravois and Marc Johnson ruled in favor of the church, overturning Miller.

“We find the facts presented in [the] plaintiff’s [lawsuit] are insufficient to impose wrongful death liability upon the school,” the appellate court said in its decision, which was handed down on 13 October and filed into the case record a week later.

The opinion referred to Devon’s death repeatedly as “tragic” – but declared “the facts of this matter … would not legally fit into any theory of recovery”.

A statement from an archdiocese spokesperson on Friday said “we remember Devon and lift him and his family in prayer” as the Catholic church prepared to pray for all of the dead in November, as it traditionally does.

Devon’s online obituary described him as a devoted player of various instruments for Rummel’s marching band. Among other things, the obituary said he was also a member of the school’s varsity bowling team and volunteered annually at a bicycle ride meant to generate charity support for people will multiple sclerosis.

One of his mother’s attorneys is Richard Trahant, who has represented numerous claimants of sexual abuse by clergy within New Orleans’ archdiocese. The archdiocese filed for bankruptcy protection in 2020 amid the financial fallout of the longstanding, worldwide Catholic church clergy molestation scandal.

In December, the archdiocese and its insurers agreed to pay about $305m to roughly 700 clergy abuse survivors. Survivors had not been paid as October ended, though there were indications that individual payments may start in the coming weeks.

In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In the UK, the youth suicide charity Papyrus can be contacted on 0800 068 4141 or email pat@papyrus-uk.org, and in the UK and Ireland Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123, or email jo@samaritans.org or jo@samaritans.ie. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.title: Unseen Harry Houdini writing published on 100th anniversary of his death
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.author: Richard Luscombe
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.text:
Strand magazine to feature never-before-seen article from Hungarian-born escapologist who was also a prolific author

Unseen writing by Harry Houdini, the world’s most renowned escapologist and illusionist, is being published in the US on Saturday, the 100th anniversary of his death.

As well as being famous for his magic acts and quest to expose fake mediums and spiritualists before he died in 1926 at the age of 52, Houdini, whose real name was Eric Weisz, was a prolific author, with more than two dozen books, short stories and plays to his name.

One of them, an article titled An Interesting Scrapbook, was never published, and appears for the first time in print Saturday in Strand magazine, a literary publication that specializes in presenting lost or hidden works by prominent writers and historical figures.

It is a detailed look at some of the performers who shaped the early days of magic as a stage production, and inspired the path of Houdini, a Hungarian immigrant to the US as a child, into the best-known, and one of the most creative and popular entertainers of his day in Europe and America.

It features images of numerous theater bills from an era of growing public fascination with the supernatural blended with an increasing appetite for unusual or fanciful acts. Houdini explores advertised performances including “necromantic miracles”, “magical delusions”, and “the greatest living wizard”.

“What makes the article remarkable is it reveals a side of Houdini that has largely been overshadowed by his extraordinary fame as an escape artist,” said Andrew Gulli, Strand’s editor-in-chief.

“Here we have Houdini the historian, painstakingly documenting forgotten magicians, theatrical performers, old playbills, and the remarkable world of 19th-century entertainment.

“There’s something rather poignant about the world’s most famous magician devoting so much attention to entertainers whose names have largely disappeared from history.”

The article was preserved among many of the artist’s other papers in the Houdini Library at the Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas at Austin, where a curated tour will mark the anniversary of his death on Saturday.

Houdini experts at the University of Michigan, and the online fan site Wild About Harry, told Gulli they believed it has never previously been in the public domain.

“[Finding] a published version of An Interesting Scrapbook turned out to be as elusive as the man himself, which raises an interesting mystery of why,” he said.

“Houdini was an accomplished author and an extraordinarily effective self-publicist. He was also fiercely competitive and protective of his professional knowledge. Could he have deliberately withheld this material because he feared rival magicians might benefit from his research? Or was it simply a project he never completed?

“We don’t know the answer, but the question itself adds another dimension to the discovery.”

Houdini was known to despise spiritualism being presented as anything other than entertainment, and dedicated increasing time in the years before his death from peritonitis debunking performers he called “charlatans” for claiming to be mind readers, or possess supernatural powers.

Several commemorations are planned globally on Saturday to mark the anniversary, including a gala and public events in Budapest, where he was born in 1874; and a séance at his former home in New York.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: This rightwing evangelical was one of Trump’s biggest backers. Why isn’t he talking about the midterms?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Elle Hardy in Dallas, Texas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Lance Wallnau has gathered supporters to talk about Charlie Kirk and school boards – with no mention of GOP

One of Donald Trump’s most influential Christian nationalist backers has privately shied away from rallying supporters for the Republican party before the midterms, instead urging them to focus their attention elsewhere – including emulating El Salvador and Poland, finding a successor for Charlie Kirk and even focusing on their own diets.

At the “As One” weekend for paying “partners” in the Dallas-Fort Worth area earlier this month, Lance Wallnau, one of the first prominent rightwing evangelicals to back Trump in 2015, spoke across three sessions about the virtues of El Salvador’s prison system, school boards and the movement’s future. The midterms, then little more than three weeks away, were not mentioned once.

Wallnau has long espoused being both “overt and covert” in Christian politics, and helped write the blueprint for Christian nationalists within the Maga movement to turn their faith from personal salvation towards political, social and institutional conquest.

Wallnau still champions Trump and Republican candidates in public. In spring, he praised Trump as “an actual Old Testament prophet king” whose “enemies are freaking out” because of his political skill. But behind closed doors, he conceded that the Maga movement is struggling to appeal to young people, and urged supporters to think about building a post-Trump infrastructure, with leaders who will outlast the president.

“Charlie Kirk’s death bothers me,” he told the weekend’s gala dinner, referring to the slain rightwing activist whose murder at a public event in Utah last year galvanized many on the right. Wallnau posited himself as the person to anoint the next Kirk. “I got to find that guy. That’s my job,” he said. “I feel more like a Samuel than a David” – a reference to the Old Testament prophet who anointed Israel’s kings.

Wallnau promoted El Salvador as one nation with “a president through prophecy”, a reference to the country’s authoritarian president, Nayib Bukele, whom he said was building a “sheep nation” – a term for the godly nations that are separated from the “goat nations” in the end times. He also spoke approvingly of eastern European nations Hungary, Slovakia and Poland, all of which have experienced hard-right political surges in recent years.

At home, he pointed followers to the power of local action. He praised churchgoers in Southlake, Texas, for taking over the school board and kicking out “progressive Marxist liberals and demonic ideologies”. He told those upset about a mosque in nearby Irving to “go vote out this city council”, and suggested the movement “infiltrate Islam”.

Speaking candidly at the partner weekend, Wallnau said that privacy was necessary because journalists “stalk me”. In a room in which only a handful of people appeared to be under 40, he acknowledged his following as “an ageing demographic”.

Wallnau, 70, is highly revered in evangelical circles. He co-wrote the 2013 book Invading Babylon: The 7 Mountain Mandate, which urges Christians to take control of seven spheres of society, from government and media to education and business. Two years later, he became one of Trump’s earliest champions, likening him to King Cyrus, the Persian ruler who was not of the Israelites’ faith, but furthered their cause.

Trump appeared to allude to this idea at a recent rally in Kansas, recalling that “a certain pastor from Dallas, Texas” had said: “He might not read the Bible as much as us … But one thing about him – he’s the greatest leader.”

During the 2024 election, Wallnau founded the Courage Tour, a travelling festival of faith and politics that toured swing states for Trump. Despite his ministry booking more than a million dollars in income from the tour, Wallnau has not sought to repeat it in this election cycle.

While Wallnau is often loud in public, his private musings are more telling – and more politically charged. He is an important cog in the Ziklag group, a secretive Texas-based Christian dominionist group with a minimum net worth requirement of $25m for membership. Ziklag’s operations were highly active and influential in the 2024 presidential election, targeting voter turnout, sex and gender issues, and Christian mobilization.

In leaked members-only videos addressing the Ziklag group in 2023, Wallnau laid out ideas for the dark-money group’s electoral strategy: “You almost hate to put it out this clearly, because if somebody else gets ahold of this, they’ll freak out,” he said. The group divided its battle plan into three operations for the 2024 election: Checkmate, which funded so-called electoral integrity groups; Steeplechase, which mobilized churches; and Watchtower, which stoked tensions over sexual identity and parental rights.

In a follow-up “strategic ministry webinar” for As One members last Wednesday, less than two weeks before election day, Wallnau acknowledged the elephant in the room. “We all have a certain responsibility … but you can’t be responsible for the whole nation,” he said, referring to the elections. “You’ve done your job. Your conscience is clear, and whatever comes out in the midterms is going to be. We’ll sort that out when it happens.”

He then urged followers to focus on themselves, rather than politics. “When you’re dealing with something you don’t like, something that isn’t working, something that isn’t clear,” he said, “there’s some seed of a greater benefit that can come out of that … maybe it’s going to be lifestyle, or maybe it’s going to be diet.”

The political content he did offer looked further ahead beyond the midterms and played on familiar far-right tropes. Repeating Trump’s claim that unrest in France was caused by immigration, he warned that “what’s happening in Europe could be coming here in 18 months”. The As One weekend, he said, had been about focusing energies on the future: “Thirty-six months from now, a lot can change.” For now, he was “pulling back” from current events towards Bible studies where “I don’t have to deal with anything negative”.

André Gagné, a professor at Concordia University in Montreal who has followed Wallnau for years, reviewed the transcripts of the events and said that private gatherings like this are a big part of his appeal. “He’s a populist,” Gagné said. “He impresses on Christians the need to get involved in societal transformation.”

Gagné said the silence on the midterms reflected strains in Trump’s coalition, even from some of his earliest, and most victorious, backers: “There’s fractures in the movement,” he said. “My sense is that Wallnau feels he has to tread very carefully with what he’s going to say in overly defending Trump or overly talking about the midterms.”

When Wallnau complains that journalists stalk him, Gagné added, “he’s actually bragging”. And his talk of Kirk’s successor was partly about himself. “He sees himself as someone that’s going to lead the way after Charlie Kirk,” he said. Wallnau’s distancing himself from Trump is not merely strategic, but practical: he has to think of who is coming next – why he is so happy to point to leaders of other nations, such as Bukele in El Salvador. “He talks about there are many Cyruses, that there are all these other very strong leaders that God is raising up,” Gagné said. “Trump is not the only one.”

Wallnau’s most recent book, The Return of the Lion, sets out the stakes in starker terms. “Revival is personal. Reformation is institutional,” he writes. “Jesus is coming back to execute vengeance on rebellious angels and everyone and everything aligned with them.”

At the gala, Wallnau closed out the evening more combatively, asking attenders to stand up with him and participate in a karate chop together. “Here’s the problem,” he said, accusing partners of half-measures. “[If] you don’t break a board, you break your hand.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: The staggering $446m Elon Musk has spent on the US midterms – visualized
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Nick Robins-Early, Andrew Witherspoon, Will Craft, Alvaro Dominguez, and Daniel Wolfe
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
The tech mogul’s midterm donations backing Republicans have made him the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history

Elon Musk has poured so much money into US politics this midterms election cycle that his donations could fund half a dozen SpaceX rocket launches or buy thousands of Tesla Cybertrucks. At the Tesla Diner in Los Angeles, Musk could order more than 31.9m cheeseburgers with the money he has spent on the midterms.

Musk, the world’s richest person, has funnelled at least $445.77m into Republican-aligned political action committees (Pacs) and groups since last year, according to US Federal Election Commission data as of 29 October. The contributions have made him the Republicans’ most prominent financial backer and the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history.

Musk’s spending is a staggering example of the SpaceX and Tesla CEO’s political influence, as he seeks to help Donald Trump’s administration retain control of Congress in the upcoming midterm elections, though current polls predict Democrats achieving a majority. The contributions are at a scale that is difficult to fathom and dwarf efforts from big name megadonors like George Soros or Michael Bloomberg, setting a new precedent for how the rich and powerful attempt to shape politics.

Only last year, Musk claimed he would step away from making large scale political donations after putting nearly $300m towards Trump’s 2024 presidential election campaign. FEC data since then shows he has not only leaned back into financing campaigns, but that his spending has dramatically ramped up as election day approaches, increasing by about $200m in the final two months of campaigning.

Musk’s money has primarily flowed into several Republican-aligned Super Pacs, with his largest contribution of $216m going into his own America Pac. The Pac has targeted 43 House and Senate races across the US, blanketting voters with television commercials, digital ads, text messages and mailers.

America Pac made 839 independent expenditures in House races and 623 in Senate races in 17 states across the country. The spending varies greatly depending on the state, however, with campaigns in battlegrounds such as Michigan and Arizona receiving more of the Pac’s support.

Musk’s Pac has spent the most in his home state of Texas, where a closely fought Senate contest between Democratic candidate James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton has turned into the most expensive race of the midterms. America Pac has overall poured more than $33m into efforts to elect Paxton, while Musk also made a $168m contribution to the Senate Leadership Fund which supports the Paxton campaign.

A large portion of America Pac’s output focuses on attack ads against Democratic candidates such as Talarico, often accusing them of being radical socialists or targeting them over supporting transgender rights. The Pac has spent $28m on anti-Talarico content, including between $300,000 and 350,000 in October on a single Google ad targeting the Texas Senate candidate.

“James Talarico supports parents being charged with child abuse if they do not support transitioning their children,” stated the ad, which was shown more than 10m times over an eight day period.

Musk has also reposted America Pac’s content to his more than 200m followers on X, the social media platform he owns. One of Musk’s posts in October amplified an America Pac attack ad and claimed: “Talarico wants to trans your kids and destroy the border.”

The nearly $446m that Musk has donated this election cycle far exceeds his contributions in the 2024 presidential race, when the tech mogul also held rallies and appeared on stage next to Trump during the campaign. While Musk has been a less visible presence in the midterms, potentially reflecting the US public’s dislike of him, behind the scenes he has greatly upped his financial support for Republicans.

Musk’s spending far outpaces all other donors in the elections, including fellow tech and finance moguls like Marc Andreessen, who also started his own Super Pac. Musk has put more money into this election cycle than what every top Silicon Valley donor, including himself, spent on the 2024 presidential election combined.

The stakes of the midterm elections are potentially high for Musk, who has closely aligned himself with the Trump administration and benefited from its lax policies toward regulating tech and artificial intelligence. SpaceX has also intertwined itself into the government more extensively, landing lucrative contracts this year for Trump’s missile defense program and the use of Musk’s Grok AI chatbot in the Pentagon.

Despite the immense and unprecedented scale of Musk’s political spending, his contributions this election are still only a tiny fraction of the centibillionaire’s overall assets.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Can Democrats win Maha voters after Trump let them down?
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Jessica Glenza
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
The party is hoping they can integrate the public health message with grassroots concern, but leave behind conspiracy theories

Chellie Pingree remembers when she moved to Maine as a teenager in the 1970s – she was one “hippie” among thousands in the back-to-the-land movement, when baby boomers fled to the sticks to revitalize small organic farms.

Today, she’s a Democratic US Representative for Maine, but still knee-deep in the organic movement. And she’s starting to see a lot of new faces – many pulled in by the Make America Healthy Again (Maha) movement, largely led by the Trump administration’s health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr.

“I just went to a conference in upstate New York,” said Pingree. “I was a speaker there with Thomas Massie, the Republican from Kentucky, on a panel talking about this coming together of liberal, environmental, organic types and Republican libertarian Maha types,” she said.

Then she ticked off some of the people there: “all these young Maha people like Vani Hari,” known online as Food Babe, “and the woman from Ballerina Farm”, citing two well-known Maha influencers.

This overlap has Democrats excited. In a midterm election where public health has been on the offensive for the first time since 2020 – including a list of high-profile candidates who are doctors and nurses – the party has sought to court Maha voters who have soured on the Trump administration over the last year. The hope is the party can bring together a coalition of “pro-science” public health advocates and those highly concerned about a toxic food system and prevention.

“I’m just thrilled that there are Republicans who are activists on these issues related to ultra-processed food and chemical toxins in our food, who want healthier school lunches for our kids, and who don’t believe we should give big chemical companies immunity if they’re poisoning our food or water,” said Pingree.

However, leaders of the loose coalition formed during Kennedy’s independent bid for president in 2024 also tend to overlap with anti-vaccine advocacy and conspiracy theory – the narrow end of what some researchers describe as the online “radicalization funnel”. Further, unlike the back-to-the-land movement, many aligned with the Maha movement have something to sell.

“One of the smart things that [Kennedy] did during his presidential run was he identified a bunch of different fringe communities,” said Derek Beres, one of the hosts of the Conspirituality podcast, which tracks the Venn diagram of conspiracy theory, pseudoscience and extremism. “He was going to Farm Alliance groups, he was going to crypto conferences, and he was in the anti-vax circles, obviously. With that, he’s just made a lot of inroads with people who became known as Maha Moms.”

At a Children’s Health Defense event in September, the anti-vaccine organization Kennedy led before he became health secretary, he even pledged to investigate “chemtrails”, the long-time conspiracy theory that condensation trails from planes are in fact toxic chemicals.

Whether Democrats can woo this coalition without alienating long-time supporters, who see the party as aligned with scientists and social programs, is an open question.

“Now, we’re in a weird period of time where there’s a lot of frustration with some of the activists in Maha and feel like they still strongly support RFK, but they believe this administration is backed down on its commitment,” said Pingree. Particularly, she added, “in the glyphosate issue”.

Maha’s well-documented fracture with Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement began in 2025, when the administration announced it would continue to allow use of the pesticide dicamba, banned in some countries and known to drift across fields. Then, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) approved a new pesticide ingredient containing Pfas, sometimes called a “forever chemical”, despite health concerns. In response, Kelly Ryerson, better known as Glyphosate Girl online, and other influencers circulated a petition for the ouster of EPA administrator Lee Zeldin.

“This isn’t Kennedy’s fault, but he seems to have absolutely no power to regulate the chemicals, even though he was put as head of this Maha commission,” said Ryerson.

Then in February this year, the administration issued an executive order describing an “adequate supply” of glyphosate as a “national security” issue. Glyphosate is the active ingredient in the widely used Roundup herbicide, linked to cancer in scientific studies, and designated as a probable human carcinogen by the World Health Organization in 2015. Bayer denies that the product causes cancer and the EPA has found that glyphosate is “unlikely” to cause cancer. In March, the justice department backed Bayer in a so-called friend of the court brief to the supreme court, and a subsequent decision blocked thousands of lawsuits against Bayer.

“We really have seen over the last few months that the White House is committed to keeping these pesticides on the market, because they’re working on behalf of the pesticide companies,” said Ryerson. “And it’s really disappointing and entirely counter to Maha.”

Other Maha priorities, such as making American food healthier, have also fallen short. Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced it would define ultra-processed food in August, but failed to actually issue a definition. Kennedy oversaw a hobbled Food and Drug Administration (FDA) during the worst outbreak of diarrhea-inducing cyclospora in the country’s history. Finally, he has made little progress on improving school lunch.

Most recently, Kennedy adviser Calley Means quit the administration, reportedly frustrated by the lack of progress.

As the midterms close in, Kennedy has attempted to find a victory. This week, he announced a voluntary program for hospitals to certify their food is healthy. Kennedy also successfully proposed changes to FDA law that allow food manufacturers to use ingredients “generally recognized as safe” (Gras).

And there appears to be daylight between the concerns typically espoused by Maha’s unofficial leaders and voters who identify with the cause. The biggest health concern for most Maha voters is still affordability. In a poll by Kaiser Family Foundation, 42% of Maha voters said lowering the cost of healthcare and prescription drugs was their most important health issue. That’s double the next biggest point of agreement, restricting chemicals in the food supply.

But for as much agreement Democrats appear to have on the top issues, there are also rifts, particularly on vaccines. Many in the Maha movement feel burned by Covid-era lockdowns, said Ryerson. At the same time, Kennedy has become a powerful symbol for why public health leaders decided to run for office in opposition.

“Since RFK Jr was nominated and came into office, RFK Jr has been our number one recruitment and fundraising tool – hands down,” said Erik Polyak, executive director of 314 Action, which focuses on recruiting and electing “pro-science” Democrats. “He has motivated hundreds of doctors, public health leaders and nurses to stand up and run for the first time.”

Indeed, the list of Democratic doctors and nurses running for office across the country is impressive. Among many, physician Amy Acton is running for governor in Ohio, pediatrician Annie Andrews is running for US Senate in South Carolina, and in one of the most widely watched races in the country, Abdul El-Sayed, a physician and public health official, is running for US Senate in Michigan.

“For all intents and purposes, Maha is now dead, RIP,” said Polyak. “After this election, I think the next thing we’re going to see is RFK Jr’s head on a platter, because we know RFK Jr is a political liability.”

How far a Democratic Maha alliance will go is unclear. Pingree gave a real-world example in her own office.

“The first time I met with Moms Across America”, an organization founded by Maha influencer Zen Honeycutt, “she gave me five flyers, and one was Pfas, one was school lunch, one was glyphosate – but one was vaccines, and one was 5G. And I just said, ‘Look, I work on these three issues; I don’t work on those two issues.’”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Men detained at Texas’s ‘dog pound’ ICE facility describe their experience – in art, letters and song
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: José Olivares
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Nearly 500 men are detained at the T Don Hutto detention facility, and many have risked sharing their experiences in a unique way

What goes on inside Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention centers across the US happens behind closed doors and high fences.

Personal accounts of lengthy detention, misery and sickness and allegations of abuse rarely reach the public directly while people are still behind bars.

But a group of men detained in Texas found a new way to communicate what they are going through in custody, despite being shuttered from the outside world. They compiled hundreds of pages of handwritten testimony and some hand-drawn art, and mailed it from inside the privately run ICE jail.

One man even wrote two protest songs and sang them over a crackly prison pay phone to the Guardian. In a solemn and defiant tone, he sang from the perspective of one detainee to another: “We are the people, raising our voice. You are my brother, brother I am. Today as you find yourself in this prison, give me a hug, I give you love.”

Others’ stories were scribbled on notepaper, between July and September this year.

“We are immigrants, we are not criminals,” one wrote. Distraught, the men blame their situation on “nothing more than the result of racist policies” by the Trump administration.

“Why is it that a simple migrant, who one day leaves for work, can end up not seeing sunlight nor breathing pure air for days, simply due to a status adjustment?” one writes, nodding to Donald Trump’s actions of detaining immigrants despite them having temporary legal status or ongoing cases.

The men find themselves “behind bars, living an experience that marks a ‘before’ and ‘after’ for the detainee and his family”, another testimony says.

The detainees are at the T Don Hutto detention facility in Taylor, on the outskirts of Austin, a place nicknamed “la perrera” – Spanish for “the dog pound” – to reflect harsh conditions.

The package of writings and art was mailed to a detainee’s relative and shared with the advocacy group Center for Popular Democracy, which shared it with the Guardian.

Many tens of thousands of people are detained by ICE across the country – the majority without criminal histories – amid the anti-immigration crackdown. The men’s reported experience is common, but their way of communicating it is not.

The Guardian received testimonies from at least five detainees after months of detention, but is withholding most identifying details for their safety.

They add up to almost 200 pages of narratives in Spanish, drawings and documents. The T Don Hutto facility is run for ICE by the private prison company CoreCivic. The men wrote that the facility makes them feel not like people but like “inventory”.

One explained that they wanted to “alert, denounce and affirm what is seen, lived and felt daily, while being detained”.

One series of drawings depicts a man waving to his family as he leaves for work, but then being arrested by ICE officers swooping outside a grocery store and locking him up. Other, sparely drawn sketches show the detention center’s bleak cells, hallways and communal areas, along with an immigration court.

The fiery testimonies make allegations of abuse by CoreCivic guards, and substandard food and medical care.

“CoreCivic plays a limited but important role in the immigration system,” a company spokesperson said in a statement. “We do not decide who is detained, for how long, or whether someone is released. Our job is to care for the people at our ICE-contracted facilities safely, humanely and with dignity while their cases proceed.”

“The safety, health and well-being of the individuals entrusted to our care is our top priority. We do not dismiss the concerns of the people in our care, and we respond to legitimate issues through established processes,” the spokesperson added.

The detainees also sent out a list of demands, including calls for their immigration cases to be processed more quickly, to be reunited with families, the release of children from other immigration centers and of detainees with developmental disabilities. They also called for investigations into the rising number of immigrant deaths in ICE detention.

“These first-hand accounts reveal more than what is happening inside a single detention facility. They expose an entire system that strips people of their dignity, separates families and treats fundamental constitutional rights as optional,” said DaMareo Cooper, co-founder of the New York-based Center for Popular Democracy, a progressive advocacy organization. “What is equally powerful is the extraordinary courage of those risking so much to speak out. Behind every testimony, every piece of artwork and every story is a human being enduring unimaginable pain.”

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said that “any allegations of subprime conditions or misconduct at the T. Don Hutto Detention Center are FALSE”.

“All detainees are provided with 3 meals a day, clean water, clothing, bedding, showers, soap, and toiletries,” a DHS spokesperson added. “Illegal aliens also have access to phones to communicate with their family members and lawyers. Certified dietitians evaluate meals.”

However, the men, who regard some of the testimonies as a collective appeal, write: “Being an immigrant does not mean you do not have rights.” They go on to say that their notes and drawings were done “for those who will be here, for those of us who are here, and for those who left”.

The Hutto facility is relatively small and detains only men. In late September, there were 497 total detainees – almost reaching full capacity, according to a review of a daily roster page. Most people were booked into the facility in 2026, with many others in 2025. Two men have been detained for more than three years, since September 2023, according to the roster.

“We know some community members in there right now – we get a lot of information about how bad it is,” said Alejandro Caceres, an organizer with the Austin Sanctuary Network, an immigrants rights group in Texas. Caceres said he had also heard repeated complaints about alleged retaliation by guards, substandard medical care and food, and the use of solitary confinement in the facility.

A Honduran father describes in his testimony how he was arrested by ICE in San Antonio, Texas, in August, after seven years in the US. He says he does not have a criminal record. He worked at a mechanic’s shop, and cycled to a convenience store during break to get coffee and cigarettes, but as he was leaving, he says, he saw a black vehicle speeding towards him.

“I thought it was someone driving drunk or under the influence of drugs, or someone who wanted to kill me,” he writes.

He described his fear as the people in the vehicle jumped out and pepper-sprayed him. He lost consciousness and woke up to officials splashing water on his face, he said.

“It was exactly at that moment that I discovered they were ICE,” he writes. The Guardian was unable to confirm his account.

Detainees also accuse guards of abuse. In late September, a detainee described how he saw a Cuban man attempt to take a piece of bread from the cafeteria back to his cell to later eat it “alongside his coffee”. The guards would not allow it, so he quickly ate it in defiance. According to the written account, the confrontation escalated, with guards beating him to the floor, bleeding. Other detainees “only saw through glass how they beat their companion”, the detainee wrote.

In a statement, CoreCivic said that incident “was reviewed in coordination with ICE, and it was determined that excessive use of force was not used”.

DHS did not respond to any of the specific allegations of abuse, with a spokesperson saying the department “are not going to entertain unnamed allegations from the Guardian”.

One of the men detained in the facility who chose to be named is Julian Osorio Garcia, an asylum seeker from Colombia who spoke by phone from inside and is the man who wrote the protest songs and sang them over the phone.

“I do not know why migrants are treated in such an inhumane way,” he said. “We have so many stories here. I have heard some situations that are extremely difficult.”

Osorio has requested asylum in the US and received a work permit while waiting for his case to be decided. But he was arrested in Texas in May, after he and a friend were pulled over by local law enforcement working with ICE – an increasing trend – according to him and a cousin, in separate phone interviews.

Osorio came to the US in 2023 with a legal tourist visa and about one year later requested asylum after being threatened by criminal groups in Colombia, he and his cousin both said. According to a Colombian judicial document shared with the Guardian, a Colombian magistrate with the country’s special jurisdiction of peace found Osorio to be an “indirect victim” of the country’s decades-long civil conflict.

Osorio’s attorney filed a habeas petition with a US federal judge in June, requesting his release while he fights his case. A federal judge in Texas denied Osorio’s petition in late October, meaning he cannot be immediately released from detention.

“It’s a migratory process that is costing tears, the separation of families, the loss of so much money for families [trying to fight their cases] – it’s leading to death,” said Osorio.

“And how can a private company profit from all this?” he asked, referring to CoreCivic.

DHS wants to deport Osorio. A spokesperson said he entered the US legally in 2023 “but chose to violate our nation’s laws by refusing to depart by the required date”.

“This administration is not going to ignore the rule of law just because the Guardian would like us to,” the spokesperson added. “Osorio Garcia will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending the outcome of his removal proceedings.”

The DHS did not respond to follow-up questions about this. Records show Osorio’s asylum case has not been decided.

In its statement, DHS also said that Osorio had been arrested in 2023 in Texas for driving while intoxicated. Court and arrest records accessed by the Guardian show that he was never convicted in connection with the charge and that the case is “inactive”. DHS did not respond to follow-up questions about the case.

The writings suggest strong solidarity among the detained immigrants. Osorio sang over the phone: “They persecute us, they arrest us, they put chains on us … Let’s all take to the streets, let’s go out en masse, we are Hispanos Free.”

One testimony says that when individual immigrants are released from the facility, the other detainees say goodbye by clapping and shouting as loudly as they can.

“Because, from here, no one leaves that easily,” one piece of testimony said.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Ian Sample Science editor
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
A mile beneath the Black Hills, scientists are building giant detectors to analyse neutrino particles – and possibly find the answer to existence

For more than a century, the mining town of Lead, in the Black Hills of South Dakota, attracted workers with a taste for gold. Now, a flagship experiment being built in the old mine is drawing scientists in search of more intriguing riches: answers to the deepest mysteries of the universe.

Construction of the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (Dune) in the former Homestake mine is due to start on Monday. Engineers will begin assembling four giant detectors inside caverns blasted from rock a mile underground.

Once switched on, the detectors will quietly spark and flicker as ghostly particles called neutrinos hurtle through them. Some will arrive from the sun and distant supernovae, others in an intense beam sent through 800 miles (1,300km) of rock from a government laboratory near Chicago, Illinois.

Observing the neutrinos could uncover entirely new science and shed light on cosmic spectacles, such as the death of stars and the birth of black holes. Scientists are particularly hopeful of solving one of the most enduring puzzles in nature: why everything around us is made from matter and not its “evil twin”, antimatter. In other words, why we, and why anything, is here at all.

“It’s a super exciting time to be working on this,” said Dr Kate Shaw, an experimental particle physicist on Dune from the University of Sussex. “Neutrinos do not make sense yet and they could open a door to new physics.”

Neutrinos are the most abundant matter particles in the universe, outnumbered only by photons, the massless particles of light that illuminate the universe. They are produced in natural nuclear reactions, such as those that power the sun, in radioactive decay and in particle accelerators.

Even by physicists’ standards, neutrinos are oddballs. The chargeless particles barely interact with other matter: about a trillion pass unnoticed through your body each second. Neutrinos come in three varieties, all with minuscule but different masses. Weirdly, they change from one variety to another, a process called oscillation, as they travel. “It’s a very strange behaviour,” said Shaw. “It’s like me throwing you an apple and it turns into a banana.”

Lead has a history with these peculiar particles. In the 1960s, the physicist Ray Davis followed miners down the shaft and built a detector from a 100,000-gallon tank filled with dry-cleaning fluid. Shielded so deep beneath the ground, the detector became the first to record neutrinos from the sun as they struck chlorine atoms in the fluid and turned them into argon.

The mine closed in 2001 and transitioned, thanks to visionary forethought, into a dedicated subterranean laboratory, the Sanford Underground Research Facility (Surf). It is already home to the Lux-Zeplin (LZ) experiment which last month reported the first potential detection of dark matter.

“We’ve gone from mining the Earth to helping scientists explore the universe,” said Robin Lucero, Lead’s city administrator, whose family has lived locally for generations. “We’re incredibly proud and lucky that Dune is happening here, and Surf, which has other experiments like LZ. Having world-class science brings new opportunities, new people and new possibilities for our local businesses and especially our young people.”

Unlike Davis’s apparatus, the Dune experiment is enormous. Made from more than 4,000 tonnes of steel, the detectors will stand up to five-storeys high and hold a combined 70,000 tonnes of liquid argon that must be chilled to -200C. Assembling the detectors should take nearly three years. Filling them with liquid argon, another year.

“This is a heavy duty engineering operation,” and a partnership with the skilled local workforce, said Prof David Newbold, of the UK’s Science and Technology Facilities Council and a Dune spokesperson. “It’s like building a ship underground.” The UK is the largest international partner in the US-led experiment and is making core detector components, critical computing to reconstruct events in the detectors, and the graphite target needed to generate neutrinos at Femilab, a particle physics facility in Illinois.

Once operational, Dune will study an intense beam of neutrinos sent from Fermilab through 800 miles of the Earth’s crust and mantle. Most neutrinos will shoot straight through, but every so often one will strike an argon atom, creating a flicker of light and a pulse of electric charge. Analysing these will reveal intimate details about the mysterious particles.

One big question surrounds the masses of different neutrinos. Which is lightest and which heaviest? The answer could reveal fundamental new forces of nature. And in an attempt to answer the matter v antimatter question, Dune will look for subtle differences between neutrinos and their antimatter twins, antineutrinos.

Beyond the beams of particles sent from Fermilab, Dune will also study neutrinos arriving from space, carrying with them fresh information on stellar explosions and the formation of black holes.

Earlier this month, the Nobel prize for physics honoured the Belgian researcher Francis Halzen, who used a cubic kilometre of Antarctica to detect high-energy neutrinos from deep space. But detection is far from the end of the story. “This really is going to be a golden era,” Newbold said. “There’s a lot more of that to come.”

https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/o.title: The Trump administration wants to give married parents money to stay at home. Will it be enough?
https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/o.author: Gaya Gupta in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/o.text:
Experts say the proposed program prioritizes parents in ‘traditional families’, ignoring the flexibility needed that all families need to support themselves

They intentionally had their children five years apart because paying for two in daycare would have been too expensive. When her first child was born, Hall had to self-fund her maternity leave by drawing on savings. And recently, Hall was laid off from her tech job, leaving her at a crossroads.

“Do we move to a lower-cost daycare? What kind of job should I look for? Can I dial back now?” said Hall, who lives in Seattle. And perhaps the most essential of all questions: “Do we need to completely 100% replace my income?”

More American families than ever consist of two working parents: 52% are dual-income households, compared to 31% in 1975, according to the Pew Research Center. Eight out of 10 of these families say the arrangement has been beneficial to their finances.

Despite this shift in family dynamics, the Trump administration has remained focused on an agenda that emphasizes a “traditional” family structure, where one parent stays home to take care of children.

As part of this agenda, the White House is considering a program that would pay parents $9,000 annually to stay at home, using reallocated funds that are now used for federal programs that typically support single mothers and low-income families, according to the New York Times.

The plan was reportedly proffered by JD Vance, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, who has proclaimed himself a defender of “pro-family” policies. The vice-president penned a Wall Street Journal op-ed in 2021 criticizing federal spending on daycare, claiming that “young children from average, healthy homes can be harmed by spending long hours in childcare.”

“It turns out that normal Americans care more about their families than their jobs, and want a family policy that doesn’t shunt their kids into crap daycare so they can enjoy more ‘freedom’ in the paid labor force,” he wrote on social media at the time.

As vice-president, Vance has continued to angle himself as a defender of families. “To the radicals who wish to abolish my family and the thousands and millions of other families across our country, we have a simple message for them: stay the hell away from our kids!” Vance said at the Republican’s midterm convention in September.

But experts and parents who spoke to the Guardian said the proposed program for stay-at-home parents prioritizes a single type of family structure and ignores the flexibility that families need to support themselves and their children.

“Families of all compositions need help right now. All families do. We should not pit families against each other,” said Chandra Childers, a senior policy and economic analyst at the Economic Policy Institute.

For Natalia Goodnow of Pittsburgh, being a stay-at-home mother of two was a temporary choice that allowed her family to save on the cost of childcare while she went back to school and pursued a second master’s degree. After she graduated, she was forced to delay her next job search after graduating because the waitlist for her child’s daycare, like many in the country, had grew significantly after the pandemic.

Now, Goodnow is balancing taking care of her children while also building up her own consulting business, which she believes will afford her flexibility to work around her daughter’s schedule. She doesn’t expect she’ll ever stop working in some capacity.

There’s also a risk to relying on one parent’s income. Even though her family is able to live “somewhat stable” on just her husband’s income, Goodnow said she’s worried that his career as a physician, combined with the responsibility to support the whole family himself, will lead to burnout.

“I have to have a second income stream created to give him flexibility to scale down, because it’s just not sustainable,” she said, pointing out that the proposed $9,000 wouldn’t be enough to match what she would make if she worked.

Jillian Whitlow, a mom of three who is pregnant with her fourth child, wishes at times that she could stay at home to take care of her children, but after launching a successful marketing business, her husband left his job as a mechanic to take care of their kids.

The choice stemmed from practicality. The cost of daycare for her children was greater than their monthly mortgage payment.

Though Whitlow’s family, who live in Texas, is in a better financial place than they’ve ever been, they still feel the pain of rising costs and are still paying off student debt and loans on their mobile home. Still, Whitlow sees the White House’s proposal as an unnecessary interference in personal family decisions.

“I would love it if there was a lot less government in all of our lives,” she said, “I would love it if each individual family had more freedom to make the decisions that they want to make about the best way to raise their families.”

“It should be up to me and my family to make that decision, and not the government pushing me to stay at home,” Goodnow said.

Childcare costs can pose a major financial burden on families. Forty per cent of households, including those that have one parent who works less than full-time, spend an outsized percentage of their income on childcare, according to a recent report from the Georgetown Law Center on Poverty and Inequality.

The White House’s plan, by reallocating federal funds from the Department of Health and Human Services that have typically gone to low-income, single-parent families, could actually making childcare even more expensive or less available, Childers said.

“The minute you start draining resources that go into funding this childcare pool, then rates have to rise on other families, some of whom may already be stretching to make it as it is,” she said.

Recent policy changes by the Trump administration may also indirectly make it harder on American families, said Liz Hipple, a policy expert at the Georgetown Law Center on Poverty and Inequality. Recent pushes to increase the work requirements for Medicaid and Snap benefits, for example, will probably make it harder for some families to support themselves.

Policies that support higher wages or paid parental leave would go much further to support families, she added.

“If the Trump administration was serious about supporting traditional families with one breadwinner, there are plenty of labor policies that they could support,” Hipple said. “Those aren’t the policies that they’re pursuing.”

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Is AI your new wingman? How chatbots are transforming dating
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: George Francis Lee and Dan Milmo
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Almost 40% of British singles have used AI for romantic advice, from writing messages to assessing potential partners

After Sam’s ex joked that her sister found him ugly, he turned to AI. Google Gemini had a look at the photo and politely disagreed. AI has been his wingman ever since, aiding his dating life by giving pep talks and vetting his messages.

The 27-year-old from Stoke-on-Trent is not the only AI-assisted romantic – a survey of 3,000 British singles published this month by Match Group, the owner of the Tinder and Hinge platforms, found 39% had used AI in their dating lives.

Relying on AI is bad, Sam tells the Guardian, adding he would rather begin dating in person, but there is a “paradigm shift in dating that’s occurring, which is really odd, where everything is expected to start online”.

The proportion of AI use in dating is even higher for younger generations, rising to 66% for members of gen Z (people born in the mid 1990s to early 2010s), and 53% of millennials (those born in the early 1980s to mid-90s).

Sam says pressure to make a good impression on dating apps means a misunderstood message could risk him losing out on dates. “Online dating … as a guy it’s a bit of a ghost town,” he says. “Rather than saying: ‘Hey, how’s your weekend going?’ it’s thinking about what I can pick up that might get a response.”

The most common use of AI across all cohorts, according to Match, is to get advice about someone they are talking to, plan date ideas, practise conversations, write a dating profile or messages, and vet whether profiles or photos are genuine. Using AI to alter a photo is a no-no for the majority of singles, the survey says.

A single mother from New Zealand, who asked to remain anonymous, says she has used AI as a dating mentor. “I did not really date before I met my ex-husband … with ChatGPT I set it up to coach me to become more secure – to not panic about any delay in messaging, to not rush into anything,” she says.

One man from Melbourne, Australia, who began dating after his 20-year marriage ended, says AI made finding his current partner faster by assessing people he “matched” with and testing his responses. “It was getting [to be] quite a lot of work, like all the chats and the profiles. So I thought: ‘How can I use AI just to sort of speed it up a little bit?’” he says.

The 51-year-old adds that the chatbot he was using helped him think twice about profiles he’d overlooked. “[With] my current partner, it was really aggressive with me saying that: ‘Nah, she’s your vibe, she just takes shit photos.’ And then I meet her at a cafe and she’s absolutely drop-dead gorgeous,” he says.

When he told his partner he had used AI in their exchanges, she also admitted to using Anthropic’s Claude chatbot to analyse his responses. He says she joked that the “two Claudes were probably just chatting away behind the scenes”. It is a risky admission, though – about a third of UK singles said they would end a date if they found out AI had been used to write a potential paramour’s messages.

But, while a few singles like to discuss how their date went with a chatbot (7%), far more prefer a group chat (29%) or their parents (20%), according to the Match survey. “Maybe our friends are becoming more distant because of technology, a little more hands off, compared to the generation before us [who] would get together in their flat or the pub and just absolutely dish the dirt,” says Dec, 31, from London, who uses ChatGPT as a “sounding board” when chatting with single men.

Dec says he uploaded his dating conversations to ChatGPT and gave it prompts such as: “Tell me what you think the red flags there are”, and: “What does this connection look like?”

Although deploying the chatbot charmer led to a number of dates, Dec worries that his “brain feels like it’s rotting because everything’s just offloaded to AI now”. He adds: “We all know it’s going to be a bit of a yes man sometimes.”

The Match survey also hinted at a robotic romantic future where autonomous AIs do people’s dating work for them. More than a quarter of respondents liked the idea of two people’s assistants talking to each other and reporting back before the people speak – even if a majority think the idea is “unacceptable”. Match’s head of trust and safety, Yoel Roth, says the company is taking a “hard stance” against bot-to-bot dating.

“In a world where people say that they’re more alienated than ever, are hungrier for connection than ever, we don’t get closer to that goal of human connection by having robots talk to each other,” he says.

Sam agrees that AI can only enhance his prospects by so much: “If I replace my humour with AI I think I’ve died as a person.”

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: ‘The sexy stuff has got to be coming to an end, right?’: Rivals star Aidan Turner on beards, ballroom dancing and putting Poldark to bed
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Rebecca Nicholson
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
His dashing lead role in Jilly Cooper’s bonkbuster didn’t hurt the actor’s pin-up status, but now, he protests, he’s 43 – and a dad

Aidan Turner has a tactical beard. For the last two decades or so, the actor has found himself in roles that have made him a smouldering pin-up. Audiences really love to look at him. You can buy mugs that say, “Today I don’t feel like doing anything … except Aidan Turner.” There are entire Reddit forums dedicated to sharing photographs of him looking hot. He knows this about himself, just like he knows that people want to ask him about it. “I do get asked these questions,” he says, a little wearily. “I do get the, you know, word ‘smoulder’ or ‘sexy’, and all that kind of shit.” So right now, he has a full beard, in the hope that he will not be accused of, for example, smouldering. “I thought it wouldn’t happen so much with the beard,” he sighs. “I thought I could get away with it. I was going for ‘dad’.”

The job of actors is to sell a story as well as they possibly can, and over the years plenty of the stories that Turner has sold have involved romance and sex. He appeared in Les Liaisons Dangereuses at the National Theatre in London this summer, and even the New Yorker noted how much he smoulders. In some ways, Turner is one of those male performers who is, well, a little bit objectified. The fact that he is a good actor, and also known for being sexy, places him in a peculiar bind. If he doesn’t gamely play along, if he points out that he’s getting a bit tired of it actually, then he risks being seen as a killjoy. Sure, there are worse burdens to bear, but at times the star of Poldark and Rivals finds himself in a curious position.

Turner is 43 now. (He is literally a dad – he and his wife, the American actor Caitlin FitzGerald, have got a small son.) His early roles showed off his ability to handsomely, pensively brood. He was a vampire in the sci-fi series Being Human, and played Dante Gabriel Rossetti in Desperate Romantics, writing moody poetry in soft light. Then, in 2015, he starred in the BBC’s hugely popular adaptation of Poldark, which turned him into a household name. As Ross Poldark, an 18th-century soldier, he loved, fought and, very famously, swung a scythe. The attention that came with it made his career, but it also put him off sexy roles for a while. Then a few years later, Rivals came along.

Rivals is outrageously fun and smutty. It adapts Jilly Cooper’s Rutshire Chronicles novels, the kind of books that would once have been known as bonkbusters, into big, brash television. In her fictionalised version of the Cotswolds in the 1980s, Cooper brought together aristocrats, MPs and cut‑throat television executives. Everyone is having sex with everyone; everyone is ready to stab their neighbour in their back, and probably have sex with them at the same time. Everyone, that is, except Turner’s character, Declan O’Hara, a serious‑minded broadcast journalist who is unusually faithful to his wife, Maud – and also dashingly handsome. So here Turner is again, fielding questions about intimacy coordinators, sex scenes and his very full moustache.

The moustache was his idea. “I say it was my idea,” he begins, then corrects himself. “It fucking was my idea.” Turner swears like it is going out of fashion. He has just finished today’s photoshoot, so we have gone to find a quiet spot to chat, and have ended up in a basement, surrounded by bikes and cleaning products and tools.
