He is out of the fancy clothes and back in his east London dad uniform of white T-shirt, navy chore jacket and jeans. He explains that he had turned up for the Rivals job with a full beard, and if they were going to shave it off, he told them, he had no intention of using a stick-on prosthetic. “You end up eating hairs all day and if you smile it falls off,” he says. “I think everyone on set has now learned the lesson of no stickies.” So they shaved him down to a moustache first, and decided they liked it, and that’s what stuck. It also gave Declan a bit more gravitas. “I don’t want to make this about getting into character or anything. All that stuff gives me the creeps, actors talking about that,” he says, squirming. “But [the moustache] is really helpful, because Declan feels older to me. Like, he’s a bit more of a grownup than I am.” Turner grew up in Dublin and has the accent to prove it, but Declan has a Westmeath accent, a bit deeper than his own, which he borrowed from his father, Pearse. “So with that, and the geography teacher outfits, everything feels more mature.”

Rivals has been a juggernaut for all involved. The TV series is nostalgic and knowing, horny and hilarious, but the new episodes find the show in a more gloomy mood. It opens with a funeral – don’t panic; I counted, and it only takes 15 minutes to get to a sex scene – and trouble is brewing for Declan and Maud’s marriage. “It’s a big one,” Turner nods, though spoiler etiquette dictates he cannot say too much.

The fact that Rivals can swing so comfortably between profound grief, camp backstabbing and joyful infidelity gives it a very particular tone. Why does Turner think that audiences have lapped it up? “I mean, I was born in ’83, and there is this yearning for that nostalgia, I suppose. And Jilly Cooper has a certain tone. She was looked over for many years. It was seen as this low-rent, smutty kind of literature, and I don’t know if a lot of people gave it a chance. That doesn’t seem to be the case any more.” He has noticed that it appeals to lots of age groups, and for the first time in a while people in their 20s are coming up to him in the street. “Rivals is funny, and it knows exactly what it is,” he offers. “It’s unapologetic. It’s on the front foot and it’s out there, going, this is what we’re doing, this is who we are.”

Cooper was heavily involved in the first season, and they were in the middle of shooting the second when the author died suddenly, at the age of 88. Turner has fond memories of her. “She was famous for throwing these parties at her house in the Cotswolds that were just exactly what you would imagine,” Turner says. “They were so much fun. The champagne never stopped flowing, and her dogs were everywhere. She was so spirited.” He was filming the immediate aftermath of those funeral scenes when he sensed that something was going on. “It was eerie already, and I mentioned to Victoria [Smurfit, who plays Maud] that this feels weird. It feels very dark, and, like, not Rivals. And then we took a break, and I knew something was up.” The line producer broke the news to the cast that Cooper had died.

Five weeks earlier, Turner says, he had been at one of those famous parties. “And she was making speeches and drinking champagne and introducing me to people. She was her brilliant, funny, filthy self.” Cooper would often swing by the set. “I’m just glad that she got a chance to see the show, to see where it was going and how it was looking, and she was really proud of it.”

Given the amount of sex involved in Rivals, it is no surprise that they use intimacy coordinators to assist with the choreography. Turner remembers the time before intimacy coordinators were commonplace, and he finds it much better, and much easier, now that they are readily available on sets. In the past, he remembers working with directors who were hands-off or awkward when it came to sex scenes. “They just kind of leave it to you. And I don’t know whether that’s a really good thing, you know, because it’s, like, what the fuck do we do? And is this OK? And does this work?” Having a professional who is there to figure that out is really useful. “I think it’s important, especially in a show like this, to sell the scene and to do what we’re doing, because there are so many different types of sex in this show. It helps us a lot.”

Turner was in his early 30s when he got the lead in Poldark, the BBC’s second adaptation of the Winston Graham novels, about a soldier returning home from the American revolutionary war. It turned you into a pin-up, I suggest. He takes a breath so deep that it could fill a Cornish tin mine. “I suppose they were positioning Ross to be that,” he concedes, carefully. “There was a sex in Ross, wasn’t there, I suppose,” he says, with a chuckle, “that previously wasn’t there.” He mentions the photograph of him taken behind the scenes, in a field, topless, with a scythe. For the last 10 years, it has appeared again and again, which, he says, is “all quite embarrassing. It kind of went everywhere.” In it, Turner is being touched up by the show’s makeup artist Jacqui Fowler, who is often airbrushed out of the shot, much to his disdain. “She’s there with the makeup brush, brilliant Jacqui, and I don’t know what she’s doing … ”

Was she painting his muscles? (I meant enhancing them, rather than adding them.) “No! That was something I fucking worked hard for,” he laughs. “I was 12 years younger. It was probably a lot easier to get in shape. But I was, like, no, this guy is a farmer. He’s on the horse all the time. We never really see him eating. When he is, it’s fucking gruel. He’s probably quite lean.” So Turner decided that he needed to get in shape, too. As with the Rivals moustache, it was his idea to go topless in the scything scene, and he had no idea that it would still be talked about a decade later. “I made some friends on the show that I’m still friends with now, and I’m proud of it. It had a really strong audience, and we tried to do something different with it, and I think we did. But all of that stuff was embarrassing, because it just kind of follows you around a little bit. But it might not have been successful if we didn’t have any of that at all.”

For a few years afterwards – until Rivals, in fact – Turner resisted taking roles that he knew would require him to be sexy. Did Poldark put him off? “It did, yeah,” he says. In photoshoots now, for example, he might politely decline to pose in a way that seems suggestive. “It just feels different, at 43, and being a dad,” he shrugs. Then again, he admits, he is here to talk about Rivals. Also, he has just finished Les Liaisons Dangereuses, that famously sex-focused play, in which his character Valmont manipulates women into bed, for sport and for the sheer sociopathic thrill of it. “And you’re, like, well, I mean, you’re asking for it, dude!” he laughs. He is nothing if not self-aware. “But then, I feel like this sexy stuff has got to be coming to an end. Right? Tell me it’s done.” I think that’s up to him. “For sure, and it is. But the roles are getting more interesting, and less about … that.”

Turner has never done social media and says he has never felt any pressure to sign up to it. “No. You would definitely get more free shit if you had a few million followers on Instagram. I do meet people and I’m, like, where did you get that? And they’re, like, oh, it got sent to me.” But he knows it’s not worth it. “I don’t need those trainers. Most people I know are on it, but I don’t really want to share those things. And I don’t think I’d be very good at doing it. I would probably get it wrong. I’d probably either overshare, or not do it enough.”

Turner does not strike me as an oversharer. He mentions early mornings taking his son to school after a late night at the theatre, or trips with him to the West End to see The Lion King and Paddington, but otherwise he is tight-lipped on life outside work. “I draw the line at the personal stuff. And plus, I’ve always just felt, like, who wants to hear from me? I always felt that, in the early days of Twitter or X or whatever. It takes so much confidence, doesn’t it, to go, ‘People want to hear exactly what I have to say in this sentence.’ Wow. The balls on that. Jesus. I’d love some of that courage.”

When not being forced to examine the embarrassment of being objectified as a man in your 40s by horrible, intrusive journalists, Turner is great company. He is funny; he is as charming, as you might expect; and he is more than happy to discuss big, state‑of-the-world stuff. Take this morning. He was listening to a podcast about Meta’s new AI assistant, he says. “They will do shit for you. They’ll order food and deliver it to a friend of yours, and they’ll make sure that if you want to get paid, you’ll get paid, and they’ll make sure your mortgage gets done every month, and they’ll do everything. But you’ve just got to give them all of you.” He realised, for the first time, that he was scared of what might happen next. “There could be a moment where it’s, like, no, sorry, Aidan, there is no money for you. We need that money for a datacentre.” The podcast talked about how helpful AI could be, as well as how destructive. “But this has already been downloaded by millions of people, and I’m, like, we’re walking straight into this fire, aren’t we? This might be coming for us faster than I thought.”

Does he worry about AI coming for his job? The late Gene Wilder’s voice has been reactivated for a Netflix reality show; Tilly Norwood, the world’s first AI actor, has been unleashed on Hollywood, to middling results. “It will get better and better, and it’s about how comfortable we are when it does get amazing and we can’t tell the difference,” he says. “I don’t know whether I want to read a novel from an AI author. I want the human. I want the connection.” Maybe he is showing his age, he says, “but I don’t want to write us off yet. I don’t want a painting that’s been generated by AI. I want to see oil and canvas and acrylic. Call me old school, but I want the humans to win that battle.”

Turner lives in London now, with FitzGerald and their son. He moved to the city in his 20s, after a few years of doing theatre in Dublin. “My first TV job brought me over, and I never really went back,” he says. “I love London. For me, it’s still one of the most exciting cities in the world.” The couple have lived in the US for short periods of time, too, though neither was keen on settling there. For political reasons? “I’m not going to lie. Guns scare me, and we have a young child, and I don’t want to worry about that every day. I know we have our own problems in this country, but the guns thing scares me. I think the healthcare system is completely fucked [in America]. God forbid you’re not very wealthy, because if you get sick and you don’t have much money, or even if you’re doing all right, it will take everything. That just seems crazy to me.”

Turner grew up in Clondalkin, in the west of County Dublin, with his brother and his parents. “We were a working-class family. My dad retired a few years ago, but he was an electrician, and my mum is an accountant.” He had a grandmother who did amateur dramatics, but otherwise there was no history of performing in the family. When Turner realised he wanted to go to drama school, at 18, “there was a certain mould being broken, there”. But, he says, he did have some experience of being on stage. “It would be remiss of me not to say that there was an unusual part of my childhood where I danced,” he begins.

He was not just a casual dancer. He danced ballroom and Latin American from the age of six to 17, and at one point he came third in the All-Ireland dance championships. “That’s weird as fuck,” he laughs. “I mean, not odd, but just not the norm for a kid from west Dublin, which is quite poor. My mum and dad spent a lot of money to fund that.” He describes the world of competitive dancing in vivid detail. “There were trophies everywhere, and we went to a competition and it was tails and suits and numbers on the back, and fake tan and Elnett hairspray and pushy mums.

“I went to schools that were quite rough, and I danced right up until I was 17,” he continues. “And I told everyone!” Was he given a hard time for it? “I don’t think they believed me, that’s my theory.” He has seen old friends who have since read about his dancing years, and they told him that they didn’t think he was being serious. “These are working-class boys, who are 14, 15, and we’re all drinking cider on a Friday night and smoking cigarettes and doing whatever else. And you tell them that you’re away to Blackpool this weekend, that you dance, and they might believe you. But they don’t want to take part in this conversation. They move away. They still want to be your mate, but they don’t have the faculties to deal with this conversation.” He gave up dancing when his dance partner got injured, and while on a break, he applied on a whim for drama school. “I was actually quite a shy kid, and there’s still a lot of that in there,” he says. Acting made him less self-conscious, and he knew straight away that it was the life for him.

Turner has roles coming up that take him beyond the heart-throb. He is waiting for work to start on Grendel, the live-action adaptation of the 1971 novel, which tells the story of Beowulf from the monster’s perspective. Is he playing a monster? “No, no, he’s a warrior. He’s a shit warrior,” he jokes. “I don’t even know how much I can talk about that. I hope it’s still happening.” He also plays the Apostle Andrew in Terrence Malick’s forthcoming biblical epic, about the life of Jesus Christ, currently known as The Way of the Wind, though Malick is, famously, not a fast worker, and it was filmed in 2019. “Surely it’s coming out soon? I don’t know,” he says.

But he has also, briefly, returned to The Diplomat, Netflix’s popular political thriller, reprising his role as the British spy Callum Ellis. And there is no denying it: Callum is a sexy guy. “Oh, come off it. I am not sexy in The Diplomat,” he says, firmly. “That is all you.” He really does think, or hope, that this era is almost behind him. “It must be coming to an end,” he says. But what if he’s got another 20 years of it left? “Oh no,” he says, laughing. Then groans, as if he cannot think of anything worse.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: ‘Never big enough’: inside the booming penis enlargement industry
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Andrew Lawrence
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
In a revealing documentary, a looksmaxxing-influenced world where ‘your social capital is tied to your appearance’ has led to more men wanting more

Man’s obsession with his member is a tale as old as time, writ large in sky-scraping edifices, in allusions that flatter (big dick energy) or offend (prick), in the countless artifacts across the ages that venerate male potency – a porn star’s description of Donald Trump’s “toadstool” penis. But it’s the booming intimate wellness industry – AKA the rash (ahem) of fillers, therapies and cosmetic procedures that have come into vogue since the little blue pill rocked the market – that most intrigued Daniel Lombroso, the esteemed documentarian who made his name at the Atlantic and the New Yorker dissecting male fragility.

“A lot of the stories I worked on at those places were kind of fringy subculture and oftentimes adjacent to white nationalism,” says Lombroso, who became aware of the rising demand for penile enhancement procedures while reporting on plastic surgery trends at the New Yorker. “I started calling all these practitioners. But to make an embedded film the way I do, you need someone who’s very open.”

A 2024 study of US Google searches noted an increase in interest in penile-enhancement injections from 2013 through 2022. Lombardo’s 90-minute film, Manhood, puts male self-esteem issues at the heart of the trend on a cold, chafing examination table. Our guide throughout is Bill Moore, a capitalist in scrubs who gives fresh meaning to the phrase bedside manner. We meet him at home, tongue-kissing a pet lap dog while snuggled up under the covers with his male partner. We behold the full splendor of his naked body, nipped and tucked in retreat from the ravages of time and his own unforgiving eye. “Nobody would suspect I’ve ever had anything done!” he says with bracing cluelessness.

We see Moore hawk outpatient penile enhancement procedures from his Dallas strip mall office for $15,000 and $20,000 a pop and tout the lowly glow-ups as career-changing, sex-life turbocharging, depression-curing – whatever patients need to hear to fork over the dough, really. “Everybody wants a boat that’s one foot longer,” one guy says as Moore sticks a long numbing needle into his nether regions. “The boat is never big enough.”

We see many of these patients (though customers is the better word, since, again, Moore is not a doctor), their faces more obscured than their ink-marked private parts. The inclination toward anonymity owes as much to the physical embarrassment Moore’s clientele bring into the room as to the irony of receiving this kind of care from an out-and-proud gay man – the megachurch pastor, the border patrol agent. It’s wild to see Moore act as a machismo whisperer to men who might perceive him as less than masculine, especially as he reflects on the guilt and fear of rejection he experienced before coming out to conservative Christian family members in the deep south (not that his mother having dementia doesn’t help).

Throughout the film, Lombroso manages to point out these and other paradoxes without casting judgment. “I’m not deep in the looksmaxxing world, but part of what Clavicular and those guys understand is that your social capital is tied to your appearance,” Lombroso says. “Does your penis size matter? Probably not. But there are all these stats about the huge percentage of American men who obsess over it, which was foreign to me. And it connects all these other things we talk about – like how many older American men don’t know how to make a best friend.”

None of Moore’s customers embodies male loneliness quite like Ruben, a father of five who is so desperate to enlarge his penis that he moves his family in with an ex to raise money for an enhancement procedure. “I have to sell my house this weekend, and I’m going to Bill after.” Lombroso recalls Ruben telling him in a phone call. “I was like, ‘OK, I’ll be there tomorrow.’ The only way to make a film like this, because I’m in New York and this was in Texas, was to fly out on a whim every time and just capture things as they happened.”

Ruben fills his days listening to Joe Rogan prattle on about the marginalization of manly men and spends nights performing at comedy open mics in bars to crickets – and zero friends in the crowd. His jokes about child abuse are as wince-inducing as the circular logic of upgrading his manhood. He believes it will help protect and provide for his family, even as it fundamentally destabilizes them. “He’s actually a very loving father,” Lombroso says. “A good guy. But he escapes into these worlds like many of us do, and I think eventually it caught up to him.”

Meanwhile, Lana, Ruben’s poor wife, overwhelmed by the succession of shocks his big dick sidequest has imposed on their lives, is pushed ever closer to divorce. “With very few exceptions, almost none of the partners in the movie wanted them to do this,” Lombroso says. “You see Lana kind of against it, but not taking too strong of a stance.”

But the film takes its strangest turn with David, a handsome young man who seeks out Moore’s help repairing the damage from an enhancement procedure botched by another dubious quasi-physician – Victor Loria, a gruff George Costanza-type who brags about growing up in a “connected” family (“We lived the Goodfellas life,” he says, wondering “when are we going to jail, basically”) and keeps a large malpractice insurance disclaimer nailed to his front office wall like Martin Luther’s 95 Theses. Loria is the film’s villain, in case that wasn’t clear.

David seems plucked from a casting call for the reality TV series Botched, a naive keen to hit control-Z after going under the knife too young and, perhaps, steer others away from rushing down that same path. But as his arc unfolds and his OnlyFans porn-acting past is revealed, it turns out he and Moore have more in common than just deeply religious parents who viewed homosexuality as an abomination. They share a bed, too – with Moore’s partner and the dog. That David risks permanent damage from this corrective procedure only heightens the stakes around the throuple bombshell.

Lombroso calls the effort to compel David’s participation in the film “one of the hardest acts of persuasion I’ve ever done. It took the entire film to convince him. We were going to use AI face replacement. But right around the rough-cut stage, when we realized he was the heartbeat of the story, we flew him into New York and showed him – and he loved it. Told his family everything. Now he’s touring with the film. It’s the best.”

Weaving between David’s feelgood story, Loria’s villainy and Ruben’s allegory is Moore – the honest broker who still lulls customers into thinking he’s a doctor, who travels to conferences to show actual doctors how to get in on the male-enhancement gold rush, and who sells his wares as an antidote to all the cosmetic procedures women can get to feel better about themselves. His massive house and impressive car collection speak more plainly to his motives in this space than his riffs to customers about self-esteem or the blarney about posting their post-op results on his company website.

Moore’s company PhalloFill, which specializes in “girth enhancement”, has expanded to 32 locations across the country. He hopes to make the procedure as common as Botox. “Bill tried to get me to have my penis enlarged,” says Lombroso. The thought never occurred. “I said my mom would never forgive me.”

But the great shame in Manhood isn’t that Moore and other practitioners in this charcoal gray area of medicine lavish their customers with patience and empathy. It’s that few see the tender treatment for what it is: gender-affirming care. “That’s why this movie has a very light touch,” Lombroso says. “So many of these things are funny and self-evident, especially to smart viewers. It’s fun to have these tough conversations and not tell people exactly how to feel in every moment.”

Manhood is now playing in select US cinemas with UK and Australia dates to be announced

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.title: ‘Being hated is very bracing’: Helen Garner on surviving three marriages and being called a ‘rotten feminist’
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.author: Emma Brockes
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.text:
Her unsparing fiction and true crime writing have made her one of Australia’s most controversial and celebrated authors. The author discusses relationships, resilience – and finding global recognition five decades into her career

A few years ago, when Helen Garner had an idea to write a book about Australian rules football, her heart soared then immediately sank. The impetus was Ambrose, her teenage grandson, who played for a local team. Garner enjoyed watching them and wanted to put this into writing. Then the dreary thought: “I’ll have to swot, read the rulebook.” People to whom she mentioned the idea assumed she’d be writing a polemic, “like what it means in society and how terrible it is and what violence means. And I’m going: ‘What a bore.’”

As anyone familiar with Garner’s almost 50-year writing career will know, there is nothing more igniting to the 83-year-old than the invitation to outrun boredom by going off in an unauthorised direction. Garner, who is speaking to me via video call from her home in Melbourne, occupies that tiny category of writers famous enough to be recognised in public. Stopped by strangers in the street, she’s often treated to their strong views about her work. As a result, perhaps, she has perfected a very Garnerian obstinacy, enabling her to resist other people’s bossy opinions which, in the case of The Season, meant no tedious explainers about the rules, history or sociology of Aussie rules football. Instead, says Garner, she envisaged following a single season of Ambrose’s U16s team, the Flemington Colts, as “a nanna’s book”. During publicity, she’d turn up to an event at a library to find “the first five rows packed with nannas; all these white-haired women with hankies in their hands. And I feel nobody writes about nannas. I mean, sentimentally, yes; but I want to say what they’re really like.”

To say what something is really like is the ethos behind all of Garner’s books and it has, on occasion, landed her in spectacular trouble. It has also won levels of devotion from readers who have turned her into an almost guru-like figure in her 80s, turbocharged by the publication last year of her wisdom-heavy diaries – which won the Baillie Gifford prize – and helped, one suspects, by her ability to combine insight and erudition of the highest literary order with a style that is at times comically down to earth. (A classic example: referring to the controversy around The First Stone, the 1995 book she wrote about feminism, Garner says: “I gave a lot of people the shits.” It’s not a line one can imagine, say, Marilynne Robinson delivering.)

The current mania around Garner is a long-overdue correction for a writer who, outside Australia, was ignored and condescended to for decades. In 1987, in a typically sniffy reference to Garner in the TLS, her work was referred to as “Mills& Boon for bohemians”, yet she is now credibly hailed as a contender for the Nobel prize, can fill 900-seat venues in New York, and has seen practically her entire back catalogue reissued in the US. (Carrie Bradshaw was shown carrying a copy of Garner’s 2014 book, This House of Grief, in a scene from And Just Like That … and Dua Lipa interviewed her on her podcast.) All of which Garner shrugs off, referring to herself as an “old kind of warhorse” who was never interested in prizes in the first place, not least, she says, because “you have to put on that look that you’re pleased for the other person”, even when – a typically bracing admission – “their book was not as good as mine”.

The fact is that Garner has always cut through the flab and waffle of so much literary culture in pursuit of something more honest. In her first novel, Monkey Grip, published in 1977 and based on her rackety life at the time, Garner told the story of Nora, a woman with a young child living in a bohemian shared house in Melbourne and on-off dating a heroin addict called Javo. Garner had arrived at this point in her own life partly as a result of fleeing a rigid, repressed childhood in the town of Geelong near Melbourne. As the oldest of six kids, she had frequently clashed with her father, a wool merchant and “a rather domineering person”, she says, who bullied her meek stay-at-home mother and kept no books in the house. After attending an Anglican girls’ school, Garner won a place at the University of Melbourne, where she spent the best part of three years in the pub. “It was a strange time. Once you get estranged from your parents, you go galumphing across the landscape seizing this and throwing out that. I look back and I see a lot of damage. We trampled through each other’s lives.”

This sense of damage would become more profound in Garner’s late 20s after a short-lived marriage to Bill Garner, whom she’d met at college and with whom she had a daughter, Alice. The pair split up when Alice was two and Garner moved into a series of hippy shared houses. It was an unstable life that had what Garner now calls a “kind of berserk quality to it – there was a lot of smashing and breaking that went on”, and only became more precarious when Garner, who had been working as a teacher, “opened my big mouth” and was fired from a school in Victoria for giving an impromptu and explicit sex education lesson. At the same time, she fell in love with a heroin addict and, a few years later, looking back over her diaries from that period, realised she wanted to write about it, embarking on Monkey Grip with the modest ambitions that enabled its fresh, uncontrived voice. “It was a private thing, writing down in a notebook what I thought about what was happening in my life,” she says. “So, I didn’t compare what I had written with anything great or mighty. I thought I’d just tell the story of what happened.”

Looking back now, she finds the novel “rather naive and undefended”. But it thrills her, 50 years on, that Monkey Grip is not only still in print, but highly popular. She was in a shop, recently, “and there was a young bloke who said: ‘Aren’t you Helen Garner? I’m reading Monkey Grip, and we’re living the life!’” She laughs and assumes a look of mock horror. “And I thought: ‘Ooh, don’t do that.’” I’d always assumed Javo had died way back, but fans of the book may be interested to know the real-life Javo is alive and well and living in Hobart, Tasmania, where he has a wife and grandchildren. After offering his spare room to Garner’s own 25-year-old grandchild who was visiting that part of the world recently, he wrote to Garner, “to say how marvellous it was to see our two grandchildren together”.

Monkey Grip, which was written with the electric, offhand energy of a young writer yet to grow self-conscious, caused a sensation in Australia and was followed by a series of short, brilliant novels, including The Children’s Bach and Cosmo Cosmolino, before Garner pivoted to nonfiction in the mid-1990s. (She’d return to fiction in 2008 with The Spare Room, based on Garner’s experience of nursing her close friend through cancer. The book has recently enjoyed an operatic adaptation in Melbourne.) And in the background, always, Garner maintained her diaries, recording her second marriage to Jean-Jacques Portail, a journalist whom she met in Paris, where she moved for a couple of years in the late 1970s while living on a writer’s grant and trying to write her second novel. Portail moved back to Melbourne with Garner, and they split up in 1985. A few years later, Garner moved to Sydney to be nearer to the writer Murray Bail, the man who would become her third and (to date) final husband, and who dominates the last volume of her diaries.

Alongside entries about fashion, art, friendship, nature and the end of her marriage to Bail, the diaries offer readers a chance to witness the epic battle between Garner’s extremely robust writer’s ego and its near-constant collapse. A typical entry, from 1997, reads: “I have to admit to myself that I feel irrelevant, small, hollow, untalented, worthless – and frightened. The energy required to maintain self-command is so great that I am always tired. How repellent one is. If only I were writing something.”

I’m curious about how Garner reconciles these two things – confidence and self-doubt – particularly in the wake of The First Stone, her first nonfiction book, in which she interrogated the case of two female students at the University of Melbourne who accused the master of their college of groping them. A mid-90s cause celebre in Australia, Garner foreshadowed culture wars to come by presenting the story as a possible overreaction on the part of the women, putting the boot in, she says, “to what I thought was a rather punitive form of feminism. I got into a hell of a lot of trouble. Really, it was quite astonishing, the amount of hostility I copped. I was thought to be a rotten feminist; a heretic. I heard that someone on a judging panel said: ‘If this book by Helen Garner even gets on the long list, I will’ … thunderous threats …’” Garner says: “I just laughed. Because I think it’s a sort of compliment.”

The First Stone was much more subtle and ambivalent than its detractors allowed, being a real intellectual reckoning with a complicated subject. Given the response, I’ve always wondered how Garner came back from it. “I had the shit kicked out of me! People savaged me. And it took me a while, but when I got over it, I thought: ‘Well, I survived that, and now I’m free. I can write what I really want. And I won’t have to see if it comes out pure.’ Being hated is very bracing. It’s not destructive. Well, it could be; if I’d published that book now … but the internet didn’t exist then. I did feel miserable and sad and I thought: ‘God, everyone hates me, this is terrible.’ But I didn’t regret it for a minute.”

Because it was the book you wanted to write? “Yeah. And I made mistakes in it; but I got a lot of amazing letters. I reckon I got about 800 and I answered every one. It was quite an exercise; someone would cover me with loathsome abuse and I’d write back: ‘Thank you for your kind letter …’ And the good letters I got were long and thoughtful, saying: ‘I read your book and I’d like to tell you something that happened to me.’ And that made me think I opened up the subject for people to talk about calmly.” It can’t have hurt that the book was a huge bestseller. “Yeah, and that really gave them the shits. And they’d go around saying: ‘Oh, yes, of course Helen’s motivation was purely commercial.’”

It helped that Garner had a career in freelance journalism to fall back on, particularly when she got stuck on a book, This House of Grief, which told the story of the trial and conviction of Robert Farquharson, who murdered his three children to get back at their mother, and which took eight years to finish while the various appeals played out. After the success of Monkey Grip, Garner dashed off a second novel, “and it was crap, and my publisher correctly bounced it back. That was a nasty moment, but they were right. Just because you’ve written one book doesn’t mean you know how to write the next one.” But while better novels followed, including The Children’s Bach, published in 1984 and widely considered her masterpiece, she moved permanently to nonfiction after The First Stone, coming to specialise in a kind of literary true crime with a series of devastating books built around high-profile murder trials.

That shift was brought about in part by her marriage to fellow novelist Murray Bail. Garner’s account of the collapse of that marriage appears in How to End a Story, her third volume of diaries, and it’s quite something; at one point, in a fury at the insidious, unfaithful Bail, she throws cups, an espresso machine and a saucepan full of beetroot soup across the kitchen. Garner writes that Bail belittled and gaslit her, and dismissed her work as inferior to his. “I thought my marriage was the worst marriage in the world and I was the world’s biggest wimp for going along with it,” she says. Since the diaries came out, however, a lot of people have said to her “‘that book is my marriage.’ And that sort of shocks me – they’re talking about a marriage they’re still in. But it can be terribly difficult. I reckon it’s the hardest thing people ever do, being married. Harder than having kids.”

She regards having her only child, Alice – at the age of 26 and without any great planning – as the greatest good fortune of her life. And the happiest she has ever been, she says, has been during these past decades of living next door to Alice and her husband and three children. Bail, meanwhile, comes out of the diaries looking very bad indeed. Any feedback from him since publication? “The answer to that is no. And either he hasn’t read it or he’s saying he hasn’t read it. I haven’t had any contact with him now since long before I published the diaries. We parted badly and painfully and it’s never been mended.” She sighs. “He also published a memoir in which he summed up my part in his life in about three sentences. I was roundly dismissed. And I went on like it was the collapse of civilisation. But. You know. Bless him.”

Given the relative literary reputations of Helen Garner and Murray Bail these days, she can afford to be generous. And, of course, one of the delights of the diaries is the schadenfreude of watching a man flex his superiority over a woman who will, in time, be regarded as one of the great writers of our age. Splitting up gave her just the impetus she needed, she says. “I felt very liberated by no longer living in close companionship with someone who had ideas about literature which were too severe and didn’t suit my work. He had this hierarchy of forms, and I subscribed to them for a long time because I’d been educated to think that as well. But after I split up with him, I relaxed into being a nonfiction writer. And I stopped doing it defensively. I thought: ‘Actually, this is my natural form.’ And I still feel that very strongly: I’m out here, and I’m good at this, and it’s really fun to do, and it gets you out of the house, rather than stewing in your own self-hatred.”

So it was with The Season, in which for the space of winter training Garner showed up every week at the football ground to watch her grandson and his cohorts play. Garner went through her customary period of thinking it was all a mistake, that the book was a terrible idea and she’d never be able to drag it over the line. The toughest experience she ever had with this kind of self-doubt was during the writing of Joe Cinque’s Consolation, her deeply affecting 2004 book about the killing of Joe Cinque, a young engineer from New South Wales whose girlfriend injected him with ‘Get in there and do it!’heroin and was later convicted of manslaughter. “I actually told Maria Cinque, his mother, that I wasn’t going to write the book. I wrote her a letter and said I’m really sorry, I’m going to have to give up, I can’t do this. And she rang me up and said: ‘What do you mean you can’t do it? We gave you our story, you said you were going to do it, you’ll do it! Do it!’ God, I nearly died of shame. I look back on that and think you need someone who’s going to kick you right up the arse. Don’t you think? You don’t want someone who’s going to say: ‘Oh, darling, it must be so hard, I really feel for you.’ You want someone to say: ”

This is Garner’s circuit, from idea to execution via collapse, shame and eventual, dogged persistence. A few days before our conversation, Anne Carson was announced as the winner of the Nobel Prize in literature, a decision thoroughly approved of by her Australian peer. Taped up on the wall of her office, Garner has a poem of Carson’s, which she looks at in times of dire need. “If I ever had a tattoo, I’d have that last line tattooed on me,” she says. “I just think it’s so marvellous.” The poem describes a stormy night at sea, fraught with peril, existential and otherwise. “And the last line is: ‘Nothing for it just row.’”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Top Democrats are fighting a billionaire tax in California. Their voters are on the other side |
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Norman Solomon
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The unprecedented measure has enormous potential nationwide. The clash exposes the party’s corporate-progressive divide

Midway through this summer, a high-quality poll found that Democrats in California were overwhelmingly in favor of the upcoming ballot measure for a one-time 5% tax on billionaire wealth.

The ratio was more than 4 to 1. But the state’s most powerful Democrats – including the governor Gavin Newsom, his near-certain successor Xavier Becerra and the Los Angeles mayor Karen Bass – have lined up with Silicon Valley billionaires who’ve raised upward of $340m to defeat the initiative.

While Newsom has led the charge against the measure, most Democratic leaders in the deep-blue state have opted to duck. California’s senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff have stayed mum on Proposition 40. The same is true of the former vice-president Kamala Harris and the former House speaker Nancy Pelosi.

“Neither wants to alienate wealthy donors or their allies in labor by publicly opposing it,” the San Francisco Chronicle noted in mid-October. “But their silence on such a high-profile measure is giving cover to the billionaires” fighting the measure.

Nine-tenths of the billionaire tax revenue from Proposition 40 would go to healthcare for Californians in need. As the New York Times reported this month, “California stands to lose around $100 billion in federal Medicaid funding over the next five years, threatening healthcare coverage for millions of low-income residents, as well as the potential closure of hospitals and other facilities.”

With so much at stake in human terms, refusal to back Proposition 40 runs directly counter to standard rhetoric from Democratic politicians about standing up to the ultra-wealthy on behalf of the disadvantaged.

The stance of Newsom and other Democratic heavyweights in the state puts them on the side of billionaires in ongoing class war. The effect is that party leaders are offering a kinder, gentler oligarchy as an alternative to the far more corrupt Trumpist version.

Overall, a semblance of party unity has taken hold with the midterm elections looming. But clashes between corporate Democrats and progressives will soon begin to escalate.

The fact that the most prominent Democrats in the country’s most populous state are at loggerheads with the party’s grassroots on Prop 40 is a bad sign, but it’s hardly an anomaly.

Every time a general election nears, party leaders fervently call for a huge turnout – but their disconnect from the party’s base discourages turnout. California’s billionaire tax proposal is unprecedented, but the response to it from Democratic party elites is part of a pattern that has undermined capacities to build populist momentum against Republicans, let alone advance progressive agendas favored by voters.

Now being vilified by an onslaught of attack ads, Proposition 40 might get buried under the avalanche of billionaire cash (with nearly half coming from the Google co-founder Sergey Brin). The proposal’s foes have out-fundraised supporters by nearly 10-1.

But whatever the election’s outcome is on 3 November, campaigning to tax the wealth of the country’s nearly 1,000 billionaires has enormous potential nationwide.

In early August, the California Democratic Party executive board, hardly a bastion of class struggle, voted to give the party’s endorsement to Prop 40. But, undeterred, Newsom has gone all-out to fight the billionaire tax proposal as well as to boost another ballot measure that would nullify any such tax.

When I contacted a former chair of the state party’s Progressive Caucus, he was matter-of-fact about the alliance of big tech moguls with the current and next governor. “When it comes to Newsom and Becerra opposing the billionaire tax,” said Amar Shergill, a Sacramento-based attorney, “you need know only two things. First, Newsom needs billionaire money for his presidential campaign. Second, Becerra needs to pay back the billionaires that made him governor. The rest of the corporate Democrats in office are some version of these stories.”

Newsom became governor in 2019, following Jerry Brown’s second eight-year stretch in the job. His unique style aside, Brown has long been a kind of prototype for the state’s Democratic leadership now typified by Newsom.

“The way you have to approach the political process is something like piloting a canoe,” Brown said in 1979 during his first stint as governor. He explained: “If you paddle a little bit on the left side, then you paddle a little bit on the right side, you keep going right down the middle.”

This year, Brown has stayed out of the battle over Proposition 40. In late October, when I emailed the former governor to ask whether he supports it, he replied: “I have not discussed the proposition. There is already a plethora of opinions on the measure.”

Weeks ago, during a BBC interview, Brown lamented: “The gains for those who succeed at the top are getting bigger and richer, and the sustenance at the bottom and the middle is getting less and less.” He added: “We obviously need a wealth tax. If Tesla wants to give Elon Musk a trillion dollars over 10 years, then the people have to take back 99% of it. Now, can you get that? No, not at this point. Can you get it in one state? No, that would not work. Can you get it in one country? Probably not. So it would take an international agreement to tax the very wealthy, so that you can’t accumulate at the level that they are today.”

Brown and Newsom share a fondness for voicing lofty principles while kicking them very far down the road, tacitly equating deference to corporate power with realism. Newsom says – with scant details – that he would support a federal tax on billionaires. Meanwhile, he claims that approval of Proposition 40 would cause many of California’s more than 200 billionaires to move out of the state, with disastrous results.

“Proposed tax hikes on the rich invariably produce grim warnings of millionaire flight which then don’t eventuate,” the journalist Harold Meyerson recently pointed out. “Even if they did in this case, as a paper for the National Bureau of Economic Research has documented, the revenue gain of roughly $100 billion that the [billionaire] wealth tax would yield wouldn’t be offset by reductions in the income tax revenue produced by the flight of every one of those 200 billionaires until 25 years had passed. If just 50 of those 200 billionaires fled, it would take a full century.”

A large majority of the 45 Democrats in the California delegation to Congress richly deserve the “corporate” label. The official website of the Proposition 40 campaign lists only two congressional endorsers in the state. One of them, Representative Ro Khanna, has emerged as California’s most visible and vocal politician advocating for Prop 40.

“It’s the most important ballot initiative in America and in the world,” Khanna declared during a recent interview on MS Now. Looking ahead, he asked: “Are we going to continue to cater to a donor class that has hollowed out jobs, hollowed out the working class, and lost us two elections to Donald Trump?”

That kind of rhetorical question could progressively reframe the race for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028.

“This is a fight for the soul of the Democratic party,” Khanna told me last weekend. “Will we be beholden to billionaire donors and offer platitudes without policy like Gavin Newsom, or will we reclaim our FDR courage and offer a bold vision for our nation’s future?”

Exactly 90 years ago, speaking at Madison Square Garden on the last day of October 1936, the then president Franklin Delano Roosevelt scorned the rightwing plutocrats of the day: “They are unanimous in their hate for me – and I welcome their hatred.” Leaders of today’s Democratic party have failed to earn such hatred.

Norman Solomon is the director of RootsAction and executive director of the Institute for Public Accuracy. His latest book is The Blue Road to Trump Hell: How Corporate Democrats Paved the Way for Autocracy

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump boosted half of US coal plants with taxpayer dollars and ‘free passes to pollute’, report says
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Hilary Beaumont
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Environmental Defense Fund analysis shows administration handed out $950m and Clean Air Act exemptions

It’s a good time to be a coal plant in the US. The Trump administration has given support to almost half of the nation’s coal plants, helping them to continue operating despite economic and regulatory headwinds, according to a new analysis by the Environmental Defense Fund.

The analysis, which looked at the 184 operating coal plants that are connected to the grid, found that 90 received support from the Trump administration through “cash handouts, free passes to pollute, and requirements to stay online past their retirement dates”.

The administration provided $950m in taxpayer dollars to 24 coal plants and handed Clean Air Act exemptions from toxic pollution limits to 70 coal plants, according to the EDF analysis.

“It’s extending the life of these coal plants,” said Surbhi Sarang, director and senior attorney at the Environmental Defense Fund. “The administration has leveraged a multitude of tools to prop up coal plants, and ultimately all of that is harming Americans even more by increasing electricity costs, by increasing pollution – it’s like Americans are getting hit twice.”

In 2015, the EPA’s Mercury and Air Toxics Standards first took effect, driving down dangerous pollution from power plants by more than 90%. In 2024, the EPA updated the standards to further reduce harmful pollution from coal-fired power plants. In the early days of the second Trump term, companies were invited to email the administration to request an exemption from the 2024 standards. According to emails obtained by the EDF through Freedom of Information Act requests, companies expressed concern that the standards would cost them too much money.

The Colstrip plant in Montana has operated for more than 40 years, affecting nearby communities like the Northern Cheyenne reservation by releasing toxic chemicals like mercury, arsenic, lead and nickel. “That’s one of the dirtiest coal plants that’s still operating in the nation,” Sarang said.

In 2024, the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards for coal-fired power plants was strengthened in several ways. For example, the standard for fine particulate matter, or fPM, reduced allowable emissions of nickel, arsenic, lead and other toxic metals from coal plants by two-thirds. According to the EDF, NorthWestern Energy and Talen Energy, which own and operate the Colstrip plant, requested an exemption from the fPM requirement.

Brian Bird, president and CEO of NorthWestern, wrote an email to the Department of Energy in March 2025 asking for a 15-minute chat about the standards with administrator Lee Zeldin. In the email, obtained by EDF, he argued that it would cost $500m to comply with the new rule: “It is ludicrous that our customers would have to cover the costs of a $500m investment for such a slight improvement to particulate matter capture,” he wrote.

The Trump administration gave NorthWestern an exemption from complying with the 2024 updated standards, which the administration went on to repeal in February.

Sarang said the Colstrip plant had not installed modern pollution controls that could reduce emissions. If it had been required to comply with the 2024 updated standards, it would have had to upgrade its equipment, she said: “It would have had pretty significant impacts on air pollution.”

NorthWestern, which became Colstrip’s majority owner earlier this year, describes the coal plant as a “dependable bridge to a cleaner energy future” that supplies reliable energy “until viable, equivalent, carbon-free energy resources are commercially available”.

Asked to comment on EDF’s report, NorthWestern said its technology at the Colstrip plant is “state of the art” for removing sulphur dioxide, and is 99.6% efficient in removing filterable particulate emissions. The company said if the updated 2024 federal standards had taken effect, it would have required it to become 99.8% efficient by 2028, costing hundreds of millions of dollars. The company said its mercury emission control at the Colstrip plant meets current state and federal requirements.

Another coal plant that received a pass from the Trump administration is the WA parish coal plant outside of Houston, Texas. Community members living nearby have called for it to be shut down due to its planet-heating CO2 emissions and what they say are ‘hazardous’ levels of particulate matter.

The plant’s owner, NRG, asked the Department of Energy for an exemption for all of its coal-fired facilities including the WA parish plant, arguing that its facilities wouldn’t be able to comply with the new standards and would need to “derate in order to comply”, taking megawatts off the grid in “critical areas”, according to an email obtained by EDF. NRG wrote that complying with the regulations “with razor thin margins” would risk the affordability and reliability of the grid.

A 2018 Rice University study found that the plant is responsible for as many as 177 premature deaths each year from PM 2.5, which are particles small enough to enter the bloodstream through the lungs, causing increased rates of respiratory diseases, heart attacks and strokes. “Our research has shown that WA parish is the deadliest power plant in Texas,” explained Rice professor Daniel Cohan.

Cohan said plants across the country were supposed to meet the 2024 updated standards. “Trump is letting them off the hook from the more stringent version of the standard,” he said.

“It lets them stay open longer,” Cohan explained. “Many coal plants in this country are barely on the edge of breaking even, and so any regulations that force them to spend more money to clean up their pollution is likely to cause some of them to choose to retire and be replaced by cheaper and cleaner sources.”

The administration defended its support for the coal industry in a statement. “The Democrats’ energy-subtraction policies shuttered American coal plants that provided reliable, affordable power to families and businesses when they needed it most. President Trump promised to revive America’s coal industry, and the Trump Administration has backed and saved more than 100 coal plants this term. By championing beautiful, clean coal, President Trump has prevented the retirement of more than 17 gigawatts of power and saved lives during heightened demand periods,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers wrote in a statement.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Affordability, AI and Iran: Americans on the key issues guiding their midterm votes
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Guardian readers share their concerns and disillusionment with the political climate under Trump as elections loom

Millions of Americans will head to the polls on 3 November in elections that will determine control of the Republican-held House of Representatives and Senate, as well as the governorships of 36 states.

The midterms come amid mounting public frustration over issues ranging from the rising cost of living and immigration to the climate crisis, artificial intelligence, big tech and the US’s overseas wars. Donald Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 36%, according to a New York Times/Siena poll conducted this month.

Voters across the US described to the Guardian their concerns and disillusionment with the current political climate, with one characterizing the country under the Trump administration as a “rogue nation, ungoverned by the rule of law”. (Some respondents only shared their first name or declined to share their name for privacy reasons.)

For many, the cost of living is a central concern ahead of the midterms, particularly as inflation reaches 3.7%.

Kathryn Warren, a retired staff member from Dare county schools who lives on Hatteras Island, North Carolina, said she and her husband had already voted early.

“We are dying on the vine in this economy. We live in a remote area and the cost of gas is taking a big chunk of our social security. Groceries and medicine are outrageous. The medicine that keeps me alive costs $7,000 a month before insurance. In what world is that reasonable?” Warren said.

A 36-year-old counsellor in Tennessee described financial pressures compounded by health issues and expressed concern about the US “sliding into an authoritarian state”.

“I have a migraine medication that costs nearly $2,000 out-of-pocket for a month’s supply. My health insurance has agreed to pay for five months. That’s it. After 24 years of chronic migraines, I have tried everything under the sun and this is the first medication that has ever reduced the pain levels, so it isn’t like I can try some cheaper, knock-off brand. But I find it absurd and financially prohibitive to spend that much on medication every month,” she said.

Vicki Stein, a 66-year-old retired marketing communications professional from Alpine Township, Michigan, said she had already voted for Democrats across the ticket.

“Working Americans can’t afford healthcare, let alone gas nor groceries due to tariffs, and children are losing Snap benefits while we blow our gold on [Israeli prime minister Benjamin] Netanyahu’s war. We can’t even trust our lettuce under this administration’s [Department of Health and Human Services],” she said, referring to a cyclospora outbreak across 27 states this summer that was traced to contaminated lettuce.

George, a 23-year-old business school graduate in Houston, Texas, also linked the affordability crisis to the administration’s policies, criticizing “Trump’s idiotic tariff scheme”.

“The priorities of both parties are clearly more in line with billionaires than regular people … It has been heartening to see politicians like [James] Talarico abandon that side of politics to focus on affordability and quality of life for average Americans. Who cares about 1% of the population when everyone is struggling?”

George also criticized the US’s war in Iran and called for the US to divest from Israel, saying: “Billions upon billions of American taxpayer dollars spent on killing children. No matter how you cut it, all we get from our investment in Israel is a mountain of dead bodies. Any politician who refuses Aipac money or promises to stop funding Israel’s perma-war has my vote and many other Americans’ as well.”

Opposition to the US war in Iran and military aid to Israel remains a driving concern among voters.

Joel Young, a 66-year-old retired civil litigator in Albuquerque, New Mexico, said: “The single most important issue in any election for federal office is whether the candidate or incumbent will approve another dollar, weapon, or material to support Israel, or support the US’s historical pattern of cover for Israel’s apartheid regime and program of ethnic cleansing in place since 1948, which has now clearly become genocidal.”

A 30-year-old machine operator and father in Bogalusa, Louisiana, who voted for Trump in 2024, also criticized the “evil war against Iran which must end”.

“Every day it continues is another day that the president scandalizes our service members, taxpayers and nation. It’s also another day of stealing present day purchasing power from embattled American workers, stealing future prosperity from our children through a climbing national debt and stealing tranquility from people in the Middle East,” he added.

Beyond economic pressures and foreign policy, voters also raised concerns about the growing influence of AI and big tech.

Dave Neps, a 74-year-old retired teacher in Georgia, said: “I’m … concerned about the AI financial bubble. This market reminds me of the dotcom crash in the late 90s and the financial crash in 2008. My wife and I lost money both times in those markets. Now I’m looking at a pension and a country that’s heavily invested in AI that so many of us don’t want. Give these guys time and they’ll just turn it into another commodity that we’ll have to pay for like cable TV.”

Joy, a 47-year-old insurance executive in north Georgia, similarly raised concerns about the expansion of datacenters and the influence of technology companies on local government.

“I live in rural Georgia where they are buying off local officials to build datacenters and the county and city reps are ignoring their constituents and offering massive tax incentives,” she said, calling for datacenter moratoriums.

The climate crisis and environmental protection were also prominent concerns, particularly among older voters who described witnessing the degradation of natural spaces over their lifetimes.

David Tucker, a 57-year-old registered nurse in Washington, said: “The climate crisis and public lands protection are my main concerns, along with protecting democracy and healthcare funding cuts. I grew up in Utah and spent a lot of time camping and fishing with my parents and siblings on public forests and deserts. Natural spaces and our ecosystem are essential for our survival.”

Similarly, Kaye, a 71-year-old resident of Bothell, Washington, said: “While Donald Trump is evil and incompetent in so many ways, the degradation of the planet is my greatest concern as it is larger than all of us and we’re so close to a tipping point that will be catastrophic. I’m old enough to have known a world with more birds and animal species; where the forests, coasts and plains were so much more alive. Our vile destruction of the land that feeds us is tragic.”

Another 78-year-old Washington resident similarly described the climate crisis as the “biggest threat to the planet and causes suffering, disease, fear, inequality”.

“A candidate with a clear track record of ethical standards, who is direct about the threat, and who can muster a coalition to face it will have my vote. This issue is bigger than political affiliation,” she added.

Immigration enforcement and fears of voter intimidation were other major concerns, with some readers expressing alarm about potential federal interference in the midterm elections.

Katie, a 34-year-old arts professional in Denver, Colorado, pointed to the killings of two Americans, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, by federal immigration agents in Minnesota earlier this year.

“Maga lost America when they murdered Renee Good and Alex Pretti. First and foremost I’m concerned about Trump’s immigration secret police, and I am voting for candidates who will defund and prosecute ICE,” Katie said.

Julie Stielstra, a retired librarian living in rural Kansas, said she was worried about the potential presence of immigration agents and armed individuals at polling stations. Stielstra said she would be working as a poll worker the following week.

“I am apprehensive about the possible presence of ICE, which has been active in my state recently … [and] armed government agents or self-appointed ‘poll watchers’ who may be intimidating at best. I trust my county clerk’s vigilance and honor, but worry about federal minions and officials who could disrupt or try to negate or overturn our ballots,” she said.

Those concerns extended beyond intimidation at polling stations to the possibility that the Trump administration could challenge the election results.

Richard Corcoran, a 63-year-old licensed clinical social worker in Lumberton, North Carolina, said: “I do not have faith that the federal government under Trump and Republican control of Congress and the supreme court will respect the outcome of this election. I expect problems in the aftermath,” he said.

Michael Pitts-Campbell, a 78-year-old law enforcement retiree living in Brookings, Oregon, similarly worried that Trump would reject a Democratic victory.

“My biggest concern is that if the results of the election are overwhelmingly Democratic, Trump will claim that the election results are false. Whether the appropriate member of the government attempts to not certify the vote or not seat the new representatives and senators, the proclamation from Trump will only widen the current political chasm,” he said.

But even among voters hoping for a Democratic victory, there was little consensus that the party would be prepared to deliver the changes they want.

Several readers expressed concern that Democrats could fail to use a potential congressional majority to enact effective change.

For a 52-year-old insurance professional in New Lenox, Illinois, their “biggest fear is that despite a likely massive Democrat wins, they will not have the guts to do what is necessary to prosecute this administration and pass laws that are sorely needed limiting the powers of the president, abolishing [the Department of Homeland Security] and establishing Medicare for all”.

D Turner, a California resident, similarly said: “I’m concerned that the reflexive centrist impulses of current Democratic leadership and advisers will assume that if they just get a majority, everything will be back to normal. There is so much hard work that needs to be done to preserve the rights of all.”

Brad Southard, a 54-year-old teacher in Irvine, California, criticized Democratic leaders for focusing “too much on courting the illusive ‘undecided middle’ to the detriment of the needs of working-class people”.

“I worry that the party will again choose to seize defeat from the jaws of victory by supporting pro-corporate neoliberal candidates and policies and refuse to pay attention to the real material pain felt by so many Americans,” Southard added.

For other voters, disillusionment extended beyond either party’s leadership, reflecting a broader lack of faith in the US political system.

Mark, a 68-year-old retiree in Parma, Ohio, said both parties had become too beholden to wealthy interests to represent ordinary Americans.

“Both political parties share the blame. The GOP has morphed into something even worse than the [Democrats]. Neither party offers policies that meet the needs of the people. Rather, both parties are captured by moneyed interests. It just turns out the GOP has openly embraced the dark side while the [Democrats] are more coy about their corruption.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Hyrox athlete who soiled herself puts ‘confronting’ matter behind her to win return race
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Martin Pegan
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The Australian athlete who sparked outrage when winning a Hyrox event in Beijing despite soiling herself during the race has returned in style with victory in the first event of the new season in Hamburg.

Joanna Wietrzyk won the endurance sports event in China last month but forfeited the points and soon faced a stinging public backlash as footage of her continuing through demanding exercises and using communal equipment with faecal matter running down her legs went viral on social media.

The 24-year-old posted a statement on social media with an apology in the aftermath of the incident before stepping away from the public eye. The Melbourne-born athlete returned to speak on a pre-race video this week where she said she was “truly, truly so sorry to everyone that I affected”.

Wietrzyk, the world record-holder in the Hyrox women’s solo event, added the attention that had stained her reputation had been “very hard” and “very confronting” to deal with before she put the storm behind her to win the Hyrox event on her comeback to competition on Friday.

“I’ve had some time to reflect over the past six to eight weeks of everything that happened in Beijing and firstly I want to say that I’m truly, truly so sorry to everyone that I affected whether they were spectators or participants out on that race floor, for my decision to choose to continue to race,” Wietrzyk said in a post on Instagram. “Having that time to reflect, I’ve really learnt a lot from the situation and I am very, very sorry for it all.”

She added: “It has been a very hard situation to navigate for me and very confronting as well, so all the support, whether it was personally or through my team has been honestly so incredible and it goes a far longer way than I can truly express right now.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Hyrox is an increasingly popular fitness competition that sees participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises at shared high-intensity stations – including a rowing machine, sled pushes, burpee jumps, medicine ball throws and lunges while carrying a sandbag.

The competition launched in Germany in 2017 and is now held in locations across the world with the 2026-27 season to include races in London, Bangkok, Las Vegas and Lyon after the opener in Hamburg.

Wietrzyk took an early lead in the Elite 15 competition when winning the fitness event in Hamburg in 56:10.21 ahead of American pair Lauren Weeks (56:24.37) and Vivian Tafuto (57:55.34).

Hyrox apologised and pledged immediate rule changes after Wietrzyk was allowed to finish and win the Beijing race in September even as she suffered from a bout of diarrhoea. Co-founder Moritz Fürste said after the event that organisers “made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race”.

New rules have since been introduced to give race organisers the power to remove an athlete if their “blood, vomit, urine, or faeces poses a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers”.

Rules were already in place to penalise athletes for minor infractions such as littering on the course, or spitting or clearing their nose on the floor.

Wietrzyk was subjected to vitriol when her identity was shared online following the incident in Beijing, prompting Hyrox organisers to warn that anyone sending abuse or threats of violence towards the athlete would be banned from future events.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120356.title: Beruf | Zu wenig Ausbildungsplätze
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120356.author: Andreas Fritsche
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120356.text:
Jugendlichen, die in Berlin keinen Ausbildungsplatz fanden, riet die Arbeitsagentur viele Jahre lang, es doch im Umland zu versuchen. Denn in Brandenburg überschritt die Zahl der freien Lehrstellen deutlich die Zahl der an einer Ausbildung interessierten Schulabgänger. Doch das sieht nun anders aus und ist ein Problem.

In Berlin hatten vor drei Jahren den damals 21.176 Bewerbern immerhin noch 16.813 Ausbildungsplätze gegenübergestanden. Diese Schere ist inzwischen noch weiter auseinandergegangen. Auf 24.716 Bewerber kommen nur noch 14.490 Ausbildungsplätze. In Brandenburg hatten vor drei Jahren 12.370 Bewerber 15.319 Ausbildungsplätze zur Auswahl. Diese Lücke hat sich vergrößert. Es gibt im Bundesland 13.299 Bewerber und 13.706 Ausbildungsplätze. Das bedeutet: Es gibt nicht mehr viel Platz für Bewerber aus Berlin. Es reicht gerade noch für die eigene Jugend.

»Derzeit ist es insbesondere in Berlin für Jugendliche so schwer wie lange Zeit nicht, eine Ausbildung zu finden.«

»Derzeit ist es insbesondere in Berlin für Jugendliche so schwer wie lange Zeit nicht, eine Ausbildung zu finden«, bedauert Carina Knie-Nürnberg. Sie leitet die Regionaldirektion der Arbeitsagentur.

»Die angespannte wirtschaftliche Situation darf nicht zu Lasten der jungen Menschen gehen, die in den letzten Jahren schon sehr viel zu tragen hatten«, findet Nele Techen, Vizelandesvorsitzende des Gewerkschaftsdachverbands DGB. Sie sagt: »Wir müssen alles tun, die duale Ausbildung zu sichern und für mehr betriebliche Ausbildungsplätze zu sorgen.«

Brandenburgs Sozialstaatssekretärin Friederike Haase meint zwar, es gehe in die richtige Richtung, da sich die Zahl der Stellen gegenüber dem vergangenen Jahr wieder erhöht habe. Doch für die BSW-Landesvorsitzende Friederike Benda ist dies Augenwischerei. Das Mini-Plus von 1,3 Prozent bei den gemeldeten Stellen könne nicht darüber hinwegtäuschen, dass in Brandenburg gegenüber 2021 »über 1600 Ausbildungsplätze weggebrochen sind, Betriebe mehr als 4000 gemeldete Stellen wieder storniert haben und unterm Strich erneut deutlich weniger Jugendliche eine Lehre beginnen konnten«. Gleichzeitig sei die Zahl der arbeitslosen jungen Menschen unter 25 Jahren auf fast 8500 geklettert.

Benda spricht von dreifachem Versagen: Erstens erdrücke eine verfehlte Wirtschafts- und Energiepolitik mitsamt selbstmörderischer Sanktionen gegen Russland die Betriebe so sehr, dass die Ausbildungsquote nur noch deshalb steige, weil tausende nicht ausbildende Betriebe komplett vom Markt verschwänden. Zweitens räche sich die jahrelange Bildungsmisere, wenn über 2300 arbeitslose Jugendliche in Brandenburg nicht einmal einen Hauptschulabschluss vorweisen könnten und Betrieben die ausbildungsfähigen Bewerber fehlten. Drittens scheitere die Ausbildung am fehlenden bezahlbaren Wohnraum für Azubis. »Statt sich die Krise mit Durchhalteparolen schönzureden, muss die Landesregierung endlich unsere Schulen sanieren, sich für Reformen in der Bildung einsetzen, den Mittelstand durch bezahlbare Energie entlasten und für bezahlbare Azubi-Wohnungen sorgen!«

Immerhin: In Schwedt entsteht ein Lehrlingswohnheim mit 60 Plätzen in Einzel- und Doppelzimmern. Dafür gibt es 14 Millionen Euro Fördermittel von der EU. »Junge Menschen können in Schwedt künftig nicht nur eine gute Ausbildung absolvieren, sondern auch preisgünstig wohnen«, freut sich Ministerpräsident Dietmar Woidke (SPD). Die vom Importverbot für russisches Erdöl betroffene PCK-Raffinerie in Schwedt ist aktuell zu etwas mehr als 86 Prozent ausgelastet. Woidke ist dankbar, dass dies »in diesem Jahr trotz aller Schwierigkeiten stabil gehalten« werden konnte.

Der Bundestagsabgeordnete Christian Görke (Linke) fühlt sich an einen »Schlafwagenzug« erinnert, in dem »haufenweise Beruhigungspillen verteilt werden«. Immer wieder höre er Ankündigungen. »Wenn aber nicht bald echte Maßnahmen ergriffen werden, wird die PCK noch totverwaltet.« Dies sei schlecht für die 3000 Menschen, deren Lebensunterhalt direkt oder indirekt von der Raffinerie abhänge, und für Millionen Menschen, die Benzin benötigten.

85.029 Brandenburger waren im Oktober arbeitslos gemeldet und 223.254 Berliner. In der Hauptstadt stieg die Arbeitslosenquote im Vergleich zum Oktober vergangenen Jahres von 10,3 auf 10,4 Prozent, im Umland von 6,2 auf 6,3 Prozent.

Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.

Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

Trotz der Veröffentlichung des »Spiegels« dürfte Rot-Grün-Rot noch nicht abgeschrieben sein. Der Linke-Landes­parteitag wird aber mit Spannung erwartet.

In Berlin gibt es sehr viel mehr Bewerber als Lehrstellen. Der Blick nach Brandenburg hilft ihnen auch nicht mehr.

Casa-Kuá-Razzia bleibt international nicht unbemerkt. Ein offener Brief um Judith Butler klagt zunehmenden Autoritarismus und Queerfeindlichkeit an.

In Berlin-Reinickendorf wurde die Brandmauer von der CDU schwer beschädigt, aber nicht gänzlich niedergerissen.

In Marzahn-Hellersdorf scheiterten die Wahlen von Bezirksamt und BVV-Vorstand. Im Fokus: der potenzielle Königsmacher CDU.

Die Autorin verzichtet auf ihr Ehrenamt als brandenburgische Verfassungsrichterin. Macht sie damit Platz für einen Kandidaten der AfD?

Die in Marzahn aufgewachsene Sozialistin Hendrikje Klein ist neue Präsidentin des Berliner Abgeordnetenhauses. Ein Zeichen von Normalität?

Kleine Solarmodule am Balkon spielen für die Energiewende nur eine untergeordnete Rolle, füllen aber insbesondere schmale Geldbeutel.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120356.title: Miete | Wohnen oder leben?
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120356.author: Patrick Lempges
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120356.text:
Immer höhere Mieten fressen immer mehr Geld eines Großteils der Menschen auf. Eine neue, vom Sozialverband Deutschland (SoVD) in Auftrag gegebene Umfrage zeigt das Ausmaß des Mietelends. Im Rahmen der Umfrage wurden etwa 2500 Mieter*innen bezüglich Miete und Finanzen befragt. Es ist eine Umfrage, die Bestürzung und Wut auslöst.

53 Prozent der Mieter*innen gaben an, sich angesichts ihrer Wohnsituation stark finanziell einzuschränken. Davon 18 Prozent sogar »sehr stark«. Seit Jahrzehnten geht es im neoliberalen Wahn aus Austerität, steigenden Kosten und Steuergeschenken an die Bonzen bergab für die arbeitenden Menschen. Nirgends ist die Lage so kurz vor dem Explodieren wie bei der Miete.

Während sich die besitzende Klasse am ureigenen Bedürfnis der Menschen nach einem Zuhause die Kassen füllt, strampeln sich die Mieter*innen mehr und mehr ab, nur um nicht immer weiter vom Stadtzentrum verdrängt, in immer marodere Wohnungen abgeschoben oder letztlich gar auf die Straße geworfen zu werden.

Also heißt es, sich zusammenzureißen. Den Gürtel enger zu schnallen und alles zu geben, nur um wenigstens den Status quo noch halten zu können. Fast die Hälfte der Befragten gab außerdem an, wegen zu hoher Wohnkosten bereits konkrete Lebenspläne geändert oder aufgegeben zu haben. Zehn Prozent haben ihre Familienplanung wegen der Miete verändert. »Wohnst du noch oder lebst du schon?« hieß es in der bekannten Ikea-Werbung der 2000er Jahre. Treffender wäre heute: »Lebst du noch oder wohnst du schon?« Es ist ein Trauerspiel, das sich angesichts der kommenden Kürzungen beim Wohngeld nur noch weiter zuspitzen wird. Statt dass Mieter*innen ihre Lebenspläne wegen zu hoher Mieten aufgeben, sollten Bonzen dazu gebracht werden, ihre Mietwohnungen aufzugeben – siehe Vergesellschaftung.

Hinzu kommt ein katastrophaler Trend. Je jünger die Mieter*innen, desto schlimmer die Mietsituation. Bei 30- bis 39-Jährigen gaben 60 Prozent an, sich wegen der Miete finanziell einschränken zu müssen, statt der generellen 53 Prozent. Bei 18- bis 29-Jährigen sind es sogar gut zwei Drittel. Wer sich jetzt noch über Gen-Z-Proteste wundert, hat den Kontakt zur Realität in diesem Land verloren. Man sollte sich eher fragen, warum es so wenige Proteste gibt.

Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.

Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

Die Hälfte der Mieter*innen hat wegen zu hoher Mieten Lebenspläne geändert. Noch schlimmer sieht es bei der Gen Z aus. Ein guter Grund für Protest. Ein Kommentar

Berlin sollte durchaus von einer Politikerin wie Elif Eralp regiert werden, die sich Sorgen macht. Ein Kommentar
