https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Elie Mystal
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The Alaska case is a red flag that Trump has no intention of accepting the results of an election that Republicans lose.

Donald Trump speaks at a rally for GOP candidates in Wasilla, Alaska.

The Democrats have a legitimate chance to retake the Senate next week. The Cook Political Report rates 13 of the open Senate seats as favoring Democrats, giving them a possible total of 47 seats. It rates seven additional races as “toss-ups.” If Democrats win four of those races, they’ll control the chamber.

I don’t actually believe any polls, anywhere, anymore, because repeated polling failures during the Trump era have left me scarred for life. But for the sake of preelection argument, we have to pretend that these pollsters have professional skills and aren’t engaged in a terroristic plot to weaponize hope.

One of the toss-up states is Alaska, where Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan is facing a fierce challenge from former Democratic representative Mary Peltola. The race could be definitive in determining control of the Senate. The seven states rated as toss-ups are: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio, and Texas. Let’s say Democrats win in Michigan and Ohio. Let’s say they split Maine and Texas—Susan Collins hangs on but James Talarico pulls through, or vice versa. Alaska could easily be the fourth seat Democrats need to take control of the Senate. It’s that important. (If you tell me Democrat Adam Hamilton is going to beat incumbent Republican Roger Marshall in Kansas, then I’m going to tell you Democrats are gonna run the entire table and Trump will need nukes to maintain control.)

I don’t need the pollster-industrial complex to tell me that Alaska is close, because Republicans are doing what they always do when elections get close: They’re trying to steal it. Last week, the Department of Justice, at the personal order of Donald Trump, filed a lawsuit to try to prevent Alaska from certifying the result of the Senate election, but only if the Republican loses.

Trump and the Republican Party have engaged in numerous forms of electoral skulduggery, including trying to gerrymander their way to one-party rule, trying to purge the voter rolls of eligible citizens, and threatening to unleash an army of election thugs wearing ICE clothing to intimidate voters at the polls. In such a corrupted world, it’s tempting to think of this Alaska lawsuit as more of the same, just another attack on democracy from an administration willing to burn the whole system down to be king of the ashes.

But the Alaska lawsuit is different from everything that’s come before, and a dangerous harbinger of what is to come. That’s because everything Trump has done up to this point has been aimed at preventing or suppressing the vote. He’s been trying to stop people from voting in the first place. This Alaska thing is trying to prevent votes that have already been cast and tabulated from counting. The lawsuit contemplates the Republican’s losing—it literally takes effect only if the GOP candidate loses—and then making that loss not matter. That is a dangerous escalation that should alert people that the Trump administration has no intention of accepting the results of an election in which the Republicans lose.

If it weren’t so obviously antidemocratic, this case would present an interesting legal issue. Alaska has ranked-choice voting, so there are actually four people running for Senate in Alaska: Sullivan, Peltola, a Republican named Gerald Heikes, and a candidate with no party affiliation named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. Yeah, there are two men with the same name running for the same office. That’s not a coincidence. Moreover, it’s probably a dirty trick. Daniel J. Sullivan is a retired schoolteacher who recently registered as a Republican and then, even more recently, switched his affiliation to “undeclared.” He has given money to Mary Peltola in the past. Even if most people know the difference between the incumbent Dan S. and the schoolteacher Daniel J., if there are even some people who rank Daniel J. over or instead of Dan S.—people are allowed to rank a total of four candidates—it could matter.

Daniel J. claims that his candidacy is not a plant or a trick inspired by Democrats. But just because he says it, doesn’t mean I have to believe it. I was born at night, but not last night.

After Daniel J. won enough votes during the primary to get on the November ballot, Republicans moved to have him kicked off. That case was litigated all the way up to the Supreme Court of Alaska, which ruled in favor of Daniel J. The lawsuit launched by the DOJ last week challenges that ruling.

The most important thing to know about that state Supreme Court case is that it happened in June. If the Trump administration had a problem with the ruling, it could have filed its appeal over the summer and had this all worked out by now. But it didn’t. It filed its appeal in October, days before the election, to make sure to cause maximum confusion and uncertainty in the election. Attorney General Todd Blanche claims that there was nothing nefarious about the timing of the administration’s appeal, but, again, I wasn’t born last night. Everybody can or should be able to see that the DOJ is trying to interfere with the election.

The other reason the DOJ’s delayed timing matters has to do with the remedy it’s requesting. Pending its appeal (which now cannot be resolved before the election), the DOJ is asking the court to force Alaska to delay certification of the results should Daniel J. Sullivan secure enough votes to influence the outcome of the election. This is the most dangerous part of what Blanche and Trump are doing. They’re effectively asking the court to rule that all votes cast for Daniel J. are suspect, based entirely on the theory that anybody who votes for Daniel J. meant to vote for the incumbent, Dan S.

We know that logic is wrong. There will be some people who honestly want to vote for Daniel J., especially as their second choice. He is, after all, probably a secret Democrat. If I were an Alaska voter, I would rank Peltola as my first choice and Daniel J. as my second, not because I am confused and not because I am trying to participate in a scam; I would legitimately want a retired probably-Democrat schoolteacher to represent me in the Senate over a Trumper like Dan S. Casting my vote aside, or awarding it to a guy I never intended to vote for, because the Republican Party thinks it knows what I meant to do is ludicrously antidemocratic. It can’t be allowed.

Indeed, I know that courts do not allow this kind of remedy, because I am old enough to remember the 2000 election in Florida. I remember the infamous “butterfly ballot” in Palm Beach county. For those lucky enough not to remember one of the dumbest episodes in the history of American civics: The presidential ballot design in Palm Beach county (pictured here) likely caused confusion for people who wanted to vote for Democrat Al Gore against Republican George W. Bush. An analysis of the election results showed that over 2,000 registered Democrats voted for Republican bigot Pat Buchanan (running as a third-party candidate) instead of Al Gore. Those 2,000 votes were more than Bush’s margin of victory over Gore in Florida; if people who probably tried to vote for Gore had successfully voted for Gore, Gore would have won Florida and the White House, and (most likely) the entire freaking world would be different.

You know what the courts said to Democrats who complained? Tough nooggies. They said there was nothing they could do. They couldn’t just give Gore all of Buchanan’s votes in Palm Beach. They couldn’t just assume that the voters who mistakenly voted for Buchanan actually made a mistake. For all the litigation that erupted after the 2000 election, the butterfly ballot was not part of Bush v. Gore. You can argue about whether election officials correctly counted votes that were cast, but you can’t argue that voters cast a ballot in error so those votes should be awarded to another candidate.

That said, the current Supreme Court is even more nakedly partisan than the one that decided Bush v. Gore. I don’t think this Supreme Court will give all of Daniel J.’s votes to Dan S. I don’t think this Supreme Court will allow Republicans to engineer a new election in Alaska if the current one doesn’t go the way Republicans would like. But I can’t be sure. Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito seem to be so deep in the cult of the Republican Party that they will vote for whatever the administration wants. If the Alaska race turns out to be the deciding seat, who knows what the rest of the Republicans on the Supreme Court will do?

Still, my biggest worry isn’t what the Supreme Court will do in Alaska. My real worry is what this means the Trump administration is prepared to do across all states. It’s trying to stop certification of results in an election the Republicans haven’t even lost yet, so what the hell do you think the administration will do when Republicans actually start losing some of these races? Every loss will be litigated on the thinnest theory of Republican supremacy, and that opens the door to Supreme Court shenanigans every day from the close of the polls to the induction of the new Senate, which JD Vance might not even be willing to oversee properly. And during every one of these legal fights, the potential for Trump to take extralegal means to assure power, including the destruction of physical ballots he doesn’t like, increases significantly.

The Alaska lawsuit proves that Trump will contest ballots that are validly and legally cast, and Todd Blanche will do whatever Trump tells him to do. I don’t think anybody is truly prepared for how dirty Trump is going to play.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Michele Goodwin, Lawrence O. Gostin, Eric A. Friedman
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The plight of immigrants under this administration provides a lesson and a warning.

Friends, advocates, and community members hold a vigil in Brooklyn to honor 20-year-old Haitian immigrant Pierre Damas Bel, who died by apparent suicide after facing the termination of Temporary Protected Status protections for Haitians, on September 4, 2026, in New York City.

With the protracted war in Iran, a pending firing squad execution, the most expensive election cycle in US history, the unaffordability of everyday necessities, outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases, relentless ICE raids and arbitrary detainments (including of children), attacks against selective press outlets, the continued demand for justice for Epstein victims and survivors, and ongoing threats to civil liberties and civil rights, what’s happening to Haitians in the United States might not register for most Americans. But the plight of Haitians living here offers a lens into how America’s light and credibility as a beacon for human rights and civil liberties is quickly fading, shamefully growing dark at rapid speed.

A vital part of the sweeping Immigration Act of 1990, signed into law by President George H.W. Bush, was Temporary Protected Status (TPS). This congressionally created program provided protection from deportation and extended work permits for immigrants experiencing natural disaster, armed conflict, or other extraordinary and temporary conditions in their home countries. The law did not provide permanent protection, and was specifically meant to be temporary, but with an important caveat allowing for review and extension of status. This mattered because armed conflict itself might not be temporary, as evidenced by the US wars in Vietnam and Afghanistan.

Now, however, instead of protecting foreign nationals who cannot safely return to their home country, the country is vilifying them.

The contrasts between George H.W. Bush’s statement upon signing the Immigration Act and Donald Trump’s public statements cannot be more glaring—and that is shameful for the United States. Bush noted that the act’s objectives included “support for the family as the essential unit of society” because the law sought to balance family reunification and employment pathways. This falls in stark contrast to the utterly false and crass campaign slogan Donald Trump spread about Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio: “They’re eating cats and dogs.”

After Trump and the right continued to amplify this untrue rumor about Haitians, the administration moved to revoke their TPS. The Supreme Court was forced to weigh in and decided, in a 6–3 ruling, to allow the revocation to proceed. Justice Elena Kagan’s dissent in the case, Mullin v. Doe, underscores our point. As she noted, President Trump’s targeted actions against Haitians must be understood for what they are—xenophobic and racist. She offered some of Trump’s statements to prove her point. “Haitians are ‘eating the dogs…they’re eating the cats. They’re eating—they’re eating the pets of the people that live [in Springfield, Ohio].’” His crudity suggests Haitians are infected with disease: “Haitians in the United States “probably have AIDS.” That their nation is a “‘shithole country,’ which is ‘filthy, dirty, [and] disgusting.’” In his more than apparent disgust toward Haitians—very likely because they are Black—he has stated that they are “poisoning the blood” of the United States. As Justice Kagan surmised, “The references–of filth, disease, and primitiveness—are shot through with racial stereotypes and tropes.” She concludes, “It is hard to imagine the statements being made today of any White community.”

Yet the United States’ dismantling of human rights is not a matter of mere crude words. The effects are serious and proof of America’s backsliding on democracy and the rule of law. Consider the death of Pierre Damas Bel. Authorities labeled his death a suicide. On August 31, near Springfield, Ohio, Bel stopped his car on the shoulder of a highway, exited, stepped in front of an oncoming tanker truck, and was killed. It would be more accurate to say that the 20-year-old Haitian immigrant was the victim of the Trump administration’s cruel and erratic immigration policies. In this case, he was one of the innumerable immigrant victims caught in the horrific trap of an administration that views Black immigrants as both unworthy of legal protection and as a threat.

Bel had only been in the United States since 2024. He was a first-year college student. He had been an honors student in high school. Pierre was a lieutenant in the Marine Junior Reserve Officer Corps and volunteered at local charities. He dreamed of becoming a doctor.

Tragically, like so many other Haitians, he was driven to depression after the administration stripped TPS from some 330,000 Haitians Bel’s asylum claim was pending when he died. Like many of his neighbors in Springfield, he was summoned to a local ICE office and fitted with the ankle monitor. And like them, he was traumatized, shamed, and humiliated—treated like a criminal.

From a civil liberties point of view, forcing ankle monitoring on Haitians in the US is a serious problem for several reasons. First, it is a departure from standard law enforcement protocols, because he had not committed a crime and did not pose a risk of harm to anyone. According to the local government in Springfield, Ohio, Haitians are more likely to be victims of crime there than to commit offenses. Contrary to Donald Trump’s statements, non-detained immigrants have a very high compliance rate with immigration appointments. Thus, this shift is not only unnecessarily invasive but also procedurally unprecedented. Second, an ankle monitor is highly restrictive, limiting the distances one may travel, affecting employment, schooling, and caregiving. Third, ankle monitoring imposes stigmatization and can result in a severe emotional strain—as was the case for Bel, according to his family members. Fourth, for an administration that claims to be fiscally responsible, the program is a clear waste of resources: Many of the individuals being fitted with ankle monitoring devices have pending legal claims and were already cooperative.

Today, Haitians in the US are being stalked by ICE. As a headline in the French publication, Le Monde read in early October, “ICE agents are chasing Miami’s Haitians: ‘No one goes out anymore, the streets and churches are deserted, people are afraid of being arrested.’” It seems that cruelty is the point. And this is why Americans should be concerned.

The president has justified breaching constitutional norms and ignoring judicial rulings based on a theory of protecting national security. This served as the underlying justification of ICE raids and lawlessness in the Twin Cities, where Alex Pretti and Renée Nicole Goode were gunned down by government agents. That is also the community represented by Representative Ilhan Omar, whose home was raided by federal immigration agents on October 12, in an effort to “build [a] case for stripping her citizenship” according to The Wall Street Journal. It was the argument used for deploying National Guard troops in Los Angeles and Washington, DC. It has also been the justification for barring news organizations from briefings at the White House.

A healthy and functioning democracy does not pander to racial stereotypes to promote policy. Both constitutional precedent and civil rights laws make this clear. As Justice Kagan expressed, Donald Trump’s “statements fairly shout, in their racial undertones and overtones alike, that race entered into the President’s resolve to remove Haitians from this country.” Moreover, a well-functioning executive does not weaponize government against law-abiding immigrants and citizens. A nation committed to the rule of law does not brazenly kill its citizens and then blame them for their deaths.

While Americans may have moved on from the plight of immigrants among us, their experiences under this administration provide a lesson and a warning. Their case shows how the Trump administration ignores the rule of law, disregards precedent, is willing to impose psychological threats and harms against innocent individuals, and cares very little about disrupting the lives of law-abiding individuals. Americans should worry that immigrants are simply the canaries in the coal mines.

Michele Goodwin is the Linda D. & Timothy J. O'Neill Professor of Constitutional Law and Global Health Policy at Georgetown University and Faculty Director of the O'Neill Institute. She is a recipient of the Polan Fellowship in Constitutional Law and History at the Brennan Center for Justice and author of the award-winning book Policing the Womb: Invisible Women and the Criminalization of Motherhood.

Lawrence O. Gostin is a Distinguished University Professor at Georgetown. Gostin is the director of the World Health Organization Collaborating Center on National and Global Health Law. He worked with the WHO and the Intergovernmental Negotiation Body to draft a Pandemic Treaty. He also currently serves on WHO’s Review Committee for amendments to the International Health Regulations. Professor Gostin is an elected lifetime Member of the National Academy of Medicine/National Academy of Sciences.

Eric A. Friedman is the O’Neill Institute’s global health justice scholar. He is also a member of the Executive Committee of the Framework Convention on Global Health Alliance, which advocates for a treaty to improve accountability to the right to health and is aimed at national and global health equity. He is a former senior global health policy adviser at Physicians for Human Rights. Friedman holds a law degree from Yale Law School and a BA from Yale College.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Séamus Malekafzali
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The attempt to strip Omar of her citizenship is part of a much bigger push for the mass denaturalization of American immigrants.

Ilhan Omar speaks to MS Now about the raid on her home.

Last week, Representative Ilhan Omar’s Washington, DC, home was raided by agents from the Department of Homeland Security. Omar has not been indicted or criminally charged, but the Trump administration has now said that it was investigating whether Omar had acquired her US citizenship through fraudulent means after arriving in the country as a 12-year-old from Somalia.

There are multiple allegations the DHS appears to be pursuing, one claiming that Omar’s father lied on her immigration paperwork to say she was 17 instead of 18, thus allowing her to acquire citizenship through her own father’s naturalization. Another allegation apparently being investigated is one that has regularly percolated through the conservative mediasphere for years: that Ilhan Omar’s ex-husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, is in fact her brother, and that she fraudulently sought to extend her own citizenship to him through “incestuous” means. The government has apparently acquired her DNA to pursue this, reportedly by having taken discarded garbage from her home (though the government has denied the account of this specific method).

The Wall Street Journal reported after the raid that the Trump administration was pursuing something that had never been attempted before against a member of Congress: denaturalization and removal from the United States. Tom Homan, Trump’s so-called “border czar,” then confirmed to Fox News that such extreme measures were on the table.

Denaturalization is in vogue right now. Deportation, detainments, visa revocations, and entry bans have all been part of the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant crusade. But there are simply not enough noncitizens present in the United States, whether documented or undocumented, to fulfill the national cleansing that the government appears to be openly salivating after.

On New Year’s Eve in 2025, the DHS posted a picture of a peaceful, unnaturally spotless beach and a perfect blue sky, with the caption: “America After 100 Million Deportations. The peace of a nation no longer besieged by the third world.” There are estimated to be roughly 15 million undocumented migrants present in the United States, 13 million green-card holders, and 3 million documented noncitizens on temporary visas. In a perfect Republican world, one where every undocumented and documented noncitizen is deported, you still only get to 31 million, well below the magic number needed to supposedly ensure America’s prosperity. Thus, naturalized citizens—those who went through all of the legal hoops, learning American civics and all the little bits of this country’s history—have to be next on the chopping block. And as a high-profile political antagonist of President Trump, Omar is an inviting target. Back in May, when discussing Omar, Trump had mockingly imitated her saying, “The Constitution gives me certain rights,” before dismissing her as a “phony” and saying she should “get the hell out.”

While Omar is not the most leftist member of the Democratic Party (she is not a member of the DSA, for instance), she is something that is arguably just as bad in the Republican Party’s imagination: a Somali American, the first to be elected to Congress.

Trump has aimed his ire at many different ethnic groups over his two terms, but he has targeted the Somali community in an especially venomous way. Days before Omar’s house was raided, Trump posted that her home state of Minnesota, which has the nation’s largest Somali American community, was “being taken over by Somali Immigrants” and urged Minnesotans to “fight back,” adding that the “Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing.” In particular, Trump promised those fighting the alleged malign influence of the local Somali community that, if need be, “the Federal Government will come to your rescue.”

Omar, perhaps the most prominent Somali American in the country, has been the prime target within this larger communal attack for years. Since she first ran for Congress in 2018, Omar has been accused of antisemitism, being “Somalia-first,” supporting multiple terrorist groups, secret communism, financial and tax fraud, both polygamy and adultery, and being a foreign agent. While most of these allegations have come from Republicans, many Democrats have joined the pile-on, in particular to attack Omar’s criticism of Israel. (This lack of solidarity from some Democrats continues even now; Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer has not commented on the raid despite its having happened over a week ago, and Minnesota Senator Amy Klobuchar only questioned the raid’s timing, while offering no support for Omar or larger criticism of the move.)

While the denaturalization of a serving member of Congress would be unprecedented, past governments have tried to denaturalize elected officials, driven by the same anti-immigrant, partisan dynamics that are behind the anti-Omar campaign. Perhaps the most notable such target was Stanley Nowak, a Polish American union organizer who briefly served as a Democratic state senator in the Michigan legislature from 1939 to 1948. Nowak had worked in the past with communist publications and organizations in the 1920s, but never said that he himself was a member of the Communist Party. Nevertheless, in 1942, Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s government initiated proceedings to denaturalize him on the basis that he had concealed his connection to communist groups while applying for citizenship. As with Omar, the aim was to use charges of immigration fraud as a pretext to remove someone whose leftist politics the government deemed unacceptable.

The case proceeded for only a few months before FDR’s attorney general dropped the matter, but it was revived in 1952 during the Truman administration, dragging on until 1958 under the Eisenhower administration, with Nowak’s citizenship being revoked and then restored later by the Supreme Court. The ultimate failure to deport Nowak could be construed as a victory for the rule of law, but nativism and a hatred of those who criticized the United States were what governed his prosecution, and those sentiments have only built, grown, and spread to new hosts since then.

Even if all 26 million naturalized American citizens were to be deported en masse, the work of building the ideal fascist state would not be complete. After all, the Trump administration has made no secret of its desire to end birthright citizenship, thus making the millions of Americans born to immigrant parents vulnerable to removal. There are also those whose parents are American citizens but are of the same irksome race that noncitizens are, like Somalis or Haitians, or of enemy nationalities, like Palestinians and Iranians, who will almost undoubtedly come on the chopping block in the coming months and years. Then there are people who, though they may be white, Protestant, and otherwise spotless in their racial makeup, are deemed to have voided their right to Americanness by opposing the state of Israel—thus “becoming Palestinian,” as Trump once described Schumer. The idea of making someone born in the United States, to American parents, stateless is no vice to certain members of Congress, such as Randy Fine, who wrote a letter this year demanding the revocation of the passports and the barring of reentry to activists and journalists who attended the funeral of Ali Khamenei, accusing them of treason, a crime punishable by death in the United States.

The breadth of this crusade is one of the reasons it is ultimately useless to note the obvious shoddiness of the case against Omar. This is an administration that recognizes no limits and knows it is dealing in deceit, a massive, systemic fraud of its own. The point of this case is to be a stress test for wide-scale denaturalization in the remaining years of Trump’s second term. Even if the move against Omar fails, we cannot rely on one of the most right-wing Supreme Courts in American history to be so forgiving toward lesser-known individuals, not to mention that every time one of these cases makes its way through the courts, the Trump administration will take notes and fine-tune its approach. Through these proceedings, the government will be able to know better what matters it can simply ignore the decisions of courts on, and what angles the Democratic Party will simply ignore either out of lack of care or silent agreement. Omar may be the story now, but there are thousands more waiting to be written with bitter hands, out of sight.

Séamus Malekafzali is a journalist and writer primarily focusing on the politics of the Middle East.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: John Semley
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Long out of print, The Tunnel returns with a timely exploration of the fascism of the heart.

Having required decades to write and rewrite, William Gass’s The Tunnel has always been a difficult novel to read. An enormously long, often gratingly obnoxious and violent book rendered in overblown prose, it is also shot through with squiggly doodles and diagrams and bawdy limericks and all kinds of lexicographical shenanigans. But that’s only part of what makes it difficult to read. Exasperatingly demanding, defiantly highfalutin, and richly rewarding, The Tunnel is also just hard to find: It was long out of print, and old copies regularly fetch hundreds of dollars in used-book marketplaces.

For this reason, Dalkey Archive has taken on the task of reprinting the book yet again. This time it has done so in full color, as the author intended, and with a companion volume called The Tunnel Reader, a special issue of the now-defunct Review of Contemporary Fiction that contains a complete publication history, critical commentary, correspondence, and the author’s own handy guide, “How to Read The Tunnel,” which helps to contextualize (and soften the blow) of Gass’s heavy masterpiece. The timing is auspicious, for not only is Gass’s book intimidating and frustrating and brilliant, but it is also a study of the ugly, often inchoate nature of the American authoritarian character, and how a crude politics of exclusion and resentment rises from the bile of a more basic resentment—what Gass terms “the fascism of the heart.”

The Tunnel has not one author but two. There’s the book’s literal author, the novelist and essayist William H. Gass, who died in 2017. And then there’s its fictional author, The Tunnel’s protagonist, narrator, villain, and governing consciousness, a bitter, bloated creep named William F. Kohler. A professor of German history at an unnamed college in Indiana, Kohler is a product of two ostensibly distinct milieus. The first is the uninspiring flatlands of the American Midwest, where he was reared and now resides; the second is the political and emotional hothouse of Nazi Germany, where he studied history and found himself “caught up in the partisan frenzy of those stirred and stirring times.”

At the book’s beginning, we are introduced to Kohler just as he is completing his work on a massive historical tome titled Guilt and Innocence in Hitler’s Germany. Its thesis is provocative: Rather than invoking the more standard explanations of culpability regarding the horrors of the Holocaust, Kohler blames not only every German but, in fact, all of humanity for what happened in World War II. He does so because he believes that all human beings harbor nasty, fascist, essentially Nazi-like instincts toward violence and the exaltation of one group at the expense of another. The Nazi Party, he argues, should not bear the stain of guilt alone, since Hitler was little more than “a wimp in wolf’s clothing” and “probably history’s most sincere man.” Indeed, the Nazis, Kohler insists, should be commended for embracing the violence that lurks inside us all: “Suppose but a whisper of our wishes leaked out and half a continent was ready to rise and do your bidding? Orders are easy. Liquidate the trailer parks. Murder motorbikers. Silence the soaps. Clean up the town. Bust up the trusts. It is the killing—hands-on and nearby—that takes fortitude and commitment.” Yet despite his own fortitude and commitment in making this argument, Kohler finds himself distracted as he attempts to pen the book’s introduction. Instead, he starts composing a bittersweet memoir of his childhood, jeremiads against his mediocre colleagues and portly wife, horn-dog reveries about his flagrant affairs, and extended exegeses on the deep, envenoming rancor that poisons the hearts of men. His burrowing deep into his own internal (and infernal) world finds its metaphorical expression in the titular tunnel, which is also not a metaphor: In the midst of all this psychic digging, Kohler begins to excavate a tunnel in the floor of his basement office, hiding the mud and dirt in his wife’s antique wardrobes. It’s not exactly clear what this tunnel business amounts to: an attempt to break loose from his stifling, sexless home life? An effort to escape himself, or to dig his own shallow, silty grave? Or merely “a gesture which will symbolize my desperation”?

Whatever the purpose, the image of a man boring into increasingly tight, dirty spaces befits the feeling of The Tunnel itself, as it slithers into the hollows of Kohler’s repugnant psychology. It is a pitiless, pitch-black map of the human soul—or, rather, of the gaping hole marking its absence.

“What works of art testify to is the presence in this world of consciousness,” William Gass declared when he accepted the 2007 Truman Capote Award for Literary Criticism. “For that is what fine writing does: It creates a unique verbal consciousness.”

Gass has sought to create this unique verbal consciousness ever since he started writing. His dissertation, submitted to Cornell in 1954, was a philosophical investigation of the metaphor. His 1966 debut novel, Omensetter’s Luck, deposits the reader into a slipstream of Midwestern consciousness, as characters in a small Ohio town at the turn of the 20th century rail and sputter against the breezy, earthy charm of a new arrival to their parochial berg. In his 1971 novella Willie Masters’ Lonesome Wife—which, in its use of illustrations and all kinds of typesetting trickery, anticipates some of the lexicographical theatrics of The Tunnel—Gass traces the internal monologues of a sex worker who may be a stand-in for literature or poetry itself. The job of the writer, as Gass outlined in one of his many essays, is not merely to describe the world but to bring one into being. For him, a book is a “container” of how humans think and express themselves, how they struggle to draw connections between experience and words. But a book is also more than that—because, for Gass, literature is something like consciousness perfected. Proust, he writes in one appreciation, typifies this high ideal, allowing the reader “to live for a while as we ought, in a fully realized world.”

The Tunnel is a grand expression of this idea, applied to an imperfect consciousness; it’s as if Proust wrote The Turner Diaries. It is not a typical stream-of-consciousness novel in the modernist tradition but a creation of that consciousness. Kohler is the text—to even classify him as an “unreliable narrator” would be senseless, as there is no external truth to judge him against. Everything that happens in The Tunnel happens inside Kohler’s mind. “It’s time,” he announces to the reader, “to hide inside my work, which is, of course, a fortress also made of language: the castle of what comes between commas.”

As much as Gass is committed to this experiment in verbal consciousness, so is Kohler, whose intellectual North Star is Magus “Mad Meg” Tabor, an excitable German historian with a diehard’s belief in “the force of fiction.” To write history, for Tabor, requires bringing it into being by turning it into literature. This idea animates Kohler’s own historical exercise as he attempts to write his way through (or out of) his own mediocrity, malignity, and meagerness of spirit. It turns out that, as we go deeper and deeper into the tunnel of Gass’s novel, it becomes harder to see the light at its beginning. Having coined the term “metafiction” to describe stories that self-consciously call attention to their status as such, Gass has composed a book that is an endless maze: a book about the writing of a book that is attempting to stop being a book and become a form of consciousness itself.

It must be said that Gass’s exercise in verbal-consciousness world-making is brilliant in long stretches. You could drain a ballpoint pen dirtying up the page by underlining great sentences (“After God created snot he made small boys with pugly noses to stuff it in”) or placing asterisks in the margins by memorable paragraphs. The book is full of hates: Kohler hates his parents, his wife and kids, his hippie students denouncing the Vietnam War, even his furniture and his own birthday. But Kohler hates himself most of all, with the usual narcissism inherent in so much self-loathing. “Hate,” as he says, “has given force and purpose to my life.”

The Tunnel’s reflections on how resentment and humiliation mutate into hatred and fascism are particularly sharp, and they are also scarily relevant in a time when such sentiments seem to have swelled in supply. A section headed “Being a Bigot” provides considerable diagnostic relevance for a present-day United States where Nazi sympathies are not just secretly harbored but openly barked. “The bigot,” Gass writes, “is a person who has suffered an unmerited injustice, one which hasn’t been put right, and woe to others if he ever has a chance to get his own back, and take what has long been his—property, power, and honor—from those who have traduced his principles and scorned his manner of existence.” And then, a few pages later, comes a full-blown rebuke of liberal notions of equality among the different races, colors, and creeds:

Because if we were each as identical as twins, I would scratch your face to hate the scratch which spoiled your looks and improved mine, while you would say the scratch set you apart and made you more interesting, and gave you a purpose in life: to scratch me back a thousand times.

These passages penetrate the mind of the deeply detestable or even just the basically jilted, offering an account of how the modest slights and gripes that most people endure in the course of daily life calcify and metastasize and become a “pandemic.” More bothersome, though, are The Tunnel’s no-less-exhaustive sections showcasing this ugly spirit with a libidinal glee. I’m no prude, but after a certain point, reading a guy whine about being under-endowed (“My weenie was, in fact, a little wormlike model of my soul”) or wax poetic about his bowel movements begins to grate—not because it’s unseemly, but because it’s tedious. In how many ways can a man call his wife fat? A rhetorical question, perhaps, but Gass is up to the task of answering it. It’s easy to imagine him and his authorial surrogate smirking, brows furrowed, like one of those bootleg peeing-Calvin bumper stickers as they gleefully micturate on some presumed standard of good taste: Oh, no! What a bad little boy! The truth is that the act, at times, can end up becoming a bit exhausting.

The preening and sniggering qualities of The Tunnel often make it feel like it’s trying too hard, but they are nonetheless crucial to the book’s larger project, which is probably a worthy one. The Tunnel goes to great lengths to be believed: Gass, with a kind of irksome impishness, works to collapse the gap between his fictional author and himself. For example, they’re both named William, and their last names have shared excretory resonances, with “Kohler” evoking the popular line of toilet fixtures. Indeed, when Kohler is described as overweight, beardless, and babylike, readers may reflexively flip to the back of the book to consult an author photo. (They won’t find one.) To make matters only more confusing, Gass had apparently lobbied for The Tunnel to be published with no author’s name provided on the cover or title page, hoping that the reading public might encounter it as some kind of genuine found manuscript.

Some of the book’s more vehement critics have tripped into the trap of conflating its exploration of Kohler’s execrable politics with the views of its author. “It is an act of ventriloquism,” Robert Alter wrote in a 1995 review in The New Republic. “What emerges is a kind of inadvertent complicity between author and protagonist.” Yet that the book allows for this ambiguity is part of the point: Gass does not merely think up the thoughts of a bigoted misanthrope; he wants everyone to be aware of the possibility that they might think them too. His sentences rise and fall rhythmically in an effort to make the ugly beautiful, and he gives Kohler considerable skills rhetorically. A description of a Pennsylvania autumn, where “the land becomes violet and mauve and pink and gold as if sunsets were its new cash crop and sprang freely from the earth,” is arresting. Kohler’s childhood memory about his routine trips to the candy store yields revealing thoughts on the corrupting power of candy: “Sugar slides things past the palate so agreeably a person might willingly swallow a roach or a smart remark from a spiteful spouse if its frosting were creamy and rich and thick enough.” There is wisdom in the midst of the bile. Kohler’s goal is not just indictment but recruitment: He imagines himself as the de facto leader of a new fascist cause, the “Party of the disappointed People” (PdP), “meant for people of broken promise, for whom there was once hope.” If beauty beguiles, as art has shown time and again, then the lesson of history is that evil can be no less beguiling, especially when expressed beautifully.

The Tunnel’s ugliest, grandest metaphor—the Holocaust—is bound to unsettle. In his “How to Read The Tunnel” guide, Gass himself cryptically calls the Holocaust his book’s “shadow subject.” Paved with the hatreds festering in the hearts of men, the road to Auschwitz was, at least in Kohler’s grim conception, an inevitability. The Nazi horrors seem fated, born of an original sin going back to Cain and Abel: “The Holocaust,” Kohler writes, “is perhaps an extreme example, the consummate pogrom, but only made major by improvements in technology.” In one section, he even describes the American fetish for automobile culture and its resulting environmental devastation and atomization of social life as worse than the Holocaust. Deploying such a world-historical catastrophe so flippantly feels deliberately offensive—and even risks diminishment: One might wince (or roll their eyes) at the basic suggestion that every perceived injustice, hostile glance, denied promotion, “ancestral resentment,” or lovers’ quarrel leads irrevocably to the gas chamber. Surely, not I! the polite reader will insist. To which The Tunnel responds with something like: Of course, you! Who else? In any event, this is not a historical account of fascism but rather a psychological and often metaphorical one. And it follows in a proud anti-Enlightenment tradition. If it was, as Adorno said, barbaric to write poetry after Auschwitz, then perhaps crude cartoons, dirty limericks, perverted daydreams, dark fantasies driving ever deathward, fart jokes, and other “obnoxious effluvium” (in Kohler’s words, but also Gass’s) constitute an appropriate—and appropriately barbarous—new form.

John Semley is a writer based in Philadelphia. His writing has also appeared in The Baffler, The New Republic, and The Guardian. He is the co-host of Slow Learners, a podcast about books.

The bad habits Emmanuel Macron will pass on to his successor.

“With this decision, the Paris Police Prefecture forbids any assembly in Bastille Square,” said the looped message delivered over a loudspeaker on Saturday to the handful of onlookers gathered near the French capital’s iconic roundabout, a usual meeting point for political demonstrations. “Police officers and gendarmes are positioned around the square to enforce this ban.” The punishment for unlawful assembly: a verbal warning, including a €135 fine pursuant to a class 4 infraction.

Like just about all of central Paris, Bastille Square was declared off-limits for the latest round of protests held on October 24, with many surrounding businesses boarded up in anticipation of a replay of the violent clashes and rioting seen one week earlier. Organizers estimate that as many as 250,000 people still made it out for this Saturday’s largely peaceful march, which received last-minute authorization to take place on a far-flung boulevard along the southeastern perimeter of the city. Nationwide, upwards of 800,000 demonstrators defied the attempts by authorities to snuff out the social unrest that has gripped France since high school students began blocking campuses in late September.

These efforts have escalated significantly in the last 10 days. Police prefects, the top Interior Ministry representatives in each administrative département, have instituted curfews in several medium-sized French towns, with similar nighttime orders covering select parts of larger cities like Paris, Lyon, and Nice. In the capital, helicopters mounted with searchlights patrolled the city from above, while by day police chiefs handed out protest and assembly bans. Further from the public eye, hundreds of individuals accused of participating in rioting on October 17 have been brought before rapid-fire trials in courthouses, with scores of prison sentences already handed down. As many as 70,000 riot police were mobilized for October 24 alone, when special military detachments were deployed to guard sensitive public buildings.

This was not a “state of emergency” as such, at least not in the strict legal sense of the special emergency powers that the French executive can claim in a period of crisis. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, for his part, has resisted calls to seek such powers, which would require approval from parliament if they are extended beyond an initial 12-day window.

But is such a designation even necessary? The clampdown on this fall’s wave of demonstrations has already seen over 10,000 cumulative arrests and countless injuries inflicted on protesters. It is a showcase for how ostensibly exceptional powers to suspend civil liberties are becoming the norm when it comes to the management of strained outpourings of opposition. Macron seemed to have even claimed a presidential prerogative over the right to protest itself, offering his “general recommendation” on October 22 “that there not be protests in the coming days.” In a patent attempt to constrain information and grassroots organizing, Lecornu has purportedly sought to prepare for blackouts on social-media sites like TikTok and Instagram.

As strategies to keep anger at bay, forceful policing and recourse to the gray zones of administrative law have long been trademarks of Macron’s presidency. More than perhaps any administration in recent memory, the outgoing president has assumed a confrontational stance toward protest—a highly incendiary strategy that ultimately serves to sideline genuine political demands. It is a governing habit that will likely be passed on to his successor.

Party politics is also porous to this kind of thinking. Since tensions began to mount in September, government officials and figures in the right-wing opposition have sought to label the left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI) as instigators. Yet Mediapart last week blew a major hole in that narrative. The investigative news outlet reported that France’s internal intelligence services—in no way a pro-LFI constituency—doubt the line coming from political authorities eager to ascribe blame for the crisis to La France Insoumise. “When we’re being asked to write word-for-word that LFI is driving the movement, even if that’s objectively false according to the consensus in the intelligence services, then we’re obviously being faced with a political decision,” said one officer cited in the report.

These are shocking revelations, especially some six months from elections. Then again, a Pavlovian willingness to blame the left is another one of the reflexes that have taken hold in the Macron years. It is also a not-insignificant ingredient in a climate that now has Marine Le Pen enjoying a strong lead before next spring’s vote. For Lecornu, the ongoing crisis is a time to make allegiances clear, between those loyal to the “Republic” and the “forces of violence,” as the prime minister said on October 20.

However irresponsible it might be to respond to political demonstrations with bloody-shirt-waving like this, it’s not new. The anger boiling over this autumn is entirely within the trend of the social conflicts that have defined Macron’s two-term presidency. French students, like the broader public joining them in recent weeks, are demanding little more than changes in policy, namely the freeing up of resources for smaller class sizes and decent learning conditions. On Monday afternoon, the government announced its first significant material concessions, including capped classroom sizes, upwards of €4 billion for school renovations, and the “replacement” of the unpopular university selection platform Parcoursup. But there’s little mystery as to why it doesn’t want to go much further. Seeking to contain a gaping state budget deficit hitting 5.4 percent of GDP, Macron and his allies above all want to avoid any hints at a fiscal deal that might mean new corporate and wealth taxation.

Macron’s best hope is that things eventually blow over, that the cost of lost class time, missed wages, and afternoons spent protesting does its work. But the events this fall have thrown into plain daylight the many trade-offs that the country has to make in a time of limited resources. For now, the protesters are also showing few signs of throwing in the towel. Cost-of-living demonstrators and students are expected to hit the streets again on October 31—this time under the banner of “defending civil liberties.” Unions have called for cross-sectoral strikes and demonstrations on November 5, pushing for investments in state services and an increase to the minimum wage. They have their own idea of what counts as an emergency.

Harrison Stetler is a freelance journalist based in Paris.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Lee Schlenker
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
Democrats have the tools to challenge Trump’s military interventions and electoral interference in Latin America—if they’re willing to use them.

As Democrats on Capitol Hill envision regaining control of one or both chambers of Congress in November, they are already gearing up to rein in the Trump administration’s imperial agenda in Latin America.

But beyond seeing the Western Hemisphere through the lens of the issues contributing to Democratic gains in polls nationwide—heavy-handed immigration enforcement, the tariff-fueled affordability crisis, high-level corruption—legislators in Washington should prioritize a robust oversight and accountability agenda that puts the brakes on the Trump administration’s reckless militarism and coercion in the region.

From the lethal boat strikes across the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, joint military operations in Ecuador and beyond, blatant electoral interference from Honduras to Brazil, gunpoint diplomacy in Venezuela, and the military-enforced fuel blockade of Cuba, Democrats can stem the tide of Trump’s so-called Donroe Doctrine—if they are willing to use the tools at their disposal and resist the bipartisan, interventionist consensus on the region that has long plagued Washington.

In response to Trump’s foreign policy in Latin America, Democrats have, by and large, attacked the administration on largely partisan issues, many of which intersect with areas affecting their constituents, including immigration policy, affordability, foreign aid, and corruption.

Democrats have challenged the administration’s mass deportation campaign, “safe third-country” agreements and gutting of asylum and temporary protected status; questioned the basis for imposing levies on Mexico and Brazil and their impacts on the cost of living; bemoaned the impacts of aid cuts on farm communities and the impoundment of funds already appropriated by Congress; and sought answers about the pardoning of the former Honduran narco-president and the security contracts of Blackwater founder Erik Prince in Haiti.

These areas of concern are undoubtedly significant and, because of their impacts on US communities and nexuses to domestic issues, should continue to be pursued if and when Democrats take back the House and/or Senate.

But wielding these select issues for partisan purposes or electoral gain should not overshadow equally pressing foreign policy concerns that many establishment Democrats have long avoided to prevent fissures within the caucus—areas that the administration itself has prioritized and could present significant blowback to long-term US interests if left unchecked.

Atop the agenda for Democrats should be the administration’s lethal boat strikes, which experts say amount to crimes against humanity, having left 240 people dead and cost taxpayers nearly $5 billion. Lawmakers in both chambers say obtaining the secret legal memo justifying the strikes and reasserting congressional authority over them will be among their priorities next year, but much more must be done to uncover the true cost of ongoing operations, sanction those responsible for serial killings on the high seas, and hold third-country collaborators accountable for carrying them out. Congress must clearly articulate that the president cannot direct summary executions against criminal suspects without due process and must withhold funds for lethal operations against presumed traffickers in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific.

Additionally, Democrats will need to obtain concrete information from administration officials about expected joint ground operations across the region under the framework of the US-led Shield of Americas and Americas Counter-Cartel Coalition. These operations have already seen US special forces deployed on missions in Ecuador and potential plans to integrate operationally in Colombia, Guatemala, Honduras, and elsewhere. Beyond standard training, intelligence-sharing, and military financing programs, lawmakers will need to press the Pentagon and State Department on the authorities under which troops are engaged in combat, the US taxpayer resources being committed, potential civilian abuses US deployments may enable, and measurable impacts on organized crime and US public safety.

Furthermore, the Trump administration’s electoral interference in the region—from issuing ultimatums to voters in Honduras and Argentina to endorsing a candidate in Colombia and unleashing a pressure campaign in anticipation of this week’s final vote in Brazil—must also face consequences from Democratic lawmakers. Congress should make abundantly clear that not only do overt US actions or statements that interfere in foreign countries’ elections set a worrying precedent for the future of US statecraft and complicate day-to-day diplomacy with institutional partners; they also establish a hypocritical standard for those critical of interference in US elections and can unduly tilt the scales in razor-thin contests.

Fortunately, top Democrats are already probing the administration’s shady dealings in Venezuela, an area that should expand to potential conflicts of interest by former administration officials now cashing in on lucrative business deals with Caracas. Not only must Democrats continue to scrutinize the neocolonial arrangement through which the Trump administration has assumed control of Venezuela’s oil revenues but also commission studies linking the Energy Department’s gold deals to organized crime, push the Pentagon on its statutory authority to take equity stakes in Venezuela’s hydrocarbon reserves, demand a return of the country’s sovereignty over its domestic affairs, and lift the comprehensive sanctions still handicapping the country’s full recovery.

Lastly, the de facto fuel blockade of Cuba, the imposition of secondary sanctions on foreign firms operating on the island, increased diplomatic pressure on countries sustaining ties with Havana, and ongoing military planning for potential kinetic or covert actions should remain a top priority for legislative oversight and debate. Reports of cronyist graft and back-channel deals between administration-linked figures seeking to swoop in and control Cuba’s key assets must also be addressed as Congress seeks accountability for the administration’s role in accelerating Cuba’s humanitarian crisis.

To pursue these issues and others, legislators have a number of tools at their disposal.

First and foremost, Democrats in the majority can call hearings and issue subpoenas—whether for administration officials, their family members and business associates to testify, or to review the text of official agreements—as Representative Joaquin Castro (D-TX) recently requested with regard to the Venezuela oil deal. They can also use the increased resources and personnel afforded to the majority to launch special investigations, issue committee reports, and convene temporary task forces on select topics.

Congress can also use the power of the purse—particularly through the annual federal appropriations process—by wielding funding restrictions or inserting reporting requirements for certain policies that, if Democrats win both chambers, have an increased likelihood of becoming law. Democratic leadership can also continue to restrain the administration by forcing floor debates and votes on the War Powers Resolution—as it has tried and failed to do over the past year on the boat strike campaign, war with Venezuela, and military action in Cuba—albeit with better chances at success come January.

And the Senate can choose to block the ambassadorial nominations for particularly partisan or underqualified political appointees for the dozen-plus vacancies at US embassies across the region and/or other top foreign policy posts charged with advancing the Donroe Doctrine from Washington.

Notwithstanding these efforts, the Trump administration will likely plow forward to reassert US dominance across the hemisphere and weaponize the economic and military diplomatic tools it has to those ends. But attempts to constrain these and related actions are well worth the fight, as congressional action can spur public frustration and mobilization over the domestic and global costs of unchecked militarism.

At the same time, vocal Democratic action may accelerate GOP dissent and intraparty infighting, creating space to further expose the frustrations and disagreements some Republican lawmakers have with aspects of Trump’s approach to the hemisphere and his apparent contempt for meaningful congressional input.

For Latin American governments, including those that have become willing, if junior, partners in Donroeism, heightened legislative action may incentivize hedging, a push to invest in bipartisanism, and a diversification of the bilateral agenda beyond security and defense issues.

Perhaps most importantly, more robust congressional action can redefine the terms on which US-Latin America relations are debated, expanding possibilities for less securitized solutions and more productive, multifaceted, and respectful ties with our neighbors to the south.

Lee Schlenker is a research associate with the Global South program at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, where he focuses on Latin America.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Israeli Elections: Fanatics, Generals, and the Question of Palestine
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Marwan Bishara
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
The central question is whether defeating Netanyahu would change Israel’s policies or simply change the people managing them.

It is déjà vu all over again in Israeli politics.

The upcoming Israeli election on Tuesday, October 27, has been called watershed, pivotal, defining, even fateful. Israel may indeed stand at a historical crossroads. But when it comes to Palestine, it has already turned the corner and is heading toward disaster.

Netanyahu’s political fortunes have weakened in recent years. The October 7 attack, the mishandling of the war, his dependence on the religious far right, and his resistance to an independent state commission of inquiry into the security failures of October 7 have all contributed to the opposition against him. He’s been indicted on corruption charges in Israel and on war crimes in The Hague.

But the central question is whether replacing Netanyahu would change Israel’s policies or simply change the people managing them.

Since the 1990s, opposition to Netanyahu has repeatedly rallied around former generals turned politicians. From Yitzhak Rabin and Ehud Barak to Ariel Sharon and Benny Gantz, the pattern has been remarkably consistent. When political leadership loses public confidence, a general appears. He promises to restore order, competence, and security.

Gantz had led the 2014 Gaza war. He later led the Blue and White Party, which beat Likud in the 2019 elections to win the highest number of Knesset seats but went on to form an ill-fated coalition government under Netanyahu.

And still, he joined Netanyahu’s wartime cabinet after October 7, 2023, alongside former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot. Both lent Netanyahu indispensable political support after his disastrous failure on October 7.

Eisenkot has since emerged as a leading political contender. His recently established party, Yashar, has been polling strongly. He hopes to repeat the familiar pattern: defeat Netanyahu by offering a more competent, disciplined, and credible form of leadership.

But the question is not merely whether Eisenkot can defeat Netanyahu or assemble a governing coalition. It is whether his victory would change Israel’s relationship with the Palestinians or simply change the management of that relationship.

The Israeli military remains a central institution in the country’s political and social life. While Israelis may distrust the government and parliament, they continue to place considerable faith in the military and security establishment. This helps explain why former generals in Israel remain such powerful political figures.

They promise to restore competence and discipline without necessarily challenging the security consensus that underpins the country’s political order. The consequence is a political culture in which strength and deterrence take priority over diplomacy and compromise. Problems become threats; force becomes the response.

General Gantz once put the Israeli mindset bluntly: “We definitely will live with our sword,” he said. “I don’t think our children or grandchildren won’t be soldiers. We must make efforts to try and not live only by our sword, but we will always be with a sword.”

The question is whether a new general in the prime minister’s office would challenge this mindset or simply manage it more effectively.

Eisenkot has become one of Netanyahu’s fiercest critics since leaving the wartime cabinet in the spring of 2024. He opposes Netanyahu’s dependence on the religious far right, the judicial overhaul, and the prime minister’s resistance to an independent state commission of inquiry into the security failures of October 7.

Like his predecessors among the generals, Eisenkot promises more competent government, institutional accountability, and a less combustible relationship with Israel’s democratic institutions.

Yet on Palestine, Eisenkot is no peacenik. His position is firmly on the right.

As head of Israel’s Northern Command during the 2006 Lebanon war, he became associated with the “Dahiya Doctrine,” named after a Hezbollah stronghold in Beirut. Its logic is to impose overwhelming destruction on areas from which attacks originate, treating civilian infrastructure as part of the enemy’s military capacity. He managed the doctrine’s replication during the Gaza war.

His military record also includes Israel’s use of overwhelming force against Gaza’s largely peaceful Great March of Return protests in 2018–19, during which tens of thousands of Palestinians were injured by live fire.

He opposes Palestinian statehood. He rejects restrictions on settlement expansion. He wants Israel to maintain its military presence in Gaza and elsewhere until Hamas and other enemies are defeated.

He may seek to curb the most violent settler excesses. But he has offered no political horizon for ending Israel’s domination of the Palestinians.

This is the central problem with the prospect of an Eisenkot-led government. His appeal rests on the promise of better leadership, greater accountability, and a more competent security establishment. Yet these promises do not necessarily entail a fundamental change in Israel’s policies toward the Palestinians.

Eisenkot could defeat Netanyahu’s Likud in the race for Knesset seats but fail to assemble a governing coalition. This is particularly likely if he continues to rule out relying on Palestinian Arab parties.

Israel could then be left in political limbo, with neither camp able to secure a majority of seats to form a coalition. Defections from one camp to the other remain a distant possibility because of the deep polarization between them.

A prolonged stalemate could keep Netanyahu in power until another election is called in the coming months, giving him a better chance of winning alongside his coalition of fascists and fanatics. His comeback would be nothing short of catastrophic. Another two years of Netanyahu and Trump? Apocalyptic.

Another possibility is a broad national-unity government built around shared security priorities. Such an arrangement could appeal to many Israelis but would be difficult to negotiate, considering Netanyahu’s long record of lies and betrayals. His decision to renege on his power-sharing agreement with Gantz after the 2019 election offers little reassurance to a potential partner.

Whether Netanyahu would accept Eisenkot at the head of a new national-unity government in return for a deal that ends his corruption trial remains to be seen. Either way, such a national-security government could amount to no more than an expanded version of the October 2023 war cabinet that managed Israel’s devastating war in Gaza.

The political question is therefore not simply who wins the election. It is what kind of leader can emerge from the result and whether his policies would differ in any meaningful way from those of his predecessor.

The choice facing Israeli voters may appear to be between Netanyahu and a more disciplined, pragmatic alternative. But the distinction between the two camps on domestic issues should not obscure their shared assumptions about security, military power, and the Palestinians.

Netanyahu’s dependence on the religious far right has helped intensify Israel’s political divisions. His opponents offer a different style of leadership and promise to restore institutional credibility. Yet a government led by Eisenkot will still maintain Israel’s military presence in Gaza, oppose Palestinian statehood, and resist restrictions on illegal settlement expansion.

The danger is that a change of leadership could make these policies more politically palatable without changing their substance.

For years, the generals have been presented as the responsible alternative to Netanyahu’s political excesses. Their credentials, experience, and reputation for competence give them an advantage among voters who want a change of government without abandoning Israel’s expansive security doctrine.

But competence is not the same as a willingness to change course. Let alone for the better.

The election will test whether Israeli voters are prepared to reject Netanyahu. It will not necessarily test whether they are prepared to reconsider the occupation, the settlements, or the use of military force as the principal instrument of policy.

That is the deeper political paradox. Israelis may reject the politician without questioning the military doctrine and national assumptions he represents.

The question is whether replacing the politician with the general will change the country’s policies or simply make their pursuit more disciplined and politically palatable.

And for those of us on the outside looking in, the larger question remains: What can or must be done so that Israelis rethink occupation and war as a way of life?

Marwan Bishara is a political sociologist and the senior political analyst at Al Jazeera English. He was previously a lecturer in International Relations at the American University of Paris and a fellow at the Ecole des Hautes Etudes en Sciences Sociales. He is the author most recently of Twelve Days That Shook the Middle East: Origins of a Genocide (Haymarket Books).
