https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Chris Lehmann
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The president’s flailing midterms campaign underscores a truth we should be acknowledging more often: He kind of sucks at this.

Donald Trump speaks during a campaign rally at the McMorran Place Sports & Entertainment Center in Port Huron, Michigan, on October 25, 2026.

President Donald Trump rounded off a hectic stretch of midterm barnstorming last week with an appearance in Sioux City, Iowa. There, after one completely unidentifiable noise and some desultory talk about extending a last-minute aid package to farmers throttled by sky-high diesel prices thanks to Trump’s feckless war in Iran, the proceedings turned to a Trump obsession: his eternal failure to land a Nobel Peace Prize. In typically cultish form, Joe Mitchell, a former GOP state representative now locked in a tight race for the state’s open second congressional district seat, proudly displayed a gold-framed certificate proclaiming Trump “Man of the Century” to make up for the long-standing Swedish snub.

Mitchell then launched into a groveling encomium worthy of a Trump cabinet meeting:

I wanted to say, Mr. President, for the last 10 years, you kept this country more safe than any other president, ever. And they’ve never given you the Nobel Peace Prize, by the way, which is a disgrace. So, what I came up with, Mr. President, is the new award. It’s called the “Man of the Century Award.” OK? It’s the “Man of the Century Award.” And I’m gonna hold this up for the artificial media to see. CNN, zoom in right here, CNN. OK? Because this man has done more for humanity and for America than any other president ever.

There may be more completely bizarre and off-base appeals to an electorate angered over the twin Trumpian scourges of escalating living costs and rampant elite corruption, but none leap immediately to mind. The voters of Iowa’s second district, like the hard-pressed residents in other traditionally deep-red but suddenly swingy states such as Mississippi, South Carolina, and Kansas, are seeking reassurance that the Republican Party actively identifies with their daily struggles in a top-heavy, inflation-racked, and benefit-starved economic landscape turning their communities into dumping grounds for data centers. Instead, they’re being treated to parodic displays of ultra-elite Oval Office grievance—and a GOP nominee whose chief qualification appears to be maximum sycophancy before the party’s Caligulan overlord.

Mind you, Mitchell was only heeding the main takeaway from the previous evening’s Trump rally in Greenville, South Carolina, where the president largely neglected his reason for being there—to tout Darline Graham, his handpicked choice to replace Graham’s late brother, Lindsey, as senator who, like many GOP candidates in formerly safe statewide races, is embroiled in a much closer general-election fight than anyone expected. Instead, he launched into a long harangue about the international awards he’s been cruelly denied—not just the Nobel Peace Prize but also the Pulitzer “for writing.” (The Pulitzer exists for books and journalism, so it’s not clear what Trump would have been nominated for, since his last book appeared more than a decade ago. Perhaps the laurel would be for fiction, a genre in which Trump has displayed unrelenting mastery while touting his record in office.)

Trump has claimed on Truth Social that his barrage of homestretch rallies are “SAVING THE REPUBLICAN PARTY AGAIN!!!” but instead they’ve been driving home a very different message, which has been clear throughout a second term where the GOP has clocked a long series of off-year electoral losses: Donald Trump is simply not very good at politics.

Yes, I know: Trump has twice claimed the presidency, and now enjoys a trifecta in Washington—albeit with a seven-vote House majority that rarely stirs out of its state of catatonia, and a Senate that won’t deliver on his pet legislative priorities like the vote-suppressing SAVE Act. But every facet of the GOP’s steeply declining political fortunes is traceable to staggeringly obtuse Trump-authored policy calls and boondoggles, from his disastrous tariff regime to the Iran War to the massively unpopular data-center offensive.

This is no doubt why Trump has such a pronounced inability to stay on topic at the campaign events meant to close out the GOP’s argument to retain power in Congress—and why his shtick is reaching a notably smaller segment of the party base. As Paul Waldman observes, the Trump rally is a once-formidable political innovation that’s now in its death throes. The shock value that earned them acres of unfiltered media coverage that worked out to an in-kind campaign contribution north of $2 billion in the 2016 cycle has clearly worn off. In 2026, Trump is playing to smaller-than-ever rally crowds; a recent campaign stop in Youngstown, Ohio was booked in a 7,000-seat facility that was roughly half-full, depriving Trump of his standard stump refrain claiming that thousands more of his adoring fans were lined up outside, clamoring to get seats that were already filled. When news organizations reported the anemic turnouts, Trump again repaired to his Truth Social following to ritually declare them ideological fabulists:

Because of their dishonesty, I have cinematographers shooting the various Arenas where I speak, in that some of the Fake News likes to dishonestly report lies and untruths. In actuality, my Events for very good Republican Politicians are probably more crowded than ever. There are no empty seats, there haven’t been for years, and there never will be. The Rallies are “HOTTER” than ever.

In a separate post, Trump said that the failure to report the Great Leader’s popularity meant that “The New York Times, and many other Artificial Media Outlets, should be arrested for their dishonesty and disservice to our Country.”

In reality, the midterm rallies are attracting a turnout down 75 percent from what his first presidential campaign saw, according to an analysis by PunchUp and The Daily Beast. And with an ironclad determination to sidestep the need to galvanize a majority of voters behind his record in office—a much taller order than the 2016 mission of demonizing Hillary Clinton and the Democratic Party on all fronts—Trump is freestyling in a fashion that defies the patience of all but the most diehard MAGA cult followers. During his original burst of rally success, the broad grievances Trump brought to the podium aligned themselves effectively with the deep sense of cultural exclusion that’s long fueled mass politics on the right: In calling out the political figures lording over a corrupt political system, Trump offered a critique of the knowledge economy’s phony meritocracy that resounded with the struggles of working Americans who felt their birthrights and livelihoods were besieged by it.

Now, however, he’s spewing non sequitur complaints, and lofting bizarre ad libs, into the void. In addition to dwelling on his award deficits, he’s held forth at length on the manly physique of Ohio Senate GOP candidate Jon Husted. He’s weathered repeated interruptions from protesters and strains of booing at several stops, which wouldn’t be all that newsworthy if the hecklers weren’t located in traditionally MAGA-steeped locales in Texas, Kansas, North Carolina, and South Carolina.

In Kalispell, Montana, Trump entertained a prolonged thought experiment about how animals felt about the Second Amendment’s protections of gun ownership, landing on this, uh, takeaway: “You know, the animals would be very, very happy to see you without guns. They would gain a lot of weight. And leave the law-abiding Americans defenseless while they set loose the savage criminals into your communities.” In Georgia, he proclaimed that the Iran War was going well for his cronies in the oil industry: “The United States oil and gas business is making hundreds of billions of dollars,” he announced with glee, after noting that his advisers had told him to avoid discussing oil-company profits before a crowd of supporters struggling with exorbitant energy costs. “I don’t give a damn, I’m going to say it—we’re making a freaking fortune.” On Friday, when the president was clearly running on fumes, stout Trump followers at a Fort Myers, Florida, rally got to savor this word-picture:

How about me. I come home, get into the building, get into a gorgeous White House that’s now fully renovated and beautiful again. So I got my guys and we took the good ones and put it on the bad one and we cleaned up everything and we skimmed the entire building. It’s so beautiful. We replaced the floor. We replaced the Home Depot one by one. The little ding, ding, ding, ding, ding. You buy the marble. It’s about a half an inch thick like this. We replaced it with statuary. The white and black. Beautiful. That was Rome. That was Greece.

It’s important to note that all these slapdash efforts arose in part because of the weak, ineffectual, and/or scandal-plagued candidates Trump has thrown himself behind, such as Graham in South Carolina, Michael Whatley in North Carolina, and Ken Paxton in Texas. In assembling this motley crew, Trump chiefly pursued one campaign credential: the ability to display maximum Trump fealty—a filtering process that crowded out more viable statewide candidates in the relevant primaries and set the stage for last-minute rescue missions in states that no Republican political operative would have imagined could have been in play this time last year. Trump’s eye for political talent, in other words, is as myopic and destructively narcissistic as his stump messaging.

Indeed, all of Trump’s rally antics last week came to be dwarfed by his unhinged Truth Social endorsement of the depraved campaign ad released by another of his handpicked protégés, Ohio GOP gubernatorial hopeful Vivek Ramaswamy. That spot features Donna Arthur, the long-estranged mother of Ramaswamy’s opponent, former state health commissioner Amy Acton, denouncing her daughter as a liar—without noting that the reason that Acton hasn’t been in contact with her mother for nearly 50 years is that Arthur sided with the stepfather arrested for raping Acton at the age of 12. In Trump’s world of patriarchal and predator impunity, Acton is simply “fair game” for disgusting drive-by assaults on her survivor’s story—a narrative that Acton has chosen not to highlight in her own campaign.

Trump feels complete license to treat an adult survivor of childhood rape like a rally protester he gleefully urges crowd members to beat up. And he clearly expects a fawning MAGA electorate to fall automatically into line; as he blurted out at another unhinged rally performance in Tennessee, “I mean, it’s amazing. When you stand up here, it’s just like… the love. I could say the stupidest things and you clap: “Oh, I love you so…’” That may still be technically true, but the acolytes of unconditional Trump love are getting smaller by the day—and the far greater legions of voters outside the arenas feel strongly otherwise. But the president needn’t be too upset by the mounting evidence of his horrifically bad political judgment; as he faces the prospect of subpoena-wielding Democrats coming to power in Washington, he can always find consolation in his growing trove of fake awards.

Chris Lehmann is the DC Bureau chief for The Nation and a contributing editor at The Baffler. He was formerly editor of The Baffler and The New Republic, and is the author, most recently, of The Money Cult: Capitalism, Christianity, and the Unmaking of the American Dream (Melville House, 2016).

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: The Culture of Experts and the Rise of MAHA
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Anthony Flaccavento
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The left won’t win over rural Americans by condescending to them.

My wife and I have been drinking raw milk for nearly 20 years. Over that period, two different local dairy farmers have used Virginia’s “herd share” rule to legally provide raw milk to customers like us, who pay to own a portion of the cow rather than buying it through a typical retail channel. For the past 15 years, our milk has come from a diversified local farm that also produces eggs, chickens, turkeys, and beef, all raised on the rolling pastures of Russell County, Virginia. We know the farmer and his family well and have visited the farm several times over the years.

This raw milk has never made us ill, nor has it sickened the scores of family and friends who have stayed with us over that time and had this milk on their cereal, in their coffee, or straight up.

Maybe we’re just lucky. After all, studies have shown that raw milk and products made from it are more likely to cause food-borne illness than pasteurized milk. For the most part, I accept those studies, so I guess you can say we also accept a higher level of risk in order to drink a richer, better tasting and, we believe, nutritionally superior product, supplied by a neighboring farmer.

I mention raw milk not to debate its merits but as a window into MAHA, the Make America Healthy Again movement. The question is how liberals handed the right a part of our base—historically left-leaning, countercultural people seeking to live, eat, and be healthier, many of whom also supported sustainable farming and organic foods. Annie Levin covered this shift well in her February, 2026 piece in The Nation, delineating a number of the cultural and political reasons behind it.

But one important reason is missing from that account: Many Americans simply want more control over their own lives and more autonomy in how they make decisions, especially regarding what and how we eat. This is particularly true in rural areas, where we tend to lean more libertarian. Much of the liberal establishment, on the other hand, admonishes us to “listen to the experts,” marginalizing or dismissing challenges to the prevailing wisdom. That’s a surefire way to piss us off in the countryside.

One example of this comes from an April 2025 edition of NPR’s It’s Been a Minute. Discussing MAHA and the relatively new phenomenon of “crunchy conservatives,” the two experts on the program cast a wide net in their characterizations of misinformation. One of them, Dr. Andrea Love, categorically rejects the health value of organic food and the ecological benefits of organic farming, while extolling the safety of genetic modification. Love, whose PhD is in microbiology and immunology, rather than nutrition, agriculture, or ecology, nevertheless regularly weighs into the debate about farming and health, including in a 2024 article she authored titled, “The organic food industry is a $180 billion marketing fraud.” Rejecting concerns about toxins in our food supply or claims that some farming practices lead to more nutritious foods, she instead argues that we should focus our health priorities on more frequent check-ups with the doctor, getting our vaccines and putting on sunscreen.

Journalist and podcaster Derek Beres, the other expert on the NPR program, places “regenerative agriculture” conferences alongside anti-vax gatherings as examples of “fringe groups” that have unfortunately gained a foothold in certain circles.

How did regenerative farming, documented in multiple studies to restore the health and productivity of damaged landscapes, offset carbon emissions while maintaining yields, and increase farmers’ profitability through reduced dependence on purchased inputs come to be a “fringe” phenomenon? Does that fringe element include the scores of agronomists, soil scientists, and other researchers from land-grant universities who present their findings at such gatherings?

If organic food is a $180 billion fraud, what should we make of studies showing higher levels of vitamins, nutrients, and phytochemicals resulting from sustainable soil-building practices, the heart of organic farming? Or of a UC Berkeley study showing that a switch to a diet of organic foods dramatically reduced pesticide residues in the bloodstream of children and adults?

Understanding the emergence of MAHA as nothing more than an embrace of conspiracies that has distracted us from the “proven” practices of doctor’s visits, vaccines, and sunscreen fundamentally misses the point. People are questioning, even rejecting, the advice of health and medical experts at least in part because they want more agency and more control over the decisions impacting their health. Rural folks in particular don’t take kindly to “just listen to the experts” admonishments—especially when some of these experts dismiss things they know to be true, like that better farming practice lead to healthier foods. You don’t have to be a conspiracy theorist to conclude that more regular visits to your doctor—if you have one anywhere near you—will not reverse the sorry state of American health.

A similarly reductionist listen-to-the-experts dogma played out during the Covid pandemic. When some Americans started taking ivermectin based on faulty information that it could cure Covid, the FDA tweeted, “You are not a horse. You are not a cow. Serious, y’all. Stop It.” It was a sarcastic and condescending potshot against the rubes. While it’s true that there is no evidence that ivermectin cures Covid, it is in fact an anti-parasitic drug commonly prescribed for people. Rather than simply stating that on its website, and cautioning against off-label use of drugs, the FDA’s tweet reinforced rural people’s perception of experts as condescending know-it-alls.

I was trained in the sciences, primarily biology and agronomy, and as a result, I’m always looking for the evidence when making important decisions. I don’t buy much of what the wellness industry is selling, nor do I reject the advice of experts just because they’re connected to the government or big institutions. But I’ve learned a couple of things that we on the left might be wise to consider.

First, the experts aren’t always right, and the advice they provide often changes over time. If you live in Appalachia, where the experts—the doctors, pharmacists, and government regulators—assured us that OxyContin was safe and nonaddictive, you know that in a visceral way.

Just as important is the second lesson, that smugness about possessing superior knowledge and understanding only exacerbates the left’s current struggle to establish commonly held truths. When our yard signs proclaim “We believe in science” or our media outlets relegate whole bodies of knowledge and experience to the fringe, we reject information from which we might benefit. In so doing, we fuel the fires of resentment and mistrust. And we help drive millions of Americans who want better health into the arms of the MAHA right.

Anthony Flaccavento is an organic farmer and rural development consultant and the author of Building a Healthy Economy from the Bottom Up: Harnessing Real-World Experience for Transformative Change. With Erica Etelson, he is a cofounder of the Rural Urban Bridge Initiative.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: “LULA!” Progressives Hail Brazil’s Stunning Election Result
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
“The people united will never be defeated!” declares Zohran Mamdani.

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva addresses supporters during a victory rally after winning a fourth term in the presidential runoff on Paulista Avenue in São Paulo, Brazil, Sunday, October 25, 2026.

Progressive leaders in the United States joined with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and global advocates for democracy in celebrating Sunday’s remarkable election victory by Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. After trailing far-right challenger Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in the country’s first round of voting earlier this month, Lula was written off by many analysts, who suggested that the largest country in South America would join its regional neighbors in swinging to the right.

Yet, after an energetic second-round campaign in which the 80-year-old former labor leader and veteran left-wing advocate rallied young people to boost turnout, Lula won a fourth term by 4.4 million votes—a comfortable 52–48 margin over a rival who was closely aligned with US President Donald Trump. The New York Times recognized the result as a “stunning reversal,” while NBC announced, “Lula halts pro-Trump wave with Brazil turnaround.”

Lula celebrated the victory with what sounded like a message for Trump, telling his cheering supporters in São Paulo, “This country will not accept being anyone’s backyard.”

From Mexico, Sheinbaum highlighted a popular victory over the authoritarian right and despair. “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won,” she said. Flashing an “L”—for Lula—sign with her hand, the Mexican president hailed the win as “a breath of fresh air for Latin America and the Caribbean.”

Sheinbaum’s enthusiasm was echoed by US Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent and two-time presidential contender, who paused his campaigning for Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan to declare, “Congratulations to Lula on his extraordinary reelection victory in the Brazilian presidential election. Lula has stood up for Brazilian workers and democracy—and will continue to do so in the next four years.”

US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) wrote on Monday morning, “Yesterday, Brazil showed the world that the will of the people is stronger than the authoritarians who try to suppress it,” while US Representative Ro Khanna (D-CA) said, “People all across the world are fighting back against extremism. With Lula in Brazil, they just won. Authoritarian leaders always attack democracy because they stand no chance against the will of their people. Trump must respect the results and not undermine Brazil’s elections.”

Sara Nelson, the president of the Association of Flight Attendants–CWA union, simply posted, “LULA!” on social media. And from New York City, where he recently met with Lula during the Brazilian leader’s visit to the city for the United Nations General Assembly session, Mayor Zohran Mamdani summed things up with a celebratory affirmation of the historic promise of global campaigners for economic and social and racial justice: “The people united will never be defeated! Congratulations, President Lula.”

John Nichols is the executive editor of The Nation. He previously served as the magazine’s national affairs correspondent and Washington correspondent. Nichols has written, cowritten, or edited over a dozen books on topics ranging from histories of American socialism and the Democratic Party to analyses of US and global media systems. His latest, cowritten with Senator Bernie Sanders, is the New York Times bestseller It's OK to Be Angry About Capitalism.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Obama Delivers a Scorching Rebuke to Trump—and Centrist Dems
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jeet Heer
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Unlike other establishment figures, the former president isn’t scared to associate with the party’s left flank.

Barack Obama has been out of office for more than a decade and is prohibited by the Constitution from running for the presidency again. But he remains a central figure in the Democratic Party.

This is true even though Obama’s ultimate legacy is still uncertain—far more than that of many ex-presidents. He made history as the first African American president, an achievement that owed much to his extraordinary charisma and political instincts. And he remains the only Democrat since Franklin Delano Roosevelt to win a majority of the popular vote more than once.

But the fact that Obama was succeeded by Donald Trump has cast a shadow over the Democratic titan’s tenure. Further, Obama’s successors as party leaders have all failed. He helped clear the field for Hillary Clinton in 2016, which ended with Trump’s election. In 2020, he worked behind the scenes to consolidate mainstream Democrats behind his former vice president, Joe Biden. Although Biden won the presidency, his term ended in disaster—and a second Trump presidency—as he pursued reelection despite visible signs of cognitive decline.

Trump ran in 2016 on popular dissatisfaction with Obama’s style of centrist leadership—frustration that was not confined to the MAGA fringes. The populist left, exemplified by Bernie Sanders, also felt Obama was too eager to shore up the status quo and had missed the chance y to push for much more populist economic policies in the wake of the Great Recession.

One of Obama’s critics during his presidency was an assistant professor at Columbia named Abdul El-Sayed. In 2012, El-Sayed wrote an article for The Huffington Post that distilled the left’s case against Obama. He lamented, “This leader has perpetuated war, violated our civil liberties, deported more people from our shores than any other president before him, and the list of his failures goes on.”

Since then, El-Sayed has moved into public service. Now he is the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, running on the slogan “Money Out of Politics, Money in Your Pockets, Medicare for All.” Accordingly, El-Sayed has tempered his criticism of Obama. Earlier this month, he addressed a reporter’s question about his past comments by asking,

“Do you love your dad? Do you agree with everything your dad has ever done? It’s a normal thing to love somebody, to really appreciate all that they’ve done, and to say, ‘Hey, here’s some things I would have done differently.’ But they still did some important things to create opportunity for you. There is no world in which I get to run for office without somebody like President Obama.”

El-Sayed’s friendlier words have been notably matched by Obama’s embrace of the younger politician. On Saturday, Obama went to Michigan to deliver an enthusiastic stemwinder in support of El-Sayed and Joycelen Benson, the state’s Democratic candidate for governor.

The speech proved that Obama has lost none of his skills as a rousing orator. He might be a retired politician, but he’s not a retiring one. He still has a remarkable ability to work up a crowd and to land well-aimed jabs at his foes, remarks that hit with force because they are delivered with preternatural confidence.

Much of Obama’s speech, not surprisingly, was taken up with decrying Trump’s failures—from the betrayal of Trump’s promises to both avoid new wars and to lower prices to the president’s corruption and gaudy self-celebration. In a passage that seems to have particularly upset Republicans, Obama noted that Trump

is very focused on home renovation. He should be on HGTV. Guy is building a ballroom that is bigger than the White House, paved over the rose garden, paved it over, put a helicopter pad on the south lawn, and then there is just gold everywhere. What’s up with the gold? I mean, he’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a cheesecake factory. It’s just gold everywhere. He is clearly not focused on lowering prices for you. People will come in to talk about the Iran war and talk about lowering prices.

Obama characterized Trump’s presidency as being riddled with “chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence.” There were also some cutting remarks about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s being “laser focused on important matters like the jawline and testosterone levels of our troops and livestreaming executions.”

This verbal shelling of the Republican administration is to be expected, although the sheer élan of Obama’s delivery was welcome.

What was more noteworthy was the subtext of the speech, where Obama implicitly acknowledged El-Sayed’s populism as the proper successor to his own politics.

Obama endorsed this agenda by saying, “Abdul is fighting for change, real change. Change that will bring an end to this war. Change that will get money out of politics and put money in your pocket. Change that will finish the job we started with the Affordable Care Act and guaranteed quality, affordable healthcare to every single American.” To be sure, Obama stopped just short of saying “Medicare for All,” but only by slightly rewording the demand.

El-Sayed is not the only left candidate Obama has endorsed. He has also backed Angie Nixon, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, in Florida’s Senate race.

Commenting on Obama’s endorsement of Nixon, David Sirota, former adviser to Bernie Sanders, wrote, “I think Obama’s incrementalism & establishment deference turned promises of hope and change into more of the same and created conditions for Trump’s ascent. But I’m genuinely glad he’s now helping candidates who embody a more populist politics & ideology than his own.”

Obama’s willingness to support populist left candidates sets him apart from prominent centrist Democrats like political strategist James Carville, Center for American Progress president and former Biden aide Neera Tanden, and Atlantic columnist Jonathan Chait, all of whom seem to fear progressive politics more than MAGA. These are all figures inordinately obsessed with disciplining the progressive left, and sometimes even calling for it to be purged from the Democratic Party.

In a recent interview with Bill Kristol, Carville said, “I would rather the Republicans keep the House by five than the Democrats win by five, because if that happens, they’re hostage to the DSA.” One can’t help but admire Carville for being so honest in laying bare, in such self-defeating terms, his core commitment: He would rather lose to Republicans than be part of a coalition where the populist left plays a prominent role.

Obama, despite his own very checkered history, doesn’t share in this folly. He fully knows the dangers of Trump and MAGA. Moreover, he seems to have accepted the critique of the populist left that the best way to defeat Trumpism is by more forceful economic populism.

Obama will never again hold office, but he still has an important role to play: not just as a critic of Trump but also as a model for his fellow centrists. His message to them is to give up the politics of the past and embrace the rising strength of progressivism.

Jeet Heer is a national affairs correspondent for The Nation and host of the weekly Nation podcast, The Time of Monsters. He also pens the monthly column “Morbid Symptoms.” The author of In Love with Art: Francoise Mouly’s Adventures in Comics with Art Spiegelman (2013) and Sweet Lechery: Reviews, Essays and Profiles (2014), Heer has written for numerous publications, including The New Yorker, The Paris Review, Virginia Quarterly Review, The American Prospect, The Guardian, The New Republic, and The Boston Globe.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Elon Musk’s Mortal Threat to Democracy
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: David Futrelle
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The world’s richest man—saying he’s “wised up” to the fiction of self-government—is leveraging his wealth to sway elections, threaten Congress, and alter the global balance of power.

Elon Musk delivers a Sieg Heil–style salute during Donald Trump’s inauguration celebration last year.

Should we worry that the world’s richest man, a self-appointed arbiter of all things cool or not, seems to have decided that democracy is deeply cringe? On the Fourth of July, while millions of Americans enjoyed fireworks displays and their dogs and cats cowered under beds in auditory terror, Elon Musk was having a conversation about the relative merits of “makers” and “takers” with a self-published science fiction author on X, the social-media platform he happens to own.

“Elon, this is the moment where you’re supposed to wise up and abandon classical liberalism,” Devon Eriksen wrote. “If you let takers vote, they will not only take more and more, they will make it more and more rewarding to be a taker.… Universal suffrage leads to universal suffering.”

As an alarmed David French noted in The New York Times, Musk’s response recalled weirdo techbro investor Peter Thiel’s infamous 2009 declaration that he “no longer believe[d] that freedom and democracy are compatible.”

Thiel may have been an early recruit to Big Tech democracy-bashing, but many others have followed his example. Elites in and around Silicon Valley, perennially angry about wealth taxes and government regulation of people like them, have become increasingly hostile to democracy itself. Eggheaded venture capitalist Marc Andreessen has declared that “democracy is fake” and holds up F.T. Marinetti, the Futurist who co-authored the 1919 Fascist Manifesto, as a personal hero. Tech entrepreneur and author Balaji Srinivasan, a former partner at Andreessen Horowitz, has become the Valley’s loudest proponent of what he calls the “network state”—a scheme to supplant boring old democracies with high-tech city-states lorded over by kinglike CEOs. Meanwhile, neo-reactionary monarchist Curtis Yarvin, formerly known as the alt-right blogger Mencius Moldbug, has become what Thiel biographer Max Chafkin calls the “house political philosopher” of the tech world’s fraternity of democracy haters; Thiel has funded his ventures and Vice President JD Vance, another Thiel protégé, considers him a friend.

It’s more than a little alarming that Musk has decided to join this motley crew. He’s obviously a powerfully situated foe of self-government, just because he’s got so much damn money, with his net worth hovering around a cool trillion. Beyond that, though, he now wields unprecedented geopolitical clout thanks to his ownership of more than 80 percent of the voting shares of SpaceX—a stake that gives him control over Starlink, the leading satellite Internet service. This Musk property is now a vital part of the tech infrastructure in 160 countries around the world—and not just for those living in rural or remote areas who would otherwise be without Internet service. Notably, Ukraine depends on the civilian version of Starlink for general communications and control in its war against the Russian invaders, while also relying on Starshield, its military-grade application, to control fleets of drones, which can be used to defend against Russian drones and to strike well behind enemy lines.

It can, that is, when Ukraine’s use of both Starlink and Starshield is unrestricted. On October 10, after Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, an irritated Musk posted that “Zelinsky has gone too far.” President Donald Trump, also angry over the refinery strikes, said it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president.” Four days later, Ukraine found itself facing extreme restrictions on its Starshield use that made it nearly impossible to successfully use its drone interceptors. Musk said it wasn’t he who had effectively pulled the plug but Trump. Trump, for his part, said that “it wasn’t me and I don’t think it was Elon”—apparently pointing his finger at the infamous invisible gremlin Not Me, or perhaps his colleague Ida Know, from the cartoon Family Circus.

After more than a week of denials all around, Musk muddied the waters further with a post on X Saturday in which he acknowledged throttling Starlink, but not Starshield, because, he said, the Ukrainians had violated its terms of services by “us[ing] it for offensive drone strikes to kill people.” Ukrainian officials replied that they not only hadn’t but couldn’t have committed such a violation, because Starlink does not, by design, work in Russian territories, with one adviser to Zelinsky remarking that it was “very strange” that Musk didn’t seem to know about the restrictions on his own technology.

Musk went on in his post to insist that the US government, not him, controls the military-grade Starshield, but then added rather ominously, “Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately. This is NOT a threat, it is simply a statement of fact.” He ended by declaring that he had “nothing but UTTER CONTEMPT for the virtue-signaling evil warmongers who push for endless slaughter and offer no realistic solution to the conflict”—presumably a swipe at anyone who thinks the Ukrainians shouldn’t immediately cede land for “peace.” Whichever version of l’affaire Starlink turns out to be true, it should now be abundantly clear that the mercurial, not to mention unelected, Musk has no business conducting foreign policy for us, and that his ability to do so is a threat not only to Ukraine but also to democracy in America.

Meanwhile, Musk can conduct the equivalent of a coordinated political drone assault on the American political system via his vast hoard of cash. According to Bloomberg, Musk has dumped more than $445 million into assorted Republican-aligned dark-money PACs in an attempt to put his big fat thumb on the scale in the November midterms. At least $158 million of that total has gone to the odious Ken Paxton, running for the Senate in Texas, Musk’s current home state; Musk is basically bankrolling his campaign.

Putting this much money into a political race is essentially a vote against democracy itself, an attempt to nudge results your way by overwhelming uninformed and uncommitted voters with a flood of paid propaganda—like the mailers sent out en masse by Musk’s own America PAC declaring, “THE SOCIALIST LEFT is DESTROYING AMERICA.” Notably, America PAC has spent four times as much on attacks against Paxton’s Democratic rival, James Talarico, than it has supporting the Republican. Musk has supplemented his PAC’s propaganda with even less subtle jabs at the “creepy” Talarico on X, where the tech mogul has 241 million followers. “There is something deeply wrong with Talarico,” Musk wrote in one post last week, adding in another that “Talarico would vote to take away your kids and transition them, not just in Texas, but nationwide. Pure evil.” Needless to say, Talarico would do no such thing. Musk—deeply estranged from his trans daughter, model Vivian Jenna Wilson—evidently takes this issue too personally to tell the truth about it.

The most unnerving thing about Musk’s political outlays isn’t that he’s spending so much; it’s that, in proportion to what he has, he’s spending so little. In politics, a half-billion dollars is a ton of money. In Muskworld, it’s a rounding error, representing only a fraction of a fraction of his total net worth. In 2022, he spent $44 billion buying what was then called Twitter and turning it into the fascist-infested hellhole it is today; that’s 99 times what he’s put into Republican races this fall. Hell, according to Forbes’s wealth tracker, Musk’s net worth rose by more than $10 billion during the time it took me to write this piece, because investors were feeling more charitable toward him on Friday than I was. He could easily dump a great deal more money into the midterms, and somehow I suspect he will.

One reason for this suspicion is that Musk is clearly feeling antsy about what might happen to him if the midterms don’t go his way. Once regarded as a sort of quirky tech wunderkind, Musk has recently seen his popularity sink toward Trumpian levels in recent days; an Economist/YouGov poll from earlier this month puts it at 34 percent. So it’s hardly surprising that some Democrats have begun to talk about hauling him before Congress to answer questions about, among other things, the skulduggery of DOGE and its enormous human cost; even a few Republicans want to ask him about just what happened with Starlink.

On a Bulwark podcast last week, tech journalist Kara Swisher remarked that if the Republicans lose the House and the Senate, the Democrats are “gonna start investigating again. You think he’s not on the list? He’s at the top of that list.” She went on to speculate that if Kamala Harris had won in 2024, Musk might already be in jail, not because Harris would have been “some avenging fury” but because there are “a lot of questions around different companies of his.”

Musk reacted with, well, fury. “Live by the sword, die by the sword,” he wrote ominously. “Sounds like Swisher really wants to go to prison.” For what exactly he didn’t say. A cat may look at a king, but apparently a journalist looking too critically at Musk has committed a jailable offense.

“Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets,” Musk added in another post, sounding like a B-list Marvel supervillain.

If Musk were just some crank on X, none of this would matter. It matters because this particular crank is, well, Elon Musk—a capricious, emotionally stunted man-baby mogul with incomprehensibly more power and money than he deserves, and who’s decidedly prone to basing most of his decisions on a mixture of strange whims and dark impulses. It is practically our small-d democratic duty to tax the shit out of billionaires like him. Yes, we could certainly use his money—but we’ve also long eclipsed the point at which his fortune has given him powers that are fundamentally incompatible with democracy. Elon Musk is a policy failure.

David Futrelle is a writer whose work has appeared in The New York Times, The Washington Post, Slate, and Vice. He writes the newsletter Brotopians.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Michigan Students Are All In for Abdul El-Sayed
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Heather Chen
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The progressive Senate candidate has won over students with his politics—and, in at least one case, his protein intake.

Parker Ward remembers every detail about his first time meeting Abdul El-Sayed. It was October 3, 2025, and El-Sayed was holding a town hall for Central Michigan University students, cohosted by the school’s College Democrats chapter, of which Ward is president. In the basement of a local Unitarian church, about 30 people showed up—half students, half Mount Pleasant community members.

“I loved listening to him, and I thought everything he was saying was awesome,” Ward recalls. El-Sayed spent his time answering the audience’s questions—discussing how people could connect across political divides, how AI policies affect students, and what community safety in the face of gun violence looks like. But as Ward was sitting there, listening intently to El-Sayed’s policy platform, he couldn’t help but notice something.

“I was like, ‘Oh my God, this dude is jacked,’” Ward remembers thinking to himself. After El-Sayed posed with the CMU College Democrats members for a picture following the event, Ward turned to him, shook his hand, and asked him the question that was at the top of his mind: “Abdul, how much protein do you eat in a day?”

“I don’t think he was expecting it, he just closed his eyes and laughed,” Ward recalls. El-Sayed gave him an answer: 180 to 182 grams of protein per day. It was, perhaps, the moment that Ward knew he was going to vote for El-Sayed.

“This dude is locked in,” Ward said. “I have to vote for him. I’m sold. That’s our next senator.”

Just over a year later, on October 9, more than a thousand students and local community members filled an auditorium at CMU to see El-Sayed speak. Where only a few dozen people had shown up to see the candidate a year before, now, the crowd was so big that some people had to be turned away at the door.

College campuses and young voters have always been a focal point of El-Sayed’s campaign. In 2025, El-Sayed held student town halls all around the state, visiting campuses from Wayne State University in Detroit to Northern Michigan University in the upper peninsula.

“It was really critical for us as we were building our campaign to go and listen to young people first, to engage them on the issues that are the most important in their lives,” El-Sayed told The Nation in January. “I see young people as being a foundational engine of this movement. And so it only made sense to start reaching out to them.”

That philosophy has paid off. In the August primary, El-Sayed won young voters by large margins, and led in major counties where the younger vote is concentrated. And come Election Day, a strong turnout from the youth voter bloc will be necessary for El-Sayed to beat Republican candidate Mike Rogers.

Over the course of a year, El-Sayed’s team has built up a network of campus fellows who run Students for Abdul chapters across college campuses in Michigan. To date, the campaign has 25 fellows, spread across 12 college campuses. Day to day, they handle voter outreach on campuses, create content promoting El-Sayed for social media, organize events, and inform the campaign of the priorities on their campuses.

“The goal with the program is record youth turnout,” said Milo Slevin, one of two campus campaign managers for the El-Sayed campaign. “Abdul has this unique and powerful ability to speak to students: to the issues that young people care about, to the values they want to see reflected in their government.”

Those youth voter outreach efforts are aided by the relationships that the El-Sayed campaign has fostered with College Democrats chapters across the state, where many of them work alongside local Students for Abdul chapters, organizing their own tabling efforts and registering new voters. The events have ramped up, too. In the lead-up to Election Day, El-Sayed has continued to visit colleges across the state, drawing massive crowds that bring together students and local community members in college towns.

Slevin said that the campaign has directed its attention primarily to eight campuses across the state, with 19 of the 25 fellows working on one of those campuses. Their target schools, which include larger state schools like the University of Michigan and Michigan State University, tend to be residential campuses as opposed to commuter colleges. With residential campuses, students are usually on campus around the clock, allowing for more outreach opportunities. Oftentimes, they already have existing political student organizations on campus, like College Democrats.

Stella Camerlengo, the president of Michigan College Democrats, which is considered a caucus of the Michigan Democratic Party, said that the chapters of College Democrats across the state were focused on “reaching as many people as we can, as quickly as possible.” Camerlengo said that members often coordinated visits to dorms, where they talked to students face-to-face about issues that matter to them, like the affordability crisis and stopping costly wars abroad. Then, they connect those issues back to El-Sayed’s campaign.

At Michigan State, where one of the largest College Democrats chapters is located, chapter president Aastha Singh said that she talked weekly with a staffer from El-Sayed’s campaign, and that the Students for Abdul chapter had become like a subcommittee of her organization.

While constitutional rules prevented Michigan College Democrats from endorsing El-Sayed before the primary, some chapters of College Democrats were so excited about him that they endorsed him independently.

At Central Michigan, prior to the primary, Ward said the majority of his chapter had either Mallory McMorrow or El-Sayed ranked first or second—supporters for Representative Haley Stevens, the moderate Democrat who eventually lost to El-Sayed, were nearly nonexistent. On July 5, when McMorrow, a Michigan state senator, dropped out of the race, the Central Michigan College Democrats immediately announced their endorsement of El-Sayed.

“The endorsement was a long time coming,” Ward said. “When McMorrow dropped out, we said, ‘Well, we don’t have anyone that would vote for an endorsement for Representative Stevens, so we’re going to go forward and endorse Abdul.”

A similar scene played out at Northern Michigan University, where the chapter bylaws require a unanimous vote for a primary endorsement. Before the endorsement, many members in the Northern Michigan chapter were already door knocking for El-Sayed. Shortly before the election, on July 23, they endorsed El-Sayed in a unanimous vote.

Summer Morrison, who leads the College Democrats chapter at Northern Michigan, said that El-Sayed embodied the ideals that young people at Northern Michigan were looking for, especially when it came to affordable healthcare.

“We have one big hospital here in the Upper Penninsula.… overall, our health system is run very thin,” Morrison said. On October 15, El-Sayed rallied at Northern Michigan with Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. It was a cold, rainy day, Morrison recalled, but hundreds of students and community members waited in the rain for a chance to see El-Sayed.

Hannah Hashem, who runs College Democrats at Detroit’s Wayne State University, said that the El-Sayed campaign reached out to her chapter in March to discuss an endorsement. When Hashem was 11, her father was deported under the first Trump administration. She has not seen her father, who was sent to the Middle East, in over a decade. A candidate like El-Sayed, then, who not only spoke about abolishing ICE, but vocally recognized Israel’s actions as a genocide, meant a lot to Hashem.

Hashem, who is Lebanese and Egyptian, also considers the El-Sayed campaign an opportunity to bring communities together. “Maybe we’ll get to have a senator who’s Muslim and a senator who’s Jewish.… I think that’s something that Michigan really needs, and something I’m really excited for,” Hashem said, referring to Senator Elissa Slotkin, who is Jewish.

While El-Sayed’s campaign fellows and the College Democrats are focusing most of their efforts on in-person organizing, they have also had fun making content for social media, where Singh says they have been able to reach many other young people.

Over the summer, Singh and Camerlengo attended a creator event where they were able to make content with El-Sayed. She came in ready with an idea, and gave El-Sayed the rundown. When it came time to film, he suggested they move to a spot in the room with better lighting.

“People love seeing candidates engaged with young people where young people spend their time,” Singh said. “It helps people understand and see these candidates in a different way.”

At Central Michigan, Ward said that even a rumor about El-Sayed can draw crowds. During a student activity fair, word somehow spread that El-Sayed would be visiting—even though it wasn’t true, as Ward was quick to tell the student press. So, the students took whatever else they could get instead—El-Sayed stickers, pins, even campaign literature. The table was nearly empty by the end of the activity fair.

“Anything that has Abdul on it or says Abdul’s name,” draws student interest, Ward said.

Before he took the stage at Mount Pleasant on October 9, El-Sayed made the time to speak to the people who had been turned away at the door. In the crowd, Ward, who got a chance to address the crowd that evening, saw professors, students, friends—even members of Central Michigan’s College Republicans. They didn’t disrupt the event, Ward said, and even laughed and clapped along at times.

Afterwards, El-Sayed came backstage and shook hands with all of the students who had worked the event. It was a small, but meaningful moment to Ward.

“When you’re a college student and you feel dejected and powerless to do anything in politics…it is empowering to realize that you can elect a fundamentally good person to office who will have a lot of power over how things work,” Ward said. “And I think that’s what a lot of young people are seeing.”

Heather Chen is a student and writer at Columbia University. She is a former managing editor of Columbia’s undergraduate newspaper, the Columbia Daily Spectator, and a former editorial intern at Defector.
