https://gothamist.com/news/queens-man-to.title: Queens man took girlfriend’s body to beach in a wagon, where it remained for 5 days
https://gothamist.com/news/queens-man-to.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/queens-man-to.text:
A Queens man wheeled his girlfriend’s body in a wagon to the beach at Rockaway Community Park and buried her in a shallow grave, where she remained for five days before police found her, prosecutors said Wednesday.
Two days after the alleged killing on Oct. 19, the boyfriend, Rogelio Lozano-Garita, 26, called 911 to report Seraphina Pereira, 35, missing, according to the Queens district attorney's office. He told police that a box holding her belongings had been dropped off at his apartment building, along with a note from a surfer who he said had found her things on the beach.
Lozano-Garita, of Edgemere, was arraigned Wednesday on charges of second-degree murder, weapon possession, concealment of a human corpse and tampering with physical evidence in Pereira’s death, according to prosecutors. He pleaded not guilty, court records show. Police said he was taken into custody Monday.
A lawyer for Lozano-Garita did not return messages seeking comment.
Prosecutors said Lozano-Garita shot Pereira in the head sometime between 2 a.m. and 6 a.m. on Oct. 19 inside an apartment at 343 Beach 54th St. The city’s chief medical examiner ruled her death a homicide on Monday and found she had been shot in the head, neck and torso, officials said.
An NYPD K-9 unit searched the beach and Pereira’s remains were found just before 10 p.m. on Oct. 24 near a cricket field near Beach 58th Street and Almeda Avenue, about half a mile from her home, officials said.
The couple lived together in Edgemere with their two young children and Pereira’s child from a previous relationship, prosecutors said. Police said her home was in Ocean Bay Apartments, a complex that is part of the New York City Housing Authority.
In a statement, Queens District Attorney Melinda Katz said that, as alleged, Lozano-Garita “mercilessly killed his girlfriend,” the mother of his children, then tried to cover up the crime.
A judge ordered Lozano-Garita held without bail, court records show. He is due back in court Friday and faces up to 25 years to life in prison if convicted, according to the district attorney’s office.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Challenges mounting to US laws enacted to aid recovery of Nazi-looted art
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Martha Lufkin
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
Reopened claims in California are testing new laws that were enacted to counteract court decisions in favour of museums in Nazi-looted art cases. The California and US federal statutes, which change the procedural rules for Nazi-looted art claims, are being challenged by the Thyssen-Bornemisza Collection Foundation (TBCF) in Madrid, and the Norton Simon Museum (NSM) in Pasadena, California.
Both museums are facing new litigation in art ownership claims that were previously decided in their favour by court judgments which both Congress and the California legislature cited negatively as reasons for changing the law. The challenges by the museum and foundation now launch the statutes towards court judgment themselves as to their permissibility.
On 19 October, Judge John Walter of the federal district court in Los Angeles said he would issue a decision in the TBCF case without oral argument, based on the submitted briefs. The museum and plaintiffs have each moved for summary judgment in the reconsideration of a claim to recover a Nazi-looted painting by Camille Pissarro, which had already been adjudicated in favour of TBCF.
The reconsideration was ordered in 2025 by the US Supreme Court, after California amended its procedural laws in 2024 to aid state residents who sue museums for stolen works of art. The legislature criticised a 2022 Ninth Circuit federal court of appeals decision which said Spanish property law applied to the TBCF case, and that under the Spanish “acquisitive prescription” principle, TBCF owned the painting. The work is Pissarro’s Rue Saint Honoré, apres midi, effect de pluie (1897). The Supreme Court vacated the decision because under California’s new procedural statute, California’s substantive law, and no one else’s, applies in claims for stolen art at museums, regardless of prior judicial decisions.
The plaintiffs, David Cassirer and other heirs of the original owner, Lilly Neubauer, justify recovery of the painting because Neubauer, a Jew based in Berlin, was forced in 1939 to sell it to Nazis to obtain an exit visa, and was not allowed to access the payment. In the renewed proceedings, Neubauer’s heirs argue that under the new California rule, California’s property law applies, “under which good title can never be acquired to stolen property”. The painting therefore must be returned to them as rightful owners. The plaintiffs also cite a second legislative change, which followed soon after California’s: the amendment by the US Congress of the federal Holocaust Era Art Recovery (Hear) Act. The amendment took effect in April 2026 and was expressly applicable to pending lawsuits.
For Nazi-loot claims that it covers, the new Hear Act bars art possessors from relying on “defences or substantive doctrines based on the passage of time”, including “acquisitive prescription”. The prior court proceedings had found that TBCF earned ownership of the painting under Spanish acquisitive prescription, because TBCF possessed the painting for more than six years without actually knowing it was stolen. The plaintiffs say that the 2025 Hear Act’s bar of any reliance on acquisitive prescription thus “conclusively resolves” all issues in their favour.
But the TBCF is challenging the new statutes. It says that the California law violates the US constitution by retroactively denying it of its vested property rights in the painting without due process, and that the Hear Act, if applied to this case to achieve that, will be unconstitutional too. Acquisitive prescription is not a “defence based on the passage of time”, but a property vesting law under the substantive law of Spain, it says, and prior court decisions in the case repeatedly found that TBCF’s property rights vested no later than 1999, “more than twenty-six years before the [Hear] Act’s enactment”. The TBCF makes multiple other challenges to the new laws, including that the new California law is an impermissible state attempt to regulate conduct extraterritorially in Spain.
The governments of the United States and California have intervened in the lawsuit, submitting briefs defending the constitutionality of their statutes. Friend of the court briefs have also been filed on both sides. A decision is expected likely by late February.
In the second lawsuit, the NSM on 14 October challenged a complaint filed in September in state court and removed it to the federal district court in Los Angeles. The claimants seek recovery of a diptych, Adam and Eve (around 1530), by Lucas Cranach the Elder. The paintings were among 800 works stolen from the Old Masters dealership in the Netherlands owned by Jacques Goudstikker, a Dutch Jew, by Nazi Reichsmarschall Hermann Göring in 1940.
Prior litigation seeking the Cranach diptych ended in a judgment for the museum. In 2018, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals dismissed the case based on the “act of state” doctrine, under which the actions of the Dutch government within its borders, including its allegedly wrongful sale of the Cranach paintings to a third party, cannot be adjudicated by US courts. The prior litigation was brought by Marei von Saher, Goudstikker’s sole surviving heir.
The current lawsuit relies on the new California law allowing new claims even if previously dismissed on procedural grounds, and is brought by Von Saher’s assignees, Daniel Gryczman and the Jewish Federation Council of Greater Los Angeles. The NSM is telling the court that the new lawsuit is a “misguided and meritless” action seeking to relieve the museum from its prior judgment, and is requesting a permanent injunction precluding the re-litigation. The prior judgment dismissed Von Saher’s claims “on the merits” andquieted NSM’s title to the Cranach diptych, the museum’s representatives say, and it asks the court to grant its requests to spare it “the open-ended threat of future litigation”.
A third lawsuit is also unfolding based on the new California law. In it, the daughters of the Czech Jewish artist Dina Gottliebova Babbitt are seeking recovery from the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum (ABM) in Poland of portraits Babbitt was forced to create while imprisoned at the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration camp. Under the process required to sue a foreign government instrumentality, the museum, an instrumentality of Poland, has not yet been joined to the case, a representative for the ABM tells The Art Newspaper, and has not yet filed a response. Babbitt’s daughters filed their complaint in September.
The Hear Act amendment is also being tested in other federal courts. One of the cases, brought against Austria and two Austrian museums in the federal district court for the Southern District of New York, is considering the constitutionality of the Hear Act’s denial of otherwise applicable defences.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.title: Queens Leaders Urge Mamdani to Acquire African Burial Ground to Turn Into Memorial
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.author: Greg B. Smith
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.text:
Queens Borough President Donovan Richards Jr. this week sent letters to Mayor Zohran Mamdani and two government agencies demanding they intervene to transform a parking lot built on top of an African burial ground into a respectful memorial commemorating the sacred ground.
Richards, joined by eight Queens elected officials, asked Mamdani and the city to buy the lot and join a growing effort to turn the privately owned lot at 47-11 90th St. in Elmhurst into a memorial. It’s believed more than 300 freed slaves are buried there in a cemetery that dates to the early 19th Century.
“In unity with dozens of community leaders and local preservationists, we urge your administration to acquire the lot and transform it into a proper memorial to the nearly 300 individuals who are interred there,” he wrote to the mayor Tuesday.
In August, The City Reporter revealed that a limited liability corporation that owns the site had paved it over and was renting it out as a parking lot. It held cars and trucks towed under an NYPD effort to rid city streets of abandoned vehicles.
The account inspired a wave of outrage by officials and local leaders at what they saw as a disrespectful treatment of the site.
On Tuesday Donovan and the other elected officials also fired off missives to Lisa Kersavage, chair of the city Landmarks Preservation Commission, asking the agency to designate the site as landmarked, and another letter to Kathy Moser, commissioner of the state Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation department, asking her to consider placing the site on its registry of historic sites.
Those who signed on included the U.S. Rep. Grace Meng, Public Advocate Jumaane Williams, state Sen. Leroy Comrie, Assemblymembers Catalina Cruz and Larinda Hooks and City Councilmembers Shanel Thomas-Henry, Ty Hankerson and Shekar Krishnan, all Democrats.
In his letter to the mayor, Borough President Richards emphasized his ongoing conversations with City Hall about the fate of the site. On Wednesday City Hall did not respond to questions about the status of those talks.
The site dates to 1818 and was taken over by the founders of what would be St. Mark’s African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1828, the year after New York State abolished slavery. The church sold off the lot in the 1930s and it was for years the site of a factory.
In 2009 the factory owner sold it to 90 Queens LLC, a developer who planned to build luxury condos there. While digging a foundation, workers hit an iron coffin containing the remains of an African American woman believed to have died of smallpox around 1835. Subsequent archaeological exploration uncovered hundreds of other graves.
The Rev. Kimberly Detherage of St. Mark’s has called on Mayor Mamdani to get the city to buy the plot and back the creation of a memorial that would honor the individuals buried there. A local group, the Elmhurst History and Cemeteries Preservation Society, has a pending request for examination filed with the city’s landmarks preservation agency. On Wednesday the LPC did not immediately respond to questions about the status of that examination.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Getting ‘woo-woo’ in the desert: Los Angeles artist launches pirate radio station
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Hannah Sage Kay
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
In May 2020, the Los Angeles-based artist Ian James received a package from Wuhan, China. It was a radio transmitter he had ordered months prior from the e-commerce site Alibaba. The seller—concerned about the scarcity of toilet paper and N95 masks in the US due to Covid-19—padded the crate not with bubble wrap and packing chips, but with masks and toilet rolls. After a long delay at customs, James tells The Art Newspaper, the package arrived “on a wing and a prayer”.
James had ordered the transmitter to use for a New Age pirate radio station in the desert called KHLZ. Beginning this past Saturday (24 October), every day at sunset the secret radio station starts its programming. KHLZ will broadcast overnight between 5pm and 9am—after the FCC monitors turn in for the evening. “It will be this ghost radio station broadcasting as though someone is asleep at the switch,” James says.
In his art practice, James often examines the adoption of spiritual technologies by corporate enterprises and capitalist value systems. His new radio station serves as something of a foil to corporate economies and federal regulatory systems. It operates off the grid as an unlicensed, itinerant broadcast featuring music and compilations from a diverse array of spiritually intoned, New Age musicians from the 1970s to the present. This programming is “good for people’s mental and emotional well-being”, James says.
The impetus for this project began nearly 15 years ago. Starting in 2012, James ran a New Age programme on KCHUNG—an artist-led radio station in Los Angeles. But in 2019, he decided to establish his own station, including it in his solo exhibition in Santa Monica.
Titled The Harmony of the Noosphere, the show drew on the writings of the New Age writer and artist Jose Argüelles, who popularised the concept of the Noosphere: the third sphere surrounding the Earth that serves as a site of human consciousness and mental activity, growing in complexity as planetary consciousness evolves. “Utopic in its goals, the Noosphere’s construction is aided by technological innovations, yet hampered and disrupted by the capitalist machinations that produce and pervert these possibilities,” reads the exhibition statement.
This precisely is the complex relationship that lies at the centre of much of James’s work. The exhibition featured wall works with stock photo-type advertisements for spiritual technologies and a live-streamed meditation session. And there were three pyramid-shaped sculptures housing a transmitter and two speakers, enabling James to broadcast New Age mixes.
While the 2020 exhibition served as the first iteration of James’s radio station, he had always planned to transfer it to a mobile facility and broadcast in perpetuity. Now, six years later, James has officially launched his station in a retrofitted caravan-turned-broadcasting studio near Joshua Tree.
The caravan came into the artist’s possession at a fortuitous and unexpected time. It was given to his partner, the painter Patricia Fernandez, just after the onset of the pandemic. James started renovating it as the federal government began increasing unemployment benefits and sending stimulus checks. “I was getting $1,000 a week or something that I was putting into this radio-station project,” James recalls. “It was stupid and crazy.”
After discovering rat droppings and mould in the caravan’s walls, James completely gutted the interior and decided to cover every surface in a faux-Calacatta marble laminate, which similarly ornaments the three pyramid sculptures inside. Inspired by a glacial cave he had visited in Iceland, James wanted to create a cool (but not cold) space, one that through material specificity—in this case, the simulacra of the oldest continually quarried marble in Italy that has been used in spiritual and governmental sites since antiquity—communicated across generations without need for explanation.
“I was interested in the fact that this marble had a simulacrum made by the Formica corporation,” says James, adding that he liked the idea of using “this repeating pattern that probably came from some small section of marble that is in another building somewhere”.
In addition to serving as a broadcasting studio, the caravan houses a growing archive of materials pertaining to the vast culture of New Age practices. It includes every issue of a Michigan-based newsletter called Pyramid Power. It also features a collection of typewritten and Xeroxed newsletters about extraterrestrial contact and interdimensional communication called White Star, given to James by the Ufologist and New Age musician JD Emmanuel—a featured guest on the artist’s old show on KCHUNG.
Alongside cassettes that James sourced from eBay—previously sold at massage parlours, spas and mediation centres—he includes the veritable all-stars of New Age music. These are people like Kat Epple (a close friend and collaborator of Robert Rauschenberg) and Iasos, a jazz student at Stanford University in the late 1960s who claims he was contacted by two interdimensional beings.
Iasos believed the music the aliens shared with him would “help humanity ascend to a higher plane of being”, James says. Only with the growing availability of synthesisers in the early 1970s was Iasos able to re-create the sounds that he had heard. He called it Paradise Music.
James had previously interviewed both Epple and Iasos at KCHUNG. “Iasos was always thinking about how the music can raise people's vibrations,” James says, “and help humanity become more peaceful and empathetic towards each other.”
KHLZ is meant to be “a benevolent thing that people can listen to and participate in”, James says. He imagines that, given its location near Joshua Tree—though it will also stream online and occasionally travel for pop-up events—the station will serve as a meditative soundtrack for people while they do yoga, cook dinner, or “eat mushrooms and run around. As you've probably seen, there’s a lot of ways to be ‘woo-woo’, so the radio station is open to those possibilities.”

https://hellgatenyc.com/renewables-publi.title: What if NYC Just Built Its Own Renewable Energy Infrastructure?
https://hellgatenyc.com/renewables-publi.author: Max Rivlin-Nadler
https://hellgatenyc.com/renewables-publi.text:
New York City's renewable energy buildout continues at a snail's pace. As of 2025, 90 percent of the power we use in the city comes from non-renewable power sources like fossil fuels burned at local power plants, while peaker plants burning fossil fuels continue to line the city's waterfront, spewing nitrogen oxide and other particulates into the city's neighborhoods during the hottest days of summer. The City has set a goal of relying on 100 percent renewable energy by 2040, but that looks increasingly unlikely, even with the long-awaited Champlain Hudson Power Express line bringing hydroelectricity in from Québec. New York's massive wind power projects are in the crosshairs of the Trump administration, and Governor Kathy Hochul has embraced an "all-of-the-above approach" to energy: approving a fossil fuel pipeline and pursuing a dramatic—and controversial—expansion of nuclear capacity in the state. 
But there has been one bright spot amidst all the climate and energy backsliding—New York City has been building out its solar power infrastructure far faster than expected, with the city expected to smash a 2030 goal for 100 megawatts of solar four years early. Solar power, unlike wind turbines, nuclear energy, or hydroelectricity, is cheap to build, and is done with no collateral consequences for nearby communities.

https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-exten.title: Mamdani extends NYC racial equity leader's term after Council pushes back on replacement
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-exten.author: Elizabeth Kim
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-exten.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani will delay his plan to replace the chair of the city’s racial equity watchdog, who has emerged as a sharp critic of the administration. The move comes after pushback from the City Council.
Linda Tigani has led the Commission on Racial Equity since its inception in 2023, after it was formed by a ballot measure approved by voters.
In recent weeks, Tigani has said that Mamdani has been pushing to remove her. She has also condemned some of his policies, specifically his police commissioner Jessica Tisch’s strategy of cracking down on low-level offenses, which disproportionately affect Black and Latino New Yorkers.
“My job is to hold the city accountable,” she told Gothamist on Wednesday before holding a rally with supporters on the steps of City Hall. “We know that any movement in leadership would undermine that work.”
The commission recently won a lawsuit in which they argued that Mandani and his predecessor, Eric Adams, broke the law when they failed to release a plan to combat racial inequity by the legally-mandated deadline. Tigani has been fiercely critical of the Mamdani administration's decision to appeal the judge’s ruling.
The Mamdani administration released its plan in September.
In her interview with Gothamist, Tigani also cited last week’s town hall where New York Times journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones grilled Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels for failing to put forward a plan to integrate public schools.
“We had an education town hall where the chancellor could not give us any information or action plans on how he was planning to desegregate the schools and increase racial equity or close racial equity disparities,” she said.
Mamdani and City Council Speaker Julie Menin, who jointly appoint the chairperson of the commission, agreed Tigani will now serve through July 2027, both offices said.
The commission is charged with advancing the goals of racial equity in city government and increasing community input into the decision-making process.
At an unrelated press conference in Brooklyn on Wednesday, Mamdani thanked Tigani for her service, and said Christopher Alexander, executive director of the NAACP New York State Conference, should be the next chair — but not until next year.
“We're excited to work with the same council to put forward Christopher Alexander as the next commissioner to pick up the mantle that Linda is going to leave behind,” the mayor said.
Jack Lobel, a spokesperson for Menin, said the Council is currently vetting Alexander as Tigani’s replacement.
Wednesday’s announcement came after city lawmakers urged the mayor to keep Tigani.
On Tuesday, the City Council’s Black, Latino and Asian Caucus released a letter sent to Mamdani, urging him to retain Tigani. News of the plan to replace Tigani was first reported by the New York Times.
"At this consequential moment, continuity in CORE’s leadership is essential to advancing its mandate and delivering on the commitments our City has made to racial equity, accountability and justice,” they wrote.
Menin's spokesperson later issued a statement supporting Tigani, saying she had met with members of the caucus and had conveyed to Mamdani their view that “Ms. Tigani be allowed to remain in her position for an extended period.”
Bronx City Councilmember Althea Stevens said members of the mayor’s office had recently made clear to her and her colleagues that Mamdani wanted to oust Tigani as soon as her term ended.
“They were very direct that she needed to go,” she said, adding that the mayor’s team never gave them a “clear understanding” of why they wanted to remove Tigani.
Stevens and other members argued that Tigani had done a good job and that the decision to replace her was not the mayor’s alone.
“We wanted to make clear that this isn’t a mayor appointee. They came to us with a name, there was no discussion of how to do this together,” she said.
This story was updated with new information.

https://gothamist.com/news/woman-charged.title: Woman charged with federal hate crimes after allegedly stabbing 2 Jewish men in NYC
https://gothamist.com/news/woman-charged.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/woman-charged.text:
A Russian woman is facing federal hate crime charges following the alleged stabbing of two Jewish men near Manhattan’s Diamond District earlier this month.
Federal prosecutors identified the woman as Anna Mochalova, a 32-year-old Russian national, and accused her of stabbing the men “with a sharp object that is consistent with being a needle.”
Mochalova allegedly stabbed the first victim around 5:50 p.m. on Oct. 21 while the man had been walking along West 47th Street between Fifth and Sixth avenues, according to the complaint. Federal prosecutors described the first man as having a beard and wearing clothes associated with the Orthodox Jewish community, including a black hat and tzitzit, the strings attached to the corners of a prayer shawl.
Prosecutors say Mochalova then approached another victim — also a Jewish man wearing a yarmulke — on the corner of Sixth Avenue and West 45th Street, just two blocks away from the first stabbing. She bumped into the man several times before stabbing him in the right forearm, prosecutors said.
Another person who was present at the scene during the second stabbing said Mochalova asked him if he was Jewish, and then apologized when he said he was not, according to prosecutors. She is is facing two hate crime charges, which each carry a maximum sentence of 10 years.
"Mochalova allegedly stabbed two men specifically because they were Jewish, an attack made all the more terrifying because the specific weapon used — and its potential contents — remain unknown pending further investigation," U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York Jamie McDonald said in a statement.
NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Mochalova’s actions struck fear “in an entire community.”
“A hate crime is a message written in violence, and this defendant’s message was loud and clear,” she said in a statement.
Attorney information for the accused was not made immediately available.

https://gothamist.com/news/ex-nypd-serge.title: Ex-NYPD sergeant sentenced to 4-12 years in deadly drunken Taconic crash
https://gothamist.com/news/ex-nypd-serge.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/ex-nypd-serge.text:
A former NYPD sergeant convicted of driving drunk the wrong way on the Taconic State Parkway and killing a Peekskill man was sentenced Wednesday to four to 12 years in prison, the state attorney general’s office said.
Tiffany Howell, 48, of Warwick, New York, pleaded guilty in August before Westchester County Judge Anne B. Bianchi to aggravated vehicular homicide and second-degree manslaughter in the January crash that killed Manuel Boitel, 61.
Howell’s driver’s license has been revoked, and she waived her right to appeal, New York Attorney General Letitia James said.
Boitel’s family said the punishment fell short. In a statement released through their attorney, the family members said they were was disappointed.
“It does not provide the measure of accountability the family had hoped for,” attorney Jonathan Roberts said.
Howell was driving south in the highway’s northbound lanes at more than 50 mph when she crashed head-on into Boitel’s car shortly before midnight on Jan. 22, prosecutors said. Her blood alcohol level was at least 0.18, more than twice the legal limit. Boitel was pronounced dead at a hospital shortly after midnight.
Earlier that night, Howell, an 18-year NYPD veteran, had helped organize a dinner and cigar event with an open bar in Scarsdale for the NYPD Holy Name Society, a Catholic fraternal group, according to social media posts.
The family is also suing the City of New York, the NYPD, the Holy Name Society and the cigar bar where the event was held.
In letters to the judge, Boitel’s wife and sons asked for no leniency. Marisol Boitel wrote that she met her husband when she was 18, married him at 20, and that he was driving home from work happy because he had the next two days off.
“She did not only kill him; she also killed my will to keep living, my dreams and our plans for now and for the future,” she wrote, asking for the maximum sentence.
His son, Marvin Boitel, wrote that his father had once wanted to become a police officer but chose safer work after becoming a father. Marvin Boitel ended his letter with something he said his father always told him: “Actions have consequences.”
Howell’s attorney, a Sergeants Benevolent Association lawyer, did not return calls seeking comment.
The attorney general’s Office of Special Investigation prosecuted the case. State law requires the office to investigate deaths that a police officer may have caused, whether the officer was on or off duty.

https://citylimits.org/11-year-old-boys-.title: 11-Year-Old Boy’s Death in Bronx NYCHA Fire is a ‘Horrific Reminder’ Of E-Bike Battery Dangers, Mayor Says
https://citylimits.org/11-year-old-boys-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/11-year-old-boys-.text:
Share This Article
The deadly blaze, which broke out early Wednesday at NYCHA’s Patterson Houses in the South Bronx, was started by an a lithium-ion battery on an electric bike, which was blocking the apartment’s exit, officials said.
This story has been updated since original publication.
A fire that killed an 11-year-old boy in a NYCHA apartment building in the Bronx was caused by a lithium-ion battery on an electric bike, officials said—renewing concerns about the potential dangers of such devices, which have contributed to hundreds of similar blazes across the city this year.
The fire broke out early Wednesday morning in the kitchen of an 11th-floor apartment at NYCHA’s Patterson Houses in Mott Haven. While FDNY crews arrived within four minutes, the e-bike that caused the blaze “was placed in the pathway of the exit door,” according to Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore, and “made it impossible for the residents to leave safely.”
Kristina Diaz, a resident of 35 years who also lives on the 11th floor and serves as the development’s captain of tenant patrol, described hearing neighbors banging on doors down the hall shortly before 1 a.m. on Wednesday, and said by the time she got to her front door, “the whole kitchen and living [room] was already smoky.”
She then watched firefighters break down the door of the blazed apartment, and described seeing one of the residents on the floor.
She said she received 72 calls in 18 minutes from fellow neighbors asking what happened, or inquiring about how they could help. “I don’t want nothing, just bring a candle for the little 11-year-old,” she told them.
Wednesday’s blaze is the second fire residents of Patterson Houses experienced this year, following an electrical fire that occurred in January and injured six.
Residents of the building expressed shock and grief. Florence Banks, 68, lives on the fifth floor and said she was watching TV when she heard firetrucks pull up to the building. She called her neighbor, and watched from the hallway windows as firefighters “were bringing people out, and pumping their chests.”
“I couldn’t take that,” she said. “I’m just shocked.”
Officials said the damage was contained to the apartment where the fire started. In addition to the boy who was killed, four others were critically injured, including two teenagers.
“Today is a horrific reminder of the danger that lithium-ion battery fires can pose,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a press conference outside Patterson Houses on Wednesday, where officials displayed the charred e-bike that ignited the blaze.
The city has seen more than 400 fires caused by lithium-ion batteries so far this year, officials said, up from 292 last year, and six New Yorkers have died in 2026 so far.
According to the FDNY, 22 of those fires this year took place in NYCHA buildings—up from 18 such fires in 2025, and 13 in 2024.
E-bikes have become increasingly popular in recent years, especially among residents who work as delivery drivers. But the batteries they run on can spark fires that are “extremely dangerous, because they spread fast and ferociously,” Bonsignore said.
“The battery cells go into thermal runaway, which makes a small fire turn into a very big fire, very very quickly,” she said.
Officials urged e-bike users to take precautions, including charging and storing the bikes outdoors whenever possible. If they do take their bike inside, they should keep it out of the way of any exit, including doors and windows, and should never charge it unsupervised.
“Buy certified batteries that come with nationally safety-certified testing laboratory approvals,” Bonsignore said. “If they are leaking, damaged, or smoking, do not use them, and do not buy off-market batteries, but use the manufacturer-recommended devices.”
NYCHA previously considered banning e-bikes from public housing properties, but officials said they recognized that many residents rely on them to get around, especially those doing app-based delivery work.
The housing authority’s current rules allow for no more than one e-bike to be charged in an apartment, and it must be kept away from means of egress, plugged into a wall, and someone over the age of 18 has to be “present and awake while the battery is charging,” said NYCHA CEO Lisa Bova-Hiatt.
“We need individuals to listen and follow the policy,” she added.
Mayor Mamdani told reporters Wednesday that further reforms will be under consideration.
“I think it is our responsibility to continually evaluate every option we have,” he said. “This is an issue that we have seen far too often.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/main.title: Trump Vows to Send Election “Monitors” to Maine After Far-Right Conspiracies Spread
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/main.author: Noah Hurowitz
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/main.text:
With voters set to cast ballots in two critical races that could help determine control of both chambers of the U.S. Congress, fears of potential voter suppression are running high in Maine.
Officials in the state have prepared for months against the possibility of election interference from federal officials, and the state remains on high alert in the run-up to the general election on November 3.
Training materials for law enforcement officials in the state, obtained by The Intercept through a public records request, were updated this year for the elections to include explicit references to federal statutes barring armed federal agents from polling sites.
In an interview with the New York Times this week, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said the inclusion of such references was a direct defense in response to the fearmongering around election integrity from President Donald Trump and his administration.
“This is the first time ever that we have had to engage in scenario planning to safeguard against potential federal interference in elections,” Bellows said. “It seems like the federal government is now adversarial to the states.”
Bellows’s office offered up the training slideshow, which cites a U.S. law that bars armed civil or military officers from posting at voting sites, to law enforcement personnel in the run-up to Maine’s primary election in June and again in the lead-up to the general election on November 5.
Nationwide, Democratic officials have expressed fears that the Trump Administration might weaponize U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement or other federal agencies to undermine the rights of voters. In New York, state Attorney General Letitia James issued a reminder to voters that federal officials may not “police the polls,” and the Arkansas chapter of the NAACP called out the assignment of federal election monitors to two counties in the state as potential intimidation.
The Trump administration, meanwhile, has sounded the alarm about the alleged scourge of non-citizens on the voter rolls, sending agents from the FBI and ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations division to probe alleged fraud. A handful of people in California, New York, and North Carolina have been indicted for allegedly voting as non-citizens, but a review of similar cases by the Washington Post found that such cases were often the result of honest mistakes.
In Maine, worries about federal interventions at polling places flared when — following a slew of social media videos from Trump allies suggesting that fraud is already taking place among the state’s Somali American community — a local outlet reported that the Department of Justice would be sending election monitors to the state.
Jon Fetherston, a journalist with the far-right Maine Wire, which is funded by conservative megadonor Leonard Leo, was seen following people in and around an early voting site at Lewiston City Hall and aggressively questioning them. (The Maine Wire did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)
Critics said the moves were tantamount to voter harassment, but Maine Wire editor-in-chief Steve Robinson later defended them as an act of election transparency. Robinson, who has led a crusade against what he alleges to be a network of fraud in the state’s Somali American community, questioned the role of interpreters tasked with helping “jobless Somali bums” cast their ballots.
In the wake of the Maine Wire controversy in Lewiston, Bellows confirmed to the Maine Morning Star that a wave of federal election monitors would be headed to polling sites in Lewiston and Portland.
The Department of Justice on Tuesday confirmed to The Intercept that it intends to send election monitors to Maine for Election Day, but did not elaborate or respond to specific questions about where the monitors were to be sent.
“We will have around 1,000 monitors in counties throughout the United States, but we will not share the full list until Election Day,” a Justice Department spokesperson told The Intercept in an email Tuesday. “All monitors must meet the same legal and ethical requirements, including that they not interfere with the voting process. Every monitor has the same role: observe for potential violations of federal law and report concerns to the Department, which the Department will review after Election Day and act where appropriate.”
Robinson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Collins Takes Right-Wing Bait
With Maine a key battleground state for control of Congress — Democratic challenger Troy Jackson is seeking to topple long-serving GOP Sen. Susan Collins, and the Democratic House candidate Matt Dunlap is seeking to best former Gov. Paul LePage in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District — temperatures are running high in the state.
Progressives in Maine worry that even without a robust federal presence at voting places — whether monitors are armed or not — activist campaigns like the one undertaken by the Maine Wire journalists could pose a potential threat to voters’ rights.
“Basically, if you were walking into City Hall and you were Black, you could expect to have this guy come up to you with his phone and ask you all sorts of rude and obviously racist questions,” said Ben Chin, co-director of the progressive Maine People’s Alliance. “We’re trying to encourage everyone to come out to vote, but it makes sense why that might give people pause. You hear a guy like that is outside a polling location, it’s reasonable to wonder, ‘Should I go down there right now?’”
In a statement to The Intercept, Bellows said the state and the city of Lewiston were taking steps to ensure that voters could cast a ballot free of harassment.
“We have received complaints about the intrusive filming, photography, and harassment of voters in the City of Lewiston by political operatives,” Bellows told The Intercept in a statement. “All voters should be able to exercise their right to vote without feeling watched, questioned, or harassed, and we take these allegations seriously, particularly when it appears that voters were targeted for no other reason than their race or ethnicity. We understand the City of Lewiston has taken steps to address the problem, and we will continue to monitor the situation.”
Collins, meanwhile, took the Maine Wire’s reporting seriously after Fetherston asked the senator at a campaign event about the role of interpreters, which he and the Maine Wire cast as “electioneering.”
“I’m unaware of those allegations, but certainly only Americans should be voting in American elections,” Collins said. “And it is troubling to me if people are being accompanied into voting booths and handling ballots in a way that is not sanctioned by law.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://gothamist.com/news/after-being-b.title: After being booed at integration forum, NYC chancellor praised by school parent leaders
https://gothamist.com/news/after-being-b.author: Jessica Gould
https://gothamist.com/news/after-being-b.text:
Less than a week after being booed by integration advocates at an explosive town hall, Chancellor Kamar Samuels got a warmer reception from a panel of parents Monday who serve on the Citywide Council on High Schools.
“I was shocked when the audience booed when you defended parent choice,” said Linda Quarles, a member of the council, a group made up of volunteer parents that advocate on behalf of all public high school students. She said fellow parents, especially those who support selective admissions, asked to “pass along their thanks.”
“There are communities who were definitely not represented at that event last week, and our families want you to know that,” Quarles added.
Fellow panel member Deborah Alexander noted that the city’s own surveys found that more than 40% of families who left New York City public schools cited a desire for more rigorous academic instruction as a reason for leaving.
Integration advocates want to reduce or eliminate selective admissions to the city's public schools, pointing to data showing those policies lead to schools that are disproportionately white, Asian and affluent. But other parents, including many on the high school council, support selective admissions, saying students deserve the more rigorous programs “screened” schools provide.
Samuels has said he does not favor selective admissions “screens” but wants to be responsive to communities, and is launching education working groups across the city.
Supporters of pro-integration policies feel emboldened by New York Times journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones’ deeply personal article on her daughter’s experience in public schools. Hannah-Jones has said selective admissions are tools of segregation.
Last week, Hannah-Jones grilled Samuels on the Mamdani administration’s plans to advance integration. Samuels demurred on specifics, saying he was committed to working with communities to develop policies. Members of the crowd jeered Samuels, saying they were disappointed with his answers.
But supporters of current admissions policies — many of whom serve on the council on high schools — say high-achieving students should be rewarded, and that any move toward integration should not result in fewer opportunities for the sharpest kids.
The stark differences between the two meetings hint at clashes to come as integration efforts regain the spotlight in the city's education debates. Past debates over integration have polarized communities, largely along racial lines.
A call for reform
The council, an advisory group, consists of elected parent leaders from around the city, including some members of the group Parents Leaders for Accelerated Curriculum and Education (PLACE). PLACE members have mobilized in the past to preserve selective admissions policies at top-performing schools as integration advocates have sought to dismantle those policies.
On Monday night, Samuels defended his participation in the town hall.
“Anyone should be able to ask the questions and the things that they prioritize, and so the fact that that’s where that conversation went is fine by me,” he said. “I have always in my work prior to being chancellor and as chancellor really committed to making sure that parent voice is a part of what is driving our system.”
Samuels said he personally supports reducing selective admissions but said policies have to be driven by communities. “I won’t always agree with everything our parents are saying,” he said, “but I do think it’s quite critical that we hear those voices.”
Communities across the city are mobilizing for a fight.
On Tuesday night, Adams administration alumni, former Schools Chancellor David Banks and his wife, former Deputy Mayor Sheena Wright, gathered several elected officials, civic and religious leaders to call for reforms to admissions to the city’s specialized high schools as part of a live taping for their podcast in Harlem.
While the specialized schools are just a small sliver of the overall system, they’ve become a shorthand for segregation in public schools.
Banks said he wanted to change admissions at five of the city’s eight specialized schools when he served as chancellor, but that then-Mayor Eric Adams told him no.
“He's a politician. I'm not casting any aspersions. But I want you to know the reason for it is this. And that's why. …He was not prepared to take that on as an issue. And quite frankly, he said, you know, Black and Hispanic communities may get a little upset. They talk about it at home, but they're not gonna do anything about it. The Asian community is very, very, very organized around this issue, and I don't blame them for that.”
Adams did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Last month, Banks acknowledged to Gothamist that promoting integration was not a priority during his tenure. He said he favored policies that aimed to boost academics across the board, especially overhauling literacy instruction. In recent weeks, Banks has become a vocal supporter of efforts to improve diversity in the specialized schools, which rely on a single test — the Specialized High Schools Admissions Test — to determine admissions.
Last spring, only three Black students scored high enough on the test to get into Stuyvesant High School, the crown jewel of the specialized schools. Overall, Black and Latino students made up roughly 10% of offers to the elite high schools, while Asian American students got 56.5% of offers, and white students got 23.5%.
Banks said last spring’s admissions numbers should be a rallying call to Black and Latino communities to activate on the issue.
“Tonight represents one of the first moments where the Black community and Latino community can begin to come together and say, ‘We have a voice in this as well,’” Banks said.
When the most recent admissions numbers for the specialized high schools were released in July, Mamdani called for improvements to elementary and middle schools to increase the pipeline of strong applicants.
“I will say that we know that a single test does not reflect the aptitude of students across the city. We know that Black and Latino students are excelling across the five boroughs, as are students in a wide variety of schools. We have to ensure that we're doing everything we can to deliver for those students at the earliest ages,” said Mamdani, who is an alum of Bronx High School of Science.

https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/yeme.title: The Incredible Shrinking Superpower
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/yeme.author: Juan Cole
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/yeme.text:
The Limits of American Might
The failure of Tel Aviv and Washington to achieve their war aims in Iran has resulted in the most dramatic American retreat from a region since the U.S. flight from Vietnam in 1975. This startling American defeat — after a generation of forever war failures and stalemates — has been thrown into broad relief by the resumption of another regional conflict that has received far less attention than the Trump administration’s sputtering war with Tehran. This fall, the forces that most Americans know as “the Houthis” have conducted a blitzkrieg in their native Yemen and have been pummeling Saudi Arabia’s aviation and energy infrastructure with missiles and drones. In doing so, they have put a spotlight on the limits of American power, and the shrinking U.S. military footprint, in the Middle East.
The long-standing conflict between Saudi Arabia and northern Yemen’s Ansarullah, or “Helpers of God,” led by the Houthi clan, heated up again in July 2026, when Saudi Arabia struck Sanaa International Airport to prevent a Houthi delegation from landing on its return from the funeral in Iran for slain Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The Ansarullah government launched its own attacks and, in October, managed briefly to close Saudi Arabia’s own airport. The renewed war has now expanded into a regional conflict, with Pakistan, Türkiye, and, recently, Egypt pledging to defend the kingdom from attack, though none of these regional powers appear eager to conduct operations in Yemen itself. Notably absent from the current conflict is Saudi Arabia’s most powerful ally, the United States, since President Donald Trump has repeatedly declined to intervene on behalf of his Saudi allies.
The typical U.S. press framing of Ansarullah as an “Iran-backed militia” is inaccurate, since the movement has local, Arab nationalist reasons for its actions and is a full-scale government that rules some 80 percent of Yemen’s population. Still, it does receive surreptitious technical and military support from Iran, though nothing like the hundreds of billions of dollars’ worth of high-tech armaments — from kits turning 2,000-pound “dumb” bombs into precision munitions to advanced air-to-air missiles — that the U.S. provides the Saudis. Ironically, Trump’s war on Iran, fought in conjunction with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, weakened the Saudis and exposed their vulnerabilities to military attack by Iranian drones and missiles, impelling them to seek a symbolic win over a less formidable enemy in neighboring Yemen. But the weaknesses exposed by Iran’s drones helped encourage a vigorous Ansarullah rejoinder.
The Incredible Shrinking Superpower
The American refusal to join Saudi Arabia’s war signals a profound degradation in U.S. capabilities and standing in the Middle East. The U.S. military had, for decades, dominated the region from a network of about 20 major bases. The U.S. Navy operated out of the headquarters of the Fifth Fleet in Manama, Bahrain. The U.S. Air Force flew missions from the massive al-Udeid Air Base in Qatar, which housed 10,000 U.S. personnel. Thousands of ground troops were barracked in Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, and Jordan. The Pentagon admitted that “Iranian strikes damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict. In addition, dozens of U.S. aircraft were destroyed or damaged during OEF.”
The naval base at Manama, one of America’s most important naval facilities and headquarters of the Navy’s Fifth Fleet, was destroyed by Iranian strikes. (Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao admitted last month that Iran “blew the hell out of Bahrain.”) The loss of Manama led to supply shortages and poor morale aboard the USS Lincoln and other ships patrolling the Strait of Hormuz, bedeviling Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.
The CIA offices at the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh were annihilated. Iran struck al-Udeid’s evacuated Combined Air Operations Center in Qatar, from which the Pentagon had directed its strikes on enemies as diverse as the Taliban and ISIL over recent decades, and rendered this facility inoperable. All U.S. troops were also withdrawn from Iraq, a process accelerated by the inability of U.S. missile interceptors to protect them from attacks by Iran and allied Shiite militias there.
Iran’s deployment of swarms of Shahed drones caused the United States and Israel to use up much of their stock of interceptors, which are time-consuming and expensive to replace. A basic Shahed costs as little as $20,000, though new hardened versions are more expensive — whereas a Patriot interceptor costs $4 million. One reason the Trump administration may be reluctant to intervene in Yemen is that if the U.S. cannot fly missions from al-Udeid, and cannot be sure any new fighter-jet fleets stationed in the region will be safe from Iran, given the paucity of interceptors, the Pentagon will have a limited ability to rescue any U.S. pilots shot down over Yemen.
America’s Profound Weakness in the Middle East
Saudi Arabia launched a war against the ascendant Ansarullah in 2015 when the latter staged a coup in the capital of Sanaa. The Ansarullah movement is rooted in Yemen’s Zaidi Shiism, though it is more radical than traditional Zaidism. (Zaidi Shiism differs substantially from Iranian Shiism, having no ayatollahs and having relatively good relations with Sunnis.)
About a third of Yemenis are Zaidis, who predominate in the north of the country, and many have long resented the dominance of their politics and culture by neighboring, oil-rich, Sunni Saudi Arabia, whose official ideology is hard-line Wahhabism, a puritanical form of Islam that insists on a literal interpretation of the Quran. Wahhabi proselytizing among the Shia enraged the Houthi clan and their followers began rebelling against the government of military dictator Ali Abdullah Saleh in 2004. But when he was deposed by popular demonstrations during the Arab Spring in 2012, Saleh gradually allied with the Houthis, and by 2015 about half the Yemeni military rallied to their side, along with some major Sunni tribes.
In response to the Houthis’ rise, a Saudi-led coalition that included the United Arab Emirates began bombing Yemen in 2015. Until 2022, the U.S, then militarily dominant in the region, provided the Saudis with strategic advice, weaponry, and in-air refueling for their fighter jets in the Yemen war, though Riyadh’s tendency to bomb civilian infrastructure rather than confining themselves to military targets caused tension between the two allies. While the Saudis and their coalition pushed the Houthis out of much of the south of the country, including Aden, they were unable to dislodge them from the north. The Saudis implicitly acknowledged their failure with a United Nations-brokered truce in April 2022, which largely held until this past summer.
The Forever Wars Effect
America’s forever wars against Middle Eastern countries that decline to accept the Israel project or American corporate neocolonialism helped reignite the Saudi–Yemeni conflict. Iran is the last major state in the region that rejects Israel and is off-limits to U.S. corporate investment, a stance that inspires much of Washington’s animus. Netanyahu was therefore easily able to persuade Trump, as a privileged visitor to the White House Situation Room, to attack Iran in February.
The glib expectation of Netanyahu and of his Mossad chief at that time, David Barnea, that the Islamic Republic would crumble if Israel murdered Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and around 50 other high-ranking regime figures proved wishful thinking. The notion that Iran was vulnerable to a tightened petroleum blockade was turned on its head by the hard-liners who ascended to power after Khamenei’s death. Largely veterans of the grueling eight-year Iran–Iraq War of the 1980s, the country’s new leaders pursued a policy of “de-basing” toward the United States, taking out its main regional military facilities.
In addition, Iran launched precision strikes at the energy facilities of their Arab Gulf neighbors who had hosted those American bases. They struck Kuwait’s national petroleum company and its fields and refineries. They took out 17 percent of the production of Qatar’s Ras Laffan natural gas facility, even though Doha had good relations with Tehran and had mediated for Iran. Tehran also struck ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz, using missiles and drones, scaring the major shipping insurers into withdrawing their contracts. Few shipping magnates would risk cargoes worth billions of dollars without insurance.
Iran threw the world into an energy crisis reminiscent of the 1970s, which would have been even more devastating had China not released oil from its vast private and public petroleum reserves and cut its oil imports from 11.5 million barrels a day to under 9 million barrels a day, a move partially enabled by its turn to electric vehicles, which saved it 1.5 million barrels a day. High gasoline and diesel prices hurt Asia more than the United States, but prices rose globally. A third of the world’s helium, essential for cooling computer chips in the production process, comes from the Gulf, and that supply was also interrupted, increasing the price of electronics.
By successfully striking Saudi Arabia, Iran demonstrated that the kingdom’s ability to protect itself is imperfect and its infrastructure is vulnerable. By blockading the Strait of Hormuz in a way that the United States had difficulty undoing, Iran demonstrated the vulnerability of key world maritime arteries, something Ansarullah had already highlighted by striking at shipping in the Red Sea to protest the Gaza genocide.
Blockade for Blockade
When the Saudis bombed Sanaa’s airport in July 2026, Ansarullah’s leadership appears to have decided that Riyadh posed an ongoing existential danger to their state and sought to strangle the Yemeni economy, just as Israel had done to Gaza. Moreover, they sensed that the kingdom could be rolled back in the wake of the failure of the Israeli–U.S. war on Iran. Just as Iran had weakened the Gulf Arab states with its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthis believed they could seriously degrade the Saudi economy by blocking Riyadh’s shipping through the Bab al-Mandab, “the Strait of Tears,” between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.
Saudi exports through the Strait of Hormuz had fallen substantially. The kingdom did, however, have an escape valve: its East-West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea. Ships loading at Yanbu then headed for Saudi Arabia’s major Asian markets through the Bab al-Mandab. If Ansarullah could make the tanker captains fearful of this transit, they could reduce Saudi Arabia’s income even further. The Houthi spokesperson, Muhammad Abd al-Salam, warned that the prohibition of Saudi shipping was only the first step in a tit-for-tat strategy of “blockade for blockade.” The idea wasn’t original. The Saudis and the U.S. had often attempted to blockade petroleum imports to northern Yemen during the seven-year Saudi–Yemeni War.
In the subsequent three months, Ansarullah deployed missiles and drones constructed from Iranian models by military engineers trained by the old nationalist government of Ali Abdullah Saleh, many of whom had joined the Ansarullah military, in what has been called a Yemeni “military industrial complex.”
Just as the kingdom’s interceptors had proven unable to prevent Iranian strikes on targets such as the CIA section of the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh, they sometimes failed to halt the barrage of Yemeni missiles and drones. Refineries and oil installations, even the headquarters of the state oil giant, Saudi Aramco, in Dhahran, were hit. In October, Ansarullah closed Riyadh’s International Airport, just as the Saudis had attempted to close that of Sanaa in July. Ansarullah also surged out of their mountain strongholds and made a major push to Yemen’s southwest coast, taking the strategic port of Mocha overlooking the Bab al-Mandab. They also moved on Taiz, an inland industrial city of nearly 1 million inhabitants, one of the last major population centers not already under their control, in a campaign that tested the ability of the small Saudi-backed government of Rashad al-Alimi in Aden to resist it.
Highlanders and Oil Sheikhs
Just as the Vietnam War was one conflict among many fought in the Third World during the Cold War between the U.S. and the Soviet Union, so the Saudi–Yemeni War of 2026 is part of the larger struggle between the U.S. and Israel and Iran. Still, just as Vietnam was more about Vietnamese anticolonialism, nationalism, and sovereignty than about Communism and the ownership of the means of production, so the Saudi–Yemeni War is about Yemeni autonomy more than it is about the loose Houthi alliance with Iran. The conflict is not primarily between Zaidism and Wahhabism, though religious tensions are part of the story, but is far more rooted in a struggle between desperately poor Yemeni highlanders and fabulously wealthy Saudi sheikhs.
The plutocratic Saudi ruling elite is closely tied to Washington and has secret dealings with the Israelis, with whom it shares a distrust of the poverty-stricken Palestinian resistance, and views Ansarullah as cat’s paws of Iran in the Arabian Peninsula and as radical republicans trying to overthrow the region’s oil monarchies in favor of populism. For its part, Ansarullah are Arab nationalists, anti-American, and seek to use oil resources for populist purposes. And they have been willing to attack Israel to defend the Palestinians of Gaza from genocide.
Last week, Ansarullah battered targets across Saudi Arabia, prompting a further pullback from the region by Washington. The Yemeni forces attacked King Fahd International Airport in Dammam. An Ansarullah spokesperson said the group also targeted the Saudi defense ministry in the capital, Riyadh, along with an Aramco site in Yanbu, and an airport in the southern city of Abha. Reports also emerged of an attack on another Aramco oil field.
“Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure,” wrote State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott in an October 21 post on X, after the wave of attacks, ordering “non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members” out of Saudi Arabia.
It’s just the latest evidence of the most significant regional retreat by the U.S. in half a century and evidence of profound American military decline. The outcome of their war with the Saudis will not determine the issue of the U.S.–Israeli contest with Iran, but the very ability of Ansarullah to prosecute it points to the profound weakening of the American posture in the Middle East.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: How the Village Halloween Parade keeps its soul
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Hannah Frishberg
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
It is a logistical fact that events tend to lose their soul as they scale up. More people means more problems, more expenses, more liability and higher expectations. To meet them, organizers generally must sacrifice some amount of quality, community and heart.
By all means, this should apply to the Village Halloween Parade, which began in 1974 as a roving get-together of like-minded puppeteers and artists and has since grown into one of the world's biggest Halloween parades. The annual event, which draws 50,000 participants and 2 million spectators, has become a city-sanctioned ordeal requiring street closures, crowd control and NYPD liaisons.
But even as New York City's artistic spirit has been flattened by rising rents and the drab preferences of those who pay them, the Village Halloween Parade has remained a beacon of creative expression, a mainstream, humanity-uniting delight that is still deeply weird.
It's managed the feat due to the dedication of Jeanne Fleming, a purple-haired octogenarian who's served as the parade’s director since 1980.
“ This is nothing like any other parade. This is really a march of spirit and creativity and imagination. So it doesn't work like anything else,” Fleming said from her red-linteled house at Rokeby, the Hudson Valley estate where she’s lived for 54 years. The parade is less than a week away, but she’s that rare artist who knows how to delegate, so at this point her plate is mostly full of what she calls “detail work,” like being on call in case of crisis, or managing the 100 or so emails she receives each hour.
“What happens is I download all the information into everybody's brains, and then I'm kind of free,” she said as a geriatric long-haired cat named Kitty lounged beneath photos of bygone parades piled next to her cluttered desktop.
Meanwhile, down the gravel path, in a cavernous barn, volunteers fix and finish puppets old and new.
This is the final “puppet-raising,” an October weekend fixture, when the greater puppet community descends on Rokeby to create, choreograph and practice the leading number, transforming the estate’s road into a stand-in for Sixth Avenue.
The process is led by Alex Kahn and Sophia Michahelles, who met and later married after working on the parade in 1998, and have lived in a house attached to the barn since 2007. Today they are leading a smattering of volunteers collaborating on various puppet-related tasks. Country singer Townes Van Zandt is crooning through the speakers and a woman is dancing with an enormous window-shaped puppet on a rod beneath the barn’s soaring rafters. Outside, others peacefully papier-mâché among winged clocks in the fading afternoon light. Everyone is at least somewhat covered in paint.
“People are so willing to do this because you're in an ensemble of 50 people, and we're all making this one tableau vivant together,” Kahn said. “And we're doing it not online and not through some mediated experience. It's happening here and now in physical space, and literally a million people are gonna see it.”
He’s standing in front of a mood board displaying various surreal printouts illustrating this year’s theme, Body and Soul, an exploration of the relationship between the physical and spirit worlds. That’s consistent with past years' cerebral themes, which utilize the puppets’ big performance not for sponsorship or pop culture mimicry but to “expand people's notion of what is possible for Halloween self-transformation,” Kahn said as various children wander in and out of the door connecting his home to the barn. “The parade is an invitation to think. It's an invitation to go deeper into some aspect of our collective mythology, and then make it visual and impactful for the crowd.”
Lake Simons, who’s been participating in puppet-raisings since 2001 and came up from Brooklyn to help prep, said “it becomes something that everyone's got their hands in and therefore it becomes more powerful. We all feel like, I participated in this magical event and my hand was a part of this.”
Indeed, there are more people interested in helping than the core Rokeby crew can accommodate, a fact they clearly feel bad about.
The volunteer power is vital as the Parade still runs on a shoestring budget. Thankfully rent at Rokeby is low, for some buildings nil, and many hands make lighter work of maintaining and bringing giant puppets to life.
As with money, many operational elements have not scaled along with the parade’s size and influence over the years, although there have been numerous small shifts: Parade progenitor Ralph Lee used to store the puppets in the shaft of a decommissioned West Beth elevator. Then for a time they lived in Fleming’s house, before eventually being moved to the barn. Fleming used to cook for all the volunteers herself; that job was eventually passed on to a longtime friend, then to the friend’s daughter.
Fleming still sees the Parade not as a job but an opportunity to create and maintain an annual moment that also serves as a throughline of meaning and belonging in many peoples’ lives.
“ I feel like what I do is I send a ping out into the universe, and then who responds?” she says. “There's one family, their mom died at 35. The kids are in their 20s now, and they come every year for her. They carry puppets and celebrate her life and who she was. There’s so much like that.”
People have gotten engaged and married at the parade. Some have even asked Fleming to imbue their dead grandmother’s spirit into puppets.
“Every kind of thing you could imagine. People just call up and say, ‘I wanna do this,’ and I say, yes, OK, now how do we make it happen? And that’s the game. That’s what’s fun. Being able to allow all these people to realize a dream that they have. That's what it's about for me.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.title: Past Due: Why CUNY Adjuncts Can’t Get Paid On Time
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.author: Aisha Baiocchi
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.text:
Scores of adjunct professors at the City University of New York aren’t getting paid on time, CUNY officials acknowledged, in an ongoing problem that has frustrated the university’s part-time teaching workforce for several years.
Some CUNY adjuncts are owed sums north of $10,000.
“First paychecks don’t come through for a lot of people, and they’ve made that standard,” Rose Shelor Moulton, an adjunct at Hunter College, told The City Reporter. “But our first month of rent is still due.”
This semester, CUNY’s Professional Staff Congress said it has received 110 complaints of delayed pay. That’s actually an improvement: Using payroll data from the state teachers union, the PSC counted just over a thousand late paychecks in Spring 2025.
The delays are due to late additions to the payroll at individual colleges, CUNY said.
“CUNY values the dedication of its adjunct professors and has worked to improve the payroll process to reduce delays, including sending reminders to the campuses before payroll deadlines for the start of each semester, making it easier to provide advance pay to faculty who are hired at the last minute or paying them outside the normal payroll period,” spokesperson Noah Gardy said in a statement.
Adjuncts and union reps said the delays are baked into the university’s hiring practices.
Lynne Turner, a union vice president and an adjunct lecturer at LaGuardia Community College, said pay delays are one of the many consequences of what she called the university’s “employment model of extreme contingency.” Adjuncts are hired on a semester-to-semester basis, according to their union contract and CUNY standards.
“We are employed, re-employed, and then re-employed again,” Turner said. “Of course that comes with problems. Late paychecks are the tip of the iceberg.”
GET THE CUNY SCOOP: Subscribe to our new weekly newsletter covering the City University of New York
According to CUNY’s most recent human resources report, the university employs 11,000 part-time faculty, compared with just under 7,000 full-time faculty. CUNY reported that part-time labor makes up 52% of its instructional staff, higher than the national average of 40%, as reported in February by the College and University Professional Association for Human Resources.
Most CUNY part-time faculty must be rehired each semester. Adjunct pay can range from approximately $7,000 to $11,000 per course.
The PSC’s data analysis shows the vast majority of late paychecks go to employees at senior colleges: in Spring 2025 there were 984 late paychecks to senior colleges, and 25 to community colleges. Senior colleges receive the bulk of their funding from the state legislature, including for payroll.
Because of CUNY’s split funding model, the payments of senior college employees are processed through the state comptroller’s payroll system. This means paperwork has to go through an extra step, possibly one of the reasons for the systematic delays.
In a letter to PSC president James Davis, a senior CUNY administrator said the principal cause for the delays is late submission of paperwork by department chairs, and said the university is working on an improved communications plan to “remind chairpersons.”
Turner said “shifting the blame” to individual department leads ignored what he called the root cause of the issue: CUNY’s reliance on temporary contract labor.
Late paychecks are standard for adjuncts, Moulton said. She is also one of over 50 adjuncts who has joined a union grievance seeking outstanding pay for teaching so-called jumbo courses, which have more than 90 students.
When the union renegotiated its contract with the university in 2023, it increased wages for those teaching courses of 90 or more. Moulton says she is owed $13,000. Her colleague Jasmine Bayron, who teaches in the geography department, says she is owed nearly double that for three semesters of jumbo courses.
Moulton is on a costly payment plan to cover her child’s daycare, which she needed over the summer in order to stay on top of bills. Bayron has taken to grading high school advanced placement exams and tutoring students for the state Regents exam, on top of her regular course load.
Katelyn Peters, an adjunct who teaches at Borough of Manhattan Community College and Hunter, said unstable pay affects her ability to teach.
“There’s all these different programs to increase retention and graduation rates,” Peters said. “But I would think that if you take care of your teachers, the people who are delivering instruction, that’s going to help improve students’ academic experience a whole lot.”
