https://citylimits.org/a-guide-to-the-5-.title: A Guide to the 5 Proposals on the Back of NYC Voters’ Ballots
https://citylimits.org/a-guide-to-the-5-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/a-guide-to-the-5-.text:
Share This Article
The five questions this year range from what to do with small, publicly-owned properties to how the city should plan for its financial future via the rainy day fund.
Early voting is underway in New York City, which will continue through Sunday, Nov. 1, and residents will have their final opportunity to vote on Election Day Tuesday.
In addition to races for governor, State Senate and State Assembly, the backs of New Yorkers’ ballots will give them a chance to approve or reject several proposed changes to New York City’s Charter.
The five questions this year range from what to do with small, city-owned properties to how the city should plan for its financial future via the rainy day fund.
Several bundle multiple changes into a single question. The Mamdani administration—which convened a Commission on Government Efficiency (COGE) earlier this year to draft the measures—is pushing them as a way to a “faster government” and to remove bureaucratic red tape. But critics have raised concerns with some of the proposals.
City Limits put together this guide detailing each question, which hundreds of thousands of voters have weighed in on already.
Proposal 1: Revocable consents and public space
When a business wants to construct, operate, or maintain “a structure on, over, or under New York City’s public streets and sidewalks,” it needs to have a revocable consent, approved by the city’s Department of Transportation (DOT).
A revocable consent is a permit to use public spaces, such as sidewalks or roadways, for a long list of structures, like accessibility ramps and lifts, benches, utility poles, planters, bike racks or kiosks, the city’s Commission on Government Efficiency (COGE) explained.
Proposal 1 asks voters if they want to include applications for outdoor dining sheds and sidewalk cafes in the standard revocable-consent process. These currently require a separate, longer approval process with extra steps.
“Restaurants can wait many months, sometimes losing an entire outdoor dining season and the revenue and jobs that come with it,” said Andrew Rigie, executive director of the NYC Hospitality Alliance, a not-for-profit trade association that represents bars and restaurants and supports the ballot measure.
According to COGE, the proposal would replace the required public hearing and newspaper advertisements for revocable consent applications with an online portal, where the public could review and comment on pending applications.
The Center for Independence of the Disabled in New York (CIDNY) and Common Cause New York, a nonprofit watchdog, criticized this element of the plan, saying it comes at the expense of “public participation and legislative oversight.”
But Rigie counters that the streamlined process still preserves “opportunities for community and elected official input,” calling it “a commonsense reform.”
“New York City can protect the public interest while making it easier for neighborhood restaurants to open outdoor cafés and serve their customers,” he said.
Under the proposal, the city could still revoke a permit if it needs to regain the public space. Community boards could still hold hearings, and DOT could decide a hearing is needed when public comments demand it.
“If it passes, it would cut the outdoor dining application process by about 75 percent from eight months to two months, saving small businesses time and money,” COGE’s Executive Director Ann Cheng said.
“It would also cut down the process for building accessible ramps, like ADA accessible ramps, by about two months, and similarly save time and money,” Cheng added.
Proposal 2: Changes to city contracting
Proposal 2 combines several elements. It would authorize the Procurement Policy Board (PPB), which sets rules for city contracting and procurement, to come up with a new pre-contracting form for certain businesses and nonprofits that provide goods and services to city agencies.
It addresses one of the city’s conundrums: that city agencies often find it very difficult to make purchases, while contractors face a complicated system that can cause delays.
The ballot proposal would authorize the PPB to amend the pre-contracting questionnaire—which both small and large companies seeking city contracts must complete, no matter the sum involved in the deal—for efficiency. It would require the board to meet regularly (at least once every three months) to develop the new form.
If this measure passes, PPB could adapt the questionnaire to better reflect the type or size of the contracts in question, COGE explained, and as in any new rule, the public would be able to comment on the proposed changes.
The city estimates that streamlining the questionnaire requirements would save up to 30 days in the contracting process, from its current average of roughly 13 months.
The measure would also reduce the workload for city agencies when it comes to annual reporting requirements on planned client-services contracts.
Instead of having to write a preliminary report, hold a hearing, and then write a final report, as the current process requires, agencies would just issue their reports each year, giving a heads-up to the vendor community about what contracts they plan to issue, the Mayor’s Office of Contract Services explained.
An additional subsegment in this proposal would make permanent a state provision (expected to sunset in 2030) that allows the city to provide online public notice and collect public comments on contracts.
Other provisions would allow the mayor to delegate certain approvals for noncompetitive contracts over $5 million to agencies, with the approval of the agency’s commissioner.
Proposal 3: Street safety projects, city-owned small lots, and office leasing
Proposal 3 combines three different measures: street safety, city-owned property, and office leasing.
This proposal tries to streamline the city’s process for building new street safety infrastructure, while keeping community input and engagement requirements in place.
Currently, when the Department of Transportation (DOT) is planning “major transportation projects“—like bike and bus lanes that affect four consecutive blocks or 1,000 feet, whichever is less—it is required to consult with four other agencies: the NYPD, Fire Department, Department of Small Business Services, and the Mayor’s Office for People with Disabilities. Certain subunits within those agencies have to sign off on the plans, in very specific ways.
If Proposal 3 passes, DOT would still have to consult with those four agencies, but without the requirement for sub-agencies to weigh in. Instead, it would be up to each agency’s leaders to decide which of their own units or subunits to consult, COGE explained.
The Center for Independence of the Disabled in New York (CIDNY) said they support this ballot proposal, calling it “common-sense efficiency reforms.”
The measure would also allow the DOT to move forward on projects at the same time that it notifies local community boards and elected officials, instead of after, when there’s a situation of immediate need, like street changes made in response to crash and safety data. Supporters say it would protect new bike and bus lane plans from being delayed or blocked by lawsuits, saying opponents often take advantage of mistakes and technical errors in the interagency consultation process to lodge legal challenges.
The city has 1,500 surplus lots, according to the Department of Citywide Administrative Services (DCAS), and City Hall says about 6 percent of them would fall under the 10,000-square-feet category that could be sold.
Under Proposal 3, plans for these lots would no longer undergo the Uniform Land Use Review Procedure (ULURP), the city’s public approval process for certain development projects, and instead go through the new Expedited Land Use Review Procedure (ELURP), which compresses the seven-month review timeline to 90 days.
The Municipal Art Society (MAS) of New York criticized the measure, not only for sausaging “three loosely connected proposals” into one ballot question, but because they say it fails to address “two of the city’s essential needs: open space and affordable housing.”
“New York City’s public land is one of its most valuable—and finite—resources,” MAS Communication Manager Viviane Eng said via email sent to City Limits. “Once sold or transferred, it can be difficult or impossible to reclaim. Decisions about its future must be guided by a comprehensive, long-term vision for the public good, not simply by short-term revenue opportunities.”
A spokesperson for COGE, Jimmy Wyderko, said the proposal would still maintain two key steps of the process for selling city-owned land. The “proposal does not change the public auction requirement nor the land use requirements on the new purchaser (i.e., if the new purchaser wants to build something beyond as-of-right, they would need to go through a ULURP),” Wyderko said in an email.
Marcel Negret, Regional Plan Association’s director of land use, said the current rules make these small lots less attractive to potential developers, at a time when the city is trying to facilitate as many new apartments as possible to address the housing shortage.
“One way to look at it is like putting them [these lots] in a better market position,” Negret said.
COGE officials said the measure would reduce the administrative burden to sell small lots.
Another part of this ballot proposal would remove City Council and the City Planning Commission approvals when the city leases office space for government employees. Currently, the city notifies the local community board and the borough president about such leases, followed by a public hearing and a vote at the City Planning Commission, and then the City Council.
Instead, the Department of Citywide Administrative Services commissioner would provide the community board, local council member, and borough president with a notice of intent to acquire the new office space ahead of time. Then the city would need to notify the Council and comptroller.
Proposal 4: Moving waterfront permitting and building permitting
Proposal 4 would create a one-stop, centralized online construction permitting hub, overseen by the Department of Buildings (DOB), for applicants looking to do construction on an apartment or storefront, or to build affordable housing. COGE says this would give applicants an easier route to getting construction permits than the current process, which requires the involvement of dozens of different city agencies. 
The DOB would have until 2030 to get the hub running. If passed by voters, it would also allow additional DOB staff to approve certificates of occupancy. 
Another point of this proposal would transfer responsibility for waterfront construction permits from the Department of Small Business Services to the Department of Buildings, where the expertise lies, officials and advocates explained.
“Right now, the process can be confusing,” said Tyler Taba, Waterfront Alliance director of policy and government affairs. “Moving that responsibility to DOB is a practical step toward reducing confusion, delays, and unnecessary costs for waterfront projects.”
Proposal 5: Setting a goal for the city’s rainy-day fund
Through a 2019 ballot proposal, New Yorkers took the first steps toward creating a “rainy day” fund to help the city fill budget gaps during economic downturns.
The city’s existing fund, formally known as the Revenue Stabilization Fund, has nearly $1.7 billion in it. But there are no specific goals for how much the city should be saving with it.
If Proposal 5 is approved, the city would set a savings target for the fund at 12 percent of prior-year tax revenue. But that doesn’t mean the city will contribute that 12 percent all at once: the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), in consultation with the comptroller and the public, would be required to develop a plan by May 2027 that would outline when the city needs to contribute and if so, how much in a given year.
The city will contribute every year as long as that criteria is met, until the 12 percent threshold is reached. Once it hits that goal, the city no longer has to contribute to the fund, but still could if officials choose to. “That is like the city’s savings account, and so it would establish a target of 12 percent of the city’s prior year tax revenue, in order to work towards long-term fiscal stability,” Cheng said.
Good government groups like Reinvent Albany and The Citizens Budget Commission (CBC) are urging people to vote “no,” on Proposal 5, saying it doesn’t do enough to force the city to beef up its financial reserves.
“Voting no on Proposal 5 does not oppose strengthening the Rainy Day Fund. It is a vote declaring the status quo is not good enough, and the city should do better,” CBC President Andrew Rein wrote in an Op-Ed in October.
Comptroller Mark Levine’s office put out a report in April suggesting that a 16 percent reserves target would suffice to help the city weather an “entire below-trend period” like a recession.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Edward Hopper biography, Kvareli Foundation in Georgia, Marisa Merz in Turin—podcast
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Ben Luke, Alexander Morrison, David Clack
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
As a biography of Edward Hopper is published, containing a wealth of new material, Ben Luke speaks to its author Louis Shadwick about his quest to find the truth behind the artist that he writes “has become more myth than man in the popular imagination”.
In Georgia, the Kvareli Foundation for Contemporary Art, a new private museum, opens this weekend. The Art Newspaper’s digital editor, Alexander Morrison, speaks to Nino Sulkhanishvili, the creative director, about it.
And this episode’s Work of the Week is E il naufragar m’è dolce in questo mare (1980) by Marisa Merz. This installation is the centrepiece of an exhibition at the Castello di Rivoli in Turin, one of three presentations in the Italian city marking the 100th anniversary of Merz’s birth. Ben talks to the co-curator of the Castello di Rivoli show, Marianna Vecellio.
- Edward Hopper: A Life by Louis Shadwick, Yale University Press, out now in the US, $40 and published on 24 November in the UK, priced £30.
- Kvareli Foundation for Contemporary Art opens on 2 November.
- Marisa Merz – La danza delle ore, Castello di Rivoli, Fondazione Merz, GAM, Turin, Italy, until 4 April 2027.

At Meredith Rosen, we get the algorithmic bondage we deserve
By David Lê
SINCE THE APPEARANCE at the 2016 Berlin Biennale of Anna Uddenberg’s Journey of Self-Discovery, 2016—a sexed-up, life-size figurative sculpture decked in athleisure, contorted to take a selfie of its own ass—Uddenberg’s reception has focused on how her sculptures relate to the social media image culture they metabolize. The critical frame has often aimed to reduce the possibilities of the works’ meaning to two options: Does it satirize the consumerist dreck of the Instagram era? Or does it cynically re-merchandise that same dreck as art? There are, of course, other options: that there may be something of genuine interest in the exacting codes of Instagram’s high femmes, that Uddenberg’s response to these protocols is more sophisticated than either opportunistic regurgitation or “critical comment.” The work might, in fact, vitiate the notion of criticality as a prophylactic, meant to enforce the barriers between the visual cultures of mass and fine art.
The stakes of this interpretive problem are uniquely high for Uddenberg precisely because her work has such an unusual relationship with social media, where it has gone viral from the beginning. In the same review in which he accused the 2016 Berlin Biennale of erasing “any distinction between creation and complicity,” Jason Farago also took a passing swipe at Journey of Self-Discovery: “From the Pergamon to this in 2,000 years.” Farago’s comment spawned a viral meme of the sculpture with this caption, employed with winking irony by some and genuine derision by others. The newspaper, it should be noted, ran a photo of the sculpture at the top of the article (a good photo editor knows how to drive traffic). A decade later, one video of Continental Breakfast, 2023, in which Uddenberg had live performers mount H. R. Giger–esque forms that evoke both baby carriers and sex slings, has reached nearly two hundred million views on TikTok. Her “metrics”—likes, views, comments—number in the hundreds of millions. She is in the rare position of being a contemporary artist whose work a broad swath of the public is acquainted with (though many see it without any real context, not necessarily knowing it is, in fact, art). Around once every six months, a user somewhere reposts her imagery and sends a new cohort of viewers running to the comments to try to understand what they have seen.
On September 30, Uddenberg, now forty-four, opened her largest New York show to date, “White Noise,” at Meredith Rosen Gallery; the second half of the show opened at Telegraph in the Czech Republic this month. Since 2021, she has largely deployed human actors in the place of the figures she introduced at the biennial; she is now returning to figurative sculpture, showing a suite of humanoids hybridized with their ergonomic Herman Miller Aeron desk chairs. Their bosoms strain the buttons of cheap gray button-down blouses; from their necks hang lanyards with ID cards and off-brand Labubus (the briefly viral collectible dolls that bear some resemblance to Maurice Sendak’s wild things). The sculptures are unique. Each is styled differently—one figure sports a skirt with an oversize zipper running down her butt; another, stilettos imprisoned in metal cages closed with a combination lock; a few wear their razor-cut bobs pulled back by a so-called “claw” hair-clip merged to an armature that looks like a viper striking its prey. Some are without legs; having fused with their chairs, they suggest both the Borg queen from Star Trek and the motorized wheelchairs used by paraplegics. An audio track pipes in a droning sound that feeds the sense of disquiet. For Uddenberg, the sculptures are grounded in her own experience working at a call center in Berlin in 2015, forced to maintain a chipper attitude in a windowless factory pumping out “customer satisfaction.” Uddenberg’s artworks have grown up, gotten jobs. In “White Noise,” she presents them in office cubicles—aediculae for the era of bullshit jobs.
With this new exhibition, Uddenberg pushes the problem of power and degradation further than she has before. There is a violence in the figures’ tortured poses, the way their “support” structures force them into submission, interposing themselves between torso and legs. The Aeron chairs’ hallmark curves are designed to keep the sitter comfortable and productive; in “White Noise,” the chairs ensnare their sitters. The tenor of the show is especially sinister in part because Uddenberg has not deployed her dominatrix-like performers, as she did in Premium Economy, 2023. We are left instead with mute drones, their eyes cast to the floor, their individuality only discernible in the prepackaged form of their cutesy Labubus.
The show offers a collage of the novel material palette we encounter in contemporary life: the padded straps of a backpack covered in “breathable” polyester mesh, the plastic curves of a stroller, crisp polyester shirting. Uddenberg’s sculptures are composites of these textures and forms, which promise comfort and adaptability at an “accessible” price. Her uncanny hyperfemmes are realized with the help of large-scale 3D printers and modeling software often used in industrial prototyping. She aims for the kind of polish one might mistake for an industrial ready-made (viewers often mistake the figures in her sculptures for store-bought mannequins). Over the past decade, her sculptures have achieved an ever more flawless finish, even as their forms have grown baroquely labial. In “White Noise,” she has allowed more of her own touch to be seen. The perfect lines of the Aeron chair butt up against a sculptor’s foam that retains traces of her hand.
The most viscerally engaging works in the show demonstrate Uddenberg’s exercise of the sculptor’s unique prerogative: to confront viewers with an uncanny version of their own bodies, remade according to an image of humanity unbeholden to nature. The contemporary iteration of this ideal, with its snatched waists, taloned fingers, and bursting bosoms, suggests a form of femme self-fashioning that is radically non-domestic, overtly online, and above all pornographic (rather than sexual). For Uddenberg, the image of the body precedes embodiment.
Uddenberg frequently invokes Martin Heidegger to describe her work, specifically his idea of a technological “mode of being” that surreptitiously determines, in advance, how we understand it and ourselves. Heidegger thought that the apparent neutrality of tool use had metastasized, coming to frame our own self-conception (and clearing the way for the constant expansion of technology). For Uddenberg, this “resonates with the idea of images as operational” instead of merely representational: The images are, in her view, almost agentic, much as Heidegger worried the technological worldview was. He famously thought that the only way out of this totalizing problem would be an exogenous, divine shock (“Nur noch ein Gott kann uns retten”—Only a God can save us now). Heidegger needed a God’s-eye view, a critical “outside” from which to see and solve the problem. Uddenberg is less interested in salvation from without than she is in the novel possibilities for beauty from within our own self-imposed captivity, the at times dark possibilities of remaking the self. She does so with a laser-like focus on high femininity that refuses to fetishize either a nonexistent pretechnological past or to imagine that the present is somehow liberatory. What she does do, and does well, is show us the world we are already in—freezing the endless scroll just long enough for us to catch our own reflections.
The sculptures will, undoubtedly, find their way to social media again. I ask Uddenberg what she makes of her work’s virality. She notes that the circular form of Journey of Self-Discovery was already a comment on social media and how it was reshaping reality. “You can think of images as operational, as opposed to representational. It’s not just that we look at something and think about whatever is symbolized. No, this does something to us. It commands us to copy a certain gesture, or to start behaving differently. My work is about this feedback loop of behavior.” What concerns Uddenberg is how the incentive structure of social media mediates how we relate to ourselves. Algorithms are engines of self-exploitation or, as she calls it, “self-bondage.” It rankles her that some assume her engagement with the desires of the online hordes is naive: “When a male artist gets a crazy viral moment, you don’t doubt that he knows what he’s doing. But if you’re dealing with femininity, then it’s, ‘Oh, you’re a little lost. Do you have any idea what you’ve actually done? You don’t understand that you don’t really have any agency.’”
The question of agency is precisely what “White Noise” is about: that agency conceptualized as “resistance to power” disavows how that agency has already been seduced, coerced, and given shape before it arrives on the scene in protest. High femmes show us this most clearly. “White Noise” exhibits the almost quaint vestiges of a world in which people in offices, rather than machines, made decisions for us. Equally quaint is the idea that art is a domain of cultural production that functions as a clean room, safe from the contaminating effects of this new environment. It is perverse to imagine that art benefits from walling itself off from these new productive forces. As Uddenberg puts it, “There’s a way of thinking about criticality as a rejection of contemporary visual culture, a rejection of what’s visually stimulating or visually indulgent. There’s a tendency to think of that work as less critical, not smart enough.” Her art demonstrates that aesthetic austerity is not the hallmark of critical rigor, and that what titillates and irritates may be precisely what is required to cut through the noise.
David Lê is a writer and designer living in New York City. His weekly newsletter, The Arcades, explores “things, broadly-construed.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.title: ‘Brasil não tem 60 milhões de fascistas, precisamos conversar com eles’, diz escritor processado por 144 pastores da Igreja Universal
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.author: Conversa Bem Viver
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.text:
O documentário “144 – Apocalipse Não”, dirigido pelo cineasta e escritor João Paulo Cuenca, terá uma sessão extra na Mostra Internacional de Cinema de São Paulo neste domingo (1º), às 20h, no CineSesc. O filme narra um momento tumultuado: após uma postagem nas redes sociais com referências à família Bolsonaro e à Igreja Universal, J.P. Cuenca virou alvo de 144 processos abertos por pastores evangélicos.
Em entrevista ao programa Conversa Bem Viver, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, o cinesta explica que a ideia do documentário nasce da superação do medo pela curiosidade. O sentimento inicial de desespero deu lugar à busca de saber mais sobre as cidades e as pequenas igrejas que tinham-no processado. Ele verificou que os processos eram muito parecidos.
“Isso foi me dando muita curiosidade de conhecer um pouco o outro lado do papel. Porque era fabricada a estratégia da igreja para fazer esse assédio jurídico. Foram espalhados modelos de ação quase iguais. São poucos modelos espalhados pelo Brasil inteiro”, explicou Cuenca.
Para realizar o filme, Cuenca percorreu mais de 10 mil quilômetros pelo Brasil atrás dessas igrejas e pastores. Chegou inclusive a cidades muito pequenas. Com isso, percebeu que não é possível enquadrar o público evangélico todo dentro de um formato estanque.
“Eu acho um erro de análise tremendo do campo progressista estereotipar todo mundo como uma coisa só e não levar em conta a fé na dimensão da análise. A fé existe em qualquer uma dessas igrejas, inclusive nas igrejas mais mercenárias ou com os pastores que você pode questionar as intenções deles. Mas as pessoas, os fiéis, a fé deles é real”, reflete o diretor.
Além de desenvolver o projeto do filme e buscar suporte jurídico para sua defesa, Cuenca também tornou público o quanto pode todos os processos, como mecanismo de proteção.
“Eu recebi milhares de ameaças de morte naquela época. E divulgar era um jeito de fazer contato com parte da sociedade que luta contra o assédio jurídico. A gente conseguiu apoios de associações de imprensa, de jornalismo, de juristas, de pessoas que ajudaram isso a virar um caso no Supremo Tribunal Federal do Brasil. Então, hoje tem uma jurisprudência brasileira que não permite mais esse tipo de caso repetitivo. Quer dizer, o meu número recorde de 144 processos nunca mais vai se repetir, porque ninguém nunca mais vai processar uma pessoa com ações repetitivas usando o Juizado Especial Cível.”
Segundo Cuenca, a intenção foi fazer um filme de escuta, para que o público possa se perguntar sobre os seus pontos em comum com aquele outro. Ele destaca a disponibilidade observada do processo eleitoral à presidência do Brasil, que teve o segundo turno de votação no último domingo (25): “Uma das coisas legais dessa virada foi uma disposição do campo progressista para ouvir um pouco mais as pessoas. Não estamos ouvindo o suficiente ainda. Ganhamos essa eleição, mas precisamos continuar com essa disposição de conversar com elas, mesmo que professem fé em crenças e estejam em campo ideológico diferente do nosso.”
O cineasta completa dizendo que nem todas as pessoas que votaram em Flávio Bolsonaro nessa eleição são bolsonaristas. “O Brasil não tem 60 milhões de fascistas, ou pelo menos ainda não tem. A gente tem que conversar com essas pessoas. E como é que você começa uma conversa? Ouvindo. Quem não tem, aprenda a ter curiosidade genuína pelo contexto do outro, de onde o outro vem, a história de vida do outro”, pondera escritor.

https://apache.be/2026/10/21/waarom-comm.author: Wouter Arrazola de Oñate
https://apache.be/2026/10/21/waarom-comm.text:
De uitspraken waarmee professor Freddy Mortier aan de UGent het racistische gedachtegoed van pseudowetenschapper Nathan Cofnas verdedigde, vormen een langgerekte keten van uiterst problematische ideeën en flagrante redeneerfouten. Dat de voorzitter van de commissie wetenschappelijke integriteit het bestaan van witte suprematie aan de universiteit op deze manier duldt, toont hoe vervreemd hij is van de kernwaarden van zijn eigen commissie.
“De stelling dat er erfelijke genetische verschillen bestaan tussen groepen huidskleur wat betreft intelligentie is perfect begrijpelijk. En ze is zinvol. Dat die uitspraak vals is, is nooit aangetoond.”
Dit waren de woorden van professor Freddy Mortier tijdens een proclamatieceremonie aan de Universiteit Gent. Hij is ethicus en voorzitter van de commissie wetenschappelijke integriteit. Het is een korte uitspraak, maar één die wel heel wat aparte schakels in de redeneerketen bevat.
Elke schakel moet sterk genoeg zijn om voldoende wetenschappelijk integer te zijn. Voorwaarden voor die integriteit zijn onder meer: eerlijkheid (zonder misleiding), zorgvuldigheid (methodologisch verantwoord), transparantie (ook over de beperkingen van de beschikbare evidentie), onafhankelijkheid (ook van persoonlijke belangen) / verantwoordelijkheid (ook voor de manier waarop onderzoeksresultaten worden verspreid en gebruikt). Let’s see.
Onbestaande categorieën
Laten we beginnen met het woord huidskleur. “Huidskleur” is een heel vage omschrijving, eigenlijk véél te vaag om wetenschappelijk te zijn. Want welke huidskleuren zouden we dan allemaal erkennen? Waar is die lijst? Daarop bestaat al geen antwoord. Zijn de “huidskleuren” keurig afgebakend en zijn ze makkelijk, éénduidig en reproduceerbaar te bepalen bij iemand? Neen, dat zijn ze zeker niet. Worden ze vooral bepaald door genen en DNA? Neen, zeker niet. (Zie hierover ook het recente stuk van een groep genetici in De Standaard).
Er is geen enkele combinatie van genen die zou coderen voor iets dat men “ras” is gaan noemen
Wat met “ras”? Wel, dat concept bestaat biologisch simpelweg niet. Er is geen enkele combinatie van genen die zou coderen voor iets dat men “ras” is gaan noemen. Daar toch genetische verschillen aan toewijzen is dus met zekerheid onmogelijk.
De volgende schakel in de redenering: intelligentie. Wat is dat eigenlijk? Het is iets dat sowieso verschilt van plaats tot plaats en in de tijd. Het omvat in ieder geval veel meer dan enkel cognitieve prestaties. Het begrip wordt niet door iedere groep mensen of door iedere samenleving hetzelfde ingevuld. Opnieuw dus iets dat veel té multifactorieel is om wetenschappelijk hele scherpe en duidelijke conclusies mee te kunnen trekken. Of om groepen mee te vergelijken.
IQ-testen zijn eigenlijk niet zo'n goede meetinstrumenten om het hele brede begrip te meten. Het is erg misleidend om de véél te grote sprong te maken van IQ-testen naar “intelligentie meten”. IQ-testen meten op hun best slechts een klein stukje van wat intelligentie allemaal inhoudt. En vooral om populaties met elkaar te vergelijken zijn ze geen goed instrument. Dat is geweten, wetenschap dus.
Van “national IQ-databases” die vaak gebruikt worden, is aangetoond dat deze methodologisch van erg lage kwaliteit zijn, en sterk beïnvloed door enkele mannen met sterke ideologische linken met witte-suprematie-netwerken. Ze worden veel gebruikt in publicaties in door leden van deze netwerken opgerichte journals, maar zijn té slecht om als wetenschap aanvaard te worden. Academici als professor Rebecca Sear hebben dit al meermaals aangekaart.
Beperkte rol van genen
Hoe meer we leren over genetica hoe meer we te weten komen welke relatief kleine rol genen eigenlijk spelen, en hoe sterk de invloed is van de omgeving waarin iemand leeft en de sociale determinanten. Voor wat betreft gezondheid wegen die laatste minstens dubbel zo zwaar door als genetica in het bepalen van iemands gezondheid.
Sociale en omgevingsfactoren (en andere) wegen veel zwaarder door dan een of andere combinatie van aminozuren in het DNA
Sommigen zitten met hun gedachtegoed nog dertig jaar terug in de tijd, toen men hoopte dat alles kon verklaard worden met de DNA-code. Dat is helemaal niet zo, en hoe meer we te weten komen, hoe duidelijker die onwaarheid wordt. Sociale en omgevingsfactoren (en andere) wegen veel zwaarder door dan een of andere combinatie van aminozuren in het DNA. Recent werd zelfs gevonden dat ons DNA blijkbaar wijzigt tijdens ons leven
Ruimschoots de zwakste schakel in de redeneringsketen staat in de laatste zin: “de valsheid ervan is nooit aangetoond”. Dit is een klassieke misleidingstactiek, bekend uit de debatkunde. Doen alsof dit de waarschijnlijkheid van de stelling vergroot of dat die stelling daardoor aan wetenschappelijkheid wint, is niet correct. Zo werkt wetenschap niet, zo werkt de wetenschappelijke integriteit niet. “Niet weerlegd” is iets heel anders dan “wetenschappelijk plausibel”. Dat iemand in die functie deze truc gebruikt, of zo’n grote redeneerfout maakt, daar moet men zich ernstige vragen bij stellen.
Oude machtsarchitectuur
De uitspraak van Freddy Mortier bevat dus een hele reeks aan aannames die allemaal op erg twijfelachtige basis rusten. Een voor een. Met veel onzekerheid. “Perfect begrijpelijk” en “zinvol” zijn daarentegen erg sterke kwaliteiten die men iets toeschrijft, zonder voldoende sterk bewijs of empirie. In tegendeel: de meerderheid van de aanwezige evidentie wijst in de andere richting. Dit kan men moeilijk “eerlijk, transparant of voorzichtig” noemen. Vraag dat internationaal maar eens na.
Welke onveiligheid houdt Mortier met zijn verdediging in stand voor de vele geviseerde studenten en werknemers van UGent?
Waar wel zekerheid over bestaat is dat tijdelijk onderzoeker Nathan Cofnas tot witte-suprematie-kringen behoort (zoals ook zijn baas professor Bouke de Vries en zijn collega Craig Willy). Dat hij in zijn blogs heel duidelijk aantoont wat zijn racistische bedoelingen zijn. Dat hij zijn eigen achtergrond superieur vindt. Dat hij gerichte aanvallen uitvoert op zwarte mensen, en niet op diens witte collega’s. Met dodelijke gevolgen.
De aanwezigheid van dit onjuist superioriteitsdenken aan de universiteit zo sterk verdedigen voldoet niet aan de integriteitsvoorwaarde “verantwoordelijkheid”. Met academische vrijheid heeft zoveel foutief redeneren ook helemaal niets meer te maken. Het zijn net zulke waanideeën die leiden tot de rechtvaardiging van genocides. Bewust gefabriceerde nepwetenschap om de overkoepelende machtsstructuur van witte suprematie — met haar verwoestende impact — te bestendigen. Ethisch kan men dit niet noemen.
Reproductie en genetica behoren eveneens tot het expertisedomein van public health. Veelzeggend is dat juist degenen die hierover het luidst spreken, over geen enkele expertise ter zake beschikken. Professor Mortier niet uitgezonderd.
Waarom vindt hij het dan toch zo belangrijk om meermaals zijn machtspositie te gebruiken om in de verdediging te schieten? Welke oude machtsarchitectuur wil hij daarmee verdedigen en behouden? Welke onveiligheid houdt hij daarmee in stand voor de vele geviseerde studenten en werknemers van UGent?
Universiteit Gent, als de verantwoordelijke “wetenschappelijke integriteit” zelf niet wetenschappelijk integer is, hoe kan je dan nog je internationale geloofwaardigheid behouden?

https://apache.be/2026/10/21/zo-deed-apa.title: Zo deed Apache in september van zich spreken
https://apache.be/2026/10/21/zo-deed-apa.author: Redactie Apache
https://apache.be/2026/10/21/zo-deed-apa.text:
Jan Peumans deed een coming-out, de Orde van Architecten stelde orde op zaken en een rassen(pseudo)wetenschapper greep naast een onderzoeksbeurs. Onderzoeken van Apache rolden in september over de tongen. Zo woog Apache de voorbije maand op het debat en het beleid.
Ik ben een doorgronde democraat. Daarom ben ik ook coöperant van Apache.
Die woorden liet erevoorzitter van het Vlaams Parlement Jan Peumans (N-VA) – ook bekend als de schalkse juryvoorzitter uit Vrede op aarde – zich enkele weken geleden ontvallen in een interview met De Zondag.
Het zou geen krasse uitspraak mogen zijn, maar dat is het wel uit de mond van een prominent N-VA-lid. Want de meeste N-VA’ers bijten nog liever hun tong af dan een positief geluid over Apache te laten ontsnappen. Laat staan toe te geven dat onze journalisten nuttig en noodzakelijk werk doen, ook wanneer hun partij het daarbij moet ontgelden.
Niet zo Jan Peumans. “In een democratie moet je ook organisaties steunen die een andere opvatting hebben”, bracht hij in herinnering, en hij voegde eraan toe dat hij daarom milieu-vzw Dryade en Apache steunt. Uitgerekend de twee organisaties die eerder dit jaar financieel werden afgestraft door Peumans’ partijgenoot Jan Jambon, die als minister van Financiën de hen reeds toegekende steun van de Nationale Loterij tegenhield.
Het kon ook gelden als veeg uit de pan naar die andere partijgenoot, Vlaams begrotingsminister Ben Weyts, die het te gek voor woorden vindt als zo’n organisatie het waagt de overheid ter verantwoording te roepen.
Dank u, mijnheer Peumans, om dat even scherp te stellen.
Anders gezegd: nee, je hoeft niet alles wat Apache schrijft leuk te vinden om onze journalistiek – diepgravend en kritisch, onafhankelijk en onverschrokken, niet gesponsord door adverteerders maar door de lezer – te steunen.
Orde van Architecten schept orde
Dat was niet de enige keer dat Apache de voorbije weken van zich deed spreken. Zo brachten we aan het licht dat de heropening van het Brusselse museum Kanal nog niet de zegen van de brandweer had, al beweerde de woordvoerder van het museum het tegendeel.
Zo nodigde de Orde van Architecten na de artikelenreeks waarin Apache wantoestanden in de sector aankaartte onze journalist uit voor een rondetafelgesprek en kondigde ze een hervorming van haar tuchtprocedure aan. Zo vestigde het Koninklijk Museum voor Midden-Afrika de aandacht op het recente Apache-onderzoek naar de herkomst van de houtskool voor onze zomerse barbecues. En schreef Apache-medewerker Tine Hens de prijs voor het beste Nederlandstalige natuurboek op haar naam met Archief van mogelijk verlies.
Turbulentie boven Kortrijk Airport
Hoe N-VA-minister Annick De Ridder Europese en Vlaamse wetten overtrad om regionale luchthavens te blijven voltanken met subsidies zodat ze niet zouden crashen: dát las je voorlopig dan weer enkel in Apache. De grote media zwegen er zedig over in hun berichtgeving rond de beruchte geheime dading met commerciële luchthavenuitbater Egis.
Maar onze onthullingen over de luchthaven van Kortrijk-Wevelgem bleven alvast niet zonder gevolg: een maand nadat Apache aantoonde hoe miljoenen winst van de gesubsidieerde luchthaven in de zakken van twee private aandeelhouders belandden, gaf de Vlaamse Regering opdracht om de subconcessie van deeluitbater FIA te heronderhandelen.
Win for life
Ook niet onopgemerkt bleef het Apache-artikel over hoe kabinetsmedewerkers die het dankzij politieke benoeming tot topambtenaar schoppen, zowat een win for life krijgen.
Intussen ging een zucht van verlichting door de UGent bij het nieuws dat het Fonds voor Wetenschappelijk Onderzoek géén beurs toekent aan Craig Willy: de fameuze “derde” rassen(pseudo)wetenschapper aan UGent – net als Nathan Cofnas binnengehaald door filosofieprofessor Bouke de Vries – voor wiens dubieuze onderzoek Apache al anderhalf jaar geleden waarschuwde. Waarmee de racistische pseudowetenschap aan onze universiteiten alvast geen extra wind in de zeilen krijgt met belastinggeld.
Tot slot nog een pas binnengelopen bericht: de Raad voor de Journalistiek heeft een klacht tegen Apache door diamantair Philippe Heilmann naar aanleiding van dit artikel, ongegrond verklaard. Dat kon ook moeilijk anders, want er stond niets in wat niet klopte.
Niets van het bovenstaande hadden we kunnen uitzoeken of onder de aandacht brengen zonder financiële steun van onze betalende leden.
Ben jij nog niet aangesloten bij Apache? Neem dan vandaag nog een betalend lidmaatschap, en geef ons meer middelen om te schrijven wat iedereen moet weten. Om kritische vragen te blijven stellen – hoe hardnekkig sommige politici ze ook negeren.

https://www.newyorker.com/culture/photo-.title: The Unclassifiable Talent of Hervé Guibert
https://www.newyorker.com/culture/photo-.author: Hilton Als
https://www.newyorker.com/culture/photo-.text:
Hervé Guibert’s ultimately unclassifiable talent brilliantly evokes the shadows, the moments of dread and paranoia, that are part of the experience of love. Doom lurks everywhere in Guibert’s world, in large part because love, as Guibert expresses it, is synonymous with longing, and what is longing but a pit stop on the way to hurt, loss, and the lover’s need to control the beloved?
Born in 1955, into a middle-class family in a suburb of Paris, Guibert, who wrote about photography in addition to taking pictures himself—he also published more than two dozen books of fiction, autofiction, and essays—was a gay man who came of age during the AIDS epidemic, a time of incalculable devastation. Guibert describes the epoch with what feels like a preternatural calm in his now classic 1990 novel, “To the Friend Who Did Not Save My Life,” in which we meet some of his friends, thinly disguised, including the philosopher Michel Foucault and the actress Isabelle Adjani. I remember reading about the book when it came out in the U.S. the following year—the year that Guibert died, at age thirty-six, of AIDS-related causes. Some people condemned the work for outing Foucault as a fellow AIDS sufferer. What right did Guibert have to tell someone else’s story? At some point, I read the book, and then I put the memory of reading it away: it was too potent, too sharp a reminder of what I had experienced during those years when quick and slow disasters were all around, and I felt ashamed of my helplessness and relative good health.
But then, about a decade ago, the writers Bruce Hainley and Jennifer Krasinski told me about a video that Guibert had made some months before his death. Titled “Modesty, or Immodesty” (1991), the hour-length work, shot by Guibert himself between June, 1990, and March, 1991, shows the artist going about his daily life in his final months, writing, talking on the phone, bathing, exercising, undergoing a medical procedure, then playing back the footage so that he can witness it, taking a holiday, and finally typing on a word processor, which continues to produce his text after he has moved on. This piece, Guibert’s single work on video, is an extraordinary film of self-dramatization: life and illness as a form of theatre. It is not a brave work—that’s too paltry a word for it. It is a powerful record of the isolating effects of AIDS, and of a patient who is running out of time and holding onto the act of creation as evidence that he has lived. As with “To the Friend Who Did Not Save My Life,” I did not want to remember the film after I had seen it; its solitude spoke of universal solitude, all those rooms filled with lost potential and the memory of the dead.
So it was with some trepidation, but also curiosity and not a little excitement, that I began looking at the volumes of Guibert’s photographs that were published recently, in elegant editions, by the Magic Hour Press. “The Only Face” is a version of the catalogue for a show that Guibert had in Paris, in 1984. The images are in black-and-white, and are romantic in a way that reminds one almost immediately of the photographer Duane Michals, another artist who worked with image and text. In the introduction to the original catalogue, Guibert wrote:
Love doesn’t necessarily make a good photograph, but the photographer’s interest, and the intelligence and imagination behind it, can contribute to the making of a picture that interests us. It’s important to remember that Guibert was a very young man when he was taking these photographs, because sometimes the romanticism of his vision draws out a kind of artificiality that feels distinctly Gallic in its love of surface beauty; one longs to go deeper, to be allowed to go deeper, into the image.
The photographs are titled—“The mother,” “The father,” and so on—and the dominant visual theme in the work is the photographer’s fascination with the play of light in black-and-white. Too often Guibert goes for mood, as in “The fiancé” and “Sienna.” In the former, we see a figure shot from the front, draped in tulle. At first it’s not clear what sex the person is, but, looking closer, you can make out black hair across his chest. It’s a self-conscious study in texture, the kind of Photography 101 assignment you’re proud of yourself for having carried to completion, but Guibert’s lyricism topples over into kitsch in “Sienna.” In that picture, we see light pouring through a window. There’s smoke in the light. Is it cigarette smoke, or angels’ breath? A thin, shirtless figure sits in a chair with arms and head bent over a table. Again, it’s not a photograph but an image about photography, and Guibert’s too-romantic love of it.
Guibert’s love of Michals-influenced gay narrative also plays out in a piece called “The friend.” A white male hand rests on a broad, darker-skinned chest. That is all we see, in medium closeup, and the contrasts are obvious—light and dark, older and younger—but the picture stops there; what we are meant to register is not so much the bodies, their stories, as the photographer in the act of becoming one. (Helmut Newton is another influence. In Guibert’s portrait “Agathe,” a wavy-haired young woman looks out at us, her open jacket exposing her small breasts.)
Sometimes, though, Guibert is helped by a subject who works with him to make an emotionally legible picture that succeeds graphically as well. I don’t think I’ll soon forget his terrific portrait “Isabelle,” in which we see Adjani lying on a bench, her face turned to the camera. She wears a light-colored garment; her right arm rests on her belly. Adjani’s dark hair, the openness of her gaze, feels less like a study in grays and blacks than like a photograph about stillness. You can see how in their time together, the time it took to take this picture, Guibert was able to move past his love of the art of photography to the point of understanding it as an instrument of connection.
Like Adjani, the subjects of Guibert’s brilliant book “Suzanne and Louise” are so extraordinary that you can’t look away from them, and neither can the artist. Guibert called this book, originally published in France in 1980 and now available in English for the first time, a photo-novel, and that’s fine, but the category seems too limiting for what “Suzanne and Louise” is: a work as great as Jean Genet’s “The Maids,” and just as chilling. We’re in another black-and-white world, this time in a hôtel particulier in the Fifteenth Arrondissement, where two sisters, Suzanne and Louise, have lived for more than forty years. The fairly reclusive ladies, Guibert’s great-aunts, have had different lives: Louise was a Carmelite nun until she was convinced to leave the order by Suzanne, a widow who was once married to a pharmacist. Suzanne has money, and Louise does not. They share a dog named Whysky, and a marriage of sorts: Suzanne is the dominant figure, and Louise her poor relation who waits on her. The prose in the book is written from the inside; when Guibert was a child, he and his family made weekly visits to these sisters, who ultimately fascinated him enough that he was able to sidestep his overly aestheticized sensibility and let these singular beings speak and act and be in ways that are constantly startling and new. “Five years ago, I proposed to my great-aunts that I make a film about them; I had started writing a script, but their refusals were so categorical that I lost of [sic] all hope of ever making it,” Guibert writes. He was able to take photographs, though, and, as the contact sheets piled up, he decided to print some of the images, “just to see, to show them.” In a book of astonishing acts of intimacy, the most revealing is in a series of pictures that Guibert shot of Louise taking down her hair—her “most intimate thing.” Long ago, a woman would send a missed loved one a photograph of herself taking her hair down. In this case, Louise’s washing of her long gray tresses is less an erotic image than an act of self-dramatization in the theatre of being. It’s not a statement so much as a reckoning, a way of showing love to the young relative behind the camera who refuses to let these women not be in the world and then leave it, forgotten. ♦

https://theintercept.com/2026/10/27/pent.title: Pentagon Fears Drone Attacks on U.S. and Foreign Bases
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/27/pent.author: Nick Turse
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/27/pent.text:
Top defense officials are expressing increasing worry about the vulnerability of U.S. bases around the world and even within the United States as cheap drone technology upends long-standing defense strategies.
The fear is mounting after a series recent attacks and threats against ground targets, including the destruction of key bases in the Middle East by Iran, plots against mega-bases in Europe, including to U.S. bombers at a British air base, and a Russian campaign that damaged European military facilities, according to two government officials.
While the Pentagon is notorious for inflating threats to press for additional funding, the officials stressed that the anxiety is real, not invented. Despite the U.S. military’s enormous budget, they say, the United States now finds itself scrambling strengthen its fortifications, protect its costly equipment, and recall personnel from some locations.
“Now all the world knows what the SecDef should have,” said one of the officials.
Foreign adversaries have taken notice of Iran’s ability to defeat U.S. air defenses using missiles and drones, they said. The officials drew specific attention to Tehran’s ability to damage or destroy bases that have been the key to U.S. power-projection and war-making for decades in the Middle East.
An Iranian missile and drone attack on February 28 destroyed Navy facilities in Manama, Bahrain, the region’s most critical logistics hub. The Combined Air Operations Center at Al Udeid Air Base, Qatar, was severely damaged by Iranian missiles early in the war, rendering it inoperable. Both were recently attacked again, raising questions about whether either will ever be rebuilt. The destruction of these bases has fundamentally altered America’s future force posture in the region, according to the officials. One of them called it a “seismic shift.”
On Friday, the Trump administration leaked highly classified intelligence to Fox News and Axios suggesting Iran has “substantially increased” efforts to target U.S. diplomats and other officials in the Middle East and beyond. The October 23 memo claimed that “the lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages.” A U.S. official confirmed the accuracy of the intelligence but questioned the motives of the “official leak,” suggesting it’s part of a case being built to justify renewing the failed war.
The leak came as the State Department ordered a further reduction in staff at multiple diplomatic posts across the Middle East, including in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. One of the officials said the move “definitely” spoke to America’s inability to defend its assets overseas. Those fears now extend to the United States, according to the officials.
Last month, buried in an unhinged address to troops in which he attacked the press and those within the military he calls beardos, weirdos, and wimps, self-styled War Secretary Pete Hegseth tacitly acknowledged the vulnerability of U.S. domestic bases, noting that the Pentagon was now “hardening every installation on American soil” against “sabotage and drones.” And last week, the Pentagon quietly began seeking advice on new ways to protect bases by using innovative advanced materials, camouflaging facilities, obscuring their thermal and electromagnetic signatures, hiding them underground, and making them more resilient in the face of successful attack by adversaries, according to a special notice issued by a top Pentagon official.
As the Pentagon refines this “base of the future” concept, Iran is teasing a “war of the future” effort that builds on its successes in throttling the Strait of Hormuz, regionalizing the war, and battering U.S. bases, according to Mahdi Mohammadi, a senior adviser to Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the lead negotiator and speaker of Parliament. “The second generation of surprises will be on their way; at the time and place of our choosing, in the manner we have devised, and with the creativity that only our unparalleled fighters can muster,” he wrote on X, teasing how Iran would respond if America ramps up the war.
Iran’s successful attacks on U.S. bases have added to the growing realization that foreign adversaries, proxies, terror groups, and lone wolf actors can use low-cost, easily obtained drones to attack the military bases, aircraft, and military personnel of the U.S. and its allies.
While Iran dominated the headlines for months, officials became increasingly worried about danger from Russian attacks. “When do we stop calling it gray zone?” asked a third official briefed on the intelligence, referring to a Russian drone attack on a massive air freighter, used to carry military assistance to Ukraine, at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany in August. One drone hit the cargo plane but failed to explode, another struck a different aircraft, and a third was found near the airport. “That’s what Putin always does. He keeps testing us, pushing us, to see how far he can go,” said the official. That official and another said that the intelligence proved there was “no question” that Russia was behind the operations. Russia has denied responsibility.
The August drone attack was part of a monthslong campaign of nonstop sabotage, cyberattacks, and psychological operations against NATO nations. “These were happening in sequence from earlier in the year, through August, through September and they didn’t show any signs of stopping,” said the third official. But the attacks slowed or stopped after President Donald Trump announced earlier this month that the United States would buy Russian diesel in an effort to bring down fuel prices before the midterm elections and called on Ukraine to stop striking oil Russian refineries.
The officials noted that Pentagon leadership has been slow to respond to the changing nature of warfare, specifically drawing attention to tactics honed by Ukraine in its war with Russia. Earlier this month, for example, intelligence suggested that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps was planning a complex drone attack on U.S. B-1 bombers used to attack Iran, and U.S. personnel at Royal Air Force Fairford air base. The plot, they said, was to launch small drones from just beyond the bases’ fenceline, attacking the supersonic bombers, which were not in hardened shelters but in the open on the tarmac. They noted that the plot appeared to be patterned on a Ukrainian attack, dubbed Operation Spider’s Web, against Russia last year. The plot so unnerved top military officials that the bombers were flown out while some aerial refueling aircraft were still being deployed to support their panicked flights back to the U.S. In addition to RAF Fairford, U.S. officials referenced additional threats against other bases in Europe, including Ramstein Air Base in Germany.
Last August, Hegseth established Joint Interagency Task Force 401 to deliver “C-sUAS” or counter-small unmanned aircraft system “capabilities to America’s warfighters, [to] defeat adversary threats, and promote sovereignty over national airspace.” But an inspector general report from January said “immediate attention” was required to protect the most critical bases in the U.S. against drones and noted that Pentagon “documents contradict one another and do not speak to certain aspects of C-UAS authorities and capabilities.” The IG found also that key “military installations, government-owned, contractor-operated facilities, and contractor-owned, contractor-operated facilities conducting critical missions” were not even designated for protection.
In March, small drones flew over Louisiana’s Barksdale Air Force Base, the home of Global Strike Command which oversees America’s bomber fleet and its intercontinental-ballistic missiles. And the IG report mentions “10 DoD installations and activities where Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) incursions have occurred.”
Late last month, the Air Force awarded a contract for counter-drone systems for Joint Base McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst in New Jersey. The military has also been looking into drone-killing technologies to defend Yokota Air Base in Tokyo, Japan; Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota; Battle Creek Air National Guard Base in Michigan; and Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina, among other facilities.
Two of the officials suggested that new Pentagon plans for military base modernization are rooted in an uneasy acknowledgment that U.S. outposts around the world — including within the continental United States — are increasingly vulnerable to complex and asymmetric attacks. A recent Pentagon inspector general report revealed Iranian strikes “damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict.”
Hegseth’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment by The Intercept.
One U.S. official told The Intercept that the cost of repairing and rebuilding these Middle East outposts could be “upwards of $50 million,” but said the “real cost” might be “far higher.” The Pentagon, however, refuses to disclose the price tag of the damage, which has only been shared in a classified briefing.
“The American people deserve to know the full cost of the Trump administration’s unauthorized war against Iran. Even if DoD has not yet determined which facilities it is planning to rebuild, disclosing these costs represents the bare minimum transparency DoD owes the public,” wrote Democratic Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Richard Blumentha, Mazie Hirono, Tammy Duckworth, and Gary Peters in a recent letter to Adm. Brad Cooper, the chief of Central Command. CENTCOM did not reply to a request from The Intercept for the total cost.
Last week, the Pentagon quietly began seeking information for “near-term” procurement and long-term modernization strategies to “move past traditional ‘pour-concrete-and-hope’ hardening” of its facilities and increase the “survivability of these installations under kinetic and multi-domain threats,” according to a special notice from the office of Dale R. Marks, the assistant secretary of war for energy, installations, and environment.
Following the destruction of NSA Manama and Al Udeid Air Base, the Pentagon is seeking ways to promote “operational capability and survivability under kinetic impact,” by employing decentralized energy grids, “autonomous backup utility systems,” innovative base layouts, and modular structures. Recognizing the need to “protect assets and personnel from kinetic impacts, thermal effects, and blast overpressures,” the military is looking at ways to harden facilities. This means employing advanced construction methods involving metamaterials designed for surviving air attack, energy-dissipating composites, self-healing materials, and “novel concrete formulations.”
The U.S. is also seeking ways to lower the profile or conceal the location of its bases through technological means. This includes camouflaging facilities and integrating them into the natural environment to make them more difficult to spot, masking their thermal and electromagnetic signatures, and creating decoy structures to draw fire.
Beyond the use of “terrain-integrated facility design,” the U.S. is also seeking to take its most sensitive facilities deep below ground. Increased vulnerabilities to aerial attack have led to a reemergence and increased reliance on subterranean warfare in the Russia–Ukraine war, harkening back to World War I trench warfare and the use of massive underground tunnel networks and bases by Vietnamese forces in the American war.
Iran, for its part, uses underground facilities to shield its missile and nuclear programs. The Pentagon, according to the documents, is interested in new methods of “high-speed tunneling,” the rapid creation of protected caverns, and “shock-isolated underground structural design[s].”
Last week’s quiet plea from the Pentagon follows an announcement by Hegseth of a FORTRESS America initiative that he calls a “national insurance policy for the American homeland.” One former Pentagon analyst, however, said it sounded more like “cutting America and Americans loose” in the event of a major conflagration, tying it to Hegseth’s belief that the military is a warrior elite superior to civilians.
“Every major military installation in America is going to generate its own power. Independent of the civilian grid. If an adversary takes down the grid by cyberattack, by sabotage, by any means, our bases stay lit. Our aircraft keep flying. Our command centers never go dark,” said Hegseth, explaining the FORTRESS concept. “We are building long overdue strategic reserves deep enough to fight through disruption. Think munitions. Fuel. Medicine. Blood. Deep enough that if the world’s supply lines break, and in a real war, they are going to break — America keeps fighting anyway.”
The former advisor said that Hegseth’s plan appeared to send a message to 99 percent of the American public: “It sounds as if he is saying to people ‘fuck off and you’re on your own.’”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://hellgatenyc.com/benjamin-button-.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/benjamin-button-.text:
When was the last time you thought about "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button"? Maybe you saw an old-looking baby, or a particularly youthful 70-year-old; maybe you studied David Fincher's filmography for a movie-themed trivia night; or maybe, like us, you caught wind of the fact that "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button," a musical fresh off the West End, is now showing at the Public's Newman Theater. 
Let's get this out of the way: "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button" the musical does not have the same plot as Fincher's strange, schmaltzy 2008 Oscar bait. Theatergoers will not be treated to any Taraji P. Henson, Cate Blanchett, or Brad Pitt impressions, and there is absolutely no whiff of Hurricane Katrina. (Yes, all that stuff is in the movie.) The musical also apparently deviates from the F. Scott Fitzgerald story that created Benjamin Button, which is seemingly a good choice based off of the short story's acutely depressing Wikipedia entry. 
Instead, "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button" follows the backwards-aging, eponymous hero from his home in Cornwall, England, through World War II (we are fucking robbed of seeing BB storm the beach at Normandy, sadly), an international journey of self-discovery, and, of course, through an epic, decade-spanning love story with a woman named Elowen who is, unforch, aging regular style.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Downsizing and debt swaps: Pace Gallery files latest UK accounts
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Anna Brady
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
In the wake of public retrenchment over the summer, Pace Gallery’s UK registered company, which serves as the parent company for all of the firm’s operations outside the US and Tokyo, has filed its 2024 accounts with Companies House.
The accounts—which were due at the end of December 2025 and filed ten months late—report earnings for The Pace Gallery Limited (“the company”) and various subsidiary undertakings in Asia and Europe (“the group”).
The group incurred a pre-tax loss of $2,429 in 2024, compared to a profit of $6.8m in 2023. Such a drop, the directors’ report states, reflects a "continuation of the sector-wide contraction in global and UK art markets as well as a continued reluctance by some clients to buy which became most pronounced in 2024 and continued through 2025 and into 2026". These market conditions led the directors to "initiate cost saving measures across the group, but despite these measures, difficult market conditions continued".
Total group turnover stood at $67.7m in 2024 (2023: $104.9m), of which some $48m was contributed by its subsidiaries. Only $4.1m of this was sold to the UK (2023: $10.7m) while $60.5m went to the rest of the world.
Net assets amounted to $2.5m as of the end of 2024 (2023: $4.5m), of which $9.4m (2023: $17.3m) was payable to the US parent company, The Pace Gallery LLC. Debts and other amounts owed falling within one year stood at $49m, compared to $50.8m at the end of 2023.
Cost-cutting measures
Although the filings refer to 2024 results, late filing meant they also outline cost-saving measures implemented this summer. “Throughout 2025 the group developed a comprehensive plan to refocus the gallery's mission by streamlining strategy, reprioritising relationships with artists and collectors, and reducing operating expenses,” the report says. This plan was first announced by Pace’s chief executive Marc Glimcher in May, when he told The New York Times that the gallery was cutting 50 artists and 50 staff. Such a diminished artist roster, the filings say, “reduced the number of full-time support roles and resources” needed, hence the concurrent staff cuts.
The group’s global footprint has also been scaled back, the filings say, “which decreased the number of exhibitions the group is engaging in, as well as lowering overheads” (the gallery’s Hong Kong space was shut in October 2025). Such consolidation “will allow the group to focus its resources, better support its artists and collectors, and return to a more efficient and profitable approach,” the filings say. Furthermore, only last month it was reported that Pace is seeking a tenant to share its enormous eight-storey New York headquarters in order to share operating costs.
The Companies House filings mention the partnership with Emmanuel Di Donna and David Schrader to form Pace Di Donna Schrader Galleries (PDS), first announced in December 2025, with the purpose of expanding the group's secondary market business. Along with the “counter-cyclical investment” in the form of a new gallery opened in Berlin in 2025 as “a foothold in Europe”, the directors believe the company is “well placed to take advantage of any improvement in market conditions in 2026 and beyond, despite the ongoing uncertainties associated with geopolitical tensions and inflationary increased in operational expenses.” The report concludes that with the above changes, the directors “have a strong belief in the future of the company and group.”
The 2024 filings also show that severance pay of $1m was paid to one key member of departing management staff, though the gallery declines to identify the employee. Advances of $5.7m were paid to artists (2023: $2.9m), of which $306,235 (2023: $9.4m) have been written down as irrecoverable, whether due to the saleability of the works held on consignment or the saleability of the artist's works more generally.
The Pace Gallery Limited, it should be remembered, is a subsidiary of the US parent company, The Pace Gallery LLC (controlled by Marc Glimcher), which—together with Marc and his father Arne Glimcher—underwrites it. Therefore, these filings only give a partial picture of the broader corporate structure and its international operations.
Debt swaps
Nonetheless it is interesting that the filings reveal a planned debt for equity swap as the UK registered entity, The Pace Gallery Limited, is unable to repay its debt of $19.2m to the US parent company, The Pace Gallery LLC. This unpaid group debt will be turned into shares by the end of 2026. “The proposed debt-for-equity conversion, part of a broader global financial management strategy, reflects a capital structure decision within the Pace group and should not be interpreted as a loss or a liquidity issue for the UK business,” a Pace spokesperson tells The Art Newspaper. The company reviews how its subsidiaries are financed “to ensure that their balance sheets appropriately reflect the long-term nature of the capital invested in those businesses” the spokesperson says. In this case, the parent company has decided that some of its investment in the UK operation “is more appropriately reflected as equity rather than intercompany debt”, they continue: “The proposed transaction is intended to strengthen the UK company's balance sheet and align its capital structure with the long-term needs of the business.”
The share issuance will not make any material difference to the running of the UK group, the spokesperson says, and on the planned move of the London gallery’s premises from Hanover Square to a smaller space on nearby Grafton Street in Mayfair, there is no news yet.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Toledo Museum of Art launches initiative to donate art books to African libraries
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Gameli Hamelo
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
The Toledo Museum of Art (TMA) has launched the initiative Africa Art Library to donate books to libraries on the continent. The museum donated around 100 books to the Koyo Kouoh Library at the Gihanga Institute of Contemporary Art in Kigali, Rwanda, earlier this year and a second set is headed to the Nubuke Foundation in Accra, Ghana, this month.
The subjects of the books cover Africa and African diasporic art as well as art history, criticism, museum education and other relevant topics, and have been selected by the receiving libraries from the TMA’s library inventory.
The idea grew out of conversations over the past four years among leaders of the TMA and African art residency spaces, foundations and cultural institutions, during which books for their libraries were among the top requests.
During the process of the museum’s current reinstallation—the first in 40 years—the team realised that “like so many Western institutions, [the TMA] did not have adequate representation of the breadth and depth of artistic traditions on the African continent, including and especially Modern and contemporary art histories”, Adam M. Levine, the museum’s president, director and chief executive officer, tells The Art Newspaper.
The TMA team travelled to African countries and bought artworks for its collection by the likes of Jimoh Akolo, the late Nigerian artist renowned for his contributions to modern Nigerian art. He was also a member of the Zaria Art Society, a group of local artists known for their rejection of Western art-focused curricula by their mainly British lecturers, who chose to embrace indigenous Nigerian art in the late 1950s to early 1960s.
“Our objective was not just to go to these places to try and find artworks but to figure out how we could partner and support these ecosystems without being extractive. Without perpetuating sort of colonialist or imperialist logic,” Levine adds.
Prior relationships and engagements with people on the ground helped select the receiving partners for the pilot Africa Art Library initiative, supported by the Accra- and London-based Gallery 1957 and its founder, Marwan Zakhem.
Alexandra Nickolaou, a fellow in African and African Diasporic Art at the TMA, is leading on the Africa Art Library project and views it as a long-term initiative. She hopes to bring other museum libraries across the US on board as partners and aims to expand and add more recipients in other African countries.
“I think [the initiative] is a really fantastic way to think about partnerships with the continent [...] making sure that these partnerships are not just strengthening repatriation efforts but also creating good lasting partnerships outside of that in other ways that have to do with art education and not just art itself,” says Nickolaou.
Over the past year, the TMA has also partnered with Nigeria’s Yemisi Shyllon Museum of Art for cultural exchanges that boost museum expertise and access, and with the Ethiopian Heritage Authority to return objects to Ethiopia. The TMA is set to reopen its galleries in autumn 2027.
