https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Art Basel Qatar releases 2027 exhibitor list as renewed threat of war looms over Gulf
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Kabir Jhala
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
Art Basel Qatar (ABQ), the Qatari state's finely orchestrated selling event in partnership with the Swiss fair giant, today announced the exhibitor list for its second edition, which will take place across the M7 and Doha Design District venues from 28 to 30 January 2027 (VIP preview days 26-27 January).
Eighty-two galleries plan to take part, a slight decrease from the 87 that showed in the inaugural edition. Among them are Sylvia Kouvali (London, Piraeus) bringing the kinetic art pioneer Liliane Lijn, and Gagosian, which will offer works by the art-world prankster Maurizio Catellan. Like the inaugural edition, almost half of participating galleries operate spaces in the Menasa (Middle East, North Africa and South Asia) region, including Marfa’ Projects from Beirut, whose stand will feature the Lebanese artist Stéphanie Saadé, and India’s Nature Morte, presenting the architecturally minded sculptor Ayesha Singh.
Each presentation will respond to the theme of “between”, which was chosen by the fair’s artistic director, the Iraqi curator Wassan Al-Khudhairi, who was the founding director of Doha’s Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art from 2007-12. She takes the reins from Wael Shawky, who curated the inaugural edition.
Who's returning—and who isn't
Exhibitor turnover is high from last year’s edition, with 35 galleries—or around 40%—not returning, including global dealerships like Hauser & Wirth, Pace, Almine Rech and Victoria Miro, as well as prominent regional spaces such as Gallery Isabelle from Dubai. Filling their places are 30 newcomers: Isla Flotante (Buenos Aires, São Paulo), Pilar Corrias (London) and Silverlens (Manila, New York) are among those taking part for the first time.
A full list of galleries exhibiting at Art Basel Qatar 2027—plus those not returning—can be found at the end of this article.
Vincenzo De Bellis, Art Basel’s global director of fairs, tells The Art Newspaper the high turnover is typical of ABQ’s format. “Across our global fairs, we see greater turnover in the sectors that are theme-led, and in Qatar that approach extends to the fair as a whole. Selection is closely tied to how galleries’ proposed solo presentations respond to each edition’s theme, so it is natural for the exhibitor list to change from year to year.”
Gallerists in the selection committee are: Lorenzo Fischi, Galleria Continua; Gordon VeneKlasen, VeneKlasen Gallery; Daniela Gareh, White Cube; Shireen Gandhy, Chemould Prescott Road; Sunny Rahbar, The Third Line; and Mohammed Hafiz, Athr.
Contingency plans
Like its competitors, Art Basel does not discuss motivations behind individual exhibitor applications, including whether some prospective applicants may have pulled out due to geopolitical tensions in the Arabian Gulf. Nonetheless, visitors planning their trip to Qatar next year will certainly be conscious of renewed bombardment in neighbouring Saudi Arabia earlier this month, and looming threats of the US and Israel resuming war with Iran. In late February, a few weeks after the conclusion of the first Art Basel Qatar, Iran launched missiles into Qatar, injuring 16 people, according to Qatari authorities at the time, and causing major disruptions to its airspace.
As a contingency plan, should the fair be postponed or considerably altered due to such circumstances, exhibitors will receive a refund of their participation fee or have the option to defer their participation to the following edition, currently planned for January 2028. Nonetheless, any last-minute drop outs will be subject to a standard penalty fee, similar to other Art Basel fairs.
While this uncertainty might deter some galleries, others will likely be incentivised by the unusually generous level of support provided to exhibitors via Art Basel's partnership with Qatar Sports Investments (QSI) and QC+, the commercial branch of Qatar Museums. This funds customs clearance, in-country transportation, consolidated storage and installation services, hotel accommodation for up to two staff members, and travel and hotel costs for exhibiting artists. In addition, from the 2027 edition Art Basel Qatar will also cover 50% of outbound shipping costs for unsold works, up to a maximum of $20,000 per gallery, further mitigating costs and risks for galleries.
Art Basel is also deepening its roots in Qatar by launching a year-round programme there to develop the country’s art market, including masterclasses and workshops designed to foster new collectors. "Our ambition extends well beyond the fair week: through our new year-round programme, we aim to deepen collector engagement between editions and contribute to the sustained growth of the regional art market," Art Basel's chief executive Noah Horowitz says in a statement.
Visitors to the second edition of ABQ will also get a chance to see the inaugural Rubaiya, a quadrennial exhibition in Doha, that will bring together more than 120 artists, including Saodat Ismailova and Rirkrit Tiravanija.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Fake or Fortune art historian donates major Anglo-Indian art collection to Tate
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
A UK collector has donated a significant collection of 50 works by artists who lived and worked in India during the 18th and 19th centuries to the Tate in London. The collection, given by the UK art historian Charles Greig, includes works by Indian artists, such as Sita Ram and Ghulam Ali Khan, and European artists, including Johan Zoffany and Rudolf Swoboda, along with British figures such as Thomas Daniell and William Daniell.
The works throw light on a “period of profound cultural, social and political change brought about by British colonialism in South Asia” says a Tate statement. Key pieces donated include three watercolours by Sita Ram who was instrumental in creating works known as “Company paintings”, watercolours created in a European style for foreign patrons. The British Library in London has a large collection of watercolours by Ram.
Greig says in a statement: “Most of the works were made in the vanished world before photography and they provide us with a visual record of our rich shared history from about 1770. Assembling this collection has been my life’s primary passion, but at no stage did I ever see myself as other than a temporary steward.”
Asked why Greig opted for Tate, a spokesperson tells The Art Newspaper: “Tate has long held a few key paintings related to Anglo-Indian history of the period, including Zoffany’s Colonel Mordant’s Cock Match (around 1784) and Indian landscapes by Thomas Daniell and William Hodges”. Greig recently appeared in an episode of the television series Fake or Fortune?, in which he assessed a portrait of an Indian woman by the 18th-century Scottish artist Katherine Read.
A free display of the works drawn from the Greig collection is due to open at Tate Britain in 2028.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.title: New Yorkers Want to Play Ball. The Toughest Game is Getting a Field.
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.author: Haidee Chu, Carol Chen, Stephen Lurie | The Pudding, and Matt Daniels | The Pudding
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.text:
When the playground at St. Vartan Park closed for renovations this spring, parents in Murray Hill rallied around one question: Where will the children go to play?
“We thought, well, at least we have the field next to it,” said Rebecca Webber, a 51-year-old mother from the neighborhood. “And every evening we would get sort of ushered off the field by an organization that had a permit.”
Across the East River, at Pier 5 of Brooklyn Bridge Park, a group of eight high school soccer players filmed a public plea addressed to Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Instagram.
“Mamdani! Three fields, three permits, this is crazy,” they said. “We just want to play and now we have to go home. … We propose that one field should be open at all times!”
At New York City’s hundreds of public ballfields and soccer pitches, casual pick-up players are feeling the squeeze as demand surges for organized games, practices and sports clinics. But even those with the persistence and resources to score a permit don’t feel like winners. League and club operators say they, too, are struggling to get enough field time as interest in recreational sports explodes.
The Parks Department permitted 48% more daily reservations for organized sports on public athletic fields in 2025 than a decade ago, according to public and internal Parks Department permit data obtained and analyzed by The City Reporter and data visualization site The Pudding. Nearly 1,850 organizations secured permits — roughly 310 more than in 2015.
The proliferation of recreational leagues and sports clinics has at times pitted older neighborhood teams against new entrants in a struggle for field time. In East Williamsburg, for example, longtime residents who’d been playing softball at Sternberg Park for five decades were surprised to learn last year that one of their weeknight league permits had been denied to make space for another group.
“Before, no one wanted this park. It was in bad conditions,” said Hector Perez, who moved to the neighborhood from Puerto Rico as a kid and now plays in the 55-and-up Los Abuelos league. In 2021, the Parks Department unveiled a new artificial turf field at Sternberg Park. That same year, Williamsburg ranked second citywide for new housing construction over the previous decade.
“And now, after the neighborhood’s been gentrified, everybody wants to play here,” he continued. “But we’ve been here the longest.”
On weekends, the park still throngs with cheers as the old-timers compete against one another, while free food is laid out for the crowd ringing the field, folding chairs galore.
“We’ve kept the spirit of baseball going — to not forget our culture — because this is all gentrified, and this is the little bit that we have left,” Perez said.
But amid the growing competition for fields, even the big leagues have struggled with permitting.
“It remains the single most frustrating aspect of this job,” said Tarek Pertew, founder and CEO of NYC Footy, the largest adult recreational soccer league and for-profit permit holder in the city.
It took Pertew three years to score a permit at Brooklyn Bridge Park when he started out in 2010, then another five years to break into Manhattan. Sixteen years later, Pertew said he’s still waiting on McCarren Park in Greenpoint, home to a football field and three baseball diamonds. His waitlist of would-be teams, in the meantime, continues to grow.
“There’s so much demand for this simple service,” Pertew continued. “And we can’t even come close to fulfilling that demand because of these restrictions.”
A Crowded Field
According to Parks Department data, the number of permitted field reservations has grown year over year at least since 2014 — until 2020, when the COVID pandemic forced New Yorkers indoors and demand plunged.
But as coronavirus restrictions began to loosen, permitted field usage didn’t just bounce back. It boomed.
Field usage continued to reach new highs, with 223,860 permitted reservations issued in 2025.
“COVID changed everything,” said Pertew, whose recreational soccer league service exploded with demand overnight. “There was this very natural biological reaction for people that wanted a physical and mental outlet with a social backdrop … It was the perfect combination of what people needed coming out of COVID.”
It was youth sports, however, that accounted for the majority of the permitted field usage during this time. Around 75% of all permitted field reservations every year since COVID, in fact, were issued for youth sports — noticeably more than the roughly 55% from a decade ago.
“In 2020, we started picking up momentum, and we started to see, ‘OK, people value it,’” Sherard Sullivan, 41, said on a recent afternoon at Jesse Owens Playground in Brooklyn’s Bedford-Stuyvesant, where teenagers scrimmaged on one side of the soccer field and parents played with their toddlers on the other. A former teacher, Sullivan founded the non-profit S.S. Soccer Academy in 2015 to serve children from three to 14. “More people aligned with our vision.”
As popularity grew, so did the competition. Sometime around 2023, Sullivan recalled, his permit renewal at Jesse Owens, where he’d been running his program for three years, was denied. His academy’s field time was instead granted to a soccer club based in Williamsburg, he recalled.
“That was one of the hardest nights I ever had in my life. I couldn’t sleep,” said Sullivan. He’d made a commitment to his young athletes that he’d get them college-ready, he said, reminiscing on the way soccer had brought him from his home country of Trinidad and Tobago to New York City, where he played in college.
He continued: “I was really devastated, because all I thought about was all the different kids: What am I gonna tell them? What am I gonna do for them? I hit the ground running and luckily it was rectified.”
In 2024, the Parks Department modified permitting rules to give non-profit organizations like Sullivan’s priority. And youth groups, as is always the case, are prioritized over adults.
But that did little to help the Harlem Jets, a non-profit that has been serving youths for more than two decades.
“We live in Harlem. We’re from Harlem, but we’re forced to come to Randall’s Island because the fields in Harlem were being utilized by other people,” its founder and CEO, Jamel Wright, told The City Reporter while coaching football on the island. “We use any field we can get that we can get on, to be perfectly honest … There’s just a lot of utilization that needs to happen with limited options.”
Wright has always had trouble securing enough field time in Harlem, he said — even after the city unveiled a new artificial turf field last year at General Charles Young Playground.
“That’s part of why we purchased our own bus, so that our kids wouldn’t necessarily have to take the M35 bus,” Wright added. “This team has 30-something children on it. But what do you see here? Maybe 15, 20. That’s because they’re finding it to be problematic to get them from over there, over the bridge, to over here.”
Wright proposed a solution: The city, he suggested, should reserve field space for neighborhood youths during the afterschool hours until the early evening.
“After 8 p.m. every kid off the field — and grown-ups can play until they fall asleep,” he said.
Ken Conyers, director of citywide athletic permits for the Parks Department, said the agency has continued to refine its permitting systems and its scheduling practices to make sure facilities are used “fairly and efficiently.”
“As demand for permits has grown, we’ve worked hard to keep pace,” Conyers said. “Our goal is to make sure everyone who wants to take part in athletics and other permitted activities has a place to do so, and we’ll continue working with our communities to meet that need.”
Let There Be Light
As the fall yields to winter, however, shorter days will begin to eat into available field time.
That’s because just 5% of the city’s 5,850-something active athletic facilities are equipped with lights, according to Parks Department data.
This poses additional headaches especially for soccer, football and lacrosse organizers. These “rectangular ballfield” sports, as the Parks Department calls them, are prioritized in the fall and winter, as opposed to diamond sports like baseball, softball and cricket, which take precedence in the spring and summer.
“Once daylight loss pushes sunset earlier than 6:00 p.m., fields become effectively unusable for working adults unless they are lit,” Pertew, who operates NYC Footy, wrote in a letter to Parks Commissioner Tricia Shimamura in April.
In the letter, Pertew also urged the city to introduce temporary lighting to expand field access, while investing in permanent lighting infrastructure in areas where adult recreational sport is most in demand.
Pertew’s for-profit organization stands to benefit financially from increased field access, to be sure. By his estimate, however, one single lit field could add roughly 1,200 hours of play each year — offering more field time for not just NYC Footy, but to all park users.
Already, the Mamdani administration has experimented with the idea in partnership with NYC Footy over the summer, as the World Cup fueled fervor for soccer. For a little more than a month, the city kept the lights on overnight at one field in every borough, opening them up for pick-up play from 10:30 p.m. through 8 a.m. for adults.
Parks Commissioner Shimamura herself pointed to the pilot as a success when The City Reporter asked in the late summer how her department can make it easier for New Yorkers to access fields and permits.
“I don’t think we’ve exhausted all of the low-hanging fruit to create more access,” she said. “In the long term, we need more fields and more lights.”
The Parks Department extended the pilot earlier this month, granting one soccer field in each of the five boroughs extended night lights until 2 a.m.
Pertew’s attention, meanwhile, is now focused on St. Vartan Park in Midtown East, where parents, children and sports organizations alike feel squeezed for play time since the playground closure.
While the City Council already voted last year to fully fund the installation of field lights on the multipurpose field there, Pertew is now offering to cover the bill for temporary lighting while the upgrades are pending, he said, so that field access can be expanded for everyone in the neighborhood — so long as Footy can be permitted to play on the field for at least one day each week to cover the cost.
Youth sports could take over in the after-school hours till sunset, he envisioned, followed by community open field time, and adult leagues in the evening.
“If you do that, you are going to drastically minimize the complaints in the conflict because youth is benefitting, community’s benefitting, and the adults get more time as well,” Pertew said. “That is what lights can do.”
Webber, the Murray Hill parent, has missed the daily kids’ meetup at their local playground in the meantime — squirt gun fights and all, she said. She spent the summer exploring other playgrounds in the neighborhood with her son, who still occasionally plays pick-up with his friends at the St. Vartan field.
The children would occasionally sit along the sidelines while the adults played, she said, choosing a player to root for as though they were watching a professional match.
“It’s really cute, so I wouldn’t want to lose it entirely,” Webber said. “I think it’s just about balance, and it’s a really hard question: Who should get the park when and who should get it most, and how do we allocate this?”
This story was reported by Haidee Chu and Carol Chen of The City Reporter, based on original research and data analysis by Stephen Lurie and Matt Daniels of The Pudding. Katie Honan contributed.

https://www.propublica.org/article/oklah.title: This Oil Company Is Linked to 1,000 Pollution Incidents and Other Violations. Oklahoma Never Punished It.
https://www.propublica.org/article/oklah.author: Nick Bowlin
https://www.propublica.org/article/oklah.text:
Reporting Highlights
- Citation’s Track Record: Citation Oil & Gas is named more than any other company in an Oklahoma database of pollution reports and other rule violations — over 1,000 times in the past decade.
- Pollution Without Punishment: Regulatory agency staff repeatedly recommended the state punish Citation. Instead, agency bosses allowed the company to restart operations without consequence.
- Regulators Rarely Regulate: Our analysis found that less than a third of enforcement cases filed by Oklahoma’s oil division since 2023 have resulted in punishment.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
In June 2023, staff at an Oklahoma regulatory agency were fed up. The state isn’t known for cracking down on oil and gas companies for polluting the environment, but for over a year, the staff had been building a case to punish Citation Oil & Gas, one of the nation’s largest privately owned oil companies.
About 30 miles north of the Texas border, toxic wastewater was gushing from the ground outside the small city of Ardmore. In the mile-wide oil field known as the Bayou, an oily sheen glistened on creeks and long streaks of salt scarred the land. The so-called purges, bubbling up among stands of oak and walnut trees, also threatened drinking water sources, drawing attention from the Environmental Protection Agency, according to a federal report.
State investigators pinned the blame on Citation’s injection wells, which pump wastewater from oil production back underground at high pressures and volumes in order to produce more oil. But this injection came with risks.
Days earlier, the agency had asked Citation to cut injection pressures in half. The company refused, prompting staff at the oil division of the Oklahoma Corporation Commission, the state’s oil and gas regulator, to recommend an official punishment through the agency’s court system.
“This will be an important case to get some of these purges stopped and particularly concerning Citation’s operations,” Danny Ray, an agency manager at the time, emailed his colleagues.
He restated the urgency three days later in an email to oil division leaders and Citation officials: “We consider this an emergency situation that needs to be addressed promptly.”
To stop the flow of wastewater, the agency temporarily shut down the Bayou’s 22 injection wells — all but three of which were owned by Citation — kicking off a yearlong fight over the terms under which injection could restart.
Under state rules, companies must not pollute, and oil and gas regulators at the Corporation Commission can revoke injection permits and issue fines to those that violate regulations.
But agency leadership ultimately did not follow staff guidance to punish Citation through the commission’s administrative law court. Instead, in April 2024, state officials, including the oil division’s then-Director Robyn Strickland, would allow Citation to restart injection at higher-than-recommended pressures.
Agency leaders’ reluctance to punish Citation reflects a longstanding pattern of Oklahoma regulators letting oil companies contaminate drinking water, farmland and people’s homes with scant consequences, The Frontier and ProPublica have found in a yearlong investigation.
In fact the commission has no record of ever fining or completing an enforcement case against Citation, the company named more than any other in the agency’s database of pollution reports and other rule violations, listed more than 1,000 times over the past decade. That’s hundreds more incidents than any other operator, including comparably sized companies. In recent years, purges linked to Citation include some of Oklahoma’s longest, most damaging oil field pollution events.
Current and former employees at the Oklahoma Corporation Commission describe top agency officials as wary of going after habitual violators like Citation. Citation has become Oklahoma’s second-largest well owner after taking over collections of aging, low-producing wells from oil giants that have largely left the state for more lucrative oil fields in Texas and elsewhere; the company acquired its Bayou wells in 2010. Regulators treat Citation gently, current and former agency employees say, because the company holds onto aging wells that are worth little — wells that could easily become a financial liability for the state if Citation were to sell or walk away from them.
A spokesperson for the Oklahoma Corporation Commission declined to answer questions about the regulatory agency’s handling of Citation’s record, noting the possibility of future enforcement actions or litigation involving the company.
“The OCC Oil and Gas Conservation Division must remain mindful of its regulatory and adjudicatory responsibilities and avoid making public statements that could potentially affect future proceedings or legal considerations,” spokesperson Jack Damrill said in an email.
Strickland has since left the agency for a job as chief projects officer for the Interstate Oil and Gas Compact Commission, a quasi-governmental organization that often advocates for industry interests. She did not respond to requests for comment.
A Citation executive declined to comment in response to written questions.
Regulators in other jurisdictions have at times come down hard on Citation, which owns wells in 11 other states. In 2017, the company settled with the U.S. Department of Justice for $2.25 million over allegations of underpaid royalties from drilling on federal land in Wyoming, though the settlement did not rule that the company was liable in the case. And in 2025, Utah reached a $700,000 settlement with the company after a crude oil and wastewater spill. Texas and Colorado have also fined Citation in recent years for violations.
“Citation has been the thorn in my side for a long time,” said a current manager at the Oklahoma agency who spoke on the condition of anonymity to protect their job. “They just operate however they want. They’ve had major pollution issues, and you can’t really touch them.”
Preparing a Case for Punishment
In November 2023, five months into the wells’ shutdown, Citation was getting antsy. Its officials had repeatedly demanded permission to restart their wells and had even challenged the state through the commission’s court to prove the connection between the Bayou purges and its operations. Regulators and company officials packed into a small conference room in the Oklahoma Corporation Commission’s Oklahoma City headquarters to discuss how that might happen. More than a dozen others joined via video.
On the state’s side, a team of consultants took the lead, displaying a report with evidence that tied Citation’s injection to the wastewater that gushed to the surface in the Bayou. The state had hired the environmental engineering firm Halff earlier that year on a $550,000 contract to investigate the fast-growing number of oil field wastewater eruptions around Oklahoma. The consultants and agency staff presented a unified front in identifying the problem: Citation’s nearly two dozen Bayou injection wells were operating at unsafely high pressures, according to a video recording of the meeting obtained by The Frontier and ProPublica. Over the years, the injected wastewater had shattered underground rock layers, allowing the toxic fluid to spread uncontrollably.
“You definitely have overpressurization,” Carolyn May, Halff’s director of environmental remediation, told Citation officials as she presented her team’s calculations, which were based on well records, field data collected by agency staff and a standard set by the federal government. “It’s allowing that rock to fracture.”
The consultants were meant to serve as independent experts to mediate any disagreements within the agency over what to do about the wastewater eruptions, according to current and former commission officials.
In the meeting, May and agency staffers ticked off a number of problems with Citation’s wells that regulators had overlooked for years. Not only had they allowed the company to inject wastewater at excessive pressures, regulators had also given out more than a dozen exemptions to testing and well-construction standards that endangered groundwater. Several wells had checkered compliance records; agency documents noted that one had been in “perpetual violation” of its permit for “nine years running,” injecting tens of millions of gallons of wastewater beyond the legal limit.
Citation’s active wells weren’t the only issue, they said. Nearby were dozens of abandoned, unplugged wells that offered the pressurized wastewater open pathways to reach shallow freshwater sources and the surface. May singled out a handful of those wells that especially troubled her team, and oil division deputy director Mike McGinnis suggested that Citation permanently plug them.
May noted that imaging below the surface by agency staff showed a distinct plume of highly polluted wastewater rising from deep underground, where injection took place. This posed a threat to the freshwater sources beneath the Bayou, she said — water that some residents rely on for drinking and cooking. “That’s our primary concern here.”
The consultants were not alone in this fear. Earlier in 2023, the Environmental Protection Agency had warned of “potential endangerment to underground sources of drinking water” in the Bayou from oil field injection. Groundwater tests taken near the purge sites showed evidence of oil field wastewater pollution, including high levels of salt, bromide and the carcinogen benzene, which exceeded the EPA drinking water standard by five times.
For its part, Citation came to the meeting armed with a very different argument: the pollution was caused by a combination of historic oil drilling and recent rainfall — not by the company.
It was a claim the company had repeatedly made, especially in the months since the agency had shut down its wells. To bolster its case, the company’s consultants had produced a series of detailed reports citing the area’s history of oil production, along with Citation’s own water testing data. Oil drilling began in the Bayou in the 1920s, a time of lawless extraction, and for decades, companies would simply dump their wastewater into large, unlined pits, allowing the fluid to seep into the ground. Old pollution that saturated the land was being flushed to the surface by rainfall, the reports argued. Each one concluded that there was no link between Citation’s injection and the Bayou pollution.
At the meeting with regulators, company representatives reiterated these arguments. Jeff Lewis, a Citation engineering manager, assured the agency that the company’s data indicated that its wells were not behind the Bayou purges and that it could safely inject at pressures higher than Halff had recommended. He proposed that the company restart injection on its deeper wells because they were separated by layers of rock from the abandoned wells that Halff identified as likely pathways for the wastewater to surface.
Agency staff did not buy this. In prior internal meetings and emails, staff and consultants had criticized Citation’s water sampling practices as biased in favor of the company’s conclusion that rainfall was causing old pollution to resurface. There was no question that old pollution covered the Bayou, but in recent purges, wastewater had pushed to the surface in significant volumes, covering creek beds in layers of snow-white salt. Old pollution would not be this forceful, according to internal documents written by agency staff.
“A purge is created by pressure and is not due to old pits,” Ray, the agency manager, wrote in a memo distributed months earlier within the oil division that urged agency leaders not to allow Citation to restart injection.
May, the agency’s consultant, echoed these rebuttals during the meeting and said the state’s evidence pointed to an injection problem. She concluded her presentation with a warning: Citation must change its injection practices in the Bayou.
“If y’all want to start injecting again,” she told company representatives, “I think we’re going to have to look at those pressures and the volumes very carefully.”
The meeting ended without a resolution.
“They Wore Us Out”
Over the next four months, Citation and state regulators would continue to debate the terms of restarting the Bayou. Neither side budged. By the time they gathered for another face-off in March 2024, oil division leaders appeared weary of fighting.
May and the Halff geologists from the consulting firm began by again insisting that Citation substantially reduce pressures in order to be allowed to restart a handful of wells. But even as they presented their case, Citation representatives including Lewis, the engineer, and Bob Redweik, a company vice president, repeatedly spoke over them. After more than two hours of disagreement, Redweik and Citation’s attorney ended the meeting abruptly. “We’re not going anywhere,” Redweik said.
Several top oil division officials attended, including Strickland, McGinnis and commission attorney Tyler Trout. They remained largely silent throughout.
The next week, Trout tried to end the impasse by passing along a memo from Citation.
“In an effort to reach an agreement and move this situation forward,” Trout wrote to top oil division officials and May, “would we consider meeting Citation in the middle as far as recommended injection pressures are concerned?”
May stood firm. “From Halff’s standpoint, our recommendations aren’t going to change,” she responded, adding that it would ultimately be up to agency leaders.
In early April, the agency went with a compromise, approving a plan to bring seven of Citation’s 19 Bayou injection wells back online. The company would be able to inject at pressures higher than Halff had recommended, though less than Citation had requested.
Current and former employees say that the decision to restart injection came from the top of the oil division, including Strickland and McGinnis, among others — bypassing staff who objected to the plan. Like Strickland, McGinnis did not respond to requests for comment.
“They wore us out,” said an agency manager who spoke on the condition of anonymity to protect their job.
Before injection restarted, three oil division officials chosen by Strickland conducted a walkthrough of the Bayou with Halff and Citation, according to an email from Strickland. The rest of the division was left in the dark. That same day, a pollution abatement manager noted in an email to the commission’s general counsel that agency critics of the plan had not been invited.
Around the time agency leaders allowed Citation to restart injection in the Bayou, staff were drafting an extensive contempt case against the company for rule violations in other parts of the state, according to public records obtained by The Frontier and ProPublica. Field staff and consultants were still turning up considerable problems related to Citation’s injection, including excessive pressures at the sites of destructive eruptions of wastewater. The staff complaint called for the agency to issue fines and to terminate well permits. But oil division leaders never signed the paperwork for the case.
There was ongoing trouble in the Bayou as well. Weeks after Citation restarted injection, field staff discovered a “severely contaminated” private water well nearby that had been polluted by oil field waste. Testing showed high levels of salt as well as the “highest levels of bromide that we have ever sampled,” according to internal emails, referring to another chemical constituent of oil and gas waste that poses a public health risk. (The landowners declined to comment because of an ongoing lawsuit against Citation, but according to court records, they do not drink from the well. The company, which has fought the family’s claims, says in a court filing that it has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars addressing the pollution on their land as part of a plan approved by the commission.)
By the end of 2024, oil division leaders had allowed six more Citation wells back online, bringing the total to 13. And the next spring, the agency closed the Bayou investigation, along with several others related to Citation, without taking further action.
Collection of New Complaints
In the year and a half since the Bayou case closed, several of the oil division staff who had pushed agency leaders to punish Citation have left the agency, as have a handful of senior leaders. Staffers told The Frontier and ProPublica they grew frustrated with the agency’s unwillingness to crack down on repeat corporate offenders that agency staff had spent months — at times, years — investigating.
Tracy Case, an attorney for the oil and gas division, admitted as much at a national conference for oil regulators in Oklahoma City in May. “I’ve been there 11 years doing this and we’ve never pursued what we call our ‘bad actors,’” she said, according to a recording of a meeting obtained by the news outlets. She explained that the oil division is extremely short-staffed while dealing with hundreds of potential enforcement cases at any one time. An agency spokesperson declined to comment on behalf of Case.
Less than a third of the roughly 750 enforcement cases filed by the oil division in the agency’s administrative law courts since 2023 have resulted in punishment so far, according to a review by The Frontier and ProPublica. The average fine given out by the agency was about $1,700. The most common punishment was a $500 fine, combined with using company insurance money to plug unused wells.
Neither the Oklahoma Corporation Commission nor Halff responded to questions about whether the consulting firm still has a role at the state agency.
At the Bayou, nearly all of Citation’s wastewater injection wells are back on, many operating at pressures beyond Halff’s recommendations. And industry data indicates that Citation has ramped up oil production to pre-shutdown levels even as evidence of new purges continues to emerge. In September, fresh layers of salt — residue of the wastewater — covered the dirt near yellowish puddles of standing water. Nearby, streaks of oil shone on the ground. The preceding weeks had been hot and dry, with hardly any rain.
In early October, an agency field staffer requested that Citation install a specialized well in the Bayou to pump out polluted groundwater, according to a report in the agency’s incident database.
A slew of new pollution complaints against Citation have continued to appear in that state database, including more than 60 spills and leaks at well sites over the past year. Among the complaints were three purges that blew out in southern Oklahoma over the last three months. All those investigations remain active, according to state records.
Another ongoing complaint against Citation originated about 10 miles east of the Bayou, where a rancher named Mike Faulkner noticed an unusual amount of salt water gurgling to the surface and flowing down a creek on his land in April. Nearby, dozens of Citation wells pump wastewater underground.
In response, Citation once again blamed the pollution on old drilling practices, according to an email from one of the company’s engineers to the Oklahoma Corporation Commission.
Nevertheless, the agency told the company to temporarily shut down some of its nearby injection wells, and, according to Faulkner, the purge on his land dried up for the first time in years.
“That tells me that they know the why and the how of that saltwater purging,” he said in July.
The agency also instructed Citation to install monitoring wells to test for pollution and to build a pit with a rock dam on Faulkner’s land to catch the polluted water, along with a fence to keep the cattle out.
But in the months since, the agency has given Citation multiple extensions on the deadline to build the dam and the fencing. In September, Faulkner learned that the agency granted Citation yet another extension — until December, seven months after his initial pollution report.
As of October, he said, the wells where the state had asked Citation to pause operations are injecting — at reduced pressure.
Faulkner said he is fed up with Citation’s yearslong pattern of degrading his pastures. But he blames state officials for their unwillingness to rein in the company.
“They’re like a spoiled kid,” he said. “They’ve just gotten away with it for a long time.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.title: A Freedom of Information ‘Christmas Present’ Remains Unopened as City Delays Rollout
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.author: Katie Honan
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.text:
The city is dragging its feet on a requirement for all city agencies to upload records requests and data to an online public portal, further delaying transparency from city agencies, good-government advocates said.
The bill, which was passed in the City Council last November, requires every municipal agency to opt into the city’s Open Records portal for data requests.
The updated bill formally requires every agency to participate in the portal and now will include Freedom of Information requests made to the City Council and the five borough presidents’ offices.
The law would make it easier to file data requests and provide more transparency on delays. Agencies would be required to upload responses within a certain time frame, allowing the requestor — oftentimes journalists — 14 days to publish a story without it being shared widely, according to Rachael Fauss, the senior policy advisor at the nonprofit Reinvent Albany.
She and other good-government advocates helped craft the bill and are now concerned because a report on its implementation due in June has still not been released.
“The law would absolutely put us on better footing to actually monitor the agencies and see what they’re actually doing on FOIL,” she said.
The bill, introduced by Manhattan Councilmember Gale Brewer, lapsed into law on Dec. 25, 2025 — “a Christmas present for the advocates who fought for it,” Fauss joked.
“If you get every agency on the open records portal to start proactively releasing records, you can get some better data about what the actual problems are,” she said.
“How do you know what the problems are if nobody’s looking systematically at them at the city level?”
‘Nothing’s Happening’
A spokesperson for the Department of Records and Information Services, Kenneth Cobb, said they planned to release the plan to Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Speaker Julie Menin in mid-November, but did not answer a question about its delay.
Brewer told The City Reporter the Council planned to hold a hearing on the law’s delay in January.
“Nothing’s happening,” she said of the initiatives the bill planned. She said she thought the Mamdani administration “should be better.”
New York City government is notoriously slow around Freedom of Information Law requests, often delaying for years before releasing information.
A 2025 analysis from Reinvent Albany found that the city government receives around 170,000 FOIL requests a year, and 16% were still open a year later. Data from the existing Open Records portal showed that response times were slowing, which they blamed on staffing issues.
Journalists often rely on the Freedom of Information Law to obtain schedules, emails, renderings, and any other data to inform their reporting — but the delays can often render the data useless once it finally arrives.
And it also can keep vital information from the public.
In September 2019, The City Reporter requested data and outside contracts related to a 911 system upgrade from the city’s technology agency.
Since then, the city’s Office of Technology and Innovation has extended the deadline 60 times. The latest projected response date is Dec. 1 of this year.
Noel Hidalgo, the executive director of BetaNYC, an open government advocacy group, said this law would ideally give everyone a better sense of how the city works.
“We’re in a moment in time where government information is one of the few things that you can actually trust,” he said. “FOIL is our last recourse in regard to transparency and operation.”

Vandaag (27/10) zal de Europese Commissie een voorstel doen om het personeelsbestand van Frontex te vergroten én om de operationele bevoegdheid van het grensbewakingsagentschap uit te breiden naar derde landen buiten de Europese Unie. Dat betekent meer bevoegdheden, maar het onduidelijke juridische statuut van Frontex blijft onaangepast. “Zowel Frontex als de lidstaten wijzen de individuele verantwoordelijkheid af.”

Cartooning for Peace is delighted to support the launch of the first edition of the International Biennial of Press Cartooning in Latin America, which will take place at the UNAM’s Tlatelolco University Cultural Centre in Mexico City from 24 October 2026 to 30 January 2027.
For this inaugural edition, the Tlatelolco University Cultural Centre (CCUT), in collaboration with CartónClub, is inviting cartoonists, illustrators, visual artists and graphic designers from around the world to take part in this international event.
The programme includes: an international press cartoon award, a ‘Cartooning for Peace’ exhibition and workshops and talks with António (Portugal), Boligán (Mexico), Darío (Mexico), Dorthe Landschulz (Germany), Nani (Spain-Colombia), Piet (France) and Solís (Mexico)…

https://gothamist.com/news/california-ma.title: California man was shot by a NJ detective in Moonachie, officials say
https://gothamist.com/news/california-ma.author: Kaya Laterman
https://gothamist.com/news/california-ma.text:
Prosecutors investigating a fatal shooting involving a New Jersey state police detective in Moonachie on Wednesday said the civilian who died had approached an undercover officer working in the area before being shot.
The New Jersey attorney general's office on Thursday identified the deceased as Roberto Castro-Quinonez, 30, of Bakersfield, California.
The identity of the officer involved in the fatal shooting has not been released.
According to preliminary information, at approximately 5:15 p.m., New Jersey state police detectives were conducting an investigation on Gotham Parkway, near the intersection with West Commercial Avenue. The detectives, operating in plain-clothes, were in the area as part of a criminal investigation, according to prosecutors.
While in that area, one of the detectives was approached by Castro-Quinonez. An interaction between the two men ensued, and a second detective arrived at the scene to assist, prosecutors said.
Shortly thereafter, one New Jersey state police detective discharged his weapon two times, striking Castro-Quinonez, officials said.
Officers attempted to perform medical aid, but Castro-Quinonez was pronounced deceased at 5:44 p.m., according to prosecutors.
The attorney general is required by law to investigate a person's death that occurs during an encounter with a law enforcement official.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

Marian Goodman Gallery in New York has hired curator Ebony L. Haynes as senior director, global head of curatorial affairs. Haynes, who will join the gallery in late November, is the first person to occupy the newly created role. She arrives from David Zwirner, where she is global head of curatorial projects. In 2020 Haynes was tapped by Zwirner to create and oversee TriBeCa outpost 52 Walker. Run by an all-Black staff, the space launched in 2021, and held seventeen exhibitions before undergoing a name change to David Zwirner Tribeca this past summer. Among the artists given solo shows at 52 Walker during its run were Sara Cwynar, Nicole Eisenman, Nikita Gale, Arthur Jafa, Bob Thompson, and Kandis Williams.
Before joining Zwirner, Haynes, who cocurated the 2024 Triennial at MOCA Toronto, was curator for the inaugural Fine Arts MFA exhibition for first-year students at the Rhode Island School of Design, Providence, and visiting curator and critic at the Yale School of Art in the Painting and Printmaking program. She also runs Black Art Sessions, an online “school” offering free professional practice classes to Black students around the world.
Marian Goodman also announced Rose Lord and Junette Teng as its new co-presidents. The pair will shape the gallery’s strategic direction and oversee its management team, which includes Haynes. Emily-Jane Kirwan, managing partner and head of sales, will leave the gallery to focus on cultural philanthropy after a fifteen-year tenure.
“Ebony is a natural fit for the Gallery,” said Teng in a statement. “She brings a strong curatorial vision, intellectual rigor, and deep engagement with artists, which aligns with our approach. Her appointment also reflects where we want to go next: expanding the ways we support our artists, creating new contexts for their work, and bringing a new perspective to our program.”
Asked by Artnews about her reasons for joining Goodman, Haynes was succinct. “How do I say this?” she said. “It’s Marian Goodman.”

https://gothamist.com/news/lithium-ion-b.title: Lithium-ion battery caused Bronx fire that killed boy, FDNY says
https://gothamist.com/news/lithium-ion-b.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/lithium-ion-b.text:
An e-bike’s lithium-ion battery caused a Bronx apartment fire that killed a boy and critically injured four other people early Wednesday, FDNY officials said.
Firefighters found an e-bike in the kitchen near the entrance of an 11th-floor apartment at the Patterson Houses, a public housing complex in Mott Haven, officials said. The blaze began around 12:50 a.m. and spread quickly throughout the home, according to officials.
“It was placed in a spot in the kitchen that made it impossible for the residents to leave safely,” Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said at a press conference Wednesday. “ We know lithium-ion batteries are everywhere, and we know how valuable they are to people's livelihoods, so we need to remind New Yorkers how to use them safely.”
FDNY officials said firefighters forced the apartment door open, then searched the apartment for victims before working to control the fire. They found one person immediately behind the door, then crawled past the flames to search for and rescue the rest of the occupants, according to officials.
All five people were rushed to a nearby hospital, where a the boy was pronounced dead. Officials have estimated his age at 10 or 11, but the FDNY told Gothamist the boy's exact age has not yet been confirmed.
The four other occupants, including two teenagers, remain in critical condition, officials said.
“I ask New Yorkers to join me in sending our deepest condolences to the family of the child who passed away, and in praying for a full and quick recovery for those who are currently battling to survive,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at the Wednesday press conference.
According to FDNY data, lithium-ion batteries have caused more than 400 fires across the city this year, resulting in 74 injuries and six deaths. That's compared to 292 fires last year, which caused 51 injuries, and just one death.
“Lithium-ion battery fires are extremely dangerous because they spread fast and ferociously,” Bonsignore said. “The battery cells go into thermal runaway, which makes a small fire turn into a very big fire very, very quickly.”
Bonsignore said lithium-ion batteries used to power micromobility devices should be charged and stored outside when possible. She said the devices should never block exits, doors or windows, and the batteries should never be charged when people are sleeping or not in the room. She also said New Yorkers should only buy batteries certified by national safety testing organizations like UL, and advised against using leaking, damaged or smoking batteries.
Lisa Bova-Hyatt, CEO of the New York City Housing Authority, said NYCHA is working to relocate and support the affected families and is assessing needed repairs in the apartment and the building.
NYCHA had previously proposed an e-bike ban at its complexes in 2022, but rescinded the proposal and instead implemented rules for keeping e-bikes in apartments after pushback from tenants and delivery riders. The rules state that residents may only charge one lithium-ion battery or device at a time, and an adult must be present and awake while it’s charging. The device must also be placed more than 5 feet from a heating source and must not block any entryways, according to the rules.
This story has been revised based on updated information from emergency officials.

https://gothamist.com/news/the-nypd-is-c.title: The NYPD is confiscating e-bikes along a clogged East Village street
https://gothamist.com/news/the-nypd-is-c.author: Willow Higgins
https://gothamist.com/news/the-nypd-is-c.text:
A tiff over parked e-bikes is escalating on a busy thoroughfare in the East Village.
An NYPD spokesperson said on Thursday that police confiscated 11 e-bikes parked along East 11th Street and First Avenue this week, where neighboring business owners and residents have been complaining for months about idle delivery bikes clogging sidewalks and curbs, sometimes by the hundreds.
The spokesperson said the e-bikes were removed because they had been parked illegally or out of concern over the bike’s lithium-ion batteries sparking fires. The department had given the owners three weeks’ warning before beginning the enforcement, and the owners will be able to retrieve their property, according to the NYPD.
Members of a newly formed coalition, the East Village Beautification Project, convened a group meeting on the block Thursday afternoon, against a backdrop of dozens of parked e-bikes, and urged the city to intervene further.
“Delivery workers deserve safe places to park and charge their bikes, but not at this location at the expense of everyone else who lives and works here," Christine Renzi, the coalition’s leader, said in a statement.
“If the city, local elected officials, and our local community board will not take this seriously, we will make sure they cannot keep looking the other way," she added.
Renzi said the coalition is advocating for bike parking to be dispersed along other nearby blocks – just as Citi Bike dock stations are distributed to multiple sites – so that the impact isn’t so concentrated.
But other community advocates worried that confiscating e-bikes would hurt immigrant New Yorkers.
“People are going to lose their means of livelihood with no warning and no education,” said Susan Stetzer, the district manager of an East Village community board, said at a meeting on Tuesday ahead of the enforcement.
A spokesperson from Cafewal, a community kitchen and local resource center, said many of the e-bikes are used by immigrants who frequent the site, and that the organization conducts weekly cleanups of the area. He said the drivers need a place to go, and would welcome more formal parking.
Mamadu Djalo, a delivery driver from Guinea-Bissau who spends time on the East Village block, said removing bikes affects drivers and their families.
“They're surviving on this delivery job, so there's nothing else to do,” Djalo said.
Djalo said that he didn’t object to spreading the parking to other areas, but added that the neighborhood is important to the workers, too.
“ We spend time together here,” Djalo said. “We are together like one family.”

https://www.artforum.com/news/ursula-von.title: Ursula von Rydingsvard, Whose Massive Wood Totems Brought Warmth to Minimalism, Dead at 84
https://www.artforum.com/news/ursula-von.author: Polly Watson
https://www.artforum.com/news/ursula-von.text:

Sculptor Ursula von Rydingsvard, known for her craggy, majestic wood forms carved from cedar, died at her home in New York on October 27 of Alzheimer’s disease. She was eighty-four. Over a career spanning five decades, von Rydingsvard transformed humble four-by-four chunks of wood into towering shapes whose puzzling bumps and hollows gave them the aura of ancient living beings. So committed was she to cedar that she eventually developed an allergy to it; she refused to abandon the material, instead working in a full protective suit. For von Rydingsvard, work was necessary “to survive,” she said in a 2019 interview, “because it’s a place to put my pain, my sadness.”
Ursula von Rydingsvard was born Ursula Karoliszyn, the fifth of seven children, in Deentsen, Germany, on July 26, 1942. The daughter of Polish and Ukrainian parents, she spent the early years of her life in displaced persons camps. The experience would profoundly shape her practice. “We stayed in barracks of raw wooden floors, raw wooden walls, and raw wooden ceilings,” she told Art21 in 2007. “Somewhere in my blood, I’m dipping into that source.”
When she was eight, the Karoliszyns immigrated to Plainville, Connecticut, where her father farmed and took on factory work, and her mother worked as a barmaid. At first, young Ursula seemed destined to follow in her mother’s footsteps, taking a job in the same tavern. “I did everything conscientiously,” she told Judith Richards in a 2011 oral-history interview for the Archives of American Art. “And I say that with regret. I wish I could have blown—the grid, the fenced-in psyche. But I am trying to still blow it, through my work.”
Eager to escape small-town life, she attended first the University of New Hampshire and then the University of Miami, studying painting and drawing. In 1969, she moved to California with her husband, Milton von Rydingsvard, who was pursuing a medical residency there. Four years later, he suffered a mental breakdown, and the pair divorced. Von Rydingsvard moved to New York with her young daughter and enrolled in Columbia University, where she earned her MFA. “I just felt like that was a place where my mind would finally have a chance,” she told Richards.
Just before arriving at the school, von Rydingsvard had turned from paper and canvas to sewn forms, having increasingly become interested in sculpture owing to its tactile nature. “You can’t grab a painting,” she told Artsy’s Tess Thackara in 2018. While at Columbia, she experimented with steel, but found the material too cold and unforgiving. Given some four-by-four cedar beams by painter Michael Mulhern, a classmate, she first used them to prop up other materials but soon found herself deeply attracted to the wood. “The cedar is like butter,” she told Even magazine in 2018. “It yields so easily; it doesn’t fight you.”
Using a pencil, von Rydingsvard marked the wooden slabs, then cut them with a handsaw, stacking, gluing, and chiseling them into monumental, glitching forms. The sculptures were frequently stained with graphite or chalk dust, whose force of presence was comparable to that of cliff or cave, capable of stunning the viewer into silence. A 1988 exhibition at New York’s Exit Art proved pivotal, with the Metropolitan Museum of Art purchasing Untitled (Seven Mountains), 1986–88, and the Brooklyn Museum acquiring Umarles (You Went and Died), 1987–88. By 1992, she had been the subject of a ten-year retrospective at Storm King Art Center in New York’s Hudson Valley, and been taken on by Galerie Lelong, which would represent her for the rest of her life.
“Von Rydingsvard uses wood to sensualize the material and to evoke feelings, textures, and things that seem impossibly remote from wood itself,” wrote Zachary Fine in a 2019 issue of Artforum. “By combining and rearranging fixed units of cedar to produce this range of evocations and effects, [she] effectively turns the units into words and wood into language.”
She continued to express herself in that same language throughout the ensuing decades. An emblematic recent work is “All the Children I Never Had,” 2018–23, which suggests a trio of escarpments marching resolutely forward despite some invisible weight dragging them down. Von Rydingsvard ultimately expanded her practice to include materials such as resin and bronze. The latter enduring material appeared in several public commissions, including the nineteen-foot-high Ona, 2013, outside Barclays Center in Brooklyn.
Von Rydingsvard earned numerous accolades over the course of her career, including a lifetime achievement award from the International Sculpture Center as well as a Joan Mitchell Award, an Academy Award from the American Academy of Arts and Letters, and fellowships from the John Simon Guggenheim Foundation and the National Endowment for the Arts. Her work is held in the collections of numerous major institutions, including the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, Kansas City, Missouri; the Art Institute of Chicago; and the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, and the Whitney Museum of American Art, all in New York.
Von Rydingsvard’s second husband, Nobel Prize-winning neuroscientist Paul Greengard, died in 2019; her daughter, Ursula Anne von Rydingsvard, died in 2022. She is survived by two siblings, three grandchildren, and three step-grandchildren.
“I feel completely different in the world where I make my art,” she told the Creative Independent in 2018. “It’s so clear to me that this is what I was born to do.”

https://www.artforum.com/news/ballot-que.text:
Subscribe to

On elections day next week, ballots in Philadelphia will include a question to formalize the office for local arts and culture—Creative Philadelphia—into a permanent part of the city’s government.
The ballot’s Question 2 asks, “Shall the Philadelphia Home Rule Charter be amended to establish and define the functions of Creative Philadelphia, an office headed by the Chief Cultural Officer to promote the City’s arts, culture, and creative economy sector?”
Currently, Creative Philadelphia exists by way of an executive order. According to Broad Street Review, a creative office was established in 1986 under Mayor Wilson Goode, but was subsequently shuttered in 2004 by Mayor John Street. Michael Nutter, his successor, re-established the office, only to have his own successor, Jim Kenney, propose eliminating it in 2020 due to budget constraints. Instead, Kenney reduced its capacity and moved it under the Managing Director’s Office.
In 2024, Mayor Cherelle Parker rebranded the Office of Arts, Culture, and the Creative Economy as Creative Philadelphia, and turned its directorship into a cabinet position with a seat at the mayor’s table. Currently, that position is held by Valerie Gay.
Gay has been instrumental in getting Question 2 on the ballot. “It was a moral obligation for us to try to become permanent instead of starting over from scratch with every mayor,” she told Broad Street Review.
The measure, proposed by Councilmember Isaiah Thomas, would also allow the office to grow its staff from ten to fifteen. The Committee of Seventy, a nonpartisan civic leadership organization based in Philadelphia, reports that the city’s art community has a large economic impact but that public support for the arts is low. The city recently slashed its funding for the Philadelphia Cultural Fund from $5 million annually to $3.5 million.
“We’re part of civic infrastructure, just like other things,” Gay said. Without public funding, “only the folks who are able to pay should have access to arts and culture … If only the rich people can pay for art, what kind of society would we be?”
