https://citylimits.org/opinion-laying-th.title: Opinion: Laying the Foundation for NYC’s Small Business Renaissance
https://citylimits.org/opinion-laying-th.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/opinion-laying-th.text:
Share This Article
“If we want a small business renaissance, we have to stop treating empty storefronts as acceptable collateral damage of financial regulatory happenstance and start seeing them for what they are: a policy choice.”
Walk down certain blocks in Lower Manhattan or Western Queens and you can count every third gate pulled down where a restaurant or bodega used to be, with its “For Rent” sign often weathered from years of exposure to the elements.
According to the city comptroller’s office, roughly 15,700 storefronts sit vacant across the five boroughs—about 11 percent of all commercial spaces—with some corridors pushing 20 percent vacancy or more. These patches don’t just look bad. They drain the life out of neighborhoods that would otherwise feel very much alive.
We’ve gotten used to explaining this away as fallout from the pandemic or blaming it on “greedy landlords” waiting for a corporate tenant. The whole story is more nuanced. New York has quietly and gradually built a system in which keeping a storefront empty can make more sense on the landlord’s spreadsheet than renting it to a local business. That is not a moral failing of individual owners so much as a policy failure—and it’s one we can fix, starting with the NYC Small Business Rent Stabilization Act, but more on that later.
First, it is important to dispel a common myth about the cause behind this phenomenon. There is no special tax deduction for keeping a storefront vacant. Owners can deduct mortgage interest, property taxes, and maintenance whether a space is filled or not, but they can’t write off rent they never collected. When a gate is down, the owner is still paying taxes, insurance, and debt service every month. A vacant storefront really does bleed money.
So why would anyone choose years of bleeding over a lower, realistic rent? Because commercial real estate in New York is financed and valued almost entirely on stabilized income potential and assessed rent levels, not on whether a local business is open on the corner. A closer look at what
actually causes this begins with a journey into the seemingly grey world of appraisers and lenders. It is in the market dynamics and regulatory frameworks that govern nearly all aspects of these few basic cogs in the economic engine where the true root cause of these undesirable external realities on the street are found.
Appraisers and lenders look at net operating income, capitalization rates, and the rent rolls, and they reward high rents from “credit‑worthy” (corporate) tenants with higher valuations and better loan terms. In hot corridors that saw a heated rent bubble before the pandemic, owners and their bankers have baked in very ambitious future rent assumptions. If those assumptions crumble, so do the numbers underpinning the mortgage.
In many cases this not only relates to the mortgage used to finance the purchase of the property itself, but often the buildings (and their typically inflated appraised income potential) are used as collateral to finance other properties, development loans or nearly any other class of financeable asset.
These chains of over-valuations that compound over time are the stuff market bubbles are made of, and the commercial real-estate market is sitting firmly atop exactly such a bubble. Seeing this from the perspective of landlords, banks and the chain of interests bound into these assets, one of the chief arguments for starting to pull the policy levers that are effectively the only cooling rods available in this kind of reactor is to govern and legislate towards an off-ramp for market
overheating, a “soft landing” to prevent a cataclysmic crash in this sector of the economy.
What this broadly translates to is: commercial rents must come gradually down. Not just for the vibrancy of our great cities to return. Not just for the dreams of ordinary people whose ingenuity, drive and natural desire is to build businesses that fill real needs and employ people meaningfully and locally. Not just for opportunity and hard earned prosperity to be within reach for people of all ethnicities and class backgrounds but also, not least, for the giant commercial real estate sector to steer clear of igniting what could be an economy-wide free-fall “correction” in the not-so-distant future.
Recent research on Manhattan storefronts shows how the prevailing logic currently dictating the business practices of lenders and appraisers creates what economists call “option value.” Landlords with long fixed leases and costly eviction rules have a strong incentive to wait for a tenant who can pay at or near the peak rent for that space, because locking in a low rent today means under‑earning for 10 years.
In New York, that incentive is sometimes hardened into contract. Some commercial mortgages now include rent floors—covenants that effectively forbid signing leases below a specified rent per square foot. When the real local market falls beneath those floors, the choice isn’t between “some rent” and “no rent.” It’s between breaching the loan by accepting reality, or enduring vacancy until someone appears who can satisfy the covenant.
From the sidewalk, that looks like stubborn greed. From the bank’s point of view, it looks like discipline. Either way, the result is the same: ghost corridors in a city that prides itself on vibrancy and street life.
The costs of this system fall hardest on small, independent businesses. The comptroller’s analysis finds that restaurants and cafés make up the single largest share of shuttered storefronts citywide. In fast‑gentrifying neighborhoods, those that survive one lease term often face a brutal reset at the end of it, as landlords try to line up their rent rolls with boom-time expectations.
In all this it is important to remember what a waste of resources the choking of a neighborhood business really is. Small businesses are not just realizations of dreams but are often built on the life savings of entire families. They embody countless years of partly unpaid work that goes into building a customer base of regulars, designing and equipping the space to fulfil its potential and so much more. Real sacrifice is made in the building of these cornerstones of our lives and real
value is created within them.
The bitter irony being that the restaurants, the bars, the cultural spaces that are the most frequent victims of this are in fact among the main drivers of the kind of neighborhood improvement that, once realtors pick up the scent, translates to gentrification and displacement of long-time residents. This only happens because perceived vibrancy in many parts of the city is scarce and concentrated in some pockets in the cityscape.
Were rents more attuned to real and actual income potentials from real and actual local businesses, the “hype” of these neighborhoods would not have to turn so destructive and exclusive with inevitable rent hikes. Were “survival rates” permitted by policy changes to rise also outside such hot-spots, these extreme zones for real-estate speculation would have much less fuel for fire.
At one Ridgewood location, my partners and I watched a promising lease negotiation collapse over this very logic. The landlord insisted on a 10‑year term with no meaningful renewal protections, in a neighborhood that is visibly transforming block by block. Friends and people we knew who had opened businesses in similar areas had in some cases seen their rents triple at renewal after a decade of building out spaces, cultivating regulars, programming culture and maintaining a staff.
Signing that kind of lease isn’t just a business risk; it’s a time‑bomb set to detonate precisely when your investment finally matures. We walked away and chose a smaller, less favorably located space whose owner would accept options to extend another five to 10 years on the same basic terms.
That kind of predictability should not depend on individual landlords. It should be the baseline expectation for doing business in New York.
The New York City Small Business Rent Stabilization Act would be a first attempt to make it so. The bill would create a Commercial Rent Guidelines Board and institute a rent‑stabilization system for non‑chain tenants, capping how fast commercial rents can rise and establishing clear renewal options for eligible small businesses. It is not a blanket freeze; it is a rules‑of‑the‑road framework aimed at keeping independently owned storefronts from being priced off their blocks every lease cycle.
Combined with a well‑designed vacancy tax, an outline emerges of how we can implement policy change that will not only revitalize our own city but reverberate around the country. A modest tax on long‑term vacant commercial space—calibrated to kick in only after a meaningful grace period—would make it more costly to warehouse storefronts as financial options. It would also generate revenue. The point is not to punish owners for every short‑term vacancy, but to make the social cost of years‑long emptiness show up in the same spreadsheets where banks and landlords currently see only potential upside.
Critics will warn that commercial rent stabilization and vacancy taxes will “hurt business” by lowering property values. But this exposes the confusion at the heart of our so‑called
pro‑business politics. For decades, when politicians of both parties have said they are “pro‑business,” they have usually meant they are pro‑asset‑holder: pro‑landlord, pro‑bank, pro‑large corporation whose primary product is a stream of passive income. The neighborhood bar that employs 10 people, the repair shop that keeps your speakers alive, the bookstore that gives your block a reason to exist after 6 p.m.—these have been afterthoughts at best.
Meanwhile, our culture has learned to worship passive income as an ideal. Scroll through Instagram or TikTok and you’ll find no shortage of being told that success is to assemble enough “revenue streams” to stop working altogether. The dream is no longer to build a business locally that answers a need in your community; it is to extract value by speculative means while someone else does the labor. In that value system, an empty storefront is not a civic failure—it’s a temporarily underperforming asset in a portfolio.
A city that takes itself seriously cannot be neutral between those two visions of prosperity.
Choosing active over passive income generators means designing policy to favor enterprises that hire people, provide services, and knit neighborhoods together, even if that means some loss of short‑term paper wealth for those who own the underlying real estate. It means accepting that a building’s “value” is not just its potential rent cash flow, but the positive externalities that come from having a bakery, a venue, or a childcare center downstairs instead of another vacant storefront.
The New York City Small Business Rent Stabilization Act and a serious vacancy‑penalty regime will not, overnight, reverse every ghost corridor or guarantee every corner store’s success. But they are a test of whether our politics is ready to be honestly pro‑business in the only sense that should matter for a city like New York: pro-family run business, pro-mom and pop shops, pro-small businesses created by craftspeople and artists, immigrants or anyone with a genuine, invested connection to their own community.
If we want a small business renaissance, we have to stop treating empty storefronts as acceptable collateral damage of financial regulatory happenstance and start seeing them for what they are: a policy choice.
Emil Bovbjerg is a leader at Small Business United, the owner of Dada bar in Ridgewood, a recording musician and long-time New York City resident.

https://hyperallergic.com/documenta-16-n.title: Documenta 16 Names Four New Curatorial Team Members
https://hyperallergic.com/documenta-16-n.author: Valentina Di Liscia
https://hyperallergic.com/documenta-16-n.text:
Documenta 16 Names Four New Curatorial Team Members
The embattled German exhibition's latest appointments, artist Catherine Opie wins a Yale University award, and Dallas Art Fair partners with … a university?
Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.
Documenta Appoints New Curatorial Team Members
Less than eight months away from the 16th edition of Documenta, the German contemporary arts festival has appointed four new curatorial team members: artist and musician Raven Chacon will serve as curator-at-Large, and Osei Bonsu, Timea Junghaus, and Noam Segal will be curatorial advisors.
The upcoming iteration, opening on June 12 in Kassel, promises to offer a space for “study, experimentation, and awakening, where artists hold right to expression alongside their artistic creation.” But artists and free speech advocates have argued that this stated mission jars with Documenta’s adoption of a controversial definition of antisemitism that includes criticism of Israel, raising serious questions about creative freedom. In a recent interview with the German newspaper Die Zeit, Artistic Director Naomi Beckwith revealed that some artists have already declined to participate in Documenta 16 over Germany's support of Israel's genocide in Gaza.
Chacon, Bonsu, Junghaus, and Segal will join Beckwith and the core curatorial team for the 16th edition — Carla Acevedo-Yates, Romi Crawford, Mayra A. Rodríguez Castro, and Xiaoyu Weng — to help shape the program's artistic vision.

https://gothamist.com/news/15-year-old-b.title: 15-year-old Bronx boy fatally shot while walking to school, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/15-year-old-b.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/15-year-old-b.text:
A 15-year-old boy was shot and killed on his way to school in the Bronx on Thursday morning, police said.
The shooting happened around 9:30 a.m. near East 171st Street and Crotona Place, near Crotona Park, according to an NYPD spokesperson.
Officers who responded found the boy shot once in the abdomen and drove him in their patrol car to St. Barnabas Hospital, where he was pronounced dead, police said.
Police later identified the boy as Javits Frimpong.
Authorities did not immediately describe any suspects, or say how many there were. Police have not said what led to the shooting.
According to the boy’s father, Thomas Frimpong, Javits was on his way to school at DreamYard Preparatory School.
Frimpong, 60, said the school called him Thursday morning to say Javits was not at school. Soon after, he said, the principal called to tell him his son had been shot.
“It’s not easy for me,” he said. “I’m here with him alone.”
Frimpong said he moved to New York from Ghana in 2000, while his son followed him here last year to live with him.
Whenever Frimpong came home, he said, Javits would come downstairs to open the door for him.
He described his son as a reserved boy who came home from school and stayed inside playing games on his phone.
"My son is always quiet, always," he said.
A few days before the shooting, two students fought with Javits at school and both were suspended, Frimpong said. He said the school told him his son was not to blame.
"I thought that was all," he said.
Frimpong said he called Javits' mother in Ghana to tell her what had happened. She and other relatives were "crying, crying, crying," he said.
Frimpong said police had not told him whether they had any suspects.
Relatives are on their way, he said, and the family will decide what comes next.
Neighbor Sherric Philips, 39, said she heard two shots in the morning.
“It was a pow pow,” she said. “It woke me up.”
The killing comes as shootings and murders are down this year in the 42nd Precinct, which covers the area. There have been 17 shootings in the precinct so far this year, compared with 27 last year at this time, according to NYPD data.
This is a developing story and has been updated with new information.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/10/29/m.title: Mayor Mamdani: Trash Containerization Protects Sanitation Workers
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/10/29/m.author: Kevin Duggan
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/10/29/m.text:
Mayor Mamdani sold the new containerized garbage collection as a godsend for Sanitation worker safety. Photo: Michael Appleton/Mayoral Photography Office
The city’s effort to move trash from bags on the sidewalk into bins on the street will make Sanitation jobs less physically taxing and less exposed to reckless driving, Mayor Mamdani and a union leader said on Thursday.
DSNY is expanding its “Empire Bins” waste collection program, which relies on side-loading collection trucks to lift and empty curbside containers. The trucks help mitigate the risks of a job that is among the most dangerous in the country.
“If we continue down this path of using these black trash bags, what we will see are continuations of injuries to workers who are doing their best to make the best city in the world the cleanest city in the world,” Mamdani said at a press conference in Brooklyn Heights. “I think we owe it to them to use every strategy we have to make their job a little safer and a little easier.”
Hizzoner and Sanitation Department officials installed the first residential Empire Bin in Brooklyn on a quiet block of the tony enclave on Thursday, after testing out the new initiative outside schools in the area’s Community District 2 over the last year.
Sanitation workers are exposed to a plethora of dangers on the job, from sharp objects in bags to drivers crashing into them as they haul piles of them across the street. Refuse and recyclable material collectors rank fifth for highest fatal work injuries, according the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The new mechanized side-loading trucks mitigate a lot of these issues, according to the head of the union representing Sanmen.
“They’re not in the back of the trucks where it could be hazardous, getting hit by cars from operating a conventional truck… and these mechanical arms, it’s much easier on their backs and shoulders, and it’s also safer,” Teamsters Local 831 President Dennis Schock said at the mayor’s press conference. “You know what? This is something that should be done and should happen all over the city.”
Crashes and serious injuries dropped 15 percent and 52 percent respectively after DSNY deployed the bins uptown, Streetsblog previously reported.
Containerized waste collection is commonplace in cities across the globe, from Buenos Aires to Barcelona, but the City that Never Sleeps has long lagged behind its peers.
Former Mayor Eric Adams set out to change that with the containerization efforts in the name of his obsession to curb the city’s rat population, and Mamdani put more city funding behind it after taking office this year.
“It is time that New York City follows the best practices of leading cities across the world,” Mamdani said. “For too long, we have allowed an exceptionalism in our politics to justify mediocrity that really isn’t acceptable.”
DSNY’s Empire Bin program is mandatory for residential buildings with 31 or more units, but optional for those with 10-30 apartments. The latter can also opt for wheelie bins that go on the sidewalk, which are already required for all smaller housing stock with up to nine units. DSNY plans to allow smaller building to share Empire Bins in the future.
The bins have been one of the few bright spots of the otherwise car-focused Adams administration. They reduced the amount of stinky garbage on the sidewalk and also cleared up space on the foot paths. All these benefits came at the low low cost of repurposing a mere 5 percent of the city’s three million — largely free — parking spaces, or about 150,000 spots, DSNY has estimated.
The agency plans to roll out 700 bins at residences by the end of the fall across the Brooklyn district, which in addition to the Heights also includes Downtown Brooklyn, DUMBO, Fulton Ferry, Vinegar Hill, Boerum Hill, Fort Greene and Clinton Hill.
Mamdani committed to expanding the program citywide by the end of 2031, two years after the end of his first term.
Next up in 2027 are Bronx Community Districts 2 around Hunts Point and 5 in Fordham Heights, Queens Community District 2 in Sunnyside, Manhattan Community District 2 in Greenwich Village, Brooklyn Community District 8 in Crown Heights, and Staten Island Community District 1 on the North Shore.
Kevin Duggan joined Streetsblog in October, 2022, after covering transportation for amNY. Duggan has been reporting on New York since 2018, starting at Vince DiMiceli’s Brooklyn Paper, where he covered southern Brooklyn neighborhoods and, later, Brownstone Brooklyn. He is on Bluesky at @kevinduggan.bsky.social and his email address is kevin@streetsblog.org.

https://hyperallergic.com/how-edouard-ma.title: How Édouard Manet's Black Cat Became a Symbol of Modernity
https://hyperallergic.com/how-edouard-ma.author: Rebecca Schiffman
https://hyperallergic.com/how-edouard-ma.text:
How Édouard Manet's Black Cat Became a Symbol of Modernity
Long associated with witchcraft and bad luck, the black feline became an emblem of artistic rebellion and urban life in 19th-century Paris.
Every Halloween, black cats return as emblems of witchcraft, bad luck, and the supernatural. Their sinister reputations stretch back centuries: starting in the Middle Ages, people associated cats with heresy and sexual transgression, and their perceived affinity with witches intensified during the trials of Elizabeth Francis and Agnes Waterhouse and their cat Sathan between 1565-1579.
But after the Enlightenment, 19th-century French artists and writers began to reclaim the mysterious and devilish qualities foisted onto felines as desirable. Alongside a new bourgeois pet-keeping culture, where caring for animals became associated with progress and enlightenment, bohemian artists and intellectuals began incorporating black cats into their work. The black cat became a symbol of independence and nonconformity, reflecting changing attitudes toward individualism and self-expression amid industrialization and urbanization. French writer and diplomat François-René de Chateaubriand described the cat’s modern independence favorably, stating, “What I like about the cat is his character, independent and almost heartlessness […] The cat lives alone, he has no need of society.” These inherited qualities of eroticism and defiance also became synonymous with the emerging language of modern art.
No painting or artist makes this transformation more apparent than Édouard Manet’s “Olympia” (1863). Historians like T.J. Clark have long hailed it as a “founding monument of modern art,” updating Titian’s “Venus of Urbino” (1534) with a stark depiction of a contemporary prostitute, her Black maid, and a black cat. The work provoked outrage at the Paris Salon in 1865: its subject matter, combined with flattened forms, bold color contrasts, and use of black, clearly rejected academic conventions. Critics latched onto the wiry black cat, whose arched back and luminous eyes seemed to embody the painting’s perceived vulgarity by showing what Olympia’s hand covered.

https://hyperallergic.com/this-years-gay.title: This Year's Gay Halloween Celebrates Women's Rights and Wrongs
https://hyperallergic.com/this-years-gay.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/this-years-gay.text:
This Year's Gay Halloween Celebrates Women's Rights and Wrongs
From the Kelly Clarkson's mechanical bird fiasco to Carrie Bradshaw's Dior newsprint dress, Gay Halloween speaks to the staying power of women's iconic media moments.
With everything that's happened in the 1,000+ lifetimes jammed into 2026, I think we've all been waiting for Gay Halloween to rehash the year in popular culture. A recently named phenomenon for the chronically online, Gay Halloween is best described as the costume-based valorization of specific media moments, however iconic, niche, or overlooked they may be.
Against the grain of sexy cat costumes and run-of-the-mill superheroes, those blessed with ✨ the vision ✨ devote their resources and talents to fashioning a high-commitment outfit about some bullshit like the hyperpigmentation meme or the disco testicles stage prop from Kacey Musgraves's concert tour.
This year, I've noticed that a majority of Gay Halloween costumes pay homage to the real and fictional women carrying pop culture on their backs. That's not to say that there haven't been hat tips to the cyclosporiasis outbreak from Taylor Farms's lettuce, the hidden death rumors that emerged from Mitch McConnell's multi-week disappearance, or other 2026 happenings that were so absurd they became memes.
I'm just saying that for the most part, this year's Gay Halloween appears to be heavily influenced by the staying power of iconic women and their enduring impact across fashion history, viral interview clips, cringeworthy plot points, salacious scandals, and diva-defined media personas. And it gets really specific, too.

https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorkers-e.title: New Yorkers enrolled in SNAP will get more money for fresh produce next year
https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorkers-e.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorkers-e.text:
New Yorkers enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program will receive more money to use at farmers markets and farm stands next year, City Hall announced Thursday.
The changes are coming to the city’s Health Bucks program, one of several initiatives that lower the cost of healthy foods for low-income residents who often struggle to buy fresh fruits and vegetables.
SNAP recipients are already able to receive an additional $2 for every $2 spent purchasing certain fresh produce at more than 100 local greenmarkets across the five boroughs, but the city sets a daily cap of $10.
Starting in January, the cap will increase to $14.
The cost of increasing the daily cap in this program, which is partially funded by the city, is expected to reach $2.3 million in 2027, officials said.
It’s a change that Mayor Zohran Mamdani said “puts fresh produce within reach and makes groceries more affordable” for low-income residents.
“Every day, New Yorkers walk into a store hoping prices haven’t gone up again,” the mayor said in a statement on Thursday. “As food insecurity rises, far too many families are forced to skip the fruits and vegetables.”
Those who aren’t on SNAP can still receive Health Bucks from nonprofits and faith-based organizations that distribute the $2 coupons.
A full list of farmers markets and farmstands that accept Health Bucks can be found on the city’s website.

https://gothamist.com/news/you-cant-even.title: 'You can't even look out the window': Asbestos dust coats Brooklyn NYCHA building walls
https://gothamist.com/news/you-cant-even.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/you-cant-even.text:
Some residents of Brooklyn's Marcy Houses are balancing their personal health against the difficulties of relocating after a steam leak deposited asbestos-laden residue on the exterior walls of two adjoining buildings there, and covered many of their windows with the white dust.
Workers from the New York City Housing Authority and the city Department of Environmental Protection were at 502 and 504 Marcy Ave. — two of the 27 buildings in the sprawling Bedford-Stuyvesant complex — responding to the incident on Thursday. NYCHA officials said the steam came from an exhaust vent for an underground line that connects with mobile boilers. Part of the apparatus sticks up from the ground and is surrounded by a wooden safety barrier, which residents have been concerned about for some time.
Some told Gothamist they had seen the steam billowing up for weeks or longer, and that it had been leaving a white powder on their windows.
“The steam kept coming up, real white steam. It would cover the windows. We can't look out our kitchen window or the room window facing that way,” said Digna Torres, 75, whose apartment was along the affected exterior wall. “And all of a sudden, the windows got white. I mean white white. You can't even look out the window.”
NYCHA officials said in a statement the residue tested positive for asbestos, and that residents of 23 affected apartments — those along the exterior walls of the buildings — had been offered temporary relocations. Four have relocated, officials said.
Torres said she’s been stressed since getting the notice on Wednesday, but decided against leaving her apartment because she didn’t want to transport her three parakeets. On Thursday morning, she said she was waiting for workers to clean her windows.
“I'm worried,” she said. “My sons are like, ‘Mom, that's asbestos. That's no good. You could get cancer.’ And I said, "Oh, my God." Yeah, it’s bad. … Right now I just wanna know when they're coming so I could do what I have to do.”
Councilmember Chi Ossé said earlier this week that nine buildings were without heat due to the same issue. By Wednesday, NYCHA confirmed it had restored heat to 234 apartments across four of the buildings, and was working to install mobile boilers for the remaining five buildings.
Estalin De Leon, 45, also lives in the buildings but in an apartment facing the opposite direction, so her apartment is not one of those considered directly affected. She said the notices regarding the asbestos still left her nervous about the building’s safety.
“Of course — I was really scared,” she said in Spanish. “I sent my daughter to stay with my sister, and I stayed behind in case they needed to come and check the apartment, but they didn’t end up checking my apartment.”
During an appearance on the WNYC show “Who’s Running This Place” on Thursday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he didn’t have updates on the situation, but said serving NYCHA residents' needs is a top priority for his administration.
“ We are looking to address not only this specific issue in ensuring that we're taking care of the health and safety of those NYCHA residents, but also delivering more in investment and attention to NYCHA than we've seen in recent decades because these are working-class New Yorkers who are being pushed out of New York through a lack of habitable conditions," he said.

The Met and Swiss watchmaker Vacheron Constantin have unveiled three original works created during the Metropolitan Museum of Art and Vacheron Constantin Artisan Residency. The brand new program took place over the course of eighteen months, and emphasized preserving and reinterpreting traditional craft techniques. The three works of art produced in the residency are Vessel by Aspen Golann, Shaping Time by Ibrahim Said, and Ruined Splendour – BRONZE DIADEM by Joy Harvey. This is one of several collaborations between the Met and Vacheron Constantin.
The residency began in May 2025. In a press release, the watchmaker shared the residency is built on three key pillars: encouraging “the development of the widest range of artistic and craft skills so that they may evolve and thrive,” challenging and expanding “the norms of traditional craftsmanship by directing it towards new forms of expression,” and inspiring “future generations through the exchange of ideas and transmission of knowledge”
The three artists used the Met’s vast collection as a source of inspiration for their new works. Golan looked into the museum’s collection of American wooden furniture from the 17th to 19th centuries; Said studied an ancient Egyptian Lentoid bottle and a thousand year old Islamic water filter; while Harvey found inspiration in ancient jewelry from Greece, India and China.
“This artisan residency program is a collaborative initiative that embodies our mutual commitment to supporting artistic innovation and cultural dialogue,” said Max Hollein, The Met’s Marina Kellen French Director and Chief Executive Officer, in a statement. “It is a thrill to see how the three artisans, inspired by their engagement with The Met collection and Vacheron Constantin, have created works that breathe new life into traditional techniques, powerfully connecting the past and present.”

https://hellgatenyc.com/hot-97-laid-off-.title: Hot 97 Is Lurching Into Oblivion, Say Laid-Off Workers
https://hellgatenyc.com/hot-97-laid-off-.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/hot-97-laid-off-.text:
Hello, Adlan Jackson speaking, back from vacation. Welcome back to Cultural Capital, Hell Gate's biweekly arts and culture newsletter, in which we deliver a critical eye on the city scene. Subscribe to it here. A little further down, we’ll give you nightlife recommendations, capsule reviews, and a recap of what’s come across New York City's last real local culture desk. But first, if you've been wondering what's going on at Hot 97, I have too—for almost a year now. In that time, I've spoken to some former workers there to get some answers.
Hot 97 is so woven into the fabric of New York City culture that it's hard to have a conversation about it without hearing the words "iconic," "legendary," and even "dream job." You probably don't even have to stay in New York to find somebody who speaks of the nation's premiere terrestrial hip-hop radio station with reverence—just find a hip-hop fan born in the last three to four generations since hip-hop became America's pop music. Hot 97's reputation as an artist-breaking home base for three decades is entwined with the genre's dominance.
Bryson "Boom" Paul, a news writer from California, was one of these admirers, so when he got a job in 2024 as a contributing journalist for Hot 97's website, he thought it was "a monumental moment for my career, pretty much, being that it was a place that's like the Mecca of hip hop," he told Hell Gate. "Going into it, I felt like it was a milestone, for real. Everybody knew about Hot 97, worldwide. It's what you grew up on: seeing it on TV and hearing about it online."
As of this month, however, the dream has faded. Paul was laid off from his freelance gig as a content writer for Hot 97's website, amid a chaotic upheaval that has reportedly included furloughs, and, former Hot 97 workers told Hell Gate, missed paychecks and firings.
Even so, former employees still speak about Hot 97 with reverence—you can practically hear them get that glassy look in their eyes, even over the phone. Jason Peters, formerly head of podcasts for Hot 97, called the former on-air staff "legends," and said "we all had real respect for the brand." The Kid Mero, the Bronx-born comedian who was hired to host station's daily morning show in January, told the New York Times it's "the Google of hip-hop radio stations."
But Peters described the mood among Hot 97 workers in the past few years as "grinning and bearing and hating your bosses, and hating your situation."

https://gothamist.com/news/trash-contain.title: Trash containers take over Brooklyn parking spaces as NYC gets garbage bags off sidewalks
https://gothamist.com/news/trash-contain.author: Liam Quigley
https://gothamist.com/news/trash-contain.text:
Trash bag piles will soon be eradicated from a swath of Brooklyn as the city sanitation department installs hundreds of trash containers in parking spaces in some of the borough’s densest areas.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Sanitation Commissioner Gregory Anderson on Thursday announced that crews began installing more than 700 “Empire Bins” on streets across Downtown Brooklyn, Boerum Hill, Dumbo, Clinton Hill and the Navy Yard. The bins will be placed in front of buildings with more than 30 units, and officials said the rollout would be completed by the end of the fall.
Mamdani and Anderson installed the first of the bins during a news conference in Brooklyn Heights. The bins will be serviced by one of the city’s newly purchased garbage trucks, which lift and empty the trash containers.
“Every New Yorker deserves clean streets and sidewalks,” Mamdani said. “For too long, New Yorkers have had to walk past mountains of trash bags piled high on the curb that offer feasts for rats and stink up our streets. We’re changing that.”
The bins could replace around 768 of the area’s 23,795 on-street parking spaces, according to an analysis published by the sanitation department. More than 31% of households in the area where the bins are coming own at least one vehicle, according to city data.
The city already requires all buildings with nine or fewer units to use a smaller official NYC Bin to wheel out their trash to the curb. Buildings with 10 to 30 units can opt into the Empire Bin program.
By the end of this year’s rollout, trash bag piles will no longer be permitted across this swath of Brooklyn, which is home to 138,000 people. Recycling bags are still allowed to be put out on the curb.
Rat sightings in Harlem dropped after the bins were installed through a pilot program in the neighborhood, and officials say they'll drop across the five boroughs if the city's waste is fully containerized.
Previous Mayor Eric Adams introduced the bins to Brooklyn last September by ordering them to be installed outside school buildings. The new rollout marks the first time the street bins will be used for residential buildings in the borough, as well as the first time the containers have been deployed in such a dense area of the city.
“I cannot recall a time when New Yorkers have not had to dodge mountains of trash bags and rats on their own sidewalks — but now, I can proudly say that those days are numbered,” said City Councilmember Crystal Hudson, who pushed legislation that mandated the sanitation department continue the rollout after Adams’ departure.
Some neighborhoods could see 10% of their available parking spots swallowed up by the trash bins.
The city plans to continue the rollout next year by installing the bins in Hunts Point and University Heights in the Bronx. Empire Bins are also slated next year for Sunnyside in Queens, Manhattan's West Village, Prospect Heights in Brooklyn, and Staten Island's North Shore.
Clarence Gilliam, who was parking his car near the Brooklyn Navy Yard on Thursday, said he has no plans to give up driving even if the bins make it harder for him to find a parking spot.
“If it gets rid of the rats, it's a good thing, but make it easier for people to park," he said.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.title: Pressure Mounts on Mamdani Administration To Address Growing Number of Small Schools
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.author: Michael Elsen-Rooney, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. This is part two of a three-part series. Here’s the first story. And sign up for Chalkbeat New York’s free email newsletter to be the first to know when the next story is published.
As a parent leader for more than a decade, Johanna Bjorken has heard plenty of stories about New York City schools struggling with low enrollment.
But Chalkbeat’s investigation last month into the decline of Murry Bergtraum High School for Business Careers — the city’s smallest traditional high school with roughly 90 students — struck a nerve.
Bjorken’s son goes to school just two floors above Murry Bergtraum in a shared building in Lower Manhattan where the students play on joint sports teams. Yet the schools feel worlds apart. While Bjorken’s son takes Advanced Placement Calculus, students at Murry Bergtraum last year had only one math teacher and two math courses, Algebra I and II. Despite having a per-student budget nearly twice the city average, Murry Bergtraum’s limited academic offerings force some students to attend night school to graduate.
“I was shocked to hear that students, some of whom may very well play volleyball or soccer with my child, have to go to night school for basic graduation requirements, and moreover, that the school’s situation has been known for many years with no action,” Bjorken wrote in a September letter to city officials.
Like school districts across the country, New York City is struggling with a small schools crisis after years of enrollment declines. What makes the city’s situation unique, however, is how many of its small high schools share buildings with each other: 72 of the city’s high schools with fewer than 250 students are on shared campuses, a Chalkbeat analysis found.
Ten months into his tenure, pressure is mounting on New York City Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels to address the increasing number of small schools, which cluster the most vulnerable students in schools with the fewest academic opportunities. School leaders and experts say that long term, the city will need to close and merge underenrolled schools — a process that can be slow and politically unpopular. But many principals feel they can’t afford to wait for that process to play out and feel a sense of urgency to ensure their current students have access to high-quality programs and advanced courses. Now, a growing chorus is urging Samuels to help small schools on shared campuses pool their resources.
“On shared campuses like ours the system accidentally pits us against each other — right when we need to share resources the most,” said Amy Piller, the principal of Urban Assembly Maker Academy, the school Bjorken’s son attends on the Murry Bergtraum campus.
Samuels indicated at a town hall last week that he’s not crafting a citywide plan and instead is asking five working groups to devise blueprints for underenrolled schools in their districts. None of those working groups includes high schools, but Samuels told parent leaders this week that the Education Department is looking at creating “campus working groups” for high schools. City officials have not shared a timeline for this work. An Education Department spokesperson did not respond to questions about how, or whether, the city is helping schools in the same building share resources.
In the meantime, some principals on shared campuses have pooled course offerings, while others have not — but are looking for guidance and support from the Education Department as they’ve seen their rosters shrink.
“They kind of leave principals up to their own devices,” said Mike Sill, the secretary of the United Federation of Teachers.
Inside the Push To Reimagine NYC’s Shared High Schools
About two decades ago, the Bloomberg administration made a big bet that small schools would better serve vulnerable students by providing them with more individual attention and ensuring they didn’t slip through the cracks. The city shuttered dozens of troubled large high schools and opened scores of small new ones in their buildings.
Small schools boosted graduation rates and college enrollment, but they couldn’t provide the same variety of extracurricular or academic options as larger schools.
As enrollment declined, some schools banded together in an attempt to provide students with more opportunities. At the Theodore Roosevelt campus in The Bronx, the principals of its six co-located schools decided a decade ago to open advanced courses like calculus and statistics to the entire campus since none of the schools had enough students to fill the courses on their own.
“It’s challenging with scheduling,” said Michael Barakat, the principal of Bronx High School for Law and Community Service. “But what’s the alternative? Kids don’t have calculus? That’s crazy.”
At the Lehman High School campus in The Bronx, the principals of six small high schools in a sprawling building agreed in 2016 to align their bell schedules so they could open courses to everyone on the campus.
“We sat down and figured it out,” recalled John Powers, the former principal of Lehman High School, who retired in 2023. “It was something we all felt compelled to do.”
Some education leaders said the city can be more ambitious in helping small schools pool resources than just sharing courses.
With nearly half the city’s high school buildings sitting “underutilized,” it’s worth trying to figure out how to use the empty space for new programs or academies to benefit all the students in their building, said Kristin Kearns Jordan, the former CEO of Urban Assembly, a nonprofit that helps run roughly two dozen small New York City public high schools.
The city recently built STEAM centers in Brooklyn and The Bronx where nearby high schools can send students to get hands-on experiences in math and science. Those centers offer a model of what the city could build on shared campuses.
“The possibilities are endless,” Kearns Jordan said.
Several of the schools on the Murry Bergtraum campus are already thinking about those possibilities. In a letter to families last month, Piller, the Maker Academy principal, said her school is a finalist for a grant to transform an unused locker room on the campus’s top floor into a shared academic space for all of the schools on the campus.
“As enrollment patterns change across New York City, large shared campuses like ours have an opportunity to rethink what sharing a building can mean,” she wrote. Chalkbeat’s story on Murry Bergtram “names a problem. I want us to be part of designing what comes next.”
Schedule Clashes and Fragmented Leadership Complicate Resource-Sharing on Campuses
Pooling resources, however, is not without complications.
Besides having schools with different bell schedules, they may also have different grading policies. Some, for example, might focus on classwork and prioritize essays and projects, while others assign more homework and exams. Principals have to figure out how to split the costs of teachers covering shared classrooms. Further complicating matters, on many campuses, including Murry Bergtraum, schools in the same building report to different superintendents, meaning there’s no single leader responsible for the whole building.
Some education leaders hope a new position Samuels created — a supervising official overseeing all 11 high school superintendents — will help streamline decision-making for shared campuses.
Shael Polakow-Suransky, the president of Bank Street College of Education and a former deputy chancellor under Bloomberg, said sharing courses can work for advanced classes and electives, but it’s harder for core academic subjects where different schools may have specific — and clashing — approaches to instruction, behavior, or grading.
“The key is how much does that shared instructional work impede on the autonomy of each school on the campus to do its model effectively?” he said.
Sharing resources often only benefits a portion of students, too, such as those who seek out advanced courses. That’s part of why it can feel more like a “Band-Aid” than a systemic solution to the small schools problem, said Vivian Orlen, the former superintendent of Manhattan high schools.
Barakat, the Bronx principal, agreed that merging schools is the “logical next step.” But for now, he said, “I would hope that there are principals all over the place who are taking advantage of the opportunity to work with colleagues.”
Sophie Hayssen and Kae Petrin contributed data analysis.

World Monuments Fund has raised $62 million, tripling its endowment and beating its fundraising goal eighteen months ahead of schedule. This will give the New York–based preservation organization a financial cushion to protect monuments around the world.
The organization’s endowment net assets are now expected to pass $100 million by 2028. The money raised will support everything from conservation training to protecting heritage sites threatened by war, climate change, and natural disasters. The fundraising drive launched less than a year ago, as part of WMF’s sixtieth-anniversary celebration.
WMF was founded in 1965 and has since worked to preserve more than 700 notable sites across 114 countries. Projects include conserving historic buildings and archaeological sites, training local craftspeople, and protecting and restoring cultural landmarks after natural disasters.
The Robert W. Wilson Charitable Trust was the main donor, with a $20 million challenge grant matching 50 cents for every dollar raised, up to $40 million. Other major contributions came from Suzanne Deal Booth, who gave $10 million to establish the Suzanne Deal Booth Institute for Heritage Preservation. Virginia James donated between $5 million and $10 million. Susan de Menil, Stephen Lash, Annabelle Selldorf, and Christian Louboutin are also on the list of notable donors.
“Cultural heritage is being lost to conflict, climate change, neglect, and urbanization faster than the world can respond,” Bénédicte de Montlaur, WMF’s president and CEO, said in a statement. “This campaign gives WMF the long-term resources to act with greater urgency and ambition.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: New York’s Socrates Sculpture Park rebuilds for resilience and expands
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Hannah Sage Kay
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
When Superstorm Sandy hit New York City in 2012, Socrates Sculpture Park, located on the Queens riverfront, disappeared underwater. With a four-foot rise in sea level, water streamed from the park into the surrounding area, which was at that time comprised mostly of factories and the neighbouring Noguchi Museum.
Fourteen years later, the New York City Department of Parks & Recreation broke ground last month on the park’s seawall reconstruction. This work, which has been unfolding at riverfront parks across the city with funds from the Federal Emergency Management Agency, necessitates that much of Socrates’s five-acre campus remain closed until its completion next spring.
A former landfill and illegal dumping ground turned green space that supports artists in the production and presentation of public art, Socrates’s founding is described by executive director Shaun Leonardo as “a radical act of land transformation”. In this same spirit, Socrates will unveil on 31 October—during its annual Halloween Harvest Festival—the transformation of a largely abandoned storage area on the park’s southern edge into a revitalised landscape featuring a long-term installation of three monumental sculptures by the park’s founding artist Mark di Suvero.
Called The Point, this one-acre expansion, Leonardo says, is an opportunity to “connect Socrates’s future to its founding story” on the occasion of its 40th anniversary. Though this parcel has historically been a maintenance and storage location to support the creation and installation of work by Socrates artists—including Di Suvero who built many of his towering sculptures at the park in the 1980s and 90s—it has steadily grown dormant. Now, at age 93, he primarily lives on the West Coast, but the three soon-to-be-unveiled sculptures have lived on-site since their creation (1995 for the earliest, 2017 for the most recent). While they are comprised of steel I-beams, like much of his work, these sculptures are dynamic and meant to be engaged with: two include a swing; one of those also features a spinning titanium element.
Di Suvero’s “work feels like drawing in space and, through that lens, you really start to see how much he thought about it interacting in its environment”, Leonardo says.
Established in 1986 by a coalition of artists and community members, Socrates grew out of Di Suvero’s nearby studio located in a defunct brick warehouse. Having brought in a team to help install his works, he also shared his space with other sculptors and gave them access to his tools. Together, they looked at the neighbouring landfill and “saw an opportunity again to extend the work they were doing in the studio into a space to develop works in public view, and in deep connection with the neighbourhood,” Leonardo says.
With the establishment of a workforce development programme—whereby residents of the nearby Astoria Houses public housing complex were hired to both clear the land and help artists fabricate their projects—Socrates revitalised the landscape while creating, as Leonardo puts it, an “economic engine of an opportunity for individuals to build up a skill set not only in horticulture, but in fabrication, maintenance, community engagement and public event production, knowing that they could leave from Socrates to full employment elsewhere”. Though the programme had fallen dormant since the Covid-19 pandemic, Leonardo relaunched it this year with a pilot edition supported by the Ford Foundation and Urban Upbound.
The factories that formerly populated the neighbourhood have in recent years been replaced by residential high-rises that are just as vulnerable to the next storm as the park is, if not more so. “What’s unique about erosion of a landfill, as opposed to a natural landscape,” Leonardo says, is that “not only has the rock shoreline disappeared, but the coast is caving in as well because of what is being eroded from underneath.”
“We have taken it upon ourselves to think about our work as it relates to climate resilience as a responsibility to both people and place,” he adds. “Much of our landscaping system has been strategic in terms of not only soil rehabilitation but also flood mitigation and providing a better barrier to the neighbourhood.” That has included, for example, cultivating native plants and restoring the habitat for monarch butterflies along their migration route.
“In order for the community to thrive,” Leonardo says, “the art has to serve an additional purpose of giving to that community and being in reciprocal relationship with the land.”

https://medor.coop/magazines/medor-n43-e.text:
Près de 85 % des entités publiques fédérales, plus de 91 % des institutions flamandes et 71 % des communes wallonnes sont liées à Microsoft pour leur messagerie électronique, et un grand nombre de sites gouvernementaux sont hébergés par des entreprises américaines. Cette dépendance n’est pas sans poser certaines questions, en particulier au temps de l’administration Trump.
Au dernier Forum économique mondial de Davos, en janvier 2026, notre Premier ministre Bart De Wever soulignait que nous aurions intérêt, en Europe, à devenir « indépendants sur le plan technologique ». Au même moment, les relations transatlantiques connaissaient une crise sans précédent à la suite des menaces agitées par Donald Trump au sujet du Groenland. Et De Wever d’entrevoir que, dans cinq ans, nous aurions peut-être à remercier le président américain de « nous avoir réveillés juste à temps ».
Le site officiel du Premier ministre belge – premier.be – ne sera-t-il alors plus hébergé sur les serveurs de l’entreprise américaine Akamai ? Et la communication électronique de son administration ne passera-t-elle plus par les logiciels du géant Microsoft ?
Le SPF Chancellerie du Premier ministre est loin d’être le seul de nos services publics à s’en remettre largement aux géants américains du numérique tels que Microsoft et Google. C’est ce qui ressort d’une analyse de 799 sites web d’institutions publiques belges réalisée par Apache.

https://medor.coop/magazines/medor-n43-e.title: Sauvons les sentiers : Les conclusions de notre enquête
https://medor.coop/magazines/medor-n43-e.author: Chloé Andries, Olivier Bailly, Philippe Engels, Céline Gautier, Quentin Noirfalisse, Louis Van Ginneken
https://medor.coop/magazines/medor-n43-e.text:
De juin 2025 à juin 2026, Médor a enquêté avec vous sur l’entrave au passage sur les chemins publics de Wallonie.
Un chemin labouré par ci, bloqué par une barrière par là, bouffé par les ronces plus loin. Des cas isolés ?
Sur notre carte interactive, vous avez déposé des centaines de signalements. En Wallonie, 4 630 kilomètres de chemins publics sont entravés ou difficilement accessibles, sur les 51 000 de la région. Au bout du compte, c’est l’espace public qui se trouve privatisé.
Mais des actions individuelles, collectives et politiques existent pour défendre nos droits à circuler.
L’enquête
Vos signalements ont été les points de départ de nos reportages. Six journalistes de notre rédaction se sont baladés à travers la Wallonie, pour entendre les revendications des usagers, des associations de défense des chemins et (lorsqu’ils ont été réceptifs) les explications des « entraveurs » concernés, des associations de propriétaires ou d’agriculteurs.
Retrouvez ces reportages dans l’onglet «Articles» ou directement sur la carte ci-contre (les pictos jaunes).
Un article de conclusion rassemble nos constats de terrain et fait le point en dix questions, de type «Qui entrave les sentiers ?», «Pourquoi est-il si compliqué de savoir si un sentier est public ?» et «Que fait le gouvernement Wallon ?».
Ressources pratiques pour rétablir le passage
Si d’aventure, vous tombez subitement sur une barrière ou un panneau d’interdiction qui n’a pas la tronche des signalisations du code de la route et ce sur un terrain qui ne vous semble pas être une propriété privée, il s’agit peut-être d’une entrave illégale.
La carte que vous avez sous les yeux a été alimentée par des citoyen·nes constatant des entraves (les cailloux oranges) et complétée par les reportages de nos journalistes (les balises jaunes). La récolte de signalements est clôturée.
Une enquête participative de Chloé Andries, Olivier Bailly, Philippe Engels, Céline Gautier, Quentin Noirfalisse & Louis Van Ginneken avec le soutien du Fonds pour le journalisme.

Depuis plusieurs années, le sentier a été obstrué et le passage empêché par le propriétaire voisin, qui a érigé des barrières pour chevaux (du côté de la chapelle/vers la commune d’Enghien) et des barrières métalliques (du côté chemin de fer/ vers la commune (flamande) de Pajottegem), pour empêcher tout passage de promeneurs sur sa propriété (agricole) - voir photos. Ce chemin est pourtant même indiqué comme accessible sur Google Maps (voir capture d’écran, avec lieu de blocage encadré en rouge). Il semble que le blocage soit bien connu des autorités, mais fasse les frais de la « lasagne institutionnelle » belge : ce sentier relie la Wallonie à la Flandre, mais semble surtout gêner les résidents enghiennois, alors que l’autorité communale compétente (au vu du lieu du blocage du chemin) est celle de Pajottegem (en région flamande). Il se dit que des courriers auraient été adressés, par le passé, par les autorités communales enghiennoises à leurs collègues flamands afin de porter la situation à leur attention, en vain. J’ai, à titre personnel, contacté l’administration communale de Pajottegem à ce sujet voici plusieurs mois, sans suite favorable à ce jour.

Je crains qu'à terme, si aucune trace attestant de l'utilisation du chantier n'apparaît pendant des années, ce chemin ne puisse être privatisé de plein droit par l'agriculteur (mais quelle est la loi exactement?). Heureusement, on voit quelques traces de pas ici, mais souvent ce n'est pas le cas.

TUBIZE: Accès au "chemin des amoureux" obstrué: un entrepreneur local y a déposé plusieurs containeurs pour en bloquer l'accès. La commune est au courant et le tolère (par peur de dépôts sauvages). Le sentier vicinal original (n°83) a été raboté à la construction de la ligne de chemin fer 106 (années 60?), mais l'accès au chemin de halage a continué pour les ouvriers des forges de Clabecq, via une passerelle, jusque dans les années 2000. Il y a eu depuis plusieurs tentatives pour le faire réhabiliter, sans succès. Il est facile pour la Ville de botter en touche puisque le sentier "actuel" ne suit plus le chemin vicinal original (qui n'aura jamais été mis à jour sur les cartes). Auparavant, on pouvait rejoindre le halage depuis la gare en 900m via ce sentier. Désormais, cela prend 2.5km pour y accéder.
Le 13 mai 2024, nous avons interpellé le conseil communal à ce sujet et nous avons remis une pétition de 800+ signatures. La Ville, qui avait d'abord invoqué d'obscures raisons pour éviter de se pencher sur ce dossier, dit désormais avoir l'intention de le réhabiliter. Aux dernières nouvelles, ils n'avaient toujours pas bougé d'un pouce et n'ont même pas de relevé exact du sentier. La Région Wallonne, qui cherche à établir un réseau cyclable structurant (mais qui a, d'un autre côté, financé un énorme boulevard urbain sans pistes cyclables à l'entrée de Tubize) se heurte désormais aux difficultés pour franchir la ville... Aux dernières nouvelles et faute de mieux, la Région envisageait d'intégrer le chemin des amoureux. https://www.chemindesamoureux.be

La vision réductrice des « savoirs situés », c’est la liste de courses identitaire : penser que la légitimité professionnelle d’un·e scientifique, journaliste ou documentariste doit nécessairement se fonder sur un genre, une expérience personnelle ou une couleur de peau.
La philosophe féministe Donna Harraway en appelle plutôt à une réflexion collective sur la façon dont les récits sont produits et par qui. Nous ajoutons volontiers : « et avec quels outils ».
« Je suis une femme, je suis Blanche, je suis de classe moyenne, je suis d’âge mûr, je suis éduquée, je suis d’origine irlandaise… J’ai toutes ces identités, voilà d’où je parle. » Ce genre de préambule énerve un peu Donna Haraway (Le Monde, avril 2026). Qui ? Donna Haraway herself. La philosophe féministe qui a forgé la théorie des « savoirs situés », dont s’inspire cette habitude de décliner son identité avant de s’autoriser un récit sur le réel. Autrefois, comme biologiste, elle observait les grands singes. Ou, plutôt, elle observait les primatologues qui étudiaient les grands singes. Elle remarque alors que, selon les époques, le genre ou la place dans la société, les scientifiques ne voient pas les mêmes choses chez les chimpanzés : certains voient la domination de mâles agressifs, d’autres (Jane Goodall, notamment) des relations sociales fondées sur la coopération. La science n’est pas « neutre ». Les récits que nous faisons de la vie des singes racontent aussi les humains qui les écrivent.
Dans Primate visions (1989), Donna Haraway porte un énorme coup à la conception de l’objectivité, telle qu’elle était alors en vigueur dans la science. Elle a conduit de nombreux auteurs et autrices à s’interroger sur la façon dont leurs identités coloraient leurs récits et à identifier des regards dominants (voir notre enquête « Les journalistes [se] racontent » p. 14). La vision réductrice de cette idée salutaire, c’est la liste de courses identitaire : penser que la légitimité professionnelle d’un·e scientifique, journaliste ou documentariste doit nécessairement se fonder sur …

Google en Wallonie
Les centres de données mettent la Belgique sous tension
Texte (CC BY-NC-ND) : Maïté Warland & Quentin Noirfalisse
Photos : Nick Hannes
Texte (CC BY-NC-ND) : Janine Meijer
Publié le
La Belgique se rêve en grand hub numérique, en terre d’accueil idéale pour les centres de données (data centers). Depuis vingt ans, Google a montré la voie, en s’installant à Saint-Ghislain, au nord du Borinage. L’expansion rapide du géant américain soulève des enjeux majeurs : pression sur le réseau électrique, manque de transparence et retombées économiques floues. L’intelligence artificielle (IA) accélère l’implantation de ces usines numériques et met notre pays sous tension.
Du fond de son jardin, Anne More contemple la vue. Devant elle, de l’autre côté de la Rue des Roseaux, de grands bâtiments gris barrent le ciel. Elle vit à 200 mètres du centre de données de Google à Saint-Ghislain, à l’ouest du Hainaut. À 68 ans, elle doit composer avec ce voisin installé ici depuis une vingtaine d’années : « Là, ils sont en train de bâtir une nouvelle extension, ça cause pas mal de soucis. Du bruit d’abord… J’ai même acheté un casque pour ne plus les entendre. » De la rue du Marais, où elle vit, il ne reste aujourd’hui que le nom : « Avant, c’était magnifique, aujourd’hui, il n’y a plus que du béton et ils se rapprochent de plus en plus. » Cette cohabitation forcée, Anne ne la comprend toujours pas : « On ne sait rien. Google construit, agrandit, et on a à peine été consulté. Je ne sais même pas ce qu’ils font alors qu’ils sont presque au fond de mon jardin. »
Ici, Google et sa société faitière Alphabet développent depuis 2007 leur premier data center européen. Vingt-quatre heures sur 24, des dizaines, voire des centaines de milliers de serveurs travaillent pour lancer les vidéos que vous regardez sur YouTube, récupérer une pièce jointe sur votre Gmail, activer le résultat d’une recherche Google. Les journalistes se (la) racontent
Enquête (CC BY-NC-ND) : Chloé Andries & Céline Gautier
Illustrations (CC BY-NC-ND) : Jérôme Degive
Publié le
En 2026, les podcasts parlent de nos grands-mères, les BD de nos vies intimes et les docus de nos photos de famille. Jadis, l’idéal journalistique exigeait que l’auteur s’efface derrière son sujet. Que nous est-il arrivé ?
« Il y a six ans, mon compagnon me dit qu’il ne souhaite plus avoir d’enfant. » La journaliste Lucie Tesnière lance son podcast (Juste une femme) consacré aux femmes qui n’ont pas d’enfants par un témoignage fort. Le sien.
« Ma mère Nathalie mourra dans deux ans. Mon fils naitra dans neuf mois. » La caméra de Caroline Guimbal ne fait pas 50 fois le tour du monde : la documentariste explore la vie de sa mère, avant qu’elle ne meure et que naisse son enfant (L’éclipse de la lune rouge).
« Mon ami Michel me tend un paquet. Cinq carnets. » Les notes de tranchées de son grand-oncle. « C’est toute une famille que j’accueille, sans le savoir, dans ma maison. » L’écrivaine Violaine Lison commence une vaste enquête historique et littéraire (« Lequel de nous portera l’autre ? ») qui mêle sa voix à celle d’un soldat inconnu.
Ces trois exemples sont tout récents (2026). Nous pourrions en trouver plein d’autres. Partout, des auteurs (et surtout des autrices) ne se contentent plus de mener des enquêtes mais nous en dévoilent les coulisses, se positionnent dans leurs récits, voire s’emparent de leurs propres histoires de famille.
Ce mouvement touche depuis plusieurs décennies l’anthropologie, la sociologie, l’histoire ou encore la littérature du réel et, depuis belle lurette, le cinéma documentaire. Mais ce qui est neuf, c’est l’ampleur inédite du phénomène et le fait qu’il touche désormais les journalistes – un métier spécifique, …

L’exil sans sexualité
Faire l’amour dans un centre d’accueil de demandeurs d’asile, ce n’est pas interdit. Mais dans la pratique, c’est presque impossible. Une absence d’intimité qui rend le parcours migratoire un peu plus lourd à supporter.
À leur arrivée en Belgique, les personnes migrantes se cognent à : des procédures administratives sans fin, un logement précaire, les traumas de l’exil et le racisme. Dans ce contexte, la sexualité passe souvent au second plan. Pourtant, l’intimité est aussi un droit essentiel au bienêtre. L’article 8 de la Convention européenne des droits de l’homme stipule que « toute personne a droit au respect de sa vie privée et familiale, de son domicile et de sa correspondance ». Il régit donc le droit pour tous et toutes à une vie affective, intime et sexuelle. Dans le système d’accueil en Belgique, ce droit peine pourtant à être garanti, relégué derrière l’urgence et le manque de moyens.
L’intimité face au collectif
Tamer est un réfugié gazaoui reconnu depuis peu. Durant sa procédure, il a vécu dans quatre hébergements différents : « En fonction du centre, j’ai partagé ma chambre avec trois à douze personnes et les visites étaient toujours interdites, il n’y avait pas d’intimité. J’ai un ami qui avait une relation avec une autre fille de notre centre Fedasil, ils s’arrangeaient pour que les colocataires de la fille partent quelques heures pour avoir un moment intime. Si la direction avait su, elle les aurait surement expulsés. » Dans la plupart des structures d’accueil, il n’est pas interdit d’avoir une activité sexuelle, mais d’autres règles limitent cette possibilité : visites en chambre régulées, respect du sommeil et de la vie privée. De la boxe à la bombe
Lors Doukaev
À Liège, on connaissait Lors Doukaev comme un boxeur unijambiste au parcours inspirant. Jusqu’à ce qu’en septembre 2010, il rate un attentat au Danemark, sa bombe artisanale lui explosant au visage. Derrière ce basculement, un parcours trouble et un dossier long comme le bras qui révèle alors les angles morts des services de police et de renseignement belges.
Il sort de la douche, encore marqué par l’effort, la peau rougie par l’eau chaude. Lors Doukaev affiche un sourire en coin, des cheveux mouillés, quelques gouttes sur les épaules. Et commence à raconter. « C’était en Tchétchénie, en 1996. J’ai marché sur une mine », rembobine-t-il, dans un français impeccable.
- Quel âge aviez-vous ?
- Je venais d’avoir 10 ans.
Les détails viendront plus tard : une aire de jeux à Grozny, une mine russe enfouie sous le sable, puis l’explosion immédiate, surtout irréversible, parce qu’elle emporte avec elle le dernier tiers de sa jambe droite.
Depuis cette scène d’horreur, d’autres parties du corps du Belgo-Tchétchène ont légèrement morflé. Le nez et les oreilles en particulier. La barbe, elle, a poussé en mode collier. Logique : le gamin est désormais un homme, qui plus est un boxeur reconnu en Belgique francophone, ce qui lui permet de dérouler sereinement le fil de sa trajectoire face à la caméra d’Alain Marcoen, réalisateur d’un documentaire sur le « noble art » liégeois – Coin rouge, coin bleu.
À Liège, on le connait d’abord pour ce statut-là. Le boxeur unijambiste. Le type qui monte sur le ring avec une prothèse, malgré la guerre, la mutilation et l’exil. Une anomalie devenue attraction, muée en respect : vingt combats, douze victoires, deux nuls, de quoi forger une solide réputation dans la salle, et notamment dans la sienne, à Droixhe, au cœur de cet emblématique …

Photos
Pendant neuf ans, Diana Takacsova a photographié le ravalement permanent de notre côte. Un territoire coulé dans le béton mais en perpétuel mouvement.
Diana Takacsova débarque un weekend d’octobre à Blankenberge. Jeune photographe slovaque arrivée en Belgique en 2017, elle est intriguée par ce petit front de mer qu’on lui a décrit comme sans intérêt. « Venant d’un pays complètement enclavé, mon œil a été tout de suite attiré par cette lumière, sans cesse changeante, du littoral et ces immenses barres d’immeubles. » Dans ses premières images, Diana Takacsova capture l’exotisme suranné de notre côte. Elle s’y rend les weekends et photographie les parties de snookergolf, les pêcheurs de crevettes, les bains du Nouvel An.
En 2022, elle s’installe à Ostende où son conjoint travaille. « À l’époque, je n’en mesurais pas pleinement les conséquences. Après Porto et Bruxelles, le choc culturel a été réel. Ici quand tu ne fais pas partie de la communauté, tu te sens vite isolée. Tu es une ‘aangespoeld’, une échouée. Aujourd’hui, j’en ris… mais sur le moment, c’était rude. » Passé le mois d’aout, la « reine des plages » se vide. Pour se remplir la saison suivante. Un sentiment de tourner en rond. Que raconter de plus profond sur ces 67 kilomètres de plage ?

Et si la Belgique recommençait à creuser ? Longtemps reléguée aux livres d’histoire, l’extraction minière revient au premier plan, portée par la quête d’autonomie stratégique de l’Europe et un MR qui brandit la souveraineté énergétique en étendard. Derrière les promesses politiques, une question surplombe : que reste-t-il réellement sous nos pieds ?
Casque jaune sur la tête, gros caillou en main : Georges-Louis Bouchez prend la pose, accoudé à un wagon de la mine de Blegny. L’extraction de charbon s’est arrêtée en 1980 et avec elle le dessein économique d’une région. En ce début juillet 2025, le président du MR a voulu faire un coup pour lancer une étude du Centre Jean Gol, le think tank du parti. « À ce moment-là, les enjeux de souveraineté étaient sur le devant de la scène, que ce soit sur l’industrie, l’énergie et même la défense », explique-t-il, un an plus tard, pour justifier son timing.
Son projet est dans le titre de l’étude : « Relançons l’activité minière en Belgique et en Europe ». À ses côtés, accoutré aussi en mineur, Corentin de Salle, directeur scientifique du Centre Jean Gol, s’apprête bientôt à publier un post sur Facebook. « Oui, nous devons rouvrir des mines et en créer d’autres ailleurs. Oui, nous avons des gisements identifiés […] Oui, cette étape peut ouvrir la voie, en créant une chaine de valeurs, à une réindustrialisation massive (mais propre) de notre pays. » Et en plus, conclut-il, cela créera de l’emploi, mais heureusement des robots feront le gros du boulot sous la terre. « Il faut foncer. » Foncer, c’est bien, mais foncer pour quoi ?

Mais derrière les comptoirs d’opticiens, l’enjeu de santé peut se transformer en bataille marketing : « 1+1 gratuite », « 1+1+1 gratuite », « 1+1 solaire »… Bref coup d’œil sur un marché qui explose.
Potentiellement, près de 8 millions de Belges sont mirauds. Selon le Centre fédéral d’expertise des soins de santé (KCE), ils portent des lunettes (95 %), des lentilles (10 %), souvent en alternance avec des lunettes, ou recourent à la chirurgie correctrice (2,5 %). C’est l’histoire d’une interview qui a dévissé. Et c’est ce qui pouvait arriver de mieux. Rencontre avec l’écrivain Antoine Wauters, à l’envers du monde.
Dans Le Plus Court Chemin, livre qui remonte le fil de son enfance dans le village ardennais de Fraiture, Antoine Wauters raconte l’habitude qu’avait sa mère de dessiner sur des bouts de serviettes en papier ou de journaux. Et comment lui dessinait au dos des documents officiels que son père ramenait de la banque (où il travaillait). « De sorte que maman […] nous a appris que l’art se pratique au dos du monde, toujours. Et que l’envers est l’endroit le plus précieux. »
Le matin du 19 juin, j’ai donc traversé la Belgique, dans l’objectif d’atteindre « l’envers du monde ». Cet envers semblait localisé dans le petit village de Becco (près de Theux), où vit Antoine Wauters. Loin de Bruxelles et Paris où le quadragénaire est devenu, par un étrange effet d’inversion, un écrivain « reconnu ». Passé en vingt ans de la poésie au roman, d’une petite maison d’édition (Cheyne), à une moyenne (Verdier), jusqu’à l’influente Gallimard, Antoine Wauters est aujourd’hui un écrivain belge « coté ». À quoi bon ?
Édito
« Le journalisme ne change rien à lui seul, écrit le Bureau of Investigative Journalism, mais il constitue souvent un élément clé d’un ensemble bien plus vaste de personnes, d’organisations et d’actions qui, elles, font bouger les choses. » Et c’est pour cela que nous faisons ce métier.
« Votre sol est-il pollué ? Consultez la carte de l’inventaire de l’état du sol. » L’administration régionale bruxelloise invite les personnes qui souhaitent acheter un bien ou démarrer un potager à regarder sur la carte dans quelle catégorie apparait leur parcelle (polluée ou non, avec ou sans risque). Pratique. Cette carte sert aussi de base à des politiques environnementales de dépollution – il parait que ça avance bien…
Sauf qu’au terme d’une enquête rigoureuse, la journaliste Lou Janssens met le doigt sur un grave manquement dans cette cartographie. 80 % du sol n’est pas repris à l’inventaire, faute d’informations suffisantes. Ces parcelles apparaissent donc en blanc. Blanc comme la pureté, la propreté ou l’absence de substances toxiques dans les salades ou le bac à sable de la crèche. Le risque de rassurer – à tort – la population est grand. Par exemple, l’inventaire ignore largement les activités industrielles du XIXe siècle qui ont pu polluer les sols accueillant aujourd’hui des habitations, des jardins, des potagers, indiqués en blanc sur la carte. Que faire de ces infos ? Les experts consultés invitent à la prudence : une pollution passée n’indique pas forcément un danger ; mais il faut aussi se méfier des effets cocktails (un peu de plomb par-ci, un peu d’arsenic par-là) dont les effets sur la santé commencent seulement à être étudiés.

Le 9 juin 2026, en Commission des Sports, de la Fonction publique et de la Simplification administrative, des Médias et de la tutelle sur Wallonie-Bruxelles Enseignement du Parlement de la Communauté française, il se passe ceci :
Le député MR Olivier Maroy pose une question orale à la ministre des Médias, Jacqueline Galand (MR).
Titre : Avenir de la radio en Fédération Wallonie-Bruxelles
Objet : Un avant-projet de décret porté par la ministre des Médias pour une future extinction de la FM au profit des technologies numériques (DAB+). Le gouvernement serait autorisé à mettre fin au mode de diffusion analogique, pour toutes les radios en même temps, à condition qu’un nombre suffisant d’auditeurs et d’auditrices aient d’ici là basculé vers le DAB+.
Contexte : Ce texte a été soumis au Conseil supérieur de l’audiovisuel (CSA) qui a recueilli les nombreuses remarques du secteur de la radio et remis un avis. Globalement, les gros diffuseurs sont favorables à un arrêt de la FM (la diffusion conjointe en FM et en DAB+ leur coute un pont), mais réclament une réflexion plus large sur l’avenir de la radio. Les radios indépendantes demandent du temps et du soutien pour assurer le transfert vers le DAB+. Portfolio
1975 marque le début du chômage de masse en Belgique. Cinquante ans plus tard, alors que les allocations de chômage connaissent une profonde réforme, Médor s’est plongé dans les archives photo de l’agence Guyaux pour raconter cette période charnière.
En 2026, près de 200 000 Belges ont été ou vont être exclus du chômage selon l’ONEM. La coalition Arizona limite désormais la durée des allocations à deux ans au maximum. Cette mesure rompt avec l’une des particularités historiques du système belge : le caractère illimité des allocations de chômage. Au milieu des années 1970, la Belgique tourne la page des Trente Glorieuses. Le choc pétrolier provoque une crise profonde de l’industrie, tandis que la première génération du babyboum arrive sur le marché du travail et que les femmes sont de plus en plus nombreuses à chercher un emploi. « 1975, c’est vraiment l’année de l’explosion, rappelle Jean Faniel, directeur du Centre de recherche et d’information sociopolitiques (CRISP) et auteur d’une thèse consacrée aux relations entre syndicats et chômeurs.
